Doorkickers in an awesome semi-realistic top-down pause/play Urban Ops tactical planning game (a lot of words, i know), focusing on police and counter-terrorism scenarios. It has exceptional value for your money, and the devs are decent enough to actually bring a good game out of early acces. That shouldn't have to be a plus, but it is.
Your SWAT team is fully levlable with it's own skill tree, seperate from the leveling of each individual team member, and the unlocking of new gear for your team, which adds to the feeling of progression and depth of the game. There are a LOT of ways to complete most levels, and as you unlock new gear you can go back and solve a scenario in a new and better way, improving replayability. Your team members die permanently (and is replaced by a rookie police officer) if you don't restart a mission where someone died, which gives every tactical decission you make a distinct feeling of importance.
For someone with basic experience with military urban ops tactics, gameplay feels intuitive and realistic in that real life techniques and equipment are successfull when applied apropriately within the game. It's rewarding that I can jump straight into the game, learn the controlls, and instantly see how a good plan works, and a bad plan don't, and know EXACTLY why.
One of the few problems i have with the game (which is completely subjective, and perhaps even a part of the intended difficulty) is that as the maps become bigger and the enemies more numeorus it becomes VERY tedious to make a working plan beforehand, and you basically have to "test" your way through the level. Another problem I have is that it gets problematic to controll bigger teams when you want them to walk the same path but perform different actions and cover different sectors, because their waypoints and routes overlap and create an unmanagable cluster. There should be a better way to toggle between the units and finalize/hide certain units' actions (maybe there is, but i missed it?).
Another thing I wish was improved is the intelligence and behviour of the AI enemies. Considering they are hardened terrorists and seasoned criminals they're pretty stupid. This is really a realism issue, and not a gameplay issue, as I do mostly enjoy the game and it's dificulty as it is.

So, you're probably sitting here thinking, "Why don't I just get Breach and Clear?". Here are a few reasons why this game is AWESOME! I got Door Kickers in the autumn sales for £2 (I'm a sucker for a bargain) already I have put 4.1 hours into the game just by playing before and after school before dinner. This game is amazing!
The sheer brilliance of the customisation means you can have all kinds of you own "classes" on top of the pre-made ones! For example, I created a line up of solely pointmen with silenced pistols and took out the targets with stealth and cunning rather than brute force. It was cool to think I could do all of these new cool tactics!
Now, I'm not one to go through a game and get three stars on every level. I just get bored. But for Door Kickers? The fact that you need stars to customise your squad means I want to 100% the game!
Also, another great thing is that the most expensive gun/armour/shield isn't nessecarily the best gun/armour/shield! It's all about how you play the game! You can also upgrade the weapon skills of your squad with pistols, long guns and shotguns! This adds a whole other dynamic to the game as you can upgrade your perks or equipment strategically depending on one other!
And of course you can name each member squad! You can be as creative as you like! You could call your "crack-shot-with-a-pistol-guy" anything from "Dead-eye" to "Sh**head" This enables you to be slightly attached to your men and be upset if they are killed in the line of fire. And yes, if your men are killed during a campaign, they will not be replaced by new men until you have won/lost the whole campaign! This makes you think about your choices more carefully during an assault on a building.
I would highly recommend this game to ANYONE no matter what games they like/play! I recommend picking it up, especially in a sale! Worth the £14.99 its sold for!

This game's primary sin is mediocrity. Paired with sluggish controls and audio issues, it takes the game from about a 5.5/10 to a 4/10.
Deadlight is a short (8 hours max) 2D platformer with the themes of grim darkness. If you've ever seen/read/heard a zombie story, the story in this game is really no different. You play as a suvivor of a zombie outbreak, trying to find his family and friends and troubled by a dark past. Really not much to talk about there.
The gameplay and controls is where I take most of my issue with the game. The main character controls like a dumpster. He is slow to turn, slow to start running, slow to stop running. The game tries to go for a sense of fluid character motion and realism, but at the same time has you wall jumping and parkouring, so the movement comes across as inconsistent. Enemies can only be killed in melee after being knocked down to the ground, so even 6 swings of a fire axe wont kill them unless they're prostrate before you. It makes for frustrating and not rewarding combat. Especially because enemies can somehow phase through you and wind up on the other side of you, causing you to perform a 3 point turn with the garbage truck of a protagonist.
In an effort to generate excitement, the game has several chase/run sequences that paired with it's sluggish controls make for a pretty unpleasant experience. If you misstime a jump/roll even without failing it completely, you will ultimately fail the escape sequence because there is no room to make up for it. So you end up trial and error running over and over the same parts that aren't difficult but simply frustrating.
Lastly, the collectibles/secrets/achievements in this game are insulting. The game chooses to reward you with juvenile achievements for completing levels. But even more so, 95% of the secrets are simply lying on the ground along the main walking path. There is no effort required on the part of the player except to hit the interact button and pick up an item and be rewarded with SECRET DISCOVERED. No, it wasn't "discovered". It was literally in the way.
Lastly the techical issues: sound randomly doesn't work in cutscenes. After some research it seems to be an audio setting for some people, audio drivers for other people, or just ingame settings. For me, it worked in about half of the comic book still shot cutscenes. Frustrating because there's no unified agreement on how to fix it.
The game isn't very rewarding to play and is barely interesting. It's okay for an afternoon if you're very bored, but otherwise I'd probably play anything else. Definitely don't bother getting it at full price.

'Journey of a Roach' is a point & click adventure game. In order to progress in the game, you collect items you find and then use them on stuff in the world or on other items you collected, as is usual in these games. But there is one thing that makes 'Journey of a Roach' stand out: as you're playing a roach, you can effortlessly climb walls and ceilings. This adds a whole new dimension to the game world, compared to other games of the genre. It also made me switch from keyboard and mouse to a controller, but a controller is certainly not mandatory to play the game efficiently.
The graphics are cartoonish but not exuberantly so. The ambient music and noises are subtle and not intrusive. The sounds the characters produce are cute and not annoying, which seemed like a real possibility to me. So I was pleasantly surprised on both counts.
'Journey of a Roach' is different because it doesn't use any words at all. No written words, no spoken words. Instead, you see the thoughts of the characters in the game in the form of a drawing in a speech balloon. This is a refreshing approach and it works well here. The only downside is that it severely limits what the game's makers can tell you, the player. This has two direct consequences:

The game world is very small: there are only 5 scenes, basically, but the game does seem a bit larger than it is because of the climbing. If you don't rush and take your time to think about what to do, 'Journey of a Roach' will take you 2 or 3 hours to finish. If you do rush (a second playthrough or following a walkthrough to the letter) it can be very short. Let me put it this way, there is a Steam Achievement for finishing the game in 18 minutes or less.
'Journey of a Roach' has 6 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 just for running the game.
The Steam Achievements are varied and add an extra layer of fun to this game. A few are story-based and can't be missed, some are completely missable, some mean collecting optional stuff and a few are real challenges, like the 'speed run' achievement I mentioned earlier.
Yes, 'Journey of a Roach' is short, but I prefer short for point & click games. There is also no deep story, but it never pretends to be something it's not. 'Journey of a Roach' is an accessible, original and fun adventure game and I recommend it, especially since you can pick it up for less than €2/£2/$2 when it's on sale. At that price, don't hesitate and give it a go. Your reward will be a couple of hours of fun and giggles.

So I heard that this was debatably the worst Call of Duty game out there, so I bought a key off of a site and decided to give it a whirl, and to be honest, I actually kinda like it.
This review will center around the muliplayer specifically, as I havent played enough of the Extinction and Campaign modes to form a solid opinion.
TL;DR: It's a fun MP experience. It has some upsides and some downsides, but I have enjoyed it thus far. Buy it on sale or from a site though, because $60 is way too much.
MP Pros:
1. Fast-paced as hell
2. The guns are cool and fun to use (especially the snipers).
3. Strike packages are back
4. It's just plain fun.
5. Lots of custimization
6. Squad Pts are now used to buy guns/attacthments, meaning you no longer need to wait to unlock everything, as nearly everything is open for unlock from the very start, be it guns, attachments, new killstreaks, Squad Members, etc.
7. Field Orders are interesting, to say the least.
MP Cons:
1. Guard Dog KS is douchey and unfair
2. I.E.D.s EVERYWHERE; they are hard to spot and you'll only know they're there once they kill you
3. Large map size and design heavily promotes camping
4. TTK is pretty fast, resulting in the afforementioned fast paced gameplay. This is fine on smaller maps (i.e Strikezone), but on larger maps (i.e Stonehaven) it becomes annoying to roam the map, find one guy, maybe get killed by the guy, rinse and repeat.
5. Sadly, not too many people online, usually 500/600 tops. You'll usually find a TDM or Strikezone 24/7 match with ease, but other modes are deserted, which is a real shame, as I heard that Ghosts' Gun Game was awesome, and nobody plays it.
6. The squad points are cool, but for some people they could disrupt the whole ranking up process.
Overall, I recommend this game. There are some good things and some pretty screwed up bad things , but I still have enjoyed myself thus far. I have only played a bit of Campaign and Extinction, but I have heard a lot of mixed opinions about the two, more so with Extinction.This is a pretty solid MP experience, but I don't honestly think its worth the hefty $60 tag. I'd recommend purchasing it either during a sale or off of a reliable site that sells games for cheap, as I was able to get the key for this game for about $7, which is a pretty good price. Just keep in mind that the playerbase will unfortunately only shrink gradually from here, so see if your friends want to play with you in case you can't find a game. There's also the occasional cheater, but nothing that we haven't seen before about 2,000 times, and I haven't run into too many cheaters so far.
Verdict: 8/10

--- Call of Duty:Ghosts ---
The campaign started out really weird. I didn't get jack♥♥♥♥♥♥what was going on from the start. As a matter of fact, the SP campaign is pretty weird all the way through. It's all over the place, but still not in a terrible way. You are in space, you are in dense jungles, crawling around avoiding detection (just like the classic "All ghillied up" from CoD:MW), you are on high-speed-derailing trains, you drive tanks and helicopters and so on. Turns me off a little. Infinity Ward could have worked a bit harder on a proper story that follow a less rough path.
I got the feeling that they just cherry-picked the most memorable pieces from their previous games and slapped a new skin over it and shipped the new Ghosts. This time you are in some kind of alternative future, like 70 years from now, but without the gadget-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t from Black Ops 3 that I found somewhat questionable...
So what saves CoD:Ghosts from falling short then? The gameplay. It's fun, it's tight, the difficulty is just right (on normal) They introduce the mechanics in a nice tempo. I played it on normal and it offered somewhat of a challange. Not like BO3, but I thought it was perfect since I'm not HaRDcoRe. I just wanna have fun.
And the game looks really good for a CoD that is 4 years old. Decent amount of detail in the levels, decent amount of polys used, but the textures is to low res for my liking.
TL;DR...
- Solid gameplay.
- Well balanced.
- Tight controls.
- Variety in the SP campaign. For good or bad...
- Sluggish weapon handling and "tame" impact from them. For some reason, in this CoD, the weapons felt a bit like pee-shooters. I want more "oomph" in my guns when I murder bad guys all willie-nillie. (The rest of your actions suffers from the same weird behavior - throwing frags and so on - is sluggish... Really strange. What works tho - as it always has - is the movement. It's tight CoD-style.
- I would prefer higher resolution textures tho. After playing BO3 or DOOM2016 this feels like a trip back in time. (which it is but anyway...)
- "Perfect length" according to me, it did not overstay it's welcome, but I did NOT like the horrible cliffhanger that they leave you with at the end.
- Imho, Ghosts is better then BO3 and maybe even BO2.
Final verdict....
Around 7.5/10 I would say, even if it has flaws like the (mostly) unsatisfying gunplay. The reason is simple. It was really fun to blast through the campaign. However, at it's current pricepoint of $50-60, I would recommend that you do some research of your own before pressing that Buy-button.

I must first throw out a disclaimer in saying that I do not think I've played enough of this game still to write a full review on my entire thoughts and feelings, so please keep that in mind and feel free to comment with your own opinions and disagreements.
Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide from what I can see has a lot of very similar elements which are comparable with Left 4 Dead. (Pretty sure that's well-known at this point though) There is a simple 4 party setup (there are 5 characters to choose from, each with different weapons) along with 'specials' that do an assortment of different things that are also relatable to the specials in Left 4 Dead. Teamwork is essential, as you fight your way through the waves of enemies that are randomly thrown at you. (Of course, some are scripted however.) There are even little missions throughout each map such as placing barrels or sacks, defending wards or breaking supports. Each of these missions break up the -potential- repetition of the gameplay, and are a welcome thing in my eyes.
Now I have lots and lots of wonderful things to say for this game. It's like it was made just for me. I love the merciless killing of clanrats, I love kiting rat ogres when I'm the last alive and I love most of all getting those 3 tome, 2 grimoire and loot die successful runs. I even, in a sick way, enjoy the runs where I throw a bomb, manage to hit a wall and wipe our entire party... though others might not quite see the funny side as much as I do. I also enjoy grinding loot, although I know a lot of people are complaining about that.. but for me it gives the game a little something extra to work with.
There is a lot more to this game than simply fighting waves of rats though, once you go to the higher difficulties, it's encouraged that you have a satisfactory knowledge of the game and decent gear. There comes a point when you can have your own assigned role for certain things, such as tanking or headshotting specials, crowd control etc. I've not played enough to know too much about it but this aspect definitely appeals to me. The game is definitely a better experience with premade parties and/or voice communication. I definitely recommend turning voip on, even if you don't have a microphone.
Here are just a couple of things I think could be worked on however. For the most part, spawns are hidden quite well.. but there have been quite a few encounters where the rats spawn right infront of me. I'm hoping somewhere down the line they will tweak this. Another issue I have is with the exotic loot. As much as I like the loot system, there is nothing to be done with exotic loot, as you can't simply merge it. I also think that numerous exploits need to be fixed. I know that one of the big exploits on Horn of Magnus is due to be fixed next week and I can't wait for that. For me those just cheapen the experience for other players. One final thing that bothers me is the optimisation (or rather lack of) for the game. The CPU-Usage is crazily high, as well as the fps fluctuating at an alarming rate. Again, this is supposedly going to be worked on, but who knows when it'll be adjusted.
TL;DR
+ Slay the rats
+ Kill your friends with bombs
+ 10/10 replayability
+ Nice graphics
+ HOLY SIGMAR, BLESS THIS RAVAGED BODY

- Exploits need fixing

- Not much lore (though it's not really lore focused.)
- Bots currently ignore the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you when you're downed.

This game is great as long as you’re playing with two other people and have excessive amounts of time or luck. If you have only two or less players then you probably won’t be playing on a difficulty higher than easy for a very long time due to the worst friendly AI I’ve ever seen. They destroy objectives, stand by as you die, get stuck, walk off of ledges persistently to their deaths, as well as a number of other problems.
The special item drop rate is also insultingly low, with the end of mission dice rolls tending to low numbers far too often. After 25+ hours of play and god knows how many matches on easy, normal, and hard, I have only received 4 uncommon loot drops. All the good-ish loot I have was made from a plethora of rubbish I have accumulated via a smithing fusion system. The fusion system is also rather annoying, requires hours of play before you’ll get anything out of it, and will not always give the desired results (which is particularly frustrating if you prefer a certain weapon).
Despite claiming issues are being fixed in the patches there is little evidence of it, to the point I’m beginning to desire in game compensation for anyone who bought the game as it currently is. Joy will quickly turn to rage and frustration as a result. You’ll waste hours on a mission only to fail, but keep playing in the hopes of getting better drops to make life easier, but they never come. The game is in an unfit state to be fully released and feels like it’s still In beta a lot of a time.
Unless you really need your old world fix, give it a few months then come back when hopefully the problems are fixed or at least vastly improved. If it weren’t for the above issues I would rate it as a must buy.

Objectively, I am only reccommending this because of the experience I had, as opposed to what I think a reasonable person should put themselves through.
I bought  the game in Alpha. I played through the completed portions until the narrative hit a dead end. I might as well have mined to the planets core that's how much I was underground. Digging and digging. To craft amazing things!
I almost completed a canal from an inland lake to the ocean. I was invested. Even when an update took that canal away, I was still filled with hope and excitemement, because I had experienced the genuine thrill of discovering a new world, with each foray into a new zone I was excited to see the knew flora and fauna.
Even when I spent hours and hours digging using an unscalable scanner interface that challenged my 20/20 vision, I had hope.
My investment in this game was so willing that I managed to get through the first frustrating 5 hours of figuring out an interface I was sure would be improved. Every time the game crashed from too much mining, or the graphics ground to a halt, I figured it was my old Phenom and an HD4770 that couldn't handle it as well as a better equipped rig.
And then two things happened. The general release. And my personal hardware update.
I don't care about the the quest and story bugs, those are tertiary.
The interface remained cramped, unintiutive, and barely decipherable based on the iconogrpahy employed. What I learned out of motivation, others would have to suffer with.
The increase in computing power I gave the game, specifically an i7-3770 with 32M of RAM running two GTX570's (2.5G RAM) in SLI showed no measurable increase in performance. A user, should, in theory be able to rotate a camera view to see a flying hostile, while things explode, without the video stuttering to catch up.
The potential is enormous, but until ( if ever ) the underlying structure of the game narrative, as well as the virtual material world it inhabits experiences an improvement to both the interface, and the fluidity of movement, I have to say- know what you're getting into. If it's on sale, and you find the world interesting, in that, you will not be disappointed. As for the rest, I am not one of those people that believes a game should be work, but the effort I expended I found personally rewarding.
That just makes me a masochist. Save yourself.

The only reason I am not recommending Deep Under the Sky on Steam is due to how poorly it was ported over from a mobile system. It can be played with a single finger on a single button and, when it's cooperating, the uncomplicated play style is suited to that equally simplistic control scheme. The trajectory of the jellyfish-spore creature is locked from the start of the level and the tools used to alter its path, as well as the order they can be used, are predetermined as well. Despite a small difficulty spike at the end, even getting the optional hidden stars isn't made to be a challenge. Everything's so relaxed and smooth that I was inclined to play through the entire game in a single sitting. Furthermore the visual style, though not quite stunning, isn't as cluttered as some screenshots make it look.
The only irritation I encountered was due to a strange indecision surrounding how to adapt to the lack of a touch screen. No in-game instructions have been altered in the transition, so when told to tap and hold that may mean to press and hold or to press again to release which itself can change from moment to moment. That can become very frustrating very quickly which spoils the chilled-out atmosphere the developers are justifiably proud of. So if a low effort, low stress couple of hours sounds like a good time, pick up Deep Under the Sky, just don't do so outside of a touch screen device.

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #45 - Deep Under the Sky
When I started playing Deep Under the Sky, it kept bothering me that this game reminded me of something I had played, but for the life I couldn't remember.  But after getting through the first Chapter, it finally dawned on me that the game I was thinking of was Angry Birds.
At first glance, you wouldn't really notice the similarity.  And really that is to this game's credit, as I don't actually intend to call it an "Angry Birds ripoff".  In fact the colorful, almost trippy, art style is quite different, and definitely what I would consider this game's strong suit.  And the music blends itself well into this trippy vibe that the game has going for itself.
It's the gameplay that has some striking similarities to Angry Birds.  In Angry Birds, you launch your birds, and each bird has a different ability that affects how it travels, but regardless of the type of bird you are still trying to take out the pigs.  What birds you play vary from level to level.
In Deep Under the Sky, you play as a jellyfish that will morph into other forms as you hit the button (which by the way is the single control in this game).  Each form does a different thing, such as launching you like a rocket in a certain direction, or curling up into a ball to roll around.  The forms you take change from level to level.
With Angry Birds, you launch your bird with a slingshot, but here you always launch your jellyfish in exactly the same way.  So the only difference in controls is the timing of when you hit the button.  In that sense this almost takes the form of a rhythm game where button timing is essential (but the timing has nothing to do with music).
While the button timing presents a challenge, it also gets repetitive pretty quick.  Each time you fail and relaunch your jellyfish, you end up pushing the same button through the same sequence, up to the point where you left off and need to change your timing.  It turns into a lot of trial and error, but there isn't any real strategy to it.  It's more a combination of luck, patience, and some amount of skill.  Just don't confuse this with a puzzle game.
While I appreciated the presentation and music, I just can't get into the gameplay enough to recommend this to anyone, unless you really happen to like Angry Birds.  I didn't quite finish my hour of gameplay and really I don't feel any need to come back to this game.  It's not something that would really keep my attention, and for that I really couldn't justify the $9.99 asking price.

Don't buy this game. At least, not through Steam. This is a mobile port tried and true, and so faithfully ported from its home device the tutorials still refer to everything as "tapping." Not only this, but if you want to play it on android it's 4 dollars base price. Here, it's 10, which is an absolute rip off unless it goes on sale for pennies.
Is the game itself bad? Not at all. In fact, it's fairly decent of a port, glaring phone prompts aside. As some of the other reviews stated the description is misleading for emphasizing exploration and the ability to turn into a ball "like Samus!" as this is more or less a physics based catapult game, with couple cute little tweaks to make it interesting. The ball transformation stuff only happens for a few choice levels too, and it's simply done as that world's gimmick. It's not a selling point, trust me.
This being said, I found the art style extremely pleasant, and the puzzle layouts to be very rewarding. While the later levels rely on trial and error, the general layout for a majority of what I've played was quite clever and implemented some interesting tricks with the variety of physic defying powers. I have to say, this is definitely a high tier mobile game and could easily be received well on Steam if they priced it more realistically and, ya know, made the steam version in any way superior to the mobile version. Of course the Store Page doesn't even reference its origins so I doubt that will happen, but I would color this game as kind of a shame, since with a bit of modification and an added area or two it would've been a great little gem.
For 10 dollars though? Not a chance. At best, get it in a bundle, or wait for it to go on a big sale. Even 4 dollars on mobile is a bit too much to ask for. Such a missed opportunity.

I think it's a fine enough, fairly simply but not too simple to the point of being tedious puzzle game. It's mostly a matter of timing, as well as figuring out how to hit everything using whatever moves you're given in each level. There's 80 levels in all, and each has 2 secret stars to collect alongside the targets needed to clear the level.
One minor gripe I had is that clearing the main objective forces you out of the level, so if you accidentally trigger the last target before collecting the star, you have to redo the level to get it. Happened fairly frequently to me.
The level design tends to be pretty good, the only really hard stuff to hit being the stars but many of the targets involve an interesting use of the mechanics given. There's a boost in the direction you're moving, a set-angle boost, a move to turn into a ball, and a grapple mechanic, given to the player piece-by-piece over the course of the four worlds. Each level has a preset order of moves and you have to use these moves in specific ways at specific times to hit all the targets.
It's a very simple game, even if I've accidentally made it sound complex; one-button control and no free movement, just controlling the moves you're given. It's a fun game for short bursts, though I couldn't take playing too much of it at one time, even despite its short length.
It's a solid enough game, no real gripes with it, though not immensely enjoyable and not immesely rewarding. Basically what you'd expect from a mobile port, I guess?

Sonic Adventure 2 is a 3D platformers that mixes three gameplay styles in one game, being part of Sonic franchise. It was one of the last games to come out on Sega Dreamcast in 2001 and can be taken as Sega's "farewell". Shortly, it was ported to Gamecube, getting "Battle" subtitle, bringing new addition to multiplayer mode and chao garden. It also had small tweaks to it and didn't have neither small Downloadable Contnet that Dreamcast version had, mostly skins, nor Dreamcast's VMU to play tamagochi with your chao.
And now in 2012 Sega decided that Sonic Adventure 2 might be great enough to get HD rerelease for PS3, X360 and Steam, with it coming to PC for the first time ever.
So, here we have our modern Steam version of the game. As you noticed, Sega decided to separate game into just "Sonic Adventure 2" and DLC "Battle". DLC adds all the new content that Gamecube version had over Dreamcast one, which isn't much for single-player game, unless you want all achievement. Technically, just "Sonic Adventure 2" is more like Sonic Adventure 2 Battle with content cut down to Dreamcast level, not real Dreamcast version, the difference being in various small tweaks. BUT it does bring Big The Cat cameos in every level back. Funny.
A big feature of modern ports is widescreens support. All of the gameplay is now taking whole space of your wide monitors, with only Full Motion Videos and some of the cutscenes still retaining 4:3 aspect ratio.
It's quite a solid PC port, I don't remember seeing any new glitches. But multiplayer is local only.
Game has both singleplayer and multiplayer modes to play.
Now, I didn't get to try multiplayer, but it's a competive one. Could be lots of fun. But the only thing I can say is that it's common knowledge that Amy is OP.
Single-player is divided into two campaigns, Dark and Hero. Each of those two have the same three gameplay styles for three characters. Speed sections are the ones that Sonic fans expect and they were greatly improved over Sonic Adventure one, making them feel tight, challenging and more designed to be the blast to replay and better your score. Mech stages aren't as fast-paced and have more of primitive shooting mixed with platforming, with the Sega's style of ability of "put few enemies under the target and then release fire to have them all killed for big score". Treasure Hunting are more of exploration of huge stages, where you have to get yourself familiar with mazey layout and then use hint system and radar to track three pieces of needed item.
And while it does improve on gameplay, it has a fault of getting on more generic territory when it comes to universe. Gone are colorful otherwordly strange levels, instead you will spend time in more generic places, like city, forest and space station. The most Sonic-like stage you will get there is egypt-style with ghosts. Spooks. Then again, these generic stages are still colorful and are nice in their own way.
Music once again changed style. It's not as varied as the Sonic Adventure, aside from stereotypical rap for Knuckles and jazz for Rogue. Everything else is mostly techno and guitar work. And yet it's awesome, catchy and you will remember them for a while! They also provide intense feel at times.
Plot is quite darker this time. Instead of seeing perspective of six characters individually, you will get storytelling from the two sides. It's not deep and got some holes in it. Strange stuff, that sometimes feel were left out. Animation in cutscenes also got improved, they aren't too hilarious anymore. They sometimes move like puppets though. And I have to say that Dark Side is done better than Hero Side. Darkies are the ones who lead the plot and deal with mystery of Shadow. Heroes are just confused Sonic and his friends reacting to whatever happens.
And I have to say most important thing. The campaign is NOT fun to play for the first time. It got a huge pacing issues that ruin fun and turn it into patience test.Those three gameplay styles are mixed together seemingly randomly and change every single mission around. They are differently paced and fit for different kind of gamers, and even if you enjoy them all, they swap around to quick to get used to. Even worse is that plot often on Hero Side's is being interrupted by Knuckles with his slow-paced gameplay. Oh yes, and some enemies are quite cheap. I have no idea how to avoid attack of liquid monsters in last levels. Though, I don't think that Mech stages enemies are cheap, it's just that after getting used in earlier stages that you can just walk until the end calmly don't get you ready to actually avoid projectiles.
But once you get through campaign, you will get ability to select any level you want... And this is where fun begins. Not only because you can select any gameplay type you feel like doing right now. There are 5 missions for every level, the first mission being just "beat the level" and the last mission always being Hard Mode. Even more, for first time ever in Sonic games, it got a rating system. Upon completing levels you will be given one of the five grades, A being the highest, based on the final scores. While time score matters there, you will get a lot by destroying gold robot, doing tricks, defeating as many enemies in a row as possible and collecting more rings. As said, Sonic games are easy to play, easy-hard to beat but difficult to master. Even kart stages start to make sense when you have mission not to touch walls, having to drift into corners (release and press jump button again while turning to get into drifting mode). Some of the mission grade A requirements are quite insane though, so I doubt that you will 100% the game easily at all.
Actually, just knowing the pace of the game after beating it will help you enjoy game more when rebeating it. Which quite explains why those who played the original version praise Sonic Adventure 2, while newcomers get bad taste of it.
You also will get to unlock Boss Rush mode.
And Kart mode, which is more of bonus game. Drifting is nice, but it's not Daytona. And characters aren't balanced around each other, some character have no chances to keep up with AI cars, who don't even make look that they their cars are being controlled in same ways.
Developer video will be unlocked in options after some amount of hours being played. Where developers will tell you few small anecdotes/facts from the development and that's about it.
Oh, and this time, getting all 130 emblems will give you not only achievement, but a little bonus level. Shame that in order to do that you have to also get emblems from Chao Garden part of game. And DLC too.
Yea, Chao Garden, that tamagochi thing. Where you have to find chao key on stage and also feed chao 10 animals you brought along. And then watch them grow. And stuff. It's not really a thing for gamers. Then again, Sonic games's main auditory are young people anyway, but still, not something traditional gamers will care about. Just grind with 10 animals over and over again.
Dreamcast actually had this little thing where memory unit had it's own control on it and you could take it with yourself as "portable handheld". Though, more like tamagochi. And you could raise chao on it when you was outside of home. Or at least find useful items for them. So it was making more sense back then.
So, not a good game to beat, but awesome one to master. Recommended to Sonic fans and those who tend to replay stages they liked, instead of abandoning game after beating it.
Then again, there isn't so many 3D Platformers on Steam right now, so may take it anyway.

The apocalypse has fallen, Nuclear War has wiped out all traces of human life, but deep underground inside a bomb shelter a host of mutated insects live on... Nope, this isn’t a new Fallout expansion, its Daedalic Entertainment’s Journey of a Roach! This comedy clicker sees the player take on the role of Jim the Cockroach, as he puzzles his way through laundry rooms, bars and ventilation shafts on a quest to save his cockroach pal Bud, so they can escape to the surface together and finally experience what life is like on the surface.
Visually, the game is a real treat. Cutscenes use comic-strip style storytelling to advance the plot and despite it being released in 2013, the graphics have aged relatively well. Levels are varied and interesting and the cutesy cartoony characters are lovingly and humorously designed - from the war veteran wasp, to the old lady spider and everything in between. Much like Machinarium, the game has no dialogue, or so to speak. Characters communicate using speech bubbles with pictures hinting at what they want, and voices are an adorable mixture of buzzes, bu-be-dees and bo-bi-dos. Combine all of the above with a quirky soundtrack and the game simply oozes humour. It’s cheerful, charming and fun.
Gameplay is presented in 2.5D style, which gives the rooms you travel through a great sense of depth, and much to my surprise – Jim has the ability to scale the walls and ceilings. This alone makes every room feel almost twice as big, and adds in a whole new dimension to puzzling and moving around. It can take a little while to get used to at first and in places it can be a little clunky, but in no time at all you’ll find yourself rather smoothly navigating your way around. It’s worth noting too, that the game offers full controller support for even more fluid control as you scuttle around the bomb shelter.
Puzzles are fair to reasonable in the difficulty stakes, and some of the item combinations feel very reminiscent of Day of the Tentacle and other old school classics, which is always a good comparison. As the game advances you will run into a few trickier parts, namely a section involving a pylon and a beam of electricity – but on the whole, there isn’t anything too difficult here. Some of the puzzles are designed with the 2.5D/Climbing mechanics in mind too, so what starts out as a little novelty, soon becomes a core gameplay element – much like the ‘thinking with portals’ logic, you’ll soon be making sure you explore every ceiling as well as the floor to help you progress. It’s a pretty unique mechanic for the genre that, for the most part, is pretty well implemented.
The game clocks in at about 3 to 4 hours in length for one playthrough, so it is on the shorter end of the spectrum – but that doesn’t feel like any sort of a hindrance. The story is funny, the characters are great, and the puzzles offer a good enough challenge. The little bit of time you’ll spend with Jim on his journey is well paced, and the game certainly never drags or outstays its welcome. There’s a little replay value here too for you 100% completion junkies - I’m not one for achievements myself, so I doubt I’ll be replaying it anytime soon, but for those of you that are, there are plenty in there that challenge you to not only replay the game, but beat it in 18 minutes. Let me know if you manage it!
One thing I will point out though, is that considering the length - at £11.99 as I write this, JoaR is slightly on the pricier side, so you may want to wait until it pops up on sale to really squeeze your pennies for every bit of value.
All in all though, Journey of a Roach is a short and sweet Point & Clicker that brings in some new twists on the age-old genre. There’s not too many developers in the world that I would say are always a safe bet, but in my eyes, Daedalic are one of them and they’ve delivered yet again with this cute-as-a-button, post-apocalyptic comedy. A good balance between fun and frustrating, solid gameplay mechanics and good design. It may never make it into the videogame hall of fame, but don’t let it pass you by entirely!

So a lot of people weren't fans of this game for a few reasons:
-Level design: many people complained that the openness of the levels, including the large amount of windows (compared to the first game), meant that it was too restrictive in terms of what weapons you could use, in that it forced you to use guns in order to chain combos and stay alive. This is a valid point, but really, people are just upset because the game is different than the last game. The last game had small areas, a few rooms and a hallway that could easily be used to string combos with a bunch of different weapons. That was great, people liked that. But the new game does force you to use guns, a lot. The Fans use guns most of the time, as well as the Soilders. So, people who don't like to use guns may be angry at first, but I think they'll warm up to it when they realize they can make some pretty awesome combo chains with them.
-Story, mostly the ending: Well, I can't say much because I don't like to spoil things (even if you think it's♥♥♥♥♥♥so who cares), but I can say that the story makes little sense unless you go out and look up a timeline or something. Still, the characters are a lot of fun, and there is a large variety within the game of what kind of weapons, tactics, etc. one may use.
-Difficulty: this might play in to the "level design" portion, but I did see a lot of complaining about the difficulty of the game. I can attest to the fact that this is justified, especially on Hard difficulty. There are some very frustrating enemies in the game (the big fat guys who only die by a magazine+ of bullets, the superfast crackheads that run after you with the quickness) that can ruin people's combos and leave them♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. One of the hardest levels for me was the prison, and many people found the ship to be quite difficult as well. But that is a part of the game people have to accept. I know "git gud" is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ advice, but if you really do find out that you can use the character's tactics and learn to shoot accuratly and quickly, as well as switch weapons with ease, you might actually find yourself happy to repeat the same level over and over to get that sick 34x combo. Just have a bit of patience and believe.
So in conclusion, it's different from the first game. If that disqualifies it for you right away, then so be it. It is a good game by its self.
But hey, if you just want more of the same as the first one, the level editor should be out of beta soon, so grab it for that! The devs said they want people to be able to make HM3 in it, so you get a full campaign editor with cutscenes and all that jazz.

The magnificent duo. I insist on calling Hotline Miami and Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number nothing short of a masterclass on game and narrative design. Go play it for yourself before reading the rest of this review.
Your objective is simple - kill. What makes this different from other quick and dirty ultra-violent games that you might find on the internet? Well, for a start, you and your enemies die from just 1 hit. This is the crucial mechanic of the Hotline games - you will die and you will die again, but you'll keep pressing that quick respawn button. You'll just keep on pressing it.
This is where the game's narrative kicks in - at the end of levels and between levels, you're given a brief period of reflection. The game literally asks you whether you enjoy what you're doing, because the thing is you don't think about the senseless violence and mayhem that you're wreaking while you play. It's lost in a haze of flashing neon and pumped-up music. While the first game is vague in its moral direction, the second employs a Pulp Fiction-style story to demonstrate the consequences of seneless bloodshed.
I could absolutely gush all day about how fantastic an experience the two games are. After playing the first, I marathoned almost the entirety of the second. It's compelling, it's absorbing and the soundtrack is immense and BUY THIS GAME RIGHT NOW WHAT ARE YOU DOING?

Amazing game and one of the best I've played.  Plenty of people will complain about Uplay and, to be honest, there are several complaints I could write about - chief amongst those would be the terrible experience getting Uplay rewards to load.
But about the game:  tremendous.  I played the game nearly non-stop because I just had to see where the story was going.  I had several different theories about what was happening to our character and the underlying island drama.  I won't spoil it but it was some of the best storytelling in a game I've seen.
The game is open for you to explore.  There is a bit of hand holding to progress some stories along.  After the first main quest (which is a tutorial of sorts), you're free to go any way you want.  The challenges of the island come from the environment, nature, and the warring factions.
Weapon selection is nice and I quickly figured out which loadout I preferred.  SMG, assault rifle, sniper rifle, and LMG.  Despite being kitted with a fine selection of firearms, I found the stealth approach to be quite enjoyable.  The knife is very deadly and the choices of "takedown" moves makes the gameplay exciting.
Despite having to play this on a lower end system - right at the bottom of the playable heap - it was a joy.
Highly recommended!  9/10   (I wish there was an option to play as a female lead, but it's understandable since the bulk of the dialog was written from a male lead's perspective.)

Deep Under the Sky is a physics puzzler (wait come back) that might be the best chillout game I've ever played. You control a crazy♥♥♥♥♥looking space jellyfish on Venus as it wanders around and produces offspring. I use the term "control" in the loosest possible way because like the screenshot says, this game only has one button. At the start of every level the jellyfish settles into place and cannot be moved. Your one button launches an egg pod offspring thing in a set trajectory. The icons in the bottom left are the different effects that pushing your one button will have on its movement. There are directional boosts, rolling, bouncing, and of course, exploding. Your goal is to get the pod close enough to the glowing stalks to explode and plant a new offspring there.
The limited controls mean puzzles tend to be pretty obvious and open to trial-and-error. Some levels have a lot of different travel powers to use that open things up more, but mostly you'll just be using your one or two directional boosts at slightly different times and seeing where your pod ends up. The game is nice enough to show you the path of your last pod, so if you were close to your target last time you can use that as a handy reference. The visuals are weird and busy in a pleasant way, and there's a lot of detail in the particle effect. The soundtrack is a perfect low-key synth thing to relax to as you fling alien spores around. Each stage has two stars in tricky places for completionists to find, and there's about 80 levels to float through. I played it for about 30 minutes and beat the first chapter (20 levels), and when I sat down later to play something else... I actually booted this up again for a bit. It's a great little filler game, not too taxing on the mind and with lots of pretty sights and sounds to keep you occupied.
This sort of game belongs on mobile devices.

The game begins with some very basic physics puzzles and quickly ramps up to more and more twitch gameplay; not only will you have to time each click perfectly, especially for the stars, but every level needs several differently timed executions, not just one. It's surprisingly addictive once things start getting more complicated, especially if you're obsessive about getting all the stars. It may be a mobile game, but it makes up for that with excellent level design that easily translates to PC. The graphics aren't much to write home about, but they do a good job, and even have that retro Ecco the Dolphin feel.
The best part is that there's no fake difficulty, it's all skill. They even show you where you last clicked, so you can do better next time, but despite that it's intuition and reflex that will succeed, not mechanical learning.
But don't trust the video. That doesn't capture the feel of the game at all.
As for price, I'm not sure the regular price is worth it, but it's often on sale and it'll keep you entertained for hours. Pick it up.
Note: When it says "one button only: The space bar" that actually means space, mouse, or gamepad button. So it's definitely no limiting you to any control scheme.

Extremely simplistic (1 button) puzzle game that would be barely tolerable on a mobile platform.
PROS:
-Art is ok
-Puzzle setup is clean and varied by levels.
-Very calm gameplay.
CONS:
-"Trial and error" gameplay that is extremely repetitive. Gameplay consists of you shooting these balls from the same starting location and trying to time a series of actions to hit targets (except you don't actually control the actions, all you can do is control when each action begins). In short, each time you miss the target you simply repeat the series of actions until you hit it.....and then you repeat that a bunch more times until you hit all the targets in the stage.
Then you move on to the next stage which presents you with a different order of actions, but the same concept of hitting targets. That is the entire game with only the order of actions changing between stages.
-MISLEADING description: There is no "exploration" or "movement" really...each stage simply presents you with a series of actions and a bunch of targets to hit, and then you go on to the next level.
Similarly, nothing here is psychadelic. Its simple, colorful graphics, but thats about it.
The video presented on the steam page (showing "gameplay) is also misleading. It shows the character moving through a variety of environments, but this is not, at all, what the gameplay is like. Your objective is to "explode" yourself near those orange balls and then respawn and repeat until you hit all the orange balls in a stage (usually about 5-7).

This game is pretty fun, but it has various unexcusable flaws. The Steam version of this controls terribly unless you use a controller. No matter what console you use, the game has a usless camera, music that is WAY too loud [but admittedly very catchy], unpredictably spazzy character animations merciless and cheap enemy placement, and way too many glitches that induce rage-quitting while also making the game more fun to explore. speaking of exploring, you get almost none of it with the most linear stage design ever. on top of all of that, only a fraction of the game is enjoyable. Sonic and Shadow's "Action Stages" are the only fun ones, of which there are only 10 in total, Dr. Eggman and Tail's mech stages had potential, but were ruined by tank controls cheap enemy placement, and ear-piercing sound effects, and Knuckles and Rouge's treasure hunting stages are an unplayable mess. The plot and cutscenes are for the most part engaging and fun to watch, despite it being inconsistent. The graphics look good, especially the framerate. Overall, this game is terrible, but thanks to the few good points and the excellent stage select that lets you replay only those good parts, I just have to recommend Sonic Adventure 2.

the card system sound cute till its implemented. think of it like this each card is in your deck is 1 attack, ability, or spell and you can hold upto 5 cards at a time from your deck and you'll get 1 new card per turn if you have under 5 cards. say you have 1 heal card in your deck this means you can only cast heal 1 time per battle. there will allways be a normal attack and 1 random card to use (its only replaced if you use it) but if you use up your deck these 2 cards are all you have. the bad thing with this is if your hand can't be used and/or the random card can't be used you can wast a turn on a card and hope for a better card next turn or use a base attack with that character. there is no discard without wasting your turn. each character does get their own deck. this system just feels so limited to other rpg's and when the enemies pummel you in 2-3 hits it makes this system seem even worse if your starting hand is bad.
another issue is your hp refills after every fight but your GD&DR (your mp. 2 use gd 2 use dr) does not and you must find glowing balls to refill some of it. you can refill GD as some steam engine things in town but i have not found anything to refill DR outside the light balls or leveling up. The mana system is just terrible: You have to manage different kind of mana based on your class, which doesn't regenerate over time/ when you enter a new area or could be restored with potions. Even worse: your max mana doesn't increase over time meaning unless you use up equipment slots for items that increase your max mana, all you get is ~3 "spells" / character until you pick up one of the mana containers that you can find on each level.

Overall, I loved this game.  I love the excecutions, I love the modding, and I love it's potential.  The basis of the game is situated around a player who has choices in the beginning, to mould his/her character, to give them a story.  After the game begins, you're down to no army, you have little money, and you must chose to help a merchant with bandit troubles or leave him and his kin to die.  After that, it's up to you how it's done.  Become a lord, get Right to Rule, and make your own kingdom.  One more thing I mentioned earlier, the mods.   Modding is one of the base principles in Mount and Blade.  It's what makes the game so intriguing.  I got bored quickly after playing the vanilla game, much like how I got bored of vanila Minecraft.  But, the mods kept it changing, they added in boats, they added in firearms, they added in whole different universes.  If you want to see some gameplay footage of this game before you buy it, I strongly reccomend going with Reformisttm on Youtube.
Paradox really made a great game when they began Mount and Blade.  I wish, that there were multiplayer campaigns and the like, and a tune-up in graphics and general gameplay.  But this game was made for the community that played it.  This game was made so the players could decide how they managed it.  Add in mods, and you have the entire world of Calradia to your command in some instances.

The sad truth is, Call of Duty campaigns and its general gameplay has lacked meaningful innovation for quite a long time. This entry is no different. While they have introduced Squads (which is, I admit, a very intriguing mode to try out), don't expect any daring attempt at innovation. In the end, this is yet another blatant money grab for our pockets, whilst "playing it safe" by staying to the "tried and true" Call of Duty formula.
As for the graphics...they are about what you would expect for a Call of Duty title. Had I not known it was a new engine, I would never have guessed, as the graphics look quite dated when matched against other recently released games.
The Story for the single player campaign also was quite unengaging, sticking close to all of the Call of Duty cliches. There was no exciting or unpredictable twists, no real attempt by the writers to get me to connect with the characters in the story. In fact, about halfway through the campaign, I realized that I didn't care what happened to any of the characters, or even what would happen in the larger scope of the war that was going on. It was a huge disconnect, and In short, it was quite boring.
As always, multiplayer is interesting, though again, do not expect any surprises. They make some changes, sure, but not large enough changes to really change the formulaic call of duty approach. Thus, if you've played multiplayer on call of duty at any time over the last 3 or 4 years, you can consider yourself to have pretty much experienced this year's rendition of it as well.
Because of the lack of MEANINGFUL innovation in its campaign or multiplayer, its lack of an engaging story, its lack of engaging characters, and its lack of graphical innovation, I have given this game a score of 2 out of 10. Call of Duty needs to break new ground. Innovate!

It's a beautiful game very reminiscent of old school Runescape. A great sandbox to enjoy with your friends. I'm giving a negative review because they've included micro-transactions into an Early Access game. I'd be fine with micro-transactions if this were an mmo. But it's not. And the argument the developer made is absolutely ludicrous.
They're justifying their reason for keeping the cash shop by stating that the game only costs 12 USD with constant regular "free" updates. I can think of multiple games in that price range that doesn't have a cash shop but still gives out constant updates (Stardew Valley, Terraria, Starbound, etc). These are all amazing sandbox rpgs with a thriving community supporting them with tutorials, guides, and even mods.
How can Ylands hope to compete with those titles if they are implementing one of the most hated aspects of video games, micro-transactions? Sure it's only cosmetics items for now, but what's stopping them from adding different progression-based items later on? I honestly hope I'm wrong because this game looks very interesting and I would love to play it with my friends.﻿
I will check back in about 6-8 months to see if the cash-shop is truly "cosmetics" only.

TL;DR: Honestly, if you have the money and don't care how you spend it, get this game. It's a great, realistic adventure FPS with a fun story. But if you're looking for the best of its genre, or a game that you can keep playing, don't get it. Ultimately, play Borderlands before you play this. Here's why:
The combat is amazing. Effective difficulty changer, hyper-realistic guns, multiple strategies optional for each problem, pretty darn good stealth system, etc. The open world is really good. I love how you have to craft things to improve your character. The main story quest is very good. You play it once and it's great... but after you beat it, you may aswell uninstall. The continuity is far from bad. It's a nightmare.
-The guns get very repetitive cause there's not many to choose from. Only 6 assault rifles, 5 smgs, 3 lmgs, 3 shotguns, and 3 snipers (also pistols and specials like bows and flamethrowers). It may sound like enough but you can actually unlock the weapons for FREE (which sucks) (by activating towers) and each weapon is better than the previous one, so chances are you'll have the 3rd-ish best weapon in the game and never switch it out before 10% of the mainquest is through with. You think you really need to unlock the good weapons anyways? Nope. I beat the entire campaign on Expert dificulty with only the worst AR (the AK-47, which btw 70% of the enemies drop so you can get one in the first 10 mins of playing.) (and I'm not an expert FPS player either... my average K/D on any call of duty is like 1/3). But this just shows you how, since the worst weapon is good enough to beat the whole campaign on Expert, don't expect to be excited about the guns. They're just kinda... there.
-Enemies get rediculously repetitive... there's only like 5-6 variants on the enemies: light, armoured, rusher, heavy, sniper/rpg, pretty much it. Helicopters, too, but even in expert mode the helicopters are potatoes. They show up, sit there, and give you a good, solid 8 seconds to pull out your RPG and one-shot them (which takes about 1 second). Don't expect exciting enemies.
-And as for side quests and pass times... It seems like the devellopers forgot about the side quests and had to get the mexican custodian downstairs to do all the coding in about 45 minutes. EVERY SINGLE NPC HAS THE SAME CHARACTER MODEL AND VOICE. The quests are about as deep as this: "Go talk to this guy." *you talk to this guy and tell him to stop being a yeasty motherflucker* "Sweet thx here's $500". That's not an exaggeration. That's actually one of the quests.You just talk to someone for someone. The pass-times are pretty bad too, except for poker, which is actually VERY fun. The others are just knife throwing games or shooting ducks from the sky. There's racing games too, but dumbl enough you're racing a clock not other cars.
-And, last but not least, Uplay. Ubisofts technology reverses the definition of technology. Let's just say it takes about 5 hours to play the game after you first download it. You don't just buy Far Cry 3 and expect to play it the same day.
In the end, if you have a lot of money, get the game. It's a FUN game, well constructed, and I enjoyed myself thoroughly. Seriously get it despite wht I said if you can afford it. However, if you're budgeting and want to find the RIGHT game that you can replay over and over again, I would direct my attention elsewhere, for sure.

Oh, Planet Explorers. The potential you had.  When it first popped up, it seemed like a decent Minecraft clone, with some MMO bits for good measure. And it even has a thing which allows you to design your own vehicles! ( Seriously, aside from prefab wheels and an annoyingly large cockpit, you make the rest out of voxels, and you can even use your own materials!) I've lost hours and hours to that vehicle creation system.
But the game itself? Pretty bland, actually. The characters are dull, the voiceovers are pathetically awful, and the AI is just... Well, the 'I' doesn't stand for 'intelligence' here.
There's also graphical issues aplenty, weird inconsistencies with the characters ( Like for eaxmple how some have voiceovers and some do not, some will give you the same quest over and over again, etc.) Also, the weather seems to sporadically decide whether your structures can block water or not. Vehicles randomly flip for no reason, and there's no way to adjust the turning radius of the cars. Flying is.... Interesting, to say the least.
It's really a shame with a lot of this because the story ( And there IS a story) gets interesting as you get deeper into it. Sadly I've never gotten much past the desert because of the bugs. And the vehicle creator ( Which makes more than just vehicles, by the way) has some huge potential. Or had. It doesn't seem they're doing any work to it at this point. As it sits it's pretty good.
I'd love to give this game a recommend, especially if it was still considered alpha/early access.... But it seems this is the complete game, and as such, I'm going to have to not recommend it, for now. Change my mind, Pathea. Make your game shine.

First off, let me say that I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Sonic games, both old and new.  With a great 3-act story, well designed levels, fun bosses (I always fight Final Hazard as a warm up when playing, great fun!), and a Chao pet raising sim I honestly feel that I can say that this is both the best Sonic game I have ever played and also my favorite (having sunk hundreds upon hundreds of hours into the Chao portion alone).
THAT BEING SAID, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME ON STEAM.
Not because of anything that Steam has done, mind you, but simply because SEGA dropped the ♥♥♥♥ing ball on the PC port.  If you want to truly enjoy all that this game has to offer, buy the Gamecube version.
Simply put, the game is buggy as all hell on PC, and multiple features are implemented but deny the player access do to SEGA's gimmick feature for GBA connectivity in the Chao garden (pet raising sim portion of the game).  Speaking of the Chao garden, in the PC version (in addition to features that were meant for the GBA/GCN) you cannot grow trees, they literally bug out and only grow halfway (both reducing the number of extra trees you can have and never producing fruit). I wonder if it's more accurate to say the space jellyfish is now my favorite aquatic or extraterrestrial creature.
As far as I know the depths of our oceans are wondrous and alien enough that Deep Under the Sky could be playing out within them, far from any depth humans have been able to reach. Bounding from the safety of their nest, tentacles swirling in the current, attempting to fertilize a waking host before their short life expires. There's something very poetic about Deep Under the Sky, its bedazzling art creating a hypnotic cycle as you run almost on autopilot, sacrificing innumerable members of this strange species in pursuit of the task at hand.
Mesmerizing as it can be, Deep Under the Sky has the inescapable issue of being so hands-off as to make me often feel like my role in it was superfluous, or at least fairly dull and extremely limited in scope. A queue of moves scrolls from the bottom of the screen, their moment of execution being your only means of interaction, and thus levels are laid out before you as you launch jellyfish out attempting to discern the correct timing to be able to reach each of the nests you need to fertilize in order to progress. It's something like being given a catapult but only ever being allowed to pull the lever, leaving the aiming to others and then entering into a series of trial and error as you work within your rigid limitations to recreate the moves of the developer. Success often felt like an accident, yet another thing I had little control over, level after level passing by but failing to leave me with any lasting impression longer than the seconds it took to load the next screen.
It's not the worst way to spend a few hours by any stretch, but the experience goes by with such little presence that it was almost like I wasn't playing a game at all, just staring at my monitor as my fingers moved on their own and I was left to leisurely enjoy the wondrous, sparkling world of strange organisms draped around a much less engaging game. I find it hard to say whether that's an experience worth your time, my memories of the game already beginning to fade, but I'm equally indecisive in prescribing you stay away so perhaps that says what I'm failing to.

A 2D (or 2.5D, if we're gonna use buzzwords) platformer about the world being overrun by zombies in the 80s. Not the most original premise but it works.
Pros:
-Visually stunning, artistry of the game creates good atmosphere for the most part.

-Short (this is also in the cons section), only about 3 hours.
Cons:
-Sloppy and clunky feeling controls. This doesn't usually create too much of an issue as the game is fairly easy, but it does serve as a point of annoyance for several sequences and it just means that the game feels less fluid.
-Most of the puzzles are uninspiring, unfun, and make you feel like you're "going through the motions"

Lets look at Deadlight not to get confused with dying light. Dead light is a 2D platformer zombie game that is designed in this comic book style in the cutscenes. I will be reviewing this game....not dying light on a pro/ con style and ending with my final conclusion.
Pro:
The game has this awsome soundtrack. I could sit on the main menu for hours listening to the moody song that plays. Actually it was one of the songs i enjoyed jamming to when playing other games...sometimes if the mood calls for it. The other songs are really good too but that main menu song is my favorite by far.
The graphics in the cutscenes are very well done. I want to say they are hand drawn in that comic book style which is very cool. It reminds me of the infamous series....the first two that were on the ps3 back then. Those were also good games but the point is the cutscenes felt like watching one of the comic cutscenes  in the game infamous. It proves that a game can be pretty spectacular to view even if it has that comic style artwork.
The story is great. I enjoyed it alot because there was development on the main character and there were very rememberable moments but that will be kept a secret. You know spoilers.
The achievements. Most are easy to get while a few will be a tad tricky but that is not the reason that is a plus. The real reason is that the achievements are named after old 80s songs like knocking on heavens door, i want it all, and others. I thought that was really cool to realize.
They have old school minigames to play and alot of collectables that adds back story. The minigames are really fun because they are old school handheld like games that existed in the 70s probably. Simple left/ right movement and an action button game. The only one i played was a guitar hero like minigame.
Con:
There are moments in the game that breaks the flow. The helicopter sequence when you are being chased is frustrating with how perfect your run must be. There are a few others but it is never fun to play a moment that has to be done very perfect else you will die.
Chase sequences are annoying. I didnt like chase sequences in outlast and i dont enjoy it here. It is a cheap way of pushing the player along and breaks the flow with how perfect it must be.
The combat is sluggish. It isnt bad for the early portion of the game since you can avoid the zombies all together but late game you will need to slash or shoot through a small group of zombies and it is not fun when at points the zombies respawn infinitly. Naturally i kill the zombies to give me all the time i need to solve a platforming puzzle but continuously spawning zombies to replace the dead ones does not make any progress feel worth it. Cleaning a room at those points feels like a waste.
Slippery controls. There are points that the player must jump up from one ledge to another or a piece of a broken ladder to another. The game sometimes registers me when i am pushing the controller up to jump up to the other section of the ladder. The character decides he would rather jump to the right to my death. Also with chase sequences being so perfect it is stressful when the controls are slippery and you do a mistake you didnt expect to happen.
The issue where in cutscenes there will be no audio. That is still an issue but atleast there is a great guide on steam that explains how to fix it. Still it is an issue with the game and even if you do the fix ive experiened some very weird moments like how my destination was blocked by an invisble wall and how the map abruptly ended when it shouldnt. How i fell through the map. It was very awkward and at the time i felt it might be game breaking.
Game mechanics that only make a presence for like 2 moments in the entire game. Changing sides on the ladder is a mechanic that can be done to avoid obsticals but it is used only 2 times and is very forgetable that you can even do something like that. The 2nd moment that i needed to change sides on a ladder i ended up dead because i forgot i could do that till the game kindly reminded me after death that it is a mechanic. If there are mechanics in the game, make sure that they are used often....more than 2.
The sewer mission was just so slow because there were traps, no combat so you must avoid zombies and traps at the same time.
Conclusion:
Overall i do believe that deadlight is a great game even if it has a few bugs or issues. I dont like how there is a few moments that are chase sequences or the entire Rat mission where your in the sewers. That Rat mission was just so slow. The music was fantastic, the graphics were nice, and the story was an experience to be had. I could reccomend this game to anyone who was curious about it but i would need to show them the guide to fix the audio for the cutscenes. No one wants to miss the tone of the dialoge or the voices of the characters. Some characters have really cool voices and get some nice dialoge. It really compliments the graphics.

The gameplay was also enjoyable and reminds me of older side-scrolling games (Prince Of Persia, Nosferatu, Ninja Gaiden, Castlevania; etc.). However, that is where the game's appeal ends for me.

This is a fun little rpg with a surprising amount of strategy to it.  Though short, this game has an interesting storyline and very different gameplay from most rpgs.  Rather than having a fixed set of skills that a character can perform every round, you, instead, have a deck of tactics that you can customize, but are randomly drawn from over the course of battle.
The graphics for this game are pretty good.  Not excellent, but most people shouldn't complain.  The gameplay is pretty simple and not particularly hard to follow.  Maps are easy to navigate for the most part, though some clickalbe objects will get in the way when you are attempting to move.  Dealing with the robot factory, this was especially the case.  The music for the game is pretty par-for-course, though there are a couple of really good songs in there that stand out from the rest.
Downsides to this game are problematic item management, a lack of stores, a lack of options for things other than combat.  The game feels a little rushed and is incomplete with the revelation that one of the characters in your party has a storyline that is completely unresolved by the end of it.  There are a few other plotholes similar to this, notably.
Overall, I would say that it's not quite a $20 game.  There's simply not enough here, but beyond this, the game is very good and fun.  It is well put together and I didn't encounter any major bugs.  Longer story, larger maps, and more access to the world and it's history would make for a better and more immersive experience I thik

With some gorgeous art style, that really suit the type of game genre, Trulon: The shadow engine strives to be a different type of RPG game with some interesting features. It is a card based RPG based based upon a book by Jak Koke, writer of the Shadowrun trilogy and The Dragon Heart Saga.
Based upon a book by Jak Koke, Trulon: The shadow engine is set in a steampunk universe where a young hunter called Gladia has discovers a plot to poison her homeland, from using the mechanical machines from the Kingdom of Maelon. After finding out about this plot and reporting it to the queen of Tripudia and realizing that they won’t do anything, she decides to set out on her own journey to find out who sent the machines and to stop their plot. This game features 4 playable characters that you will meet across your journey in a few locations that you will come across in the course of playing this game.
Trulon: The shadow engine strives to be a unique type of RPG game. The gameplay is based upon a basic card based battling system with a turn based system and some RPG elements thrown into the mix. Attacking enemies are fairly straightforward, you click on the card you want to use and then click on the enemie(s) you want to attack. There are about 50 cards in total for you to discover over the course of the game, with each one having a specific function to them. Some cards are physical and can attack from one enemies, to multiple enemies, some of these can then either add or take away a buff on your character with could ultimately win you the battle. There are also defensive or magic cards that you can use on your character to avoid an attack for a single turn. It’s very easy to pick up and play, all of the cards are self-explanatory so there isn’t much learning involved in this game, most of the time it’s up to luck of what cards you draw and the strategy of when you use your cards. Unfortunately, there isn’t all that much variety in the cards each character can use, therefore it’s not a very in-depth system that other types of cards games do have. There are a few ways that you can obtain new cards, you can acquire these cards from opening treasure chests, obtaining them from quests that you have completed or from battles that you win. Creating your own deck for each character is rather simple and straightforward, some cards can only be equipped to a certain character in the game. A unique mechanic about this type of deck creating is that there are different types of mechanisms that you can quip on your characters which will add special bonuses during your battles. Some of the special bonuses include being able to set your enemy on fire, the damage repeats over time, adding defence for the next turn or increasing your attack power for your character. There is a nice variety to discover and create so you can build a pretty wide amount of unique characters throughout the game.
The game has some really nice joyful atmospheric music when you are in the cities, and then when you are in the battle the music jumps to a little bit more serious and sometimes intense music. Although this is nice and all, sometimes this can get a little repetitive and therefore you end up not wanting to listen to the music at all whilst you play the game. Adding a bit more variety of music to the game would makes this game shine a bit more, but other than that the music is fairly nice for the first couple of hours playing the game.
The art style of the game to me give off a sort of retro feel to it. The graphics for each of the characters are well done, and seem to be polished to be the finest that it could possibly be. All of the areas that you go into seem to be really vibrant in their colours and give off the atmospheric sense that you would imagine. From the day towns to the night cities, the art style really shines throughout the game as you play through it.
+ A unique type of RPG mixed with a card turn based system
+ Very easy to pick up and play
+ Very nice art style to fit the genre
+ A simple point and click game
+ The dialogue of the characters is well written
+ For the first few hours the music is really fitting no matter where you are
+ Story is interesting and fun, along with a few optional side quests
- No trading cards
- Not much variety of cards for each character to use
- Only way to save is to save and exit the game
- Music can get a little repetitive after a while
- Asking a bit of a heavy price
If you can get past the heavy price, and the music that gets a little repetitive over time, the game itself is definitely worth the money. The characters and story are interesting, as are all of the people you meet along the way on your journey. The art style is very vibrant in its colours and gives off a sort of retro feel to the game. The combat system in the game is a really nice change from the classic RPG battling system. Would definatly recommend this game.
