Rainbow Six planning phase as a refined standalone game.
This is a top-down pausable real-time strategy where you guide a squad of special forces through various missions (hostage rescue, bomb defusal, arrests, evidence grab or plain good old terrorist hunt). Before the start of the mission you are able to set up a plan and then watch it play out - however you can adjust it to your liking at any moment and have a limited direct control of separate fighters. Furthermore every fighter is customizable with the ability to select a loadout suitable for various tasks (akin to SWAT4).
The game comes with several campaigns and a huge amount of single missions, as well as a battle generator. Missions have a degree of replayability due to random enemy positions and numbers each time. If that's not enough there is a built-in mission editor - meaning you can also download many great user missions from Steam Workshop.
Steam Workshop further offers more variety by having mods that add new squad skins, new weapons and gear.
The only downside of note is an interface, which no doubt was affected by the mobile version - there's a lot of scrolling and clicking through to get to the stuff you want, especially after you've installed some mods. The game also gets repetitive after a while - same as its "bigger" brethren - classic R6 and SWAT series.

There are currently 227 people playing COD: Ghosts on Steam; the servers are all empty and the few that have any players at all seem to be occupied entirely by griefers. Not that I care much about multiplayer, but you'll have to forgive me if I concentrate entirely on COD:Ghost's single-player mode.
Which, of course, is going to consist entirely of moaning because - like all Call of Duty Games - the single-player in Ghosts is terrible. I know, complaining  about the sub-par gameplay of the console-era Call of Duty games is like pointing out the brilliance of our nearest star or reminding everybody that water is surprisingly liquid, but I'm still surprised at how bad the single-player portions of these games are. I mean, the developers pour tens of millions of dollars - the bulk of which go into the story mode - into these titles and I've never heard anyone - neither critic nor player - heap anything but scorn upon the single-player mode. The usual excuse is that people buy these games for their multiplayer, but I don't buy that; why spend so much on a game-mode nobody uses? There's obviously a significant segment that enjoys these stories.
I will give the developers credit though; it's nice to play as the villain for once. The protagonists are brain-dead goons with severe daddy-issues working for a tyrannical empire with weapons of mass-destruction ready to be unleashed on the world. In a clever twist, you fight against the heroic rebels who turn those weapons against the evil empire, and - as protagonist - you are forced to use guerrilla and terrorist tactics to fight back against the underdog and.... wait, what? That's /not/ what the story is about? Because it sure felt like it. Despite all the rah-rah gung-ho America-is-awesome patriotic nonsense, it's hard not to feel as if I were the bad guy as I snuck into a city or unsuspecting enemy base and massacred and tortured the unsuspecting populace, especially after being shown that America had an orbital death-platform at the start of the game. And the hero got no points for smart, being - once again - completely unable to open doors without help and being punished if he strayed ever so slightly off the expected path. The game was so tightly scripted as to remove all agency from the player; it's almost as much a "walking simulator" as "The Beginner's Game" or "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" (except at least those games allow you to freely wander about at your own pace). I got so tired of it that I ultimately stopped even trying and I still finished the game. I ambled calmly through the hectic firefights when the game expected me to run; I didn't shoot the enemies except when I had to, and when I was forced to pull the trigger I did it haphazardly, never once using the iron sights. That I still got to the end of the game just goes to show how pointless my actual involvement was.
Ghosts also felt oddly gimmicky, even for a Call of Duty game. In one mission, you are controlling a robot dog, in the next you have an remote sniper, then the usual death-from-above segments first popularized - and later overused - by the Modern Warfare games. I got the impression the developers were throwing anything at the wall, hoping one of these modes would "stick" by catching the interest of the player. None of them did. The game even featured a weird alien-shooting "horde mode" (not part of the main story line, fortunately) that felt so out-of-field that I was left more befuddled than engaged.
Ghost's doesn't quite match the nadir of the franchise that was "Black Ops" but it does absolutely nothing to revitalize it either. I remain confused as to why this series has such prominence in the marketplace.

Journey of a Roach was a game I gambled on and won. I saw it come up as a Steam advertisement, and after having seen a dozen or more “stupid” games being advertised, something in me decided to check out one of them. I picked this up for a few dollars, and it sat unplayed for most of a year.
By the time I dusted it off last week, I was pleased to find that it was exactly what I was looking for. Simply put, it is an adventure-puzzle game with a very simple and intuitive interface, and yes, you are a roach.
I enjoyed almost every aspect of the game. I laughed, felt sad, smiled, and felt my eyes go wide on a few occasions throughout. It is a short game, but that is something I count as an advantage. I feel that I got everything I wanted out of it and did not waste time on repetitive content.
Journey of a Roach is a single-player game, but in retrospect, it would have been fun to sit down with a friend and figure out the puzzles together. For the most part, though, I think it is perfectly great in solitaire.
There were a few things that distracted from the fun of Roach. The first thing I encountered was the music. Early in the game, the music is so terrible that it was making me sick. There were bendy, modulated, sickly notes during one puzzle, so I turned it off. By the end, the music was better, but I did not listen to it most of the game just in case.
Second, as with any puzzle game, it is very hard to get all of the clues fall within the perfect range of difficulty for a wide range of players. Journey of a Roach did a good job; in fact, most of the time, I realized later that there were subtle clues I missed. Nevertheless, there were a couple of times where I felt quite frustrated. Once, I looked it up after having spent thirty minutes on a single part of a puzzle, and it turned out that an idea I had thought might work but did not realize was actually doable (negative metagame thinking) was the right thing. In the end, this is a minor negative: that things that should be doable are not while others you might not expect are.
Third, and this may be the biggest negative for me, the camera follows your perspective at all times. Oh, and you are a roach, remember? I am no entomologist, but it appears roaches can walk on walls and ceilings. If you are even remotely prone to motion sickness, …holy roaches, buckle up. I learned to squint, look away, or lay my head back while exploring certain parts of the game.
All things considered, Journey of a Roach is a great game that does exactly what it sets out to do. If you are thinking about it, just buy it and have some fun.

If you've done it in Minecraft, you've done it here.
A shameless clone of Minecraft and many of its mods, Ylands puts you in a survival situation and expects you to figure out how to make a living out of the world ... to no further end. 90 Percent of the reason Minecraft isn't trending anymore is market saturation. The rest of it lies in the "Death of the Author" phenomenon where something created by an Author becomes the property of others to do with what they please. And when you carbon copy an experience with little minute changes but slap in a Micro-transaction mechanic, you're guilty of plagiarism on the one and being lazy on the other!
What makes me angry is there the failure to Remix the idea. You mine, you craft, you build things. You start out crawling in the dirt and then climb out of the muck to build a really awesome castle. And just like Minecraft, once you've done that, you have run out of things to do. There's no level above 'Make something Awesome.' Once it's all been built and mined out, you're done. Ylands doesn't even pass muster as a 'Minecraft-but.'
Next is the micro-transactions in the game. Having a proprietary currency separate from the game that cost additional money is a deal breaker in every sense UNLESS THE GAME WAS FREE. Ylands want's 12 bucks as current and then an additional 50-60 dollars USD for me to have all the content currently available in the shop? And lets not forget other reviewers who've dumped more hours in to find that some of the items (mostly the static ones that I can see) don't follow your account. They are stuck in the world in which you placed them and constitute value robbed from you by the game.
Then there's the questions about privacy raised by user Ni†oXo†iИ regarding data being taken by the game. I don't have the credentials to argue about that but simple data collection by the programmer should be fine as long as it's all laid out in the open.
It's wrong to talk about entitlement when a game barely rising above a clone of Minecraft wants me to pay additional cash for other content and might be spying on me or my computer. I have no faith in this game or its potential and recommend staying clear, at least until the developers get out in front of this bus and put a halt to some of this suspect behavior.
Tldr; Don't settle for anything other than a Post-Minecraft game. Build something more! I'm getting a refund.

ZUP! is a physics-based puzzler that, while incredibly short, is oddly satisfying as well. Your task is to remove any and all obstacles that prevent the blue block in each stage to rest securely on the green platform below. Doing so will award you access to the next level. The game sounds simple enough and it is relatively so, even throughout the 40+ levels it has to play through. While that may seem like a significant amount of levels to keep you busy, you’ll find yourself breezing through them quickly.
The charm that encapsulates ZUP!, in my opinion, is that it isn’t frustrating. Sure, the difficulty could be increased dramatically to better challenge the participant, but I didn’t mind as I sat down and exploded blocks across the screen; I found something this simple to just be, well, fun, regardless if I completed the level or really progressed at all. The handful of levels I kept failing miserably at still had me smiling, even after watching myself fail again and again.
It is important to say, however, that ZUP! is painfully short, despite boasting well over 100 achievements. The main issue I had with ZUP! is that by the time I became fully engaged in it, the game was over. I prefer a meticulous approach to games, scouring every inch and trying everything I can. However, with just a mere 23 minutes of gameplay I was done; I had completed everything there was to do. I felt cheated, teased with a marvelous, yet simplistic idea. Even now, I feel as if I’m floundering as to say anything else about the game. There’s just not much substance to it.
On a final note, as mentioned earlier, ZUP! does come with practical and useful achievements for those looking to dress up their Steam profile. While this shouldn’t be a positive to the game itself, I suppose one could consider it a consolation prize in the end.


Overall, ZUP! never tries to be something its not; the game is solid for what it is, albeit very short and not all entirely taxing when it comes to problem solving, but that being said I still had fun. When it comes down to it, that is all that matters and despite the obvious issues with the game’s longevity, I enjoyed what little time I had in it. With that being said, I would still recommend the game, but I feel other players will agree that it falls short of its true potential.

For me, it is quite difficult to decide on this game.
Do I like this game? Yes, absolutely.
Could it be better? Yes, absolutely.
Do I recommend it? Kinda...
Lets go into detail:
I have bought this game quite a while ago and played only the story mode (as it was pretty much the only thing working back than, even though the story wasn't finished). Back than only a few quests and only a "small" part of the map was accessible (I say "small" here, but it still took like 10-15 minutes to walk from the east edge to the west edge of the map).
This meant, that I played the relatively few quests several times and gotten used to them.
Unfortunately, new players obviously don't do that, they (logically) want to play the story in one go... and this - I think - is one of the reasons, why new players have issues with this game. To me it feels like, this game was optimized for players already familiar with the game mechanics - for players that took the time to just play around for hours and tested everything out.
The game gives players a lot of options - without explaining how to use them best. That's up to the player to figure out.
One example: The building system.
You get two types of blocks (voxel blocks and blocks) - no explanation what the actual difference is... just figure it out for yourself.
Then you can pick the type of material - again, no explanation what the difference between them is. Also no explanation, why you can use some type of materials (like diamond) and not others (like titanium).
If you chose voxel blocks, you can pick texture, if you chose normal blocks, you can pick one of several shapes.
Once you have set all that up, you can start, right?
Well, no. You have to make sure there is nothing in the way of your building, so no peacefull animals, no NPCs, no piles of dung (seems so irrelevant, but especially on larger builds, dung lying around is SO annoying) and especially no enemies or aggressive animals... because they will obviously ♥♥♥♥ things up - and again on larger builds, it is pretty much impossible to not be interrupted several times because of attacking animals.
And I haven't even started on the clunkyness of the camera during building...
As for the creation system:
(For those unfamiliar: The game has an editor in-game, where you can create various stuff, like vehicles, weapons and decorative objects - all based on voxels, objects can be saved and reused in other replays or be shared with others)
The interface is somewhat difficult to learn, but once you get the hang of it, it is acutally quite fun to use and relevant to the game. For example, I created a rifle that is way better than the early models available in game and also cheaper to produce. I can use that rifle in every replay now. The only issue here is, that you can not repair it unless you have a colony set up...
One thing I do however not understand about the editor: Why can't we use glass (or transparent materials in general)??
In short / TL:DR:
Planet Explorers is a fun game, if you like to figure things out for yourself and are not easily frustrated, if it doesn't work as you expect it to. There is pretty much no limit to your creativity here, especially with the creation system.
However: The game does have bugs (both in quests and the base systems itself), that make it very hard to really enjoy it in the long term.

"There's such a severe lack of polish," is something I've uttered many, many times while playing this game.  Most of the bad things you may have read about it are probably true, as are most of the good things.  It's all going to boil down to what kind of gamer you are, and how much patience you have.
I'm not exactly sure why a sandbox crafting/exploring game is so heavily formatted to be like an asian mmo.  Everything from the UI design, the grinding, the bad voice acting, to the game flow of doing all the quests in one area and getting sent to another and doing it all over again.  I spent years playing that sh*t, and PE doesn't win any points with me for using it.  The story is actually pretty decent, but is badly delivered because of the limitations of this format.
Combat is clunky, at best.  Hitboxes are awful.  AWFUL.  From early in the game you'll be sent against absurd "bosses" that are usually impossible to kill at the time you receive these quests, or at the least without a great deal of grinding.
I'm going to be blunt: the game isn't finished.  There are people who will argue that a tacked-on sequel-bait ending to the story technically means the game is done.  But not if it's still somewhere in a Beta state, if you ask me.
And yet..... Somehow.....  The game has some bits of real magic in it.
When you crash land on the planet, everything is new and vaguely terrifying.  Is that a tiny stegosaurus?  Is that a large, ferocious plush bunny?  Animals roam this MASSIVE totally destructible voxel landscape in multiple biomes, and apart from some weird fetish the devs obviously had for multiple eyes, all of the alien species are distinct from each other.  There's some REALLY good visual design here - it just happens to be badly optimized.
The soundtrack is almost equally decent, although there are strange long periods of total silence because the game doesn't have enough ambient noise to compensate.  The game even has an integrated way to listen to your own music while you play.
And the crafting.  Ohhhhhh the crafting.  We're not just talking about things you can make, and orient when building a colony.  We're talking a brilliant creation system where you fabricate basic parts, and then add material pixels however you like.  People have made all sorts of things in various categories, from flying pirate ships to weapons and armor from other games/films/real life.  I didn't dig too deeply since I stuck mostly with templates, but there's a lot here.  You can even go back and edit your creations later.  THIS is the meat of the game.  You run your colony, you hunt, farm, mine, and make stuff.  If that's not really your jam, the other elements of the game aren't going to do it for you.
It doesn't quite last.  Not all of it.  At some point you've been to every biome.  You've seen every species and kicked its *ss.  You have so many raw materials you hardly ever need to harvest anymore.  Colony management can be just as clunky as most of the rest of the game.  At some point you'll just want to wrap up the story, and the story will delay you, usually in the form of travel, or grinding.  I'd estimate there's probably about 40 hours of story, and no, it doesn't end in a good way.  But if you like to make things and do all that other sandboxy stuff, you'll be entertained for much longer than that.  The game has alternating moments of "Wow, that's kind of amazing," and "Wtf happened?  Was an intern in charge of this?"
There's some good stuff here, it's just that the devs bit off more than they could chew.  Word on the grapevine is they can't do any major code changes for PE, but they're taking on other projects to get funds for PE 2.  I look forward to it.

So after playing this for a while, I can sort of review this game. I'm about 2/3 through the story mode at 26ish hours of gameplay, which is pretty great for that 10 bucks I spent for the game on sale.

The music is alright, but only changes in different biomes, or that one battle theme that plays whenever you're fighting something.
Now that's all the good things and we get to the bad things.

All in all, if you want to try it, I say go ahead. I played with a friend the whole time and it was pretty enjoyable. BUT ONLY if you can deal with bugs and low FPS you'll get while playing it.

A very nice little puzzle game, with really beautiful graphics (for a puzzle game of course) and a good, relaxing OST.
Each of the 25 puzzles are country-themed, making you "travelling" around the world through the stained-glass panels you have to put together. And these stained glass panels really are well-designed. As long as you've a fondness for this kind of things, the art-deco-style graphics tryly makes this game stand out among the plenty of puzzle games you can find of Steam.
The controls are simple and intuitive, with the pieces on two circles around the puzzle, easy to turn, even with when you use a pen tablet instead of a mouse. So you don't have to sort out anything, just to look at the pieces. Plus they are automatically rotated in their right position when you take them, which makes the game even easier.
Because yeah, there isn't any difficulty here. Of course, this is a puzzle game and not Darks Souls, but even so, none of the 25 panels have any particular tricky details that could made them longer than 10 minutes to complete. (In comparizon, I sometimes spent ~2 hours on some "Pixel Puzzles".)
So, obviously, the game is *very* short and can be fully completed in two, two hours and half at most.
However, it's still a very enjoyable game, beautiful, relaxing, with a unique feeling of his.
Maybe a little expensive for what it is at full price, but don't hesitate to grab it during sales.

Glass Masquerade is a nice jigsaw puzzle game.
It reminded me of
: the puzzles are really mosaics, which means the puzzle piece shapes correspond somewhat  to outlines of picture elements. To really do a proper jigsaw on the computer, you'd need about three 4k monitors or you simply haven't got enough space to put all the parts. AP limited the amount of pices you could access; GM gives them to you on "scrollable" rings (which are really 4 bins), but it roattes them for you and blanks out the colors until you pick them up. At that point, the colors come back and the proper rotation is restored; the game would instantly become a lot harder if it wasn't.
Also, having a frame helps a lot, even if you have "hint pieces" turned off.
The interface is well done and feels smooth, the game is fun to play. The only drawback is that it is short; with 25 puzzles taking 6 to 16 minutes, it's only a few hourse long (I needed 2 hours for 11 puzzles). I'm enjoying every minute of it.

Now before I go into my review I want to make one thing clear. I love this game. It is a very cool experience for those looking for a tactical strategy challenge of commanding a swat team breaching a building. However, there are just a few things that ruin the experience for me in some cases.
First: The AI
The biggest problem that I have with the enemy AI is that they constantly open doors and just run out of them without and moments thought instead of posting up and keeping there guns trained on a door as they should be doing. Watching my guys mow down half of the enemy on one level just because they kept moving down a narrow hallway instead of fortifying themselves really broke my immersion.
Second: Lack of Surrender Option
If I was playing a military game, I wouldn't have a problem with my troops just gunning down unsuspecting enemies, and inspite of what people might think, SWAT team members are NOT allowed to open fire first unless they give proper warning and demand surrender from the enemy. The fact that this doesn't happen, and for a game that I assume is supposed to be simulating SWAT team breaches, really is disappointing when you compare it to something like SWAT 4 which this game seems to emulate from a strategic standpoint.
Third: Irratation
Now while some people may get the joy of going through a level for an hour trying to create the perfect plan, that isn't me. I'm the kind of guy who likes to do a level only a few times and not have to rely on trial and error mechanics to complete a level. And when I do complete one I don't feel sastisfaction at all.
Fourth: Progression
To be fair, I'm not sure what progression system I would have chosen for this game, but I don't know if a star system like on mobiles games would have been the route I went. Really makes grinding extremely annoying. Plus I end up just not using most of the weapons and only go for the ones that are the best in the game.
Fifth: Hostage Death = Restart
This is probably this most frustrating aspect of this game. I'm not sure what real life SWAT would consider a hostage being killed a failure, but being forced to restart the entire level just because one hostage out of like 12 gets killed is overly punishing. Especially if you consider that the SAS (I know its not SWAT but still) raid on the Iranian Embassy was considered a success even though a hostage was killed in the siege.
Sixth: Price
For a game that is $20, it just doesn't feel like it is worth $20 in the end. (I would recommend this game for $5 when it goes on sale but no more) DISAVOWED. $5 definitely pick this up, $10 sure, $15 eh pushing it but would still recommend, $20 no (at least for me). Some people might think this game is worth $20, which is perfectly fine if they believe so, but for me personally $15 would probably be a better base price tag.
Overall, its a great concept and a good game, but it needs to lower its price and work on some of its flaws before I can change my review to positive.

Insurgency is a multiplayer, tactical first person shooter. It implements elements of realism, in an attempt to increase player immersion and promote teamwork. The game is primarily set in Iraq, however some maps are set in Afghanistan.
There are two teams available, the US Marines and the Insurgents. Teams are structured around two squads, for a total of 16 maximum players per team. Within this team structure are limited player classes, such as the Rifleman, Support Gunner, Engineer or Marksman.
There is no on-screen crosshair and the players must use the iron sights of the game's weapon model to accurately aim the weapon.
The maps are small but this does not mean that there is no tactics involved.
Insurgency: Modern Infantry Combat is one of the most realistic source mods out there. At the beginning it is hard but once you play for a few hours, you start to get the hang of it.
If you want a more modern graphic you can look for the remake "Insurgency".

The quick for the tl&dr readers: Good concept, great potential, currently only PvP or PvBots, campaign to come later, UI not fully matured yet and difficult to navigate for new users, a few bugs and glitches here and there, servers not very populated.
The more detailed version: So I knew this game was in a pre-release format when I bought it. I've always been a fan of the Heavy Gear games and lore, so this is a fan-based purchase. I saw this game pop up on Kickstarter and I wish I had been able to be a contributor. Since I wasn't able to, I decided to pay the $39.99 for this game here on Steam.
Now, for a fan of the franchise and being used to the pricing of fan-related products, $39.99 wasn't a big deal for me if it goes towards polishing this game up. However, a new player who is just into mech-style games will probably be disappointed,
(hint hint to some of you out there...).
Here's my list of pro's and con's, IMHO;
All in all, the game needs work. However, there’s plenty of games that started out with similar issues. Look at Warframe for example. When I first played that game there were all KINDS of bugs, and the game art wasn’t all that great. As time went on, however, the community who played and funded the game helped it grow, and now look at it. Any game can be great if it has a good community behind it.
Now, as far as recommendations go, I will recommend this game. The reason being is that this game does have potential, it can be fun as-is once you get to the actual combat, and if you have patience you’ll probably see this game grow and change for the better over time. Should you buy this for $40? Well, do you want to contribute to a game and help make it
more than that $40? It’s up to personal preference. Personally, I like to be at ground floor when games like this start off. Gaming communities need early players to help form a strong backbone for an expanding player-base, ya know?
Hope this review helps.

Everyone's been saying it, Vermintide is just like L4D2 and it's 100% true. If you've played L4D2 at all and loved it then there's no need for me to tell you that this game is a must buy.
Instead of having zombies for the millionth time we are now fighting against hordes of rat creatures, the vermin. You will notice "specials" in the game which are all very reminiscent of the "specials" in L4D2. They throw poison, there's a large rat ogre, there's a machine gunner, an armoured brute, a rat that pulls you away and a rat that pounces on you. The music in this game is also another big plus. It starts to get really tense when a wave is incoming which really adds to the atmosphere.
The game is set in what seems to be a london-esque city during the plague. The game has different acts which are basically just different maps which get progessively harder. There's no real story except that you are trying to fight off the rats that are trying to kill all of humanity. You'll also notice that the maps are also very similar to L4D2 in the sense that some require you to collect barrels of oil or wheat and place them somewhere. Though it feels the same they do change it around a bit and is quite nice.
Now to get to the meat of it. The biggest difference of all is the combat. Since the setting is c. 1600's you now have a bigger emphasis on melee and you still have a secondary ranged weapon which would be a gun, crossbow, bow or fire staff dependant on your character. The combat is really good and is very satisfying. At the completion of every level you can roll to receive a semi-random weapon of variable quality, the harder the difficulty the better the weapons. You can collect 5 weapons on the same quality to forge one of the next level. You may also salvage weapons to unlock abilites of higher grade weapons. This to me is a big plus for replayability, it allows a player to reach an "end-game" something that wasn't present in L4D2.
Though my one and only disappontment is the last level of this game. They have you go into the leader's lair, The White Rat so now you're thinking that there's going to be an epic boss battle at the end. Nope all you have to do is place some barrels here and break some chains. Done, last level was a big let down, would've been nice if it was more story driven with a boss battle.
All in all what I'm getting at is this game is a must buy if you're looking for a new and refreshing 4-player co-op horde killing survival game that isn't the same old zombies and guns in a modern day setting. Don't wait for L4D3 and buy this now!

Trulon: The Shadow Engine:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The region of Tripudia experiences an increasing surge of monsters, especially near the village of Meadow Hills. The Mayor of the village needs a monster hunter to resolve this situation straight away. As your father (who is the master monster hunter) has been injured in your last battle, you are now the one who needs to step up. Where has this eruption of beats come from? Or, who is behind it?
Trulon: The Shadow Engine is an RPG / TCG style of game. You will be playing Gladia, the daughter of a great monster hunter.  As you travel along your journey, you will find quests and will be rewarded with experience points upon completing them. Some of the quests will involve interesting puzzles. Experience points will go towards your characters so they can reach higher levels and so on and so forth. You will meet other characters who will join your party, and you will need them, let me tell you.
As you visit locations you will notice chests lying here and there; open them and you will get additional cards for your deck, or mechanisms (upgrades) for your characters. Make sure you collect the Gaudium Orb - this orb will regenerate your magna and will also give you some experience points too.
The combat phase is turn based but you will use deck cards to activate action from your hero. As you level up, you will face stronger enemies and some will be able to knock down some of your characters with only two turns if you do not have the right deck of cards. At the end of each encounter, and of course if you are the winner, you will be rewarded with experience points. Every here and there you will be prompted to investigate an area. You will be able to accept or decline the search. Sometimes you will face tough foe but other times you might find some great goodies, which will be totally up to you whether or not you investigate them.
The graphics in Trulon: The Shadow Engines are great - you will swap from pixels (moving around the map) to nice 3D graphics in specific locations. In terms of the control, it is a point and click system and it works fine. I have not encountered any issues with the game so far.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Good Story-line in a Steampunk world
-	Good, colourful graphics
-	Over 50 cards to use
-	Good number of upgrades
-	Interesting puzzles
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
Trulon: The Shadow Engine is a well-structures RPG/TCG game with a good story-line in a steampunk world.  Great game to own!

In the undiscovered recesses of a faraway planet, beautiful and strange organisms live and breathe in a psychedelic Venusian world of dancing lights and metroid-like organisms. Similarly psychedelic to the visual style of the game is the soundtrack, with its equally as trippy and ambient qualities that build up and evolve with each successful move you make.
Deep Under the Sky uses a one-button control system that while incredibly easy to use is surprisingly deep in execution. The objective of each gorgeously organic stage is to fertilize each glowing plant with the debris from the exploded amoeba-like jellyfish that release from the base you control. As simple as that sounds reaching each carefully placed plant and spreading your pieces far enough to fertilize them will be a matter of careful aiming and finesse as you surpass each obstacle and navigate each twist and turn of the maze-like passageways.
Releasing your little jellyfish and aiming their trajectory with split second perfection is a zen-like experience almost akin to a surrealistic and extra-terrestrial Skee-Ball, the game is all about accuracy. As the levels progress your jelly-like projectiles become faster and force you to think quicker about deciding when to employ your various maneuvers.
You start out utilizing the simpler skills mostly involving rocketing your pieces in a specific direction, nudging it into the right direction when timed properly. As you move on more hazards and obstacles to work around are introduced and you're quickly navigating elaborate series of bouncepads to reach the proper destination.
By the second world you gain the ability to morph into a ball to roll across surfaces and gain momentum as you descend any hill. This is also important for squeeing into seemingly impossible tight fits à la Super Metroid. Timing the start and release of your ball form just like anything else in the game is incredibly important and adds even more reflex based skill to how you play. This feels really good, and again reminded me of some kind of psychedelic Skee-Ball or Pinball even more.

All the elements that make for yet another beautifully strange creation from the minds of gems Incredipede and Pineapple Smash Crew. If you're looking for a fun and simple way to relax with the added effect of being visually and audibly stunning then come and chill out Deep Under the Sky.

Play as everyone's favorite blue Hedgehog in Sonic Adventure 2, which was developed in 2001 by Sonic Team. Sonic Adventure 2 is available on many consoles, but the game was originally released for Dreamcast.


In Sonic Adventure 2, Eggman (Doctor Robotnik) has plans to take over the world by using a secret weapon that his grandfather created, that is how he meets Shadow the Hedgehog who offers to help Eggman take over the world.
There are two stories that are running parallel to each other in Sonic Adventure 2: the Hero and Villain stories. You play as: Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles for the Hero story. Shadow, Eggman, and Rouge for the villain story.
A couple new characters were added to the franchise in Sonic Adventure 2; Rouge the Bat and my personal favorite, Shadow the hedgehog. These additional characters were created to balance out the game play and give you a second set of characters to play as through the game a second time.
Unfortunately not long after this game was released, Sonic Team went crazy with the characters and decided to make a game with all of Sonic's little animal friends. Generally overwhelming the standard sonic-gamer-fans (some/most of the characters had existed in comic series and other minor video games before release. But it was the first time many had seen them in a big name game).

I hate to knock the controls ...but the most obnoxious part about this game was definitely the controls. It was annoying to control the camera and movement, with a controller when I played Sonic Adventure 2 on the GameCube; it didn't improve at all when playing with a keyboard and mouse.
Other then the obnoxious controls, the game itself is pretty fun and there are many different ways to complete levels, get unlockables, accessories, level ranking, including a mini feature with "Chao".
Call me a sucker, but half of the reason I bought this game on steam was because I loved raising Chao, and I hated sharing the GameCube with my brothers while we all raised our Chao. So I purchased the game, and got that out of my system... mostly.
To be more specific, Chao are little alien-looking-creatures with a dot that hovers above their head. (Just Google it, okay?) Depending on how you raise your Chao they will look different and you'll unlock two new area's depending on the Chao you raise and who you raise it with. I personally liked to raise them with Villains so they all had the most adorable evil smiles. (Yes, I'm fan girling, yes I play the Sims, Shaddup.)

Ugh... Do I need to mention this part? There are steam achievements, but there is only one "freebee" achievement, the rest are awarded for completing long objectives (such as beat the game, beat it with the other team, raise a villain and hero Chao, get all of all the things, get "A" on each level)
I'm currently sitting at 7/15 achievements there is only one or two more achievements that I think I can get, the rest are too difficult to get without putting an ungodly amount of time into the game to get perfect ranks on ever single level.

Sonic Adventure 2 is priced at $9.99 I personally waited until a steam sale before I purchased the game. There's enough content to play through the game for 9+ hours , however unless you already know you like sonic games, that's a bit of a risky purchase. You would be better off buying this game on sale, or playing a sonic game that is much easier on the controls.

I'm on the fence for this one, I found the game more enjoyable then annoying, but I've always been more patient with video games than most people. If you want to buy a Chao Growing Simulator, this is the right game for you. If you want a solid Sonic running-speedy-blurry-graphic-game, you should probably skip this and look for another one.
I Recommend this game to Sonic Fans, GameCube/Dreamcast owners, and anyone else who might be mildly interested in trying out Sonic Adventure 2.

Though quickly I started to see the other side - voiceacting was poor from the beginning, somewhat overdone and overacted. "It happens" I thought, "let's see forward". At first it went pretty well, even though the controls where horrible. I'm a lefty, so everytime I remap my keys from WSAD to arrows and keys around that. Here it's a bad idea - with any other keys mapped than defaults some of them just stop working - for example no way to make a sprint jump on remapped controls. Yet, at first I liked it.
At some point the game started to became weaker and weaker. Especially after I met "The Rat". From this point everything sucked - the story fell apart (WTF is wrong with this guy ?), the level design became pointless and difficulty level jumped too high. And it made it in most stupid way - the game begin to require a pinpoint accuracy in every move. To get to a higher level you have to jump from exactly correct point, otherwise you won't catch a ledge. To jump over an obstacle you have to start your jump exactly at precise point. Same goes for zombie fighting - you even cannot kill a zombie fight away, but have to make it fall to the ground and than perform a "fatality" - otherwise they will just rise back. Good luck if you're fighting a group of enemies. And usually the game doesn't give you a second chance - if you don't get it right first time, you die and start from the checkpoint. Result - I died in this game more times that in the first Dark Souls game !!
Finally - the lengh of the game. I did it in 6 hours, only because I left it paused once when I went to walk my dog. Otherwise I would have finished it in 4 hours tops. I feel honestly offended.

I refunded the game, let me tell you why. The game is titled as a rhythm game. Now that being in mind you can expect many different types of rhythm styles in the type of game especially when you increase the difficulty, examples: Speed increases, more enemies/blockades spawn, etc. Now that is not this game, it's difficulty increases with patterns, allow me to explain. As you may see in the pictures or video above there are 2 types of notes and 4 different colors, arrow keys and then the color keys of your choosing. Two of the difficulties: "Relaxing - Each intensity movement mode requires the same button/key press for all obstacles; a relaxing way to enjoy your music. Normal - The type of obstacles (and associated color input) depends on the musical key of each specific beat." As the difficulties go up it is adding more of a challenge by, examples, of using different colors and keys or adding more keys to an action. I of course don't have much time on the game but as the game that it is, it seems good if you are into that kind of difficulty change with patterns rather than speed and such. That is why I refunded it is because I prefer games that offer more speed and extra intensity. A good 6 or 7/10, especially when you note that steam workshop works with your character and know that you can of course use your own music.

Now before I go into my review I want to make one thing clear. I love this game. It is a very cool experience for those looking for a tactical strategy challenge of commanding a swat team breaching a building. However, there are just a few things that ruin the experience for me in some cases.
First: The AI
The biggest problem that I have with the enemy AI is that they constantly open doors and just run out of them without and moments thought instead of posting up and keeping there guns trained on a door as they should be doing. Watching my guys mow down half of the enemy on one level just because they kept moving down a narrow hallway instead of fortifying themselves really broke my immersion.
Second: Lack of Surrender Option
If I was playing a military game, I wouldn't have a problem with my troops just gunning down unsuspecting enemies, and inspite of what people might think, SWAT team members are NOT allowed to open fire first unless they give proper warning and demand surrender from the enemy. The fact that this doesn't happen, and for a game that I assume is supposed to be simulating SWAT team breaches, really is disappointing when you compare it to something like SWAT 4 which this game seems to emulate from a strategic standpoint.
Third: Irratation
Now while some people may get the joy of going through a level for an hour trying to create the perfect plan, that isn't me. I'm the kind of guy who likes to do a level only a few times and not have to rely on trial and error mechanics to complete a level. And when I do complete one I don't feel sastisfaction at all.
Fourth: Progression
To be fair, I'm not sure what progression system I would have chosen for this game, but I don't know if a star system like on mobiles games would have been the route I went. Really makes grinding extremely annoying. Plus I end up just not using most of the weapons and only go for the ones that are the best in the game.
Fifth: Hostage Death = Restart
This is probably this most frustrating aspect of this game. I'm not sure what real life SWAT would consider a hostage being killed a failure, but being forced to restart the entire level just because one hostage out of like 12 gets killed is overly punishing. Especially if you consider that the SAS (I know its not SWAT but still) raid on the Iranian Embassy was considered a success even though a hostage was killed in the siege.
Sixth: Price
For a game that is $20, it just doesn't feel like it is worth $20 in the end. (I would recommend this game for $5 when it goes on sale but no more) DISAVOWED. $5 definitely pick this up, $10 sure, $15 eh pushing it but would still recommend, $20 no (at least for me). Some people might think this game is worth $20, which is perfectly fine if they believe so, but for me personally $15 would probably be a better base price tag.
Overall, its a great concept and a good game, but it needs to lower its price and work on some of its flaws before I can change my review to positive.

Door Kickers is a solid game and you might enjoy it (the crushing majority does, as it seems). But for me personally, it was a disappointment. I was really hyped about this game according to the trailers, there was no demo, and the game didn't live up to my expectations.
I expected this to be more arcade-like, instead it's more of a planning/puzzle game. That wouldn't be a problem, but I don't like how it's implemented. There are basically two modes you can operate in: full-ahead planning or realtime mode.
So, in summary, I felt that I'm either frustrated by inadequate controls in full-ahead planning mode, or that I'm repeating the same short-time realtime plans over and over again, until I finally finished the level. I couldn't enjoy it.
There are some technical issues as well, which annoyed me:
Aside from the technical issues, I like sound effects of this game, music is OK, but I don't like the graphics. First, the absolutely top down perspective doesn't look good, just a bit of isometric view would work much better. Second, the graphics are ugly and blurry, and the texture quality (or artwork quality, however you want to call that) is low. I have correct resolution set, but the whole game looks upscaled and far from crystal clear as I expected.

It's not the monetization scheme that bothers me -- though others might claim that's the biggest problem with this game. Sure, you have to either grind for thousands of hours OR pay an exorbitant sum of money to unlock everything. But that, really, has become a bit of the norm these days. I played enough Planetside 2 to be quite familiar with equipment paywalls.
No, in the end, the game just isn't very fun. Not if you're looking for a good, exciting FPS. (If you're looking for more of a WW2 simulation, then this might float your boat).
Some might blame the matchmaking. Yes, the matchmaking is terrible. Almost every battle is lopsided. But there is a distinct reason for this: you cannot adapt to your enemy's strengths and weaknesses. Once you've locked in your character, you are pretty much set. If you have a sniper and the opponent comes with all tanks, you're pretty much screwed. If you have no anti-tank rockets, you're pretty much screwed. If the enemy is sniping the heck out of you and you're just a newbie-ish infantryman, you're pretty much screwed. If they have a LMG and you just have the stock equipment, you're pretty much screwed.
Outside of battle, you can grind for hundreds of hours to unlock all the equipment, to level up your tankmen and recons and paratroopers and etc. Or you can pay. But if you're a new player, or if you're just a mediocre player, then you pretty much have nothing to do. You run or bike around with your semi-automatic rifle and a grenade, you do your best to storm buildings, and you get waxed. You try to snipe, only to find your gun is absolutely terrible for sniping -- and you're either 1,000 hours away or $25 away from unlocking it. You try to tank...except you can't; it's locked. You try to anti-tank...except you can't; it's locked -- and even if it's not, it's absurdly expensive to try.
In BF and in Planetside 2 -- other 'vehicular warfare' games -- you can unlock new weapons, sure. You can grind or you can pay, sure. But when a tank is rolling into your base, no matter how skilled you are, no matter how much you've paid or played, you can find ways to deal with it. You can adjust, adapt. You can change your strategies. You can pick up rockets or heavy guns -- heck, you can hop in a tank or airship of your own.
There's none of that here. This game is the ultimate paradigm for 'The strong get stronger, the rich get richer, and the rest get eaten alive.' And ultimately, it makes the game tediously, terribly boring.

Have to say, pretty bloody good.
I spent two to three weeks making my way through the 25 or so hour main game, and I really enjoyed it. On paper it's a bit "samey", with repetitive taking over of enemy bases, and climbing radio towers to reveal the map, but it somehow gets away with it. The characters are great, likeable, and surprisingly real! The missions are generally pretty good fun too - it's  a fun game. It looks great still, and runs perfectly.
It's main failing is its greatest strength; the open world. It's great, and expansive, and reasonably varied, but it means nothing ever really develops. There's no push towards an end goal, it just meanders its way there. The sense of urgency you get in a properly designed level is never there... There's also the slightly disappointing quicktime style fights for the main bosses.. A shame, but unavoidable for this kind of game I think.
But overall, great fun, but I won't be rushing to get Far Cry 4 any time soon, as I expect it to be much more of the same, and there's only so much one can take.

This is a fun 3D-2D platformer in which you need to get to your group that you get separated from. On the path to finding you regroup you will come across "shadows" (zombies) as well as traps and a few other obstacles both in the form of the living and the un-dead.
You will find a few weapons in which to help defend yourself including two different firearms and the traps mentioned above; can also be used on enemies. The graphics for this game are decent but very dark in terms of color and lighting to give that feel of post apocalypse feel. The cutscene animations are in almost a comic book style of animation which personally; I think looks and works really well.
This game is not too long and can be completed in 3-5 hours on your first playthrough dependent on skill level, but if you want to torture yourself (as I did); then you can try the games nightmare mode which is exactly the same as the normal mode but with only 3 checkpoints throughout the entire game, if you die; you start at the beginning of the act.
I definitely recommend this game but be warned there is a good chance that you will die a lot, and if you try nightmare you might shout a lot. In terms of re-playability there are collectibles but if you are looking around in your first playthrough there is a good chance you will find a lot of these. Also, try and get it on sale, I would be happy to pay full price but some people may not be considering the length of the game and only one additional game mode which may not even be considered by some.
Which brings me to my one disappointment; no horde/survival mode :(
Patience and quick reactions will definitely be a benefit if you buy this game as well as love for the platform genre and atmospheric gameplay.

A side-scrolling platformer set in a post-apocalyptic city of Seattle, Deadlight puts you in the shoes of Randall Wayne who's trying to find his friends and family after being separated due to certain events.
[MAY CONTAIN SOME SLIGHT SPOILERS REGARDING THE LOCATIONS OF THE GAME]
PROS
[GAMEPLAY]
As a platformer you'll be maneuvering through houses, buildings, warehouses, and any other common structure within a city all the while escaping the gaping clutches of the "Shadows" (An alternative term used by the characters ingame for the zombies).  The game also provides some rather easily solved puzzles which adds an enjoyable twist to the just running around through levels. Aside from Randall's physical prowess of being able to jump great distances and run for a considerable amount of time, he can also wield an axe which he can use to breakthrough obstacles or use firearms such as a pistol and a shotgun.
[SOUND]
Given how the game is presented to you as a form of a narrative, you get to feel every moment through the soundtrack of the game whether you're reliving Randall's memories or you're surrounded by Shadows, Deadlight makes sure that you 're truly living the moment.
[Graphics]
I was surprised to see the level of detail for an indie game like this. Traversing through the different locations in the game you'll see the wreckage of different areas in the game such as skeletal apartment building barely being held together, and while you run through it, you'd see thing happening in the background such as a zombie pinned under debris, a bus in flames, and a plethora of other things happening in the background.
CONS
[VOICE-ACTING]
Unfortunately this is where the game's charms fall flat. You'd eventually learn to put up with Randall's voice but as you meet more and more of the characters especially during the New Order stage, you  begin to see where they had to compromise on the budget of the game.
[STORYLINE]
Aside from the horrid voice-acting, Deadlight's story is linear and predictable. You're pretty much set out to just reunite with your friend and family while the game doesn't try to even explore on the background of the virus (except for a few details in the notes that you find throughout the game) but the world-building just isn't there.
Side note: There have been certain times when I've encountered a few glitches where I'd suddenly be transported from a short distance to another when maneuvering the different areas of the game but nothing groundbreaking.
RATING: 6/10
Should you buy:  Buy it on sale for 50% above.

If you're a fan of jigsaw puzzles and beautiful art, Glass Masquerade has you covered. It's a simple game with intuitive controls, a relaxing atmosphere, and with nothing to get in the way of the colourful stained glass pictures that come to life as you piece them together. Recommended!

We all have one of those games that we turn to to help us unwind and relax after a stressful day.
In my case, it's not Glass Masquerade, but gods damn, if it ain't beautiful as hell. The music is lovely, and the puzzles are fairly challenging at times, all while providing some gorgeous stained glass designs as a form of reward for completing them.
There are, sadly, a couple of gripes, but they're pretty small ones.
The first is the issue with empty spaces not being the size of the pieces you'll be handling. More often than not, you'll be spending extra time trying to figure out where a shard will go, and wind up glancing over the exact spot time and time again, simply because the space is much smaller than the actual piece.
The second gripe is that some puzzles have outer pieces, but the frames don't immediately tell you this. This means that you may spend several minutes trying to find a space for one shard, only to realize close to the end that it doesn't even go in the main design.
Really, it's not a bad game at all, and this is coing from someone who isn't a huge fan of puzzle games.
Again: Great music and visuals, decently challenging puzzles, and the ability to track your times with each puzzle for constant improvement, but is slightly hampered by size issues, as well as unclear areas where a part needs to be.

Glass Masquerade is a beautiful game featuring 25 jigsaw puzzles that can be solved within 2-20 minutes each depending on the puzzle's difficulty and your own skill. By default the game will help you with a couple of edge pieces at the start, but you can disable it if you want to add another layer of difficulty.
The puzzles consist of 10-100+ pieces which are turned upside down until you click on them. This might seem a little bit annoying, but you really have to go by the shapes to solve these puzzles. Each puzzle piece will have a different color and a golden border that will only disappear after it has been successfully placed. This will make the later puzzles difficult, but luckily they also all have weird shapes that could only connect with one other piece.
It is a very relaxing game that offers a beautiful soundtrack. You can just jump right into the game during the day and solve one puzzle if you need a little break or you can play through the game in one session without it becoming tedious because the puzzles distinguish themselves pretty nicely. You won't feel like doing the same puzzle twice in a row.
One negative thing in my opinion is that you can't zoom out of the world map. It's not that necessary, but scrolling from one end of the map to the other is incredibly frustrating and you're forced to do so since the path to unlock new puzzles goes in both directions. A couple of people are also complaining about the regular price (5 bucks for 3-4 hours), but I do think the quality justifies it.
Overall I recommend Glass Masquerade to everybody who's looking for an unique and beautiful jigsaw puzzle experience. And if you're new to puzzles and want to try one out, this is certainly the type of game to start with.

One of the most beautiful casual puzzle games out there, and I play a lot of them. The music is nice and there never feels to be a rush to complete puzzles while you're doing them, even though the game will save your best times. In this way, Glass Masquerade is a very peaceful experience and ideal for people who want to relax after a stressful or busy day.
I also love the theme of each puzzle. Each one symbolizes a different country, and showcases its culture or history. This leads to a game that ties together well and gives the player motivation to keep playing and collect all of the artwork. That is something which I don't think is easy to do with a jigsaw game. With other games I'll usually just do one or two and then come back later when I want to kill time, but this game truly drives me to keep playing... THAT SAID...
As others have pointed out, there is a lack of content. For the price of 2-5 bucks (currently it's on sale for $1.75) I don't see it as a big deal, to me it's like paying for a movie to get a few hrs of entertainment... but realize that unless you enjoy redoing puzzles you will probably only get 3 to 5 hours of enjoyment out of this.

Call of Duty: Ghosts is the 10th installment in in the main Call of Duty series (excluding spin-offs). The game has recieved tons upon tons of critisism, and I understand where people are coming from. I personally got the game for $5 AU ($3.50 US) and, I played it and thought the campaign was alright. With some over-the-top action sequences even in outer-space or under water, it makes it a quite cinematic experience, however these levels only last a few minutes each. The rest of the game is decent, however, dull and repetitive. Most of the game is literally just a bland shooting-box with no character. For the price I payed however, it was alright. For new-comers to the series, I don't recommend starting on this game, as for most long-time Call of Duty fans (like myself), this was an easily forgetable game in general. For other long-time Call of Duty fans however, if you haven't played this game (most have, however), I do not recommend it. If you are just buying this game casually to play in your spare time, I say, if you buy it for as much as I did, GO FOR IT! It offers overall some pretty good gameplay, even while repetitive. The story of this game however, is so boring. While a couple of interesting plot-lines, most of it is just boring with a really dissapointing ending. If you're looking for some good Call of Duty Multiplayer, while still a pretty decent community playing, the multiplayer is horrible, not in terms of gameplay, but I'll explain why. The maps in this game, ARE WAY TOO BIG! You will get lost. Lost and stuck. Lost and stuck with hackers. It's dreadful. There is no sense of direction at all, whatsoever. Mulitiplayer however is fun, if you are just getting it to stuff around and be silly with it (eg, troll, smurf, etc. None of which I have interest in however). The game in a nutshell isn't horrible. For a spare time, fun. For a new-comer, ok. For a long-timer, disease. It really depends on what you're into and how long you've been playing for.

I was looking for a change of pace and a way to relax. Journey of a Roach did not disappoint.
The art is cute, the puzzles are logical and challenging enough to make you have to work at them.  They are interesting enough to make you want to.
The hint system is intuitive in that if you are stuck, you can click on one of the characters, or an item and a picture will appear that gives you a hint of what they want and/or what you need to do. I liked this aspect because it was a natural part of the game and you do not lose points (spend money/credits) if you need a hint (as in some other games).
No on spole - very suitable to a game where  you just want to relax and not listen to the characters talk. The music was not obtrusive, and added to the atmosphere.
The only time Bud got annoying was when he kept squaking at the end of the game waiting for me to rescue him (avoiding spoilers here). But it made sense under the circumstances and added to my desire to fix his problem as quickly as possible.
Took me a few hours to finish the game (though I admit, I was playng the game before bed and the last hour was like a book you can't put down). I was a bit groggy, but was enjoying the game and didn't want to leave Bud in hot water before I went to bed. At times the puzzles were making me a bit frustrated, but once  I solved them, I could only blame myself for not figuring it out sooner. When the light bulb finallly lights up above my head, it is satisfying.
The climbing on walls mechanic is very cool as well. It takes a little getting uwsed to, but adds to the puzzle element. You need a decent 3-dimensional sense to figure it out. The life of a roach indeed.
Recommended game for a fun, challenging few hours.

As a huge fan of RTS and RPG genre, this game came as a refresher after long hours spent playing Total War series. While the manner that you play this game is similar to the aforementioned, RPG elements and a sandbox aspect make this game much more interesting to play.

Firstly, if you are fan of fancy graphics, this game may not be for you, because map graphics could be called appalling, but in a sense it will not distract you to take away the sense of the game from really enjoyable part of the game. And that is building up your armies from scratch, feeding them, keeping their morale positive and high, and of course levelling your units. Seeing your rabble become knights, huscarls, axemen, archers, elite warriors of your small company, and guiding you to your own cities, villages and in the end empire.

Battles are pretty dynamic and well designed. And on higher difficulties strategy that you propose for your battles can be your undoing or a chance for a great victory. As I witnessed by myself, when in a battle for a city I lost most of my knights and elite archers, it was a Pyrrhic victory. While you can always rebuild your armies, it can be very tedious work. Melee battles are so tens, and keep you on your toes all the time. Storming the cities with your troops can be really exhilarating, while fighting on the walls and trying to fight of the defenders and archers it can test your reflexes to the limit.

There are some shortcomings, repetitiveness is one of them, but it's same with most of the game, as AI is not the smartest. Graphics is also one of them, but still decent for a game not to be called ugly. But even this doesn't kill the charm of the game, in a sense it just asks you for more fighting, and this is a major virtue of this game. And the biggest one is that it hooks you so much, that in the end you can loose sense of a time and even social parts of your life :).

For me, this is an amazing game and its worth every penny.

Title: Warhammer: End Times – Vermintide
Genre: Action, Indie
Developer: Fatshark
Publisher: Fatshark
Release Date: 23 Oct, 2015
Review copy was supplied by the publisher.
-------------------------------------------
When team based games are done well, they are one of my favourite type of games. These types of games force players to work together and help each other, which is a lovely change from trying to absolutely destroy each other in competitive matches. Left 4 Dead 2 is one of my favourite team based games, in fact, it’s probably one of the few games that focus on team playing that I still play today. The problem is that Left 4 dead 2 is quite an old game now, and with no view of Left 4 dead 3 on the horizon, I am so glad that Warhammer: End Times – Vermintide has been released – It is the breath of fresh air that I really needed.
I really don’t want to keep comparing Vermintide to Left 4 Dead, because it makes it sound like a bad thing, kind of like I’m saying “Oh, don’t worry about playing Vermintide, it’s just Left 4 Dead but with rats” – because this isn’t the case at all. It is Left 4 Dead with rats, but it is also so much more than that, and I recommend playing Vermintide if you are either a fan of melee based combat, team based games, the Warhammer universe and/or Left 4 dead.  Vermintide is a horde game, this means that the enemy (Skaven) will be attacking you in massive hordes with some special Skaven being thrown into the mix to keep you working with your team and to keep you on edge. Many games have tried the horde game mechanic, but very few have done it well. Warhammer: End Times – Vermintide has done it exceptionally well.
In Vermintide you can play as five different characters each with their own playstyles.  You will quickly find a character that you will prefer playing as, and most likely stick to playing as. I have yet to unlock the achievements for playing as three of the characters because I’m just having so much fun with the other two! Each character is brilliantly voice acted, and often engage in conversation with each other randomly when playing a level, in these conversations you can easily come to enjoy a certain character’s personality which makes playing as them all the more enjoyable.
The combat in Vermintide is where the game shines the brightest. Each swing or stab with your melee weapon will give off a satisfying sound as you watch a limb from your enemy fall to the ground. Shooting arrows from your bow into hordes of oncoming skaven makes you feel like you are Legolas from The Lord of The Rings, which will never grow tiring.  Hordes of skaven will be attacking you, so you will need to make sure that you block and time your strikes well. There are no triggers or indication on screen to tell you when to block, so you need to watch the enemy and see when they are swinging their weapon – This can get difficult when you are surrounded, so make sure that you push some of the enemies back to give you time to take a few of them down. Each character needs to work together to watch each others back, especially considering the special enemies that can strike at any time. Similar to the special infected in Left 4 Dead, Vermintide has special enemies. Special enemies have their own way of striking ranging from the Gutter Runner that will pounce on you, leaving you defenseless – To the Rat Ogre that is a giant monster that your team will need to focus all attacks on before it manages to wipe all of you out. With a good variety of these special enemies, it will keep you sticking together with your team so that you can help each other in times when you cannot help yourself. If you stray away from your group, you will probably wish you didn’t.
The game looks amazing and the world is beautifully crafted. I’m not really familiar with the Warhammer Universe, but with the limited knowledge I do have – this really feels like a Warhammer game. The world is dark and dreary and has a great old world fantasy charm. There are plenty of amazing sights that you will see when you walking around the game. The problem is the game has such intense combat that you will probably miss some of the great things that you can just stand and look.
There are thirteen missions each with their own challenges and objectives. Some of these objectives range from getting to point A to Point B and then defending an area, some are collecting objects and putting them in a location before escaping. Each mission is fairly short, so you can easily blitz through the entire game before you know it. Replayability is massive in Vermintide, these missions are designed to be played and played continuously without getting boring, and Fatshark have succeeded there. The levels are extremely linear with only a small choice of diversion in some parts, and each time you replay it will be the exact same level – One of my favourite team based games is Contagion because of how well the levels change each time you play it, one time a door may be open, another time it may be locked or blocked and you have to find another way to get to the objective. I would have loved it if Vermintide had a similar mechanic, it would make replaying of the levels much more fun than it already is.
As well as the satisfying combat, the loot and leveling will keep the replayability very high. Every time you end a level you will gain XP to level your character (even if you fail). However, if you succeed in a level, you will get more XP and a chance to roll some dice which will give you a chance of getting some good loot items. You can have a higher chance at rolling for a better item by collecting Lore Books and Grimoires that are hidden in a level. Each level will have 3 Lore Books and 2 Grimoires. For every one of these that you bring back to the end of the mission, you will get an extra die to throw, granting you a higher probability of getting a better item. Be careful though, a Lore Book will take over the healing item slot in your inventory, and a Grimoire will take over the potion item slot, as well as lowering your entire team’s max health (so please only take the Grimoires if you are with a good team)
Each item that you collect or unlock can be upgraded at the forge to make it slightly better and giving it an attribute such as X% chance of doing Y. If you have a bunch of items that you do not want, feel free to combine them with items of the same quality to turn them into an item of the next quality up, you need five items of the same quality to combine to get one item back of the next quality up. If you just want to destroy an item to get its components back, you can – These components that you get back are used to upgrade other items.
Optimistion is currently a massive problem. It’s doesn’t run great at all times. I get constant FPS drops when large hordes start to attack, and I’m running an i7 4770k and a GTX980! People have reported drops to as low as 10fps at times, although I have not had drops this bad. The drops really ruin the combat experience, making movement of my aim all jittery at times. People have also reported many crashes mid-game, which means you will lose all progress. I haven’t had any of these crashes. Vermintide also does not support dedicated servers just yet, although Fatshark have said that this may be added. No dedicated servers can be extremely annoying, especially when Vermintide does not have host migration. If the host leaves/crashes mid-game, you have to restart the level.

Pretty stained glass pictures, pleasant music, and a pretty good system/mechanics for playing the puzzles.  I'm not great at these sorts of puzzles, but I found this game pretty good for a pleasant, rather than frustrating, challenge.
So I do recommend it.  It's a good price for a few hours of putting together pretty pictures.
Replayability is limited.  You've got the set puzzles.  You can replay them at any time, and try for a quicker time.  But coming back every few weeks or months or something to try again seems worth it.
There are some downsides.  Pieces often don't seem quite to scale for where they fit, so that takes a bit of getting used to.  Stained glass means not the most clear pictures, so that makes it harder to put them together based on what's on the pieces.  You only see the pieces as a silhouette, which only show the image and align to the correct angle for placement once picked up.  But as you get used to it, none of those are all that frustrating.

Glass Masquerade is another of my SG wins, and one I'm particularly fond of. It's basically stained glass clock puzzles (like normal fit pieces together type puzzles), each puzzle with a different national theme. You start with France, which is functionally your tutorial, and from there, you unlock neighboring countries as you complete puzzles on a world map. That's pretty much all there is to it although different countries have different puzzle difficulty levels.For me, this is a 15-30 minute at a time type game, and I imagine I'll wrap up the remaining puzzles over the next few days.
The actual artwork looks really nice and the puzzles are challenging enough.
I think this one merits an 8 out of 10.

This isn't the easiest review to write, which is odd because this is a _very_ simple game.  In fact I felt half-mislead by the presentation, which seemed closer to Pandora's Box or The Fool's Errand than an elabourate jigsaw puzzle game.
Glass is an attractive game.  It sounds good, it plays well for what it is, and the presentation is rather lovely.  It is very light weight, not overly complex--put pieces together, make a picture, move on with your day.
And that I suppose is why I don't recommend it.  There is no depth; a Level 5 puzzle simply has more and smaller pieces.  (A question: why use a 5-point difficult system when no puzzle goes below 3?)  While tha'ts not shocking in what is a jig saw puzzle game, it also only has 23 puzzles that all unlock rather quickly.  No randomization, no variations, no difficulty levels.  Once you've done all the puzzles, the game is over, something that takes about 4 hours.
Hardcore puzzle fans won't enjoy it, casual puzzle fans won't find enough substance.   A shame.

Where to begin? This game, as it is now, is a horror show. Below are a few reasons why:
1: The capture radius for an objective is huge. In H&G you are tasked with either attacking or defending certain points on the map. Defence of these points is simple: DON"T LET THE ENEMY NEAR THE OBJECTIVE. Attacking is more complicated you need to remain in the area long enough to turn the objective to your side and if the enemy outnumbers you or matches your numbers than the capture is either halted or reversed pending on numbers. The issue is that all that is required to capture a point is to be near it. This isn't fair due to the amount of automatic weapons avaliable ingame. All someone with half a brain needs to do is find a good camping spot with an automatic weapon and that's it. The way captures should work (to make the person capturing it vulnerable so people would be forced to protect him) is if someone wants to take an objective they need to A: stand near the radio at the objective and B: Need to hold the interact button (as though they were unlocking an enemy vehicle). This eliminates everyone camping and forces teams to cover one another as the man capturing the objective can not defend himself.
2: You don't spawn in your objective if the enemy is nearby. I don't know who was the genious behind this one. If you chose to spawn at an objective that's under assault you don't spawn inside the objective where you can mount a successful defence but are instead spawned OUTSIDE your objective THOUSANDS of yards away! This now gives the enemy free reighn and almost guarantees a successful capture. While you have to run across open ground in a sense ATTACKING the objective you're supose to be DEFENDING! This in turn provides easy kills for the defenders as most will roam the perimiter with tanks jeeps and the like slaughtering anyone who comes near. Oh and this can happen if even a single soldier even ENTERS the area AROUND the target! They don't even have to be actively capturing it yet. Which means that all you need is someone to ride up on a bike, go prone somewhere, and wait while allies pick off the defenders already present, as no new men can spawn there due to "sir campsalot" it's again an easy capture.
3: The weapons accuracy at range is insane. Getting killed from outside your view from a sniper is to be expected, as that's a snipers function. This however shouldn't extend to LMG or SMG weapons! I have been in effect "sniped" by both LMG wepons like the MG 34 and SMG weapons most notably the MP 40. Both have rediculous accuracy at range which isn't realistic. Whoever designed this game doesn't know how bullets work.
4: Prices are too high: In game purchases and "micro-transactios" have become common in the gaming industry. Never before have I seen such insane prices for currency as are in H&G. The cheapest they offer is roughly $8 (U.S. Dollars). They have no $5 option, an option that most other games have. Add to this the fact that even items that can be bought with the games credits cost tens of thousands of credits! This would require weeks of grinding (as you earn practically pocket change for playing). Is the development team so inept and irresponsible that they wasted their money and are now reduced to sucking their player base's blood to survive? Honestly it's not woth the money.
5: Pay to win: Ah the bane of all MMO's. This game allows you to purchase EVERYTHING with GOLD (the game's version on real money). This translates to one thing: "you don't have to work for anything" you can buy the biggest tanks the best guns right off the start even of you don't have the proper rank or ribbon, fear not! Your soldier not the rank you want? No problem, just give us enough money and you can BUY a soldier at the highest rank!
