NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Trulon: the Shadow Engine is a console-style RPG in an original fantasy steampunk world, with combat based on a battle card system using cards you collect as treasures throughout the game. The game has previously been released on mobile devices and now it's come to Steam.
You play as the young Gladia, in training with your father, the great monster hunter. Your father was recently injured, however, so you must investigate a recent outbreak of monsters in the village near your house. In typical console RPG fashion, you follow along this main plot line as it twists and turns, and as you do you gain levels, abilities, and treasures by beating up monsters and doing simple side quests for people you encounter along the way.
If you've played any console RPG from the last 20 years you'll have seen most of it before, but Trulon does it well. It looks nice, the battle system works fairly well, the music is pleasant, and the plot is interesting enough given the original steampunk-style world.
Graphics - Trulon is pretty. It has a last-gen cartoony console feel like many mobile or Wii RPGs, but it does look nice. The engine is 3D, but the screen is fixed in a high isometric viewpoint. A number of post-processing effects seem to have been added or improved for the PC release and although graphical options are limited, from my experience if you have an even half-capable PC you shouldn't need to turn anything off.
Character and monster graphics are a bit more cartoon-like than the world around them and look a bit like they've been pasted in, but the effect isn't too distracting, and the big-eyed anime-style characters are well drawn. Due to its mobile roots, Trulon's interface graphics are quite big and easy to select.
Sound - Background music is pleasant and sound effects are decent. There are no voices. Sound overall is nothing remarkable, but is solid.
Gameplay - If you've played any console or high-end phone/tablet RPG then you'll be familiar with Trulon's gameplay. You talk to people to and gain and complete quests in 'safe areas' like villages, move to the world map to access other areas (perhaps triggering encounters on the way), and move to dangerous combat-enabled areas to complete your quests and advance the story. Trulon is mouse only, and you only need one button: everything is controlled by moving the pointer and left clicking or dragging.
Battles can be a bit annoying as you have only limited battle cards available to you at a time, and even with only a small number of cards in your active card inventory you can still find yourself waiting for turn after turn for one of your most useful cards. The battle system works well enough; just prepare to be a bit frustrated on occasion.
Character progression is automatic: when your characters earn enough experience to go up a level, they do, and their increases in statistics are shown to you. Customisation is limited to equipping them with up to three pieces of gear (each with different beneficial combat effects), and choosing which battle cards each character has equipped.
The biggest complaint I have about the gameplay is that there is no map. A world map showing discovered locations and the routes between them, as well as your current location, would have been a very useful addition. Local maps for each of the quest areas wouldn't have gone astray either, as some of them are just big enough to mean that I forgot where I was on occasion.
Pros:
+ Original and interesting game world with fantasy and steampunk roots
+ Big, colourful graphics and pleasant atmospheric music
+ Easy-to-use interface
+ Achievements to make it a bit more interesting
+ Great writing! Very few, if any, grammar errors
+ The game allows you to reconfigure your equipment loadout after losing a battle, before trying again
Cons:
- Very short: only 'over seven hours' according to the Steam game page
- Combat can be a bit frustrating when you just can't get the cards you want to appear in your 'hand' and have to keep retrying the same battle
Trulon: the Shadow Engine is a great game. I've had a lot of fun with it so far and I expect to finish it very soon. Trulon: The Shadow Engine is a game that is very much a mix of styles. The look and tone of Trulon is bright, colourful, soft looking, but its story is something a little more complex than one side good, one side bad, but it is a game that's lacking a bit of punch
Trulon: The Shadow Engine is a mix of traditional JRPG gameplay with card battling and deck building. There’s an overworld, the occasional random battle, levelling, even items to equip. The levelling in particular makes a real difference to characters, gaining a level can make challenging areas bearable. I have to admit, there were a few areas where I felt the need to go and gain a level or two, the simplicity of the early game is, every so often, rocked by spikes in difficulty
The card system and deck building are where the depth of Trulon comes in. Winning fights may earn you a card, which can be equipped to selected fighters. During battle you’ll be presented with a handful of cards from your personal deck, plus a couple handed to you each turn by the game, these are essentially your moves. Certain characters can only use certain cards, Gladia for example never learnt a healing move, but she was my go to if I wanted to cause a lot of damage, conversely Valencia can alter enemy stats, even get them attacking each other. you have to be careful though, the cards coming from your deck can only be used once per battle, burn your stun moves, dodge moves, or even healing moves too early and you could be in real trouble.
Characters can be equipped with perks, activated by special cards, that, as well as attacking/healing/whatever, will also bestow an affect on you or the enemy. It may be that using a card will give you some HP back, set the enemy on fire, or even let you pull another card, but once you spend enough time with the game you begin to build these perks in to your strategy, thinking a couple of moves ahead. That’s not to say combat is without its flaws. Because you don’t have control over which cards are in your hand you can find yourself screwed, if you need a heal spell and all you’re getting is defence perks the fight can be over pretty quickly. Which is another problem, later on, especially when you’re fairly comfortable in terms of victory, fights can feel like they take an age. It’s hard to know what could have fixed this, but fairly routine fights can feel like a bit of a trudge to the point I was avoiding some of the random encounters.
Trulon’s one big problem runs right through everything it does, namely that it doesn't engage you. It lacks punch, something that shakes you out of the automation you've slipped in to from the combat. Some more dramatic music would help, or at least changing up what’s there, particularly if someone is low on health. More in the way of animations too, graphically, while it’s nice enough, it can come across a little flat. Also displaying how close people are to levelling up at the end of the fight, make it so I feel like I'm making progress, pull my attention back to the game.
The story too needs something. It's not a bad tale, two nations suspicious of each other, it hints at something more, something bigger. It will be interesting to see if the 'phony-war' angle does feature in the upcoming book, certainly there's some apt parallels to be drawn from the naive populace. That said there's a lack of drama to how it's delivered, a handful of still pictures, one-paced text. It's hard to care about it. Especially true for what happens to the characters, there's no meat behind them, they just kind of exist, despite playing through the game you still feel like you've learnt nothing about them. Not a huge problem in and of itself, but it is indicative of a greater problem
I don’t want to be too hard on Trulon though, it’s good, surprisingly good. I expected a quick knock around of an rpg, superlight but easy to burn through, what I got was a decent challenge, with moments of real strategy. While the limitation of cards can come to the forefront, not giving you the hand you need for example, when you chain together a huge series of moves, combining your party’s efforts in clever and powerful ways, you can really see the potential of Trulon. For example, I equipped one of my characters with a perk that meant she could be triggered to have another turn, combining that with ‘Haste’ for extra turns, raising stats, stunning enemies, then using other characters with cards that dealt more damage to stunned enemies. Rinse repeat for a few turns, then freeze the enemies with one of my other characters, ‘Shadow Dance’ the next turn to draw attacks that will be dodged... When the cards fall your way you can wreak havoc.

Trulon: The Shadow Engine is a game I’m really enjoying, but I’m not entirely sure why. It’s a pretty run of the mill JRPG with a somewhat interesting combat system, yet there’s something about the look, music and general theme that I really enjoy.
The most interesting part of Trulon is the combat system. While it has your normal JRPG non-sense it takes a book out of Collectible Card Games by making the abilities you used based off a card deck. Your deck can be as large as you want, but you’re limited to 4 cards in your hand at any one time, after every turn you draw new cards and the action continues. Outside of your deck you have two ‘Wild Cards’ which are randomised cards (to an extent), meaning you’ll never been in a situation where you cannot do anything. This allows for classic card game situations, where you can set up awesome wombo combos, be incredibly unlucky or top deck that card that is the difference between victory and defeat. Overall it’s a pretty solid system, though early on in the game with a limited card pool it is a little stale.
The game controls well, looks nice and has an easy going soundtrack. It makes the experience very enjoyable and even easier to digest. There’s something nice about just running around, exploring the world and finding new monsters and new loot. The only thing that takes me out of this enjoyable experience is the slow and repetitive combat animations, and when you use another window the game pauses. There are a lot of situations where I’m waiting for the NPC to do its turn, or I’m sitting through a loading screen and I just want to tab out for a second to check out some news or social media, this time does add up, and it's just frustrating when I need to sit through this combat sequence that I have no control over.
If you want an enjoyable JRPG style experience this is the game for you. The interesting card system mixed in with the pleasant setting and atmosphere makes for an enjoyable experience. There might be no ground breaking gameplay elements, or a story that makes me question my existence, but it’s just nice sometimes to kick back, with a drink in one hand, while I slay monsters with my squad with the other.

And suddenly there is the warehouse room where you have to use a machine to move boxes, which adds a stealth mechanism to the game — you get noticed, you go back to cockroach prison. This room is so bugged that it's game breaking. Two ants notice you at the same time? Instead of throwing you to jail, they notice you alternatively in an infinite loop (while you can't move, quit, or access the menu)! An ant notices you while you're behind two stacked boxes? Infinite loop! Meaning that you are stuck, can't do anything, only Alt+F4 gets you out of it. SHAME! I hope for you that you saved the game soon before. This is the room where I stopped playing, out of frustration and dismay.
Oh, and let's not forget lack of V-Sync causing MASSIVE screen tearing everytime you move, and the overly cartoonish voices that are just GRATINGLY annoying, and you got there the perfect mix for me not to recommend the game.
The spider room was cool though so I'll give an overall... 3,5/10. Bargain.

I'm not sure if you could say "the creators poured their love into the game".
The art is nice and befitting of both the game and its genre as well as the beautiful background music.
However that's where the game falls short: The genre.
So Journey of a Roach is a Point and Click-Adventure with some puzzles that literally require you to randomly click around in order to find the solution.
It is incredibly slow-paced. So much that you could actually say, it's stretching playtime.
As for the story:
The whole story is completed in less than 2 hours, if you've played the game before probably not even an hour.
I approve of Indie studios making their own (maybe first) games, but there's so many better games out that it hurts my feelings to even have wasted 2 hours on this game.
If anything you could say I did it for the art style.
To sum up:
The idea certainly is nice, so is the art, but as far as story telling goes, this game still has a lot to learn.
If I'd have to rate it: 4.5/10

If you're a fan of rythm games like Audiosurf or Beat Hazard, you're gonna love this one.  If you're not familiar, this is the gist: you pick an audio track (and it can be ANY audio track, whether is included with the game or any of your choice saved in your PC, and while music is preferable, it doesn't have to be) and the game generates a stage that you have to sort through, with environment and obstacles shaped by the audio.
In the case of Audiosurf, you race a hovercar picking up objects.  In Beat Hazard, you fight enemy ships with your own and in this one you run through a platforming level.  In each of these games, avoiding obstacles is a must, but in this one is specially important.  Note that both the layout of the stage and its difficulty depend a lot on the pacing of the audio track chosen, and it can from relaxing to maddening.  You can experiment with a lot of different tracks to figure out what kind of challenge you'll like better.
Note that besides the chosen track there are other ways to reduce or spice up the difficulty.  The game uses four directions and four color buttons.  A gamepad is recommended, particularly if you're familiar with the colors of the buttons, which makes playing less confusing.  In this regard, choosing to play with a keyboard might count as adding an extra layer of difficulty.
Your character moves automatically.  The gameplay consists on pressing the correct button/key when your character walks/runs over the colored prompts.  In the easiest difficulty, the prompts are separated by areas.  So you'll walk through a bunch of yellow prompts, then sprint through a bunch of pink ones, then run through a bunch of blue ones, then go back to pink, and so on.  Harder difficulties mix them up more and start making you press two buttons/keys at once in certain areas.  Difficulty is actually customizable if you want to pick and mix handicaps.
All in all, it's the ideal kind of game: easy to learn, hard to master.  It can work as a relaxing experience or a challenging one.  With an appealing visual style and music that's literally how you choose it to be you can't go wrong with this one.

First off: I wish there were more options than yes and no to judge on a game, and it's especially true for this one.
Now now... Warhammer The End Times: Vermintide is in no way a bad game. Well, it shouldn't be at least.
As you probably know or guessed, it's a 4 player, CO-OP based game and the comparison with Left 4 Dead or even Payday seems kind of obvious. The main difference with this game is that it's mostly melee based. Well duh, it's based on Warhammer, not 40K.
It's a pretty good thing really. Feels refreshing and all that.
Now why am I not recommending this game?
Thing is, I cannot recommend it AT THIS POINT. This might as well evolve in the future and I'll edit my review accordingly, but as of now, I'd say stay away from it and wait for the devs to actually do what they're saying.
There are a number of issues with Vermintide, I'll try to list all I can think of. First, let me begin with the fact that there are no dedicated servers and that the netcode is absolute garbage, resulting in desync, lag (that can easilly cost you your life) and other happy stuff.
1) Melee. It's a great idea to have a melee based FPS, especially when successfull titles like Shadow Warrior or Dark Messiah opened the way. Problem is, Vermintide seriously lacks feedback in that regard. Most of the time it feels more like you're sweeping wheat than actual Skavens. As a result, you'll often end up taking hits thinking you killed a mob when you missed it, or them, if you aren't careful enough.
2) Distance. Now I know the game is supposed to be melee based so of course, that ain't where it's going to shine, just like how most FPS don't shine on the melee side. Still, the ranged combat aspect could very well use some polishing, with a better feedback for example or, mostly, not having your allies push you as you're aiming. Which brings us to the third problem...
3) CO-OP. Cooperation is vital in this game. More so than in L4D or Payday. The game is unforgiving, and if you leave a team mate behind, you can be sure as hell he's going to die. Problem is, the game severely lacks anything in that sense. Some audio lines telling you that you left a team mate behind could fix that, though the audio could be revamped as well as it's not loud enough. Add the special enemies bugs like the Packmaster pulling you behind houses or the Rat-Ogre sending you all the way down, below buildings, and COOP becomes really tedious.
4) Variety. EDIT OF 11/27/15: Previously, I complained about the fact that we are only fighting rats when Warhammer has such a large story. What I didn't know is, Vermintide is a part of Warhammer lore so it makes sense, as they would have needed to program an entire new AI for new enemies, had they not been rats. However, the point still stands about the lack of variety.
The maps are very similar, the objectives are dull and you just end up missing that feeling of satisfaction whenever you complete one, resulting in the farm of the same 2 maps over and over for the loot. It can also be quite tricky to tell a rat from another, including specials, or from a pile of bricks. Everything is grey, it's night time all the time. It's... boring.
5) Equipement and loot system. Great idea in itself. It makes for the replayability, and it's always interesting to get new stuff or customize your gameplay a bit more from just the classes. Problem is, the loot system is totally unrewarding, you end up grinding and grinding never to get the weapon you so want. The fuse system is a good idea, you fuse 5 weapons and you get another one... problem is, the forge works based on the weapons you input. So it's great to get a better quality hammer if you have 5 hammers, but what are you gonna do with all those 1 handed swords? I'd say, give us some more options as to what we can get. Let the players choose which weapons they want, and let the die choose the quality and bonuses. Easy enough fix ain't it?
6) Performance issues, desync and a various set of bugs are common, so beware.
Finally. The game has great promises and I could very well see this becoming as popular as Payday or Left 4 Dead, but certainly not at this point. I'm kind of addicted to it, but god damn am I going to be mad if they don't give that potential gem the polishing it so needs! I'm not exactly sure why the game went out of beta so early... marketing strategy?
This is honestly the best Warhammer game I've ever played. Loot system can be a load of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ from time time, but it's a fantastic first-person class-based horde mode game.

Door Kickers is a top-down real-time tactical shooter (shooter in leiu of a more appropriate term - the shooting is automatic and your buds are very competent at running and gunning) in which the player controls a team of SWAT (?) (Armed police, S.T.A.R.S., whatevs) operators tasked with completing an objective at a given location.
The objectives typically take the form of a. Kill all the bad guys, b. Arrest a certain specific badguy, or c. Rescue a bunch of helpless hostages.  In most cases objectives of the B & C variety can be over-ruled by killing all the bad guys anyway.
During each mission, your task is to choose and path your operators through the building/mission-zone.  This involves selecting means of entry, equipping your team with the correct weapons and breach equipment and otherwise generally co-ordinating your buds so they can support each other by fire, hold down certain angles, throw flashbangs and grenades and escort hostages.
The over-world gameplay takes the form of a squad roster in which you may allocate each operator to a specific skill class alongside individual stats and some (seemingly inexhaustible) operator avatars.  From here the player can choose to play a single mission, to gain star economy for in-game upgrades, or embark on a longer campaign - a series of missions which, perhaps with the exception of the first, are enormously expansive and super intricate.
Gameplay is nice, ergonomic and smooth and for the vast majority entirely mouse driven.  Though played in real time, the mechanics hinge a lot on the ability to pause and re-plot paths for your dudes.  Cheevos await anyone who can execute an entire mission from a single plot-line before the mission.
I have only two gripes about the game really. First, the throwing of flashbangs or other grenades through closed doors is somewhat sluggish and counter-intuitive.  Often, though you've set him to peek the door after he throw's the grenade, your trooper will sit idly taking bullets to his non-mobile♥♥♥♥♥
Secondly, and perhaps minorly, I would love to be able to export my ossom mission completion playthroughs but this function while tantalising me constantly, is not available on Mac.  Devs, plz fix.
These tiny gripes aside, Door Kickers is a fantastically gripping game with a well thought out single player campaign.  The weapons and equipment are good in vanilla and, I must say, enhanced tenfold by Gunworld's IoV - Instruments of Violence item pack.

**This summary contains minor puzzle spoilers**
While the game wasn't quite what I expected, I ended up enjoying it a lot. I particularly liked the creative puzzle design, which requires you to be observant and really get into the logic of the game and its world. For example, you'll find yourself having to electrify yourself to use your own body as a battery, or dump radioactive waste on fish food to make a cute goldfish mutate into a giant monster that explodes out of its aquarium. It's all good, wacky adventure fun. I also liked the simplicity of the story and the complete absence of any dialogue in favor of speech and thought symbols, the latter feature (in combination with the fact that you're playing as a cockroach) actually reminded me a bit of the excellent Bad Mojo, which is always a good memory to invoke.
In summary, Journey of a Roach is a somewhat brief but thoroughly enjoyable and very charming adventure experience.

Okay , one hit kill headshots are understandable , but having instant death torso shots is just over powered.  You'll be pushing towards a point and then bam , dead from a guy hiding somewhere in the trees. Better go find a bike. 3. HE rounds for aircraft.  Always being shot out of your plane really ruins the dogfighting experience. You don't have much chance against HE , especially in a P-38. 4. United States. I thought it'd just unlock the aircraft , but no , it also takes away your ability use rifles and fight in certain kinds of fights.  Had I known that I would'nt have made that character a pilot.
In conclusion , this game has potential to be really good but it just isn't there yet.

$10 - Early Access to the game, bare minimum rewards for showing support to the project early
$25 - EA, a gear, and some swag
$40 - EA, 1-2 gears, a large amount of swag.

Zup! is an achievement-laden simplistic puzzler in which you use explosive red cubes in the hope of landing a sole blue one on a green platform to complete each level. It is a game of trial and error and basic physics that is extremely short and far too rewarding; however for such a respectable price, it can provide a good half hour of entertainment.
Most of the 50-odd levels in the game are fairly routine and there isn't really a gradual difficulty increase until the latter levels. You will fly through the game with achievements raining down and only towards the end does this game begin to shine as a very intriguing concept that just plays it too safe early on and for the majority.
With 118 achievements that all can be earned within 30 minutes as you sail to completion; this aspect alone will interest many users probably more than the game itself. Zup! is an excellent idea that just needs a bit more depth, challenge and better level design.
If you have a few spare pennies or want to give your Steam achievement counter an easy boost; this game is ideal. Beyond the easy achievements, length and lack of difficulty; Zup! could have been ingenious but instead is far too generous. A sequel that focuses on complexity instead of generosity would be highly welcome but depsite the shortcomings here; it's hard not to recommend the game for the price and achievements alone.

Alright, since this is a simple puzzle game, I'm not going to go into much detail.
You have 3 types of building blocks (Literally) which have different functions that appear on a platform in each level and 2 additional types you will encounter as you progress through the game. There are a total of 40 levels altogether.
*Your objective is to have the blue square land on the platform
**The blocks you'll come across later in the game
***Will stop in its tracks if interacted in any way
Like I just mentioned, you have to get the blue square to land on the platform in order to move on to the next level. The early levels only require you to use the red blocks in order to launch and aim the blue block toward the platform. The later levels may require a bit of timing and strategy (But it's not
hard). Honestly, it'll probably take you about 30 minutes to 100% the game so you don't have to worry too much.
Zup! has a unique concept different from other puzzle games that was executed quite well in my opinion. I really enjoyed playing this even though it was really short. Also since the achievements are very easy to get and most of them are a plethora of letters and even symbols, this game makes a great alternative to LYNE; so if you want to customize your achievement showcase, then the achievements will provide you a wide variety of customization. The amount of customization will be even bigger if you also have LYNE achievements to go with it.
In conclusion, Zup! is a simple, yet satisfying puzzle game that Achievement Hunters and most people will enjoy. As most people would suspect, this game is most likely intentionally made so that people can easily get the achievements for use in their achievement showcase.
I highly recommend you should. Super easy achievements you can use for customizing your achievement showcase, good gameplay, trading cards; what more could you want for $0.99? Well, except if you want a challenge, then this isn't for you. Consider taking a look at
as an alternative option!

This a great game that gives freedom to do as you wish and play how you like in an immersive medieval atmosphere. I will now breifly describe the combat system, party sytem and world map.
The combat system can be annoying at times and takes a while to 'master' but it is rewarding once you get the hang of it. It is based on clicking and dragging the mouse in different directions to produce different movements in game. All you have to bear in mind is that you are drawing the weapon back to let it go, so for instance clicking and dragging the mouse left will make the blade swind right as you have to take the weapon left in order to do so. This can be frustrating at times as you occasionally forget to think in opposites and miss your target completely but in time this decreases and enjoyment increases as enemies fall before you.
The party system seems simple enough right? you just hire people and they fight for you and that is correct but when it comes to upgrading and wage scalling it can be annoying. With upgarding units you will often have a choice between two upgrades, the two different skill paths for the unit, and in this case you may wish to know more about said upgrade before you buy it right? well there is no info just a choice that is irreversible as clicking on either of the upgarades selects them. Whilst this will probably only happen once per unit type it means that you now have a new choice to either stick with your new unit or disband it and start again, of course it entirely depends on the type of units you like best and want to use but as i said it can be annoying. The wages of each unit start out reasonable but VERY QUICKLY become rather costly and as basic units are little more than arrow fodder this can be a serious barrier to progress in the game, whilst there is no 'problem' with this i mention it only as a caution to improve your experience.
The world map is fantastic and is both suprisingly large and small. Large in the respect that it has 6 factions with 4 cities each and host of villages but small in that it can be traversed with relative speedand ease. This will be down to personal opinion again but as with the party system it is just a heads up. My real advice to download the HD world texture pack form the workshop as this greatly improves the visual experiance. I have put the link here
the other thing you need to know is that each mod acts a seperate copy of the game and so a new game would have to be started if you played the native version then added the mod afterwards.
Hope you find this useful.

I've always loved creating things and seeing those things put to use in a game. It's what drew me to modding, what makes Space Engineers one of my favorite games of all time, and why I love survival games. Now with that said, Planet Explorers has set the bar for me. Any survival game will let you make things. Minecraft will let you make houses and castles and god knows what else. Space Engineers will let you make starships and stations and a whole pile of other things. But never have I seen a game that lets you design things as basic as your weapons and armor. And it's not just allowed, it's encouraged! Sure the voxel system takes a little getting used to, but once you figure it out the possibilities are literally endless. Got a favorite gun from another game or a movie? Bam. Make it. Like someone's clothes in a show? Bam. Make it. Want to drive around in the Oscar-Meyer Wienermobile? Bam. Make it.
Gameplay-wise PE is a little rough. Like any open-world sandbox game there are issues. For some games those issues can be a deal-breaker, but PE? In this case, the pros FAR outweigh the cons. Sure the graphics can be a bit janky at times and I can't help but wonder what the dev team's primary language is ('cause it sure as hell wasn't English), but the game itself is solid. The crafting system is steamlined, the gathering isn't nearly as sadisticly grindy as most survival games, and the worlds are interesting to explore and colonize. I can easily lose myself for hours on end with this game, which is nice given that I recently started working for a different company and am now working the graveyard. With nothing to do but wait for calls to come in, this game makes the time in between fly by.
All in all I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys surivival games or is looking to try one for the first time... and I'm always excited to see what both the community and the dev team have in store for us.
P.S.: Be careful when setting up a custom map. It's quite easy to end up with something that looks like a 20-square-kilometer setpiece for Waterworld. @.@

I play games while being very critical, and so thats how I'm going to review the game for others, to help you decide if you want to play Deadlight. Lets start off by saying the game is absolutely gorgeous, and has attention to detail, especially in the beginning with secret entrances and well thought out situations to raise your adrenaline. However towards the end, the game unravels more and more, and begins to seem rushed. It becomes obvious that the storywriters didnt put a lot of thought towards building up the necessary atmosphere, so we end up with non-realistic and often annoying characters and  the ending feels rushed, unoriginal, and not satisfying. The same loss of enthusiasm can be said for the programmers as well. While in the beginning the game ran smooth except for a few annoyances with the control, at the very end of the game we encountered multiple bugs, making the game feel impossible at times until we realised it was a bug that prevented us from progressing. This only makes it feel even more like the ending was rushed, especially when we consider the multiple unrealistic scenarios, such as enemy soldiers not shooting at all, characters skipping trough locked doors, or just rooms that you find yourself in that have no entrance doors, only vents... All in all the game was enjoyable, especially the graphic design, but thanks to the rushed ending I cant give it a positive review.

We all have some darkness inside. No matter who you are, what walk of life you come from, everyone has a little voice inside that tells us to do evil, to steal, to mock, maybe even to do harm. But we all (I'm hoping, dear reader, I can include you in this) push those thoughts away... Either by pushing them down as deep as they can go, or letting them drift out of our minds like a mistaken fart in the wind. We survive our day to day lives because we have the ability to know right from wrong.
But then suddenly ZOMBIES OH GOD. Or "shadows" as they are named in the game - and an apt name at that. These aren't just typical zombies. Yes they slouch around, trying to bite you, and only a head shot will kill them, but when they appear, they are always coming out of the shadows. From the background, from under your feet. They come from the dark places in a ruined city, and they are coming for your flesh.
Deadlight is the story of Randall Wayne, a park ranger who is looking for his wife and daughter in the midst of a zombie outbreak in Seattle. The city is ruined, there are Shadows everywhere, and all you know is that everyone is trying to get to the safe zone at the stadium where the military is supposed to protect the survivors. We don't know why Randall was separated from his family first, but through cut scenes drawn in a scratchy motion comic we learn more and more about what happened to everyone, why we are in the situation to begin with, and what we have to do to find his wife and daughter. Along the way you meet old friends who you thought died who can help you on your journey, and...Interesting denizens of the underground.
The game mechanics themselves are pretty straight forward - it is a platformer. Try to jump and shimmy and crawl through different obstacles, using what you find along the way (such as weapons and fire axes) to solve different puzzles; all while trying to avoid the dark for fear it will rise up with no warning.
This is not to say there are jump scares. When they start moving, the shadows are slow and deliberate - which I find to be far more distressing in some ways.
The overall art is wonderful. The city's very spirit seems broken, as you climb through shattered glass, boarded up doors, and climb up neon signs that are falling apart as you go. Everything is fluid, and even through this is a 2D platformer, shadows and other enemies do come out of the background, as if they are walking down an alleyway towards you. Again - scarier than jump scares in many ways.
The shadows. The dark part of our hearts that we try so hard to forget and try so very hard to push down is really the focus of this story. This isn't a tale questioning if we are any different than the zombies. This is a story about one man fighting against his own darkness, his own fear, his own self-loathing to find and save the only two people he has in this world. He is fighting his own shadows. He is fighting back the darkness both physically and emotionally.
Can he do it? What happens when he finds his wife? His daughter? It made my jaw drop to the floor when I found out.
This is a great game for playing when you have nothing else to play but it gets boring after about 15 hours.

What a great game!
There is literally no down side. The only thing that hurts it, is actually one of it's better points. That being that it is too open ended to be played any one way.
The level of challenge is up to you. Can you pre plan an entire mission without losing any troopers? Will you try to make arrest or just shoot everyone? Will you go the stealth way, the hard way, the quick way? Any way you choose will require very carfull planning. It's a simple game containing near infinite complexity. The one corner you fail to check, is the one that gets some one killed.
So what do you get for your money? Everything but multiplayer (which is still being considered). It's one of the most replayable games I've ever played. 100 stock single missions, 6 big campaigns with a hardcore mode that save permadeath of your officers. You can always do any of this more perfectly, or all preplanned, or step by step, and if you run out of fun in about a year or 2, there is a easy mission / map editor and if that wears thin, it's already modded and workshopped to epic magnitude. It's RPG, TDS, RTS all in one.
It shows you how to play, but never tells you how to play. If I told you how the game is played and a what I think of each aspect it would take 10 pages. Just watch the vids and keep in mind what I said. Best 20$ game this year. I'm gonna keep an eye on Killhouse. They seem to love the craft. I feel the feels inside for them. Sniff....

The new Insurgency standalone game is sadly a product of it's time, and a while a good game in it's own right, it has lost the feeling and atmosphere that made the original mod so great. Here there are no small tweaks or attachments to give you an advantage over the enemy in certain situations, only raw and gritty combat where instinct, reflexes and teamwork separate the victors from the defeated.

Make an yland your home. Craft yourself an improvised weapon. Tame a horse companion. Lay the foundations of your soon-to-be great base. Gather more resources. Shape the land anyhow you like. Brew potions. Dive into the caves. Find rare Ylandium. Figure out the recipes for the most advanced tools and guns. Design your car. Will it be a racecar or an ambulance? Build a mansion illuminated by lamps powered by your generators. Craft a boat and visit nearby ylands, full of new materials and animals. Make yourself a ship and explore the distant waters. Maybe you will even find some shipwreck or submarine, who knows? Gather resources, craft, explore and create. Too much for you? Start a multiplayer server with your friends! Of course, you can "just" create if you want. Grab yourself the propeller pack and powerful tools like Annihilator and Terraformer. You can build anything you can. Not just from the items found in the game. Improvise, disable the grid and combine them. Paint anything you want, in any color you want. Open the Editor and add a role to the player. Make the torches light up whenever you are close to them. Let the bridge collapse below a specific circumstance. Craft a whole new game in the Editor! This looks like an infinite number of ways how to have fun. But we have just started. Ylanders are still early access players. Join our classy community and explore the future of Ylands!

Its Left 4 Dead with rats, loot based equipment and melee weapons.
Long version.
I know nothing about the Warhammer franchise, but the idea here was to make a cooperative action game in the vein of Left 4 Dead.  Being Warhammer brings new things to the table, such as magic and melee weapons, rather than mere guns.  Also, there are five different heroes (classes) you can play as.  This obviously takes place during the conclusion of the initial Warhammer franchise.  Don't get your hopes up, you will not be fighting the gates of hell (Chaos) alongside Orks and Elves like in Warcraft.  This game is focused exclusively on fighting the Skaven, rat people that are rightfully treated like a plague rather than a race.
Because you are fighting with more melee weapons and less guns, surviving in Vermintide requires finesse.  You are not meant to slash away and "trade hits" with the Skaven.  Your alternate fire lets you block attacks or push to knock enemies down.  Just like L4D, you should not be getting hit in the first place, and the block button is a tool you need to familiarize yourself with.
Unlike Left 4 Dead, the character you select matters.  You can choose from one of five characters, each a different class.  Victor is the lanky Witch Hunter, armed with dual pistols and a deceptively powerful rapier (because headshots matter, even with melee weapons.)  Sienna is a Bright Mage, and despite her name, uses very black magic, burning everything around her with unlimited fire spells.  Bardin is a Dwarf Ranger with increadible melee attacks.  Kerillian is a boisterious, concieted Elf called a Waywatcher, fighting in a classical elf fashion, with lots of bows and arrows of varying power, and blades of varying sizes.  Markus is my favorite.  He is an Empire Soldier, a veteran with varying swords, hammers, and incredibly powerful, slow guns.
The Skaven are as dangerous as they are silly, and are far more versatile than the zombie hoards of L4D.  They have their usual hoard attacks that come in waves, cued by music just like L4D.  There are also more threatening specialist Skaven that require teamwork to defeat and punish players who wanter off alone.  Packmasters sneak up on players from behind, drag them away with a mechanical lynch and strangle them to death.  Gunners single out players and unload bullets from their "Ratling Gun," requiring a different player to flank them.  Gutter Runners are assassins, rapidly dashing on top of players to pin them down and stab them, only to vanish as soon as they are threatened.  Stormvermin are dangerous tanks that require heavy attacks to pierce their armor.  They are the only class, that when seen patrolling, can be ignored through stealth!  Globadiers hurl glass globes of poison gas and self destruct when damaged.  And of course, there is the Rat Ogre, a devastating enemy that requires a team's full attention to bring down.
Completing quests guarantees you a single piece of loot, but at this time, a lot of people are not happy with the loot system.  The conclusion of each quest yields a single, predetermined dice roll, and each die that lands with a symbol increases the quality of the loot.  These rolls are predetermined, but thankfully, are bound to the probabilities that the dice would have if they were real.  The standard dice cast have very few sides with symbols.  You get better dice and odds within quests.  Occasional treasure chests reveal Tomes, additional Dice, and extremely rare Grimoires.  They take up the slot you would typically use for health items, limiting your ability to heal yourself.  If you and your team can carry more of these items to the finish, your probabilities of getter rarer goodies increases dramatically, and playing on higher difficulties improves your odds too.
There are 13 missions with five difficulties, if you were concerned about length.  But don't get too exited, you will not be ready to move from Normal to Hard mode for a long, long time.  You need to have blocking, pushing, and headshotting down on lock, your teamwork needs to be stellar, and although it can be done with plain (white) gear, you may want fancier tools to get by.  I'm still not ready for Hard yet.
The graphics are nice, but I'm not happy with the art, even thought its probably true to the fanchise.  I find the game's color scheme so grimdark, that I personally attack the elf thinking she's a rat because of her cape has a fur coat on it (good thing you can highlight allies in the options menu.)  I tell this to other players, and some said they do that for the dwarf :D
If you like L4D at all, this is a must, and it should only get better as the developers continue to fine tune the game.  Just don't expect plot or a happy ending of any kind.  Its called End Times for a reason.

In Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide, you play as one of the five unique heroes and work together with up to three other players in a fictional town named Ubersreik to save the town by doing various missions while killing every Skaven (rat-men) that gets in the way.
While showing many similarities to Left 4 Dead series, Vermintide differs in the sense that it puts a lot of emphasis on melee combat, kind of like Chivalry. Ranged combat is possible but there are a lot of restrictions, mainly the limited amount of ammunition you get.
* Character interactions with each other showcases their unique personalities nicely, rather than just five generic characters that looks different
* Having many ways (decapitation, caving heads, explosives, etc) to kill rats is satisfying
* Collecting books and grimoires adds challenge regardless of difficulty, and can improve loot quality
* Levelling also rewards you with loot, so your progression isn't halted should you find yourself not winning often.
* Different characters having different playstyles adds variety and replayability
* Rat Ogres make L4D Tanks look like babies
* Cannot sprint - You will have to rely on your own dodging and parrying skills if there are no one to cover you
* Optimisations need improvement - CPU/graphic card usage remains high even for high-spec computers
* Matchmaking is 'First come, first serve' rather than lobby browsing (You deal with the same people for a particular map until slot is filled, forcing you to play different map or host your own lobby).
* Weapon balancing needs work, some weapons are underpowered making them undesirable
* No shared equipment besides trinkets (already somewhat rare itself depending on luck)
* Rewards don't fully justify difficulty - Common weapon is possible reward for nightmare/cataclysm difficulty
* Unpredictable spawns can feel rather punishing at times even on easier difficulties
* Bot intelligence makes solo play rather unfun
* Curse those near unstoppable, physics defying Zeratul rats- Oh sorry wrong game, I meant Gutter Runners
Despite these flaws, Vermintide is still very promising as the development is very active, and you can expect a lot of these issues to be resolved in the upcoming updates.

Long story short: don't buy it unless there is serious sale and you are a fun of the genre.

CoD:Ghosts is your average CoD with a slightly better campaign and a slightly worse multiplayer. Let's ditch the obvious first : the graphics are okay, but not breathtaking and absolutely not optimized. The sound does its job, and the gameplay consists in clicking on heads. Woaaaah.
I have a particular affection for this game's campaign. The story avoids the usual trap of being more complex than the game does really need,and that's really for the better. You know what you fight for, something that was not that obvious in some previous entries. The emphasis on the variety of situations is welcome as well. Space is love, space is life. But what retained my attention is a very particular (if not unexpected) twist that would be criminal to spoil here. To me, it simply flet that, for the first time in the whole series, an episode tried to tell its story using specific game-design mechanics. That twist is the only reason I'll actually remember the game. And to be honest, I tend to forget CoD's campaigns as soon as they are over.
What kills the multiplayer are the maps. They're too big. CoD is about frenetic close-combat. Game Over. The zombies/aliens mode is fun tho. Nice try, but not enough to my taste to compensate for the failed deathmatch.
At its actual price, this game is not worth a buy, the campaign being short and the multiplayer boring. For ten bucks or less tho, it makes two enjoyable afternoons, which can't be spitted over.

All in all: If you're familiar with Early Access and the bugs that come with it, can pay the price of admission, and enjoy team-based mech shooters, this is the game for you.

I don't really want to give this game a red thumbs down. And I'm probably still going to stick around and see where it goes because I do find it interesting.
But frankly that's largely because I was able to get the game for free on a newsletter promotion. And unfortunately price is a large part of whether a game is worth it or not.
I won't mince words here- the current price is way too high for the current product. Sure, sure- early access, blah blah blah... but it really feels very, very early and more like an in house alpha than a public version. I will not recommend the game in its current form with its current price regardless of game potential.
The game of course has plenty of that. There's a sad lack of mech games out there today and any new mech game is welcome in my books. I haven't played the early Heavy Gears, although I believe they ran parallel with early MechWarrior games, which I do play- a lot. This isn't a MechWarrior style game with tank like controls. Gears perform like a very heavy, clunky FPS character and feature abilities such as wheels on their feet to skoot about quickly.
This isn't a bad thing. The game still feels like a mech game and unique is good. There seems to be an indepth component and limb damage system too, which is another plus, along with a lot of mech customization.
So as you can imagine, the game is full of potential, but right now- it's rough as anything. I don't know much about the developers but I have a suspicion they're somewhat small or inexperienced, and they have a mammoth project ahead of them.
I'm looking forward to seeing where Heavy Gear Assault goes, and I'll update my review once/if changes come for the better.

I connected, ran into him, and started shooting.  None of my weapons seemed to do any damage at all, and eventually he just ran off a cliff and died.  I disconnected.

This game needs a LOT more work, and I couldn't recommend this game for even $10, let alone the outrageous $40 the developers are asking.

I bought Planet Explorers during a sale and did not touch it for a long time, but as soon as I started I just wanted to continue playing. There are not that much games that keep me playing long into the night.
I think this game is a highly underrated one. You can mostly compare it to Minecraft, but with Story mode and built using an older version of Unity Engine (but still looking good enough for me).
Compared with "hardcore" survival games like 7 Days to Die, the survival aspect is not developed that much. You need to eat but not trink, you need to defend your camp but the game gives you strong weapons to do that. So it is not that "hardcore" but a lot more relaxing, and that's a good thing for me. You can enjoy exploring the land, hunt some animals, grow plants, build houses.... I like it.
The base building system is easily the best I ever saw in any game. You can choose between blocks or voxels to place, you can choose shape (round, triangle, cube etc...), size and texture of the blocks, you can place several at once, rotate them, you can undo your last few placed blocks... you can even save complete buildings as blueprints to quickly build a copy of it. Absolutely awesome.
And I'm not even starting with the ingame item creation editor. Do you want to design your own sword, gun, vehicle or helicopter? Do you want to customize it completely, pixel by pixel? You can, if you are creative enough (I'm not. :)) Every creation has some fixed parts that need to be placed (a sword needs a hilt), the rest is up to you. The damage of the sword comes from the material you choose (wood swords are worse than steel swords) and from the amount of material you use.
Combine this with NPCs that offer quests (you that you have a reason to do or craft something) you get a survival/exploration/base building game that offers great value for your money. I even like it more than Minecraft.
Sure, it could use some polishing. Unity 4 games should not drop below 30 frames (7 Days to Die Alpha 10-11 never did using this engine), there should be options to change color saturation (everything looks a bit bright and colorful for my taste) and programming could be a bit more smooth (first game start after PC is started is without problems and the game runs smooth, but if I quit the game and restart it, second start takes forever and ingame autosaves makes the game freeze for about 3 seconds. I need to shut down the PC completely to fix that). But hey, it's only 20 Euros... I leave more money at the cinema for a two hours movie and popcorn.
Multiplayer is very entertaining (coop story mode and sandbox mode) but suffers from some sync problems. Sometimes you miss some of the other players animation, if you talk to an NPC the other does not see the dialogue, and setting up a dedicated server is a little bit tricky, but it works. Too bad that no one seems to play this game online any more, so you need to bring a friend or two.
Short form: I'd give this game 8/10. There are a lot of games on Steam that are worse and more expensive.

In Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide, you play as one of the five unique heroes and work together with up to three other players in a fictional town named Ubersreik to save the town by doing various missions while killing every Skaven (rat-men) that gets in the way.
While showing many similarities to Left 4 Dead series, Vermintide differs in the sense that it puts a lot of emphasis on melee combat, kind of like Chivalry. Ranged combat is possible but there are a lot of restrictions, mainly the limited amount of ammunition you get.
* Character interactions with each other showcases their unique personalities nicely, rather than just five generic characters that looks different
* Having many ways (decapitation, caving heads, explosives, etc) to kill rats is satisfying
* Collecting books and grimoires adds challenge regardless of difficulty, and can improve loot quality
* Levelling also rewards you with loot, so your progression isn't halted should you find yourself not winning often.
* Different characters having different playstyles adds variety and replayability
* Rat Ogres make L4D Tanks look like babies
* Cannot sprint - You will have to rely on your own dodging and parrying skills if there are no one to cover you
* Optimisations need improvement - CPU/graphic card usage remains high even for high-spec computers
* Matchmaking is 'First come, first serve' rather than lobby browsing (You deal with the same people for a particular map until slot is filled, forcing you to play different map or host your own lobby).
* Weapon balancing needs work, some weapons are underpowered making them undesirable
* No shared equipment besides trinkets (already somewhat rare itself depending on luck)
* Rewards don't fully justify difficulty - Common weapon is possible reward for nightmare/cataclysm difficulty
* Unpredictable spawns can feel rather punishing at times even on easier difficulties
* Bot intelligence makes solo play rather unfun
* Curse those near unstoppable, physics defying Zeratul rats- Oh sorry wrong game, I meant Gutter Runners
Despite these flaws, Vermintide is still very promising as the development is very active, and you can expect a lot of these issues to be resolved in the upcoming updates.

Door Kickers harks back to a time when gamers were thought to be intelligent. A little bit of information is given to the player about gameplay mechanics and the rest is left up to them to figure out through trial and error. This, in part, is why there's no "do it this way to win" approach to informing the player. Inspired by the planning stages of Rainbow Six, with a SWAT aesthetic, and turned into a feature length game, it all makes sense. A player must learn to play the game much like they must learn to understand how to deal with the situation in which their troopers find themselves. Or be left to suffer the consequences.
Although it's possible to make arrests and to subdue assailants with a taser, that's not where the emphasis lies. The opponents you're dealing with are all presumed to be heavily armed and willing to kill you on site based on the knowledge that they most likely already have. Once you understand that, the gear and equipment options available in-game will make a lot more sense. That is why this game is more comparable to Rainbow Six than Swat 3 or 4. It's not about getting a conviction but dishing out the punishment because the verdict has already been made.
I highly recommend this game. But that recommendation entirely depends on the type of gamer you are. This game is for the thinker. Sometimes you'll make a plan that will take a few seconds and so will the mission. Other times, you'll spend a few hours only for the mission to fail. It's not the game's fault, nor is it yours. That's just a harsh reality and simply a matter of learning from such mistakes. If you want mindless satisfaction, are looking for a game that plays itself, or were born yesterday, this is not the game for you. This game is a challenge, your enjoyment will entirely depend on whether or not you'll accept it as such and rise to the occasion. So the question is: do you accept the challenge?

I got this game gifted to me by a generous friend and was interested to play because I wanted to try a refreshing point-and-clicker with an interesting artstyle. I was pleasantly surprised with my gameplay experience.
The aesthetics are very nice - the amount of detail in the game world is high. During brief cutscenes, the artstyle switches to a charming, fun cartoon appearance. The music and sounds are good and add to the positive, comical vibe emitted by the gameplay. Much of the game consists of you travelling throughout an extensive bomb shelter, trying to fix all of the troubles caused by your roach friend/brother.
The controls are simple and easy to learn - I recommend using a controller to play, but the keyboard and mouse combo work fine. There is a quick tutorial that helps you understand the mechanics of the game. Clues are constantly given, and trial-and-error will help you progress through the game most of the time. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with point-and-click adventure/puzzle games. Most of the puzzle solutions are intuitive - or at least hinted at heavily when you interact with said objects.
Gameplay consists of you moving around different rooms of a bomb shelter, usually solving problems for other people in order to progress. As a cockroach, you can walk along walls and the ceiling, changing the orientation of the camera if you do so; you cannot jump, only walk. You can pick up items of interest, combine them in your inventory (if applicable), and use them to interact with the world (indicated by a puzzle icon over an item). Unlike many point-and-clickers, you can actually move your character around without using the mouse - something I found refreshing after playing many mouse-only point-and-clickers.
Another nice thing I appreciated in this game is the depth of puzzles - many times, you have to do an extra step to solve a problem. For example, there is a part where you need to collect baby flies that are located throughout a set of rooms. One of the flies is racing in a circle around a makeshift track - to capture it, you need to place a net on the wall, repair it, and physically block the fly's way so it goes around you (straight into a ramp that launches it into the net). These type of dynamic puzzles help prevent the game from getting stale.
Overall, the game is a very well-done point-and-clicker that makes up for its simpler storyline with fun, comical puzzles. If you are interested in the point-and-click genre, then you should definitely give this game a try. I normally try to avoid mentioning price if I feel it is unnecessary, but I do think that the retail price ($16.99 CAD) is a bit steep. At the time of writing this review, the game is discounted at 88% ($2.03 CAD), and that is more than a fair price for the value you are getting.
Recommend!

Deadlight isn't a long or particularly original experience, but it is fun while it lasts and that's really what matters.
I don't always go into a game expecting full originality, that's a pretty difficult feat nowadays, what with most topics already having been covered in one way or another, but that doesn't stop Deadlight from being an enjoyable game. The storyline leaves a little to be desired, it's not worth writing home about and character development is mediocre at best, but it's the gameplay that shines. Your first go at Deadlight will be very much an experience of trial and error, where in most circumstances you will be encouraged to use your initiative to solve the issue, but don't take too long, there will more than likely be zombies ready to chomp on your♥♥♥♥♥
Deadlight is similar to games like Limbo or This War of Mine, so expect gameplay similar to that.
Never feeling overpowered or too overwhelmed for circumstances that don't require it, gives the game a nice sense of balance that'll keep you playing addictively. Let's be honest, this isn't a game that'll take you too long to complete, you are more than capable of completing it within a few hours, but that said, it doesn't outstay its welcome either.
There are a few quetionable design choices here and there, mostly interface related, as well as some moments of head scratching, though because of lack of direction or just puzzle solving freedom, one may never know. Also it should be known that this game was clearly designed with Xbox in mind, so don't expect PC friendly intuitivity right off the bat.
If you can put aside the minor flaws, there's a good game here, not groundbreaking, not original, but enough to make it a fun experience.

This is understandable however, in order to force you to play certain maps in a specific manner which I fully accept in order to fully participate in the creator's vision. The soundtrack of course is fantastic enough to keep you playing even in the face of increasing frustrations. Another interesting aspect is how after being frustrated with dying you can instantly get your frustration out on the unlucky victim of whatever weapons happen to be in their proximity.
Excellent soundtrack and a sequel that builds on the original in many of the right ways. The confusing story and inability to freely use masks you unlock on all subsequent levels are the only small downfalls of this game. All around I would give this a 4/5.

Sonic Adventure 2 does so many things right, but to truely enjoy the game...you have to pull through some sections that you will either LOVE or HATE. Details below
(I recommend playing this game with a Gamepad. I use this a reference when I use the terms "A", "B", and such. I am talking about a Gamepad)
SA:2s story is divided into 3 parts,
,
, and
Each story has 3 character each with their own play Style.

Continuing where Sonic Adventure 1 left off, Sonic escapes custody of the Military (CITY ESCAPE SONG PLAYS HERE), and encounters Shadow. Shadow Sends Sonic back into Military Custody and its up to Tails to break him free. Knuckles is off on his own for a majority of the game, collecting Master Emerald Pieces (Per Usual), which takes him to different parts of the map each with their own theme (I will touch on this later on)
After Sonic and Tails reunite, a series of unimportant events occur, blah blah blah, and Sonic has to go to space to destroy a Super Weapon. And go figure, the weapon is run off of the power of the Chaos Emeralds.
Eggman is infiltrating a military Top Secret base to uncover an "Ultimate Weapon", which he discovers is Shadow the Hedgehog. Shadow talks about a mission he must fullfill, and commands the Dr. around so he give the Dr. the "True Ultimate Weapon".  Shadow and Dr. Eggman team up with Rouge to recover Chaos Emeralds to power the Ultimate Weapon,  the world is about to blow up, end story.
After both campaigns are beaten, there is a secret story.
Speed sections have you running around at the speed of sound, got places to go have to follow my rainbow.
These parts of the game make everything worth while. Speed sections are fun, fair, and varied.
The only complaints I have are in the Shadow campaign, the Forest level has many glitches that it easy to die for no reason, but otherwise, I love these parts of the game.
Back in the day, having varied gameplay in your game was seen as innovative. Nowadays, going from a speedy high-octane part of the game to a slow paced "Hot and Cold Meter" style of hunting for gems is seen as a sin. If you can forgive this games age and its willingness to push these sections of the game on you then will enjoy the experience as a whole, way more...otherwise these sections of the game are hated by most of the community.
As Knuckles/Rouge, you are placed into a map with three emerald boxes on the bottom of your screen. You are challenged with exploring the area waiting for one of the gems to flash Green (Close), Yellow (Closer), or Red (Very Close) to find the pieces of the Master Emerald. Scattered throughout the levels are hint Robots, that will give you three hints as to the whereabouts of the hidden pieces.
Hold down A, move your cursor around to lock onto enemies, and release to kill them all.
This is how you kill enemies in these levels of the game. Although you CAN run up to badies and bash them (Which is a stupid idea), and you CAN manually aim at them (Easier said then done), holding down your A button and moving your laser around is the best way to kill enemies. And as far as i am concerned, it is the only way.
Here is where the problem lies: For 90% of the level, you holding down A, which causes a high pitched
sound to play non stop as long as you are holding down A. Sure the laser dies after a few seconds, but you can (AND SHOULD), hold down A again right after, just in case there are enemies off screen you dont see because the camera is trashy on these levels. Or who knows what, but holding down A gets SO ANNOYING, but is needed.
Like I stated above, the camera is trash in a mojority of these levels, and yet they require platforming on certain parts. Yuck. Levels like the Egypt and Space level as Eggman have certain angles that mess with your depth perception.
I do not enjoy these levels in the slightest.
SA:2 features a small side area of the game where you raise a Chao by giving it Power Core-ish bits you find when killing enemies, and animals. You can spend your rings in a Black market area to feed fruit or give gifts to your Chao. Each chao can be named and used to play mini-games, such as racing and fighting (But you have to pay to fight).
Show your Chao enough love, and you unlock a Chao Heaven!
Abuse your Chao and you can unlock Chao Hell...which is much cooler...
This little addition makes the game more enjoyable, and when you replay missions you are achieving something in itself when your return to your garden to upgrade your Chao.
The game is dated, we can all see that, so some courtesy is due.
+Decent Story...for a Sonic Game
+Fun Gameplay
+Chao Garden
+Good port
+Bosses are fun

This is the most disempowering simulation I have played.
That is not, to say, that it isn't also an excellent simulation. It's a mediocre game, but a phenomenal simulation. Maybe not for its efficacy of allowing you to do what you want, but for its complete obstinance in making that anything other than easy. If you have fantasies of living in a medeival land and being a roamnig hero, beholden to no-one and helping the common man, prepare to be bored out of your mind. The peasants mostly want to be left alone, and when they do want things it's things like grain. Or cows. And when they actually have problems you want to help with, like bandit attacks, they don't ask you to hunt bandits for them. They ask you to teach them how to defend themselves. Everything they ask for is reasonable. That's what makes it so numbing. Eventually you abandon your desire to be a roving, solo hero. (Perhaps you are sick of being run down and gored to death by a practically untrained mercenary who just coincidentally owns a horse, which elevated him to the status of a god. So you get a few friends and wander with them instead. You do some good deeds. You train some peasants. Whatever. Your small warband starts asking for pay. You realize you can't just keep a dozen skilled warriors on retainer without producing an income. You start working for guilds. Then lords. Your warband grows.
Flash forward a bit and you're collecting taxes, refusing to give the collected taxes to the lord you're collecting them for, razing villages and selling their valuables, growing rich on your mercenary war-profits by collecting pay from a liege whose wars you never actually help with and going mad with transitory power.
I mean, if you want power. And frankly there isn't much else to aspire to, despite the level of simulation. Sure, you can romance a few noble ladies. Or men, depending on your gender, but they predictably require far less romance. But that process is ardurous and takes agonizing months if not years of letter writing and 'visits'. "I need to see you, love!" "I am here!" "Okay, later!" +3 affection.
Wow.
Maybe you want to lead a kingdom. Become a rogue power taking castles and villages and coming to lord over a vast army.
Well, your army size is limited by your Leadership. Better grind that. Not that it matters, your enemies scale so their armies are always bigger. Lords who you need to woo into your service take months if not years of letter writing and 'visits'. "My friend, we should speak!" "Okay." "We have spoken, goodbye." +1 affection (sometimes). So...you'll never in any reasonable timeframe get what you want.
So it's an excellent simulation of medeival life. You can't really get what you want. The most effective short-term gains come from screwing over peasants, and your success can be instantly destroyed at the whim of a lord that glanced at you across a field and happens to have a larger army.
Who am I kidding? The game's rigged. They -all- have larger armies.
...actually, that doesn't sound very simulationist.
Worth playing. Not at full price. Thank god it's on sale all the time. Don't spend more than five bucks.

Cover system is very mediocre, with your troops more or less being a gun that you point with your mouse. No dynamic AI, no functional cover shooting. What you have is a game that consists of everything that made the old Rainbow Six games good, but without the same polish that made them fun. Fun diversion for a few hours, but not an 8/10 game.

This game seems amazing. I only managed to honestly play 5 minutes of it on and off. The rest of the 15 minutes I spent in this game consisted of massive frame loss and bugged sounds and music. Before anyone plays this I'd thoroughly recommend you read the "Early Access Game - What the Developers have to say:" section of the store page to understand the scope of the project that we're sitting on and the potential this game has to be great.
Secondly, I'd like to say that the development team has been running on skeleton crew for a long time (until recently at least) meaning that development of the game sadly to drop to a crawl speed so although yes it's been in development a long time but it's being handled by a group of devs who are literally doing this for the love of mecha games and seeing it through to completion through thick or thin. I think people have some sort of misconception that because it's been around for a while it should be further along but it totally depends on personal expectations. The back-end updates have been huge and they've been pushing to get a solid foundation on which to build the rest of the game, which I feel they now have (despite some wonky control options *cough* prone *cough*).
I'd also like to stress that AI controlled bots ARE IN THE GAME, look for the "Training Grounds" servers where you fight in "wave survival" mode to fight AI. If no players are on, fight the bots, they are challenging.
So all that said, lets get to the game itself...gear combat feels solid, I enjoy the pace being somewhere between Hawken and MWO. The running and SMS mechanic adds another level of control to the game as well, feel you're losing a fight? Jump on SMS and burn rubber out of the combat zone and try to split up your enemy take them out one by one. I like how the gears aren't absolutely overladen with weapon systems and you can only take into combat what you can carry effectively, the variation in weapons should have something for everyone in there, personally the VHAC (very heavy autocannon) is my favourite by far. Jump jets do exist in the game to add some vertical lift but I tend not to use them on my gears so I won't comment on that. Couple of things about movement that currently bother me is the prone problem (known bug developers are working to fixing) and no kneeling (yet), gears still feel a little too 'floaty' when they jump though just need a bit more weight added in there. Despite the issues I have with the movement system it is currently going through an entire revamp (hence prone broke in the first place) new animations, new movements etc are all being worked on so I'm excited to see what that brings.
Maps look good for the most part, San Lopez is definitely my favourite, with or without sand storm lol. Tershaw valley if your system can handle it, is certainly one of the most beautiful maps in the game but it eats resource with all of the vegetation on it so I'd avoid playing AI bots on it with a minimum spec system, not so keen on the unfinished maps but obviously early access right now is understandable whilst they're texture artists and modelers work on different assets. Zero G map is coming as well in orbit around Terra Nova as well, if you host your own server in game (yes you can host your own system :D - this is a MASSIVE positive for me where you can tweak all your own numbers and really personalise your own Heavy Gear Assault experience) you can see the Horizons map that is the Zero G map.
The Gears themselves look superb despite being a different art direction to the original TT models, although with the addition of interchangeable armour pieces you can literally create a totally unique and personal gear and there's no paywall for colouring your gears either, you have access to the entire colour spectrum and over 30 different material types for primary, secondary and tertiary aspects of your gear, this is a huge amount of customisation available to the players for nothing!!!
The UI is slightly clunky but not unusable and with a bit of familiarity you soon get used to zipping around it, and it doesn't really affect my ability to blast apart other gears which is fine.
So overall the game is in early access it has got bugs, they are being reported and fixed as fast as Stompy Bot can manage, the devs themselves went through some really tough times and have come out the other end stronger than ever so again it shows the dedication that Stompy Bot have to their project. The gear combat is a solid experience and the customisation options for both personal server and the gears is off the chart. So despite being a basic arena gear combat experience right now we have the beginnings of a VERY promising mecha game that gives people an alternative to what's on the market right now.
Things I'm most looking forward to in no particular order:
1) Spitting Cobra Southern Heavy Support Gear
2) Melee Combat!!!!
3) Corporate and e-sports modules :)
