The game is free so there's that, keep that in mind whenever I mention any of the games many flaws, its free, so if you want a battlefield fps set in WW2, then here you go, just don't spend your money on this trash.
Also they will claim the game isn't P2W you can earn everything in credits.
They then will never mention that wages are constantly decreased (how you earn funds to buy things and repair) that upkeep for weapons is increased, (YES for EVERY bullet you have to spend funds to replace and repair your gun).
Which makes it when you first join a upward battle, as you will die to more experienced better equipped players which often means they have two badges vs your one.
You can get vet but it costs 76,000 for a single day, 600k for 30 days, that isn't play time but like a subscription where it runs out even while you're away.
This makes it impossible to earn the vet sub early on, until you rank up enough to get enough money just to break even with your upkeep.
So to summarize,
You start the game with beginners gear, in the same games with vets with more badges and better guns, and more upkeep. You have to count bullets and grenades to make sure you don't break the bank, meanwhile they are blowing your car up with bazookas and anti-tank rifles with wild abandon.
And the people who claim it isn't P2W claim that throughout this you can just purchase a vet sub, when this whole process is to frustrate you to buy gold or vet membership.
The balance updates are also geared to this, making factions go through a cycle of severerly nerfed and buffed, so that you get soldiers of each faction starting the grind over encouraging you to once again pay out
Off the topic of the P2W model. Flaws include.
-Squad
You can get put into a squad randomly, which includes people with hardly any playtime, if your squad leader neglects orders or is even AFK, you can't leave squad once battle begins. This is especially annoying when you want to back up another line but can't spawn there because your squad leader needs to switch over spawns, but he can only do that when he's dead.
You can't edit your squad unless people are in it, so unless you have a friend who will wait patiently you will have to hurry to upgrade while you wait for battle with some pubbies.
-Vehicles
Oh boy, the cars defy physics, I am almost positive a swerve is a meter or a rng mechanic, as it makes next to no sense.
A car will swerve the exact same way every time, the cars are purposely awful to encourage you to get a badge to make up for it, however there are 1-3 badges so useful you will never take those, UNLESS you are a vet because you have 1 to spare. Cars especially german cars are incredibly slow to get going, even when facing down hill.
Other qerks, if you are in the driver seat and switch over to passenger then hit E you will exit always out the drive door.
Occasionaly while pressing E you will not leave your car, incredibly annoying still not fixed since beta.
-Gun balance
Awful as well, I won't go into specifics, as the gun balance and stats change frequently, but I will mention the equipment points they take up.
Most guns take up 5-7, meaning you have enough room for only 1 accesory maybe two if you take a gun with 5 points.
I have no idea who uses the extra slot granted by vet membership, unless its a complete utility class using a pistol.
Bringing up pistols, they hit harder then a rifle, as accurate as one too, the only reason you can't effectively snipe with them is the bullet dissapears after a distance.
-RNG headshots
Apparently you hit close enough to someone's head if you roll right you get a headshot. Really stupid.
-Match balance, you can end up with a tank of half tanks or half planes, a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when the other team is mostly infantry.
-Still no new maps
-I'll be updating this as I come up with more things I dislike.
But again keep in mind the game is free.

'2.5D Action/Shooting/Puzzle Platformer' built on the Unreal game engine.
It's a good game but the story is grim and it does not have a 'hollywood' happy ending. (although I have not seen the alternative ending, yet)
The game is seperated into three 'acts' with act one starting off relatively easy and then act two and three becoming increasingly more difficult. You get to use a slingshot, revolver, shotgun, and a fire axe at different stages of the game. You have limited ammo and need to manually reload your guns. You have a stamina bar that depletes while swinging your fire axe, sprinting, or hanging from things by your arms. So you are not really able to take on large swarms of zombies, you have to out manoeuvre them. You find supplies but they too are limited in quantity and in rarity. The game uses a checkpoint system that is very good although in the later stages there were a couple of longer gaps between checkpoints that will cause frustration.
Having previously completed games like 'Braid', 'Limbo', and 'Planet of the Eyes' I am experienced enough for the 'puzzle' aspects of this game. I didn't have any trouble finding all the secrets or knowing what I had to do to progress to the next area.
The game has an online leaderboard with score and progression tracking, both globally and with your Steam friends which is quite cool.
Overall I enjoyed my time with this game. I have unlocked all achievements except one. Do I think I will get the final 'nightmare mode' achievement? Probably not. It takes about 4 hours to complete a run through give or take an hour. I played the game with an XBox 360 controller.
If this sounds interesting to you then I recommend to give it a go.

The animations of Melody (the main character) herself are very stiff due to the way she's drawn in the game. Since her body parts are all non-stretchable static images that are simply moved and rotated, she cannot be very flexible. This does allow easy creation of alternate characters for her, though. Some people have reported getting motion sickness from playing this game due to the continuous scrolling from right to left, but I find that I can solve it by simply playing on a smaller screen.
Due to a mix of no updates, poorly implemented controller configuration and lack of polish, I wouldn't suggest this over other play-your-own rhythm games. This opinion may change with future updates, however.

As others have expressed, I really tried hard to like this game, but it all feels very underdeveloped and unrefined. After playing this game for over 30 hours or so, I wanted to compile a list of things that I had a problem with, for those hesitant about purchasing this game as I have.
*LONG load times: Regardless of which mode you play on (Story, Adventure, Build), you'll find yourself having to fast-travel around the large maps provided. However, each and every time you fast travel, the game has to load in. I've experienced loading times as long as 5 minutes or more and in worst case scenarioes, even had to reload an autosave after the game froze \ crashed.
I understand that games do need to load in lots of data at a time, but having to wait so long just to get back to my colony is ridiculous and tiresome.
*"Story" Mode needs more STORY and character development: I cannot stress enough that there needs to be more STORY in Story Mode. When you first begin Story Mode, it will give you an introduction cutscene showing you and a group of colonists travel the stars on board of a starship. Only moments later, some kind of event triggers and you and your shipmates get shot down and crash land on an alien planet, where you have to survive on.
The story then thrusts itself upon you as you pick up the pieces. The characters that you meet say that they have met you on board the ship you came in from, but use the stupid excuse that, "Oh you must have hit your head and forgot who I am" thing, over and over again. I'm sorry "Gerdy" and "Dr. Allen," but I don't know who the HELL you guys are, as the game never gave me much of a chance to meet you prior to this event.
*The voice acting is TERRIBLE: After the introduction cutscene in Story Mode, you'll quickly notice that after talking with the first NPC you see how robotic and how stale and flat-toned the voice acting is. Most people you talk with in conversation don't even sound like a human in real life voiced them; i.e. they sound like a voice similar to Microsoft Sam. It honestly sounds like the voice actors recorded in the bathroom stall at their studio \ home.
This is an issue because with a game focused on "Story" and "Character Development," it's really hard to get immersed with all these different characters you meet along the way with the dialog so bland and boring. Either hire more talented voice actors or allow us to read text-only dialog, like in Adventure Mode.
*The same BGM (background music) over and over: You can count with one hand the amount of BGMs that are in this game, as there aren't many to go with. It's not so bad at first, but after a few hours you begin to resent the music so much that you eventually disable the music altogether.
*The majority of the questing is BORING: If you've played an MMORPG before, you know the routine: go from Point A to Point B, collect and kill stuff, and turn the quest in. If that's something that interests you, though, then this game will be great for you, as there are a PLETHORA of these type of quests.
*Monster fighting is BORING: Enemies come in 2 varieties, just 2: Charge and attack you straight on with maybe 1-2 abilities, or ARMAGEDDON TERRORS that shoot laser beams and missiles at you.
The enemies that just charge and attack you may have some abilities that also knock you around literally like a rag doll. Fight with enemies that use knockback are as follows: hit them a few times, dodge roll back, hit them a few times, etc. Repeat this and you win.
Then there are some enemies that are like if Godzilla fused with a Gundam and proceed to start a mini-war with you. If you're playing on Normal like I did, they a virtually impossible to kill, unless you have great gear, a vehicle with weapons on it, or an hour or two in real life to spare taking it down.
That's not even to mention that one of the only "difficult" parts about the enemies is that some of them can take A LOT of damage, e.i. they are damage sponges.
*Skill tree system extremely limits to what you can or can't do: In Story Mode, you don't have the opportunity to use the skill tree system as you are with Adventure Mode, so when I saw the option, I thought to myself, "Oh cool! This should make the game more fun!" ..... It didn't and made it pretty frustrating at times.
The skill tree system in Planet Explorers uses skill points that you can allocate to different skills, such as mining / chopping faster, gaining more materials doing those, doing more damage with weapons, etc. You get these skill points by killing monsters(2-8 SP each), mining(1-2 each node), chopping trees down(1-2 each tree), etc.
Maybe you think to yourself, "Well, the map is a pretty big place to just be walking around only, so I'll go get the parts and make a vehicle to ride around in!" You take the time to gather everything you need, maybe even pimp out a custom vehicle ride in the vehicle creator. When you try to "Export" the vehicle into the game, though, you'll quickly realize that you need a specific SKILL to even Export something from the creator to in-game (which will cost you hundreds of skill points to farm up to that point). So say you farmed up everything and got the skill to Export the vehicle to the game. You place down your sweet ride and you're about to ride it, but OH WAIT! You need the specific skill to even DRIVE the damn thing (costs another 90 skill points). You see where I'm getting at?
To even do the most basic gameplay functions requires you to unlock specific skills within the different skill trees. Can't use your new tool or weapon? Get the skill for it. Can't use a specific type of building block or building block shape? Get the skill for it. So on, and so on.
I have played many sandbox survival games for many years and this is the first time I've seen such a system as appalling as this system. If you're playing this game on Adventure Mode, make sure to uncheck this broken system and just stick with the default.
*Food and sleep meter doesn't have much of an impact to gameplay: I never once felt, during my 30+ hours of playing, that the food and sleep meters had any significant consequence against me. I never had the thought that, "Well, my food meter is almost depleted. I better go eat something before I starve to death." There's doesn't seem to be any weight or impact of the gameplay with the current food / sleep meters, other than just losing some stats temporarily.
*NPC Followers and NPC colonists never shut up: This is just a minor point, but every time either an NPC follower or NPC colonists is in need of something, they will vocally tell you that they are in need of it. (I.e. "I need more ammo!" or "I'm too sleepy to work!"). They will NEVER SHUT UP about it until you give them what they want, much like a toddler does when they want a toy real bad.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I could go on and on about many different aspects about Planet Explorers, but the point I'm trying to come across is that this game needs MORE work on it.
There's lots of potential in this game, such as the in-game object / weapon / vehicle customization system (very easy to learn, fun to use), and the NPC followers with the colony feature (colonists can farm crops and material for you, base defense, building stuff, etc), but everything else around it needs refinement.
If what I said above didn't dissuade you, as a customer, in your interest to this game then I suggest you at least download the demo of this game before purchasing and find out yourself.

is a throwback to mech-centric platform/action games of old.  With tight controls and rewarding gameplay, this is a short but fun experience and one you are likely to want to replay several times, especially with a friend.
If you choose to, you can get through most levels in seconds by not killing everything and collecting all the gold.  You miss out on all the score bonuses (but can get a time bonus) and – by not getting the gold – you miss out on repairing any damage to the mech.
On the default setting, it took me around an hour to complete, but I had continued a few times.  As I got into further the game, the mechanics of the game became apparent and the controls are tight and responsive – one highlight is the use of the shield to bounce higher – a clever mechanic that you do not need to complete the game, but is satisfying to use.  The ‘sticky’ grenades are another highlight and you can aim them through small openings to damage the enemy.  The controls are well designed and are fully configurable.
There are leaderboards for all the difficulty settings, and this game is best approached with that in mind.  It is easy to get through all the levels and the bosses are not difficult, but to get as far as you can without continuing is where the game shines and has that ‘just one more go’ factor.  This is a game you can return to when you feel like destroying stuff.  It has local co-op too, which is bound to increase the fun.

Journey of a Roach is a point and click adventure game with a stylistic twist: as a cockroach, you can climb on nearly any surface, including the ceiling. This allows the main character, a cockroach named Jim, to traverse levels in a uniquely three-dimensional manner, with his main goal being to rescue his friend from a gang of kidnapping ants. The wall-crawling feature, along with the game's charmingly excitable characters, creative level design, and user-friendly puzzles, makes for a pleasant point and click experience.
Like most point and click adventure games, the main goal in Journey of a Roach is to collect various items and then use them in the correct locations. Often the items are in hard to reach locations that require creative climbing to get to. Sometimes you might have to combine items in your inventory so that they can be used to solve puzzles. The puzzles themselves are fairly straightforward, with nearby NPC's often giving small clues whenever you happen to get stuck.
At first the level design in Journey of a Roach seems rather simple, but as you go on they grow complex. The levels are often big and have several different branches of items to collect for multiple different puzzles at once. However, instead of overwhelming you, the amount of puzzles allows you to bounce back and forth between them when frustrated, minimizing the time you'll spend blindly wandering about wondering what to do.
Solutions for the puzzles, much like the chattering, nonsense voices of the characters in Journey of a Roach, are often silly and happily humorous. At one point I was asked to bring an ant a burger and I fashioned one out of a piece of sponge, a shoe, and a handkerchief in order to continue onward in the story. The game ends on an equally laugh-worthy and heartwarming note, making it a great game if you want a quick, light-hearted adventure.

For a game called COD Ghost, there's a surprising lack of
in it.
Overused jokes aside, Call of Duty ghost is one of many Call of Duty titles set in roughly the present day. My own experiences with the series are limited to CoD 1, 4 & 5. While shooters are not my main genre, I don't dislike them, and the previous games that I played were quite good shooters.
This review is going to focus on the singleplayer aspect of the game. Currently there are less than 150 players playing this game, and that seems to indicate that multiplayer community is not exactly thriving.
You can tell that this game was given a big budget by just looking at it. The game looks quite good, with relatively detailed character models, animations that look believable and so on. The environments look good, with a realistic amount of "clutter" items, foliage and other such things. And for a game with so much going on, it also runs surprisingly well on my humble machine, indicating that it's well optimized.
One area where the game looks oddly bad is in its reflections. There are a lot of supposedly reflective surfaces in this game, from camera lenses, to most doors that you're not supposed to open, to shop windows where they don't want to model the inside. These reflections seem to be portals to some other place altogether, as they don't actually reflect their surrounding, they just show a totally different part of the level, in glorious low res (the reflections look really blocky, as if they've used a texture meant to be viewed from a long distance).
The game lacks a real visual identity. Apart from the (rather nice looking) underwater sections, the game looks like any other modern military shooter. While this is to be expected, they could have picked some more visually interesting environments. That would really have helped the game stand out from all the other modern military shooters.
The sound of the weapons sound beefy without going overboard, and help make using the guns feel more satisfying. They're not "realistic", but they fit the tone of the game. Voice acting is quite good, with voice actors who seem to take their roles seriously, and who do a good job at portraying their characters. This helps prevent the game from feeling too hammy, something that otherwise could easily have happened had they hired worse voice actors.
In a not so distant future a nation has built a space station capable of firing weapons of mass destruction at any location in the world. Feeling threatened, another nation hijacks the space station and turns its weapons against its former owner.
A band of elite soldiers infiltrate the nation, and coldbloodedly murders civilians, blows up an oil platform and ruins the power infrastructure by blowing up their power plant.
Oh, and you're playing for the team that clodbloodedly murders civilians and blows up oil platforms and power plants, and who builds space stations with weapons of mass destruction. I'm not quite sure how I'm supposed to feel like I'm playing for the good guys. The game starts with your space station getting hijacked and several cities gets targeted. A few years later the US is fighting a losing war against South America, and the game early on shows how evil the South Americans are when they execute a group of civilians. This is framed as something terrible. But then a little later your team does exactly the same thing, shooting a person who cooperated with you in the back of the head, and this is portrayed as something good. I'm honestly not sure how aware the story writers were of these inconsistencies, if it's an intentional jab at the audience's willingness to just accept things if they're framed a certain way (it would not surprise me if it actually is).
Most of the game is a hunt for a former member of the team, who after getting tortured or something switched side (the game never makes it clear what happened, all just alludes to it), and is targeting his former team members.
There's nothing wrong with a really stupid action story, sometimes those can be really entertaining. CoD Ghost takes itself a bit too serious for its own good though, and the story is so inconsistent in its tone that it's very hard to take it serious. There's some unintentional humor to be had in the story of this game, but had it either taken itself less seriously or been less stupid, it would have been a far better one.
The gameplay is your standard shooter fare. It's not evolved much since Modern Warfare 1. Move through mostly linear levels, shoot enemies who come in waves, and repeat. Quite frequently the game tries to mix things up with sections where the gameplay changes completely, to varied results. At one point you're playing a stealth section as a dog (which could have been rather good, had it been more fleshed out and longer), at another you're swimming in a reef, and then you're controlling a tank in yet another section, or a helicopter, or a gun drone... The list of things goes on and on, and many of these non-standard shooting sections could have been good, had they not been over so quickly.
The game is, as stated above, really linear, and most of the time the game does a good job at making it feel like you're not just being tunneled through it in a very specific way, as the level designers have been good at making the "right" way be the most obvious way to go. This is good level design. No need for constant UI markers showing you where to go when the level does it for you.
Sadly the arenas where you do most of the shooting are not very entertaining. There's very little room to actually move about, you're forced to just move between a few pieces of cover and take potshots at the enemy. And on the few occasions where there were a way to move around and flank the enemy, the AI got so confused that it would just sit there, in front of cover (from your perspective) and not do anything. The AI was clearly not made for any more advanced tactics than "sit & take potshots". This is not a problem unique to this game, both EA's Medal of Honor & Ubisoft's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier has the exact same issue, and those games have level design that makes it far easier to exploit. Also, unlike in this games, I was not able to break any triggers by just moving too far ahead in CoD: Ghost.
CoD Ghost is not a terrible game, but it's not particularly good either. Many of the small non-standard shooting activities are over just as you'll start getting a feel for them, and the actual shooty bits are not as fun as they should have been, due to how the arenas are designed. The story is also really stupid, and inconsistent, and sadly not in a way that makes for prime popcorn action material. If you can get it for ~5-8€, it's worth a shot, if all you want is some mindless shooting, but at its asking price of 60€, even at 75% off, it's far too expensive.

On the surface this looks like the lovechild from a coupling between Audiosurf and Exit Path.
As a long term music rhythm game lover, I was thrilled, sadly this game falls short in a lot of ways.
While the lack of "sync" between the automatically generated obstacle courses and the music they are based on is an issue, my main gripe is with gameplay mechanics.
Unlike most rhythm games that give you a score the closer you are to the "sweet spot" of a perfect hit (be it too late or early) this game allows you to hit marks very early and is SEVERELY punishing if you are even a split-fraction too late. A miss in this game removes the obstacle course, respawning your character further ahead and only then showing the up and coming buttons again. Not a perfect jigsaw puzzle game, but the artwork is beautiful.  You don't know what the image is as you piece it together, so it's largely just finding where irregular shapes fit. Good ol' forgotten genre of "Beautiful Puzzle Games".

This was a lovely, if brief, puzzle game. I started playing thinking the images would be created from pictures of stained glass creations from all over the world, but it appears that they are all original artwork representative of the various peoples and places. (DLC idea?) The odd shapes that align with the natural divides between pieces of glass add a kinesthetic challenge more complex than the experience of traditional jigsaw-shaped pieces. It was fun to see how often I could see where a piece belonged before clicking on it so it would auto-rotate to the correct orientation, and how often an obvious fit would elude me until I did.
As I see others have noted, the pieces look larger before you place them in the puzzle, which often means they don't look like they will fit. I suspect that this might be intentional, with the solder between the glass pieces being represented both in the pieces already placed and in the loose pieces. It's something that I quickly got used to and was only a significant source of confusion in my first puzzle, but one which I periodically had to consciously compensate for all the way through. I think it has to do with the way the brain interprets shapes as ratios of, say, length to width, while the extra size given to the pieces before their placed does not seem to be proportional. This means that the piece that fits into an opening may seem a lot less "spindly" than the opening itself.
8/10 Would consider buying a DLC and will almost certainly replay the existing levels at some point.
Minor issues directed more at the devs than the players:
I never got the hang of where to click and hold if I want to rotate the unplayed pieces vs where to click and hold to pick up a piece. All the way to the end of the game I was making that error. The hit box for the pieces is larger than the pieces, and the hit box for the inner ring seems to extend into the inner edge of the outer ring. Maybe a grip strip would help clarify?
Early in each round, as you rotate the supply of pieces, the mirrored pieces on the other side of the board rotate along. It took me a little while to realize that each ring was not a single supply of pieces, but that the left and right side of each ring were separate sets of puzzle pieces cycling separately even as they looked like they were cycling together.
On several levels there were pieces of glass dark enough that it wasn't easy to see which parts of the board were unplayed space and which were not. Canada was one where, when placing the final piece, it looked like there were still a few openings and I placed the last piece based on shape. It's a minor thing, but a distinct backdrop texture could allow a better ability to compare shapes without limiting the palette of the final images.
The game reacts a little oddly to an accidental right click while dragging a piece. The piece gets returned to the unplayed supply out of place. The worst effect was when it was placed on top of another unplayed piece, and I could only pick up one of the two. There are no situations in the game where a particular piece has to be played before the other, so once I played the piece that I could pick up I was able to play the other.

So, let me explain why this game is not great at all ! While graphically the game is amazing and while the gameplay feels truly great... There is absolutely nothing that would make me recommend this game !
1st, the community is oftenly a bunch of ragers against new players... They will yell at you quite often for not succeeding a mission since you don't get anything when everybody dies... And it happens really oftenly !!!!
2nd, the missions are really long, sometimes too long ! Objectives are not well explained and if you do not know the map, be prepared to wander around some maps for a bit ! It wouldn't be a problem normally but when the maps are so huge, the risk of dying so big and that you do not get anything even if you do reach the end after a very long play time...
3rd, you'd better play with bots... however, they're not even that smart but they do tend to stay around you... While playing with bots is better than with humans, they do a lot of stupid things which will make you get all killed and fail the mission ! It will make you go nuts and rage !
4th, the difficulty is horribly high even on easy... You are not allowed any mistakes ! You really feel the action, the intensity and why the game is called vermintide as enemies are endless (you won' t get time to breath) but healing items are scarce and it's first found first served most time, some players play more in a team spirit but it's really hard to communicate with the way the chat system is made when communication is so important... So much action, no time to really say anything either. We might salute the diversity in ennemies wich are all hard ! And if you don't stay a team, the ones who grabs you and kill you in a couple seconds without being able to do anything but waiting to be rescued (at the condition the team is not trying to rush) is really frustrating !
5th, the number of maps really really low, even if big.., Unlocking the 2nd wave of maps is really difficult and you will just see the same stuff over and over.
6th, you lose interest in the game really quickly, playing more than 2 or 3 maps in a row is really really repetitive and will make you lose interest really fast... Loot doesn't change anything as the loot is mostly uninteresting.
7th, you don't anything than hit and parry, sometimes fire a gun, a bow or a crossbow but the gameplay between character is all the same and this is the biggest flaw ! The mage doesn't really feel like a mage ! You don't have the time to really charge your attacks which slows you down and they burn you (ya right? for a fire mage!) and you're most likely forced to play with the sword as there's no way to stay back and bomb the ennemies from afar =/
The game really lacks of diversity, of special skills which would help to differenciate the different classes and help to renew the gameplay ! No tanks, no healer, no mage, no DPS... all characters are the same, none makes more damage.
8th, The loot system is bogus, the difference between weapons, even the epic ones (supposedely) are really minor except for the bright mage... the devs wanted new players not feeling disadvantage compared to older players and avoid any kind of big level difference (ya, there's a crappy level system which doesn't change much TBH)... let me tell you they failed big time ! The forge system is quite crappy as well and you can't upgrade your weapons as you wish to make them more powerful, it's all out of luck !
9th, The atmosphere is really great and skavens are coming out of everywhere! You really feel the panic and the tention...the battle feels very good but the good things really stops there... You will enjoy it for a couple hours, maybe even think I'm wrong as the game feels amazing then you will wonder why you even should go back to it! No PvP and no way to really support your team other than staying next to them and slaying everything the game throws at you which really feels overwhelming, sometimes in a good way, sometimes in a bad one.
Conclusion: I really can't recommend this game! I was hoping for something great while waiting for games like Battleborn or Overwatch... I was wrong ! The lack of diversity is a major handicap !
If the devs come out with abilities and more classes, ennemies and levels, the game might be really great (but some hardcore fans and ragers will tell you this is a bad idea and the game is perfect as it stands... I don't think this is the right thing to do, defend devs who partly failed in a major way), but as it stands... Pass your way ! Go to borderlands or go back to it or better, wait for Overwatch or Battleborn !
This game really doesn't deserve more than 5/10 because you will either love it and be a hardcore fan or be quickly disapointed with the game mechanics which will bore you to the death after a couple games !

Vermintide is a fantastic game. When all you need is some visceral, powerful violence, this game delivers fully. This game offers a Left 4 Dead type of on-the-move, hoard based gameplay with a gritty melee combat, a looting and equipment system, 13 maps and 5 difficulty settings, 5 classes, and tons of loot to find. Vermintide is a well-crafted game with a combat system that keeps you coming back, bloodthirsty for more rats to kill.
But I can hardly recommend it.
While the combat system is competent, though iterative, the combat alone does not carry the game. This game suffers from a myriad of problems that really hamper it and obstruct your enjoyment of the game.
First off, optimization. It's awful. To save space, I'll at least say I'm running a mid to high range system with an AMD R9 280x, and even on the absolute LOWEST setting, I regularly experience sub-30 FPS. Looking on Reddit and the forums, many others suffer from performance issues, especially other AMD users. This alone gives me enough reason to not recommend the game - to push the game out so quickly out of early access when it could hardly play is a bit of a disgrace. But it doesn't end there.
Second, the loot system. It is not uncommon to play for dozens of hours and not get a single new weapon for your main class. You get one piece of gear per game, excluding bonuses, and you must roll for a random piece of loot. The issue that comes with this system is while I can be tolerant of rolling for rarity, the type of equipment you get is entirely independent of the class that you're currently playing. Essentially, morely likely than not, you can expect to get equipment completely useless to you, and it is not uncommon to never get a specific type of equipment that you're looking for for hours on end. While the loot system is a healthy addition to a L4D formula, it's hampered by how flawed and frustrating it could prove to be.
Third, hosting. This game makes the same mistake that Payday 2 did - making the game entirely dependent on the connection of the host. Should the host disconnect, the whole game ends. Game crashes because,  y'know, the game was rushed out and all of the major bugs weren't wiped out? Too bad. Somebody's trolling the entirely team and decides to end the game moments before you escape? That's it for you. At least Warframe gave you a chance with host migration, but this game? Not even the slightest. Irritating doesn't even begin to describe this issue.
Fourth, uninspired loot. As if it wasn't bad enough that looting ends up being a massive pain and an unrewarding experience, the rarity and the auments that the weapons could come with are hardly exciting. Remember Diablo 3 on release? Remember how meaningless the gear you find were? Well, this game suffers from the same problem. Augments are often uninspired, boring passives that barely distinguish a rare weapon from a regular common one. 20% to not use stamina when pushing? 5% chance on hit to have a 30% increase in attack speed for 5 seconds? I can barely contain my excitement. Even Blizzard realized how unrewarding their own loot system was before they changed it - I could only hope  that Fatshark realizes the same.
Well, there you have it. This game is barely a good enough romp in the park if you just want a hoard-based, stabbing simulator, but all of these problems present make it unworthy of a full-price purchase. Performance issues aside, the other issues I've listed make this game too frustrating of an experience to appreciate outside of a cheap thrill. My only hope is that these issues be resolved soon, and I will happily change my review to a positive, because for what it's worth, it is a fun game - it just pains me to see all of these issues getting in its way.
EDIT: The loot system since writing this review has been changed. You now have an option of which loot to craft using unwanted loot through a new system available at the inn. However, this does not preclude the issue of boring, uninteresting loot. Even with the advent of red rarity loot, the augments and abilities are STILL dull and uninspired. There is almost literally no difference between an orange and a red weapon aside from their color. And honestly? There was barely a difference between orange and white weapons to begin with.

I enjoy survival and crafting games, but the biggest problem most of them have is a total lack of purpose beyond simply not dying.
They usually very quickly become boring and repetative because in game life, even more than real life, mere continued existence is simply insufficient as a motivator for the endless tedium and overly-elaborate crafting systems that lazy developers throw at us in order to disguise the fact that there is only a sketch of a premise for these events to be occuring as they do, or worse, no premise for their game and the player's reason for being there at all.
Too many times have I played such games and tossed them aside because it's just another "I'm here, because I'm here, because I'm here, because I'm here..." game. Pointless. Useless. Devoid of purpose or meaning. You may of course have that experience with this game too, if you wish to do so in Adventure mode, etc., but I prefer having some story.
Planet Explorers is not one of those pointless games. Playing through story mode once just racked up 96.8 hours of interesting and fun gameplay for me.
While the dialogue and voice-overs themselves are bit on the amateurish side, the scope and breadth of the story as well as the concepts it seeks to convey are actually quite impressive even by triple-A title standards. Every effort you go to has a purpose. Has meaning. Right from the very beginning.
Constructive purpose, no less. This is important, as most of these kinds of game when they have a premise at all, it is based solely around defense against onslaught by one kind of ravening hoard or other after the apocalyptic downfall of all human civilization. Usually lame♥♥♥♥♥zombies.
To be sure, Planet Explorers also takes place in a post-apocalyptic world. It just wasn't our apocalypse, or our world. Yet.
The story has a little bit of everything. Humor and meloncholy sadness. Drama and light-hearted fun. Treachery, betrayal, vengeance. The triumph of hard-earned peace and safety along with the horrors and loss of a senseless war no one involved can afford.
The thrill of real exploration and survival in a harsh environment with the odds stacked against you from the start. Not because of one single reason or agenda, but because half a dozen agendas or more and the chain of events they set in motion converge to create an unforseeable disaster from the viewpoint of any one group.
Why are you chopping down a tree with this dinky little starting cleaver? Because old Gerdy was in the lifeboat with you and didn't fair as well in the crash. Now you have to craft a shovel to dig up the medical supplies that got buried when you came down.
Why are you bothering to design your own armed aluminum hovercraft in the creations editor? Because you can sneeze a hole in wood and besides, you want your colonists to look badass when they fly four of them in during their show of force for the Puja in your efforts to bring them to the negotiation table for a peace treaty.
The game actually strikes a very good balance in the players themselves between the impulse to get more done so they can see more of the story and the knowledge that they must pace themselves, or be caught unprepared at a crucial turn of events in that storyline. A story which has a lot of twists and turns that most often really are very much an unexpected surprise, which is almost always based around a 'Big Thought' concept.
That's hard to find in nearly any genre of entertainment these days, much less a survival/sandbox/crafting game. This is stuff you usually only see handled in any way by hard and high-level Sci-Fi novels. And even then, only rarely are so many disparate such concepts brought into play for one story.
I would love to see the implied sequal made and would happily buy it in early access.
These developers did this the way games should be done. They created a world and a story, then built a game around that, rather than building a game, THEN hiring writer to give it an excuse for existing, automatically hobbling any creativity or flexibility in the resulting story, or it's method of delivery.
I could be wrong about that, but even if I am, I must still credit them based on the grounds of their giving the writer(s) a great deal of freedom to tell an interesting story with their platform.
I mean really, when was the last time you actually CARED about your NPC colonists in a game? Knew them by name, personality and profession? Sorrowed if they died, beyond a mere loss in your colony's efficency or production or some such?
Story matters. Purpose in this kind of gameplay matters. Yes the game has some minor faults, but they are made less obvious and more minor because of the engaging story and sense of exploration. Easily overlooked.
Game developers who wonder why their games are being ripped apart in reviews by players on techincalities of gameplay mechanics need to look at this game and realize that the reason it's happening to them, is because they have offered the players nothing else by which to experience or evaluate their games.
No Man's Sky being perhaps the most recent and glaring example of this downward trend on a lazy treadmill. A game which reached legendary status as and has subsequently become synonamous with the very concepts of nihilistic futility and uselessness of effort.
This game really does make you feel like you are exploring a new and interesting world, while still lacking in enough specific detail to allow players to fill in the blanks with roleplay if they like, or just fleshing out in their own minds for fun because the concepts and scenario are compelling to think about.
This game was on sale when I bought it, but it would be well worth the money to experience, even at full price. It's sadly pretty much one of a kind.

Summary: A very short point-and-click game with a whacky art style and standard item puzzles which are enhanced by movement mechanics. Recommended, though the shortness of the game may warrant waiting for a sale.
Long story: I enjoyed my time with Journey of a Roach. The art style is a bit ugly, but whacky enough to be comical. The story is silly, but nice and often amusing. The puzzles consist almost exclusively of items and are generally unchallenging: the biggest challenge is usually finding the items. Once you have them it is usually easy to figure out where and how to use them. The ability to walk on walls is integral to some puzzles, both in getting close to items, areas and in approaching a problem from the right direction. This adds some extra flavor to what would otherwise be a standard point-and-click adventure game. Additionally, there are some collectables which encourage keeping your eyes open.
The game is short. I finished it in around 2.6 hours according to steam and the game features an achievement for completing the game in 18 minutes. Personally I do not mind short games as much as games which drag it out longer than their story can support or purposefully waste your time. However, the shortness of the game may affect whether you want to buy it at full prize or wait for a sale, so keep it in mind.

I'll admit this is one of the most nostalgic games for me. I occasionally listen to the OST still to this day and might leave the soundtracks on repeat for hours at a time. I'm also part of that group of people who thinks this is one of the better 3D games for Sonic, mechanically. It's true that newer Sonic 3D games have improved on many of the unique issues that arise when developing for a unique character like Sonic, but the gameplay in SA2:B just feels the most controllable. I admit the breakneck speed effects of more recent Sonic games feel more genuine to the character, but this one game still feels the most controllably fluid for me. Then again that might just be more of the nostalgia showing.
Unfortunately, I think this is one of those games that you don't
like until you've played through it a couple times and have a good feel for the quirky camera and the level layouts and upgrade collections - and a game controller (you really ought to play this one with a game controller).
The story wasn't all that amazing to me as a kid and holds even less value to me today - however the premise of Sonic still having an actual attitude and characters having personality archetypes that relate to their traditional reasons for existing, beyond filling a role as "[acquaintances of the protagonist character]," is something that makes me perhaps a bit dissapointed with the direction of the franchise since such days of the past.
All the Sonic fandom crap aside - Generally speaking, I'd recommend this game to anyone with a game controller and a thing for arcade games.
Edit: After playing this on PC with an xbox controller for a few hours - I hate to say it, but it handles much worse than I recall from the Gamecube. So much easier to get caught off-course and have a sudden momentum halt just from gently swiping a polygon the wrong way. It's definitely not as enjoyable as my nostalgia recalls. I may set up the gamecube again someday to compare how the GC version plays against the PC version - it definitely feels different in a bad way. In addition to the controls feeling really over-sensitive, the game has several audible and visual glitches that are new to me - most occuring during the rouge/knuckles maps where you tend to observe the maps in detail while seeking the hidden pieces.

Visually, the game is nice enough and the Steam Workshop option for having custom skins is a nice touch as well.
Where the game doesn't excel is as a music game, or worse yet as a rhythm game if you think of it as one. The danger of allowing anyone's music is that you have to cater to a lot of different problems. Even songs with fairly regular beats may not follow the rhythm that's most prominent, or the percussion. This on its own wouldn't be a problem, if the game had better visual language.
Unfortunately, tempo shifts are dealt with by a change in the color of background, possibly a change in your avatar (walking, running, flying), and happen pretty abruptly. This makes it very hard to quickly adapt, or in some cases to even tell what your timing should be. Some sort of visual cue to show "beat lines" would be immensely helpful in mitigating this situation. It's also a shame because it means often a lot of the space on the screen is wasted - if your runner is walking, there's not really any advantage to looking at the right half of the screen.
The algorithm itself isn't bad, but after playing Audiosurf 1 and 2, Beat Hazard, and even Rhythm Zone, I'm pretty familiar with these sorts of automatic detection methods and how the song will interact with the game. Melody's Run is actually surprisingly versatile - if the gameplay engine was better I'd enjoy a variety of styles.
There are other visual issues - some of the motions will cause your avatar to be leaning as they slide along slopes, which makes it unclear which part of your runner you should be tracking to figure out timing. Tight pairing of arrow cues are also very tough to figure out since it's a bit of trial and error to figure out where exactly different arrow cues start, and combining them with the guesswork of where your runner's "hitbox" really is at the moment can be ugly.
Another issue is that some of the up arrow cues have you jump off cliffs. Unfortunately you can't see what's below you until you're almost on top of it if the jumps are long and tall. Sometimes this means you're going to have to react immediately as soon as you land, and that breaks up the feel of following a rhythm.
When you miss an arrow cue, you'll trip, bump your head into terrain, etc. and despawn. A bit later you'll spawn again, further on the track since the music keeps playing, and this is also handled poorly. There's no slow phasing in, you'll just pop up out of nowhere meaning you lose your sense of what pace you're running at (especially if you happen to despawn across tempo changes). This often results in extra misses, or even spawning immediately after an arrow and "missing it", leading you to despawn again. Not only does it make playing the game futile sometimes, but it's exceedingly punishing and could be easily avoided.
Finally, the game has some performance issues. I don't have the best machine out there, but it's more than a "minimal" machine by a long shot. I had to turn down the performance settings, and kill a few video settings, otherwise midgame sometimes the game would freeze for a bit, the last few moments of buffered music would loop endlessly in an annoying stutter, my runner would jerk forward and fall into the ground, and then the game would catch up 5-20 seconds later, flinging me further down the track and guaranteeing a miss, not to mention player confusion. In a music game, real-time (or the illusion of real-time) response is paramount - and the audio getting messed up during these portions makes it even worse.
tl;dr Game had potential, is a fun casual run, but suffers from some bugs and visual design choices that detract from gameplay. If you're looking for something to do while listening to your music, this game's not a bad way to add some color and keep your hands busy, but that's about it.

Recommended.
Story...
There's not much of a story for a pure puzzle game, but I didn't expect anything more. The idea is very simple; explore the world via puzzles. That's it, and it's fine the way it is.
Gameplay...
It was both challenging and rewarding. There were varying difficulties, from three to five - and five being the most challenging. The puzzles had different shapes, which made some of them quite difficult. They certainly were different from normal rectangle ones, for instance.
There was also this interesting trick. Depending what route you went, you could come across puzzles with the difficulty rate being five. After finishing it and unlocking the next, that puzzle's difficulty could be four. I actually ended enjoying that, since I could test my skill and then relax a bit more with a more easy puzzle.
Art...
The art was really pleasant to look at. As I don't know much about stained glass art, I'm not sure if they are "real" or just made for the game. Either way, they were pretty and I even learned some history from them.
Music...
At first, it annoyed me. The music itself didn't sound bad, but my focus drifted because of it, especially if the puzzle was hard. After I finished the last five puzzles, the music didn't bother me at all.
Conclusion...
It's a nice, short game that can offer either challenge or relaxation. There's no time limits, so there's no need to rush to get that one achievement. You might learn new things from playing the game. However, I think the price is just a bit too high for a game that will take two to three hours to finish. Unless you buy it on sale.

Deadlight is a nice little side scrolling platformer. You can tell it was developed for something like Xbox Arcade. The controls are hardly perfect with a controller, but with the in-game prompts they are playable. The story is obviously linear, but my recommendation at some of the "tougher" parts, remember the controls. For example, a few times I was running back and forth like the l33tzor parkour daddy that I am, ducking Zombies to and fro, and couldn't find the way to the next section. Until I was like, oh yeah, ducking is a thing. Same thing with swinging quickly around gates during some of the chase scenes, instead of calming dropping from the gates and subsequently getting murderballed. The game mechanics aren't hard, but some of the puzzles do make you think for a second.
But to the crux of the reason why this game is worth spending a few bucks on, the story is quite good. Journey of a Roach is a short but cute 3D Puzzle Adventure slash Point and Click game and a result of a colaboration between German P'n'C veterans Daedalic Entertainment and the relatively young studio Koboldgames from Switzerland.
You play as Jim, a cockroach living in an underground bomb shelter that is controlled by an army of ants. When your cockroach buddy accidentally crashes through the floor and gets captured by the ants, you set out on a quest to rescue him, end the ants' terror regime and find a way to get out of the bomb shelter and to a peaceful place somewhere else.
There aren't any actual dialogues in the game. All of the communication between the characters takes place in the form of incomprehensible sounds (sort of similar to baby mumbling) and comic bubbles with drawings that show what the characters try to say. Some of those illustrations are pretty hilarious and probably wouldn't be remotely as funny, as if the characters would actually say 'I found this plunger. Shall I put it on my head?'. It's not the kind of humor that makes you laugh out loud and spit your drink on the screen, but it's amusing and cheerful throughout the entire game.
While the game is advertised as a Point and Click game, it hasn't much to do with the usual pre-rendered, stiff and sometimes blurry enviroments known from other P'n'C games. It's actually best compared with The Walking Dead where pretty much everything is in 3D and where you can freely move around while still retaining the classical P'n'C feel of finding objects, combining them, solving puzzles and so on. Due to the comic style of the visuals, you don't have to worry about blurry textures or anything, either - it all looks sharp and just sooooo cute. :D
Being a P'n'C adventure at its heart, the game adds some welcome addition to the fairly worn out genre as it basically plays like a sidescroller where you control Jim with WASD (or the arrow keys, respectively) and the actual item handling is done with your mouse (you can also use a gamepad, if you wish to do so - works great). To add to that (and since you're a cockroach, of course) you can also climb on walls and ceilings to progress through the levels, reach items or just avoid being seen by the ants.
It takes a bit getting used to and you sometimes accidentally climb a wall or a crate that you just wanted to pass, but overall the mechanic works great and gives you another way of freedom to explore your enviroment.
Puzzle-wise, the game is fairly easy as most puzzles only consist of picking up items, combining them and using them on something or someone, but since it's mostly quite obvious what has to be used how and where, they shouldn't provide that much of a challenge for experienced P'n'C or Puzzle game players. However, since the devs probably tried to also appeal to a younger audience, it wouldn't have been of much use to incorporate ultra-hard puzzles that you can't solve without consulting a walkthrough, so I'm generally fine with that.
Beating the story took me roughly 3 hours, which is rather short for a game like this, but personally I will always prefer shorter games with tight gameplay over games that artificially extend the playtime by repeating the same levels or gameplay elements over and over.
Once you've played through the game, there's not much else to do apart from hunting the remaining achievements, however, there's one particular achievement that requires you to beat the game in less than 18 minutes, so that adds at least a bit of challenge and replayability to the game.
Journey of a Roach is an extremely cute, cheerful and overall fun game for a relaxing evening, so if you like P'n'C games (especially with a gameplay twist) and don't get putt off by the game's length, make sure to check it out!

Review--Coming from playing audiosurf for quite a while and various other Rhythm games, I have to say that I am a little bit disappointed with this title. The concept is cool but the execution needs work. The rhythm algorithm can be decent sometimes but most of the time it just feels like a bit of a mashup of inputs with no real “sequence” behind them. The only inputs that line up the best I would say are the drum beats. There are cool moments when the stars align and everything seems to work together but in the short playtime I’ve had that only has happened once. I know not to expect perfection but there are other rhythm games out there that do a much better job.

Do I recommend this game? Yes. Absolutely. Here's why:
-Intuitive leveling system; As you level up, you get points to spend on your trooper's skills, like better "draw speed" indoors, or the ability to make anyone using a silenced weapon hold their fire if they aren't in direct danger. Pretty rad.
-A kind of currency: You earn stars for completing levels, the better you do, the more stars you earn, and you spend those stars on weapons and equipment for your troopers.
-Can be played real-time, or with the "Pause" option, for those who want to take a tiny bit more time to think about their plan.
-PERMADEATH: This is something that a lot of games don't do anymore. If you are in a Campaign (and only in campaigns), and a trooper dies in a mission, you lose that trooper (and his individual level and skills) forever, and he's replaced with a green trooper.
-A pretty fun soundtrack
-A small, but adequate variety of missions: Elimination, Hostage Rescue, VIP Escort, Bomb Defusal, House Calls, Drug Busts, and Arrest Warrants. (Some missions may have multiple properties of each kind of mission, like a bomb defusal mission might have hostages and evidence to gather (drugs)).
Now here's why I WOULDN'T recommend it to some:
-For those with short attention spans (this guy..) this game can get pretty dull at times.
-Very frustrating level of difficulty later on. Enemies have strong body armor and spam grenades, which has the capacity to instantly kill your troopers or kill civilians, resulting in a more difficult (or instantly failed) mission.
-High learning curve: Do NOT, I repeat, DO NOT expect to play as well as the player in the videos, even if you're a strategy game guru. This game punishes hasty mistakes to the max, and early newcomers will have a hard time adapting to the controls and gameplay.
There are plenty of other reasons for me to recommend this game or not to others, but these are my main ones, and the reason I love/hate this game at any given time.

You may like 2 a little bit more than 1, or a little bit less depending on what you like, but it is an awesome game either way.

First of all, I won´t say this game is bad, but it has many flaws.
The game is fun and all, but it gets lame after you finished all the levels on whatever difficulty. The only reason to play though all this again is to get better items, so you can beat it on harder difficulties.
But there is the point.
Getting new stuff is a victim of totally bad game design. You only get to throw some dices and hope to reach the numbers 0 - 7 and you can´t even always get the stuff you want for the class you wanna play all the time.
So you will have to spend hours and days!! to gather stuff, so you can at least use it in the forge.
There are ways to get better dices, but to get the full of it you HAVE to play with others which makes the singleplayer option nonesense.
That brings me to the next problem: the BOTS or AI.
So this game is just Left 4 Dead in the Warhammer universe, but the AI is worse than in this lovely zombieshooter.
The way I see it, the Bot AI in L4D is supposed to keep a little distance to zombies and special zombies while shooting them to shreds, the AI in Vermintide is supposed to beat the S out of every enemy they see... and that is the problem.
The AI will often fall way behind because of ONE enemy they just can´t hit right and if they´re not ported to your position, BAM!, assassin strikes or something else, one bot less.
They don´t have the priority to help other bots or even YOU, "you´re on the ground? not my problem, first I have to slay this ONE rat that´s just not holding still".
They don´t even use their weapons right! I have never seen the Mage Bot use her staff and I use it nearly all the time, I have also never seen the Waywatcher use the bow on spechial enemies, which is supposed to kill special enemies on one hit, when I play as her I always use the damn bow on special enemies.
So imho there are some changes to be done:
1st - make it easier to get items, or at least to get more items in one mission
2nd - the AI needs a total makeover, why not make it possible to give them orders, like "attack that target" or "pick that up"?
Other than that it is a nice game and I bet it´s great if you have friends to fill all the places, but there are people out there who prefer to play alone or just with one other person and those people also pay money for this game, so you can at least give them something for that money.
And because of all that, I just can´t recommend this game. At the moment you just pay for annoying flaws.

This is a great game about booping rat snoots, and has a strong left 4 dead vibe while remaining in the Warhammer universe. The gameplay itself is similar, but it has a progressive loot system, leveling, and 5 playable heroes over 13 maps.
It has some things going for it:
-Fun heroes
-Various gear to play with
-Plenty of versatile missions for it's price tag
-A fairly nice and detailed dark gothic enviroment set deep in warhammer lore
-Lots of rats and types of rats to slay
-Incredibly well voiced dialogue
-Sarcastic ***** of an Elf for you to hate
Also three real problems that seem to have been noticed by most folks
-Performance issues, that seem to be steadily improving each update, but there is still some FPS loss on even high end machines on lower settings.
-The loot system is basically flat out frustrating and most people are not enjoying it. (You need to roll at the end of a successful mission and even if you are lucky and get something half decent, you have to melt down other gear to unlock one of that weapons base bonuses, and it rolls for how much of a bonus again, via RNG. The entire system is RNG based, but in a way that mission rewards do not feel like rewards)
-A lot of hitbox and clipping issues. Any time a problem comes up that causes an exploit where heroes can beat a mission earier or such is fixed within days, but issues like the Rats that can hit well beyond their actual reach, grab you through walls and pull you through them, teleport around, etc etc... don't seem to be getting much attention
That being said, the game is throughly enjoyable regardless, especially with a group of friends. I highly suggest taking a look, more so if you enjoyed Left 4 Dead or melee based FPS games.
Edit: There does not seem to be any content coming for this game fast; and that is really what a game like this needs to stay relevent.
Edit2 July 2016: Still no real heavy content for this game, and given the grind to unlock stuff, I would say it's worth a visit but not a game you will stay with.

I bought this game in early release about a year ago but was too busy to play it until recently (late February 2017).  But I kept up with the reviews, and saw a lot of thumbs down for it.  My experience has been the great with the game, and I'm guessing that a lot of players who gave bad reviews jumped right in to story mode.  I did the opposite, I went in to build mode first because I like exploration games, and also because I wanted to see what the game could actually do.  I have played build and adventure mode, but not story mode yet.  Keep in mind this game was billed from the start as an “open world sandbox adventure RPG game,” and I love sandbox games.
Build mode:
This is the sandbox aspect of the game, and it's fantastic.  The worlds and scenery are utterly gorgeous, and the adventures you can have are enormous.  I jumped in to this first to see what the developers achieved, and it's really nice.  You get all the weapons, some template air/land/water vehicles, turrets, jetpacks-- if it's in the game you get access to it.  Playing this mode first helped me figure out how to use the GUI, controls, and how things worked overall so it was definitely the right move.  Besides being beautiful, it had some nice touches like the music changing with the terrain type.  It was awesome to fly around a helicopter in the desert at night with search lights and then to return to my base by finding my campfires.  I built a quad and tore up the sand, so much fun.
Cons of build mode:  As feedback for the developers I would say that while the fun level of build mode is top notch, what made this great experience feel sterile is the fact that you're completely alone.  Not even a single animal.  There were animal sounds by the beach, but no animals.  Bird sounds, but no birds.  It would be a great touch to add some passive animals just for scenery, or to practice one's hunting skills.  The ability to add an NPC follower or something might be nice too, but non-threatening animals I think are a requisite to complete the beautiful picture of nature they have painted.  This solitary player presence affected the replayability of this mode since it gets boring to play around as the only living creature in these huge worlds.
Adventure mode:
This mode is where you essentially jump in to a map and have choose-it-yourself adventures.  It's the same beautiful scenery, and the seed-generated map I got was the stock planet Maria.  I covered about half of the map and found at least four different kinds of environments so far.  But superimposed on to this grandeur that I saw in build mode was animals, NPCs, and quests (and even dungeons), a nice old school touch that I didn't expect.  In this mode you get the RPG features, like having to gather resources and work the tech trees to advance.  I'm glad I did build mode first so I understood what to do and how things work, which made entering adventure mode even more fun for me.
Cons of adventure mode:  I didn't notice too many negatives about this mode, but one that I saw was glaring.  I think there were two difficulty level choices (easy and normal) for adventure mode, so I took easy just to be safe because I wanted to explore it.  Well, some hit-point related things definitely were not easy.  For example, my NPC follower and I were crossing terrain and these two huge birds started to attack us.  A single strike from a bird resulted in the lost of 75% health, not what I would expect on an “easy” setting for sure.  The same was true for entering one dungeon, we got wiped out pretty quick by the NPCs there, so making sure that the easy setting means “go have fun in all areas” should be considered.
Miscellaneous:
I didn't get the crashes a lot of people reported.  I ran version 1.6 of the game, and I was on a mac mini with 8GB of ram and Intel 4000 graphics.  The game ran very well, with slight lag in the finer special effects but not enough to ruin my enjoyment of the game overall.  I did have a problem with the game consistently loading though.  It would get stuck on the company logo screen and not move on, so I'd have to keep force quitting it and keep trying.  I found a similar “mac loader” problem in the forums so I hope the developers can smooth this out.
Summary:
Planet explorers is a great game, and top notch exploration game in my opinion.  I logged 35 hours on it in the first 3 days of playing it was so much fun.  While it's no longer in early access, it's still a version 1.x of a very large, intricate, and ambitious game.  I supported the developers in the EA phase because I wanted to see it work, and I have done that for other games like Kerbal Space Program.  So if you expect a finished product out of the box you should stay out of all EA and 1.x release games, but if you want a great game where you can build, explore, quest, and just have fun then Planet Explorers is well worth a look.

This game is one of the best I have ever played. I purchased this game on sale, not knowing anything about it, and just thinking the screenshots were cool. I got into the game, and went first into the Custom Battles mode.
The custom battles are fun, but they get old quick. There are only three maps for field battles, and two for siege. They are fun, however, though I feel as though the custom battles are done much better in other DLCs and expansions like Napoleonic Wars and Fire and Sword.
After about a week of having this game, and just playing with the Custom Battles, I decided the game was good enough to recommend to a friend. I decided to try out multiplayer, now that I had a friend to play it with. I will never play anything other than duel mode in Native multiplayer. Players are too good. I like to play this game realistically, but I guess others do not.
Only recently did I start playing the singleplayer, and oh my god, it is amazing. The world is so expansive, and each character has an expansive backstory. The player has so many options. They can decide to be a honorable lord, and to fight to expand their king's kingdom. You can be a harsh bandit, and steal from the rich. You can even form your own kingdom, and appoint lords to fiefs that you conquer.
There is so much below the surface of this game. If you swear your fealty to a lord, you get to see all of the internal strife in the kingdom. You can plot with lords to ♥♥♥♥ over other lords, you can participate in campaigns, complete specialized missions, the possibilities are endless.
Napoleonic Wars is a solid DLC expansion for Mount and Blade: Warband. It adds a lot more content to the game, with bigger and better custom battles, and a much more reasonable multiplayer. Unfortunately, it doesn't have a singleplayer. But worry not! You always have M&B: With Fire and Sword! The multiplayer in Napoleonic Wars is much better than that of Native. Because the guns alone aren't very accurate, and it takes a very long time for each player to reload, players aren't the immortal beings that they seem to be in Native.
If you are looking for a combination of Skyrim and Total War, this game is for you! And even if you get bored, but download one of the thousands of awesome mods.
This game is extremely fun and addicting. Then when you atart to add all of these mods, so much fun.

I usually avoid buying casual games, because there's a seemingly unlimited supply of free ones, and the simplistic gameplay and objectives usually get repetetive quickly.
This one is something special.  The audio, visuals, and gameplay are all very pleasant and relaxing.  It didn't take me long to finish all the puzzles, but I'm content redoing them.  Maybe I just really like clocks. I've spent a lot of time playing this on my laptop while waiting for appointments, airport layovers, or just trying to fall asleep.
There's a few issues with the game that don't necessarily need fixing, but they do take some getting used to, if you're accustomed to putting together table-top puzzles.  The edges of the puzzle pieces overlap in ways that often make it look like a piece you're holding is too big for the space where it belongs.  Unplaced pieces are only shown as silhouettes.  You can't see what color they are, or their actual size until you're holding them.  Unused pieces snap back to their original place on the wheel when you release them, so you can't group them with similarly colored pieces.
If they release more puzzle packs as DLC, I'd be happy to continue supporting this one.

I absolutely loved this game on my Gamecube years back, and when I found a PC vesion, I was excited to revisit what many Sonic fans consider a masterpeice, this game is not a masterpeice.
So the game is split up between 3 sections, Speed (Starring Sonic and Shadow), Mech shooting (with Tails and Robotnik) and the Treasure Hunting (Knuckles and Rouge)
When most people talk about how fun the game is, they are usually talking about the speed sections, and they are some of the most boring Sonic levels I have ever played.  They are all extremely linear and feel mostly the same (set aside a few level gimmicks like a truck).  These were the most fun this game offers though.  The Mech shooting is trying to cappitalize off the Gamma's playstyle in Sonic Adventure 1 and it is not nearly as fun now.  Imagine the Sonic levels, only slower, god awful controls, and has guns.  (So basically it's Shadow the Hedgehog)  The treasure hunting stages are the worst.  There is this "radar" that doesn't show you were the treasure is half the time because it wants you to find them in a set order...  really?  The controls were actually decent during these, only this game does not work very well on a keyboard.
The graphics are ok enough considering how old the game is at this point, but the sound, oh god the sound!
There are some nice music tracks but it lacks variety, 95% of the music in this game is metal, with the only exception being the occasional smooth-jazz or cheesy raps.  During cutscenes the mnusic drowns out the characters so I can barely hear them, which isn't to bad because I'm not missing much here.  The plot is chock full of loopholes, missed oppritunities, unexplained crap, and is generally an uninteresting mess.  Sonic and Robotniks voice actors aren't terrible, but everyone else does an either mediocre job, or one that makes me want to shave off my ears *cough Tails cough*
Oh yeah, I almost forgot about the chao garden, I applaud the devolpers for how deep of a mode this is, and I see the appeal, but it wasn't for me.
This game has aged horribly, even people who played it growing up will notice how lack-lester of a game it really is.

The sequel done right, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is a fantastic game that is better at most aspects than the first game. It answers many of those questions left after the first game, while giving even more new unanswered questions.
Gameplay-wise it hasn't changed much. It gives you an option to play most levels with different characters and corresponding playstyles, some of which are new to the series(like dual-wielding or controlling 2 characters at once). You might notice that overall second game is more gun-oriented, though.
Story is quite well-done, but requires you to know about things that happened in first game to fully understand what is happening. Developers also left a couple of easter egg levels and moments in game that may be non-canon, but provide you interesting alternative storylines.
What made this game extremely popular, however, is its soundtrack, and Wrong Number is even better at it. Music is what gives this bloody violent and chaotically hard game its pulse, sometimes being the only thing that makes you even after 1000 deaths press R and try again.
Overall, I'd call this game a diamond in indie game world. Fans of full melee combat in first game might be slightly frustrated, though. Strongly recommended to play this right after first game.

This game has a very "retro NES / SNES" type of vibe to it which is great!! Combine all those elements with the feel of few of the modern indie titles (Limbo is the main one that comes to mind) throw in some guns & fighting mechanics and it makes for one amazingly beautiful game. Probably the best part of this entire game is the artwork done in the backdrop - I actually found myself almost dying to a hoard of zombies multiple times because I was stopping to admire what was going on in the background. The enviornment surrounding the main character can be described as "alive" and the devs did a great job immersing you into a living hectic world.

Personally, I  would 100% recommend this game if you're a fan of Indie games, Retro Oldschool style side scrollers, and of course Zombie games!! I have never posted a review for a game before. I have never felt the need to... before now. This game is, speaking honestly, one of the worst games I have ever had the displeasure of playing. The concept shows promise, but any redeeming qualities stop there.
From the moment you start the game, you are assaulted by a story and dialogue that would be better suited for a third grade chapter book than any serious game. The main character constantly waffles back and forth between trying to be a stoic badass, or a compassionate, bleeding-heart, post-apocalyptic saint. Note, this is not between scenes, this is line to line, and combined with the less than satisfactory voice acting, results in a performance I would never subject myself to again. The story is cliche and worn out, with random, out of place characters thrown in for the hell of it, and scenes blatantly ripped off from other media.
Now, let's get to the game mechanics. In a word, clunky. Even without the myriad bugs that plague this port, the combination of a physics engine and a platform game results in slow, unresponsive movement that is difficult to control. For example, to climb through a window, the player may press 'up'. However, the game is slow in its response, frequently leading the player to press 'up' again. By this time, the character is finally moving. He climbs through the window, then immediately climbs back out again, leading the player to spam the 'up' button repeatedly to avoid the "shadows" (seriously?) on the other side. This leads to a long, infuriating wait while the character proceeds to climb through the window as many times as you pressed the button. This is only one of the many complaints I have regarding the actual gameplay.
Overall, I must say I regret my purchase of this game and the hour+ I wasted playing it. It was not worth its price despite the fact that I purchased it for 80% off. If anyone bothers to read these reviews before buying it, please, please, please, do yourself a favor and take your money somewhere else.

With each character, you get specific weapons with the ability to change these weapons, Upgrade them and basically level up your weapons. In addition to Gems/Trinkets.
