Warhammer: The End Times - Vermintide is a four player first-person co-op game that borrows heavily from the Left 4 Dead series. I make the comparison early because the similarities are obvious and abundant. Fat Shark have taken Valve/Turtle Rock’s design for the popular zombie-killing franchise and transplanted it into the Warhammer universe, borrowing level design and objective ideas, pacing, UI elements, enemy types and the mechanic of the ‘AI director’ who changes enemy and item placements and types when replaying levels. Even the way the camera pans around at the start of each level before zooming in behind the players is done in exactly the same way as Left 4 Dead. However despite the myriad similarities, there are a few crucial differences that set it apart enough that is shouldn’t necessarily be labeled as a lazy rip-off.
The biggest thing differentiating Vermintide from that other series is the clear emphasis on melee combat. Your primary weapon will be a sword, hammer, axe, mace or some other object designed to cut, bludgeon, or crush your furry opponents. The melee focus isn’t surprising given the developer’s background with War of the Roses and War of the Vikings, and the combat system in Vermintide is a good one, though not perfect.
What is a problem is the poor optimization. The game looks good, with nice textures and lighting bringing the environments to life and imbuing many with thick atmosphere, but during the already messy large combat encounters, the frame rate tends to tank. Even when lowering the settings considerably things would slow down on many levels on my reasonably powerful PC. For this reason, I would advise those with weaker systems to give this game a miss, at least until it has seen some patches to help improve optimization.

Released

Onyx Lute

18th of November, 2016
Singleplayer
Glass Masquerade should be regarded as a relaxing distraction from all the digital killing encouraged and required by the vast majority of video games nowadays. And even though Steam’s flooded with indie puzzles, Onyx Lute managed to create an artistically unique game which so far has no direct rival for its genre. Bear in mind that this is the dev team’s first released project and you will understand just how promising are both Glass Masquerade and any future titles or direct sequels. Many more countries to visit and visually represent, Onyx.
If you’re attracted to stained glass and/or Art Deco like I am, you certainly don’t need a lot of convincing before you actually purchase this game. If you’re relatively new to art and architecture, I shall provide some context for both the terms I mentioned earlier. Stained (or colored) glass has been invented and perfected over the course of several centuries starting from the Middle Ages. It is an art form closely associated with religion and places of worship, but fortunately in our present times, this particular type of glasswork has been used in a larger spectrum, from intricate objects (such as the clocks simulated in this title) to lamp shades. I won’t bore you with the production details, but as you can imagine, it takes great skill and effort to produce or maintain/repair stained glass.
Art Deco is my favorite architectural style. Evocative of a bold new direction in design and while it was first shown in 1925’s Paris, Art Deco is the visual representation of urban progress in many American cities of the 1930s and predominantly, New York. Of course by the start of World War II, Deco design was implemented everywhere from household appliances to means of transportation. A bygone era in which Bugatti was still an original French symbol for automotive art and luxury. In fact, nearly all cars manufactured in the ‘30s were influenced by Art Deco regardless of their brand.
So you have an art house 2D puzzle video game which is filled to the brim with eye candy, without being perceived as ostentatious. All that Glass Masquerade needed now is a topic that its Steam counterparts rarely feature. Animals, plants or cars and ships were out of the picture. What about national symbolism? Yes, that would be quite fitting for the visual style and remain a novelty at the same time. And so it was decided that the puzzles you need to assemble shall address symbolism itself. On an international scale, since the game features 25 nations from all over the globe. You have a puzzle clock for each and every such nation, with no apparent reason for their selection by the dev team. I’m certain that there isn’t a single country on Earth who wouldn’t have enough cultural merit, worthy of being put on display for all to admire. The only problem for Glass Masquerade would be that once you’re done completing those 25 unique clocks, there isn’t any replay value to be found. So perhaps (free) DLC with more nations or a sequel are to be expected once the game reaches the recognition it deserves.
The gameplay mechanics of a classical puzzle game are self-explanatory, don’t you agree? I shall focus instead on the interesting assistance you receive from the game, after you start assembling a new national clock. You have so-called “hooks” for the first few puzzle pieces on the edges, just enough to form an outline and guide you towards piecing together the entire thing, in a timely manner. The developer estimates that it takes around 4 hours to finish all the 25 nations but I think a keen eye coupled with a sharp mind could accomplish this mission in just over 3 hours. Perhaps replay value might stem from attempting to beat your initial time of puzzle completion. They do vary in complexity/difficulty as far as I’ve noticed so far. Overall, Glass Masquerade is worthy of any Steam game collection and it just might be a game in which all players can receive a full set of Achievements, once they finish it. Trading Cards should be implemented too but even at its current price tag, the game is nothing short of great value. Have a break from all that frenetic shooting and relax while admiring art and national symbols.

PROS:
+ Simple and doesn't require a time commitment
+ Very colorful and has some amazing designs on the clock faces
+ Rexlaxing (although puzzles DO record how long it takes for you to complete them, time records are there for you and not meant to make you rush)
+ Low system requirements, so even an underpowered laptop could handle it
+ For this type of puzzle game, the options menu has a lot of features in it
+ Steam Cloud
+ Inexpensive at $4.99 USD (although I purchased it on sale at $3.74 USD)
CONS:
- Almost too simple and straightforward
- Very short (I literally finished the entire game in four hours and I was taking my time) although the store page makes note of this itself, so it shouldn't come as a surprise
- No alternative modes of play
- Not immediately obvious where every puzzle piece goes (as in some clocks have pieces that go on or around the outside of the clock while others don't)
- No reference images to work from, so you're walking into each puzzle blind
- Puzzle pieces aren't always "to scale" so sometimes the piece will fit into a slot that's smaller than it looks
RECOMMEND: Yes. Despite there being some drawbacks to the game, it's a fun, very nice-looking title that's relaxing and easy to learn.

If you're a singleplayer guy like me, then you should absolutely ignore all the negative reviews and get this.
While the setting demands quite some suspense of disbelief (US in a losing war against a "South American Federation"), and the story is no more than standard fare, the campaign is still a *very* enjoyable action romp. We get to fight with the usual special ops tactical team, climbing skyscrapers, stealthing through the Amazonas, infiltrating enemy installations - but also as tank commanders, helicopter pilots, as divers, and even in space - the whole shebang.
Also, we have a dog - how cool is that?
It's still a straight shooter, though: no "safe house" with thousands of useless "crafting" and costume thingies (like in BO3), and no inclusion of "strategy" game elements (like the out of place "strike force" missions in BO2). I for one appreciate that, sometimes less really is more.
The graphics are very good (much better than BO2 and at least on par with BO3) and the controls feel precise and responsive, with a controller at least. I especially like the lean-and-peak-(and-shoot) from cover where the possibility to do so is highlighted by an unobtrusive yellow arrow.
Granted, you will see the end credits after about 8 hours already, but there's alot of replay value due to the variety in mission design. In contrast to BO3 this game will stay on my hard disc for replaying the campaign every now and then.

Half of the time you're interrupted by in-game cutscenes or thrown in a poor simulation where you have to sneak up people with your trusty canine companion, which gets ridiculously boring after the first time. I like the alternative-history take on the singleplayer campaign, but to say they took 'creative liberty' would be much of an understatement. There's also very, very little personality in the game's characters. You really don't care for them.
However, CoD's known for its multiplayer, which should also provide you with the most replayability. Unfortunately, it's terrible. I can't even think of anything positive here. It's boring, continiously re-hashed and all but one of the maps are poorly designed. And as always, the massive amount of DLC's divides the playerbase. I'm not really sure whether the DLC is still worth it by the way, as the playerbase is quite small already as it is.
But what makes the game truly bonkers is this: You can buy 2 weapons for real cash, like a DLC. The SMG variant (the Ripper) of these DLC weapons is so ridiculously overpowered, you're guaranteed to up your K/D rate if you get it. Lets break it down for you: You're paying for a game, then to actually have a fair fight, you're required to pay for an OP gun. I'm not kidding. It's absurd. If you're wondering if Activision's not out for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t cash-grab, here's your proof.
Do yourself a favor, if you're still contemplating buying this game, consider seeking help at a psychiatrist. You must be insane if you were to really give this game the benefit of the doubt.

I booted this game up again recently and played through the story mode.
I really enjoyed it, so it took about 44 hours.
Looking forward to more story, but it plays well to this point, with a rich storyline.
Graphics are good and gameplay is similar to a mmorpg style control system.
Part of the fun of the story was investigating the event that preceeded your arrival to the planet, even outside game I was thinking about what had happend based on the evidence I had at the time.
Building your own bikes, cars, aircraft and aquatic vehicles was also great, though I admit mine were mostly just adjustments from the useful templates. I didn't get around to building Cloud's Buster sword, but I'm sure I'll look into later.
Run down of the gameplay:
I started with a stone knife and leather armor, got a jetpack and enjoyed flight the first, built a small helicopter and got shot down by the locals. Built up a base and then packed it up and moved it to a more defensible location.
Built a train track halfway across the map and fought some sea critters becuase why not?
All in all, for the pricetag you get an adventure and some fun game mechanics, which, while not perfect, are fun to explore.

Wow. What a piece of absolute garbage. The developers really dropped the ball on this one. Bought it while in Early Access, because there were a lot of great ideas. Played it then. It wasn't awful at its stage in development. I thought, "I can see this making a great game someday." Well, that someday came.
Cons:
- Music is just godawful. When it doesn't sound like some cheesy background score from the shopping interface in the Sims, these abysmal vocal tracks play. Why on Earth would I want to listen to music with lyrics in this game? They're not even good lyrics. It sounds like someone on the dev team got their mom's church band friends to record a song for charity. Seriously does not help the tone.
- The character creator interface is not intuitive. I appreciated being able to change my hair to literally any shade imaginable. Other than that, serious lack of ingenuity. Nothing special about it. Might as well have made the player a specific protagonist for all the flavor it adds.
- The cut scenes are blatantly unfinished. No score plays throughout. Voice acting doesn't fit the character models, and sometimes it doesn't even sync. Once again, there is no definitive tone. So I'm stuck wondering what the h3ll I'm supposed to think or feel. This is STORY mode? Where's the story? Might as well not even be part of the game.
- Skipped the tutorial because it was not compelling. I got this far, through the boring character creator, that awful song, a cut scene that made me want to puke, what incentive do I have to sit through what is no doubt a crappy tutorial as well?
- Started on the planet. Right away, the game wants me to talk to some lady who's not feeling well. Probably because we were in a crash. Hang on. I just crashed on the surface of an alien world and you want me to CHAT WITH SOME CARSICK NPC?!?!?!? I then decided to run around. For some reason, this PC game about EXPLORATION has the worst camera controls imaginable. The mouse is virtually useless. The camera slowly turns to point in the direction my character is running... WHAT!? IS THIS 1995!? You have a mouse. USE IT. Oh well. I ran around, picked up some fruit, then I jumped into the ocean and experienced some glitching when I tried to swim. That was the last straw.
Seriously. This game had a ton of potential in development. All squandered because someone's mom's church band wanted to do right by God. ♥♥♥♥ you, God. This is trash. I wish I'd never survived that plane crash in Alaska when I was 11.

Another amazing Sega game, and arguably their final good one of the Sonic franchise. It is just as memorable and fun as the original Sonic Adventure game, but lacks the 'small' amount of free roam it used to have. You select from two teams: Hero and Dark, from which you play as 3 characters in a sequence of missions until the end-game and final boss, which I won't talk about as I wouldn't want to spoil it for anyone.
I played this game when it came out on the Dreamcast, just like Sonic Adventure, and was never disappointed. It as another one of those games I could play day in and day out and holds many memories for me. You are assigned a grade for each level, E, D, C, B and A - A being the best. There are 5 stages to each level with a different objective so that you won't be left with nothing to do. Unless your a pro like me of course;) Ahem, anyways...
Once all stages are complete with Hero and Dark stories, you unlock a final story.
Now let's not forget why we all really play any of the Sonic Adventure games...CHAO!
This game features 3 Chao gardens. A Neutral, Hero and Dark. Hero and Dark gardens can only be unlocked when you have raised a Chao with the respective sided characters. The Chao land features a school, where you can buy items at the Black Market, put your Chao into classes to be taught dances, drawing, instruments and other nice abilities or go to the Fortune Teller to get a badass name. Many hours will be spent here, just like in the previous game. You can send your Chao into races as always to win medals and items for your Chao and also put them into karate matches if you have the DLC.
All in all, it's an amazing game and plays smoother than Sonic Adventure did originally, however both amazing games!

I really liked this game. One of my favorite Sonic games out there, up there with Sonic Unleashed, Adventure DX, and Generations. If you are a Sonic fan, definitely check Adventure 2 out. (Unless you're one of those picky Sonic fanboys, who hate every Sonic game that isn't on the Genesis.) Anyway, you can customize the controls to your liking (My preferred controls are WASD to move around, SPACE to jump, and SHIFT to use a certain ability depending on which character you are playing as.) In this game there are 3 stories: Hero, Dark, and Last Story. There are three different gameplay styles: Speed stages, Shooting stages, and Treasure hunting stages. The Speed stages are for Sonic and Shadow, the Shooting stages are for Tails and Eggman, and the Treasure hunting stages are for Knuckles and Rouge. (There's also another gameplay style that's introduced at the end, but I'm not going to spoil anything, so you'll have to find out yourself!), along with Boss stages. I ADORE the Speed stages. They are amazingly well-designed, and every bit of them is entertaining to run through. I guess the Shooting stages are okay, too, but they can be boring at times. However, one of the things I hate about this game are some of the Treasure hunting stages. Since the emerald pieces spawn randomly, you never know where to look, and the levels can drag on for up to THIRTY MINUTES *Cough cough* Death Chamber *Cough cough*. The boss stages, however, are AMAZING. I especially love the Egg Golem fight with Sonic, the King Boom Boo fight with Knuckles, and yes, even the extremely hard Biolizard and Finalhazard boss fights. I don't have much more to say, as the story is quite long and I can't explain it all in this quick review, so I'll leave it at this. If you like Sonic games, get this game. It is definitely worth your time.

I first saw this game while searching through the deep dark slums of the farthest-back pages of Steam, and was not immediately encouraged to get Door Kickers. It just looked like a bare-bones, top-down shooter with some mediocre ‘tactical’ elements tossed in. I let it be for a while and then came back to it a couple of months later, then decided “what the heck, I’ll buy it”. I had a total blast for the first week, just playing my way through various missions and unlocking various weapons and armor, but after that, I found myself getting really bored. That is, until I discovered the workshop, and let me tell you; that is what makes this game so great.
Gameplay wise, Door Kickers really stands out. None of your soldiers are too overpowered (unless you download god armor from the workshop), so you need to use every last drop of tactical knowledge to keep them alive. Nothing is more frustrating then spending twenty minutes working out a plan and then having all of your troops mowed down by some guy with a machine gun hiding behind a bulletproof couch the instance they kick down the first door. To actually complete a mission you need to buckle down and focus, or you are going to end up with only one guy, cowering in the corner, waiting for someone to come and yell a stereotypical phrase at them then blow your final guy’s head off.
All in all, Door Kickers won’t blow you away, but if you like tactical games, then you’ll have some fun with it. If you don’t like those games, then this is probably not the game for you. The graphics aren’t great, but the workshop makes up for that by having new stuff constantly made every day for you to try out. So give it a try if you feel like it, but if you don’t like this type of game, then don’t waste your money on it.
6.5/10

Deadlight is a sidescrolling platformer/zombie/parkour mashup, something that sounds like a wonderfully fun idea. Sadly, the controls are very clunky and unresponsive, ruling out the "platformer" elements as even remotely enjoyable. The plot is the usual zombie apocalpyse survivor story, it's honestly boring, but this is a game; Deadlight's bad storytelling could be forgiven had the actual gameplay been fun. The gameplay consists of standard slow and slippery platforming and puzzle solving, ontop of really clunky fighting mechanics that leave you more and more frustrated because again, the controls don't work as smoothly as they should. The game *looks* great, and that's about all it has going for it. If either the story or the gameplay was enjoyable Deadlight could have been a fantastic game, but it falls flat on its face.

I've been playing rhythm games all my life, including lots of Dance Dance Revolution, Guitar Hero, Rock Band, Sound Voltex, Beatmania IIDX, Jubeat, etc. Having played audiosurf and Bit. Trip. Runner., I found myself interested in this project back when it was proposed on Steam Greenlight, intrigued by this new idea of a runner/rhythm game with computer generated levels, recognizing a similariity with Vib-Ribbon, which I have never played. When it was succesfully released on Steam, I decided I would try it later. Well now I have and here's the rundown.
I have played through these songs in testing it:
MAX 300 - Ω (actual BPM 150 (was detected))
Saber Wing - TAG (3/4 timing (detected that it wasn't 4/4))
Shades of Grey - Fracas
Blind Justice ～Torn souls, Hurt Faiths～ - Zektbach (contains slowdown at end)
CHAOS - DE-SIRE retunes
The Good:
beatmatching is on point (even recognizing when I threw it a song in a non 4/4 timing)
relatively accurate tempo evaluation (I fed it songs I knew the bpm of and it gave me the correct bpm)
nice, clean visuals
warns player of potential low frame rate (which can mess with gameplay)
The Bad:
Cannot account for time signtures outside of 4/4 (resulting in odd levels with s♥♥♥♥♥tic notes)
does not account for more gradual bpm changes (granted, that is likely difficult with computer generated levels)
locks it's note generation to the beat (1/4, 1/2, and whole notes only) resulting in simple rhythmic patterns
The Different:
difficulty comes from the number of inputs (1, 4, 8, and specific combinations of 8)
I prefer more rhythmic complexity when it comes to timing, so that's why I enjoy playing DDR, SDVX, IIDX, and the like and with this game locking out anything shorter than a 1/4 note, it really feels less entertaining to me. for those entering the rhythm game sphere, this may be some nice fun zoning out, but for people like me, I cannot reccomend it.

I am personally biased in favor of most things Warhammer. However, while the gameplay is fast and the controls are fluid
I recommend this game, but with a few caveats.
Overall: First impression, this game is gory! There is a lot of rat blood and brains and it stains the environment frequently in great volumes. Overall, the gameplay is fast, though a few of the system designs can be frustrating. The potential for equipment upgrades comes only upon succesful completion of a mission. And, since this is a cooperative game your chances for loot are largely dependent upon other people playing well. Mission failures will typically happen near the end of a scenario, which can make the player feel as though the previous 10-20 minutes were a waste of time as the only reward for a failed mission is a small amount of XP. Play with people you know and you are sure to have fun in small doses. Longer sessions can be repetitive.
First the game runs very well on mid-high end systems. I consistenly run 30+ FPS with little noticeable stutter. System specs listed at the end.
Graphics: Screenshots are pretty, especially if you are able to turn up the quality. The art team did a great job with environment and lighting design. The player characters have great textures and animations, with one exception (see below).
Gameplay: The gameplay is smooth, though it is oddly hampered with design choices with animation and feedback.
Where this game falls short from a presentation standpoint is with the animation of the enemies. This is a quite large shortcoming in my eyes. The textures are not an issue. It is specifially the way the rats are animated and interact with the player that makes them appear flat. This can make it difficult to judge their distance from you. Combine this with the fact that the player's attacks are animated the same whether they impact an enemy or not and the player is frequently wondering whether what he is doing is actually effective. This general lack of combat feedback can be frustrating, especially for a new player. I feel that this is a mistake that a more seasoned staff would not have made. Providing combat feedback to the player is crucial in any game.
Another design choice I oppose, though some would disagree with me, is that there are simply too many rats! Their AI is typically to simply charge the players, take a few hits and die. A vast majority of the enemies encountered behave in this exact pattern. Several times per level the players will encounter one or two 'special' rats which can truly make things difficult for the group. This is where most player deaths come from. A majority of the rats slain in each level will pose absolutely no challenge to the group UNLESS one of these special rats is present. In my opinion they may as well not even exist as they are simply filler when faced on their own.
I'm hoping that future patches and expansions refine rat animations and show improved enemy AI to make low level encounters more interesting. I have not experience the game breaking bugs which others have reported.

This game is a classic jigsaw puzzle game. I would certainly recommend it, but at a discount. Here is the practical breakdown:
CONS:
1. The game is too easy and short. No piece rotation and odd boarder shapes made it not challenging
2. There are no difficulty settings, so you can't make the puzzles harder by having it broken into more pieces
3. Pieces do not exactly match the openings they fit in. If it kinda looks like it fits, try it.
4. The pieces are in rings that spin. This is more annoying then helpful and sometime the wheels spin on one side and not the other to reveal other pieces you did not know were hiding.
PROS:
1. Absolutely beautiful. I would actually love to have a time piece that looked like some of these.
2. The shapes of the pieces were also interesting making the game more engaging.
3. The music was relaxing and changed from location to location to prevent it from being too repetitive
4. Puzzles were stylistic representations of something having to do with the country they are for as did some of the music
***RECOMENDATION***
1. In the settings for the game, make sure you deselect the starting clues. The game was already too easy. I cannot imagine how much faster it would have been with help.
All in all, I really enjoyed the experience of piecing these beautiful artistic works together. If you are in the mood for something quick and visual, this is it.

This game is one of the best I have ever played. I purchased this game on sale, not knowing anything about it, and just thinking the screenshots were cool. I got into the game, and went first into the Custom Battles mode.
The custom battles are fun, but they get old quick. There are only three maps for field battles, and two for siege. They are fun, however, though I feel as though the custom battles are done much better in other DLCs and expansions like Napoleonic Wars and Fire and Sword.
After about a week of having this game, and just playing with the Custom Battles, I decided the game was good enough to recommend to a friend. I decided to try out multiplayer, now that I had a friend to play it with. I will never play anything other than duel mode in Native multiplayer. Players are too good. I like to play this game realistically, but I guess others do not.
Only recently did I start playing the singleplayer, and oh my god, it is amazing. The world is so expansive, and each character has an expansive backstory. The player has so many options. They can decide to be a honorable lord, and to fight to expand their king's kingdom. You can be a harsh bandit, and steal from the rich. You can even form your own kingdom, and appoint lords to fiefs that you conquer.
There is so much below the surface of this game. If you swear your fealty to a lord, you get to see all of the internal strife in the kingdom. You can plot with lords to ♥♥♥♥ over other lords, you can participate in campaigns, complete specialized missions, the possibilities are endless.
Napoleonic Wars is a solid DLC expansion for Mount and Blade: Warband. It adds a lot more content to the game, with bigger and better custom battles, and a much more reasonable multiplayer. Unfortunately, it doesn't have a singleplayer. But worry not! You always have M&B: With Fire and Sword! The multiplayer in Napoleonic Wars is much better than that of Native. Because the guns alone aren't very accurate, and it takes a very long time for each player to reload, players aren't the immortal beings that they seem to be in Native.

Backed this game way back in 2013, tried running it on my potato, gave up, forgot about it.
Installed it on a whim and 75hrs later... wow!
Now, let's start with the bad: This is definitely
a buttery smooth polished triple-A game. Planet Explorers has every mark of an over-ambitious idea that the developer struggled to fulfill.
Gameplay is a tumorous mass of many different systems that range from kinda fun to passable to downright infuriating. I could pick nits for days: The durability system is rage-inducing. The combat could use a
of tweaking. The creation system, while cool in and of itself, has only a marginal effect on gameplay.
That said, there is about as much jank and brokenness here as there was in Skyrim or FO3 at release, and those
triple-A titles with a similar premise.
Now that I took a dump on the game, here's why you should get it:
Planet Explorers gets a thumbs up and a permanent spot in my "good games" bookmarks because it captures the joy and wonder of exploration. Up until the very end of the story playthrough, the game consistently delivers moments of "whoa, this is awesome," or "what the hell is
? I should poke it and see what happens."
There are several different biomes - not a new concept. Yet, unlike those of some other games, the biomes of Planet Explorers actually look, feel, and sound different. There is an astounding amount of (visually) unique flora and fauna. The landscape is sprinkled with several landmarks and points of interest that are
marked on your map until you find them (unless it's for a quest). Sure, my companion NPCs may be teleporting repeatedly into midair behind me, but I don't care because I'm hang-gliding through a massive freakin canyon with like three kinds of weird lookin' birds flying around and HOLY ♥♥♥♥ IS THAT AN
UP AHEAD?!
A word on the story: It's actually pretty good, and, dare I say, engaging! The pacing of the story is interesting as it progresses from pure survival, to exploration, to colonization. There are a few twists and memorable moments. I was also pleased that, despite the glitchiness of the game systems, I did not run into a single case of the story getting stuck or quests getting messed up.
TL;DR: The gameplay systems are quantity over quality due to overreaching ambitions, but the atmosphere is freakin A+ good. 8/10, would explore again.
Aside: The original kickstarter for this game asked for only $100k, and got $140k. Comparing this to all the KS's that got millons and produced jack diddly (looking at you, Broken Age), I'm impressed with what these guys managed to pull off. I'm sure they had other sources of funding, but the fact that they managed to spin up with so little is still impressive.

Journey of a Roach is the second Cockroach-themed game I've played in the last 3 weeks. What's happening to the games industry right now?
Journey of a Roach is a short adventure game (see it like a point n' click game, but with actual freedom of movement) set in a post apocalyptic world governed by radiation worshipping ants. Yeah, sounds believable!
The premise is very simple, but quite charming as well. Your one cockroach friend finds a flower in the middle of the barren wasteland the world has become. And he's quite enamored with it, and runs to tell you... But, unfortunately, he falls underground, and is later impriosed by the Ants.
And there your journey starts, finding your way into their base to rescue your friend, and finally see the beautiful flower.
The presentation of this game was very well done! It's certainly very light-hearted, and even... childish, but in a good way. The only voice-acting is gibberish (in a pretty frantic way, which was funny), and the characters' thoughts is told through pictures and some comic-book like cutscenes.
The cartoony art-style is nothing to write home about, but it fits the theme, and it looked good enough.
The music was also good in relation to the theme, and the overall vibe of the game, but it's nothing I'd listen to outside of it.
The sound design was pretty good, although I could see the voice acting being annoying for some people. I enjoyed it, even with gibberish, they managed to get the point across, and the tonality always fit the character's mood.
In this case, I'd say the whole is better than the sum of its parts! Nothing particularly spectacular, but it all works towards the same goal, and it ends up working out.
How's gameplay, then?
Well, you work your way down, solving a set of puzzles in each floor. You go around collecting items, and trying to combine them until something works. The solutions are usually pretty over the top, and they make sense only after the fact, which can be a bummer. On the other hand, each area is small enough that you won't be backtracking a lot to experiment with stuff, and everything can easily be solved without feeling too frustrating.
One aspect that I hate about point n' click games (which is pretty much the go-to genre for adventure games) is that movement is very limited, and lacks control, is sluggish, etc.
This game eliminates that, having you walking with WASD, which I found really good. It may seem a little thing, but it makes a significant difference to me.
The problem with the movement, is that, well... you're a cockroach, and so you can crawl on walls and the ceiling. Which results in the world constantly moving around, which gave me some serious motion sickness. And this was probably my main problem with the game, everytime I played it, I felt sick, and so I tried to get done with it as soon as possible (not bothering with completing it after finishing the main story).
So, if you have any problems with Motion Sickness in video games... probably pass this one up. Disregard if you think you're fine with it.
So. You go to the several rooms of each floor, and try to solve the characters' problems, in a step towards finding your friend.
The solutions are all pretty silly, usually leading to a chain of reactions that will be amusing, but certainly not very predictable (which is a minus in the puzzling, but again, it's not a major problem).
You'll try to dress up like a radiation-worshipping ant, you'll help a Spider with her baby flies, and you'll launch a nuclear rocket. What could go wrong in this game?!
It's a very simple game, and can easily be finished in 2-3 hours in your first playthrough. The story is amusing, it'll make you smile at times, and it's something good not to worry about. If you're interested, get this, enjoy it, and then be done with it.
There are also "secrets" to reward exploration, and some optional actions for achievement. I haven't bothered with it simply due to motion sickness, but it's good that's it's there!
I like Journey of a Roach for what it was. Nothing groundbreaking, but certainly a charming little adventure game.
P.S.: There was a sections in which they tried to give the game some sort of challenge (?), in which you had to walk through a vent, with blazing "fans" that would get you back to the beginning of the section. However, the perspective was a bit off, and it just felt pointless and out of place. You could easily just not see the fan correctly and get killed. But it was also very short, and once you passed a fan, you could deactivated, so it wasn't frustrating or anything, because of that decision, which was a good call.
But still, I have no idea why it was there, it wasn't very good, it was also very short, and overall out of place, with poor perspective.
It didn't affect my enjoyment of the game, but it was a design decision that I just didn't understand, so I'll leave it here.

Overall a pretty fun game, but there are some downsides to this, what is essentially, platformer. If you have a few bucks and want to kill a few hours, I would recommend this game, but that recommendations does not come without a few caveats.
Story:
The story unfolds in a pretty interesting and creative way. You learn about the world by what is left behind by others and in the form of diary pages. Aesthetically, the game is solid - the Unreal Engine still looks nice. In between "stages" the world is played out in almost a sketched- comic book fashion.
Controls:
The big thing that holds this game back from being great are the controls and the "gotcha" moments - read - unfair deaths. There were many times when I would be playing and would want my character to one thing, but instead he did another which caused me to fall to my death, or be killed by a trap.
Mechanics
Speaking of traps, there is a portion of this game that you must navigate that is filled with them, and this is the "gotcha" moments. You don't die because of lack of skill, or understanding the controls, you die because the games does not make it clear enough what is going to cause your death. There were even a few parts where I wanted to jump from one part to another, but it wasn't explicit as to what was the background and what was in the foreground - that was a bit frutstrating.
Overall:
A solid experience with an interesting story, but held back by, at times, frustrating controls and unclear death mechanics.

I have a love hate relation ship with this game.   I've played through the campaign with bots and others online, and when the game works, its great!
It's currently plagued by a few all too annoying bugs though.
Let me explain.   If for some reason the connection drops and you lose a player, theres about an eighty percent chance the game will start the level over.  If the host quits, or drops, sometimes your entire party is disbanded and you find yourself back at the red moon inn.
Lets talk about latency.  Eventually you learn your weapon's reach and timing to the point where you can kill hoards of rats without ever taking a blow, but if you're connected to a host thats super far away, or somewhere along the route your connection takes a squirrel tries to nest inside one of the CDN rooms, that timing will mean absolutely nothing.
Loot is also a problem.  I dont mind the roll after matches, i think the tomes and grimories are a fair way to boost your odds of getting a decent roll.  I do however no longer feel thrilled when Im lucky enough to get an orange drop(highest tier) either by roll of the dice or fusing.  All you can do with an orange item is upgrade it.  you cant scrap it, you cant trade it.  So even if its horrible, (And believe me, some of them are) you are stuck with it.  You'll find yourself looking at it wishing you could just throw it away.
Here are a few things I like about the game.  It's tense.  The atmosphere created by the music and hoardes of ratmen while you have good or bad teammates at your side will actually wake you up and pull you in.
The Development team is extremely friendly and will even play alongside you if youre lucky enough to join one of their games.  Their names are green and theyll even finish a run with you before disappearing back into the fat shark shadows of mystery.
In its current state, I definitely reccomend trying it out, but buyer beware:  The connection bugs and loot rolls that plague late game will turn you off eventually.  Fighting your way to the end of a level on catacylsm only to have the game decide to start you over because someone disconnected is the absolute worst feeling imaginable.
Full of noobs, your time spent in this game will be that of failing a mission over and over. But you know what you don't need a good team for? uninstall

Open world sandbox allows you to just free-roam and shape your character as you please. There are MANY good mods out there that add so much more to the base game. My first character, Queen Elsa, raised armies to siege castles and ended up ruling her new kingdom of Arendelle by eliminating all the other factions. No doubt, combat is a big focus of the game but is not always necessary in certain situations. Your character can make profit through trading and hiring sellswords for protection. Instead of forming your own kingdom, you can choose to fight for any of the current ones, starting off as a mercernary and ending up as a vassal. Mods can add much more options such as a variety of weapons/armor, increase the usage of diplomacy, or enlarging the map with more locations.
This is a game that is unquestionably worth its price for the amount of hours you can get out of it.

I found myself sucked into the medieval world rather quickly once I began my journey and grew used to the controls.  There are a multitude of things you're not very sure of when you begin your journey but the open world and long range ratifications of choices makes this a very good choice for those strategy game lovers.  On the other hand the 3rd person action sequences also keep the twitch gamer in me awake while I direct my troops to execute a flank, it's very balanced and satisfying.
The downsides would be massive amount of grinding / repetitious activities you have to undergo and how "larger" fights are just a bunch of smalelr fights chained together.  I can see this being a rendering and performance issue but there is definitely something a little disheartening of playing a 920 vs 800 battle played out 70/150 soldiers vs 70/150 soldiers at a time.  Still the only real complaint would be some colision problems when seiging castles and how annoying the interface is at times when trying to access certain options through dialogue and pointless running through the same town to speak to a npc (because they just didn't add the option to the town menu).

Originally I got this in a Humble Bundle, and I have to say I'm quite surprised. Pleasantly so.
This is a gem of a point-and-click adventure game that is neither too easy or too hard. There are some places where you may breeze by easily (and I love a good relaxing game like that), as well as others where you'll be stumped for a little bit. The length of stumped time depends on the individual. I've never personally been good at solving puzzles, so it might have taken me longer than it will you.
But that's okay! If you like point and click adventures, and a good dose of back-and-forth breeze versus challenge, you'll love this game! Add to it that that the sounds these adorable little creatures make will have you squealing if you've any sense of cuteness.
The gameplay itself offers some decent versatility, since you can either use WASD for movement, or just click around. Another fun feature is the thought bubble hints of sorts, though I won't go into more detail than that. The storyline is addictively sweet and genuine, with a lot of character.
It's not really a game I can personally pick up and play for the entire day in one stint, but it's definitely not a game I will easily put down after a few minutes (looking at some of the games in my library, especially point-and-click ones, ugh). I keep coming back because it's a very easy-going, wind-down and relax type of game. It's just amazingly well done throughout, and won't tax you for brain or reflex energy.
I hate insects, by the way. But after playing this game, it ALMOST makes me not want to kill another cockroach I see. That's how effectively adorable it is. The controls are well done in my book, the inventory is easy to use and not at all laggy or clunky, the achievements are fun to get (even the side ones that aren't necessarily part of the storyline), it has steam trading cards, it has character, it has personality.... What more could you want from a game?! And it's not greedily priced, so I'd definitely say it's worth your money.
Choose. A dinner out somewhere that will last you 30 minutes, or a game that will last you many hours? I think people fail to consider the way they'd spend their money otherwise when it comes to games.
Definitely recommend!

While staying just as violent as the original, this addition seems to have a more meloncholy vibe. Yes there is still the fast music and the punishing combat, but all the anger of the original is gone and replaced by a mellow sadness. The cutscenes play slower more calming music, the narritive is more clear and focused. Every character in this game seems troubled, but unlike Jacket, more defeated than enraged. The combat, while it still keeps your pulse up, trys to be more strategic. Many users have complained about the designers use of windows, but i enjoy it. They aren't giving you what you want, they want to keep things unfair. I found myself planning my attacks more precisely than the first and i felt much more rewarded. The gameplay is still mostly unchanged, aside from the smaller collection of masks. Each mask is much more gameplay changing than any mask in the original game. The fans kept me entertained right up until their unfortunate demise. Overall what really defines this game is the music and storytelling. The combat is excellent as would be expected, but the music has much more diversity and style than the original. The soundtrack goes perfectly with the story to make moments feel more emotional. I found myself genuinely invested in the characters, hating some with my whole heart and loving others to death. In the end there is no happy ending. This world of death and violence simply cannot get one, perhaps it doesnt deserve one. However there is peace to the ending. The violence is over, the rush has faded, and like a long, hypnotic fever dream, it fades away. Goodbye Miami, your neon lights are gone for good, did you ever really find peace? Heroes & Generals brings back the WWII era for the first person shooter genre -- and it does so solidly. With historically accurate weaponry, impressive graphics, and fun gameplay, this game is certainly one of the more solid titles out there. Especially for a free-to-play game. While many may complain about the premium content, I do have to say that my experience so far has been fairly balanced. As I play, I've found myself not needing to invest in other weaponry, and that well-placed shots and patience with the standard firearm can reak havock on the enemy. I love its tactical approach to combat, really making you cling to cover as opposed to running out in the open.
Tanks are the only real downfall of this game. Players must buy RPG rounds, which are often times more expensive than the tanks themselves. Ultimately infantry have a very limited capacity in taking down opposing armor with any chance of success. However, I see greatness in this title. Not to many games could return to the World War II era and put a unique spin on it, but Heroes & Generals manages to do so. The game is tactical, immersive, and well-produced. Aside from the occasional Beta bug, this game is fantastic. I certainly recommend this game.

Planet Explorers is a game about exploring alien hostile lands while trying to survive and build your own kingdom. Does it make the exploration worthwhile or shoots itself in the head, let’s find out:
Planet Explorers contains 3 game modes: Story mode, Adventure mode and Build mode.  The story mode is where the real meat of Planet Explorers lies. You start off in a ship that crashed on the surface of a strange planet with only a few supplies at your disposal. From here on you need to scavenge various materials, complete objectives while fighting various hostile creatures and explore the planets and thus the name.
Everything about Planet Explorers screams MMO. From the graphics to the mundane quests, Planet Explorers checks off every box in a MMO genre. First and foremost, you will be grinding a lot to create weapons and buildings but that is expected of a survival game in this age. What really impressed me was the variety present in the game. From the creatures that populate the planet to the amount of weapons and diverse buildings you can build inside the game, everything is varied and creates a truly alien atmosphere.
When you start a game, you are given a few biomes to choose from including grasslands, forests etc. All these biomes are different not only in their visual style but in terms of their fauna. Every new biome had me looking for every new creature I could find and see what it did. Unlike a game like No Man’s Sky where the wildlife rarely attacks you or differs in their actual nature instead of only appearance, the creatures in Planet Explorers are a sight to behold and they cause you to flee in terror when you realize you do not have the proper equipments to actually withstand the mighty beasts. Even the smaller of creatures which appear non-alarming from a distance can easily overtake you when they approach in hordes.
It’s a shame then that the combat in Planet Explorers is utterly lacking in depth. While the weapons are diverse, the feedback of these weapons are nothing more than firing a water gun. You don’t actually feel the impact of a sword striking a massive beast or a gun actually killing an enemy. The hitboxes in the game feel off and there is a certain disconnect between the player and the weapon he is wielding. The movement is also very clunky and the animations are very poorly designed.
The building in Planet Explorers is pretty great though. When you have done the required grinding and are ready to build something magnificent, the building system comes into play. It is easy to use and if you have the required materials, you only need to pick and place the wanted blocks. It is one of the biggest strengths of Planet Explorers aside from its creatures and definitely has appeal to it.
What lets it down though is the UI. While the diverse amount of weapons are good, it hampers the UI down. There are a lot of icons cluttering up the screen and you will more often than not lose an important item in your inventory because it gets so filled up and is difficult to separate from your other items.
The Adventure mode is pretty similar to Planet Explorers. Here, instead of starting on a crashed spaceship, you start out in a town and get quests from various NPC’s. What separates it the most from the story mode is the fact that you can choose the biome on which you want to start and you will most likely get a headstart because of the available resources in the town.
The Build mode is a mode where you are given a biome free of every creature and are left to explore and build. This mode is good for the people who really want to get in depth of the building system and such.
There is also a certain lack of polish to the game which suggests it should have been in Early Access for a few more months as I am doubtful that the devs will continue to support it as they have been till now. The multiplayer is also pretty much dead and I was unable to join or create any game with other human players.
There are both good and bad parts to the game’s visuals. On one hand, the biomes look so diverse from each other and create beautiful vistas along with terrifying new creatures which intrigue your inner explorer while on the other hand, the human character models and the fighting animations are really bad. There is also a lot of texture pop in and that causes the player to break out of immersion.
From the get go, you are treated to one of the most beautiful soundtracks that could have accompanied this game. From the menu to the world itself, the soundtrack is so soothing and melodious that I found myself constantly just drowning down in it. There is no voice acting as to speak of but some of the creature sounds were simply amazing and to the point.
I would have more heartily recommended Planet Explorers had there not been a slew of other survival games on the market. It has some really nice ideas and has a huge potential but is still in need of fixing. Had it still been in early access, I would’ve hoped for the required polish but since it’s fully released, I have to recommend it but only when on a sale.

Had this game for a while and finally decided to play through the Story mode again.  I played through the story a couple of years ago and it ended in the middle of the story, so I wanted to see if it went any further since release.  I managed to finish it this time around to the very end.
That being said.  Not much was improved since my original playthrough to this recent playthrough.  Yes.  The story can be completed.  The beginning of the story was very interesting, but after a while it just felt like elements of gameplay were thrown on top and the story was rushed.
The game had (has?) a lot of potential, but it was thrown away due to the disjointed story pacing coupled with the technical issues that still lurk in the game itself.  Nothing about it seemed smooth and organic.  Things happened so suddenly both story wise and technical wise that the story was barely holding together.
That being said.  From what I got of the story, it IS an interesting multi-layered story set in a very beautiful world (most of the time).  The game has a great range of freedom, at the cost of glitchy engine problems.
More time could have been spending nailing down these issues.  More time could have been spent on things like underground systems (which when you get down to it, all the underground cavern systems are butt ugly and featureless).  This same blandness flows into the mountains and canyon biomes.  Seems most of the time was spent around building up the initial plains area you start in (which is gorgeous) and just starts going downhill from there.
There was a great game being made here.  But it becomes quite obvious as you progress, that a lack of passion and attention petered out at the later stages.

I can not truthfully say that "Sonic Adventure 2" is a good game. But I still play it a lot.
There are three primary gameplay scenarios. Sonic and Shadow run through traditional platforming levels, Knuckles and Rouge fly through scavenger hunts, and Tails and Eggman shoot through gauntlets. The running levels are the best aspect of the game; while they can have significant control issues, Sonic feels good to play. and levels like City Escape are entertaining. I don't mind the scavenger hunts, even with their camera issues and a radar that only shows one target at a time. They're not good enough to stand on their own, but are a change of pace at least. The shooting sections are the only ones I completely dislike. Just tapping the fire button will get you through most levels,  and enemy fights almost entirely hinge on who started firing first.
Much like the original "Sonic Adventure" the narrative is oddly ambitious and serious. A single plot is told from dueling perspectives: the heroic Sonic, and the villainous Shadow. They see many of the same events, but we discover different parts of the story depending on who we play as. Now, I'm not someone who inherently dislikes this tone shift from the 2D games, which just had the light-hearted premise of Sonic rescuing animals from Eggman. But the execution of "Sonic Adventure 2's" story is quite awful. The English voice acting is bad, the animations are sloppy, and the narrative is disjointed. While some of the story problems can be explained away by the different perspectives filling in gaps, the results are two conflicting storys where neither feels complete. And even if you edited them togather, there are still unexplained jumps in the story and inconsistent charaterization. The scenes where Shadow, Rouge, and Eggman discuss their plans on the space colony ARK are the epitome of everything wrong with this games narrative.
Yet, even with all these problems, I still put a lot of time into the game, both on Steam and on Gamecube. The reason is the Chao Garden. In between the action stages, you are able to visit small creatures called Chao, and raise them however you wish. You can power them up with animals you find in the main levels, and have them compete in competitions. This part of the game could have used more activities for your Chao do, but it is a surprisingly deep feature. Half my playtime of Sonic Advnture has been in service raising these mysterious little creatures.
So, my feelings on "Sonic Adveture 2" are contradictory. It is not a good game based solely on its core features: the running, scavenging, and shooting. But the Chao Garden was enough to to keep me playing. There are probably other games with better dedicated pet sims, but "Sonic Adventure 2" did a respectable job.

While staying just as violent as the original, this addition seems to have a more meloncholy vibe. Yes there is still the fast music and the punishing combat, but all the anger of the original is gone and replaced by a mellow sadness. The cutscenes play slower more calming music, the narritive is more clear and focused. Every character in this game seems troubled, but unlike Jacket, more defeated than enraged. The combat, while it still keeps your pulse up, trys to be more strategic. Many users have complained about the designers use of windows, but i enjoy it. They aren't giving you what you want, they want to keep things unfair. I found myself planning my attacks more precisely than the first and i felt much more rewarded. The gameplay is still mostly unchanged, aside from the smaller collection of masks. Each mask is much more gameplay changing than any mask in the original game. The fans kept me entertained right up until their unfortunate demise. Overall what really defines this game is the music and storytelling. The combat is excellent as would be expected, but the music has much more diversity and style than the original. The soundtrack goes perfectly with the story to make moments feel more emotional. I found myself genuinely invested in the characters, hating some with my whole heart and loving others to death. In the end there is no happy ending. This world of death and violence simply cannot get one, perhaps it doesnt deserve one. However there is peace to the ending. The violence is over, the rush has faded, and like a long, hypnotic fever dream, it fades away. Goodbye Miami, your neon lights are gone for good, did you ever really find peace? For those who attempt to play this game on Windows 10, it will crash every 15 mins or so. THERE IS A FIX FOR THIS:
Thanks to SamaelShih, it has been figured out that TabletInputService forces FarCry3.exe to crash, when enabled. To solve the crash problem:
1) Open Task Manager
2) Go to Services
3) Identify TabletInputService (Touch Keyboard and Handwriting Panel Service)
4) Stop the service
5) Launch FarCry3
Service could be re-enabled, when you're done.
Enjoy!

Okay. Let me just say:
I beat this game with 100% achievments in 16 minutes. Not once in a game I have ever played have there been "Achievement Unlocked!" showing up from start to finish. Seriously. This game floods your bottom right corner of your screen until you complete the game.
SCREW LYNE. GET THIS.
We all know why you're here, you want to be able to spell things out in your profile showcases. Well, this game's got you covered. In addition to having every single letter, each letter has an alternate background for each achievment (look at the achievements to see what I mean) which fits better for some people's profiles. In addition to that, Zup also has symbols. Lyne does not.
Good:
- You can beat the game in 16 minutes without knowing what you're doing the first time.
- Calming music.
- Not impossible to get 100% achievements like most other puzzle games.
- You can get the achievements without getting bored of the gameplay (unlike LYNE).
- The only thing you need to beat this game is a simple click of a mouse.
- This game is better than Lyne because unlike Lyne, this game gives a letter achievement for each level rather than each "world". In Lyne, you have to complete 26 levels for each letter achievement. This game, only one level. With that being said...
Bad:
- I mean, I guess it's too short? But in reality, blame the english language for not having enough letters and symbols lol.
8/10 I guess? I mean, it's a straight upgrade from Lyne in terms of letter achievements, but if we look past that, you have a game who is calming with simplistic gameplay and graphics. I don't really see myself coming back to this game, but it is probably something memorable at least.

Hahaha. This is genius.

This is exactly what ZUP! did.
I finished the game in 15 minutes. The gameplay itself is decent, entertaining enough so that farming my achievements wasn't a chore.
But the real power in this game comes from... well, everything outside the game.
The achievements are great, you get every letter of the alphabet, in 2 colors each, for more customizing options for your profile. You even get special characters like !, ?, ~, #, $.
The emoticons are also very smartly done. They're solid-colored squares, which is VERY useful for people doing emoticon art. Again, another genius idea.
Even the badges and backgrounds are interesting enough that people may use them for their profiles.
They really thought of everything.
To me, this game is a must-buy for people that like customizing profiles... and it's not because of the very average gameplay. I respect that:)

Journey of a Roach is a rather short adventure game which is pretty easily completable in one sitting  (there's even an achievement to speedrun it in 18 minutes which only took me two tries.)  It uses silent storytelling with simple cutscenes telling the simple and rather nonsensical story.  You play a cockroach in an inhabited underground area populated by other bugs.  The game is very strange with a lot of the things that happen not making a whole lot of sense to me but it all fits pretty well with the bug civilization theme.
The game is unique in two aspects: First you use WASD to move around rather than the mouse like most adventure games, and second, being a bug, you can climb on walls.  There are restrictions however since the camera is in a fixed position so you can't climb on the foreground or background walls.  The camera rotates to follow you which can be disorienting but it works well for the most part.  There are a few places in the game where you will get stuck trying to climb on things but it's easy to get out.
I find that the weirdness of this game doesn't lend itself well to puzzle solving, but the game tries to give you hints through thought bubbles when you inspect objects.  I find it still ends up being on the obscure side which is unfortunate.
I also had strange performance problems in the last section of the game with the game stuttering badly despite my computer having far more power than the game needs.  I posted on the community hub about the problem so hopefully the developers can fix it, but I haven't heard back at this point.
Overall I find this game hard to recommend.  It's rather expensive for the length of the game and the lack of much of a story.  There's a lot of better adventure games out there, and even for $5 more I'd recommend them over this.

Journey of a Roach is a short but sweet adventure game in quite the unusual setting. Playing as a roach you have to move around the scenery on the walls, ground and ceiling. The game also has a collectable achievements and multiple achievements tied to replaying the game; one for beating it without saving, one for beating it twice and then the challenge of the game...beating the game in under 18 minutes. The speedrun might take a practice run or two of the game  to be able to pull it of but its very doable.
3-6 hours (depending on the amount of attempts for the speedrun)

Gently melt the butter in a small pan over a low heat. Place the digestives in a plastic bag and crush to fine crumbs using a rolling pin; you can also do this in a food processor. Tip them into the pan with the melted butter, stir to coat, then transfer to a 20cm springform cake tin (9cm deep). Using the back of a spoon, press them into the base, making sure you seal the edges. Place in the fridge while you prepare the next stage.
If using leaf gelatine, place in a bowl, cover with cold water, soak for 5 mins, then drain. Pour 3 tbsp boiling water over the soaked gelatine and stir to dissolve. If using a sachet, see Know-how, below.
Place the crème fraîche in a small pan with the muscovado sugars and a pinch of sea salt, then gently heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon until the mixture liquefies and the sugar has dissolved. Give the mixture a quick whisk to get rid of any lumps. It should be warm, roughly the same temperature as the gelatine solution. Stir the gelatine and vanilla extract into the crème fraîche mixture, transfer to a bowl and cool.
Place the ricotta in a food processor and whizz until smooth, then add the crème fraîche mixture and whizz again. Pour this on top of the cheesecake base. Cover with cling film and chill overnight.
Run a knife around the sides of the tin, then undo the clip and remove it. Transfer to a plate or leave the cheesecake on the base for ease of serving. Pile the fudge flakes in the centre and dust with icing sugar. Cover and chill until required.

INSURGENCY: MIC is a decent HL2 mod that has recently been rebuilt as it's own standalone game.  Back around 2010 was arguably the glory days of MIC.  Back then, there were always servers up and running, and active clans, and a great community.  However, as time went on, more people seemed to stop playing, and client-side modding became more prevalent.  This game became ruined as a material hack became popular and more servers failed to enforce sv_pure 1.
I'd say that less than 100 people are ever on at once.  Very few servers are ever populated, and even then they're eastern European servers with bad latency and a lacking community.  This mod is dying but hopefully it will live on in the standalone.
The game itself isn't too shabby.  There's Marines and Iraqi insurgents.  Each team has two squads, and each team has a few specialty weapons such as the RPG-7 or M16 with grenade launcher.  The game comes with maps that are all well made and provide a good atmosphere.  A fairly popular map was a rehash of de_dust2 from CS:S.  Weapons damage is more realistic, and there's no crosshairs.  The game is more immersive than Counter-Strike: Source and typical last-gen FPS games.
7/10 for nostalgia, but I'm not going to sink any more time into this one.

Decisions, decisions...
I honestly LOVE this game, it's so charming and so addictive.
HOWEVER
Even after doing calibration, I find the music is still just a few milliseconds out of sync with the button prompts, and when I try to get precisely into the beat of the music, I end up missing steps.
Also, I'm colourblind, so I would appreciate a function where we can decide which colours appear, or if someone could somehow mod the button prompts to be controller-based, like with my Xbox 360 / Xbone controllers.
For example, I have problems with blues / purples and yellows / greens.
This is especially difficult in this game, where I often have just a fraction of a second to notice the prompts indicating the direction of the button.
The reason mods aren't completely effective for this is that colourblindness is SUCH a nuanced condition that it's practically different for everyone who has it, so we should be able to adjust the colours ourselves from within the customization menu.
Lastly I'd recommend some different animations / actions to shake up the gameplay a bit. This game is seriously fun, but after a while you lose interest in what the character's doing and just focus on trying to 100% the song.
Perhaps introduce a story mode? I think you could really get something creative & engaging out of that.
Also: THOSE YELLOW ORBS CAN GO TO HELL.

A generic open world FPS with a lot of stuff lacking that would have made the gameplay interesting,
- Very few weapons and not many customization options (0-2 max attachments). They're also easy to acquire, so you won't have the pleasure of upgrading your gear for very long.
- Can't skip cutscenes.
- Boring "walk slowly through a corridor while on an acid trip" sequences.
- Hunting doesn't reward you with much money.
- Outpots you capture are never attacked (defending would have been fun)
- The loot system is terrible. You loot money, ammo, and useless junk that fills your inventory and which you can sell for more money. And I do mean pointless: you can't do anything at all with it besides selling it.
- The crafting is bad. You just need to get 2-4 skins from a single animal to craft bigger ammo bags. So... just find said animal, kill it, and there you go. Drugs are easy to craft too, they require a few plants and those plants are everywhere on the map. There's just no challenge gathering crafting materials, they should have done away with crafting entirely and made you purchase upgrades instead.
- The skinning animations are... Well, you skin animals by cutting them open and taking their guts, leaving the rest of the carcass behind (skin included). Oh well.
- Looting bodies is often difficult because the same key is used to swap your weapon with the dead enemy's. It's hard to get the "loot body" prompt without getting the "exchange weapon" prompt instead. Also, in order to speak to characters, skin animals or loot bodies you have to stand really close to them and aim at specific parts of their bodies (often you need to stand on the right side of them) otherwise the prompt won't show up. Getting the prompt to show up can take a few seconds of moving around. They must be really skilled programmers because no other game has ever managed that one.
- The minimap doesn't zoom out far enough when you're driving. You have to constantly open the big map to see where you're going.
- Loot and secret items you can collect are displayed on the map with pin-point accuracy. No searching involved.
As for the story, it's poor and badly written.
- You don't feel any attachment to your friends you're supposed to rescue. I wasn't even sure if my girlfriend was actually my girlfriend or just a crush until mid-game when she said she loved me. Neither characters even showed affection to each other until much after she was rescued, instead they felt their old couple arguments were much more important.
- Your friends make a big deal about how you're starting to enjoy killing and are turning into a monster... I didn't get that feeling at all. I just see a sheltered rich kid who is threatened by dangerous people, who nearly faints the first time he has to kill omeone in self-defense, and somehow he manages to single-handedly defeat them and rescue his friends in the process. Combine that with the adrenaline rush you get in a fight and I think anyone would be exhilarated to be kicking♥♥♥♥♥like that in that situation (also, acting tough is probably the only way to stay brave and keep fighting when all common sense tells you that you can't win this fight, you can't save your friends, and if you try you'll just get killed in vain).
- One of your friends is being used as a sex slave and the story just glosses over it. I mean, the abuser is bragging to your face about what he's doing to your friend, and your character doesn't even show the slithgtest bit of anger. Your character does express annoyance that the same abuser sends you on pointless quests though. Priorities, I guess.
- Plotholes: the intro has a pirate tell your brother that he cut up one of your friends. Except he didn't, they're all alive. And you and your brother never even acknowledge he said that, neither character asks which friend it might have been or anything. The game jumps straight to "Let's go save our friends, we just know they're all alive!".

What happens when you blend great ideas and a solid backdrop with lackluster implementation and a lack of playtesting? The sad state of Vermintide, which is such a great game in theory and only a mediocre one in practice.
There are plenty of other reviews that focus on the technical issues, and many that focus on the community ones, but few truly highlight how poorly designed certain systems are.
A loot system "designed" to create a hook does the opposite. The flexibility of choosing a difficulty mode fragments a community rather than unites it. The lack of "newb help" incentive leaves an experienced playerbase with no reason to stand fresh players. A poorly-conceived core gameplay loop is never explained to those who didn't spend days in Left 4 Dead. Melee combat is the star when its feedback is not given the proper UI considerations.
These are but a few of the issues that currently plague the game, a game I wanted to love so desperately.
Put this back in the oven; it's not done yet.

Не каждый раз я вижу игру, которую пройду на все 100%, толком не успев моргнуть глазом, но при этом ощущения неудовлетворения - нету.
Это обзор на минималистическую игру Zup!, где основная тема - взрывы.
Что у нас тут есть. Менюшка для мобильных, около 40 уровней, квадратные блоки разных цветов, имеющие разную роль:
Синий - главный блок, от которого зависит прохождение уровня. Ни в коем случае не ронять в пустое пространство.
Желтые - обычные, существующие для интерактивности после нажатия на красный.
Красные - взрывающиеся, приводящие все на уровне в движение.
Фиолетовые - обычные, намертво твердые, существуют "просто потому что".
Зеленые - движущиеся, пока не прикоснешься к ним, после чего становятся как фиолетовые - намертво твердые.
Ещё на виду у нас "дверь", по которой понятно, прошли мы уровень или нет, и шестиугольные "облака". ... Ощущение, что последние не просто так висят в воздухе.
В чем же задача это минималистичной игры? Честно скажу, я не сразу понял. Сначала я думал, надо взрывать блоки так, чтобы на поле остался только Синий блок, ничего лишнего. Как потом выяснилось, на деле все ещё проще: надо просто добиться, чтобы Синий блок упал на поле.
Когда понимаешь механику игры, а она тут такая же минималистическая, как и музыкальное сопровождение, понимаешь суть игры, а потом видишь, что у тебя ачивки пулеметной очередью выбиваются, ты начинаешь подозревать, что игра какая-то слишком простая. Однако на удивление, наверное зависит от характера самого игрока, игра не надоедает вовсе. Её можно использовать как расслабляющую нервы после работы/учебы/ссоры, и возможно это даже действительно поможет.
Плюсы:
- Минимализм во всем: графика, музыка, механика.
- Взрывать блоки не надоедает, ибо полет все время разный.
- Годиться для перерыва на чашечку чая.
Минусы:
- Разнообразие уровней начинаются слишком поздно.
- Очень маленькая продолжительность и малое количество уровней.
Оценку не буду ставить. Не потому что это мусор, а потому что мне на эти циферки пофиг. Тем более на такую игру.
Единственное, скажу. Есть подозрение, что у игры есть сюжет. Это как минимум говорят некоторые ачивки.

The art style in this game is neat.  With the hash marks on the walls, it would almost looks like a Dr. Seuss environment if there were fewer straight lines.
The game's shortcoming is its puzzles.  I've got several adventure games under my belt now, but this one had some of the most illogical, silly, pointless puzzles I've ever seen.  A good adventure game sets up a logical progression of events that gets you closer to your end goal, but this particular game ends up rather devious in the way it forces you to think about your surroundings (not in a good way).  I think that the puzzles could be more logical and interesting if the interface were better at explaining how to perform certain actions.  There are no spoken or written words, so your success depends on your ability to interpret the pictures and thought bubbles that appear above characters.  To me, that wasn't very fun.
Journey of a Roach tries to be cute, funny, and witty with its few puzzles.  It works for the first half of the game, but in the second half, instead of ramping up the challenge, it ramps up the frustration.  Play a Monkey Island adventure if you want to see witty puzzles done right.

A short game (you even have an achievement for completing it under 18min), but a really funny one. It has some great puzzles, a quite uplifting story with some very charismatic characters full of good intentions, and it doesn't overstay it's welcome.
It has the twist that unlike most adventure games you move the character with WASD or arrows keys and use the mouse only to click on what you want to interact with, provided it is within range. As you play a roach, you get to walk around not only on the floor but also on the walls and ceiling, which provides a neat mechanic and some skill based gameplay, as you do have to watch your step sometimes and time your movement.
To wrap it up, it is a great game, worth taking a look. Oh, and it has no dialogue, all the clues are drawn and so even the little ones who can't read can enjoy the story.
