I can personally call this one of, if not the, greatest Sonic games made.
You have 3 types of stages and 3 Stories. The Hero Story has you playing as Sonic, Knuckles, and Tails to save the world, where Dark has you play as Dr. Ivo "Eggman" Robotnik, Shadow and Rouge to destroy the world and build the Eggman Empire. The LAST Story.... well, that's for you to find out. Overall the story is interesting. Sonic has been framed because of Shadow (Shadow only shows up at night, so it's easy to mistake the 2... I think). After trying to escape, the entire military is chasing him, so Sonic aims to clear his name. Tails gets caught up in the trouble, while Knuckles tries to repair the Master Emerald after having to pry it from Eggman. On the other hand, Eggman is trying to find a secret research project done by his Grandfather and meets Shadow who shows him a weapon capable of ultimate destruction, but requires Chaos Emeralds, while Rouge gets caught up in jewel collection. It is an interesting story, and gets dark (heh) at times. It is how a story should be in a level based game. There, but not overbearing. Interesting enough to keep me going, but not distracting enough that the stages are bland in comparison.
In terms of gameplay, you have 3 types of stages. Race, Shooting and Hunting. Race stages are get from start to finish, while trying to rack up a high score, done as Sonic and Shadow. They are mostly about speed too. Shooting stages have you in a mech-suit trying to blow up as much as possible for a high score while traversing stages, done as Tails and Eggman. Hunting stages have you scowering a stage for 3 of ___ (though it's usually Master Emerald Pieces), and using a limited number of hints to guide you, and these are done as Knuckles and Rouge. It's a nice mix that keeps every type of gameplay fresh. And after you beat a stage, you can do challenges in the stage. Usually it is "Beat the stage", "Get 100 Rings", "Find the Chao", "Finish within a time" and "Finish Hard Mode" (which you have to win in order). As you go through stages, you get more powerups, to which every stage (But the Last Story ones) has at least one, but you need to explore to find about half of them. However, other than "Magic Hands" you need almost all of them, so it is rewarding to explore stages.
There is also the Chao Garden, where you can raise a Chao and is almost it's own game. Chao adorable little creatures that evolves based on what you do to it.... and if you are anything like the people I know, you are cruel ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s for kicking them to raise them (and that isn't a joke. You can actually beat them up and they cry. How do you feel now, you monster?). Based on what you bring them, their stats go up and as this happens how they interact with their world changes. Lots of flight? Watch them start gliding through the air the moment you turn your back? Lots of swim? Watch them show off! Then you can bring them to "School" and they learn more things to do such as play an instrument or draw. When you have a few Chao that can do similar things, they actually group up and do these. There has been an instance where I saw an 8 Chao Jamboree in one corner. And then you can put them in contests to race or fight.
The music is also catchy and fitting. It's amazing how much a good soundtrack can complete a game.
That said, it does have some demerits. There are some audio sync issues in cutscenes. "Ha you aren't even go..." "I'LL MAKE YOU EAT THOSE WORDS!" ".....ood enough to be my fake." Also, for Tails lines specifically it sounds like it's that person who is forced to read in class. Some cutscene animation could use improvement, but otherwise that's about it.
Summary: A great game with a lot in it. A lot of variety to keep things fresh, but not too much that it's overwhelming. Has a great story that doesn't get in the way, and has a lot of extras to keep you coming back.

I'm not a fan of the Call of Duty series. Not because they're bad games, but because they take the brightest of their staff, dedicate 100% of their efforts on multiplayer, and invite a homeless man off the streets to toss together a quick campaign for them(Not litterally, but you know what I mean). More and more games are following in their example and it's cancerous. It makes me fear for the future of games. Multiplayer is supposed to be an extra, a neat thing to do after you beat the campaign. The Modern Warfare series were the first ones to have a good, well written campaign that was capable of tugging at your heart strings.
Then comes Call of Duty: Ghosts. I bought it hoping for a decent campaign, and to be able to play with my friends who are all CoD nuts. Ghosts has the best campaign of any war game I've ever played. The Ghosts lore alone was enough to motivate me. I found myself wanting to do pushups while I watched the cutscenes, and I'm not the type to work out. As far as I recall, I've never bothered to buy a CoD game on both console and PC, but Ghosts is worth it.

wow, this game gets a lot of hate.  So does Modern Warfare 3.  I started playing CoD games late into the lifespan of the franchise.  MW3 was the first one I purchased, so that one really set the stage for me.  I then purchased BO:II and didn't enjoy it as much as Infinity Wards work.  So I have a (positive) bias towards the IW games.
After putting off this purchase for years but really wanting to buy it because I was drawn to the lore and the art style, I wanted to finally give it a shot, and I'm glad I did.  I enjoyed every minute of the campaign, and I absolutely love the multiplayer.
I originally bought this with the MP in mind, because I wanted a change of pace from MW3 and BO:II multiplayer, but I was worried the population would be too low.  Not only did I end up completing the campaign first because it was so good, but I enjoy great multiplayer matches as well.  The population has never been above 150 players when I've been on, and I don't know how accurate that metric is, but I've never had a problem joining a game quickly and having a cheater free, competitive match.  The sound plays a much bigger part in this one than previous entries in the series.
One caveat:  the campaign gave me tons of grief from game crashes until I got a handle on things.  I have to run the game in Windowed mode without borders to get the full experience without audio dropouts or game crashes during cutscenes.  Same for multiplayer.  It will eventually crash if I don't run WIndowed without borders.
On to the presentation side, the game looks absolutely stunning, and the campaign does truly feel next-gen.  Many times I was presented with breathtaking visuals, this in mid 2016.  I'm running this on a Sandy Bridge i7-2600 with an AMD R9 390 attached to a Freesync monitor, and it looks gawgeous.  I run at 144hz with no vsync and no screentear.  At 1080p, everything is maxed out except for the Nvidia specific settings like HBAO+ and dynamic hair for the dog.
You have to run the game without setting the aspect ratio to AUTO or else it will use DPI scaling.  Just FYI.  If you're tech savvy and can troubleshoot game crashes, I'd recommend picking this up.  It's an amazing game if you can get it to run.  I was able to get it to run, and I made it a point to get it to run.  I had to try many things, but in the end it was worth it.  It would have been better if the game had better compatibilty, but once I found it's sweet spot, it's been solid.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a fun co-op to play with 3 friends.  The AI is challenging.  The skill cap is high and not necessarily gear dependent.  The crafting is simple, easy to grasp.  Good variety in weapons, maps, and each character has distinct differences.  It looks great graphically.
With that said, Vermintide is extremely frustrating.  The combat system feels sluggish and clunky.  The dodge is only seems to work 3/4 of the time with the small range of the dodge and the reach of the rats; it is challenging, but it doesn't feel right.  Weapon attacks queue, meaning if you double click it will do 2 attack animations simultaneously.  This does not make for responsive gameplay, which matters a lot in Vermintide.  The attack queue is especially noticable when using slow attack speed weapons.  If you aren't playing with friends you will have a difficult time getting through maps on Hard, much less Nightmare or Cataclysm.  Disconnects and crashes plague this game, expect someone to drop out 1/3 matches.  All this on top of the ridiculous loot system.  You must roll dice at the end of each match for an extremely small chance to get what you are looking for, and the item is likely to not even be for the class you are playing. YAY!  Even if you do have a good roll and get the Exotic you wanted, the item traits could be complete crap.  But say you are super lucky and get all the traits you dreamed of on your Exotic, you still have to unlock them in the forge with a chance to get between X%-X%.  Good luck!

Ending statement: Fantastic potential, I'd love to recommend. But it's broken at the moment. Not unplayable, certainly, but floaty/glitchy/makes-you-sigh-y enough to make you quit out of frustration. I'll perservere though, hoping this game will get patched and i'll flip this to a positive review.

Journey of a Roach is short but sweet. Unlike a lot of point&click adventure games the puzzles are not the result of "adventure game logic", but rather rely on exploring the 3D environment (including up the walls, and across the ceiling). Some of the trickier puzzles use actual line of sight.
The characters and visuals of the game are cartoonish and cute (a mix of cel shading and 2D cut-scenes), while the music is light and bouncy.
Journey of a Roach is a short game coming in at roughly 3 ~ 6 hours for all achievements. A single play through will usually net the majority of the achievements without even trying.  One achievement for completing the game in under 18 minutes usually requires multiple attempts to perfect but is a good indicator of how short the game can be.
If there is one minor criticism of the game, it is that manoeuvring around doorways and other edges can be tricky. This is the result of being able to walk up almost every surface, and many other games that have attempted similar things have suffered in the same way.

During a 50% off sale, the dev Vulpe told me this game was worth more than £7, and that it was the cheapest it was going to be. I quote him directly: "The game will not be discounted lower than 50%". I like to think of myself as a generous man, but his comment on the price not going any lower only brought out my love and desire to take on a challenge. The waiting game began. Months and months passed, and the summer sale had begun. I see Door Kickers with a 60% off tag, but my excitement is contained. Not even a grin or smirk is shown. I wasn't going to give in this easily. It's 3 minutes until the new daily and flash sales begin. I refresh the Steam store at 6PM on the dot. I browse the deals, and to my disappointment, Door Kickers has not been discounted further. A week passes and the 60% is still there.  Not a single daily or flash has contained this game. My mind is filled with Vulpe's manic laughter, I hallucinate him & Gabe knocking at my door. I have nightmares where they tear my wallet from my pants and spend all my money gifting Door Kickers to people I'm not even friends with. I want to take the plunge, but my instinct tells me it isn't over yet. I've been sitting at my computer for 4 days straight now. Just waiting for new sales, refreshing over and over. I haven't slept. I haven't eaten. It's 6AM. I refresh the store for the morning flash sale. There it is. Door Kickers, 75% off. I sit in silence at first. I feel relief, and I feel pain. A tear falls down my cheek, and I click add to cart. I pay £3.75 and the game is mine. I sit back in my chair as the game installs, and laugh like I've lost my mind. I did it, I thought to myself. I persevered and reaped the rewards.
I'm 3 hours into the game, and I start crying. Vulpe, you were right; I can confirm this game is worth more than £7. Thank you for this emotional journey. Well played, Vulpe. Well played.

Great tactical game. Takes a bit to get used to the UI but it works well once learned, it's not a standard rip-off of the Starcraft of C&C interface and this is why people might have a bit of a learning curve before you can get into the gameplay. It only took my an hour to get almost everything memorized, not that bad. This game has random maps, pre-made single maps and campaigns. Going through the single maps alone would take a long long time. Campaigns can take a while especially if you have to restart some particularly overly hard missions. Once you play all those most games would be done and become boring, right? Luckily there is a random map generator. You can set size and enemy parameters, and since you don't know exactly what you are going to run in to it ends up being fun for long periods. Even if I have 5 minutes I can run one or two random killhouse maps. Or if I want to spend 3 hours playing a tactical game I can and it still doesn't get dull.
Tactically there are various ways to overcome each scenario. You can lockpick a locked door or break it down, or you can use special tools to lockpick it faster or break it faster but these tools take up an inventory slot and are heavier. Or you could use a breacher with a shotgun, but that shotgun becomes the primary weapon and is only useful at short range. There is a give and take to each option and all are viable pending your playstyle and how you want to approach that whole level. And this is just locked doors. The constant variation in the maps and multiple ways to approach each type of situation keeps it varied. Some maps you cannot flank the armored guy and have to face him head on, if you do not have the right equipment you will likely suffer. Sometimes there are too many rooms to flashbang each one so you have to adapt to opening doors and clearing rooms in a different way sweeping around the corner from a wider angle. The game doesn't feel dull even after a long time playing. Gameplay is top-notch and the devs plan on adding to it with co-op and multiplayer eventually.
This game has longevity, it hasn't gotten dull yet and I have plenty of hours in it already. It can be played in short spurts or long sessions without an issue. It's a tactical game that requires some thinking. Controls are more than functional and become natural to use with a little bit of time in the game to do exactly what you want down to smaller details like how you want to walk around a corner with a sweeping curve instead of walking straight in. There are various classes that all play differently and can change your play style immensely from one map to another depending on team loadout. You can respec your doctrine points aka skills and you can change classes freely any time you want. I have nothing but good things to say about this game so yes I recommend it. It has been on sale a few times but even full price this is a good one to pick up.

Almost immediately after I’m spotted, the bad guys kill the hostage. I take a brief moment to unleash a string of curses and rack my brain. There must be another route I can take, another plan that would give this scenario a happy ending. I tinker with the map and reset, and soon I hear a meaty splat as the hostage gets killed again.
Door Kickers is a game about cops kicking down doors, and these doors are a lot of fun to kick down. It is also very hard, and I love it for that. Played from a top-down, pausable view, this is the game that happens when Rainbow Six’s planning stage grows up and finds a home on a modern engine. It is also one of the most finely detailed, cleverly executed puzzle games I’ve played in years.
Fog of war
Each mission in Door Kickers starts with a deployment phase. Within this phase, I see the target house as a set of blueprints, atop which I can change shooters’ equipment and starting positions. As missions become more complex, the deployment phase becomes where I make some of my most important decisions. Door Kickers is a great tactical game because it is a great question generator:
Are there narrow hallways? Will all firefights be up close? Are there hostages? Do I have sharpshooter support? Is there furniture? Is there evidence to save? Do the bad guys have bigger guns than me? Every piece of information changes the ideal approach and forces adaptation.
After the deployment screen, the mission begins with time paused. From the paused overview, I drag paths for officers to follow, change the direction they’re covering, and order them to breach a door. This simple array of options becomes a complicated choreography of death pretty fast. In later missions, my eight officers follow a dance routine with hundreds of steps, pauses, shooting angles, and go-codes. Giving these orders is straightforward and malleable, but the interface is missing some important functions. If I give two units overlapping paths (walking single-file next to a wall, for example), I don’t have any way of selecting one trail over another when I want to edit it. To work around this, I have my units walk behind and to the side of each other, but that’s frequently a poor decision, tactics-wise. With eight officers in a narrow hallways, it also gets downright silly.
Some of the other limitations of this system are simply built into the game engine: there’s no crouching or leaning, so the game’s combat takes place entirely on a two-dimensional plane with straight lines. It rarely feels as flat as it is, but there are occasions where I would love to stack a crouched unit under a standing unit, and these are the times when the game’s simulation feels most like a puzzle game and least like a camera looking down on a real-life SWAT situation.

So, here's my final verdict for Far Cry 3. Well, I'm currently doing my fourth playthrough of the game (been doing every difficulty) And I still enjoy it just as much as when the first time I played it. I guess that tells you a little bit if the gameplay/story is good, if not, let me go deeper into it.
Story:
Without spoiling anything, I'm going to briefly tell you what the game is about. You're jason, some guy who was on a nice trip with his friends until everything went downhill. You find yourself caged with your brother on an island full of crazy pirates.
Then you have Vaas, in my opinion one of the coolest villains ever in video game history. Actually, I'm not gonna tell you anything about him, why don't you just get the game and take a look yourself? Throughout the game, you become more powerful, powerful enough to decide you want to take down the people who run the Islands. Are you able to do so, though? You can only find out yourself. There are 2 different endings.
Gameplay:
Far Cry 3 offers a LOT. It's not your regular shooter, no, It's more like.. Hmm, It's quite hard to say really. On Rook Island, you can find plants, animals and useful gear to upgrade your Jason with. You do this by crafting either ammo pouches, medicine, or useful items that can make hunting a little easier. There's quite a lot of different weapons to find/buy, and they all seem to be pretty damn well done. I didn't find any guns that seem underpowered. A single playthrough of the game should take you well over 20 hours, maybe even 30, if you take your time to explore the amazing landscape and secrets the island has to offer. I don't want to go on too much, so I'm just gonna leave you guys to decide wether or not to get the game. Would I recommend it? YES. Absolutely YES. There's nothing you can go wrong with here. Oh, before I miss it, this game support MODS. If you want more of a challenge, try out Ziggy's Mod. It makes the game a lot more challenging by removing the hud, spotting and free weapons.
My final verdict for Far Cry 3 is a 9/10. Only because it wasn't a perfect game, I still wish the multiplayer could be worked on a bit more, but the 9 goes to the singleplayer alone. Thanks for reading my review, and I hope you'll get your hands on this amazing game. :)

I know it says that I haven't played the game much, but I don't think I need to play it any longer than I have. I don't plan on it.
I'm just going to start by saying that I knew that this game was in early access a while ago. I hadn't heard that it released back in November, Earlier today I was playing it, and I was thinking to myself, "I wonder when they plan on releasing this."
I thought this because this game should never have been released. It's so clearly unfinished.
PROS:
A fairly nice atmosphere. The game looks pretty good, and the planet itself seems to be well thought out. The environments are consistent and look alright. The biomes are nice, too. Lots of variety.
Many NPCs to talk to and trade with. There's a few quests in the 'story' mode, but they seem like placeholders that are still holding a place that will never be filled.
The crafting/building system is pretty good, honestly. It's very creative and works well. The building system is also pretty good.
There's plenty of exploration to do, as the map is fairly large. It's fun experiencing an alien planet for yourself and seeing how the developers interpreted a completely unfamiliar situation like that.
Gonna be honest here, I can't think of anything else that's good. Moving on.
CONS:
The sound design in this game is horrendous. It seems like all of the voice acting was done in one take, and all of the music is either incredibly repetitive or just unoriginal. I ended up turning it off because it was mindless noise that was slowly driving me crazy.
All of the textures look like the artists' first attempts at creating them. Most are low resolution placeholders still, and are just unappealing to look at.
The animations for both your character, other NPCs, and the animals (except for the birds, weirdly enough) are incredibly ugly. They don't move naturally and are clearly either unfinished or placeholders, or they weren't cared enough about to finish.
The voice acting for the NPCs that you can talk to is mostly atrocious. Sometimes it's missing entirely, sometimes it doesn't line up with what's on screen at all (the NPC will say something completely different or leave out lines entirely).
The dialogue system is god awful. Your character is either as stupid as whoever decided to release this game early, or they're a sarcastic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. There is no inbetween. You don't have an option, either; it's pretty common to get two choices when talking to an NPC: [sarcastic or stupid comment] or ["No, I'm busy now"]
The quest system is completely broken. I can't get it to work half of the time. Most of the time, your questlog is empty entirely. You have to speak to NPCs for them, and while this isn't an issue, it's not immediately obvious who you have to talk to. At one point, the quest system stopped giving me story quests. I talked to the guy who was *supposed* to give me the next one and he didn't have any dialogue options.
At that point, I gave up and decided to climb the tallest mountain I could find. It was here that I experienced the joys of the animal pathfinding in Planet Explorers.
If a hostile animal sees you, they will NEVER give up trying to get to you unless they are physically incapable (like falling in a river, or dying). Flying enemy spots you? Give up hope for trying to lose it unless you can kill it, because the stupid thing will follow you to the ends of the earth (maria, i guess) trying to kill you. The same goes for land animals; they have a stupidly long detection range, and the moment you enter it, they beeline straight for you.
I bought this game for $25, and it was not worth that amount, at all. If you can get this game for less than $10, or even $5, then I'd say it'd be worth a few hours if you're bored. Otherwise, don't bother. The developers are clearly done with it other than the occasional bug fix update or tiny addition.

This is one of those games that SHOULD be in early access. For the price they are demanding from you for this, it's unfinished and buggy.
LIST OF ISSUES:
The character models are not pretty to look at and are constantly shaking on screen (that could be just me). There isn't a whole lot of customization or armor/clothing choices to make up for it either. As someone who cares a bunch about the look of my avatar, having good armor and weapons to look forward too is great gameplay incentive. But that is missing here.
At one point, all of the items in the game got their labels switched around. For the rest of my playthrough, dirt blocks were called "Carrot seeds" and arrows were "Motor Tires" for example.
The world is very nice looking and vast, but it's empty and uneventful, besides the plants and trees you can gather. If you're going to make a BIG world, you need to actually HAVE things IN it.
The audio work is a mess. Random sounds come from all sides of you and hardly ever sync with the actual direction it's supposed to come from. The ocean could be on my left and the sound of the ocean will come from the right side. Animal sounds and other similar sounds are so much louder and jarring than eveything else and are completely imbalanced. And while we're on the subject, the voice acting is laughable at best.
I know this game is focused more on exploration (hence the name) but the "survival" part of the game is lacking. It's more of "meter babysitting" than it is actual survival. It's just a distraction rather then feeling immersive.
The one saving grace of this game is the fact that you can shape the land around you freely. You can dig straight into the ground and dig a tunnel, which I actually found fun. Too bad that and nearly every kind of terra-forming in this game is so damn tedious. Chopping a tree can take so SO long, up to 45 seconds sometimes and the digging in incredibly inconsistent. One time you might dig out a bit of land but then the next consecutive clicks only progress you a few centimeters it seems.
In short, the first hour or so made for a good laugh but after that there's not much else to look forward to. And my hopes sunk low when I read around and saw that apparently that haven't done much to improve the game since 2014.
So I'll keep following this game, but I'm definately refunding it for now.

It's like Mine Craft or Landmark with actual gameplay. Don't get me wrong, I like both of those games too, but after building my sky castle in Minecraft I just always hit a brick wall. What to do with it? Well Planet Explorers tries to answer that question. It has huge enemies that can attack your settlement. It has quests, characters, weapons, vehicles and all sorts of stuff.
I should mention the negative points too though. Well... Everything that I just listed there doesn't work all that great. The game looks like a 10 years old MMO (Star Wars Galaxies comes to mind) and the animations range from ok to horrible. There are many bugs and just weird design choices, can't move while mining? Why?
It's really easy to beat pretty much any enemy if you just are patient enough to run in circles and hit them in the back. They are mostly slow and not very smart.
Also I recommend you just skip all the parts where the game tries to hold your hand. In the very beginning there is a tutorial that I guess would have gone through everything in excruciating detail. Thankfully there was a door with the word "EXIT" just behind me. I ran straight though it and was eternally grateful I did. The game does a good job teaching you the ropes as you go on, the tutorial was really unnecessary.
So there you have it. It feels like an unfinished game that has had a very limited budget made by people who had a huge vision. They had a ton of stuff they wanted to put in and not enough resources to actually succeed.
Still, somehow they managed to make a game that is definitely worth your while. And just for making a Mine Craft-like game that actually feels like a complete game rather than a fun tech demo is a feat in and of itself.

Vermintide is Intense. 4 player Co-Op. Hack, Slash, Block and Shoot your way through hundreds of Skaven (Rat Men). Cutting off heads, and limbs. Cutting Skaven in half, All in a first person shooter setting. Just intense almost non stop action. Different enemy types require differnt means of dispatching them, Armored units requiring head shots ect. Makes every battle different and keeps your party on their toes when in combat.
Item rewards such as weapons and trinkets keep you coming back for more. Playing to get the best weapons and the trinkets that boost or defend your character and play style the best. The forge allows you to combine trash weapons and Fuse them into something better. You can also smelt down special weapons to ore and use that to unlock upgrades on your higher tier weapons. Such as a chance to heal the user when killing with that weapon, or replenish your ammo from using that weapon, and even a chance to instantly slay an enemy of any size.
Takes some work and a lot of killing to get the best items and become the ultimate killing hero. But when you do master the Normal difficulty there are 3 more levels to challenge you. Hard, Nightmare, and Catyclism. Each providing higher end rewards for the increased difficulty.
The game is new but it has an endless possibility of growth in the future. Such as new characters to play, and new campaigns. Currently there are 3 Acts, each with 4 missions in each Act. But all this is waring agains the Skaven. A campaign against the Green Skins (Orcs) could be next.
If you like non-stop action. Intense hack and slash killing with friends. With many levels of difficulty for the best of the best gamers. This game is for you.

Deadlight is a Spanish plattformer Zombie game that uses graphics with 2.5 technology. The game focuses on a group of survivors of a Zombie Acopalypse, trying to get to a safe heaven in a world overrun by undead, called shadows. You take the role of Randal Wayne, one of those survivors and a former forest ranger from Canada, who is also looking for his missing family, dissapeared during the chaos that followed the Zombie outbreak.
I must say this is one of the best zombie games I have ever played. It offers a different approach to the genre, paying a tribute to the old plattform games of the 90s, and getting elder players like myself to recall those long time gone fun gaming moments from childhood when playing plattformers, like for example the mytical Heart of Darkness.
The only con I can find is its lenght, the game is rather short. I would have liked it to last more.
Anyway, it is worth to buy it if you find it with price reduction. You won't get dissapointed.

The game isn't terribly long, and some people seem to find the puzzles too easy. Unfortunately, the story is a missed opportunity; the handful of characters, including the protagonist you're playing as, have little depth. I find myself caring about them more than I thought I would, but I'm not really sure why; I don't really know them, and it's a relatively generic "two people separated by the apocalypse" story.
Gamepad support seems fine, although I only played with an X360 controller.

I had my eye on this game for ages, ever since I first searched for rhythm-based games on Steam that uses your own music and found the selection to be sorely lacking. I bought the few that seemed promising at the time - Audiosurf, Soundodger+, Beat Hazard, Symphony - but none of them succeeded in grabbing and keeping my attention for very long. Melody's Escape looked good but it was in beta for a very long time and I hesitated to try it without a sale to act as an incentive. Luckily for me, it went on sale a few months ago and I finally bit the bullet. I'm happy to say that I wasn't disappointed.
The mechanics of the game are really simple: choose the music you want to play to (the game comes bundled with a few songs as well), then choose a difficulty mode and start playing. Melody will run/jump/slide/fly at random and it largely depends on the song. Sometimes she'll also do these neat Matrix-style jumps where everything slows to a crawl for a brief instant. I find the syncronization to be pretty accurate as a whole, but I've never been super picky so your mileage may vary. You can also customize Melody's appearance-- there are several pre-existing options within the game and if you want something fancier, there's an array of user-created mods available in the community as well. (Side note: I'd recommend using a controller to play this game over using the keyboard!)
The best part about any own music-based game is the fact that you're only limited by the amount of music you have in your library. There's no risk of being bored (or disappointed) with the music selection, or being forced to purchase additional tracks just to play a song you actually like. Most of the music I like will never be commercially available to play with, so I appreciate this freedom of choice.
Granted, there are some drawbacks to this game. While I never experienced any motion-based headaches or nausea like some have reported, I do find that faster songs tend to put some strain on my eyes and things can start to blur together after prolonged gameplay. I definitely would not recommend playing this for extended periods of time. On the other hand, I find it really enjoyable to open this game up for 15-30 min of quick gameplay to unwind after a long day at work. It doesn't require much thought, and the presence of a relaxing mode means less pressure to play like a pro (and lower chance of royally sucking at the game).
The fact that you choose your own music to play can also be a double-edged sword: though the music is of your own choice (and let's face it, whose music tastes are as good as your own?), this can often mean 4-6+ minutes of non-stop gameplay depending on the length of the song. I'm starting to think that part of what makes other popular rhythm games like Taiko no Tatsujin so fun to play is the fact that they purposely trim the songs into shortened versions to make it just long enough to be a challenge, yet not long enough for you to feel bored or frustrated. And trust me, it's frustrating when you screw up towards the end of a 5-min song and mess up what would otherwise have been a perfect streak. I'm far too lazy to edit songs just to use them in the game though, so I guess I'll have to put up with that.
In a nutshell, I definitely would recommend this game. Just be mindful of the length of time you play -- and also the length of the song.

So, here's my final verdict for Far Cry 3. Well, I'm currently doing my fourth playthrough of the game (been doing every difficulty) And I still enjoy it just as much as when the first time I played it. I guess that tells you a little bit if the gameplay/story is good, if not, let me go deeper into it.
Story:
Without spoiling anything, I'm going to briefly tell you what the game is about. You're jason, some guy who was on a nice trip with his friends until everything went downhill. You find yourself caged with your brother on an island full of crazy pirates.
Then you have Vaas, in my opinion one of the coolest villains ever in video game history. Actually, I'm not gonna tell you anything about him, why don't you just get the game and take a look yourself? Throughout the game, you become more powerful, powerful enough to decide you want to take down the people who run the Islands. Are you able to do so, though? You can only find out yourself. There are 2 different endings.
Gameplay:
Far Cry 3 offers a LOT. It's not your regular shooter, no, It's more like.. Hmm, It's quite hard to say really. On Rook Island, you can find plants, animals and useful gear to upgrade your Jason with. You do this by crafting either ammo pouches, medicine, or useful items that can make hunting a little easier. There's quite a lot of different weapons to find/buy, and they all seem to be pretty damn well done. I didn't find any guns that seem underpowered. A single playthrough of the game should take you well over 20 hours, maybe even 30, if you take your time to explore the amazing landscape and secrets the island has to offer. I don't want to go on too much, so I'm just gonna leave you guys to decide wether or not to get the game. Would I recommend it? YES. Absolutely YES. There's nothing you can go wrong with here. Oh, before I miss it, this game support MODS. If you want more of a challenge, try out Ziggy's Mod. It makes the game a lot more challenging by removing the hud, spotting and free weapons.
My final verdict for Far Cry 3 is a 9/10. Only because it wasn't a perfect game, I still wish the multiplayer could be worked on a bit more, but the 9 goes to the singleplayer alone. Thanks for reading my review, and I hope you'll get your hands on this amazing game. :)

The game is awesome.  I'm not going to go through and address every complaint on this review page but I will say that almost all of them are unwarranted IMHO.  A lot of the negative reviews seem to think that this is a pay to win game but it isn't.
You only gain a small advantage in actual battle by spending real money, and that is from being able to equip a 2nd combat badge.  They are situational and far from OP or anything approaching it.
Spending real money allows you to gain exp faster and yes you can buy new weapons with money if you want but you can also get them by EXPing and it honestly doesn't take that long.  The time spent EXPing makes you more skilled at the game so it's kind of neccesary since the competition is harsh, you have to work to become a good player and be successful.
That's another thing about some of negative reviews on this page, the combat in game is fine and mostly balanced.  Battles can and do go either way all the time.  Tanks are a little OP, but so are airplane bombs, and headshots, the point is you learn work arounds and how to adapt when necessary.  There isn't really anything OP because everyone has acccess to everything, real money or not.  You just train longer if you don't pay (just play the game!).
As far as not being able to switch to different character loadouts, yeah, you have to level another toon to be able to switch to them in a match.  You load up your seperate toons with different gear such as SMG/anti tank or rifle/grenades or whatever.  Also pretty easy to do and yes, a little time consuming.  But this is one of those games where you have to grind EXP and level up for a long time, A.K.A. a kill to grind type MMO.
You have to spend time playing the game and grinding out that exp in order to get good enough at it to compete with the good players in game.  Which kinda seems like the point of online gaming from the get go if you ask me.
Of the rest of the complaints, some fall under simply not having enough time in game to figure out good work-arounds for problems, they are there.  You can be successful under almost any conditions once you've experienced enough.  Yeah, this game is good.  Learn from the experience and you shall succeed.  There really isn't much negative here besides the occasional bug (betas do that).
It's a fantastic game.  Easily the best FPS I have ever played in a gaming career that started at atari and hasn't stopped!

Is a side-scrolling puzzle platformer, it emphasizes exploration, and it boasts breathtaking art direction. But is Deadlight as good as the Out of This Worlds and Flashbacks from which it clearly takes its inspiration? No, but it’s still really good!
Deadlight is set in 1986 – a time when the absence of modern communication devices amplifies the sense of despair and isolation. Seattle-area resident Randall Wayne is a mess. His wife and young daughter are missing, he’s having painful flashbacks to when he lost his family, and, oh yeah – the city, country, and presumably world have been overrun by.....
You guessed it.
This is a great alternative to the usual Zombie games out there. In fact, it’s Deadlight’s presentation that surprised me most of all. Quite simply, its aesthetic is gorgeous, with a silhouetted Randall in a darkened foreground running for his life in front of a drab, muted, crumbling city.
Which leads to the controls. At times the controls seem wonky as you stager around looking to figure out what to do and at times the platform jumping can be brutal. Oh yeah, Randall is incapable of swiming. So if you land in water for whatever reason, YOUR'E DEAD! Avoid water.
And always remember:

A very enjoyable co-op game which takes alot of its gameplay and defining features from L4D. In terms of bullet points:
The Good:
. Each character is fun to play, each with their own personalities and weapons of choice

. Game plays very smoothly and a very nice choice of graphic options (ALSO FOV!)
. Enemies are very L4D-ish, which is not bad in a certain sense (what aint broke dont fix), however, they have been themed around the skaven and slightly tweaked to fit the theme of the world of Warhammer
. A decent amount of missions  and a good amount of difficulty choices
The Bad:
. AI can be very clunky/derpy/buggy on various missions and can sometimes be useless when they try to pick you back up
. Loot system is very RNG based, sure you can reduce it but sometimes the RNG gods give you the middle finger
. Some maps can be incredibly difficult at times due to their length or placements of objectives such as barrels
. Cannot have 2 of the same character, although this is understandable becuase of lore and balance reasons
. There could be more varying objectives to do instead of the 3 main ones (defend, BARRELS, break 4 things)
Overall:
The game is very enjoyable even with the issues pointed out above, although i will say you should never play with the bots atm until their AI has been improved and have become less buggy. For a warhammer game, it is very good and is in the top 5 warhammer video games in my personal opinion

I wish there was a "neutral" option but there isn't so I will attempt to remember to update my review If/When new updates come out that change the game.
Overall Problems:
* The game plays like it was Very rushed with very little planning or attention to detail.  It has a very complex building system but no explanation as to how to use it, this could be tolerated in an Alpha game, but this should have been fixed before the game left Beta.
* The dialogue by followers is very cheesy and not vey well thought out as is most of the dialogue in the story.
* Folowers don't obey the settings like passive, stay ect. They also can't help you do anything but attack stuff and cut down trees. they do not mine resources or even collect water.
* There are no real directions or explanation of anything in game, you have to fumble through figuring out how building in every mode works and map settings if you are playing adventure mode.
* No tools to collect resources fast, everything is collected by hand, the colony "processor" will collect resources but much slower than you can collect with the lowest level tools.
* Everytime night comes around you get tons of notices that your colonists are too tired to work.
* Your colony Weapons can destroy your own base parts and your own vehicles.
* Colonists don't make their own food, you have to make the food and put it in the storage.
* You have to have all the resources for building in your personal inventory even if you are building with the colony replicator.
* There are still alot of Alpha level bugs.
Story mode:
The story is okay, nothing that I would reinstall the game to play again. The conversation text is full of typo's and outright wrong words in places, and the story just ends.
Adventure mode:
Adventure mode has several settings, but there is nothing explaining map setup, or tool level progression if you choose that option.  There are also not enough options in world genereation.
If you start with all items scripts already learned and there is no need to interact wil NPC's at all, if you choose to start without all the scrips already learned and you have to do alot of quests to learn to build what you need to start a colony.
Resources in this mode seem to be very deep in the gound with no settings that let you bring them closer to the surface that I was able to find.
Multiplayer:
I Played on several servers, the major problem I found was that other players can simply enter build mode and take any materials you place, on one server players just picked up and took all my colony buildings without being part of my colony.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
I will recommend this game if you can find the game on sale for $12 usb or less, don't get me wrong, it's an okay game once you figure out how to do everything but I don't think it's worth the $25 usd price they are asking for it.

I'm coming up on 300 hours with Planet Explorers that goes back to mid-alpha.  Most of my time has been spent in Adventure mode where I can roam the open world and do what I want, when I want.  The open sandbox nature of the game melds well with my playstyle.  As a voxel based game, using the Unity 5 engine, you can change the landscape around you.  Dig down to mine for resources, tunnel out a mountain to lay a monorail or flatten the mountaintop.  Map sizes range from an 8x8km map up to a 40x40km map - which seems huge.  The land is populated by creatures that could be docile or hostile - up to you to find out which is which.  There are also NPC factions that may be friendly - or not!  :)
To me, the biggest strength of the game is the creation modes.  There are two.  First is the Build mode that allows you to create buildings and bases in the open world.  Choice of blocks is a bit limited to square blocks or others based on a 45° angle.  This means you can, for instance, build a symmetrical octagon but not an equal sided hex.  Addition of 30/60° blocks would open up many more possibilities.  Also, blocks are 'fixed' in orientation.  One face of the block will always face north.  Even with these limitations, people have created some incredible things.
The second mode is the Creation mode that allows you to build items from weapons and armor to vehicles that drive or fly.  Orientation of the blocks is somewhat limited here too, but you have more freedom than in the Build mode.  Using things like the mirror modes in the creator, you can build objects that are symmetrical and can then be painted and decaled to give your creation a finished look.  Creation of items can often start with a question of, "I wonder if I can create...".  Many hours can be spent finding the answer to that question.  If you look in the Steam workshop, you can see some awesome things that people have created.  For people who have spent some hours in the Creator, some of these objects can leave them shaking their heads wondering, "How in the world did they do that?"
In short, if you like games like Minecraft, but with a better resolution - of the blocks, at least, give this game a try.  There is a demo, so you can try it out and see if you like it.  I like it, obviously - with the hours I have put in it and will continue to do so.

Hotline Miami was an indie game developed by Dennaton that came out of seemingly nowhere in 2012. It had wonderful, action packed gameplay and an asthetic style reminiscent of the neon colors of the 80's. Its soundtrack was one of high-octane, pulsing techno tracks from artists such as M|O|O|N, Perturbator, and El Huervo. In my eyes and many other's, it was a gem to be remembered. In Hotline Miami 1, there is a sort of vaugeness to the story that lead enough questions open to rouse a lot of curiosity, even though story wasn't the game's focus. In Hotline Miami 2, we focus more on the story, looking into what happened before and mostly after the events of Hotline Miami and how the protagonist's actions lead to another rise of bloodlust and horrifying aftermath.
I won't give away a lot of details to the game, but there are some differences in the original and the sequel. In the original Hotline Miami, for the most part we followed a young man, dubbed "Jacket" by game's fans. Jacket carries with him several animal masks that grant him specific abilities, such as having lethal punches, survive a bullet or two, or run at lightning fast speeds. In Hotline Miami 2, this changes drastically. Having more focus on story, the game will progress throughout the vision of 13 playable characters, each with their own special abilities, though these abilities do seem a bit lacking in comparison to the many masks Jacket could dawn in Hotline Miami. To compensate for this, each character (to my knowledge) has a base ability to be able to survive a single bullet.
As we see through the eyes of the many characters in the story, a lot of questions are answered, and the ending ties the series up in a way so that a resolution may be made. Speaking in terms of gameplay, Hotline Miami 2 seems to eventually forget what made the original so great, which is quite disappointing. The original Hotline Miami strived greatly  in close quaters combat and the ability to vary between melee and gunplay many times in a level. Hotline Miami 2, however, features much larger levels than what the game's mechanics really work well with. In the beginning, this is only somewhat noticeable but it eventually grows to a point where the experience grows to be frustrating. The challenge many times seems to be not so much in chaining a combo together as much as trying to understand how to pass through a level in one piece. This becomes much more prominent in hard mode, but is still noticeable enough in the game's original difficulty.
To briefly touch on the characters of the game, we see through the eyes of Beard, the man who met you at stores in the outro to missions in the first game. This time, we see him during the early 80's, before the events of Hotline Miami, where he fights as a soldier in Hawaii. Handsome and cunning detective Manny Pardo follows closer to his own rules than the law, but this is all necessary to find the evil and infamous Miami Mutilator. His friend, Evan Wright, is a writer who seeks out to right a book about the events of Hotline Miami. His missions uniquely present the possibility of non-lethal approaches, something a bit out of place for the bloodbath that is the Hotline Miami series. In the wake of Jacket's arrest, while some viewed him as a psychopathic murderer, others saw him as a hero. The Fans consist of 5 vigilantes who copy the acts of Jacket, wearing animal masks and indulging in slaughtering any gangs they find. The son of the Russian boss, the final villain in the first game, makes his apperance late in the second one, slaughtering the rival Colombian gang with his own. One of these members, The Henchman, is an Afro-Russian who we touch upon lightly and look into his life, seeing what gang influence has changed him in his attempt to retire.
We also see actor Martin Brown, who acts out horrific scenes of slaughter as his character, The Pig Butcher. Donning a pig mask, and wielding a hammer, he cracks skulls and splatters brains in his slasher flicks. Many interpretations can be made to this character in specific, some people think he may have been actually killing and just hallucinating it as a movie. Looking more to the past, we also see some past characters from the first game and look more into their fates. Jake, the man found dead in Hot and Heavy, is a xenophobic racist American patriot. He signs up for 50 blessings, only to find a snake mask in the mail one day and a marked out address. Given the alternative history to Hotline Miami 2 where the soviet union is still well and alive in 1991 and occupies Hawaii, Jake is more than happy to spill the blood of some Russian gangsters to help "save" his country from the red menace. Finally, we meet Richter, the rat-masked failed assassin of Jacket. We find him caring and tending to his mother while he can, trying his best to disguise unwilling murders from her.
Though Hotline Miami 2 suffers flaws in consistency of level design and gameplay from the first, the soundtrack is still just as amazing. Many of the artists return to compose new tracks for the game, and some new artists even get their start in the OST. Notably, the soundtrack feels a bit darker and more dramatic than the first at some points. While there is still the great techno rush and amazing feel, there are also darker tracks that set an atmosphere of fear, unknowing, melancholy.
Though Hotline Miami 2 is not a perfect game, I would still say it's worth a shot. With the level editor (Hopefully!) coming soon, there should be more replayability and chance for design and sharing in the community. Give it a shot, but come in with a grain of salt. Preferably, bring your salt shakers, instead.

A great action platformer with puzzle elements, Deadlight is a game you'll remember. The realistic gameplay fits the narrative that you're just an ordinary guy who can easily end up dead when trying to cross a street. The platforming aspect is realistic and still enjoyable as hell with quite a bit of variation: often you have to stop to figure out how to get out of a building, other times you're in a flow and tackle obstacles without a problem, and sometimes you have to race with time, turning platforming into an exciting action sequence.
Maybe the most memorable thing about it is its unique atmosphere of the post-apocalyptic 1980's Seattle, reinforced by its grim visuals which is dirty and beautiful at the same time. The narrative is not forced on you, and some of its most interesting parts are delivered via greatly put together environmental storytelling and hidden collectibles. Most of the voice acting is cool, and the soundtrack is awesome as well, fitting to Deadlight's dark atmosphere.
The combat is not the strong point of the game, but it shouldn't be either, because it's about survival, not about killing 'em all. I've preferred the fireman's axe, because managing your very limited stamina proved to be an interesting mechanic, a source of a lot of tension.
The controls are sometimes a bit awkward, for example executing grounded zombies can be done by holding down the strike button, but I often ended up just doing a light strike instead, which often got me killed. Also, the interactive layer is sometimes hard to distinguish from the background.
If you like platformers and prefer games with short but intense gameplay, I bet you'll like Deadlight. It's not just another zombie game. :)

REVIEW UPDATED
Sat, Sept 30th, 2017
I update if patches release. Or if I come up with anything worth mentioning.
Note: The game has dropped dramatically in price, so I'm changing my review to, recommended for Gamers that want to relax and explorer/build random stuff.
Planet Explorers, is a game that (to me) had/has massive amounts of potential- but all the updates dodged ALL of the REAL issues with the game. Causing a lack of depth, in most aspects. Storyline/quest execution is bad and the game is not finished, plain and simple, but on sale, you could still get alot out of it, for very little.
::PROS::
Love the creative aspect. It has kind of 3d editor that allows you to eventually craft just about whatever you want, down to the smallest detail. Armor, weapons, vehicles (jets, cars, air ships, copters, etc), a base, turrets... all kinds of potentially fun stuff; However, polish is needed to make this quick / fun. Most creative crafting system Ive ever come across though, by a LONG shot. People say it is hard to use, but I had no issues. Navigating in 3d space needs work
You can ride animals (should be much a smoother process)
Mineral mining (can be boring mining, but it is not over the top boring, so it is fine.)
Terrain editing. Mining resources and using them allows you to shape terrain. Mining itself also has an effect on terrain, such as leaving jigostic holes in the ground.
You can eventually set up your own camp, and fend off beasts. Adding various upgrades will allow you to farm, train AI skills-as well as followers, let AI run A shop, repair/upgrade gear, etc. Needs fine tuning, more depth, better quests. It's functional, for the most part.
Semi large open world to explore.
An okay solo story mode.
Decent co op. When it works.
80+ hours of game-play to get A solid (non rush) play through.
Has replay value.
Adventure Mode. It sets the world up for A random solo rpg-esk game. Everything is randomely generated. You have the use of A very small talent tree. The donwside is the world generator needs work, and can spawn you at impossible starting locations (like underwater in the middle of the ocean). Can make npc's unuasble also.
Character creation tool. Face details, hair, height, fatness, skin color / hair color, name.
Custom Mode. Choose what% your terrain will be of each biome / choice of the use of talents or not.
Has tall trees and mountains. High sky box, vast landscapes, ocean, rivers, (*sings*) and lakes that were use to). Which feel nice.
Quests. The game has them.
Has sci fi guns. Would love to see more Variety... however you being able craft your weapon to look like whatever you want helps, but still. Basic functions of each weapon (or weapon kits) need some uniqueness/creativity. Just spit-balling here, but maybe some ability mods for weapons, like changing the element of it to fire, ice, poison, etc? or maybe make it you where you change the rapidness of a weapon with some sort of draw back? These are just typical examples. Think unique and creative Devs.
Has A NPC recruiting system. You can take NPC's with you on your travels, or just leave them behind at base camp. The Npc's also have various talents that you can use to your advantage, like bonus damage in combat, gathering.... that's just about it. Sure there are A couple more, just cant recall them currently. They need many more, would add A whole new layer to the game. Currently as is you instantly just think, Meh, liking the idea but nothing is really done with it.
Graphics maxed out looks... okay. Good luck with that though.
::CONS::
Should NEVER have left Early Access. Unpolished elements in game make it very hard to feel immersed. Character walking into large trees when chopping them (every kind), glitching to vertical surfaces when jumping on them, allowing you to climb almost any veritcal surface. Creatures walking on vertical surfaces (serious emersion killer here). Un-responsive Followers; often ill finish A battle before My AI buddies even ingage ..sometimes over 20sec, or worse, they dont engage at all! Not engaging happens around 3-12 battles. AI followers have issues traversing terrain, causing them to telleport all over the place, often being one of the cuases of not engaging the enemy.
Followers wont engage large deadly creatures.
Single player needs A lot of love (*sings*whole lot of love!). Ever since the co-op players starting bitc-hing endlessly, the campaign has greatly suffered. If co-op is what your after you will find far more modding Minecraft to whatever you want it to be, as well as get some mental stimuli. What you cant get in Mincraft is an awesome solo player campaign. I guess you can't get that playing Planet Explores either.
Almost nothing but fetch quests, and A few kill monster quests. Plot holes in story. Very... basic writing. Not mutch happening here quest / storywise, sadly.
Not rewarded for exploration. Meaning ore, basic quests, creatures, and terrain is all your going to find in story mode.
The humanoid species on the planet (one of, if not -the-, primary plot point) serves little to no purpose and almost never utilized.
Needs more Humanoid enemie varieties.
Fear; you never feel afraid for your characters life causing quests to be that much more dull.
Game is too easy.
Still not optimized enough, and runs pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ even on damn good gaming pc's.
Ground vehicles need phsyics ajustments in how they interact with terriain. They need shocks. They tip far to easy. Abit more horse power for hill climbing also.
Un-realisticly Pointy/Sharp/Jagged terrain (big issue causing ground vehicles to be that much more useless)
Dungions in Adventure mode have almost no effort put into them. Walls and floors look super tiled, with ugly, and repetitive textures.
Physics are wonky at best.
AI (though improved) is Mediocre.
Building large amounts can DRASTICALLY slow down your pc.
Trees, grass... well, anything involving nature is just, okay, looking.
Needs more to make the planet your on feel alive. Bugs, birds, wild life, and sounds (or lack there of), etc. Where are the insect/animal sounds at night? or far off beast howls? give me something! How about some voiced NPC banter in camp or in battles. The game is missing soooo much AUDIO.
Including sometimes being unable to hear what npc's are saying at all when you right next to them, crappy/no ambience, causing the game to be very un-atmospheric. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sounding effects. Needs better Vehicle sound effects across the board. Wish they hired me, could of done the game justice.
Needs visual effects.
Ranged combat is sluggish, melee combat is almost useless. Devs should be thinking action melee combat; fast paced, fun /addicting, Or at minimum Darksouls melee combat.

Cant enter most buildings, and most look awful.
Not enough in-game music, and out what little music the game does have, one is worth listening to.
The game has some cool concepts but do to the sloppy core mechanics this game may never reach it's true potential. Planet Explorer devs preferred to focus on adding co-op content instead of making A strong core (smooth combat, fun and function controls, sound, good effects, etc) for single player. Content comes after the core, not before.
::Final Verdict::
The game is worth playing IMO, just go in knowing it is not complete and it never will be. Play your own music. This game first off is a visual feast, alien critters (that must all die for my throne of meat) really look strange and for the most part unique. Except for the monkey things that throw poo and have audio like chittering monkeys... It looks and sounds like an alien world with the same ol biomes given a bit of a twist to make them stand out a bit from the norm... Best example would be the mushroom mountains in the grasslands.
Character customization is in depth enough to make you look different from other people, although i'm willing to bet in multiplayer it comes down to recognizing someones hair and outfit. Speaking of outfits, BOOYAH! The late game outfits again look and feel futuristic, with glowing lights, weird angles and questionable monotone with flavor color overlay schemes... but still far future.
People are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥+ Don't get attached. It's good to see a game with political undertones, because as a green ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I know humans are great at snubbing one another. Right off the bat (Drumroll) Martians and Earthlings (Ba-Dum-Tiss) don't like one another. See even in the future, humans gotta human. In the Story-mode of the game this plays out fairly well and has a good thread to keep RPGers asking questions, and if the option were available, sides would be picked. And some NPCs (Hailey! My blue haired Martian anime sweetheart!) die. Of course if your totally prepared a *few* can be prevented... But that was an alien invasion to fort Badass II that was not prepared for 250 laser turrets, a fully trained combat squad with top end everything... and me, sipping spiced cider watching a futile invasion. (Although some deaths are purely scripted and try as I may with overwhelming destruction, some deaths can't be prevented.)
Now for the bad...
The audio, omg the audio! 95% of the time it was immersive and really reeled me in. But there are moments... Looking at you monkey things. That rip you right out of it, or sent me into fits of throwing my headset across the room. The main music track is glorious... till it hits the high notes that make a beagle howl in pain. Some of the settlement items drown out spoken dialogue with their droning and some you wonder if they even work from being too quiet. Turrets will literally make you crap your pants! (I had to wear pull-ups about 20 hours in.) Especially the gatling turrets. Most people are willing to unzip and let a warm stream of truth leave a messy if slightly briney coating all over the spoken dialogue, myself, not really... It's bad... almost on unprofessional levels. You can read along the words in the text box don't match up, some people are faking accents, Some have residual background noise, or were recorded too quietly and had to have the volume cranked up post production, or just failed with getting and using a popper. Still I have heard and cringed at vastly worse... So I'll give Pathea a pass for just trying to coordinate audio, rather than using a central recording studio.
(It's tough man.)
Usefully useless NPCs. A major facet is colony / resource management. Thus you get people to lord over, and hooboy, do I like commanding weak humans into a pure force of fire wielding death monkeys! And some of them right out of the gate come skilled for such an endeavor. And others make for an exellent fall back crew to be trained up to fill roles highly needed by the legion of "don't you even think of invading alien scum!". The biggest detractor is in storyline mode whereas it's nearly non-existant in adventure mode. You get a guy like Chen who makes for a great first string soldier to train your defense force, but due to quests he's too busy (aka the scripting wont allow it.) Forcing you to train at least one duplicate (who hopefully does not die) to play both primary task and trainer. This happens quite a bit, and super late into the story mode you will have acess to some very skilled individuals who are sorely needed for maximum effect for the colony as a whole, but are nothing more than window dressing after becoming part of your team. Yeah Tank, F-you too buddy... Nice skill set you have there... The farmers could use you man, oh you can't be assigned... And I can't just up and shoot you in the face... crud. (But I'll totally give a pat on the back for adding the Korean girl-child. Having a young person of mid-teen years added immersion to the fact it was a COLONY SHIP and not everyone would be old farts, quite immersive.)
Questing is not really rewarding... kinda. Okay again the RPG elements are spot on, I can't dish on that... not even force a slippery wet fart in the general direction of story questing, both Story and adventure modes do a fairly good job of rewarding the player in that aspect. Do mission = unlock more of the adventure to be told with some sugar sprinkles on top... the pretty colored sprinkles like on cup-cakes. But the side missions is where I can definately squidge out a wet fart with the power to break my thunder buckets gravitational pull. Whats the point? Okay in some cases, you may unlock a follower who will be your high maintainence combat buddy... That's cool. But for the most part, the basic filler fetch quests Do X, Craft X, Gift X, yield nothing... Like that chocolate factory guy (NAME COPYRIGHTED) The same one who angrilly exclaims you get nothing. Side missions are a filler for now that mostly give nothing in return. Grumpy Goblin.
And to the Fugly... the things that make your toes curl up in terror like waking up next to you best friends dog naked.
(Don't ask.)
FIRST Whisky Tango Foxtrot Pathea? Adding theme music to Chen?!? (Latest update) Look if it was an April fools update, I would totally understand. But it drowns out dialogue during story missions. Actually drowns out everything. It is so loud and breaks the living hell out of the fun factor I got to the point of trying to lock him in a box filled with live grenades.
Pull it out, pull it out now! This is one baby (the theme song) that needs smothered in the crib!
The unskippable repeating wonder credits. Okay kudos on the ending and where it leaves us salivating for more... mmm freshly smothered baby meat... Fact is once you hit the credits your new old friend will be Ctrl + Alt + Del. Theres no other way to stop it, and it's on a loop... it just keeps going on and on, like this review.
Random gen NPC mutants from planet X. Random generator needs tweeking so everyone doesn't look inbred. Nuff said.
Seriously though, Despite my belching. This game is filled to the brim so far with many "oooo neet!" moments, excellent crafting, a intriguing story overall, and reminders that you always need to be prepared. So in closing, Like Survival / Exploration / RPG? Definately Get this game!

If you liked L4D then this game is for you. The difference is that there are variations within the classes / characters that greatly change how you will approach the game. Playing mostly as the dwarf with shield and hammer I thought that being a melee centric character would get boring, but instead I found it enjoyable playing the tank role. No fear as i wade into the horde of rats, shield bashing a way through as my team covers my sides. You're constantly checking your blindspots as the skaven will surround you, attacking them or pushing them away before they can land a hit. This game rewards you for precision striking as headshots really matter against armored foes and artful dodges against rat orges.
The loot system is RNG, you can increase your odds by finding better dice, carrying tomes or grimoires which make the mission harder as you have to find them and carry them to the end. It can be annoying in the sense that you may end up with too many good weapons on one character when you've been trying to farm for items for another.
Still for the price it's a fun game and I wish more people played it.

The gunplay is okay, the sounds are pretty well designed, the voice acting is terrible. There are several weapons that you think you can use, but they are just part of the map itself. The animations for the zombies climbing obstacles are terribly done and as a result, hilarious. The map's are mazes, they have so many different directions that lead to dead ends. Every aspect of your movement is either slow or doesn't work half the time. On top of all these things the concept itself is flawed. When you die, you become a much too overpowered version of the undead. You can sprint faster than any human and you are constantly attacking no matter what if you are sprinting. It's even a one hit kill to any human players. Close to the end of any game someone will likely die, and as a result that one player who was bad enough at the game to die (or glitched off of a building) comes back as a zombie and kills everyone else. It is very rare that you will ever win a game, and while that might not be bad, the game is simply not at all fun enough to lose every time at. Don't waste your money, as there is a different, free zombie game with out the "coming back as a zombie" mechanic. It also has working servers and a game that isn't nearly as clunky.

This gloomy contrast stricken game pushes you along a narative that is somewhat addictive if you enjoy the zombie survival genre. Deadlight is a side-scrolling action platform game by developer Tequila Works, initially an indie title, but now published by Microsoft.
You play Randall Wayne, a hard-bitten, haunted man in search of his wife and daughter in a post-apocalyptic North America inhabited mainly by zombies (or as the game calls them, shadows).
Deadlight's graphics are top-notch, even now, years after the game's release. The game is played side on, and you control Randall as a silhouette, similar to Vector. Animations are fluid and Randall's parkour abilities are unbelievably good, not really in keeping with the rest of his background and persona. But they do look nice.
Between and sometimes within each level are graphic-novel-like cut scenes. These are okay, but look a little out of place when compared with the rest of the game's graphics; personally I think the developers would have been better off with scripted cut scenes using the game's graphics engine.
Special effects are excellent, too, including great smoke and very effective 'dream-like' effects in some of Randall's hallucinations.
There's not a large amount of variety in the shadow enemies, but what is there looks good and is again well animated.
Performance-wise, Deadlight runs well on a gaming laptop that was top of the line the year before the game's release, although there are a few particularly busy scenes where the action slows down a touch.
Music is forgettable. It wasn't bad, but I don't remember anything about it being particularly good either. It does its job well enough.
Sound effects are good, with zombie groans and various grunts and action sounds. Weapons are suitable, if nothing out of the ordinary.
The game is supposed to be fully voiced, with Randall's somewhat over-the-top and slightly too intense soliloquys filling most of the voice track. I say 'supposed to be' because there seems to be a bug whereby the sound cuts out during some of the cut scenes, and doesn't return until the next level of the game.
The game plays like a mix between a parkour runner like Vector and a two-dimensional action platformer like any number of other games -- Shank comes to mind first, although obviously Deadlight takes a much more serious approach. You control Randal's movements directly, running, ducking, rolling, jumping, and climbing through a series of mostly very well designed levels. There are a few doozies, though: the helicopter being a good example.
Controllers are fully supported, so I played exclusively with an Xbox 360 controller. This was frustrating: I often found myself climbing up or down ladders or edges rather than moving past them, turning was too slow, and far too often the game left me facing the opposite direction to what I intended, causing Randall to leap to his death. The timed sequences in particular demonstrate the sloppiness of the controls, and you'll probably find yourself doing one or two of them over and over until the Controller Gods decide to smile down upon you.
Deadlight also features combat, using a slow and rather annoying fire axe and two ranged weapons: a pistol and a shotgun. This lets the game down a bit, though; combat feels like there's too much luck involved due to the sloppy controls and randomness of 'killing blows'. I often found myself just ploughing through the shadows in search of the next medkit, because I just couldn't be bothered with the chop-chop-chopping of heavy axe work. Some of the animations are slow enough to be painful, here, though, and the addition of a very restrictive stamina meter is more frustrating than welcome, given the number of times you'll have to swing your axe.
The story in Deadlight starts out interesting, and very similar to The Walking Dead. But it quickly becomes derivative, bland, and all together rather silly, with the often poor writing quality, plot holes, and too-powerful voiceover work making a bit of a mockery out of the seriousness the game tries to portray.
Deadlight includes Steam Achievement integration, but you'll have to be very dedicated to get all of the achievements, and some of them don't always register when they should. There are also a few other bugs I encountered, like freezes when accessing the menu, problems with alt-tab, some interactive objects not working the first time even though they were highlighted, and some ammunition disappearing when starting a new level. None of these are game breaking, though.
Pros:
+ Absolutely fantastic graphics
+ Mostly great level design making for fun and impressive parkour platforming
+ An interesting setting (to start with, at least), particularly if you like The Walking Dead
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Story is silly and overdone, as well as being poorly written and edited in some places
- Over-the-top voice acting
- Combat isn't much fun
- Control is loose and unwieldy on occasion
- Some bugs
Deadlight is an impressive game. The generally good level design and parkour platforming fun make up for the boring combat and sometimes sloppy controls, and the graphics are absolutely fantastic. Just don't take it too seriously, and try to pick it up when it's on sale.

I have always loved top-down shooters, strategic games, and SWAT. So it was a no brainer for me to pick it up when I saw it on sale. But I did not expect how fun this could really be
It starts off really easy, with just simple room clearing. Eventually, you start taking down larger and larger crime. stopping bank robberies and executions, raiding warehouses for dope, and just plain killing bad guys. There is a huge trial and error to it as well. As you get more into the game, you tend to lose a SWAT member or two (if you suck like me anyway). However, executing a plan with no dead SWAT members is just such a thrilling moment. The most memorable moment I have had, with only a few hours into the game, was when I lined up two teams of two outside a confrence room, and they both busted in at the same time. They all lived, and it was all great, until the bathroom shotgun guy killed one of my men.
There is also a lot of weapons and customization options for you to utilize. Various assault rifes, pistols, shotguns, etc. The twist is they are all part of a class system. One class has only pistols, when another will have assault rifles, or another will have shotguns, heck they even have a riot sheild unit.
On a performance standpoint, the game runs really well and is very responsive. Sure, graphics aren't like "Woah, EXTREME REALISM" but they definately are good, especially for a top-down shooter.
Finally, the last little nifty surprise was the map editor. When games have map editors, their life is extended a lot. They also have the ability to upload to the workshop along with other weapon, outfit, gameplay, and more mods!
Overall, I would reccomend this as long as you don't expect it to be the speed of a first person shooter. It is much more strategic, which is something missing in a lot of games now adays. If it's on sale, definately pick it up.
