It's only April and I can already tell this is my GOTY.  This game is just amazing.  If you haven't played the first game, pick it up when it goes on sale, see if you like it, then buy this.  More people need to expierence the Hotline Miami games.
Hotline Miami 2 is different from the first game in multiple aspects.  For starters, in HM1, there was one character (two actually) with tons of different masks with different play styles to choose from.  In HM2 however, we are introduced with many different characters, but with less playstyle choices.  I see this as a good thing.  Instead of getting use to one playstyle, such as running in a room and shooting everybody, you might have to play as someone who can't pick up weapons and can only kill with their fists.  It keeps you on your toes.
The story is expaneded on much more in HM2 than HM1 (You could make an argument that there isn't even really a story in HM1, but whatever.)  Without trying to spoil much, the background and lore behind the game is much deeper than it seems.  You can find newspapers scattered throughout the entire story explaining a lot of things.  I'll leave it at that.
The combat is amazing.  I've been farming a level to try and get the genocide achievement (kill 50,000 enemies) and being able to chop down 14 enemies without dying is satisfying.  Of course, if you do die you can get right back in extremely quickly, so that's not a problem.  There's also a lot more gunplay in HM2, which is nice since HM1 didn't see a lot of gunplay.  I've also heard people say the combat is much floatier is HM2 than HM1, but I can't confirm it.
My one gripe with this game come from level design.  Windows will be your worst enemy.  Running down a hall when suddenly, BLAM, someone with a shotgun off the screen blasts you away.  The levels are just so huge that when something like this happens, you'll have to go through that entire section again.  It's annoying, but you learn to deal with it.  Just always check for enemies before running down a hallway.
Tons of replayability.  There is a hard mode which unlocks after beating the game normally, and there is a leaderboard system.  I just went through the game a third time to get A+ and S ranks on every level (230th in the world on the final level, yeah!).  It's also fun to try and beat your friend's scores.  The level editor is coming ot soon as well so there will be no reason to stop playing this game.
The soundtrack is easily the best part of the game.  It's just amazing.  There are no words to describe it, you just have to experience it yourself.  (The music on the deathwish level is so good.)
TL;DR : Buy this game please

Vermintide is one of those rare games where it's pretty much a rip-off of a great game but where it expands upon it in pretty much all the right places, and underline that pretty much. The Warhammer setting works amazingly with the L4D2 gameplay, and the slight changes over the special enemies combined with the different class purpouse system, with 5 different classes to choose from, adds an RPG like feel to the whole game that really makes you appreciate the effort of the developers in keeping the game as close as possible to the Warhammer universe. Bombs, health packs and potions, all remind you of the '09 valve classic that inspires this game and it's pretty much a blast to go back to campaigning with your friends against countless enemies, scarse supplies and the all new quest for the sweet old loot introduced in Vermintide. The five difficulty levels on each level also add to the replay value, aswell as improving your loot and rewards from completing missions.
Teamwork is essencial in Vermintide and, pretty much as L4D, its live toguether or die alone. Small aditions like patrols to hide from, loot mice running arround and special tokens that increase your end-level rewards also add a fresh feel to the game to break from the monotonous routine of doing the same levels over and over again. The levels themselves come extremely well designed, with 13 very well crafted levels that brings the city of Ubersreik to life in a very dark, gritty way and that follow the journey of five heroes trying to save the town in the Warhammer: End Times setting. The sound design is very good aswell, creating an enjoyable atmosphere throughout the gameplay. The games controls are very much like L4D's with improved, more visceral melee combat that makes combat a very fun experience, with body parts flying arround and piles of corpses painted with blood crowding the heroes as they follow their missions. At the end of each turn, you earn experience towards your player level, something which seems to have no effect other than an ego-booster but it's fun to watch your number grow. The search for loot is also one of the games most atractive points, making you strive for better gear and making your risk leave behind health supplies, or even health points, in order to bring back special Tomes and Grimoires that make your end-mission loot better.
The game is not, however, perfect in what it attempts to do. One of L4D2's most incredible parts was the Director 2.0 AI that pretty much reacted to every move you made in your matches, creating uniquely balanced, varied and challenging experiences for the players and at the same time improving the overall replay value of the game due to how enjoyable it made it. While I find Vermintides AI competent, I think at some point it proved to be quite unbalanced in some aspects, and I won't talk about the usual BOT mind numbness. The game can at some point attack you with large number of very, very difficult opponents, from Rat Patrols to Ogres, and at some points I've met the game sending them all at once against an already debilitated team with very scarce supplies. While I appreciate a challenge, several times I came across impossible to go through situations that would be impossible even at full health, at least in the Nightmare or harder difficulties. Some balancing issues in the technical department make the game run not-so-well in it's highest graphical settings, with unstable framerates plaguing it at some points, something on which the developers seem to be working on, to their credit. Some bugs and exploits are also yet to be fixed, but two patches since the game and its release make me hopefull that the developers are fully aware of the incredible potential of their own game. The games loot system, besides being one of the games most fun mechanics, is also one of the most frustrating due to how limited it is in your part in the looting process. At the end of each match, you roll a set of dice that decide which reward you get from a pre-set random scale of items. Although the items themselves are varied and well designed, the system makes it very hard for you to collect the pieces you want, and it's so frustrating to see that item you so desperately need be lost due to you rolling your dice not too low, but too high!
Overall, Vermintide is a wonderful game full of personality, grit, violence, teamwork and fun. If you enjoy collecting loot, killing mice, RPG-like classes, spending time at an inn jumping arround while you wait for your next mission in your quest to save Ubersreik, L4D's gameplay, the Warhammer setting or any of those combined, then you'll probably love this game. It has it's flaws, but it's also being developed by a dedicated independent team that has struck gold with their revival of one of Valve's most revered classics, and I hope they continue to improve their already great game. The memories Vermintide brings back are priceless, the long nights of L4D2 campaigning, victory, defeat and frustration were sorely missed by gamers all over, and this game's just right to fill that space until valve releases some info on the third instalement of their series. Whether you play alone or with your friends, you'll find many hours of excitement and fun in Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide.

This game can be fun at first, but after I got a little over half way through it I had had enough of its problems. One big problem that tons of people have, myself included, is that there is no sound during cutscenes. I mean there is sometimes, in about 10% of them. The rest of the time they start out with one second of sound then it goes silent, or there just isn't any sound at all. The game's biggest asset is graphics. It looks great, especially the backgrounds. But after not playing the game for over a year and thinking "why haven't I played this in a year but still have it installed" I quickly remembered why.
Despite its presentation and marketing, it is not a zombie game or a survival game. It is a pure platformer and the platforming often isn't very good. You constantly die from dropping too far, missing a jump, not doing something in time, not parkouring right because of sluggish controls, dying because of being control-locked after breaking free from a zombie which causes being unavoidably chain hit into death, or running into a purposely designed death trap put there to get 100% of players on the first try. If not dying, I'm always trying to figure out what the ♥♥♥♥ I'm supposed to do next. That's another big problem for me when I play, Just about every new area I come to has me having to jump around and wonder what the ♥♥♥♥ I am supposed to do. It doesn't ever take long to figure out, it is just incredibly irritating because once I figure it out it's like are you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥kidding me that's all I had to do? But that's just the way the game is designed; half bad platforming half bad puzzles. I mean puzzle action games like Trine are great, but in this game the best way to describe it is like I said, very irritating.
Melee combat sucks too. You run out of stamina from swinging an axe maybe six or seven times at most, which is very ill conceived because if your guy has enough body strength training to parkour impossibly like he is in Assassin's Creed, why can't he swing an axe more than a few times? I'm in terrible shape and I could swing an axe more times than that without becoming tired, especially if my life was at stake in a zombie apocalypse with zombies coming at me. Either way, melee combat is just sluggish and slow and axe swings can and will leave you open to being hit or grabbed even with plenty of stamina.
The last and biggest flaw for me was how like I said if you get grabbed by a zombie and have to press the button a few times to get loose, when you get loose your controls are locked for a brief moment and your guy just stands there allowing another zombie to hit him or latch on. It can put you into a unavoidable chain of hits that leads to a quick death. Oh and the game sometimes has p-ss poor checkpointing.

I really tried to like this game, partly because I like zombies, partly because I like platformers like the first Prince of Persia, Flashback and the like, but the fact is: this game is bad. Deadlight appears a good game in the beggining, and I played it trying to forgive it's problems, but after some time playing I gave up. One of the main problems with this game, at least for me, is sadly game design. The difficulty is VERY artificial. I died a LOT of times because something fell over my head, enemies apeared out of nowhere, the floor fell, you name it. But the game failled completely to tell me a hint of what to expect. You know the first Dark Souls, in that you used to find hints when bad things were about to happen? You won't find them here. Other design decision was very strange too. For example, you are running away from zombies, but you, for whatever reason (a zombie apeared on your way, you fell in some trap, whatever), have to slow down before going to a door. Barriers in this game have simbols that demand you to do some action to go through them. The actions are kicking the barrier pressing a button, running through it (the character hit the barrier with his shoulder) or using your axe on it. This door have a simbol "run through". But you are not running anymore, so you die. "Hey, but why should I kick or shoulder♥♥♥♥♥♥while I have A ♥♥♥♥ING AXE?" - I don't know. But ok, I wound forgive some of these parts, consider it's a game, some good games sometimes do that too and blablabla if the controls weren't SO BAD. You see, every time you press a button, there is some lag in your character actions. At first they won't be a problem. But when thing start getting harder, you start dying because your character refuses to act. Sometimes it becomes pretty ridiculous. You hit some zombies with an axe, they fall, you take your pistol, aim, and one of the (slow) zombies is capable to get on and grab you before you are able to shoot anything! And yeah, your axe just stuns zombies. They are immune to axe damage... There are other problems, but I will stop here. I know some people like the game because of the story. Some even say the gameplay is secondary and that "the game is about the story". I found the story to be pretty uninteresting, to say the least. But I didn't finish the game and certainly won't even try to do that only because of its story. I don't know, I simply can't recommend Deadlight to anyone...

This is almost a very good game.  It took installing it again to remember why I quit playing it.  So, drawbacks first and then what's so great about it.
Drawbacks:
If you're not playing in the equivalent of creative mode, so that you have content, then you have two modes: story and adventure.  In story, there are timesinks as you gradually gain access to scripts that allow you to produce better and better items.  But by the time you have a thriving colony, there's nothing left to work toward except the end of the story.
If you play adventure mode, then you bypass all of the grinding because you begin with all scripts.  However, this renders the majority of scripts useless because you'll skip straight to the best items.  This is the better option for exploring and building a colony.  However, the drawback there is that you only get four NPCs and there's no guarantee that any of them will join your colony.
There are reportedly more NPCs out on the map, in many cases, very far from your starting point.  But the map is not infinite, which means that your progress is still capped.  Once you've built up your colony and recruted all the accessible NPCs on the map, there's nothing to work toward.
How to correct these drawbacks:
Literally all it needs is a tech tree for story mode and new NPCs that join the map to be recruited in adventure mode.  The tech tree would allow the player to choose what to access first, rather than wander until NPCs with the necessary scripts are discovered.  It would still be a bit of a timesink, but the player would have more control over how that timesink is progressed through, and could prioritize goals.  As it is, later scripts are often found at the same time as earlier scripts, rendering even the explore-to-advance angle pointless (ie, finding the script for a copper bow at the same time as iron bow and pistol).
Having new NPCs wander onto adventure maps would allow for expansion of colonies to encompass the map, providing a long term, ongoing goal of expansion.
What makes this game great:
I hate to use the word "potential" when it's so close to realizing that potential.
Imagine Rimworld with a RPG built on top of it, where you control a single character directly.  Imagine first person play in that game, with the ability to design custom items and structures to use and share with others.   Imagine skill trees for your colonists, vehicles, and diverse challenges on the map.
I'm clicking "Yes" that I recommend this game, but I do so with the wish that we could click a "Maybe" option.  The fact is that this game is very close to being something awesome, and at least where adventure mode is concerned, it would be very simple for the developers to realize its potential.  But as of this review, they haven't.  The result is that a rich game leaves you feeling empty, like it could have been so much more, and the simplicity of what it is missing tacks frustration onto that sentiment.
Addendum:
It may be possible to put something together in the World Editor that would alleviate the adventure mode problem.  Perhaps, for example, a map with enough NPCs that can be recruited to make it worth playing.  The first problem is, the DPI scaling for the World Editor is so horrendous that on a modern 4k screen, it can't even be used.  The second problem is that even World Editor maps are randomly generated, and editing terrain (along with practically all other functionality in the editor) is non-intuitive, slow, and frustrating.  All the reasons you can think of to use a World Editor, are reasons not to use it in this case.
I still think that this game can realize its potential, but I'm disappointed that it hasn't gotten there yet.  In this case, it appears that the developers begin with the assumption that people want to play the game, when instead they should stop and think about what would motivate people to play in the first place and then build on that.

This game is surprisngly addicting. At first glance it may seem like a game that you'd get bored of after an hour or two of playing, but it manages to keep you hooked.
The gameplay is simplistic, and even on harder difficulties, it doesn't get that much more complex (unless you are not very good with hand-eye coordination and/or rhythm). But that isn't the big thing of this game; it's the algorithim.
This game uses an algorithim to determine how many notes and "obstacles" there are in the song you're playing, and this, in my opinion, is what makes the game addicting. This algorithim, while not perfect (I'll get to that in a little bit), is still very competent. Whenever you put in a song, it not only determines where notes and obstacles go, but it also determines how much the notes are spread out, and also does its best to sync the timing of the notes with the beat of the song (which always puts a smile on my face whenever I'm "in the groove"). This allows for experimentation of different songs, and this what keept me engaged, and may keep you engaged as well.
It was a lot of fun seeing how the algoritihim interpreted my music, and sometimes it was surprising. It pays more attention to detail than you'd expect. For example, I was playing a song and it had a lot of "static" sounds for effect, and the algorithim payed attention to this and actually made the song kind of hard. But that's also what made it fun.
The only drawback to the algorithim that I can think of is that it shines brightest when you put in electronic songs. If you're someone like me who enjoys non-electronic music. You can still have fun, but it is a little disappointing to know that the game doesn't consider players with other musical tastes as well as it could've.
To end this off, the game is highly moddable and I love it. The game doesn't have a lot of costumes for Melody when you start off, but there are a LOT of good costumes out there thanks to the game's community. It can really make your Melody feel unique when you find something that you like.
TL;DR - Good game. Algorithim is a really interesting idea with a really good (but not perfect) execution, high modability, and good for experimenting with music. 8/10 from me :D

I like this game! It's basically the first game, again but with a lot more characters, a more screwed up story and twice the rage. This time though, you will need to use guns, no questions asked.
PROS
-Gameplay in general is still great, with the intense music adding on
-Soundtrack is amazing, I personally think it's even better than the first (while maybe not as memorable, it really made me feel chills at certain parts)
-Graphics are rad, slightly less ugly than the first and still a gory masterpiece through and through.
-Story. It is way more prominent (and convoluted) than the first one. Gives a lot of back, front, and side stories to the first game.
-Wayyyyy more characters, and more ways to play. Twin Swans with a gun and a chainsaw, a writer who refuses to kill or use guns, the son of a russian mob boss, and a soldier with a resupplying gun and combat knife are just a few of the playable characters. This game will force you to switch it up a lot, so be wary.
CONS
-Mainly the increase of gun reliance and windows here. Far too much hide and seek with enemies, and bullets from across the now huge maps can kill you from somewhere you can't even see.
-The gameplay is not as smooth and flowy as the first, something I really don't like. Sometimes this can be negated I find with the Tony mask, which is my favourite mask in both games. It gives you a lot of stopping power, even against those big goons.
Overall, this is a great game much like the first. I would give it an 8.8/10.

This review was written just over a week after release and with around 8 hours of play both in multi and solo play. I may update this review if any of the cons on my list are fixed.
TLDR: If you love first person melee combat, fantasy settings, multiplayer co-op horde mode type gameplay and are generally a sucker for games that have MMO style equipment loots drops then you need to play this game right now.

The main gist of Vermintide is some really nice locations and a ton of Skaven or rat-people to kill, randomised waves of weak enemies with some more powerful enemies thrown in to keep things interesting. Anyone who's a fan of first person melee combat should not hesitate to check this title out, unless of course they have connection problems and are unable to play games online (see AI section). There are 5 heroes to choose from and there is some nice variety here, a couple of the characters are slightly more tank based and can equip shields, while other are a nice mix of melee and ranged damage with 1 character specialising in pyromancy. Maps are pretty big with lots of little side areas which really encourage exploration.

This game is very easy to pick up and play, especially if you've ever played one of the Left for Dead titles as it is very similar in many ways. The only things that really take some getting used to if you're an inexperienced gamer are the Wizards overheating mechanic, which is essentially a 'press and hold reload', and then the blocking/pushing mechanic which has charges that replenish once you stop blocking or pushing. As always with these types of games staying close to your team members is a key part of success, especially on the harder difficulties. Nobody should be ashamed to start off on the easy difficulty as the equipment you start off with is pretty average, but moving up to normal and then hard should not be a problem once you have some gear.

There is a really interesting loot system in place that rewards you based on certain actions taken during the missions. Certain item pickups in the form of tombs and grimoires can affect dice rolls, these rolls happen at the end of the mission to determine how good your rewards are. To carry these pickups though you will have to sacrifice your healing item slot, so its like a bit of a gamble. The loot you can acquire and upgrade consists of melee weapons, ranged weapons, head gear and other trinkets. There is an overall level but its not tied to any of the 5 characters, so you do not need to level them up individually.

The AI as it stands now is pretty bad, they do not really help with map objectives which is quite annoying, however they are OK in combat but they can really get stuck when it comes to dealing with certain types of special enemies and quite bad when it comes to reviving you when you go down. In some cases they will be standing right next to you and do not revive. As far as I can tell there is no way to ask them to do something, like request for them to heal you or pickup a particular item. I fully understand that this is primarily an online game but it IS advertised on Steam as having 'Single-player'.

Vermintide is a gorgeous game, some top quality texture work especially on the main characters and enemies, I did notice a couple of the weapons had slightly lower res textures but I've only really played with lower level equipment so it may well be that higher end weapons have had more effort put into them. The levels are a visual treat and offer some nice variety in terms of locations, colour palette and lighting, even town areas have a really nice amount of detail and I feel that visually the maps did a fantastic job of immersing you in the experience.

sound design is pretty good, standard atmospheric noises and nice weapon sounds, but nothing outstanding like the sound design you might find in Battlefield or Dead Space. I love the voice acting, the characters often say some pretty funny things and regularly talk about what's going on around them and call out when they see pickups or a dangerous enemy. The music in this game was created by Jesper Kyd, who worked on the music for franchises such as Borderlands, Hitman, Assassins Creed, SoulCalibur and Mortal Kombat. Its quite raw and very well done, not the typical orchestral type of score you might find in other fantasy games or films.

Overall I was quite happy with the amount of options of offer, there is both controller and mouse/keyboard support, FOV slider, only a couple of anti aliasing options though, optional frame rate locks to 30, 60 and above, motion blur toggle, depth of field toggle and the ability to just generally scale the graphics quite far in either direction with many other options like texture quality, light sources, shadows and all that good stuff.

First "tactical" game I've seen in a while that actually deserves the name. One of maybe three games I've played ever, wherein you could actually use real-world tactics, and those tactics not only work, but they work in-game, for the same reasons they work in real life. Button-hooks, cross-overs, "slicing the pie", etc. etc. This could be used as a kind of "sim-lite" for real-world operators-in-training, who just want to see tactics in action, while exploring why they work. Beyond that, it's a fairly entertaining game, giving you all the gear choices, squad-building, and planning that you need for a game to actually be "tactical", a term that is either misused these days, or avoided for fear of losing the instant gratification and hand-holding market. With both one-off missions, several campaigns (with more to come, apparently), random mission generator, and Steam Workshop support, there's endless hours of play available.
I do have some relatively minor complaints, though. For one, any tactical game that uses a weapon and gear unlock system breaks my immersion just a tad. Real world units don't have to unlock weapons and gear. They simply use what they feel best fits the task at hand. So I kind of wish they would have gone the classic Rainbow Six route, where everything is at your disposal from the get-go. Also, there are some rather unrealistic balancing issues. Targets wearing body armor are human bullet sponges. I've watched in amusement, as my full-armored operator unloaded round after round of 5.56 from an M4 into one of these vested "tangos" at point-blank range, only to watch the target giggle, scratch his nuts, wink at my wife, and blow my up-armored operator away with a few rounds from his sub-gun. I'm sorry, but no vest exists that will stop a full-powered rifle round without at least incurring incapacitating trauma on the wearer. But no mind, it's just a game after all. Just frustrating at times.
I've also gotten the sense that the developers understood "rate-of-fire" to be more important/significant than stopping power, which is ridiculous. I'm not claiming to be one of them, but if you talk to anyone with any experience in a job where firearms use and training was in the job description, they'll tell you that 99.9% of the time, you're going to use that full-auto weapon in semi-auto mode, and you're trained that way for a reason. Accuracy and stopping power are what keep you alive, and rate-of-fire negates accuracy, and therefor also negates stopping power (because you're not hitting anything), as it increases. But again, not a big deal. It's just kind of awkward when you get the sense that your MP5 on full-auto, is somehow proving more effective than that M4 with well-placed shots.
All in all, this is a great game, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys tactics and planning! I've already put an obscene number of hours into this one, with many more to come!

Now that I have had enough time to make up my ideas (10 hours) I'm going to express my opinion.
The game is definitely GOOD. The fun is there while playing and it's clear. L4D kind of fun? sure. As good in every aspect? No.
The game glitches in many points, and is also very heavy to run (read: not well optimized). I am having troubles even on medium low details to keep a steady 60. When you are surrounded by 37 rats trying to eat you, dropping to 37 fps is not great. Seems like they are not going to patch it. It is playable but insanely CPU demanding (i5@4.5GHz here).
While playing you get rewards (weapons) and by rolling dice at the end of every game you may win further loot. This makes replaying every mission a more enjoyable thing. You rank up with XP and get better equipment. With better equipment you are able to go on with difficulty.
What the game lacks is its own identity. It really feels like L4D but is not. If you ask me the name of a mission, I would not tell you which one is it. If you show me a screenshot, I can't say whether it's mission X or Y. Most places look the same, while L4D had a precise feeling of the location in every stage of every campaign and I think it was a good thing.
It is definitely worth trying this game though but be prepared for bad framerate if you don't have a powerful CPU.

My friends and I have waited years to play this game because of it's time in early access but it was worth the wait, for us at least.  I'm normally not a fan of building or survival genre games but this one has captivated me.  We purchased the game at least two years ago and have tried it off and on since that time but didn't want to put in a lot of time until it was finished because we didn't want to have played it all and not be able to enjoy it when it released.  So here we are now and I'm glad we waited.  The game still have some minor issues that need resolve but the devs are so far handling those issues in short order.  The devs are also pretty responvie on the forums and seem genuinely interested in player feedback.
What I love most about this game is it's versatility.  It has a great story mode that can be played in either single player, multiplayer or on a hosted server.  Mulitplayer games can also be co-op, survival or PvP and there is also an adventure mode which is an open world quest and dungeon crawler style map.  The maps outside of story mode are also all procedurely generated with dungeons, caves, etc.  in addition to that, the options for building are seemingly limitless.  You can build your own weapons, armor, VTOLs, ground vehicles, ships, submaries, personal robots and buildings.
Plus the colony system is a lot of fun for me.  It's like having a small scale sim built into the game.  As you encounter NPCs in the game you can invite them to a colony that you establish and assign them certain roles.  They can be medics, workers that can repair, recyle or enhance gear, farmers and more.
The in game editor is also very powerful yet fairly simple to master with a little time and patience.  I am still pretty impressed with what can be created on the fly without having to drop out of the game to create custom models and whatnot.  You can not only build the body of your design but also create custom materials using your own textures (based off of a default material), place your own decals on your items and more.

First "tactical" game I've seen in a while that actually deserves the name. One of maybe three games I've played ever, wherein you could actually use real-world tactics, and those tactics not only work, but they work in-game, for the same reasons they work in real life. Button-hooks, cross-overs, "slicing the pie", etc. etc. This could be used as a kind of "sim-lite" for real-world operators-in-training, who just want to see tactics in action, while exploring why they work. Beyond that, it's a fairly entertaining game, giving you all the gear choices, squad-building, and planning that you need for a game to actually be "tactical", a term that is either misused these days, or avoided for fear of losing the instant gratification and hand-holding market. With both one-off missions, several campaigns (with more to come, apparently), random mission generator, and Steam Workshop support, there's endless hours of play available.
I do have some relatively minor complaints, though. For one, any tactical game that uses a weapon and gear unlock system breaks my immersion just a tad. Real world units don't have to unlock weapons and gear. They simply use what they feel best fits the task at hand. So I kind of wish they would have gone the classic Rainbow Six route, where everything is at your disposal from the get-go. Also, there are some rather unrealistic balancing issues. Targets wearing body armor are human bullet sponges. I've watched in amusement, as my full-armored operator unloaded round after round of 5.56 from an M4 into one of these vested "tangos" at point-blank range, only to watch the target giggle, scratch his nuts, wink at my wife, and blow my up-armored operator away with a few rounds from his sub-gun. I'm sorry, but no vest exists that will stop a full-powered rifle round without at least incurring incapacitating trauma on the wearer. But no mind, it's just a game after all. Just frustrating at times.
I've also gotten the sense that the developers understood "rate-of-fire" to be more important/significant than stopping power, which is ridiculous. I'm not claiming to be one of them, but if you talk to anyone with any experience in a job where firearms use and training was in the job description, they'll tell you that 99.9% of the time, you're going to use that full-auto weapon in semi-auto mode, and you're trained that way for a reason. Accuracy and stopping power are what keep you alive, and rate-of-fire negates accuracy, and therefor also negates stopping power (because you're not hitting anything), as it increases. But again, not a big deal. It's just kind of awkward when you get the sense that your MP5 on full-auto, is somehow proving more effective than that M4 with well-placed shots.
All in all, this is a great game, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys tactics and planning! I've already put an obscene number of hours into this one, with many more to come!

Hey you! Yes, you!
Do you like games where you get relentlessly spawncamped?
Do you love 0 team-cooperation?
Do you enjoy totally unbalanced weapons and vehicles?
How about having to grind 10s, even 100s, of hours to get basic equipment just to compete?
On top of that, would you like a game that has the visual appeal of a PS2 and the sounds of a cap gun shootout?
Boy, then do I have a game for you.
While this game does have potential, there are huge problems with it. Being that it is free, I understand the grind. That said, it should be possible for new players to have access to weapons that at least make them capable of competing and then there would be slightly better weapons to work for. Currently, American starting weapons will utterly destroy you as a starting player. Beyond that, it takes so many shots to kill another player you lose a lot of the intensity of a gun fight. Having to shoot someone 6-8 times, it stops being a gunfight and becomes more of a patience simulator. Also, the movement is terrible. Your only real choice is to stand. The movement crouching or, god forbid, going prone, is so slow it makes it totally worthless. Add that to clunky and slow transitions from one position to another and it's even worse. If I had a dollar for every time I've been killed by a sniper moving from prone/crouched to standing, I'd at least have enough money to buy a different game. Really, moving on foot at all is a bad move in this game. I really can't emphasize how bad the gun sounds are. This is such an irritation because it would take literally, minutes to fix. I'm not just hating on this game, It has a lot of potential to become an excellent game, but currently I would not reccomend it to anyone until a few things get fixed.
To reiterate
>Bad weapon sounds
>No team-cooperation and no encouragement to do so (Mics would be a big plus)
>Very poorly balanced early loadouts; America significantly more powerful
>Too much grinding for basic equipment
>Generally more powerful, but balanced, small arms
>Fix the movement, at minimum crouch and prone MUST be fixed

Walls didn't seem to work nor did buildings. as the NPCs just sort of ran through them and I'm sure i kept getting rained on. Along with this is player inventory and colony inventory. I feel that the player should be able to fabrecate items from ether storage location. NPCs should build more things along with what they gather. Complete ISO items, wepaons, armor, defense weapons etc. I would also remove scripts from the store(s) if the player already has it learned.
- Missions. There are ton of them which is awesome. Some of them can be very . . . confusing on what to do. Probably need to introduce a more indepth mission/quest log with details of where things can be found (I'm thinking more along the line for the gathering misions). We have a monster wiki in-game, might need to expand that to include the different plants as well.
- Mining/Lumbering are pretty easy from the start through out. The Drill and Chainsaw IMO are worthless with the current development behind them. So we get stuck with a space game mining ore with a pickaxe and lumber with an axe. I think, the development team might need to look at taking all the gathering tools and merge them into a single item (like the Matter Manipulator in Starbound)... The current system to me seems half baked and not thought out. We have space traveling humans, I'm sure their ship wasn't crafted by men and women farming ore with pickaxes. Some of this I understand is because they don't want us terraforming the entire planet.
Overall, besides my nit picking on development choices. The game was fun and I will return to it often to spend more time... Need to perfect my colony building and location.

Personal Rating: 5 of 10
Its very difficult to review this game. The story and plot is good, the island is vast and combat is satisfying at times. However it falls really short on variety and many things don't gel together.
Story is simple and straight foward but the plot did raise my eyebrows several times like the shocking kind which is good.
The island is self is split into 2 part with the latter being revealed later in the game. The map is huge but I think mainly its because its empty and repetitive. The island looked the same everywhere with the same encampment, building, random places of small interest, mountain top and temples here and there but beyond that, the island is practically empty. For such a huge island there sure is no jungle. Don't expect different settings like snowy mountain, huge swampy area (there is a small and rather under designed one) or perhaps some remains of previous civilization. The reason I've said this is, there is proof of war bunkers, ancient temples and some large abandon facilities but these just isn't enough of other structures or towns to support it.
Towns and encampments are plenty and scattered everywhere but they are really dead is coal. NPCs are decorations mostly that does nothing except for some that gives out quest. Not lively at all.
Speaking of side quests, apart from collectibles, none of them span across a few series of repetitive quests like kill 250 of this and collect 50 of that but if you combine all of them together you get your fill series of repetitive nonsense lame side quests. Some side quests may obviously hide some meaning behind which others may find it funny or offensive but to me, I deemed them really unnecessary.
Voice acting is alright but some NPCs voice record quality is clearly poor and bad also. Main characters are clearly stands out from unimportant NPCs as they are livelier and some are designed really well. Music is okay but it does gets on my nerve after a while because its so repetitive and some soundtrack clearly kills off the mood. Some main characters are overly done though which can be annoying. Thank heavens the interaction time with them isn't that long.
The story mission is not really that long and the developers really hike up the challenge really really fast. Enemy A.I. is alright but once you find a flaw to exploit it seemingly easy. Weapons are plenty to choose from and yes they do have different characteristics which you can clearly feel but I feel they can be a little more hard hitting. You can customize weapons and even apply skin on them but its very limited. What surprises me the most is the animals. There is actually quite a few variety of them but lacked of characteristics.
You can earn levels and money doing quests and looting but thats that. Collectibles unlocks written stories and provide nothing more. Each time, I was hoping the next collectible will unveil more location or puzzle but nothing really. Money allows you buy stuff. I was really excited at first but again dissapointed me as fast as it got me hyped up because you can only purchase weapons and customization. Ammos and med kit are practically useless as there are plenty around. Further more most of the weapons can be earned for free. Leveling up earns you a skill point and yeah the skills are quite useful nad gives you a sense of progression.
You can also craft items in the game but personally I think it is a cheap gimmick. Imagine this, you needed leather to holster weapon. To carry more weapons you need more holster. But each holster requires different leather to craft. Its like her lets make use of the animals you know since its there but yeah its really redundant. You won't feel any sense of achievement there just finally I get more slots. You can also craft a variety of syringe that boosts/gives you certain ability for a short period of time. I only find 1 or 2 of them useful. In order to craft syringe you need to forage some plants. There are just too many of them lying around which practically makes them worthless.
If you ever watched the trailer, it was really good. I thought that finally it went back to its root (Far Cry 1) but the actions you see in the trailer is more like in game ability kind of thing and not the actions you control of feel satisfy when you execute them. You only need to push a button at the right time. The antagonist that appeared on the trailer also sends shiver down one's spine. You hoped to see more of his insanity but no it doesn't really fills the expectation void. The character just don't expand.
Overall, the game feels like it was designed by many department. Some did great while others pitched the idea, implement it for the sake of having the feature there in the game but these features don't simply cannot fit into the puzzle together and other aspects of the game cannot fully utilize one another to the fullest.
Note that there are also some game breaking bugs too. Collecting collectibles doesn't save the game so if the game crashes (there are no quick save feature as I can't see the key mapping option), you need to repeat the process which is a pain. At times, if you land with the wingsuit you may clip through the ground. Missions contains plenty of unmarked checkpoint. If you somehow managed to bypass them you need to reload as the game won't progress.
This game is good for casual open world game that packs some action. There are little things in the game that may surprise you or you may notice some small features that should be there.
This game is complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and that's exactly why I love it.

I really, REALLY didn't want to do this, but I have to. Look, I love the first game, it's probably my favourite indie game of all time, but this? What the f*ck, Dennaton?
This game basically consists of open as sh*t football field sized buildings made of freaking glass that are packed with dogs, fat dudes and gun-wielding enemies that react to you in a nanosecond and kill you off-screen. This game is f*cking hard, but not in a good way like the first game. It's hard in a frustrating, unfair and b*llsh*tty way.
In Hotline Miami 1, when you died, 90% of the time it was totally your fault. This time around though 90% of your deaths are due to the god awful level design or to some cheap glitch, which leads me to my next point: on the technical side of things, this game is a f*cking mess. It has tons of bugs, the enemies react more like robots than ever, and there are some "special" enemies like the dogs and the prisoners that run at a supersonic speed to try to strangle you that can just teleport through doors, and if you are even near a door when one of them is chasing you have absolutely zero chances of surviving.
By the way, HM2 has terrible input lag by default because turning VSync off in-game doesn't work, you're gonna have to do it manually through your graphics card's control panel. Wish I f*cking knew this earlier, because I played through the entire game INCLUDING HARD MODE with that horrible input lag at first.
The game carries something that was a minor annoyance in the first game and turns it into a major one: there's no way to know what weapon you'll get from a pile of guns. Since the best strategy to kill enemies in this f*cking game is to show yourself for a second to lure them to a corner you'll just end up with dozens of weapons stacked on top of each other, and then you'll try to pick up one of them to kill that fat guy that is running towards you quickly and you'll just die horribly because you picked up a gun with no bullets or a melee weapon.
Speaking of which, thanks to the way the levels are designed, using melee weapons in most of them is completely unviable. Hope you like doing nothing but using guns to try and snipe enemies two screens away while constantly holding shift for the entirety of the game, something that contrasts greatly with how you could exclusively use melee weapons to complete most levels in Hotline Miami 1 (with the exception of picking up a gun for a second to kill fat guys and enemies that are out of reach, obviously).
Another thing that heavily frustrates me is how you are now unable to score points by knocking enemies over, unlike the first game. With very long execution animations and no way to get points, it can become infuriating to accidentally knock over a mob of enemies and lose your combo. So I never even try to go for highscores here, which is something I loved doing in HM1, because it's just a freaking nightmare.
And then there's hard mode, which is just pure b*llsh*t. I'm willing to believe this is just a sick practical joke implemented by Dennaton to laugh at our faces. It depends so much on luck it's not even funny, try the same strategy over and over again until you eventually get it right. It's pretty much impossible to finish the game on hard mode without cheaply dying at least a couple hundred times.
Some people might appeal to the braindead ad hominem argument of "you're just bad at the game" while ignoring all of my points entirely. Mate, just check my f*cking stats for both this game and the first. I got all the achievements, which means I finished the game on hard mode, and I'm able to get an S ranking on most stages with relative ease, so these opinions are coming from someone who actually understands both Hotline Miami games very well. I don't wanna come off as being pretentious here, but some people are just unbelievably dense.
One thing I feel like could have been done to improve the game quite a bit would be the implementation of a system where, after you beat the level for the first time using the character that's supposed to be there for the story, you could choose any one character when you play that level again, just like the LEGO games. Maybe let you play as Jacket (with all the original masks) and maybe even Biker. From a story perspective that wouldn't make sense of course, but why should that matter? Fun/Replayability/Variety should be the priority here. Another thing that would definitely improve the game would be just, y'know, actually having some good level design?
But credit where credit is due, the soundtrack is absolutely incredible. Go and listen to Roller Mobster, The Way Home, Run, Le Perv, In The Face of Evil, Bloodline... Hell, just listen to the entire goddamn thing. Also, graphics look fantanstic. Very stylized like the first game while still being able to pack much more detail into every level. Only problem is, that detail can sometimes make enemies harder to see, and there were times when I died to an enemy that was behind foliage or something like that, but again, that's more of a problem with the level design than anything else. Animations are also pretty good and generally smoother than the first game. And finally, I actually think they did a pretty good job on "expanding the lore" in this game and tying everything together with the first, but (without spoiling anything) the ending was just awful.
So, in conclusion, if you're a HUGE fan of Hotline Miami 1 you might want to grab this for the story, but if you're just looking for some reckless, fast-paced and fun gameplay you're better off playing the first game.
And just to top this review off, here are a few quotes from some people that I found throughout the internet about this game that I liked enough to save and I find very hard to disagree:
"The majority of the levels feel like they're ripped from a hardmode fangame: They're poorly designed and unfairly hard."
"Everything about this game feels unfair. You're forced to hold down shift to basically have any chance, and even then some unseen enemy will still snipe you from across the map."
"What killed Hotline Miami 2 for me was the level design, the maps are way too big. In those large spaces you spend more time holding the shift key to look ahead, taking cracked shots around corners at off-screen enemies. It breaks the flow, and for a game like this, flow is very important. The original game seemed like it was designed to encourage reckless behaviour, it told you that it's okay to die. But now, carefully clearing a floor, only to be instantly killed by an unseen sniper a screen away frustrates me to no end."
"I thought the level design really took a nose dive in the sequel. It forces you to be slow, to constantly hold down shift to snipe down far away enemies or be killed from off-screen. It's so linear, there's typically one way to solve a level and beating it feels like learning a choreography. Having to constantly "pull" enemies through a chokepoint got boring pretty fast."
"The level design in many areas was just bad, having obnoxiously long levels that take minutes to retry and far too much reliance on cover based shooting and camping.
Also, that ending was terrible. I understand what they were getting at with it and how it was to spite people who wanted more narrative, but we already had that idea done to death in a much better way in the last game and it didn't need to be done again. It comes off as lazy and pretentious rather than intriguing and interesting and maybe that was the point, but I still don't like it."
"The bottom line is that Hotline Miami 2 is not fun. If you don't find the idea of meticulously grinding for 40 minutes on one level repulsive and are the type of person who doesn't get frustrated that the game feels completely unfair towards you, the player, then yes, you might enjoy the game. For those who don't find pleasure in being curb-stomped by a poorly designed game, pass on this one."

I'll review this as a port. The game itself is fantastic and one of the best games of the dreamcast/gamecube library.
-Some of the cutscenes are still pre-rendered. And by that, I mean they came straight from the Dreamcast. Numerous times, I saw some of the cutscenes run in 4:3, while the gameplay is 16:9. That shows Sega laziliy ported this game.
-Camera controls feel off. You rotate the camera by pressing RT or LT(I use an xbox 360 controller). However, pushing RT, rotates the camera to the left of your character and vice versa, and the camera will only move horizontally. A handful of times, the camera will point at a fixed angle.
-Except for adjusting resolution, there are no graphical settings at all.
-The same goes for audio settings. The only settings available are language spoken and mono/stereo.
-You cannot change the interface language while running the game. You could in the Dreamcast and Gamecube versions, so why take that out?
-The music is untouched from the original DC/GC version, which I find to be a mixed feeling. It's nice that they kept all the songs, and listening to the familar tunes brings back memories, but an updated soundtrack would've been better.
-The multiplayer battle mode is DLC, which is a huge red flag in my book. Battle mode was available from the start in the GC version, and should be available from the start in this version.
-Customizable menu has also been locked out as DLC. Is Sega turning into Capcom now?
-In some of the cutscenes, the lip sync is a bit off. Again, Sega is being lazy with the port.
I recommend getting this game only if:
1. You've never played it before
2. You don't have a Gamecube or Dreamcast
3. You're like me and love it enough to buy it a second time

Set within the Warhammer lore, Vermintide is a four player co-op survival game based in the fictional city of Ubersreik. Under attack from endless hoards of vermin known as the Skaven, four unlikely heroes must use teamwork to stand a chance against overwhelming numbers.
When starting the game for the first time, players will first notice the lack of any tutorial or practice arena as they find themselves thrown into a tavern which operates as the mission hub. Players can select missions from the tavern which will then find them a game or allow them to host it themselves. This Is where I met my first problem within Vermintide, confused and with no information I found myself unable to find any games. After checking the forums I found that servers had been disabled for maintenance. After maintenance I joined my first game and soon found that games were managed with a peer to peer system. It seems unusual that matchmaking must be taken down and all games must come to a halt when the game lacks the use of dedicated servers. Many games that run with a peer to peer system can find games without needing a matchmaking server. After finally getting into my first game I immediately got to the fast paced hack and slash I had been waiting for.
Combat within Vermintide can be described as “simple yet satisfying” as it lacks depth but still provides a gratifying experience. Weapons operate with a simple system which takes into account damage, reach, knockback and speed. With a total of five characters, each character having their own selection of weapons there is plenty of variety to find the weapons to suit your playstyle, be it defensive, one hit wonder or crowd control. Shields are great for players who want to defend their friends and keep the tide of vermin back. Two handed swords to slice huge groups into a pink paste that leave you somewhat slow. Fast daggers with little reach for devastating damage against a single target one at a time. With each character having their own arsenal with its own variety you can play as any character you want, however you want to play. If the loot system lets you. Each weapon has the option for a quick and heavy attack, the differences between the two attacks depend on the weapon used. Players looking for heavy depth won't find it here but those looking for a tactical hack and slash will find it satisfying for many hours. While combat is basic there is a simple learning curve which is heavily focused on movement management to avoid taking damage. There isn't really too much to say, simple but effective and sometimes simplicity can be much more satisfying then complexity.
Teamwork is a heavy focus of the game, as four players will be the victim to a number of special enemies that excel at killing anyone who strays alone. The Packmaster carries a hook which can pull players away from the group amidst the chaos of a hoard, reminds me a little of the smoker from Left 4 Dead. The Globadier prays on campers by covering large area of the map in a toxic cloud. After taking enough damage he'll suicide and explode into the group, heh that reminds me of the boomer from Left 4 Dead. The Runner rat pounces around the map and once it catches a player it will leave them helpless as it claws away. Okay I hope I am not the only one starting to see a pattern here. The biggest and final special enemy is known as the rat ogre, a huge mass of muscles that flings players around the map. Considered the boss of each map they take teamwork to take down with the heaviest of fire-power. Yep.. it's a tank, it looks almost identical with similar sound effects complimenting it. This game is Left 4 Dead and it's not subtle about it in any stretch of the imagination. Four players fighting through mindless hoards of enemies as they progress through the map, looking out for special enemies that are specialized at killing anyone who wanders off alone. Yes, this is Left 4 Dead with rats and we'll come back to this! Disregarding the extreme similarities these enemies still work well, forcing the team to quickly change tactics to adapt to new threats.
When looking at the characters, elf caught my eye and was immediately my first choice. After completing my first mission I was rewarding with two new weapons, a mace and a magic staff. I scratched my head a little as I soon realized neither of these were for the character I actually wanted to play. This brings with one of the greatest and most frustrating issues with Vermintide, the loot drop system. After each mission players roll six dice in an attempt to get better loot. Unfortunately the loot selection is completely randomized leaving even a perfect roll with frustration as you get another item not for your character. Currently after playing roughly 30 hours as elf I own 3 exotic staffs for the mage but have yet to find a single bow for the elf I enjoy using. It can destroy the motivation to play as you feel unable to play as the character you enjoy most. Better gear for other characters constantly piling up, never to be used if its for a character you don't enjoy playing. This issue desperately needs attention and can be a real killer for the game for those looking to invest a lot of hours. While the game offers players a number of ways to play, if you simply don't find the gear you need to play that way it can only harm your motivation to play.
A number of other issues I also experienced was poor optimisation and numerous bugs. At periods of gameplay my framerate would remain consistent but the game would slow down as well as separate occasions of high frame rate dropping. While these issues were minor I soon found myself with a long list of little things that irritated me as I played.
Lets get back to the elephant in the room, this game showing extreme similarity to Valves Left 4 Dead games. With many enemies having identical roles and combat being almost identical in many aspects  its clear that heavy inspiration was taken from Left 4 dead. Is this a bad thing? No, not on its own. In gaming many games have taken inspiration from earlier titles and improved upon them, I don't feel there is anything wrong with it as long as it finds its own place within the market. This leads us to the question, does Vermintide have enough originality to give it its own identity? If you already owned Left 4 Dead, would it be worth buying? My answer would be yes, but only just. While its clear that both games are extremely similar, a focus on melle combat over guns and medieval setting does give it enough to become its own branch in the co-op survival genre. Though you can complain all you want, I'm still going to call the rat ogre a tank every time! Old habits die hard.
Putting the similarities between Vermintide and Left 4 Dead to the side, lets look at Vermintide on its own merits. This is one of my reviews where I read through it and feel I didn't give enough praise. A number of bugs and issues throughout the game can be frustrating however with everything said the core concept is an entertaining and challenging hack and slash. Great weapon variety leave open a number of playstyles that all have their own role within a team. Defensive or aggressive there will be a weapon set that fits you perfectly, with that said Vermintide needs a lot of polish to smooth its rough edges. Will the developers give this title the polish it desperately needs to be something sensational? We'll have to wait and see.
If you're looking for something to play with your friends it's definitely worth looking at and a sure buy if you see it on sale! At full price, be cautious and aware of the game's faults before you spend your cash but many people will be satisfied with their purchase. If the game gets continuous support from its developer and improve some of the major issues, i'd happy suggest it to anyone who enjoys cooperative gameplay.

If you've played Left 4 Dead, it's basically more of the same but with less special infected (there's only the bullet-sponge that is the riot-gear zombie) and more objectives.
There are also different gamemodes available. Things like Escape, where you try to do exactly that, while completing objectives along the way (unlock this, go here, press this, hold off against these, etc), Evac, where you go around collecting survivors to escort to safety, or the true PvP gamemode where you hunt each other when you're alive and have to watch out for zombies.
If a player dies, they come back as a zombie. This will usually ruin the game if you're in a small team, because for some reason they take a lot more damage. They also bob and weave which, combined with their pings, means you miss a lot before they're tearing at your face. But in a large group, it's usually not a problem.
But I mostly enjoy the Escape maps. Completing objectives as they appear on the phone you use to tell you were to go has a satisfying sense of accomplishment. While you're killing zombies, you're keeping an eye out for things like key cards, boltcutters, or keys, just in case they're useful later. It brings a sense of teamwork, when each person gives up a valuable weapon slot to carry an item that we might need later. And it all comes together when you've fought through hell, got down to your last clip, and then you find a locked door that you can open with something you've saved that whole time. All the goodies waiting behind, ready to re-kit your team into killing machines.
All in all, a game I enjoy wasting a couple of hours on here and there, though I would advise to wait for it to go on sale (the full price is a bit steep, in my eyes).
Edit: I would like to mention this: if you become a zombie, you only get 4 lives and then you enter spectator mode for the rest of the game. A terrible idea, really, and I hope it gets changed.

Often regarded by fans as "the best Sonic 3D title ever!" Sonic Adventure 2 is a must buy for anyone who loves Sonic, or good platforming in general. A nice story told through 3 different "arcs" with fun gameplay and lots of replaybility, this game is truly one of the best Sonic games ever.
Pros:
+40-60 hours of gameplay
+3  diffrent types of gameplay each with fun mechanics
+30 different enormous stages to explore (each with 5 missions to keep you playing)
+Great soundtrack with memorable tracks (Live & Learn, City Escape, Sonic's Theme :D)
+CHAO RAISING (onion headed mutant/animal babies racing and beating the crap out of each other!!!)
+Secrets and hidden goodies EVERYWHERE!!!
+Multiplayer is fun (for the most part)
Cons:
-Repetitive and boring kart mini-game (you have to play it twice in the story, plus another 11 times in missions and mini games if you want all 180 emblem -_-)
-Some glitches here and there
-Lip syncing is messed up during cutscenes and voice acting sucks sometimes (Not Eggman, he sounds AWESOME :3)
-Questionable development decisions (WHY are the bounce bracelet and light speed dash activated with the same button!!!??? Why can the radar only detect ONE emerald at a time when it could detect ALL in SA1??? >:0)
*In conclusion. should you buy this game? ABSOLUTELY YES!!! For only $9.99 this game is definitely worth every penny!!!! It's fun, challenging, will keep you busy for quite a while, and will show you what the Sonic franchise is capable of making.

This is an enjoyable yet highly frustrating game mired by conflicting design decisions and implementation as well as a suspect UI and control scheme that has clearly not been created for PC.
7.0/10 as of 29/4/2015 (14 hours of gameplay)
On the positive side, it's a lot of fun at the basic level and replaying single levels over and over again is very rewarding using different tactics and weapons. Attempting to complete levels using a single trooper or one complete plan is even more engaging and rewarding.
The game fails when you start unlocking further upgrades/weapons/setups and attempt some of the more complicated levels. This is where you need some intricate planning and split-second decisions and reactions count. And this is where the poor UI fails and where the design flaws start to actually matter.
Some of the really annoying issues include:
-inability to sync moves beyond the A B C D go-codes. Frozen Synapse does a WAY better job at that.
-you can't change a trooper's angle of view and swap weapons/reload in the same move. One action will cancel the other so either you have to unpause, execute the 1st action, pause, and queue up the 2nd one, or you have to create a redundant move point in order to queue up your 2nd action. You should be able to queue up 2 such basic actions simultaneously.
-you can't edit or move any waypoints in the middle of a chain. Everything after the point of edit is deleted and on those long complicated levels this is SUCH a waste of time!
-in some levels, the game forces your troopers into very small quarters and trying to select them and order them around becomes a nightmare. There's no SELECT ALL feature so trying to get your troopers onto the 2nd floor is very annoying. Also the way the game selects which troopers are moved between floors seems pure random. I've failed so many missions because I kept switching between floors trying to get everyone in one place and end up being flanked and killed during the time I've wasted.
-I've no idea how this game expects you to play it in real-time mode with such bugs and weird control scheme. Some keyboard hotkeys would be nice.
I'm still recommending it because I've got my fair share of fun for the price I've paid; I got the game on sale for 50%. Until this game becomes more PC friendly, I wouldn't recommend getting it at full price. The ability to mod and create/share your own content is awesome but I really need tight gameplay and proper user-feedback to enjoy this game the way the developers intended me to.

In general the game is pretty fun (almost exactly like the L4D series), and looks pretty good too. Overall, I would recommend it, especially if you have friends to play with. However, rather than spend ages on a wall of text, here's a brief summary of the main good and bad things about it (in my opinion) ..
- Classes are varied and distinct
- Decent amount of achievements to go after
- Graphics are pretty on point, even at low settings
- Combat is dynamic and interesting, and damage seems fairly distributed through the classes
- Music and sound are pretty decent
- Reasonable variety of enemies, although mostly prosaic
- A good number of maps once you unlock them all
- Difficulty curve is fairly smooth
- Forge system seems pretty flexible, especially at lower levels where item unlocks cost few materials
- Loot rewards are generally OK, especially as you can fuse items together for an item in the next tier
- Inventory/item management is intuitive and straight forward
- Interaction between characters is pretty funny at times
- No versus mode
- There's barely a story here, so you kinda kill stuff for the sake of it (without much context)
- AI bots are almost entirely useless if you play alone
- Occasional crashes/DCs, which is better than it was, but still not 100% even after beta
- Some maps are far more difficult that others, even on easier modes
- I would've liked to see other game modes, beyond those based around the 'story'
- Rolls at the end of a successful mission, with all tomes etc gathered, often don't reap the reward you hope it will
- A little too 'RNG' for some
- Very few ways to get trinkets easily as you advance
- Occasional block mechanics not working, or not working consistantly
- More gear (armour, weapon skins) needed at lower levels
- Some enemies, maps, and specials' spawns need to be balanced

Incredible game. I spent a large portion of my childhood playing this, whether it was racing, force-feeding Chao or doing Mad Space hide and seeks with my cousin.
Aside for the obvious HD remaking, it hasn't changed. It's still that great exhilaration I remember. And now that I'm older and a much more adept gamer, I feel the need to perfect it :) halfway there already!
There are three types of stages, meaning you're three times as likely to get hooked on the game's playstyle! There are Sonic and Shadow's racing stages, obvious objective there. There are then Tails and Eggman's shooting/recon stages where you must reach the end leaving as much destruction in your wake as possible. And finally, my favourite, Knuckles and Rouge's treasure hunt stages, where you are equipped with a proximity radar which flashes a colour depending on how far you are from the gem you are trying to find. The objective is a best-of-3 gem hunt.
Seriously, if you're a fan of single player campaigns with astounding replay value and games where you can spend many hours playing to perfect your score or shave milliseconds off your time, this is a high HIGH recommendation.

Hotline Miami 2 is the beatiful sequel to the original. The gory combat, intense action music, soothing cutscene music, retro graphics and feel. I just love this game so I though I'd review it
PROS:
-More Gory and Intense Action. Enemies can now be sliced up with a chainsaw or mowed down by a barrage of Machine gun bullets. To me, this is an iprovement on detail.
-A new soundtrack that completes the feel of the sequel. Unlike the previous one's soundtrack which was perfect to getting high to, this one is more loud and intense and fits each scene of the game correctly in my opinion.
A better story. This one had a more clear story. It was as cryptic as the original but required you to pay attention to detail to get any of it really.
CONS:
-Bigger Maps. This is actually a bad thing when you die in one hit. Enemies have the eyes of an eagle spotting you from an entirely different plant and either rush you down like a jumpscare or pop you skull like a water balloon with some bullets.
-Less Masks. The game doesn't have the same mask system as the last one but it does have multiple characters which helps progress the story. But not everyone wears a mask. Only the Fans and Jake wear masks whereas the Son picks a skill to use and Beard use a different gun. It removes the variety in the gameplay.
-Glitches. "Chargers" and dogs can rush you through walls, you get stuck in corners, Ash glitches into furniture and enemies can get stuck in walls.
The Second Game is a really good game for some. Others is a disappointment. Personally I still enjoy the game for it's flaws.
FINAL VERDICT:
8.2/10
P.S. This game might get a 9 if it the editor ever comes out.

THIS IS NOT A RUN-AND-GUN GAME.
Now we've got that out of the way, you should understand why some of the negative reviews exist.
Also, I got to this game after it had existed for a long time, so I can't complain about any dev process.
Reasons why I like this game:
-It's not COD Zombies, L4D, or any other highly unrealistic zombies romps I also enjoy on occasion.
-You have to manually reload. (Ikr? guns don't reload themselves in reality, either.)
-You only get one life. Once you die you're a zombie - kinda like if zombies were a real thing.
-It's terrifying at times. (Zombies are scary things. They're not funny, or cute. Not in any way. This game shows you why)
-Offline splitscreen play. (2 players is all I've been able to try)
-Being a zombie is fun, and almost it's own game. (you can gather a horde, track the humans, and other stuff)
-Stealth is really a thing. (No really. you can do most of a level with a melee and have a pretty easy time of it)
-Randomization. (you may know the level, but you still have to search for the keys/bolt cutters, etc. That smg one time might be a melee or nothing another time. It keeps you on your toes)
-Bullets are a limited resource. (spend them well)
-Small inventory. (4 slots for weapons, healing items, keys, etc.)
Reasons why I don't like this game:
-It's hard. (I rage quit often, and then pick it back up after a long break.)
-You only get one human life. (I really wish this was an option for when you want a more casual game)
-Why do keys take an inventory slot? You can put that on a belt loop ffs!

I have a really strange feeling about this game. I enjoyed it, thus thumbs up, but I would be really careful about recommending it to anyone. Unless you know you are into such games, don't buy it. It has nice storyline, and I spent hours downloading and tweaking helicopter models, but there is not much beside that.
The main supposed feature of the game - dig anything, build anywhere and whatever you want - it is not there. Yes you can dig up any terrain, but there is little sense doing that. You need to dig mines for resources. slowly with wooden tools first, then faster and faster, as you progress through iron, steel, diamond and ultimately CheatEngine universal digging tool, giving you literally billions of any resource in a couple of seconds, because farming in singleplayer is not something I fancy doing during this couple of free hours that I can spare for gaming.
Apart from mines, there is nothing to dig for. I never found any caves apart from those from the plot, I never needed to build a bridge, dam or any other stuff that took hours of my time in Minecraft.
You can design literally any vehicle, item, armor, weapon, but this design is but a skin. Mechanics-wise that will still be the very same default game object, just reskinned and with tweaked numbers. Vehicles are treated as single objects with HP. You can make a dumb sheet of steel with driver, weapons and engine just sitting on top, or you can make an intricate APC with components shielded by armor, and both these variant will work exactly same. When HP drops to 0, it explodes, can't damage a weapon, engine, or kill the driver.
Functional buildings are all pre-made, so you just dig resources and 'buy' a power plant, which is just an object. I remember fun I had, designing monster plants in MC (where you literally build a facility with real output from irrelevant stuff that was not specifically meant for that purpose), nothing of the like here. Building a colony is little fun after you figure that you just need enough even land to place a bunch of buildings-objects together, but can not really design anything meaningful by yourself.
Guess were it not for the story, I'd spend way less time in the game, and I have no idea what I'd do in it now. The story does it though, long, catching, true-like, with well-written texts. So, if you are looking for an adventure, that should be fine. If you want advanced Minecraft, it's not that. Not that at all.

As a passionate early adopter of survival, sandbox games, I was quite excited when I first got Planet Explorers. Having play-tested the game all the way through it's early alpha and beta phases, on release I decided to start from scratch and complete the story mode without prejudice.
First things first to add some perspective. As a very ambitious sandbox game from a small indie developer, Planet Explorers has exceeded expectation and delivered what was promised. Of course it is rough around the edges and needs polishing here and there but it is playable from start to finish without any major/game breaking problems.
Pros:
- Good optimization (on a laptop with old-ish GTX860m max settings, a stable 50-60fps; alpha/beta < 30fps)
- Solid tutorial
- Compelling story line unraveling at your own pace
- Adventure mode with some unpredictable/surprising results
- World editor for custom tailored multiplayer games
- Voxel world implementation to par with alternative bigger titles
- Item editor/workshop implementation (easy to use component/parts based design)
- Colony building; finished the game with minimal protection but a proper base (from workshop?) should simplify defense
- Multiplayer co-op/versus games (re-playability and fun)
- Good value for money (40+ hrs to finish story mode, with some workshop experimentation)
Cons:
- UI looks dated and dialog font is ugly; some conversations sound computerised (or badly acted?)
- When a big battle ensues, fps suffers, e.g. base/colony defense (surprisingly turning grass on/off had no impact!)
- Tutorial should be part of the story mode (skippable), as to ease new players into the game (spaceship views of Maria etc)
- Story line is linear and predictable. Near end of game becomes a little grindy. No re-playability value here
- Limited workshop implementation, ugly item icons, fiddly; no in-game steam workshop access
- Item editor is cumbersome when you try to export an item in game (back and forth switching to create required components). A shopping list implementation would made a big difference before completing and exporting a complex item.
- Voxel world works great for extracting resources, not so for filling up holes/terrain etc (box voxels, no smoothing)
- No accurate damage to complex creations (e.g. helicopter 30% damaged costs almost 100% in repairs but it returns 80%+ mats when recycled!! Doh!)
- Atrocious AI pathing!!! The biggest flaw of PE!!
- Some over-powered editor creations, make mince-meat of elite enemies (I've used skeli helicopter 190kph, M16 etc etc)
- A number of broken quests (
for some off the top of my head).
- Broken follower commands; stay doesn't work at all, defend often interferes with quests (dismiss to avoid shoot outs)
- VIP colonists with temperament; can't get any proper training in, as often they are busy (doing what exactly?)
-----
TD;LR: Despite the above short-comings, I would recommend Planet Explorers as a well worth "value for money" experience. I thoroughly enjoyed it and can't wait for the sequel (?). I believe it should have stayed in beta to the end of 2016 to fix all the bugs still lurking but nevertheless it is what it is. For creative people and custom PE game hosts, it would provide countless hours of fun. 7/10
