Planet Explorers is a game full of adventure. The game has your basic 3 playable modes: single player, multiplayer and design modes. I been playing the game for several months and followed the updates.
The main story line is a exploration spaceship crash landing on a "unknown" planet. Your quest is to create your own colony while trying to figure out the reason behind the crash. The story line has several hours of different types of quests. Like other games of the genre, the story line will have quests such as protection, escort, and gathering. What really sets a side planet explorers story mode, is the design of the building system in the sense that you as a member of the crew, that is now scattered through out the continent, are in charge of creating you very own colony. The creation of the colony is not a location specific task, meaning that you create it where you want. That freedom is one of my favorite aspects of the game. You can recruit almost all the members of your crew, even make some of them your companions.
The colony system will allow you to manage your colony and colonists according to your desire. While not all the materials are produced at the colony, you are able to assign jobs to your colonists. After creating the appropriate machinery they can farm, train or work at a factory. Certain characters will have perks that will boost some of the tasks, combat and healing. The game features a nice menu with easy navigation making it very easy to manage your colony. You have access to this menu from every location but some of the tasks require you to be within the colony e.i. storing or retrieving items. You can even recruit some of the vendors to your colony giving you easy access to some of the prime materials needed to create whatever you want.
The other highlight of the game is the creation system. This is a design system where you can design your very own vehicle. The game allows boats, ground and air vehicles. It also allows the creation of robots, tools and weapons. The creation system allows single or passengers vehicles that will increase in fire power, speed and durability depending on the parts added to the design. A lot of components of the game rely on electric charge and will deplete over time. Some of the more complex designs require a lot of work to create all the parts, but they are some shortcuts like purchasing from vendors.
I only have played the single player in exploration and story modes. Exploration is a randomly or pre-generated map where you can play with out the basic main story line. AI still offers quests and AI colonies are generated for both friendly and unfriendly races.
I purchased Planet Explorers as a early access. The game is now in V1.0.3. I can say with confidence that Pathea followed through and I am very pleased with the purchase.  If you are unsure about the game please try the demo. It offers around 2 hours of story and it should give you a good idea if the game is for you.

"Pills here!" one of my teammates yelled out with a slight accent as we rounded the next alleyway, mimicking a cry that L4D and L4D2 veterans everywhere would know.
I half expected the dwarf to belt out, "I hate stairs" as we traipsed down into the hidden cellar.
We jest, but it's a good comparison.  Vermintide evokes so many feelings of the Left 4 Dead series that I'm half wanting to check more into the development team at Fat Shark, to see if any names are the same.  Far from being a lazy copy, however, this feels more like a distinct enough iteration that it feels more a homage than the sullying of something sacred.
If you've enjoyed Left 4 Dead, pick this up.  If you enjoy Warhammer Fantasy, and like me, cannot control yourself when you see something with the Warhammer label and see it in your Steam Games list before you remember what just happened, pick this up.
If you do not like team based FPS's that require the presence of 3 other thinking beings for progression, skip this title.
The melee in this game is great.  Each weapon (and there are several!) for each class (And there's an extra!) feels unique enough that once you've started to accumulate enough loot, your distinct playstyle can be utilized in any party with at least 4 of the 5 characters.  This means that once you've really got a grasp of the game, you'll never really have to worry if someone's playing the elf, because, hey, the Witch Hunter is close enough, etc. Once you've figured out how the blocking and pushing works, you'll find that the once "suicidal" one handed/no shield or two handed weapons start to shine in their own rights.  And there's nothing better than cleaving 4 rats in half with a great swing of a 2handed sword.
Ranged weapon ammo is sparse enough that depending on the class you'll likely not be randomly wasting shots or you'll find yourself wanting.  You also have enough variety here - from the elf's various bows to the differing crossbows and handguns/blunderbusses.  The dwarf has a grudgeraker - a glorified shotgun.
Add on top of this the loot system - and you've got some longevity to character progression.
If there's one downfall to the game, it's that it's close enough to the Left 4 Dead franchise that you can't stop comparing the two.  And that's where L4D's polish is going to make this game's attempt start to turn sour.  On its own merits, Vermintide excels as a team based FPS - but where things like the AI director is involved, or bot AI, lighting cues, or even how the special ratling spawns work, you can't help but know that L4D is just ... better.
Don't let that take anything away from this game though.  When the Tank- I mean Rat Ogre starts charging in, while you quaff a strength potion, don't feel bad for yelling "HUNTER!" when you see the green blades of an assassin pierce through the night sky.  If L4D is something Vermintide aspires to, it could have done a much worse job.
7/10
- Some levels seem unnecessarily brutal - and some of the difficulties just appear to be impossible with the way things work (friendly fire and harsh special spawns).  Wheat and Chaff, I'm looking at you.
- RNGesus can make you feel like you've just wasted a lot of time, if you're rolling nothing but 1-3 all night for loot.
- 13 unique levels are a lot, but by comparison to L4D's extra modes and community maps, it feels measly.  Here's to hoping they open this up to the community for map making!

I saw tons of potential in Deadlight. It looked to be a fun journey through a post-apocalyptic wasteland. For the most part it is, but there are a few flaws that really hold it back from being a truly great game.
One of the first problems to jump out at me is the voice acting. Some parts are ok, while other parts are really lackluster. The protagonist sounds like a grizzled veteran who has seen much of the apocalypse. For the most part, this works well, but there are moments when the lines sounded forced. This applies not only to him, but to everyone in the voice cast. They usually do alright, but there are moments that can really take you out of the immersion when done poorly. Additionally, sometimes the dialogue does not even make sense. Early in the game, you speak with a dying character, and the protagonist is completely unconcerned with him and only worries about his friends. The dialogue does not even fully make sense, and it feels like a few non-sequiturs are thrown in.

The plot is fairly standard for a post-apocalyptic zombie game. You’re separated from your friends, and you miss your wife and kid, who may or may not be alive. Yeah, yeah, we’ve all heard this one before. There are some interesting bits where Randall has flashbacks, and I enjoyed those glimpses into his psychology. They are very quick, though, and I would have liked to have seen some more development in them.

The 2-dimensional platformer was an interesting choice, and I feel that for the most part it works well. For about 75% of the game, it’s clear what is on your plane. The other 25%, however, is when you aren’t sure if you can grab a ledge or if it’s in the background. This can lead to frustrating deaths and not being sure where to go.

I’ve seen others complain about the controls being unresponsive, but I had no problems with it. I’ve been able to make all of the jumps fairly easily (with the exception of a few that required very precise timing). I played with a gamepad, so I don’t know if that made a significant difference or not.
The music in this game does a good job of putting you in the survival mood. During the opening of the game, I remember hearing it complement the action on screen and being surprised at how well the two went together. It is used sparingly, but to great effect, I feel. Additionally, I feel the sound design is another strong point in the game. The sounds of creaking floorboards underfoot and the splash of water in the background all help contribute to the game’s immersion.
The best part of this game by far is the immersion. They really paint a believable picture of a world that has been ravaged by a zombie apocalypse. I love the post-apocalyptic setting (thanks, Fallout, for getting me hooked on that) and this game was exactly what I wanted in that regard. Just exploring the world that the developers created was a great experience. I loved scavenging in the various locations in the game. They felt believable. My only complaint is that the protagonist can break the immersion with his comments at times. Sometimes, when taking in the world, the protagonist would make some stupid comment that would break my sense of immersion. This kind of goes back to the voice acting complaint I mentioned earlier, but some of it also is a problem with the writing. The protagonist does not fit the world as well as he should. His comments tend to separate the player from the world instead of drawing him in.

Overall, this game is a pretty fun ride, despite its flaws. I enjoyed my time with it and will miss the time I spent in this world. It is by no means perfect, but if you can look past some of the game’s weaker elements, you’ll find an enjoyable time here.

This will be my first review on steam, but I shall do my best anyway.
This game is an interesting answer to a gripe fans of the Build/Survival genre for a long time. Most games of this nature are rarely unique and often feel like digital cut-outs of something like Minecraft (which in its self is virtual Legos), but Planet Explorers feels different. Not only is Planet Explorers different, but it feels as if the creators genuinely cared for the title they were working on. The game uses a system for creation that feels a bit like it may have been used by the developers themselves, when a Planet Explorer player says that you can build or create anything they mean it (you have been warned).
Now that does not mean it does not have problems.
- The graphics are not all that impressive 7/10
- The sound needs some serious work 4/10
- The procedural generation has many many flaws -/-
- The worst of all are the controls 2/10
The controls are seriously in need of work. There are three control schemes; the first being similar to many MMOs with the mouse cursor having free movement across the screen and requiring the right mouse button to move the camera, the second is an awkward version of the first with the cursor locked and mouse movement directly translating to camera movement, and the third is a wonky hard to use first person camera. In my honest opinion this game would have done well with a simple over the shoulder third person shooter camera angle.
In conclusion the game is very fun for the niche gamer, but without a proper control scheme it will not hold much appeal for the average gamer (and many Build/Survival players as well).

This review is based on multiplayer story mode via LAN.
Bought an played on 17 Nov.
UPDATED 26 NOV
I wont explain to you all what the game is about since you most likely have already watched a few videos and read the game's description. If not, take the intiative to do so before reading on.
Here I will provide a list of findings from myself and my gaming partner playing through story mode on "LAN" setting.
My considered PROs.
--------------------------------
1) Single player game mode doesn't require an internet connection.
2) Creativity. This needs further clarification. You can design your own gear, and vehicles with a combination of premade 3d parts and voxels (cubes), which includes a somewhat rough ability to colour them as well. Once designing is complete, as long as you have the required materials in your inventory you are able to bring this design into the world as a fully usable/interactable object, as well as it will upload this creation to Steam's workshop.
If you aren't the creative sort, you have the ability to download other people's uplaoded creations.
3) The world itself is huge to try and fit as many different land types as possible onto a single island.
4) As long you wield gear bought from NPCs or crafted from your replicator, combat doesn't last long against almost all opponents you face.
My considered UNSURE OFs.
--------------------------------------------
1) Quests mostly consist of gathering specific items, talking to particular people, moving to a specific location on the map and killing specific critters and buildings. There are singular instances of getting the player to make use of user created content, introductory tool for players to make their own content.
2) Few quests require the construction of objects you do not have access to unless you find other specific NPCs to do their quests as well. When you do gain the object scripts (recipies or crafting papers you learn how to build stuff from) through quests they are useless since you will automatically already know how to produce them. Inventory clutter.
3) There is no inventory limit of any sort. While not a bad thing in of itself (and certainly not an issue unless you are looking for some kind of realism XD), it is rather amusing to be able to just pull a colossal boat / car / tank / flying machine / buidling out of your pocket and when you are finished using it, able to pick it up and put it back into your pocket. If there is a limit, I have yet to reach it.
4) There is no levelling at all here to be done. A character's strengths and weaknesses are directly tied to the gear you wear and wield.
5) illnesses exist but are an incredibley rare occurance since they require very specific things to make them happen. A rather pointless addition.
My considered CONs.
--------------------------------
1) LAN requires players to have internet access. ( wtf )
2) Quitting a LAN game, PE_Server.exe will continue to run the background which counts as the game still running. Need to manually close it through the windows task manager.
3) Syncronization. Cause delays in actions, and animations to not play when they should.
4) in LAN game, characters and NPCs ignoring player placed blocks. This will lead to NPCs impossible to interact with should they be several layers under placed flooring. NPCs will also plant crops under player placed blocks should there be any fertilized soil under them.
5) Some items created are largely useless. Created swords wont ever be as effective (roughly 1/3 as effective in fact) as those you can buy from NPCs or build from their scripts, uless you are planning on having over-the-top huge anime swords). Vehicles are largely useless except the helicopter, and even then you only need to use it to get to a destination once as fast travel exists.
6) To edit any of your custom creations you will need to build an entire new one. You can get back all the materials for your original custom creation by recyling/deconstructing it however, it will need to have 100% durabilty to refund all of its materials used. You can't just add to your custom object without rebuilding the entire thing. I personally understand the reasoning for this choice however it creates the next point below.
7) Any kind of recreation of custom item will be put into steam's workshop again. No, this doesn't replace what you've already put onto the workshop.
8) Steam workshop clutter from everybody having created something. You'll see a host of copies of the same named thing and no idea how any of them a re different, if at all.
9) The controls for creating custom things is not explained in detail anywhere easily.
10) Some of the game's missions are very vague. Good thing there are people who will answer how to complete them. There shouldn't be a requirement to look up an outside source to understand what a quest requires a player to do.
11) Talking with an NPC does not stop them from wandering off. This doesn't affect conversations, as they can still be finished. Shops, however, close once the NPC moves a certain distance away from the player.

The experience is ok as a casual thing. Still there's a lot of room for improvement and from my opinion should still be in early access given the large number of issues present.
I paid for this at full price. Developers these days a pretty eager to just shove their product out there regardless how complete and functional it may be. I wouldn't recommend this as it is right now, not until it gets some major fixes. Also it would be wise to change the "LAN" aspect since this isn't LAN at all.
I'll try to keep this updated with the help of anyone who kindly informs me of my mistakes or game updates.

Still feels like Early Access to me. Too many rough edges, literally and figuratively, to recommend as a "finished" product. With another year or so of balance and polish there might be something here for sandbox fans.

A true tactical game, where tactical means planning and not camping. Making sure that each member of the team knows what they are doing before hand, and executing the plan pefectly is a great feeling.
With a good multiplayer, it would redefine the entire tactical genre (hopefully planning returns to other tactical-genred games).

This game really makes you think before you send your teams in. Best blend of tactics and strategy I've ever played in a game. Every mission is different and really makes you put thought into it. So many weapons, armors, and secondaries. You can breach a door with a shotgun and send a squad in with assault rifles with a sniper set outside a window to cover them going in.
My favorite part of the game is how you can divvy up your movements into sequences. For instance, once you plan your teams' routes, you can divide their movements to into sections. So. you can have one team sneak in and clear an area silently and cut off an escape route and begin phase "A" where another team will blow their door open for a loud entrance and move in. You can then set phases B thru D for movement after things are clear, certain enemies have been eliminated, etc.
It's probably the most satisfying when you're preplanned movements finish a mission without pausing it to readjust.
I would suggest maybe a headswivel option for when one of your routes end. This would enable one or more units to watch all around them so they don't get snuck up on.
I would also suggest a little more user-friendly map creation.
Other than that, this is a must-buy game for those interested in a truly amazing tactical/strategic SWAT game.

I know this game is not for everyone but it is a blind purchase for fans of the first game.

If anyone needs me, I'll be replaying Hotline Miami 1.

Every now and then, a game comes along and fills a gap in the market that I didn't really know needed to be filled - Door Kickers is one such game. Inspired in no small part by the planning phases of late 1990s Tom Clancy games, Door Kickers is a thought provoking adrenaline rush of anti-terrorism action-puzzles.
There's two ways you can play Door Kickers. You can either take advantage of the ability to pause & issue commands in real time, edging your way through a level one command at a time, carefully assessing your options before pushing onwards... Then there's the right way - You plan everything from the get go. One continuous stream of commands that'll see your trooper(s) go from room to room, checking their corners and, hopefully, never leaving themselves open to an ambush. The sense of accomplishment from laying down a perfect plan that requires no tweaking after the mission starts is pretty special, and adds so much challenge to the game that you'll be entertained for hours and hours.
Levels vary wildly from simple elimination jobs, to bomb defusal, hostage rescue, and evidence gathering. No two levels are the same, and thanks to the numerous ways to approach each, there's potentially no limit to replayability. Replayability is also helped by a multi-tier challenge system & a pretty strong community modding scene. The in-game custom level generator makes designing & sharing levels with others really simple, and it's fun to see how challenging a level can actually be when designed by someone other than a sensible developer.
Character variety is a-plenty as the game has a generous amount of specialized classes & customization, along with veterancy rewards and dedicated fighting styles. Completing campaign levels in the best possible way will require a well rounded squad of multiple talents, but be warned - Death is permanent in campaign modes, and it's possible to lose a talented officer in just one poor move.
It's not all great, though. Music & voice acting is less than mediocre, while the graphics are pretty much just fit for purpose. There could also be very slight improvements to mission planning, but the developers have proven their intent to better the game, and it's by no means bad right now - It just could be a little better, that's all.
Overall, Door Kickers is a resounding recommendation. A collection of standalone tactical puzzles, campaigns & UGC, all wrapped in an attractive enough package with amazing character customization & challenges galore. If you're in any way  intrigued, then jump in without hesitation.

BEWARE - If you will potentially want a refund (which you likely will)
If you attempt to play multiplayer, despitethe fact you more than likely wont get it working port forwarding or no, when you quit the game leaves a process running in the background and continues to count as being played by steam. So even though we only loaded it up and tried to get a multiplayer server going a couple times; it sais we have played for over 15 hours each making a refund more difficult. Make sure when you quit you lookin task manager for the process and end it manually.
Now my experience from playing on my mates account (what drove me to misguidedly buy it in the first place)
1. The item creation is really cool, played around making my friend items on his computer, however being able to make your own items is the only good part of this game and once you see the game itself, even this is lacking.
1.1 the item creater looks extensive however it is missing core parts which effectively mean that items you will find in game will be better than what you can create anyway. eg, you can get 2H melee weapons in game, you cannot make 2H weapons in the creator. You can get many different 1H hilts in game, but can only use the first 3 low tier ones in creator.
this put a massive dampening on the only good part of the game.
2. Graphically it is uninspiring and extremely dated, which I can excuse if the gameplay was fun.
3. The gameplay is not fun, starting out doing the very first quest in adventure mode and I got swamped by about 8 NPC humanaoid enemies which hit like trucks and you basically cannot damage. Sure, you can kite them around for half an hour shooting them with your rubberbands (bow) or hitting them with your wet tissue (sword), but it isnt fun.
3.1 combat is woeful, despite being able to double tap to dodge, dodging does exactly nothing for you.
4. Audio, The sound is quite calming and nice which is a good thing and likely designed to stop you raging at game mechanics.
5. Multiplayer, the "multiplayer" basically does not work,we tried creating a private server with port forwarding set correctly and noone could see the servers, regardless of which one of us set it up. You can create it via a proxy server based god knows where and then 90% of the game mechanics are broken by the latency. eg die (because the first NPC you talk to in town spawns about 15 high level mobs with firearmswhile you haven't even made a wood bow) and then cannot respawn, BUT you can drive your nameplate around ....
6. As mentioned, when attempting to make a server it created a background process which does not exit when you exit the game, racking up hours and preventing an easy refund.I have a suspiscion that this is intentional because there is no way in hell this game is in release standard.
7. The environments are boring and extremely vast nothingnesses, games liek 7 days  to Die also have this but the environment still feels alive and dangerous somehow, not so here.
8. The AI, should just be renamed A.
I could go on, however in summary; I had quite a bit of enjoyment creating items to use in game which I could copy from my mates computer easily enough, however that is the end of the fun in this game, there are soooooo many bugs, features that down work and lack luster mechanics that it is obvious this game is still in alpha or EA.
It is definately not in release. or worth ~$30 asking price, to expand - this is I tihnk the only comment I have made on steam in the many years and games (even ones I regret buying) that i have asked for a refund.

A survival co-op game that has you going around doing suicidal missions against hordes upon hordes of skaven (rat-men) with three of your friends? Count me in!
The feel of the combat is really nice and gritty, and it is easy to learn but hard to master. The higher difficulty settings that this game provides really require you to understand (to a degree) some combat concepts like chokepoints, dodging, stamina, and working with your teammates.
The loot system in this game is a really nice addition, making the game even more and more replayable.
Some problems with this game include optimization issues on PCs that should be able to run this game on full 60 fps but only run it on 48+ fps (you are warned), some rare bugs that make the game not that fun to play (I have not run into any of them, thank god), and since there can only be one of each character in a game sometimes you might not be able to play what you want unless you want to wait even longer.
All in all this game is a solid pickup if you want a Left 4 Dead Style game that his its own quirks and lore.

Only for people who have friends or Discord/TS/guild. You simply HAVE TO HAVE VOICE COMMS. And somewhat regular or good people to play with. Easy difficulty gives crap loot, and some missions on Easy mode are near impossible to complete with random people. You will repeatedly find yourself very confused, with stuff obscuring your view, disoriented and not sure what you're doing wrong, or did wrong. You will also often not be able to play the class you want to play, since you can only have one max of each type of hero for each mission. There is no way to practice the different classes with different gear, except just run and stab/shot/explode things inside the inn, which is a little silly. Do not start off playing Wizard, confusing mechanics with different staffs and you will constantly die as you have to reduce overheating, which hurts you, which means you lag behind and you die a lot more. Or maybe I'm just bad. If you're not bad, and you have friends, or a guild or people you regularly play with, this might be the game for you.
If anything goes wrong, and you drop connection or whatever during a run (some missions take 20min), YOU LOSE EVERYTHING.
In summary, good game, beautiful townscapes, but it's only good if you have friends or know how to get people to play with regularly. Discord works, as does belonging to a Steam group, I suppose. Maybe I should stick to Turn-Based games since I'm bad. You'll also find it very hard to get groups for Normal mode, most people very quickly moved on to Nightmare/Cataclysm, which is frustrating and difficult and lots of very specific teamwork involved, and one person ♥♥♥♥♥ up and you're all just wasted and frustrated and angry after 20 min of work.
Price is right wrong depending on your available disposable income. Cheap enough for me, so no worries. But repeatedly spawning into a mess of a melee away from your companions is a bit ...not fun. A fairly simplistic game really and its damn fun! A beautiful and enjoyable execution of a proven co-op formula. Between the slaughtering of massive hordes of mutant rat-men and the dice-roll system for the loot...it ends up being quite fun and addictive.
Taking advantage of a winning formula for co-op gameplay, Vermintide emulates the Left4Dead experience in many respects. Too name a few, the hordes of rat-men that randomly surprise you; the special enemies with unique abilities that often spawn at the worst times and incapacitate a teammate; the medkits that can be used to heal said teammate. There are many similarities, but there are enough differences to make the game feel fresh and distinguish itself.
In particular, the melee combat is quite an improvement over Left4Dead. It just feels good. The blood and gore of hewn rat-men will satisfy any bloodlust. The AI is done very well and the seemingly endless spawn points will continue to surprise you--even with your back to a wall you're rarely safe, as the enemies climb out of sewers, holes in walls, and drop from rooftops.
The atmosphere and visual experience is top-notch. Starting with the camera panning across the map, you get a feel for the level of detail and the dark, war torn world you are entering. One of my favorite parts of the experience in this game is seeing the menacing Skaven (rat-men) scattered around the maps: haunched over--seemingly feeding off a dead body; perched on rooftops overlooking the streets--sillouttes against the sky; leaning against a wall in an alley off the street--ready to pounce on you when you are unaware. I was pleasantly surprised that those rats in the distant backdrop, climbing over rooftops would quickly make their way onto the playable area of the map and hurl themselves at you if you didn't pick them off beforehand. The feeling of a "Vermintide" is definitely there.
If you're looking for a fun and addictive co-op game that is fairly easy to learn and still a challenge to win; a game where you can casually hop into a mission to fight the hordes with your friends; and a game where you can chop mutant rat-men into a bloody mess, then this is a game for you.
Thank you for the fun time Fat Shark and keep up the good work. I foresee the coming of DLC and I hope Fat Shark delivers something of substance unlike some other developers out there who have chosen to drown their games in half-baked, overpriced fluff.

It's been 13 years since this game was first released on the Dreamcast, and 12 years since it was ported to the GameCube.  The Gamecube port was the one I considered to be the better experience and was the version I played the most. As the years went on, and as more Sonic games were released, I found the reception to this game to be more and more mixed. Some people still claim this as one of the best Sonic titles out there, while others consider it one of the worst. While I certainly don't consider this game to be better than the classics or even the more modern games like Sonic Generations, I do still find things to enjoy quite a bit in it. The real meat of this game are the Sonic and Shadow stages which focus on traditional speed and platforming. Those stages are usually the reason I keep returning. I may dabble a bit in some Pumkin Hill here and there, but I usually stay clear of the treasure hunting and shooting stages.
When talking about the PC port overall, I find it to be very acceptable for what it is: a solid port. This is not an HD remake, it's the exact same exprience as the Gamecube version just with widescreen, 1080p support, and a different controller. So if you didn't enjoy the game in the first place, this version probobly won't win you over. However, if you don't mind that it's a basic port, then I absolutely reccomend you pick this up. For only $10, it's a steal (especcially if you pick it up on a Steam sale like I did.) It's better than going out and looking for a used copy of it.

Sonic Adventure 2 was a title most Dreamcast owners were curious over about how different it would handle things over it's predecessor, and back in it's day it was met with mixed reactions. (Very much like the first Sonic Adventure) Usually most people praise the gameplay sections of Sonic and Shadow for the more straightforward platforming action gameplay, but berate the clunky platform and shooting-segments from Tails/Dr. Eggman's stages, and the incredibly large and oftentimes tedious stage design of Knuckles/Rouge's treasure hunting stages. Although met with mixed reactions, Sonic Adventure 2 was overall regarded as one of the better outings SEGA's mascot has received in his 3D career.
With the game's release on Steam, I've tried this game out after I played the Gamecube port many years ago on, and personally I think it's a pretty decent port with HD graphics, a curious leaderboard system for the really hardcore fans of this game, and the 'Battle' content originally from the Gamecube port as DLC, which includes a pretty decent 2-player vs. mode and a overhaul of the main menu theme and other minor extra's.
The game's divided into 3 main gameplay modes, which you tackle as 3 characters on both the Hero and Dark side of the spectrum, complete with their own set of stages. As explained above the characters' gameplay styles are very drastically different, and most newcomers will often struggle with even finishing alot of the stages past the first few ones in the story, because of the somewhat harsh difficulty curve in the stage design. A new mechanic introduced in this game was the ranking system, in where dependant on how fast you cleared the stages and how well you overall did in your run, the higher the score, which is oftentimes easier said than done. Frequent issues were the rather clunky camera angles that shifted all over the place during gameplay, and you can't manually control the camera while moving around, alot of the enemies in Tails/Dr. Eggman's stages wold often spawn out of nowhere and collide with your character, taking a big chunk of damage and risking their high score streak, and that you can only detect one objective out of 3 at a time in the Knuckles/Rouge stages, and they usually randomize with the locations of the items, requiring you to both know the large stage layout and also collect them as quickly as possible, making A-ranking alot of the stages quite a difficult task in itself.
There's also the Chao Garden in where you can raise your virtual pet Chao, either for time-wasting fun, or to have them compete in races or karate mini-games. It's a nice  distraction and improvement from the Chao Garden system in the original game, but raising them can be very time-consuming (unless you use a in-game glitch mechanic to abuse it) and you have to remain in the actual Chao Garden to wait for your Chao to mature and grow better stats. It's a alright inclusion, but nothing I would spend time on personally.
Flaws aside, Sonic Adventure 2 is still a title worth playing if you're a big fan of the blue hedgehog and it's a moderate price on the Steam Shop. Just don't expect too have a easy time on the game if you're trying to shoot for all the unlockable content in the game.

It's not a mindless shooter, and if you play it like one you're going to get frustrated.  Unlike some other ones out there, you can't just run and gun most of the time. But if you learn your weapons, if you have a good team to play with, and if you think laterally instead of bashing your head on an objective, then it can be fun.
There are a good share of bad things about this game. The more you level up, the more money you get per match and the better stuff you can buy, but in the beginning it's really a slogfest. Be prepared to work hard to complete goals, and don't be surprised if the opposite team is just flat out better than yours. Also, be prepared to spend money on your guns. I know why they do it, it's a cash shink to even out things so you don't get super overpowered quick, but whether or not it's ballanced, in the beginning it feels cheap.
In the end, I like it. It's the slow kind of game where I feel like if I think smart about what I'm doing, then I can make the difference between winning and losing. If there are tanks, start laying mines. If you're getting shelled from far off, sneak behind the tank and plant explosives on it (very satisfying), if the enemy is holding an objective too hard, circle behind and start sniping people moving to teh base, they'll naturally come to look for you and that's fewer people defending that base.
(Oh, and I've played a lot more than 8 hours. Most of that was on a friend's account though. I've put about maybe 25 hours into it)

Hotline Miami is a top-down 2d game where you must eliminate a number of enemies on each level, requiring twitch reflexes since everything including the player dies in one hit. The game is moderately difficult, but the skill ceiling is high if you aim for good scores on each level.
It's very simple to describe Hotline Miami 2 if you have played the predecessor: It's more of the same. So if you can't get enough of the gameplay and aesthetics get this one too. Levels are longer and the story is more fleshed out, more convoluted but both are not necessarily strictly improvements from the first game; Since you die easily and have to restart each level each time you're incentivized to play more cautiously, which is goes against the scoring system in the game (rewards aggressive and reckless playstyle).
Adding to this is a level design with frequent long corridors where you cannot see the other end on the screen - but the enemies can - and they will shoot you from off-screen! This is terribly annoying throughout the game and although the levels are overall well-designed they commonly have these off-screen enemies. This makes the long levels even worse.
Should you get this game? It is a question of how much Hotline Miami gameplay will satiate you. I think the first game is enough for me and if you're new to the series I'd recommend that you get the original first instead - and if you absolutely cannot get enough then get this one too.
The gameplay is simple but strangely satisfying and the artstyle and excellent soundtrack adds immensely to it.

Hotline Miami 2 manages to satisfy with it's fast speeds, challenging design, gory visuals, satisfying kills, and mindblowingly fantastic music (which, in my opinion, manages to TOP the original's stellar ost). Another aspect that should be brought up is that the story is actually suprisingly interesting and captivating, it's confusing and crazy, but it'll most likely keep you interested at the very least.
As far as problems go, the game is far more restrictive than the first game. While in the original you get to collect and choose different masks that give you different abilities for almost every level, this game has it where you very rarely get to choose different abilities, making the design far more linear and tedious. Most will also dislike how LONG and open the levels get, I personally didn't mind that some levels were so long (kept me on my toes) and enjoyed how open the levels were (made things really intense, I loved being forced to improvise in those situations) but it's very obvious that I'm in the minority there.
Overall I'd give Hotline Miami 2...3.5 Tony the tigers: Frosted Flakes out of 5.

Note on controller support: this game fully supports Xbox controllers, however when you open it from Big Picture you'll notice that it states that it supports keyboard only. That is because when you run it it first starts a launcher, and that is where you enable the controller. Start the executable directly after doing so, though, and the controller works fine in-game without needing to access the launcher again. Just make sure your controller is on if it's a wireless controller before you start the game. Press the Xbox button in the center of your controller after starting the game and you should be greeted with the Steam overlay (Big Picture) or the Game Bar (Windows 10), which means the game has detected your controller. If the game does not accept your controller inputs, then it did not detect your controller and you must start the game again in order to redetect it.

A simple game based on a simple premise that is surprisingly addicting.  The beat and rhythm detection engine does very well, but when it doesn't, it makes the game difficult.  And under this circumstance, set on intense difficulty, can be more frustrating than a back-to-back Marathon of the Dark Souls Series.
From what I can gather, when a track is selected, It analyzes the track for predictable rhythm patterns, intensity levels, snare and bass beats, and vocal patterns to assimilate a profile that, if successful, sets up an obstacle course that the player can predict based on the nomenclature of the song. Key strokes coincide with some aspect of the music without making the gameplay monotonous.
When it doesn't work... it takes a calculated guess.  But at least it lets you know ahead of time that, 'Hey,  I can't get the beat in this track.'.  Then the level becomes... interesting.
It adapts to certain genres of music better than others. I found that the detection engine does not like older hard rock and heavy metal. like Motorhead's 'Thunder and Lightning'.  It did like Motorhead's 'When the Sky Comes Looking for You'. It didn't like Testament's 'Electric Crown', but did like Testament's 'More than Meets the Eye'. This leads me to suspect it has something to do with how the tracks were recorded - the enhancements made on more modern music recordings do better.
All in all, a good buy on sale just as a button warmer or relaxation game. 8/10 Would Faceplant into a Wall on a Missed Keystroke Again.

I've had this game for ages now, possibly before steam.  I'm not sure where I got it fist.  Perhaps Desura?
Anyway, this is a very interesting game.  I've only ever really played the story mission recently but previously the adventure mode was pretty lacking.  this may have been addressed.
Probably the best thing about this game is that it's a fairly unique experience.  I guess if you gave minecraft a plot it would be this game.  It's fun to explore and the creatures are unique and challenging.  Probably what makes it stand apart is that this is a RPG where you build your own town and your own vehicles.  I can imagine a lot of people would go nuts with this but I found it a bit tiring.  Just give me some pre-fab stuff so I can get on with it.  Thankfully this does seem to be the case and I'm sure there are mods to add some interesting designs without needing to sink time into their design.
That's not to say that it doesn't have any flaws.  The inventory management seems to be completely absent so as a result you hae limitless slots and no weight limit.  So you just keep everything you find, which is a lot.  I think I'm carrying around about 5k dirt blocks atm which are about 1 meter cube each.
As you can probably imagine this throws the economy into disarray.  Meat is the currency (I guess because it's a survival game?) but it never goes off and is quite plentiful.  There is no levelling or experience so quests just seem to keep the plot rolling along.  Yeah, there are rewards but you can just buy them for meat from the NPC as soon as you meet, so these feel largely pointless.  The more I think about it it just seems that this game is ment to be played in sandbox mode because the plot, while interesting seems fairly tacked on.
Combat feels a bit cluinky and relies on what feels like aut-targetting for melee and using a ranged weapon puts you into an locked in over the shoulder mode ala Resident Evil.  They're not terribe, but it's not revolutionary either.
While these sound fairly critical I still had fun with it and I suspect that the sandbox mode is the more interesting mode over the story.

I have been a long term Contagion gamer so feel qualified to write a fairly unbiased review.
TL;DR Each of the reviews you see below praising the game but critcising the developers are accurate.  It is that simple.  Also, team killing is rife which completely destroys the gameplay and forces individuals to use the easier non-TK servers which quickly become boring.  The developers have also taken no action against the numerous trolls who use certain choke points in the levels to ensure that gamplay is stopped.   The game community is almost completely extinct largely due to the developers shocking attitude to their customers.
LR;  When I first started playing Contagion last year the Developers were embroiled in a lengthy update process.  The community was disnechfranchised including certain individuals who had supported via Kickstarter and were still waiting on rewards.  I decided to let that slide and decide for myself.
The gameplay is good with tense moments and very acceptable graphics using the CS engine.  To the developers credit some of the levels are huge, the biggest in the Steam library by some estimates.  Nice use of fire and shadow makes for interesting human versus zombie battles.
Once killed a human player becomes a zombie and must attack and kill/turn the remaining human survivors.  However this creates a unique dynamic because once killed you drop your weapons and ammo.  Players naturally want certain weapons or more ammunition and team kill individuals to get it which forces the majority of the community to use non-TK servers which are far easier to beat because the zombies and objectives are easier to achieve with more abundant ammo.
Zombies are blessed with the ability to track humans, summon NPC zombies and direct zombie hordes.   Quite often the zombie players win if they are experienced and know how to ambush.  However if the humans are experienced then becoming a zombie is chore because the humans bunch at choke points...due to the fact that once a zombie is killed a certain number of times they become a spectator to the game.  So experienced players simply find an alley/corridor and wait.  They kill zombie attackers over and over forced into the alley until they become spectators then continue with the objectives.   The only way to win is hope that a new player is within the crowd and will make a mistake leading a gap in the team.
Because of the dev attitude, the team killing and the trolling, the game's user base has dwindled and you will often see the same 10-20 people hopping between servers some of which alleviate their boredom through trolling the levels to make them uncompletable.  Examples include stopping people from using critical elevators or preventing NPC characters from being rescued by leading them away from the exit zones.
Unofrtunately the user base has also dwindled in part due to the shocking attitude of the developer Tatsur0.  I had read numerous reviews on Steam and on the gaming press about his attitude to paying customers but disregarded them.  However as the updates dragged out from weeks to months to over 9 months it was hard to accept his constant refutations to customers.   In the end a bug-riddled update was issued with new maps but missing promised weapons, skins and game modes which are apparently "coming soon".  The developer response on the forums is always "I promise nothing" and "Go play other games."
People who criticised the developers were continually banned whilst trolls and team killers cannot be dealt with unless you supply video-evidence to the developers.
During my supportive period I even wrote a lengthy strategy for the developers (I have launched several apps and work in App Development) about how to really engage the audience during updates and prevent users leaving.  It was so well received some of the gamers even said I should be hired.   The post was ignored with a response "We don't have time to do any of that stuff."   I shrugged that off and continued to pour time into the forums and the game.
My decision to exit the game came after Tatsur0 refused to acknowledge the fact that Windows 10 renders the game unplayable (no sound, stuttering).   After I flagged this and asked how many users were planning to take advantage of the free Windows upgrade my topic was flagged as spam (under the heading "Not relevant to Contagion") and the response was
"Users know we don't support Windows 10 so Valve handle refunds."
I cannot in good faith recommend that new users devote any kind of time to a game whose community has almost disappeared despite being a pretty good game.
I honestly hope the Developers learn how to deliver a better customer service experience to the community that keep them in business.

Sonic Adventure 2 is a classic that brings back huge amounts of nostalgia for me, but in all honesty, the game hasn't aged very well. 3D Sonic games have always been somewhat iffy, and while this title is no exception, its rough moments can still be overlooked.
Putting the Chao Garden aside (one of the best parts of SA2B), the game is pretty decent, though some levels might frustrate or annoy players with questionable design. The plot is a little bit janky at times, and the cutscenes could use a lot of work (oh god... the lip-syncing), but the core gameplay is still very enjoyable. There are a few different game modes as well, so the gameplay tends to remain interesting and avoid repetitiveness.
However, the one part of this game that always brings me back is the Chao Garden. Chao are small, cute creatures you can raise as sort of a side-game, but the garden has a
amount of depth to it. You can raise and take care of them, enroll them in kindergarten, give them toys to play with, put them in races, they can interact with each other on their own accord, play instruments in bands, and the list goes on. You can raise them to be good or evil, and their appearance and personality will be reflected by it.
If SA2B was a staple of your childhood, then by all means pick it up; it's the exact same game you know and love. If you haven't experienced it before, I would still recommend it (if not just for the Chao Garden), but just be aware that it's far from perfect.

My first review ever so bear with me.
To start of with the good things:
- Huge world
- A lot of customization
- A ♥♥♥♥♥on of exploration
- Enormous amounts of things to craft and build
Now for the "less good things"
- The music is absolutely terrible. It's so cringey that I almost wanted to refund the game right away before I even loaded up singleplayer. It really sounds like something Family Guy or South Park would make a complete episode about.
- The combat is awful to say the least, it feels really sluggy and most of the time you will be bashing your left mouse button because there is no option to hold it down and keep attacking. Also a lot (all?) of the enemies won't even flinch when you hit them with a 5 meter long sword, making combat feel more like a turn based system then action.
- The movement is buggy as hell and is very unresponsive, feels very unpolished.
- Dungeons, those pop up randomly on your map, and most of the time come in forms of a huge mountain with an entrance or some desolate factory which you can enter. Thing is, these things are so big and pop up randomly, making them vanish just as quick again if you just run slightly from it. Very immersion-breaking, they also make some weird noise when they show up which sounds like a seagull being strangled by a string of plastic. The dungeons itself feel mostly empty and get boring really (i mean really) quick. The mobs in it are way to strong for their level and take a lot of hits before they actually die. I wouldnt consider this a bad thing if the combat itself is actually good and responsive, but most of the time mobs just miracolousy dodge my attacks despite me standing half a meter from them.
- The map drawing and fps is low considered to other games of the same caliber, but this could be due to the slugginess the game itself already has.
Overall this feels like a game which hasn't been polished at all, also the fact the devs consider this game "finished" makes me suspicious for the future for this game. I do not recommend this game for this price at the moment.

Your character will happily spend the rest of eternity producing a dig animation on a target that both you and the game know are out of range, and this happens often since you absolutely cannot move at the same time as digging.  Very fundamental things are tedious.
Movement, mining, and some very important UI interactions (the scanner in particular) are extremely poorly designed and suck the fun out of what could otherwise be a game with some unique positives.

Another early access game pushed out the door prematurely for the sake of profit. A lot of incompleteness.
- No dynamic AI pathfinding; waves of attackers cannot detect player-made bridges, so will stand still and wait to die if they cannot find a path. Even your own colonists are unable to use staircases.
- Quest triggers inexplicably fail frequently; I had to load a previous save on at least six seperate incidents in the story due to the game not detecting me having brought certain NPCs to the objective point.
- Indoor dungeons have no ambient sound, no footsteps, no sfx for moving objects, etc.
- Storyline ends abruptly and without closure
The game itself has potential for excellence, but it feels like one where the developers dreamed too big and ran out of budget near the end, so had to launch it without polish. A few more months of polish and it could have earned glowing reviews.

Door Kickers is none of those things. Door Kickers is a polished, finished and well designed game. The designer didn't try to do anything that wasn't needed but didn't left anything that was needed out either. There is clearly an attention to detail. It's one of those games where programmers spent hours resolving issues that you probably don't even realize but they are there to make your whole experience much better than average, so they are worh it. Graphically the game looks amazing and the Interface is very smooth feeling that is part of the game and not really just an interface.
It is a small game, yes, one that you probably won't play every day during a long period of time but it's still very worth the money. Highly recommend if you are looking for a game to enjoy without needing to highly commit to it.

Don't buy this game.
I got this quite cheaply on a steam sale a while back, and I definitely don't recommend this game.
Here's why:
It hardly does anything to innovate, the gameplay mechanics are way too simple, you can walk, jump and every so often use a weapon which is extremely ineffective. Other than that, they don't do anything original whatsoever. The game is based around a double-clichéd story. A world invested with zombies after a catastrophic event and a man trying to find his family in the chaos. Unfortunately, they don't give propper background for the story which makes it confusing at best. As for the protagonist, you can hardly make an emotional connection, the voice acting is great but the writing is poor. The controls are quite clumsy too, although I didn't try a controller, the mouse and keyboard controls are uneasy. This often leads to very frustrating deaths. The game is packed with puzzles, but often they don't give any hints on how to solve them, or the hints are too obvious removing any form of challenge. The puzzles are not very innovative either, just boring find a way to get to the other side of 'object X'. It runs pretty smoothly and the visuals are not bad, especially the shadows look quite nice, but then again, it's just a 2D game. The maps are pretty simple too and you're never in the same place for very long in order to enjoy the view. Then lastly, the game is really short, so you can't really connect to it and by the time you get familiar with the game you're alreay halfway trough. You can beat it in under 5 hours. And there are no optional objectives or any collectibles interesting enough to strech your game length. Just the linear stroyline. Perhaps, had it been a bit more interesting, or had there been a co-op mode I could have recommended this game. But, as it is, this game is so incredibly mediocre it's actually bad. I'm not just bashing on this game because I hate it. I tried to enjoy it multiple times, and at first it was really charming, but eventually it gets so dull you don't have the motivation to keep on playing. I tried to write a review as objective as possible, and therefore I definitely think you should not waste your money or time on this.

Seriously one of the greatest zombie games out there. Even in singleplayer.
Pros:
+ great graphics
+ very detailed designed levels and scenery
+ various modes that change up the game (coop & pvp)
+ great atmosphere, everything together sets up a real feel of being in a zombie infested world
+ traditional slow zombies (occasionally some walk a bit faster towards you)
+ the zombies are a real threat
+ stealth (although its not so great, but I like that its still there)
+ splitscreen coop! I love that they did this on PC! Its awesome and works smooth
+ a variety of weapons
+ very little HUD information, the game itself is in focus. Get messages and objectives on your ingame phone
+ some elements are randomly generated, like item placement or objectives
+ teamwork is key
+ various characters that you can choose from, no other player looks the same on a server
+ steamworkshop support
+ free DLC and additional content patches! I love it, its great the devs care so much about their game and community
Cons:
- aiming does not feel 100% right. Its kinda awkward if you clearly aim at the head, but it doesnt get counted as a headshot, but nothing too bad
- the phone is practically useless in pvp. You can send text messages to peoples phones, so they ring and you can locate them.....but its almost guarenteed to kill you, when you are focused on your own phone. Nobody uses this system in pvp
- there should be more maps, for the asking price the game still is great with the content (most workshop items are backgrounds for the ingame phone....I hope the community adds more maps)
- the stealth system is not working as it should. Sometimes zombies spot you from far away even if you are crouched and sometimes they wont notice you standing upright , when they are just not facing you. Its kinda hard to tell how stealth was implemented. But there is a melee stealth kill system, so it has to be there.....
Overall its a fun coop AND competitive shooter. Zombies are a threat in high numbers and really give you the creeps when in a tight spot. I love to play it from time to time and think its one of the best. The asking price is very acceptable and the devs include more content for free. I totally recommend it for every zombie fan.

Many of my friends and I are into zombie co-op games, so naturally Contagion is one of the titles which we would try on. Before I begin on descirbing the game itself, the first thing I would like to mention is that the number of people on my friend list who has the game, which is 21, is higher than the number of total players currently in game at the time I am writing this review. So, unless you can find yourself a good team (this is an 8 player co-op zombie killing game), please be prepared to face zombie hordes yourself. There will be one or two players in certain servers, but they will most likely leave half way or rambo about and turn into a zombie before you can realize what is going on. You will be real luckly if you can meet a quality player or two in any server. Truth to be told, this game has seen better days in terms of player count.
There are some merits to the game itself. First of all, as a realistic zombie apocalypse co-op game, the game is rather well-made, graphically speaking. The game itself uses the source engine, so expect something along the line of Left 4 Dead. The game mechanism is rather simple and bare, so as to make sure that you don't get too much on-screen help. There will only be a health and stamina bar; you can carry 4 items of all types, some essential in solving in-game quests; you will only be able to see the silhouettes of items when you go near them. Realism, so yes, that's all you get. The enemies are simpler as well, as there will only be two types of zombies, one the normal ones where you can kill with a bullet in the head, if you are able to place it there accurately that is. The other is a "riot police" zombie, which soaks a lot more lead before you can kill it. Bullets are as scarce as they are sacred in the game, so think before you shoot if you can help it. Oh and you won't have a crosshair so you will need to depend on iron sights unless you are using a shotgun.
Having said all that, the game itself is really not bad, though there are major problems elsewhere. Firstly, this game has a poor finishing. In the game I was playing before writing this review (and left because I was alone and I got overran halfway), I was pushed down a ladder by a zombie. That wasn't the problem, the problem is that, after being pushed down and suffering some dammage, my gun model disappeared! It won't be much of a problem if this is another game, but do not forget that Contagion does not offer any corsshair. So, what happened is that, I can't use my iron sight because the model has disappeared! The problem was solved by switching to another item (a card-key) and back, but shouldn't this bug be fixed at some point? Also, I have had issues with map skins. I was playign an official map and all reflective surfaces (and glasses) turned cyan after I did some alt-tabbing. You will know that vision is real important in this game if you are familiar with it, and it is not a simple matter of being irritating when glasses turn into solid cyan. If you can't see what's behind, hordes can close in a lot easier. Trust me, it's fatal.
And did I mention that zombies tend to get stuck a lot? Yeah, though I am not complaining.
Also, let's not forget that Contagion has an extremely weak game community. There's just a handful of players here and there, and there really isn't much of a back-up community to support the game. Not much custom maps, same old boring official maps with the same quests again and again, it gets repetitive. There are some die-hard fans, though most of the players I met are those who came back after a year or so to clear everything again, and then leaving it to gather dust in the vitural game shelf. I am one of them.
So, my final words will be that, do not get the game unless you know what is going on and what you will be expecting. You'll most likely enjoy a lone adventure for an hour, maybe with a random teammate or two who has 300 ping, and then grow bored with it pretty soon. Nothing too fancy about this game that is worth the money.

Game feels very polished with fantastic graphics (on ulta) but lacks replayability due to the lack of content - too repetitive and it just becomes a frustrating farm fest (because of the rigged rolls).
Here are some of the pros/cons:
Pros:
- Great Level design.
- Challenging difficulties
- The forge (which allows you to fuse 5 items together for an upgraded item), Upgrade item and Salvage is a really cool idea.
- The special Skavens really promote team play. Since if you get caught alone you're totally screwed.
- Devs seem to be listening and targetting player concerns (Hopefully we'll get more maps soon).
- Runs really smoothly on well built systems (I have an i7-5420k, R9 295x2 (crossfired) 16mb, 32gb RAM). Slight FPS drops at certain non-key locations of various maps (ex: when looking at a caged rat mid level of the Wizard tower map) - nothing to fuss about.
Cons:
- Insufficient maps. Game get's boring really quick. I'll play maybe 1-2 maps a day and then quit for the day.
- Multiplayer/Matchmaking needs some refining. Sometimes you could sit there searching for a game for a long time.
- Bots were given Artificial Stupidity instead of Artificial Intellignece. Game is really not geared for solo play.
- Ability upgrades on items are not very diverse and you can't tell in game - for most item attributes - when they "proc"
- Pretty confident that the rolling system is rigged to keep the rolls low so people could keep playing for those item upgrades (even if you get the bonus dice). This system is actually very frustrating. 50+ hours of play and I think I've rolled a handful of times over a 3.
- Host-switching is not available - as such, if you are playing a map and the host leaves, the map resets... Yes.. even if you're seconds away from the end (I'd classify this as the biggest flaw of the game).
- Lack of in-game options (Graphics mainly).
Hopefully, they'll adopt CD Prokekt Red's example and release some free content (maps) to add more life to this game since in it's current state you only need a few hours of play after completing the game to move on to another game.
Would upvote the game if they fix the host-switching, rigged rolls RNG, and add more content via patches (not paid DLCs).

Currently at the time of this writing I CANNOT recomend this game based on the grounds that the Development team has ignored UI issues presently in the game that make it hard for people with certain visual impairments or general vision loss to actually enjoy the game.  And as for someone who DOES in fact have a visual impairment this grealy effects my ability to enjoy the game to it's fullest potential.  it should be noted as well that these issues were brought to the attention of the Dev team during the beta phase of the game's devlopment as well as suggestions that could be implimented fairly easily to rectify said issues.
Presently there is NO UI SCALING in the game and all though some text areas have been addressed and text has been made larger in some respects.  But even at 1080p the current scaling is currently unaceptable.
Alos many of the UI Elements in the game, buttons, interface backgrounds and even some text rely heavily on the color blue.  for people who cannot percieve the blue color spectrum I would strongly suggest avoiding this game until the UI is darkened to create a stronger contrast to make text and other UI elements visible.
Also there may exist some recent gracphics changes to the display of collected items and or resources that could also make it difficult for individuals with varying degrees of color blindness to enjoy the game without furstration.
Also there is what I percieve as missing key information in quite a few tooltips within the game mainly in game creation and the onscreen map interface that you can see in the varous screenshots provided.  So it is mainly guess work as to what these features do or how they impact world generation.
As for the game itself.  There really is a lot to see and do and a lot of thought has been put in to both the story mode and the adventrue mode.  I am actually glad to see that they made changes to adventrue mode that in a way bring it more in line with story mode.  If you're wondering how you could compare the two.  Story mode is just that a story based adventrue that could be used as a very long tutorial for Adventrue mode.  As for Adventrue mode,  think of it more along the lines of the sandbox type game you would expect, i.e. Terraria and or Minecraft, (But of course with much better graphics in both cases)
As for the overall dificulty of the game as it has been explained by the dev team, there really is no real difficulty settings for the game even though the user is presented with an Easy and Normal mode settings.  there might be some slight changes in enemy toughness but it's not enough to really play the game on Easy difficulty settings.
One of the nicest features of the game though is the ability to create your own items through the built in ISO editor, this allows you to make weapons, armor vehicles and other items that can be used in the game.  it does take awhile to figure out how things work, but once you do you can make some really interesting items.  the only draw back to the system is there is limitations on some weapons on how powerful you can make them.  So ideas of the 50 barrel shotgun are out the window with this one.
All and all is it a good game, Yes I would say it is, but also as I said, for someone with a visual impairment the game is not user friendly and not recomended at this time.

Deadlight is mostly OK, but it is plagued with persistent irritations. The atmosphere is good, the 2D action within a 3D world lends to a nice modernized retro style, and the gameplay is generally interesting, although it is not without its issues.
The controls take some getting used to. Be prepared to die a several dumb deaths until they do. Then when you think you are used to the controls, be prepared to die several more dumb deaths when you miss a jump and touch water, when you don't roll as expected and you get hit by a spike trap, when you miss a fence or a ledge grab and get mobbed, when you try to jump over the top of the fence only to hang there and be caught, etc.
The protagonist really should not be traveling alone through a hostile world. He becomes winded after seconds of activity, he is pretty terrible at fighting, he cannot swim at all, and he isn't much better at jumping.
The game also suffers from what seems to be a glaring technical issue: the audio rarely plays during cutscenes and may stop abruptly even when it does play (at least on my system and supposedly those of many other people), so be prepared to spend the duration of those cutscenes reading subtitles instead of looking at the pictures. Turning off the subtitles seemed to result in cutscenes playing audio for a while, but after the audio abruptly stopped I was left with neither audio nor subtitles, so that experiment left me worse off than when I started.
If my recommendation options were "Yes", "No", or "Maybe" I would not hesitate to give Deadlight a qualified "Maybe" to allow for those inclined to suffer repetetive platforming, poor controls, dumb deaths, and broken cutscenes. Otherwise, it's a "No" from me.

Rage zombies were never my thing. Nothing against them but to me the slow shambling ones are the way it's done. If your a fan of oldschool zombie movies- There ya go. It's got that feel to it. Voice acting-A lot of work went into this. It's not stellar by any means but there are two radials with different sayings for most of them. Top that off the characters will be louder or quiet based on certain factors (If the person is crouching or havent done any movements yet - the voice of character will be quieter than usual. If character took a shot or someone near by shot - they will speak loud. They will also speak loud when they were running for quite long time or there is action going on).  If someone goes down, they become a zombie and can call the horde and hunt down thier former friends. I always had a lot of fun with it and it helps with the immersion which is a big thing in games for me.
-Modes-
There are a fair number of modes for this game. I look at some of the games coming out nowadays like Evolve (Don't get me wrong I enjoy it, I play it, but it was too much for what it was) that are essentially one game mode stretched to thin. The same could be said about a lot of games, some would say it about this one, but at least they tried. I tested some of the other ones, none were as much fun as coop.
Con
-The graphics are dated-
This isn't a deal breaker for me but it is for a lot of people "OMARGAWRD THUR GRUAFAX".
-The Co-op is unintuitive-
It's true, there's not going to be any Left 4 Dead highlighting of objectives. You have a cell phone that you check that tells you where to go / what to do. You have to actually figure it out for yourselfs, i.e. where the basement is, where the helipad (the roof) is, and so on. To the devs, this would really be my only gripe. Some things are easy to figure out, others can feel absurd. Play the police station and try finding keys the first time, you'll probably get the idea. I had friends drop this game just based on the fact they were tired of running around, sometimes dying because we couldn't find some objective. If you intend on playing coop, and new to the map- look up a guide of the map. You'll thank me. I'm not saying the Dev's should implement highlights, but something a little more informative with messages would vastly improve this game imho.
-Not really a SinglePlayer Experience-
The story will be the same regardless, nothing grandiose. Just the same mission or surviving alone. This game is meant to be played with friends. I have heard that there are griefers online, and people have complained about it in the reviews. There are griefers in any multiplayer experience. It's not the dev's fault. Seen it in Ark, Seen it in Payday, Seen it in Left 4 Dead, Seen it- You get the idea. Hell any survival game with limited resources is begging to be griefed. So- Play with friends if it bothers you, or find a good coop server. I have personally never had the issue of running into griefers on this as of yet, but have only played on online servers a handful of times. Those times I did, people were greedy with ammo, and weapons, but didn't grief.
All this being said, I would reccommend this game. There's still some things that could be added that could improve it, but if you're a fan of old school zombie movies like I am, then get it. Maybe wait till it goes on sale if the price tag is too high for you, but worse case scenario - If you don't like it well good news everyone steam has a return policy now. But play it with friends. All games are more fun that way, especially this one.

I had this game pop up on my store page around last July or so.  I didn't really think much of it at the time, so I passed it up and browsed for other games.   Fast-foward to December and I find myself looking at this game again in my queue.  Okay, fine.  Let's see what this game's got.  I watched the trailer, bought it, played it, and still am playing it.
The best way to sum up Melody's Escape is a simplified, yet stylized version of Guitar Hero (being the only other music game I have played).  Instead of a guitar, you control Melody as she runs through an obstacle course created by the game based on the music selection.  There are jumps, slides, kicks, dives (corresponding to the arrow keys), and at really intense parts she even flies.  In between those obstacles, there are colored spheres which correspond to WASD that you have to hit usually in time with the beat.  Difficulty depends on the music selection:  Higher beats per minute, higher difficulty.
Here's what I consider to be the game's main appeal:  While the game does come with 5 or 6 songs, all of which are very fun to play by the way, the game also can scan your music directory and add songs you own to the playlist.  Want a new way to enjoy that new song you just downloaded?  Play it on Melody's Escape.  It does not require you to make the course or do any sort of modifications.  Just select the song and the game will create a custom course based on the beat of the song....usually.  A rating is given based on how well the game could analyze the song, ranging from no tempo detected to excellent, and is for the most part dependent on the song's quality.  Some songs, especially instrumentals with no percussion, won't have a detected tempo but are no less fun to play than an EDM song with an excellent rating.  It can be hit or miss but the game does a fairly good job of matching the course to the song regardless of genre.
Overall, this game is very fun and very relaxing at the same time.  If you want a game you can unwind to, this is the game.  Graphic requirements are reasonable so if you have a low end machine, you can enjoy it as well.  There also seems to be a good workshop following for this game so if you want to customize Melody or the interface in any way you can do that.  And it's a good game to enjoy

Just to be clear - My review is only about the single player campaign (SPC). I don't play any multiplayer at all. I don't care about it. For me, it's all about what drives the story.
And the SPC is freaking awesome. I have zero idea why this game gets so much hate. It is a great thrill ride. You get to play both as a soldier and an attack dog. You have your run-and-gun sections and more stealthy ones. You avoid a Venezuelan hit squad in the jungle, infiltrate a high riser, escape on a zipline, be on a tank, attack helicopter, scuba diver, a shootout in space and that's only a partial list. Hell, you even get to avoid getting killed while carrying your injured attack dog to safety. That part really got to me. I love dogs, and this one sounds exactly like a real live one, so throughout the game, I really started caring about it a lot.
The conversations sound authentic. The mood the story sets is great. Production values are excellent. I particularly enjoyed the "kill silently" parts. It really made it feel like I'm in a real life spec op squad.
Again - I can't comment on multiplayer. For me, multiplayer in a shooter is pointless, but the SPC is HIGHLY recommended.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
