What's black and white, mixed with gothic environment and zombies all over it? That's right! It's Deadlight.
Deadlight is an action adventure platformer developed by Tequila Works, S.L. and published by Microsoft Studios in 2012. The game follows the journey of Randall Wayne, a man searching for his family that has drastically disappeared when the zombie apocalypse came out. The world of the game takes place around the year 1980 in the beautiful surroundings of the Seattle city. Because of an complication, Randall gets separated rather at the beggining of the game from the group of survivors that he was traveling with and spends most of the time trying to reunite with them and find a safe place in which to shelter from the horrors that will eventually find you through the course of the game.
When you actually start the game, you will know very little about what has been happening and the game throws you directly into the action but with time you’ll manage to find various journal entries that will slowly begin to shed some light on the horrifying events that have taken place since the end of the world started.
I have to warn you here. This is not your typical zombie game! Zombies are overpowered just as they should actually be in reality. You can only kill a few of them on the whole duration of the game so you should keep that in mind before buying the game because you will not find the Rambo style of killing zombies in Deadlight. The game encourages you to find ways of sneaking around them while continuing the journey of finding where your family is.
The game is based on the action-platformer genre at heart, but the driving story and the deeply environmental graphics makes it feel much like one of those adventures of Tomb Raider. Cinematics consists of motion comics with voice overs, which are more enjoyable than you think they would be. Randall will guide you through flashbacks of his past occasionally, making you understand the story better, and there are diary entries lying out there for you to find that will add more plot to the story, as well as some extra curiosities introduced by the ID of some strangers and newspaper clippings. Through the course of the game you will also find first aid kits lying around which will help you in the most appalling moments. And let’s not forget about the extra bullets that will save your life a few times. There are also a few "handhelds" to be found between the chapters, which will unlock some nice games to play within the extras menu.
The controls for jumping can be a bit suffocating at times, but the auto-save function will ensure that you don't have to repeat much of the section if you’re used to the feeling of dying a lot while playing a game.
The game also introduces you to a lot of diversity, as some areas are puzzle-heavy, whilst others are action-heavy, depending on where you are in the story. And I have great news for the achievements hunters! You can always go back to the main menu and choose 'Select Scene' if you think you've missed something. There are three chapters to choose from, and each chapter has specific scenes you can go back to with complete information on how many secrets you’ve found. Finishing the game also unlocks a new difficulty, Nightmare Mode, which is the same as the standard play, except that you will have only one chance of doing everything right, because the game will only save between each chapter.
- Support for Achievements, Trading Cards and Steam Cloud.
- Cinematics can be skipped (a relief for the achievements hunters or even for the people that want to just replay the game).
- Keyboard and mouse controlls can be re-mapped.
- An impressive work has been done on the soundtrack. I can still remember every beat of the main melody, that's exactly how nice it was composed. I highly recommend you picking up the DLC if you have the extra cash on you.
- The settings menu includes options like: turn on/off for things like Object Highlights, Hints, Vibration, Vsync and Subtitles; sliders for Music, Sound Effects, Dialogue, Gamma and Graphics Quality; and you can also change the resolution and choose between making it fullscreen or not.
- The game can be alt-tabbed for multitasking very easily and the music of the game doesn't hear when you're out of the game.
- Cutscenes play out like motion comics, an wonderful opportunity for the comic lovers.
- The voice acting is so good that you will start caring about what happens to the main character next.
- Hidden collectibles, secrets and time based leaderboards are probably enough to convince you to replay Deadlight after you've already finished it.
- The developers will introduce you to a new feature they've invented. 2.5D graphics with zombies in it! I have to tell you, this really surprised me while I was playing.
- Controllers can't be re-mapped.
- Leaderboards page doesn't work, saying that you need internet connection when you access it. The solution to this problem has been found, but it's a bit tricky and unpleasant. To see the leaderboards page, you have to block almost everyone from your friend list, till you get less than 100 friends. And that's it, it will most likely work now.
- Jumping is a bit weird, but that's understandable because this is a port from the Xbox 360 one.
- The game is only 4-5 hours long.
Deadlight is one of those games that made me feel in love with it from the very first time I've heard of it's launch on Steam. This may be my favorite indie game from the year 2012 and while the game may be a bit short (5 hours length), it does exactly what the developers dreamt to accomplish. To terrorise the gamers around the globe with the music, atmosphere and story it has, to put the fear into them so hard that they will remember this game for the rest of their lifespan. You get a realistic story-driven horror game that is centered in a apocalyptic zombie world. My advice is that if you're an addicted apocalyptic person as me, you should totally buy this game without thinking, it has the potential to thrill you, to captivate you and to make you cry, all those in a very short period. In just 4 hours you are thrown in a train of feels. You don't need to care about the bad reviews the game received, the game may have a different impact on every person, from my perpective the story was very good written and the actors have done a really good job in making you have a close connection to the surroundings the game puts you into. I couldn't stop playing till I didn't find myself at the end of the game. From my perspective, this game is an hidden gem.

Wow, this game is a blast!
I hadn't rly played any rhythm games prior to Melody's Escape, but liking the design and concept I decided to give it a try - and I'm glad I did!
In short, you use the WASD keys and the arrow keys (when using a keyboard), and need to press the right combination of keys to match the symbols on the screen, which also matches the rhythm of the song you're currently listening to. The concept is very simple, and once you get used to the controls it all comes very naturally.
At first I tried the easiest difficulty, "Relaxing", and it didn't take too long to master it. Next I moved on to "Intense", and suddenly things became a whole lot more difficult. Poor Melody kept crashing into stuff all the time. However, after some trial and error, I managed to get a decent hang of it. Especially when the songs were not too long or too complicated.
Finally, I moved on "Overload", the hardest difficulty. And honestly, this is where the fun begins. After you go Overload, you never go back. When trying out a new song for the first time, you wlll most likely fail horribly. However, slowly but surely you will improve little by little, and it feels oh so good when you manage to string together those long combo chains. Currently I have played the game for 8+ hours, but I have not even come close to getting a perfect run on Overload.
The rhythm recognition works very well. Some songs felt like they worked better than others, but pretty much all the songs that I tried, from a wide variety of genres, were more than playable.
One of the best parts of this game is that the fun never ends. You will never run out of songs, which means you will never run out of new stages to play. And the game is very addictive.
.
This will be one of those games that I will keep installed and ready to play whenever I feel like taking Melody for a quick run. And I
get a perfect score on Overload eventually. It might just take a while.
If you like music - get this game.
If you like rhythm games - get this game.
If you like good games - get this game.
It's definitely worth it - even at full price.

Five and/or seven out of seven, depending on the quantum state of Dr. Allen Carter's interpretation of the afterlife.
It ain't a perfect game by any means.  It's very unrefined, even after release; voiceovers of inconsistent quality, text sometimes reading more like a foreign language than English, story left open-ended, performance issues here and there, an end-game cutscene that makes the Uncanny Valley look shallow in comparison, those sorts of things.  Planet Explorers has its trouble spots, to be sure.
Underneath that bit of rough, though, is a diamond, raw as it may be.  This game's got good bones.  Unlike most voxel-oriented games (including ones in the public spotlight much later), Planet Explorers offers the ability to build things on a smaller scale than terrain and buildings; vehicles, weapons, and even (to an extent) body armor are all able to be custom-designed by the player, and sharing these custom creations online with other players is an absolute breeze using the in-game workshop.  Both the pre-defined map in "Story Mode" and the procedurally-generated random maps in "Adventure Mode" offer spectacular landscapes.  The wildlife feels both familiar and alien at the same time, and the storyline - while rough in execution in many respects - is believable and engaging.
Most importantly, though, is a development team that has demonstrated itself to be committed to working with players to fix problems and continually improve the game.  Communication has been bidirectional and top-notch, and the developers are quick to squish bugs as they're reported (even amid the influx of post-release feedback).
All in all, a great game.  Rough around the edges, sure, but shiny and clean is for AAA shops; Planet Explorers is an example of an Early Access game gone right even amid the risk of things going horribly wrong (as tends to be the case for games with even a fraction of the scope offered by Planet Explorers).

Whether you gets hours and hours of entertainment out of this game (like I did) or get annoyed with it probably just depends on what you're looking for in a game.
If you're looking for a game where you can explore, gather, craft, DESIGN & build at your own pace without worrying about frantic optimization and balance, this game is for you. Combat is passable, but not exceptional.

Voice acting is not the best.  The engineer in me cringes at some of the mispronounced technical jargon.

I was certainly able to look past some of these underdeveloped aspects of the game and still derive a ton of entertainment and satisfaction playing it.

-Horribly bad optimization as of now (if you own an i7 intel chip, at least). The game for some reason feels the need to tax your CPU more than your GPU which makes zero sense (with frames capped at 60 per second, I'm always using at least 60% all the way up to 90% of my CPU while only relying on 40% GPU at most during gameplay. Really, really bad idea.)
-Repetition in enemies, they POUR cannon fodder at you in the form of clan and slave rats, and it gets repetive mashing M1 constantly just to wade through the horde. Feels less like you slaying monsters and more like clearing vines in a rainforest, as if they're just obsticles rather than a threat, especially at the lower 3 difficulties.
-Difficulty scaling is wacky to say the least. Easy and normal are cake walks, while hard is relatively easy with even a decent group. All of a sudden Nightmare is kicking your♥♥♥♥♥ and Cataclysm requires either really good gear or insane co-ordination.
-A lot of the difficulty comes from the fact the horde just ends up doing chip damage, making block and push so mandatory it doesn't feel that fun anymore as you're usually on the defensive. Reducing the number of enemies but making the fewer numbers more deadly would help greatly.
-Pacing is, well non-existant some times. A few levels constantly throw enemies at you, making the chaos somehow tedious and frustrating rather than tense and fun. Seriously if you kill 1000 enemies in a level it's just boring after a while.
-Loot system can easily ♥♥♥♥ you over and there's not much you can do about it. The way loot is distrubuted in this game is frankly annoying. At the end of each level you roll 7 dice, which all have 2 "winning" sides to them (you can alter the dice in game by finding tomes, grimoires or loot dice) and you get loot based on how many dice land face up. This then gives you an item which could be for literally any class, meaning if you get extremely lucky and get a rare or legendary, it could easily be for a class you hate. There's a crafting system which partially alleviates this frustration, but it's still a lot of RNG.
It sounds like I hate the game, but I've played 20 hours at time of writing and still enjoying myself. If you can deal with the loot system being wonky and the tedium of horde based enemies, you'll love this game.

I've now played about 60 hours in story mode, most of it on the final build. In that time I've experienced one crash to desktop and three slowdowns so bad I had to quit and restart, but overall I've had a very good technical experience on max settings. The game looks great and the gameplay is fun and varied. Some of the locations are absolutely gorgeous and the design on some of the creatures is very impressive. Creation is a blast, but if you don't enjoy the process (understandable, as it does get rather fiddly) you can just as easily download ISOs or use ingame templates and items. Item creation is not a must to finish story mode, it's just another fun thing to do. The soundtrack is amazing. I'm probably buying the OST too, and that's something I've only ever done for one other game.
Combat is pretty basic. Once you get decent weapons, there's not much of a threat. (Tip: almost everything can be circle-strafed to death.) There's enough of a challenge to keep it engaging, but it's not very complex. You've got your attack and defense, ranged or melee, and that's pretty much it. I'd call it elegant rather than simplistic, but YMMV.
There's some negatives. The voice acting ranges from bad to atrocious, some plot twists are really awkwardly handled and most of the NPCs spend their days stuck in walls and falling through terrain. This is never gamebreaking, at least not in my case. My character does a lot of clipping through walls and getting stuck on the terrain, but never to the point where I have to reload. Neither me or an NPC have ever gotten irrevocably stuck, but it is annoying. Your own Minecraft-style buildings and vehicles can look jarringly blocky and out of place in the beautiful smooth landscape if you're not willing to spend many, many hours lovingly crafting them. Add it all up and you end up with a game that's very engaging, but not very immersive.
Still, the good outweighs the bad by a very large margin, and patches are still being put out. Fan created ISOs are already out there and there's some good stuff. I'd highly recommend this game. If it looks appealing to you, give it a go.

I must admit that I have an unnatural attraction to play zombie apocalypse games, so I was quite eager to see what Deadlight had to offer.
At this point in time, I am quite sure that most people reading this review are familiar with the concept of zombie apocalypse. If not - here is the concept in broad strokes: Due to some mysterious reason (either virus outbreak, genetic mutations or just something strange in the water), the recently deceased start rising back as flesh eating zombies (which from now on will be referred as shadows, to be consistent with the game nomenclature), killing and infecting everyone they scratch or bite. Only a selected few manage to escape the outbreak, and this is  where  the struggle for survival begins - not only from the shadows, that are just looking for an healthy snack - but also from ruthless groups of survivors that prey from the weak.
So, it is in this setting that we find our character - Randall Wayne -  traveling alongside a small group of survivors in hopes of finding a reported "Safe Point" in Seattle. We meet the group when a member just got bitten (as invariably happens) and head shot by Randall for the greater good . It is common knowledge that gunfire will attract shadows to you as fire attracts moths, so soon enough the group is overrun by shadows and Randall is separated from all the others. I could continue telling the story, but all in all it is textbook generic and doesn't bring anything that we haven't seen before.
However, the story is not the big selling point of deadlight. For all old timers that kept on playing games from the 80's and 90's, this is a good opportunity to play a 2D platformer that has a similar feel to the original Prince of Persia.
The atmosphere of Deadlight is also a very strong point. The backgrounds on all sets are amazing, very detailed and bring a certain degree of dark realism when portraying a dying world. It is interesting to see that the opposite happens with the characters that bring life to Deadligth's universe - they are mostly dark outlines of them, shadows as it may - which makes the choice of denominating the zombies as "Shadows" an intriguing creative decision, to say the least.
There is also a never ending supply of shadows. Stay too long fighting in one place, and more will come. Fire a couple of shots, and soon enough you will be  be swarmed. Bullets will not settle the score - they will only buy you extra few seconds to escape. That being said - it is also quite possible to finish Deadlight without firing many shots, as long as you time your actions just right.
The controls are all you can expect: They are responsive and simple. However, they also bring a negative point that clearly indicates that this is a console port - they are mapped in such way that makes the combination of some actions (double jump or sprinting + crouching) an awkward task. Most people will find this as a perfect excuse to unleash their rage  and justify their failures every time Randall dies...
... and he will, that I can guarantee!!! Even though there aren't any particular difficulty spikes, there will be plenty of events that will catch you off-guard. From platforms falling, being swarmed by shadows, shot by humans, or situations that will require nimble fingers, there will be plenty of opportunities to get Randall killed. But not to worry, Deadlight auto-saves regularly, with checkpoints conveniently placed to let you retry as much as you like until you reach a state of perfection.
To simply sum it up in one sentence:  the mechanics, the puzzles and level construction - all of those elements blend quite nicely with the dark environment and great visuals of Deadlight.
If you are feeling inspired, it is likely that you will be able to finish the main story in one sitting. Even in the hardest setting, it took me only a couple of hours to accomplish that. However, it also brings great replayability value. Each act / scene will record the time taken to complete, and you will be compelled to play them over and over again, just to find all the secrets or to improve your time. The plus side is that you can select the act / scene you want to play, as long as it was completed once. This is a great feature if you want to train the most difficult parts before tackling Nightmare mode. And what is "Nightmare" mode, you ask? Upon finishing the first run, we are given the opportunity to play Deadlight in a mode where there are no check points - meaning that you only have one shot to complete it from start to finish. Die once, and you are back to square one. Personally, I haven't completed this one, but a little shadow told me that people who have will gain access to an alternative ending that may be rather enlightening.
So, if you have Deadlight lost in your steam library, just enjoy it, and let me know how it went.

Deadlight is an action adventure platformer developed by Tequila Works, S.L. and published by Microsoft Studios. The game follows the journey of Randall Wayne, a man searching for his family across Seattle during the aftermath of a 1980's event that has decimated life on earth. Welcome to the zombie apocalypse. Randall inadvertently gets separated from the group of survivors that he is traveling with and spends most of the course of the game trying to reunite with them and find a safe haven. When you start the game you know very little about what has been transpiring but over the course of the title you manage to find various journal entries that slowly begin to shed some light on the horrifying events that have taken place since the end of the world started. You'll have to stay alert and be quick on your feet because, like in any great zombie game, death could be just around the corner.
Deadlight incorporates oldschool gameplay in the style of the 2D platformer which is a method of gameplay that once dominated the industry a long long time ago but is seldom used today outside of indie titles. I myself have always been a fan of the sidescroller so I was very much looking forward to playing this game. In my opinion, sidescrollers are best played with a control pad but since I don't have one I was forced to use a keyboard and this was not a problem.
Visually this game is quite stunning. It uses a mix of 3D environments and highly detailed models combined with 2D sidescrolling gameplay with all of it presented in beautiful HD graphics that really enhance the atmosphere of this decimated world. The sound quality is also very well done and really immerses you within the game. Gunshots, the wind blowing and dogs barking it all sounds splendid.
This game was really a lot of fun and the puzzles were challenging but I'm not too bright so you may disagree. Wanting to know more about Randall's life and the events leading up to and after the apocalypse kept me playing through to the end as I desperately tried to avoid certain death at the hands of bloodthirsty zombies and sheer stupidity. Deadlight really gave me a healthy dose of nostalgia from the good old days when platformers were king but the gorgeous high definition graphics and top notch sound quality quickly brought me back to the present. This title proves that you can indeed have the best of both worlds. Fair warning though as this game is quite short in playtime. I was able to finish the title in about six hours so that means the average gamer could do it in four or five...I like to dawdle. Yet another console-focused game crappily ported to PC. Full of little (and big) grievances which all add up for an annoying playing experience for PC gamers, some of which I'll list here. The main menu can't be navigated with WASD. It expects you to double-tap keys, which is completely inexcusable: it's awkward as hell on a keyboard, and why not just bind that action to one of the hundred other keys we have to play with? And the final straw that broke the camel's back - you need to press LSHIFT, LCTRL and A simultaneously to sprint-roll left. Try it right now: start with your standard WASD hand position, and then move your fingers over to those keys. See how clumsy it is? And in case you were wondering, nope, the game does
recognise RCTRL. Other moments in the Garbage Controls Hall of Shame include pommel-horsing fences seven times before the game decides to stop you on the side you want to be on, and attempting to jump straight up but instead vaulting ten metres right into one of the yet another bed of electricity(???) because you weren't at a complete standstill when you pressed Space.
Other bad points: "Secrets" and other world-enrichment miscellenea are lacklustre AF. Also, all the voice acting is bad, except, weirdly, for those two generic goons with five-second cameos at the petrol station. The bad voice acting has the secondary effect of making the already sub-par story feel even worse.
Good points: the art is nice, and although the controls make this hard to know for sure, I think the level design is actually pretty good. If I were playing this on a console, I probably would have enjoyed it. But I wasn't, so it was annoying, and that annoyance brought all the other amateurish elements into a harsh light.
Lots of fun.

A big budget title made by the creators of Left4Dead by the name of Evolve launched earlier this year to much negativity due to it's sickening lack of content, lackluster multiplayer modes, disappointing business practices, manipulative marketing campaign, and several hundred dollars worth of DLC skin and character packs. Now the game is all but abandoned and it was pimped out to be the next best thing since sliced bread.
Now, here comes a long another Left4Dead style, horde based, class based, multiplayer coop heavy title by an indie dev known mostly for RPG's, and by god does it put Evolve to shame. On top of not only looking better visually, having a good amount of content, better gameplay with more satisfying classes, more weapon variety, more enemy variety, better pacing, and even better written dialog between characters, it is all being sold for $30. In an age when a title like this could be sold for twice that with about $50 worth in season pass garbage and skins if sold by a big budget publisher, one has to wonder what world these developers over at FatShark even came from.
The answer? The world of Warhammer son! The attention to detail is bar none to only the Relic Dawn of War and Space Marine titles. The setting is great, with highly detailed locales filled with secret passageways, chests, alternate routes, houses, rooftops, sewers, forests, harbors, magic lairs, YOU NAME IT! The controls are fluid and extremely satisfying. The combat is visceral and diverse while not feeling too complex or overly simplified. It looks great, and it sounds great with excellent voice acting from the entire cast with lines of dialog making this old (Mid 20's) Warhammer fanboy wheep with joyful tears of manliness.
Sadly the game is not perfect (Knew this was coming) as it suffers from numerous bugs and performance issues, but nothing game breaking. While the loot in the game is interesting and extremely satisfying to get, it is sadly hampered by RNG dice rolls that will happily screw you over as much as reward you. The grind is real, my commrads, and the community is sadly as RNG as the loot drops since you have a high chance of running into A-HOLES that kick you randomly, curse you through the chat (Mute your damn mics, I mean it), or never stop boasting about how they played the game in beta and/or how high their level is. Play with friends ladies and gentlemen, the game is cheap enough to afford at least two people. The bots are horrible to deal with, never leaving your side, and never picking up Tomes (Essential to have better luck with RNG) nor healing themselves or even YOU appropriatly.
Despite all that the game is a freaking blast to play through. Grab some friends, grab some mead and have a bloody good time for hours and hours of grind, fun, and rat murdering. Think the Orchid man if he was written by Tolkien.
8/10. Can easily be higher once the devs churn out those free content updates and DLC (which I will happily support)!

A tactical strategy game that you can play in 2 modes, Real-Time or Planning Mode ( Kinda like transistor ) and kicking doors never been so fun
The game has a very large set of levels and its possibly endless, Around 80+ levels on Single Missions, And Also a lot of levels On campaign mode, And a lot of community created maps (Via level editor) And Theres also a Random Mission Generator which is really cool!.
you choose the map size the scenario and the difficulty, so yeah I meant it when I said Endless...But the fun does not last that long well it depends on your taste, gonna get to this in a moment.
You can customize every Swat member of yours, changing their gear and what not, Changing from assaulter to breacher and stealth or point-man Pistols, or pistols+rifles or shotguns or swat shield...etc.
Fun to use equipment's, such as a spy-cam to peak through a door and you move it left or right, or a breaching charge to plant on a door and blow it up to knockdown/kill enemies, And of course flash bangs, Stingers and more.
On each level you get stars which you can use to unlock more Equipment's , Stronger/heavier shields or armors or weapons just an example.
I really like the game control, You can assign your units to ( A(alpha) B(Beta) C(Charlie) D(Delta) ) And assign plans to each which they will execute after you press the assigned button on UI or keyboard, Really good to coordinate your unit movements ( Shields first, snipers last) and execute the perfect plan which takes some serious thinking.
At some levels you also get a sniper that auto-locks on targets on your sight, You can press Tab to order him to switch to another target and S to take the shot.
The enemy responds are pretty clever, they don't just mess around, you'd usually need to flashbang them or flank them or use any method to distract them to avoid allied losses.
The game music is very good and gives you the mood to focus on your plans, or pumps you up to go break sh*t and kill everyone.
Game levels are pretty great, Although there are a lot of levels you don't see them getting repeated.
Game difficulty is pretty hard, And keeps getting harder as you go on.
Single Mission Mode, Is a set of 80+ levels that you play each with its mission and different level layout, You could skip the first ones and jump to the last.
Campaign mode, Has no story its just a set of levels that you keep on playing with limited swat units, when you finish a level with some causalities they don't come back in the next level so you have to be careful and usually restart when they die, Around 5 Campaigns each is about 4 to 9 Levels, with completely different layouts, It also has the caption ( More to come ) so thats good I guess, they want to add more.
Leveling up your squad to the next level gets you access to the next Class ( Which I mentioned earlier the Stealth or Breacher .. etc )
Apparently there are (Doctrines) points that you get awarded by leveling up your squad level, And use them in a Skill-Tree to give you more abilities and accuracy and more.
Of-course you level up by receiving the exp award at the end of every level.
The game has a lot of achievements, At first they are easy to obtain but the later ones are pure hell this is fun for grinders.
Level editor is easy to use, And power it with your imagination, Create a hostage rescue, Annihilation, DrugBust, Arrest, Robbery, Vip Secure, Stop the execution And of-course Defuse the bomb.
2 mods that already exists that adds some levels and a few stuff ( Christmas mod, Template mod )
So now after all the good has been said let me tell you about the other side.
Although the game is really good it has its own fair share of cons.
Sometimes my units becomes dull and throws the bomb although I specifically stopped the action by pressing the delete icon, and sometimes they also become very slow to react when an enemy appear that i'v been waiting for, takes them time to take the shot and sometimes they'd kill my units before they even reacted to seeing them, I don't know if this is how the game wants it to be just saying.
I really dislike it when a unit throws a Bomb it has to wait before making a move, I understand that's how it works in reality but most of the time the delay backfires because it reaches them after the effect of the Flash-bang wore off, and it goes there to die.
Some levels are fairly hard and others are insanely unfair and frustrating, reach the point where you just keep on doing it again and again and again and going full-throttle until your units mans up and takes the shot accurately and miraculously you win.
Reason why I said ( Apparently there are doctrine points ) Its because I saw it the first time I launched the game but forgotten about it, And the game has no hints or anything to show me or remind me to use it in main-menu, I was missing around my rank and accidentally saw it lol... Which brings me to the next point.
Lack of tutorials, I don't mind this but if you are the type that wont go without them just a heads-up (There is a how to play guide)
Units becomes stupid when they collide with each other, they just stop and do not perform their next action instead of turning around the unit or object.
There is a bugged level in campaign which made it impossible to me to finish the 2nd one ( so I skipped to the next one )
In which a mission where I'm supposed to secure the VIP and bring him back to the safe zone, And usually killing all hostiles gets the job done and leaving no need to get the hostages but this one required it, So I go set next to him so he'd follow me but he never did, Played it around 9 times already and never got to finish it....was incredibly frustrating.
LIKE I mentioned at the beginning of the review after a while the game may gets boring depends on your taste.
As for me after around 7 hours I started getting really bored, Although the game has a lot of different levels, The feeling stays the same, Be careful and quick to finish the mission blah blah, Gets a bit boring in my own opinion, They should'v made a way to spice it up with more challenges and stuff, Again thats just me, There are people who played this for over 25+ hours and did not complain at all.
If you don't want to read all that
:
1 - Tactical-type game that requires strategy and thinking, Difficult but fun.
2 - A lot of levels to play, And a random mission generator, Campaigns and Community Maps.
3 - A lot of Weapons, Utilities (Gadgets) And support gear to unlock.
4 - Customizing every unit in every mission to make it best suitable for the current level.
5 - A lot of achievements to grind on, Trading cards and Steam-Cloud.
6 - Great game music and sound effects, gets that thinking mode of yours pumping.
:
1 - Sometimes it gets kinda frustrating on how some levels are ridiculously difficult compared to later ones.
2 - A few clunkiness in character movements colliding with each other and slow reactions in some cases.
3 - A few bugs I found on certain levels which made some impossible to finish and the rest just 10 times harder.
Also something I really liked about the game.
The terrorists are not portrayed as Arabs, They always make terrorists in video games to look and sound like Arabs *cough*Cs*Cough* and more games ... It frustrates me makes me feel discriminated against sometimes although i love those games, BUT it was really refreshing and nice to see a game that made a different approach.
TL;DR
A game for the tactical shooter fans, definitely worth its full price, Hard as HELL and takes some LONG♥♥♥♥♥time to complete, and even longer to 100%, And to get all the level ups and unlock everything, i'd say 30+ hours.

Personally one of the best games in a while. Grinding a perfect game out of this took 44 hours, playing just about every day. And immediately after that, I'm already missing it. It did not start to feel boring or repetitive at any point.

You can carefully (and sometimes a bit tediously) plan out the entire mission, and then relax while watching it success or fail, after which you can adjust it for a rerun. If you don't feel like planning, you can go ad-hoc blasting away in real time, merely pausing in some tight spots.
There are some annoyances in the planning, but nothing deal breaking. Addictive game that is fun, quick and easy to start and play a couple of maps - and then a couple more.
In the achievements point of view, I liked the fact that achieving everything takes a lot of work, but is eventually accomplishable by anyone. Waiting for added campaign, or better yet, Door Kickers 2 <3 (there is community content for now)

Was unsure about this game on my first playthrough, but the more I've played it and dug up on the thematic and narrative ties in this game, the more I love it. Fans of the first game may need to reserve their opinions and let them settle before jumping to conclusions, but I believe Dennaton Games made precisely what they were aiming for.
With the level editor in tow, fans of the first game were always bound to basically extend the levels of Hotline Miami 1 on their own, so the developer set out to create a more unique narrative-focused experience with a focus on undermining fan expectations. Much of the story here is reactionary to player-expectations to the first game(from what I can gather anyway) and as such, it may annoy many players that were simply looking for more Hotline Miami 1. The level designs especially have been stretched in a way that may grind on certain players' nerves, but they -also- present very unique obstacles that I'm not sure would've ever emerged from players given the new level-editor, so I'm happy with the overall product.
While my initial review probably would have been more critical, I find myself relating this game very closely to MGS2 for those of you who are aware of what Kojima was aiming at with that game. In undermining fan expectations, the game said more about the serving medium and brought about a lot of interesting explorative themes I don't get in many other places. And yes, the music is as strong as ever in this game. <3

A big budget title made by the creators of Left4Dead by the name of Evolve launched earlier this year to much negativity due to it's sickening lack of content, lackluster multiplayer modes, disappointing business practices, manipulative marketing campaign, and several hundred dollars worth of DLC skin and character packs. Now the game is all but abandoned and it was pimped out to be the next best thing since sliced bread.
Now, here comes a long another Left4Dead style, horde based, class based, multiplayer coop heavy title by an indie dev known mostly for RPG's, and by god does it put Evolve to shame. On top of not only looking better visually, having a good amount of content, better gameplay with more satisfying classes, more weapon variety, more enemy variety, better pacing, and even better written dialog between characters, it is all being sold for $30. In an age when a title like this could be sold for twice that with about $50 worth in season pass garbage and skins if sold by a big budget publisher, one has to wonder what world these developers over at FatShark even came from.
The answer? The world of Warhammer son! The attention to detail is bar none to only the Relic Dawn of War and Space Marine titles. The setting is great, with highly detailed locales filled with secret passageways, chests, alternate routes, houses, rooftops, sewers, forests, harbors, magic lairs, YOU NAME IT! The controls are fluid and extremely satisfying. The combat is visceral and diverse while not feeling too complex or overly simplified. It looks great, and it sounds great with excellent voice acting from the entire cast with lines of dialog making this old (Mid 20's) Warhammer fanboy wheep with joyful tears of manliness.
Sadly the game is not perfect (Knew this was coming) as it suffers from numerous bugs and performance issues, but nothing game breaking. While the loot in the game is interesting and extremely satisfying to get, it is sadly hampered by RNG dice rolls that will happily screw you over as much as reward you. The grind is real, my commrads, and the community is sadly as RNG as the loot drops since you have a high chance of running into A-HOLES that kick you randomly, curse you through the chat (Mute your damn mics, I mean it), or never stop boasting about how they played the game in beta and/or how high their level is. Play with friends ladies and gentlemen, the game is cheap enough to afford at least two people. The bots are horrible to deal with, never leaving your side, and never picking up Tomes (Essential to have better luck with RNG) nor healing themselves or even YOU appropriatly.
Despite all that the game is a freaking blast to play through. Grab some friends, grab some mead and have a bloody good time for hours and hours of grind, fun, and rat murdering. Think the Orchid man if he was written by Tolkien.
8/10. Can easily be higher once the devs churn out those free content updates and DLC (which I will happily support)!

TL;DR: Left for Dead with swords, and that's a compliment.
So after playing a fair amount I can now say that this game is a blast. Seeing how this is a Left for Dead clone and everyone knows it, I will simply discuss what sets this game apart from the game series we all know and love.
First and foremost it's the melee combat. This game is all about it, and even though there are ranged-focussed classes as well, melee remains an unavoidably large part of the game. And it works well enough. I am kinda missing the option to differentiate between strikes (instead of light/heavy they could have gone full chivalry and made left-swing/right-swing/overhead/stab attacks), but the hit detection and feedback are awesome. I am especially enjoying the dwarven hammer, which gives a satisfying thump and will bounce off armored targets but just sweep lighter targets along. The feedback is phenomal and feels brutal. Swords were a tad less over-the-top, but they still feel sturdy and hard-hitting. Also blocking. Whereas in L4D you have to shoot infected before they can even hit you, there is no such ranged option in Vermintide. Blocking, shoving and dodging are essential to prevent being damaged. This makes large hordes and being surrounded particularly dangerous, as you cannot block all around you, and you can't dodge anywhere when there's rats everywhere. It makes it all feel a lot more engaging than just mindlessly blasting the hordes. It makes staying together even more important, as a good group of commons can and will kill you, and in L4D I didn't even see commons as a threat.
Then there's the five classes, which all have a unique role. There's a crowd-focused melee, a single-target melee, an allrounder, a crowd-focused ranged and a single-target ranged. Collectible loot gives some flexibility in the role a character has, and of course all the character have the ability to fend off hordes, some are just better at it than others. The loot system will drop you a single weapon after each mission based on a dice roll (yes, literally a virtual dice roll), with some items scattered around each map that give better chances for rare ones, and grimoires that lower max hp for the rest of the mission in return for a fairly hefty boost to your odds. Failing a mission, however, nets you nothing.
The enemies are virtually the same as in L4D2, there's commons, armored ones, and a range of specials like the spitter, stalker, smoker and tank. Of course all reskinned as rats. They do the same job as the ones in L4D2, force teamwork. If you stray too far, a packmaster will simply sweep you up and hang you. But I feel the rats are a welcome change in the zombie-ridden gaming scene. I like having a horde game with more inspired characters than your every-day zombie. Speaking of inspired characters, this game does a phenomal job of bringing the Warhammer lore and universe to life. The characters have clear personalities that are reflected in each line of dialogue and there's a clear story for every mission. There's not really a story mode, but it's more like an overarching story and a bunch of lore interwoven in the individual missions. Combined with some ridiculously gorgeous levels this game does suck you into its universe. The detail even comes back into some cool weapon discriptions and cosmetic description, though sadly the background on weapons is reserved for the rarest ones.
Some of the less awesome parts of this game, however, have to be the fact that the game is very short if you wouldn't replay it (hence the 30 dollar price tag I suppose). With 13 missions that aren't much longer than 30 minutes at best, and some missions being only a few minutes, about 5 hours would be enough to see it all. You'd have to be the kind that seeks a challenge on the more insane difficulties to really get your value out of this one. The fact that more difficult mission yield more interesting loot will help with that. There's also the fact that matchmaking is rather dumbed down (though it covers the basic options) and the fact that the inventory and crafting system are represented with a forge and your storage chest. Perhaps this is keep immersion up, but it is also less functional than a good old menu. Now you'll have to virtually walk, which is tiresome. Another minor gripe is that while playing, the busy streets and weird architecture combined with the in-style HUD can't help but slightly disorient you and have you lose your overview. L4D did an amazing job of making clear what you have to do and what the team's status is, Vermintide is just a little less in that regard. However, you will get used to it to the point where you'll barely notice it once you start to learn the levels.
Gameplay-wise my major gripe is the 'a.i. director', which is also taken from L4D and 'intelligently' spawns enemies and hordes. I found that on occasion, he was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Though he is essential to keeping the replays actually worth playing, he can also pull the most enfuriating and unavoidable ♥♥♥♥. He has to be there, but he has to be smarter. Spawning a rat-ogre on a cliff-walk is not okay. Neither is spawning a suicide bomb on us just as we're getting in the escape vehicle. Then finally, the mission length and difficulty are wildly irregular. One mission can be a 30-minute adventure while another is a 3 minute cake-walk. They all look awesome and they have a varied setting though, some taking place underground or in the woods, others in the city, at the docks etc. I never found myself bored with the scenery, it all has a very grim and gritty vibe to it that actually brings across the end-world feel.
So, in total, this game is well worth the 30 dollar price tag for anyone who enjoyed L4D or anyone who enjoys hitting vermin with metal. Qualitatively it's still a step below L4D, but not a large one, and it's uniqueness is a welcome change. Judged as its own game, this stands well above the average with one of the best co-op experiences combined with a super cool setting, and I can only hope that in these uncertain days of gaming, the devs will continue to support and care for their community. Adding in some more maps in the form of paid DLC would be most welcome, but let's not turn into Overkill Studios. Please. I have trust issues.

I've been playing this game on and off since the very beginning of the Early Access.  It's one of, if not my favorite game in the Sandbox/Open World/Survival genre.  You should consider this as an early access review since I haven't yet played the release version of the game.
What sets this game apart from other games like it is that it has an epic story and feel, and the story mode can be played coop.  It's a "go at your own pace" story where you do quests and/or side quests which usually reward you with gear/recipes. However, you can also skip all the quests and just purchase most of the gear/recipes at the npc shops if you prefer to do it that way.
The scenery is awesome and many locations feel epic.  This is because in story mode the terrain was hand crafted and not randomly generated like other games.  There are plains, deserts, huge forests with giant trees, etc. each with different creatures.  The creatures and vegetation are some of the most unique and alien I have seen in any game.  I believe in the adventure game mode the terrain is randomly generated but I haven't played that mode much yet.
The crafting system is very unique and you can build custom weapons, vehicles, boats, helicopters, etc. and the materials you use matter.  NPC "shops" exist where you can buy most of the recipes or if you are patient you can do quests which usually reward you with recipes and/or items.
Once you have discovered a point of interest in the game, you can spend the game's currency (meat) to fast travel between any point of interest, It has a unique mining system where you can scan for ore deposits, and you can put comments on the map, so you can get back to the deposits later. The voxel terrain is destructable, and contains underground caverns to explore.  You mine for ores, cut down trees, hunt beasts, etc. to get materials for crafting.
I personally really like the sound track.
I can't think of much not to like about this game. I guess bugs were probably the greatest deterrent a while back.  Multiplayer had some syncing issues when I last played it a few months before the release but most of the bugs were tolerable at that time.  I'm guessing they have fixed most of them for full release and I can't wait to do a full play through again now that it is out of early access.
The game also has several other game modes.  I haven't tried them so I won't comment on them.  The coop story mode is almost everything I have always wanted in an Open Sorld/Sandbox game.
I highly recommend this game.

Sonic Adventure 2 is what 3D Sonic games should aspire to be! Admittedly, I might be viewing this game with a certain level of nostalgia clouding my viewpoint, but Sonic Adventure 2 is really just awesome. I first played this game on the Gamecube and it is one of those few games that I never considered boring to play. Sonic Team really knew what they were doing in this game (I wish I could say that about some of the later entries in the series).
For starters, the pacing issues of the first Sonic Adventure are just gone. There are six playable characters in SA2 much like the first one, but you don't have to start the story over and over for each character. Instead, you just play each character's stages as they occur in the plot, which is far less jarring. Additionally, there is no Adventure Field in this game, so there is no longer the tedium of searching for random items or areas to advance the plot between levels.
There are two storylines that you get to follow: Hero and Dark. There is some overlap between the two stories, but the overlaps are mostly for the boss battles so they don't particularly last that long (and they tend to involve each rival character pairing). The dynamics between the characters are much improved, and the conversations feel a lot more natural as a result (though this might just be because of a better localization effort). There really isn't a wasted moment either as every scene plays into the overall plot.
The most interesting part of Sonic Adventure 2 is how they managed to capture the length of the 2D Sonic games. This isn't exactly a long game for either storyline, and each side can be easily beaten in one sitting. The game never feels stale either because of the variety in stages. There are three different kinds of stages. The first type involves Sonic or Shadow and, much like the original Sonic games, simply requires you to get to the end of the stage in an expedient manner. The second type involves Tails or Dr. Eggman, and you use the lock-on abilities of chicken walker mechs to rack up chains for points. Finally, the third type of stage involves Knuckles or Rouge, and you have to search for items hidden within the level using a hot or cold kind of radar system. In addition, there is one driving stage in each storyline, but considering that this game is mostly an action platformer, the driving mechanics are understandably terrible (the vehicles don't really have any maneuverability around corners).
The game ranks you based on how quickly you completed a stage (or rather how highly you scored, which includes a time bonus for completing the stage quickly). The ranks add a nice layer of depth to the game and are an easy way to measure how well you performed in a stage without needing to continually reference your personal best. Rank A's are appropriately difficult to achieve and are extremely satisfying to obtain at the end of a level. Unfortunately, you will more than likely be good friends with Rank E on your initial playthroughs of different stages, especially if you die at all. Unlike the early Sonic games, the score isn't cumulative, so it will reset to zero after every death. Essentially, any death far into a level pretty much guarantees a Rank E finish, so there is a strong incentive to survive from beginning to end. Though I found that Sonic and Shadow's levels are hard to get a high rank even if you survive to the end of the level.
After completing a stage in Story mode, it is unlocked in Stage Select and there will be an additional four missions to accompany the stage, each with their own scoring requirements. For example, the second mission of every stage in the game requires you to get 100 rings as fast as you can. So even after completing the somewhat short story modes, there will still be plenty of content to go through. Through completing stages and achieving high ranks, you will be rewarded with emblems of which there are 180 in the entire game. I believe it is possible to get all 180 emblems, but will require considerable patience (I've only just acquired 90 emblems which easily took over 20 hours of play time). The emblems based around the mini-games within the Chao Garden are particularly difficult as it requires raising the perfect chao, but nothing compares to the difficulty of the additional driving missions (one of which involves avoiding hitting cars with exceptionally large hitboxes and to make matters worse...the cars can hit you from behind).
The Chao Garden was an interesting concept in the first game, but it is expanded upon greatly in this game. The Chao are a kind of digital pet with stats and life cycles, and thankfully, this isn't just a tacked on feature in the game as it is integrated into normal gameplay. Each stage has animals hidden throughout and the enemies will also drop items called Chaos Drives. Using either the Chao key hidden within one of the boxes in the level or accessing the garden directly through stage select, you can give the Drives and animals that you collect to the Chao to raise their stats. The higher the stats of a Chao, the better it will be able to perform in the Chao Race or Chao Karate mini-games. The Beginner events in either of these mini-games aren't so difficult, but it will be very time consuming to beat anything higher than that. The Chao also get a Hero, Dark, or neutral affiliation based on which characters show the Chao affection. There is a considerable amount of depth surrounding the Chao Garden and it is almost like getting a second separate game in addition to Sonic Adventure 2. I wish other games had bonus content with this level of depth.
As for the actual playing of Sonic Adventure 2, you can comfortably use a keyboard or gamepad. When I played with the keyboard, I mapped the action buttons to the number pad and kept movement on WASD. It is very playable with that setup, but the game was originally intended for a gamepad, so use one if you have one. The graphics have aged well especially with whatever touchups that were applied to the PC release, but don't expect it to be several generations ahead of the original's graphical look. I must say it is wonderful to be able to play this in 1080p resolution.
The physics are a lot better than Sonic Adventure, but there is still the occasional odd moment (luckily, you are unlikely to fall off of loops like in the first game). The rail sections over bottomless pits can be some of the most frustrating parts of the game and sometimes the game just won't register contact with the rail resulting in many cheap deaths. Besides the rail sections, a few of the boss battles can be downright picky about what constitutes a valid hit. Beyond that, I wouldn't say I have any complaints about the game mechanics (though the cheapshots from enemies and environmental hazards that Sonic games are known for are still as frustrating as ever).
Just like usual, Sonic Adventure 2 has a great soundtrack. Who doesn't want to sing along to the first level's ever popular "Escape from the City"? The rap lyrics in Knuckle's levels are unquestionably terrible, but it's composed so well that it actually ends up being good somehow (at least, I thought so). My favorite music is all the songs in Rouge's levels.
As for performance, I played this on both a GTX 560 Ti and GTX 780. The game was completely stable on the 560 Ti, but I did encounter random display driver crashes with the 780, so your mileage may vary. The screen would go black and the sound would loop, but the game would ultimately recover from it after a few seconds (and luckily, the action would pause during that time, so the few crashes I experienced never ended up too catastrophic).
I fully recommend checking out Sonic Adventure 2. It's one of those games that I feel shows off what an action platforming game should be like. It might very well be the best 3D Sonic game that we're ever going to get at this point in time.

TL;DR: Spent 2 hours asking friends "Where the ♥♥♥♥ are you?" and "Where the ♥♥♥♥ am I?" in Steam call.
Long Review: Got the game with 2 friends. We spent the first 20 minutes failing to join each other's servers. Decided to just meet up on someone else's server.
First server we joined, we spawned on opposite sides of the map. We tried looking for each other while searching houses for weapons and killing the occasional zombie. We found hardly anything. Other people joined the server. One of them found me and shot me. My friend got shot soon after. We decided to find a new server.
Second server, we spawned on opposite sides of the same map, again. Other people joined the server, again. Still can't find my friends. I hide in an attic, look out the window, and see 4 zombies walking into my house. I wait there with my ax held high ready to take them on like I'm in L4D2. This is not L4D2. 3 zombies climb up the ladder. I swing and hit 1 of them. The other 2 get up into the attic. Suddenly, there are 6 zombies attacking me. I die. My friend joins the other players and they bunker down in a house. I spawn as a zombie, gather a hoard, and start hunting down my friend. Meanwhile, my other friend died and got turned into a roach. I stepped on him.
Third server we spawned together in a prison. Other players were already further ahead in the map. We ran around and eventually found them. From there the game consisted of struggling to find small items like keys and bolt cutters to open doors, fighting a couple docile hoards, and then searching for more keys or locked doors. Players who knew what they were doing charged off ahead, while my friends and I got lost and frustrated. The maps really have no indication of where you need to go to find key-items or doors. We ran this map a couple of times before leaving mid game.
I might change this into a positive review, if I can get a good game going. I haven’t given up on it yet. But at this time, I’m giving it a negative review b/c it felt clunky and things like creating a private server did not work.

Options include sliders for Music, Sound Effects, Dialogue, Graphic Quality, and Gamma (Brightness.)  Resolution goes up to 1920x1080 for me.  You can turn on/off Object Highlights, Hints, Vibration (for controller,) and Subtitles (under Audio Settings.)  Keyboard and mouse controlls can be re-mapped, though I used the controller (which cannot be re-mapped.)
I was immediately sucked in by how atmospheric the game is, reminiscent of a cross between
, and
(because ZOMBIES!)
The game is really an action-platformer at heart, but the driving story and deeply environmental graphics, sounds, and voices make it feel much like an adventure.  Cinematics can be skipped (but why would you want to do that?) and consist of sepia-toned images with voice overs.  You will play through flashbacks, and there are diary entries you will find which add to the story, as well as little extras like the ID of strangers, newspaper clippings, first aid kits... Oh, and don't forget bullets!  There are also a few "handhelds" to be found, which are games to play within the game.
The controls for run-jumping can be a bit sticky at times, but the auto-save function ensures that you don't have to repeat too much if you die.  Speaking of running, there ARE running sequences similar to -- but not as hair-pullingly frustrating as --
.  I had to repeat these sequences three to five times, max, and they're not very long.
Some areas are puzzle-heavy, whilst others are action-heavy, depending on where you are in the story.  You can always go back to the main menu and choose 'Select Scene' if you think you've missed something.   There are three chapters to choose from, and each chapter has specific scenes you can go back to, complete with information on how many secrets you found;  ie. 2/3.  Great for those who like to 100% their games!
Finishing the game unlocks Nightmare Mode, which is the same as the standard play, except that the game only saves between each chapter.  Nightmare indeed, especially when you consider that the controls for jumping WILL mess you up, and you WILL die.  I think I'll just skip this part.
There are achievements to be had, but I can't see getting all of them.  For one thing, you'd have to meet a friend on the leaderboard for one of them (solution
-- Thank you, P0nz!,) and you have to complete Nightmare Mode, sooo... Yep, I won't be getting all of them!
I absolutely loved most of the game, but the final area of the game was too much action and not enough thinking for my tastes.  Overall I'd say it's absolutely worth playing!

Door kickers is a fantastic top down shooter, but not quite like every other one.
What sets door kickers apart is its almost 'blueprint' type of plan and play. The base of the game is you have a squad of customizable soldiers that you must guide through a small area in a strategic way while taking as few casualties as possible and comleting the objective. The objectives range from anything from saving hostages, to disarming bombs, to simply killing every enemy and more.
How to command each soldier is relatively simple, click and drag a path for them to follow. If you want to get fancy you can even right click and drag an arrow to where you want them to look at different points on the path making for effective straffing manuvers. You must plan your path carefully because you are not given the location of your enemies and therefore it pays to be strategic. If you do futz it up, there is a pause button that you can activate anytime durring the mission and replan your squads next move.
Obtaining new equipment for your soldiers is like other games with a progression system. as you progress you get points to spend on new equipment such as heavier bullet-proof vests, new weapons, riot shields, etc.
Although the customization may make the game seem unfair and favor you, it counters that by giving you a ton of enemies or the satisfaction of knowing that you planned just right. For example, if there's a room of 10 enemy soldiers right in front of you and you only have 4 guys, you're not going to send them all in with ligh armour and tiny pistols. What you can do is customize your squad to have heavy armour, have 2 swap out their primary weapons for riot shields, and the others to carry assault riffles and stack up on each other providing heavy fire and protection in the trade off for mobility and a quick trigger finger. It's these trade offs that make the difference in how you plan and make the strategic aspect of the game very inportant.
There is also a skill tree menu for your soldiers. Along with unlocking new equipment you can 'train' your team to give them boosts such as aiming faster, more accurately, following up with a second shot to make sure the enemy is dead, hold their fire for those who like to be stealthy, and so on and so forth.
The game also has a number of little things it will throw in from time to time to help it feel a little more 'real'. This includes an uncertain amount of baddies on many levels, 'cause who knows if they called for back up of not? You occasionally get a sniper friend to help you because back up never hurt you either (in fact, it seems a little overpowered, but I'm not complaining). Your soldiers CAN die! After all those missions you go through together, all the promotions they've earned, all the gear you've given them, and they just one day *pew pew* and you just have to sit there for a minute wondering why you were so foolish and sent your commerade out into a blaze of fire and know you lost the best soldier on your team *sniffle sniffle*. (Quietly whispers) "He was so young..." Ok, now back to what I was saying. You must also tell your crew to reload because contrary to many games, you don't just majically know when to reload, you first have to walk into enemy fire, pull the trigger, realize you're out of ammo, and get shot in the midst of reloading because you forgot to tell your poor soldier to reload. This isn't to forget that there is a cover system in the game. If you can pull out and behind a barrel to give yourself adequate cover for a moment, it could really save you in a pinch, and if you're like me, give an oppertunity to reload. Before I get too far off topic I should mention that you do gain new soldiers back ofter a few missions, they may grow on trees in this game, but that doesn't mean it's an instant replacement.
Door Kickers also assists you by adding stealth mechanics also (but let's be honest, guns aren't the quietest things).
The line of sight really is your best friend in this game because as long as you can intrude it by hiding behind a door or something (Are you happy now? I mentioned doors just like you were waiting for), you can use this to help get into a good spot to take down the enemy from all sides, or over all to your advantage depending on the plan. In adition to the line of sight, you should also try to be relatively quiet unless you bring out the big guns. This is thanks to a small sound system they threw in so you can't simply blow up doors and have ever enemy go "Hey, you hear something?" and the other guy say "Nah, it's probably just the wind" *cough* skyrim *cough*.
Now although It's easy to slip up (like me) and forget to reload (like me) and get your people killed (like me), your not completely hopeless. The fix to being an idiot (guess like who? yup, like me) is to add a somewhat self sufficent AI, so if your soldier runs into a tough spot or gets shot by someone out of their line of sight, they can do things like turn to them and shoot them, or if they're heavily armoured and can take a few hits to buy some time before dying and their clip ran out, they will try to reload it. Although it may not seem like it, this small bit of AI that can help take care of little things can really help win a mission.
Now, finally you say, "Okay, I beat the game, what now?" Well, the good people that made this game thought of that and have little side objectives such as complete a level without causualties ot in a certain time frame or something to help add some play time. When you finish with that there's even more. They even threw in a random map generator to add even more hours of play. You just have to put in what you want, things such as: nuber of enemies, map size, if you want fog of war, etc. and out pops a map for you. Pretty nice, huh?
Given that the game is called Door Kickers, you may be reading this and say "Hey, what's with the lack of busting down doors?" and so this goes out to you. You can:
-pick the lock
-use a crowbar
-C4
-Blast if open with a shot gun
-open it and chuck a grenade through
-make a sound to lure the baddies and have them open it for you
-whatever else you can think of doing, you got options, be creative and knock yourself out.
Rating: 9/10

There are many open world sandbox survival games on Steam, a lot of which are still in Early Access / active development, and even though the market is currently saturated, there are some titles that stand out from the crowd due to unique features or simply having enough to do to appeal to a wider audience.
Planet Explorers is one of those. It even has voxels.
Sure, it has the usual story mode on a hand-crafted map,  and a more open world approach in the way of adventure mode with procedurally generated maps, of which many other games also have. And because it's voxel-based, you can always change the terrain to your liking.
The game sports a rather impressive array of flora and fauna, as well as a much larger selection of ores than many other games offer,  for players to utilize in crafting, building, and just as basic currency since most merchants will buy most items or raw materials.
Then there's the camera modes - not every game has zoomable third person AND first-person. Though admittedly, this game's first-person feels uncomfortable at best. The third-person view, for me, is far more attractive.
Combat is awkward and lacking, players flailing about clumsily as they attempt to strike down creatures and enemies in melee, and desperately trying to see a thin white reticle against a light or white backdrop in ranged combat with a mouse that feels as if the sensitivity has been turned all the way up leads to much frustration.
Yet, all that aside, I find myself playing the game more and more. Why? Because it's a huge world, with unbelievable freedom, and though the graphics aren't AAA quality, the overall experience and malleability of the game more than makes up for its flaws. From standard foot travel to motorbikes to cars and trucks to boats to aircraft to actual railways and railcars, even though it does offer a fast travel option, there are far too many better methods of travel and transportation to make good use of.
And that's without even mentioning the creation feature. I have yet to see any game that offers the ability to custom-make a weapon or vehicle one subvoxel at a time, add mandatory sub-components like a hilt, handle, engine, tires, propeller or whatever, and simply export it from the creation screen and wait a few seconds for it to pop into your inventory. Go ahead. Name one other game that has this feature.
I love this game. I've been killed by bandits, drown while digging my way out of a cave, flipped my fugly cars and bikes while travelling over the unforgiving terrain, murdered by creatures I couldn't even describe without sounding like I was looking at an imaginative child's drawing (it has short hair, like a polar bear, and a horn, and two tentacles flowing from its back, and sharp claws and teeth, and six legs...). And yet, I've also driven my own creations across the various biomes, built towers that loomed over the landscape, climbed said towers, jumped from their apex, and soared across the land on a simple crafted glider.
It has flaws, sure, but it more than makes up for those with its features and replayability. If you're looking for a game to play with your kids, or just looking for something that feels like a fresh, modern Minecraft, you won't find many games that can hold up to Planet Explorers. And for the price? I estimate that by the end of the year, I will have spent less than 10 cents per hour of entertainment.
To me, that's one hell of a bargain.

Contagion is a first-person, cooperative multiplayer that takes various approaches and scenarios of a zombie apocalypse into a video game. Contagion is a sequel (?) or a spiritual successor (?) to Zombie Panic: Source, which is a free multiplayer mod.  Does the game stands apart from other zombie games? Is it worth playing? What about the replay value? Let's find out.
Contagion has a problem on standing out from other zombie games. There is no uniqueness or distinct flavor for this game. Escape Mode is one of the most common gameplay feature where you (and your friends or other players) have to do objectives while trying to get to the extraction point and not being killed on the way there. Escape Mode does have a "moderate" replay value, but most of the time is wasted on backpedaling to an old area to get something or do an objective. This leads to quick boredom and it kills replay value. This mechanic seems familiar to Left 4 Dead's AI Director system in terms on what items are located (along other things), but to go back to a cleared area to do an objective is a bit, odd. In the other hand, Escape Mode can be enjoyable if you have a group of friends to play with (and if your friends
enjoy it). Escape Mode seemed to have died out very quickly and that gameplay feature is the most popular one. Try to play PVP mode? Good luck on that.
The main problem for Contagion is that the player population is very low and the daily numbers are abysmal based on Steam Charts. Contagion does have sale promotions on the Steam Store to get other gamers to buy the game (as it was shown in Summer, Halloween, Autumn, and Winter Sales), and the results varied. Overall, Contagion is typical, bland, and certainly identical to other zombie games. Contagion was in development for a good amount of years and doing a Kickstarter to help "fully" develop the game is in question that the reader or gamer would have to judge for themselves.
A summary...
1. Is the game worth $20 or regional equivalent? Definitely not.
2. Are there updates and DLCs for the game? As far as I am concerned, there was a DLC recently released as a update (and it is free). However, the time span between updates are terrible.
3. Replay value? It varies from "moderate" to downright dreadful.
4. Sale price of $5 or less (including its regional equivalence)? Your choice. For me, it is not.
I would not recommend it unless you are an avid gamer who likes zombie games. It's a buyer's beware, and take serious accounts from pros and cons for the game from different reviewers.

Deadlight has very few things going for it. The story is passable, and the parkour works most of the time.
The rest of the game is a bit of a pain to get through. Melee combat is absolute trash, with "shadows" taking anywhere between one and god knows how many hits to take down. While this might be an attempt at realism it bogs down everything and makes swinging your axe and unpredictable mess--and that's if the game registers the axe as actually connecting. Ranged combat isn't much better, with aiming being slow and Randall having to sloooowly turn around in order to aim in the other direction. This isn't so bad against shadowy opponents, but late game delay is killer.
The game is also incredibly padded, with an absolutely unneeded hospital sequence and a sewer level before that wich reeked of poorly designed puzzle elements. Concerning the sewer, there's also a side character that is brought in, brought up multiple times throughout the remainder of the game, and dropped without an explanation as to why the opposition wanted it so badly.
Of course, most of this padding may come from how easy it is to die in this game. Like LIMBO is has an overload of "trial and death" segments where if you mistep even a slight bit, you die. This wouldn't be as big of a problem as it is if they didn't show up one after another in a seemingly endless series of ill-deserved deaths. The fact that pinpoint precision is needed and outside your line of vision obstacles can throw you off just exacerbate things. This does not include the CHAIRS OF DEATH, small obstacles that serve no purpose other than to dramatically knock Randall over--and they can't be jumped over, or avoided in any way. So, if death is behind you and your timing is slightly off, be prepared to start an entire segment of the game over again.
Now, as I said, the story is passable. What isn't, though, is the complete lack of audio that can occur during cutscenes. This is apparently a very popular bug with the player base, and it's a shame that one of the few things that keeps this game from being LIMBO levels of bad is cut out at times. Still, a word must also be said about the quality of the writing--melodramatic works well. Of particular note is the line "that blood in your saliva is the only real thing."
The game isn't absolutely terrible, but I can't recommend it because all of the flaws just keep it from getting anywhere good. If it's on a very, very good sale and you're a completionist concerning zombie or parkour sidescrollers I suppose you can press on through. Otherwise, leave this one to rot in the shadows.
