This is probably the first game I've ever played that truly deserves the label of "sandbox". The game opens with the possibilities of being a warrior for hire, liege lord, merchant, delivery person, roaming bandit, roaming bandit hunter, bandit hunter hunter, and all the way up to king of all the land or any mix in between.
More importantly, every one of those choices has real consequences on the gameplay! No namby-pamby paragon/renegade bars that go up so that every action is black or white in the eyes of all society. Heck no, in Warband slaughtering a village of innocents is considered bad to the innocents, but the Kingdom at war with theirs will be tickled-pink you killed all those women and children (you monster!).  Letting a rival Lord walk away after a fight could make him grateful for sparing his life or enrage him to a blood-feud for the embarrassment, depending on his personality.
It goes on, but the main idea is that every action holds weight but also holds a different weight for every party involved! This leads to moment to moment gameplay being a a massive turmoil of balancing relationships so that villagers will still gladly join your party, towns don't kick you out on sight, and the local warlord of the week doesn't drop a hammer on your head because you boned his daughter three weeks back when he was still just another penniless gob♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
All told the gameplay is deeply involving and fun, even with some odd buggy quirks and shallow mechanics. Oh, and every character model looks like a sprite-rip of Cloud Strife so don't buy it if you are into that whole "graffics" thing.
(Nitpick: The combat sections play themselves at higher levels, but there is a sort of fun in watching your hordes wash over the enemy as well I suppose.)

Bought this game quite recently, but already I love it. It's a great overhead 2D game where you control a SWAT team and have to command them tactically through hostile situations. Here's a quick overview:
PROS
(+++) Mission Variety -- There are many types of missions: there are "clear all hostiles" missions, hostage rescues, domb defusal, arrests, friendly escorts, and even a mode where you must collect evidence before criminals destory it. The game has plenty of "official missions", which are pre-rendered maps with variations of these missions; you can play these many times to improve your results and earn medals. It also has campaigns, which make the injuries and deaths on your squad have permanence and require you to safely lead your men through each mission. Most importantly, however, is the random mission generator, which picks maps at random and assigns varying scenarios and missions, or genreates maps for you to clear; this is especially fun when you set the genration options to random and aren't sure what you'll get in terms of enemy strength. Finally, there is a map editor and the ability to download other people's maps, and with the devs themselves adding new missions and campaigns as the game goes on, the challenges won't likely run out anytime soon.
(++) Squad Scaling -- Throwing a little RPG into the mix, the game provides you with experience -- both for each trooper and the squad as a whole -- after each mission. These can be used to unlock skills for the whole squad, and each trooper will increase their own stats as you use them. You also unlock more weapons and equipment as you earn stars for completing missions quickly and without losing men, and its fun to level and gear up as you beat more and more missions, making armored or armed enemeies easier to handle.
(++) Enjoyable gameplay -- The enemy varieties and randomness in each mission gives each scenario a freshness, and requires you to keep thinking through encounters instead of just doing the same thing over and over (although the restart button is there when you need it). It's a great experience if you've ever wanted to command a SWAT team and hear them shout "Clear! Clear!" as they systematically put bullets into hostiles.
CONS
(-) Controls/Interface -- Once you get used to them, the path-drawing/command-giving controls are fairly intuitive and work 90% of the time. However, as I've found with a few top-down tactics games, you don't always get the full level of control you'd want when working with your men. In certain cases, such as when two trooper's paths overlap or giving orders that stack commands on door opening, you'll misclick and put your shotgunner in front of your riot shielder or send a man through a door backwards. There are a few things the interface could do to alleviate this (such as perhaps showing unit paths one at a time, or giving a little more control over what order door opening actions are performed in) but overall it is a minor problem that usually causes little trouble once you know what to watch for.
(-) Squad Scaling -- I know this was under PROS as well, but I found that my squad was fully trained and upgraded with the gear I wanted after only a few hours of gameplay. The rest of the upgrades, then, just felt like I was unlocking gear for the sake of using up my XP or stars, and now, though I still enjoy the missions, I've run out of things to unlock. Perhaps adding more unlockables or more squad skill trees would help keep advancement fresh as the game is played longer, though the focus of this game is on individual tactical missions and not squad progression.
OVERALL
If you ever dreamed of virtually barking tactical decisions over radio to a SWAT team engaging hostiles, get this game. Hours of fun for sure.

This game is fresh to me. I haven't played anything quite like it. You can't do campaign mode right away, you have to play a few single missions and level up first. This is basically to get you warmed up for the campaign missions because campaign there is perma death. Your task force officers rank up too, and your level points get you better gear. Basically a mission operates in 3 phases
1. Deploy mode. Select your officers and deploy them onto the mission site in a selected area.
2. Planning mode. This is where you trace out the movement and actions of each officer. There are a variaty of options on how to do this depending on rank and equipment.
3. Execution mode. This is when the mission starts and your men begin to perform your plan, you can go back to planning mode at anytime and redo the plan
or if you're feeling brave you can do the planning and execution simultaniously.
At the end of your mission you are graded by speed, deaths, and overall performance. 3 star ranking gets you more XP which can be used for more lethal officers and tactics.
Planning mode gets complcated quick, you can customize it to do so many things like switch weapons, look in certain directions, don't move again until enemies cleared, and there are even wait for order Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, or Delta so a certain officer will wait until you click the order and then continue as plan.
This game is quick paced, and a great time killer. I think I will enjoy it for a long time, classic replay value.

Tired of the simplicity of Minecraft and sick of waiting for Starbound?  Sick of Zombies and tired of Bambi killers but still want to survive and thrive?  I know I was, and boy am I glad I stumbled onto this.  I feel like I may have passed it over in the past because of bad reviews but as they had recently taken an upturn I decided to give it a shot.
Now I can't speak to the multiplayer aspect (As it's in alpha I can only assume it's sketchy at best, but that's to be expected.) but the single player is excellent, the story (which I'm only a few missions into since I jumped right into adventure mode at the start) has been interesting so far.
Here's a few aspects that make me want to play this over minecraft clones:
Need creature parts but tired of running around hunting?  Set up some turrets and throw down a creature lure.
Tired of running everywhere?  Build a rudimentary vehicle and ride into the sunset.
Ten story creature?  Grab allies, outfit them with whatever you can find/buy/create yourself, make turrets, tanks and Take. It. Down.
I'm only twelve hours in and have barely done more than get iron weapons, a few turrets, and dug a few really impressive tunnels (Which I was way more proud of than anything I ever built in minecraft.) and made a few rudimentary shelters to keep the rain off my head (which didn't work, it is [or was when I wrote this] an alpha.).  You can also build gods-know-what in the creation engine which is far too daunting for me to even touch at the moment, or if creating from scratch isn't your thing I'm sure you'll be able to download untold numbers of things others have created via steam in the future (Or now sans-steam with a little know-how).
All in all you should keep an eye on this one, and if you have the extra cash go ahead and buy it.

I won't go into a lot of details of the gameplay. If you want a review on that look further in the other reviews. My review is based on two things: my experiance playing the game as of nearly 2 years ago and the current build of this game as of July 12, 2016.
I remember a time when Alpha builds were considered proof of concept builds that were for in-company testing only. The product at that point had enough in it that the vision and basis to continue developement was clear and sound but would lack enough content to release publically for beta testing. Beta builds of a product meant that they has passed the preliminary in-house testing and featured enough development and content that it was suitable to release for public beta testing.
This game... this game came out on steam early 2014 and now, 2 years later, it hasn't even entered Beta stage testing.
What does this translate to? Well it doesn't mean it is a bad game. It doesn't mean that this game won't ever be completed. It isn't a prediction on the quality of the game when it is finally completed. What it DOES mean is that if you are thinking of getting this game... DON'T. Seriously, just don't. At least not yet. Come back in 5 years when this game MAY have finally exited beta stage and moved on to full release. Until then you are going to just end up paying $25 for a glorified psuedo demo with less content and more bugs than a real demo.

Updated review.
Before the end of the Open Access period, the developers made a number of changes to Heroes & Generals, some very good, some very bad, but overall, positive. One of these was to completely overhaul the mechanic that allowed players to buy instant top-end characters and thus dominate the game. You now have to unlock weapons and higher-ranked characters through experience, rather than just being able to buy anything at any time with gold.
The most recent change, prior to this review, changed the maps, adding in a lot more cover - this makes the game a lot less playable for the 'bunny-hop' players and recons (snipers) but a lot more playable for more tactically thinking players. Again, it's swings and roundabouts, but overall they're trying to move in the right direction. H&G is still sometimes massively frustrating, but overall,it's going the right way.

It's been too long since Warhammer's Fantasy world got some love,
too much has been spent on WH40k, instead of what i think, should at least be 50% of both.
So finally, one came out, and let me tell you the devs did a really good job.
so firstly,
the Pro's
* Beautiful environment, really captures the 'dark fantasy' of Warhammer quite well
* Fun L4D style Coop gameplay, with melee working out very well
* Loot increases your power, but not by so much that you NEED it, MMO's spring to mind
* A few classes to choose from, but i suspect more will be added soon, each has their own strength and weakness
* Very supporting and active Dev team, actually the most 'concerned' Dev team I've ever seen
* Everything feels really 'Warhammer', the devs really have a deep understanding of the world
Now every game has cons, so does this one, so here they are
The Cons
* Some optimization issues, overheating issues, and the like, hopefully these will be fixed as soon as possible
* The loot system can feel unrewarding at times, getting 10 whites in a row is a bit offputting
* some repetitive gameplay, a few of the maps feel exactly the same, and there could be a bit more 'moves' with your weapons
* without spoiling, I find the ending a bit 'anti- climax'
All and all this game is what I'd call a 'Diamond in the rough', the more the devs add and tweak, the better it gets!
Don't listen to all those complaining 'its too short' people, most of them abused a few early release exploits and are now complaining that they got all the gear too fast, kids will be kids
I'd rate this game a 8/10, but a possible 10/10 if the devs continue to work their magic!!!

Skill based co-op horde game
A little exploration, maps are good and not too linear, tomes/grimoires/scraven dice (bonus chance to roles) are a decent way to encourage exploring/completing all the side quests
Loot system: Decent, could be a bit more fleshed out imo (Diablo 3 style). Loot is incredibly hard to get, and practically imposisble to get your ideal weapon (red weapon of your choice + 4 traits/abilities that you want). Maybe implement some sort of system where you can sacrifice Oranges (tier below red) to choose one of their abilities to put into your red weapon.l
Incredibly hard to get loot due to the ease of failing a mission due to being unlucky or a simple mistake. (when you fail, your 30 minutes have been a waste, no satsifactory compensation for at least trying. <- Fixed by having even a little compensation after a couple checkpoints. Rewards don't have to be great, just 'enough' to make us feel like we're not wasting our time)
Maps: Variety is good, but there should be some kind of encouragement for using the 'random maps' option rather than selecting the easiest map to farm for loot. E.g. extra Loot die for choosing random maps option
Combat: Melee combat is great, ranged combat is good and not too overbearing
Difficulty: Incredibly difficult. First game we played on easy (easiest difficulty), wiped a couple times getting used to the combat. Played on normal, wiped again. Got better, played on hard, wiped again etc.
Nightmare/Cataclysm are practically impossible to complete w/o a decent team who know what they're doing.
I don't mind the skill-based combat and hard difficulty of the game.
Downsides of the game: Declining playerbase (this is apparent to all games, but this game needs a tad better longevitiy than just 'get red weapons' or 'complete all maps on hardest difficulty' -> because there is not reward in doing so. The reward for completing these is nonexistant (rewards not provided by game, only reward is self satisfaction).
Devs need to have a better reward system for the game, it is extremely frustrating to play for a whole day and feel like you got nowhere in terms of progression.
Since weapons/items/loot are the progression in this game, they should be more fleshed out.
Upside: Fun game with friends if they are into skill-based melee combat with a desire to 'be good'. E.g. if your friends get frustrated easily at hard games like dark souls, then don't encourage them any further.
Lots of blood (can turn off in settings) to suit the warhammer theme.
It is a solid melee coop skill based horde game, but in my opinion the progression as well as loot need to be reworked to make the player feel like they are accomplishing something by playing the game.
Also, since playerbase is not that large (in comparison to say LoL), much of the time is with bots who need to be made smarter. E.g. help you with map objectives, prioritise getting you up from dying state.
Also, firnedly AI is good when fighting melee (very proficient).
OVERALL: Good game if you like it for what it is. Even better with a group of friends who like this sort of game. Of course not perfect, and I hope they 'fix' or change their loot/progression system to encourage players to keep playing. Keeping the difficulty as it is is fine, no need to make the game easier gameplay-wise, just change the reward system to not make the player feel like they wasted their time.

I'm going to start this review by saying this is my favorite game of all time, so I may be a bit bias.
Section 1:  Story
The story of SA2 is just a tad deeper the most sonic games, like SA1's story was.  Sonic has been mistaken for a black and red counter part called Shadow, who was released by Dr. Ivo Robotnik (Eggman), in hopes of taking over the world.  Shadow hopes to uncover his past and fufill his promise of destroying the world to Maria, as the last thing he remembers is her death.  Shadow tells Eggman that if he delivers the 7 Chaos Emeralds to the Space Colony Ark, Shadow will grant him any wish.  Eggman wants to use this to wish for world domination.  Sonic, with the help of his sidekick Tails, are there to stop Eggmans plans.  The first emerald Eggman tries to locate turns out to be the Master Emerald, which can give power to the other 7 Emeralds.  Eggman tries to take it with him, but Knuckles breaks the Master Emerald before Eggman gets away.  Now Knuckles is trying to peice together the Master Emerald while Rouge the Bat tries to steal the shards for her own greed.
I only have one problem with the story.  Knuckles and Rouge seem thrown in at the last second because SEGA felt they had to have Knuckles in, and Rouge because Knuckles needed a rival.  I'm ok with SEGA putting them in, but make them at least a LITTLE BIT relative to the story.  Rouge just ends up hanging out with Shadow and Eggman, and Knuckles only meets up with Sonic and Tails one time, then doesn't show up again untill the final mission!  They don't do ANYTHING to the story that couldn't have been done if they were both just dropped entirely.
Section 2: Atmosphere
Most of the hero stages (Knuckles, Tails, and Sonic) are preety upbeat until the near-end of the game, when they get serious for reasons that will be explained if you play the game.  The Dark stages (Shadow, Eggman, and Rouge) however, are vastly different.  Shadow's stages have the feel of knowing you are superior to everyone else, and you solve problems yourself because everyone else can't perform as well.  The Eggman stages feel as if you are evil and proud, and if anyone doesn't like it they can talk to your lasergun.  The Rouge stages have a mix of undercover, super spy and that you got this, and it's no big deal.  The art style feels a bit like the old sonic games, but mostly like a new fresh game like most other sonic games feel.  The music is the beautiful harmony that SEGA brings with nearly every sonic game, blending with the levels in a wonderful way.  I have a gripe about the amosphere too, as good as it may be.  When SEGA was making the US version of this game, they never bothered to fix the ever prominent cutscene issues.  Characters commonly cut each other off, talk simultaniously, and to top it all off, the voice sync sucks.  The problems are STILL in this version, even though they had PLENTY of opportunities to fix this.
Section 3: Gameplay
Ever played a 3D sonic game?  Well that's Sonic and Shadow's stages in a nutshell.  Fast-paced platforming action with enough tricks up it's sleeve to keep you playing.  Tails and Eggman's stages take a different approach, doing a third person shooter-like approach in mech suits.  It's O.K., but not quite as good as the Sonic and Shadow stages.  Finally we have the ever-hated Knuckles and Rouge stages.  They could have been very fun, but a few small things kept it from being perfect.  The way it works is that 3 items are scattered along the level, and you have to find them.  To aid you is your radar, which tells you if you are close to the object, and Floating TVs that give you hints.  The first problem with this mode is the camera.  In enclosed spaces, you always have to fight to see where you want to.  The second problem is the radar.  The radar only picks up the item it wants you to find.  This means that if you are near one of the items you need, but it isn't the one the radar wants you to find, you could be right next to it and never know.  The third problem is the combat.  Combat in the treasure hunting stages can be clunky and it can be very easy to miss.  Thankfully there isn't a lot of combat in these stages.  There is also a place you can unlock and go to called the Chao Island.  There you can raise Chao with fruit you find on the island, Chao Drives, and animals.  Chao Drives and animals can be found in the stages.  You can also go to a small Chao area to buy things with your rings, such as Chao Eggs, Fruit, and other things.  You can also send you Chao to school, where they will learn certian skills, name your chao, and check your chaos stats in the same area.  There is also a seperate area where you can race a gainst other chao, or if you have the Battle DLC, play karate against other chao.  Speaking of Battle, the other things you get from it are a versus mode, and a kart racing game.  The Kart racer is a bit boring, because there are no power ups besides a boost.  The other battle modes are just the story levels exept your racing in the speed stages, dueling in the mech stages, and trying to find the certian items first in the treasure hunting stages.  The chao mode can be hit or miss with players, but I adore it.  The VS mode can a great way to battle your friends, and there is always a good character for beginners.
All and all, this is a great game for beginners to the sonic franchise, a solid game for experianced players, and with the Battle DLC, a good place to battle it out with friends.  The game has a few flaws, but there's plenty to keep you playing.

There’s always a dangerous line to travel when a sequel is made, especially when the previous installments are successful or have a healthy modicum of acceptance from consumers. Straying too far from the original formula can make the sequel feel removed and disjointed from what made the previous game good, and sticking too close to the original can come off as lazy or apathetic. Dennaton certainly did not have an easy job on their hands making a sequel to Hotline Miami, and while the gameplay from the previous game is as strong and snappy as ever, what additions were made end up bloating the new installment while punishing the player for playing wildly.
Oddly the biggest disappointment I have right out of the gate is the story-telling. The first game was quite memorable due to the story, which kind of didn’t really care if you were following along clearly or not. Sure, with enough observation and putting puzzle pieces together you could get some idea, but it never really stopped to explain things, just chugging along to the next scene to give you more violence and combos to build in order to get that high score. In Hotline Miami 2, I can’t help but feel like there was damage control because of that, and now there’s too much story being fed to the player. Many characters are brought in to flesh out the narrative, like the Fans who are following in Jacket’s footsteps, or Evan, the journalist writing about all the mayhem and getting involved in ways he wasn’t hoping for. Yes, this does mean you get a nice break between segments to be in someone else’s shoes and potentially have different playstyles (Evan’s lack of killing, the Fans acting as Jackets’ different masks from the first game), but I can’t shake the weird feeling that between Hotline Miami 1 and 2, it felt like there was an obligation to play catch up and bog down the game with narrative just for the sake of putting some clarity to the mayhem.
The second major disappointment comes from the larger, more densely populated maps the game throws you in. While bigger maps should mean more attack strategies, higher scores and longer combos to chain, we mustn't forget that a single, errant mistake means death and restarting the screen. In the first game, playing like a madman often had the end result of clearing screens by the skin of your teeth, adapting in the middle of a skirmish and having very hectic, though incredibly satisfying victories. A death would cost you very little, and only during the later acts when the maps got larger, and more risky did you have to slow down and plan a bit more thoroughly. The player was nearing the end of the game, so the increase in difficulty was to be expected. In Hotline Miami 2, the difficulty of larger, more involved maps starts far sooner than in the original, and is expected, reckless, wild rampages will be shot down far more swiftly and feel much more painful in the process. It’s not the difficulty of the game or the easy death of your character that’s the issue, it’s that the bigger maps that almost seem to demand that you lure waves of enemies into a bottleneck before you horribly end their lives time and time again, and any improvisation during a frantic deviation from this strategy has a high cost regarding your time and patience. Having to clear a level using turtle tactics and purposeful pacing rather than going bonkers through the place and getting a poor score/rating at the end of it all was a frequent reminder of why the first game was far easier to digest and have bloodier enjoyment of. And doors somehow have gotten worse. WORSE.
The soundtrack for me is the biggest shining point of this sequel, as while the first game had a far more memorable OST that stuck with me afterwards, Hotline Miami 2′s music feels much more solid across the board in out of game listening, but it lacks that memorable punch that the first soundtrack had. To say that the music is the most noteworthy part of the game doesn’t entirely speak poorly of Hotline Miami 2′s gameplay which, excluding the need to take encounters on a lot more slowly than intended, it remains as it was in the first game.
Even if we exclude the reported problems that rose during the Steam launch of Hotline Miami 2 of controller play not functioning, Windows XP support being sketchy and the fact that the godforsaken executable did not work on day one for many consumers, I walk away from the game feeling incredibly disappointed on a personal level, while feeling frustrated on the technical side of things. Yes, it is more Hotline, but the attempts of sticking to the original formula while shoving borderline fanfiction-esque narrative upon me made things more and more difficult to swallow, and the ending itself feels like a gigantic middle finger to the player for going through everything they had to see things through to the end. I can only recommend Hotline Miami 2 to those who greatly enjoyed the first game or those who found the first game much too easy. Too much disappointment has remained on a personal and technical level, and it’s because of this that I must unfortunately say that for anyone else curious about Hotline Miami 2, it’s a pass - The first game is your much better bet.

Far Cry 3 is an action packed adventure. You have multiple objectives you can do and they don’t have to be done in order or you can simply never do them! You can find relics, raid outposts, explore, find treasure chests, and many more endeavors within Far Cry 3. The campaign reminds me of college students on vacation and things go south and rather rapidly. I don’t want to spoil anything, but the story itself contains mysteries, mystical happenings, and a crazy adventure that won’t leave a bad taste behind like other action adventure titles.
The game itself is open world and both islands are living, breathing entities. Whether its people driving around, guards patrolling, or a lion prowling in the tall grasses of the jungle, there is always some form of activity going on in the background or around you. To explore this vast world, one can obtain ATVs, vehicles, boats or air gliders and enjoy the beautiful scenery of the Rook Islands. The scenery has lush jungles, waterfalls, white sandy beaches, clear blue waters, swamps, and green grasslands. The developers put a lot of thought in this game and it seems they added a bit of every biome in this title.
You’ll notice outposts and telecommunication towers – the outposts provide you with a means of fast travel, a place to sell/buy items, and local militia to fight near your proximity. The telecommunication towers help you reveal large portions of the map so you can prioritize your next adventure or continue your way on the campaign. There are a few factions on the islands, but I won’t go into them since they may or may not be a spoiler (I’d rather be safe than sorry).
With any open world game there is customization or crafting (most of the time) and this game delivers, even though it is on a smaller scale than other titles. Your crafting consists of killing wildlife and using their hides to make a bigger holster, a bigger ammo bag, etc. in order to obtain more items (ammo, syringes, etc.). You can customize guns (paint, scope, magazine, etc.), but don’t assume the customization is big compared to Battlefield titles or other shooting games. They do bare bones on customization with guns, but they do improve a big portion of the stats relating to the gun (aim, ammo capacity, range, etc.). They could have added more customization/crafting options in the game, but I did like the quests that one must obtain to maximize their crafting potential.
The UI was clunky at times; I’d have to press multiple times of ESC to get back to the game as one example. The game was well enough to ignore the clunkiness of the UI and the game has a few years on it, so it isn’t ‘modernized’. I didn’t have any FPS drops or bottlenecking when playing this title. I never experienced any crashes or delays or audible problems that sounded off or distant. The voices were done in a way to have an emotional experience and trying to connect with the player when going through the campaign and experiencing the hardships from protagonist, his friends, and his enemies.
A title like Far Cry 3 needs no spoilers and I truly think most people who like action adventure games will enjoy this title. I might not have done everything (finding relics, treasure, etc.), but I did finish the campaign and I would recommend this title to anyone. There are still a lot of content for me to finish, so this game is worth its price.

Contagion is a first person zombie horror game created by
and running on the source engine in which you play one of eight characters who have to survive in a zombie ridden world. At the moment there is four main gamemodes which are Hunted, Escape, and Extraction. In hunted you experience tense Pvp battles with players online whilst at the same time fighting off zombies and scavenging for supplies and ammo. In escape you follow objectives sent to you via an ingame phone to escape (as the name suggests) the area you are currently in.
And finnally: in extraction you have to help rescue Ai by taking them from one side of the map to the other via a Gps on your in-game phone.
The main thing I love about this game is the atmosphere; every second and every turn is an intense moment. Most of my time playing this game I spend with my heart beating rapidly as I brace myself for a zombie encounter. This atmosphere is mainly brought on by the difficulty which comes from the random infection chance when hit from a zombie meaning any damage could be fatal and also the scarcety of ammo. The maps in these game are truly amazing. The game feautures a system which randomizes the map everytime so you will be experiencing a new adventure with each playthrough. Aswell as this the maps feauture tight spaces and lots of corners which adds a cloustrophobic ephect of if you see a zombie: your more or less going to have a heart attack. Whilst talking about the maps I feel the need to mention the amazing soundtrack and also sound effects used within the game which make up for the mediocre voice acting. These two things combined mean that you will feel as though you are actually there walking through those tight halways listening for the rumble of a nearby zombie. The graphics on this are what I would expect for a game of this type; not astounding but they dont need 4k graphics to give me a true horror experience. Moving on, within the options menu we have a wide variety of options to customize our experience and to provide the needs of those with a microwave computer, which is what I would expect for a non-port. A small mention I am going to give because I think it could be a good feauture but hasnt been used to its full advantage yet is the workshop support. This alows people to make custom maps and zombies which could bring the horror to a whole new level. So far not much good content has surfaced but I have high hopes for the future. Now onto the multiplayer side of things: you can join a random hosted server via a search from the main menu after selecting your desired map and gamemode. This means you can either play co-op or the mode named hunted in which players converse in heart renching pvp battles and fight to the death. I feel this gamemode is a really nice addition to the game but I feel it is lacking some larger maps. The main thing that seperates this game from other zombie games though; is the infection feature. This means that when you get hit by a zombie there is a chance of you becoming infected and being a zombie. Signs of this is the noise slowly distorting and the colours on your screen slowly fading. This adds a really cool aspect of the game which gives you the choice of whether to tell your friends that you are becoming infected or sneakily bite them while they are not looking! I feel this adds a new dimension to the co-op  gameplay. Also if you die during a game you will respawn as a zombie which I think is good because it rids the game of a boring spectator mode. Time to talk about my favourite feature in the game: the co-op. There is nothing more fun then hoping intom a game of escape with my friends and experiencing the horror together. It also adds a lightheartened twist to the game. Finnally I am going to mention that a free Dlc has just been released containing a new gamemode, some new maps, charecters and weapons. I think it is good that the developers are still supporting their game and I hope to see more things like this in the future.
Something I dont like in this game is theHud though this is mainly prefrence and is not game breaking. I just feel that the Hud feels like some 90's shooter and isn't very polished. Mainly the wapon slots in the top right corner. But as I said tis is just preference. My main problem with the game is the terrible Ai. It is truly unpredictable: sometimes the human ai will walk into walls and sometimes they will do as meant. Sometimes the zombies will chase after you and sometimes they will stare into space. I just feel this ruins the immersion and otherwise perfect atmosphere. Another problem is that the deddicated servers are not very reliable and thematchmaking is pretty appalling. This can be avoiced by sticking to hamatchi co-op like I do. But I feel like I am missing a big chunk of the game witrhout hunted which would be hard to play on hamatchi unless I had alot more friends. Something that is a minor problem is the lack of story. I say this is minor because the game doesnt really need a story because all you really need to know is that you are getting away from the zombies but I just felt like a small chunk of the game was missing for me. Another thing that isnt really bad but some people could find bad is that the game is very slow paced and you are not just running at hordes of zombies with a chainsaw. Im saying this could be bad because some people may expect this from a zombie game. My final complaint is a few small bugs such as when you scroll down the texts on your phone by left clicking: you cant scroll back up. These bugs are minor and can probably be easily fixed so Im not to salty about them.
Contagion is an atmospheric zombie horror that will have your heart beating rapidly but dont go in expecting a fast paced run and gun. A definite buy if you have a co-op partner.

I bought Melody's Escape quite some time ago and I'm surprised it took me so long to review it, and to to put it simply, I love it.
It takes the rhythm based gameplay made popular by Guitar Hero and turns it into a side scrolling platformer style experience, and allows you to play your own music in the same way games like Audiosurf and Beat Hazard do. When combined together it's a great experience. Whether you're cruising to video game rock, pirate metal, symphonic metal, country, or almost any piece of music, you can have a great time with this one.
Plus with the workshop support you can change the basic avatar into a number of different characters, from Goku and Megaman, up to humanized versions of the cast of MLP: Friendship is Magic if you're so inclined. So you could technically change the avatar to look like Link and put him through a heavy metal/EDM mix of the Legend of Zelda theme. Or, well any sort of combination really.
That's the beauty of it. A game like this just says "here I am" and it's up to you to make the experience through your own choice of song, and avatar. I should also mention there are four basic difficulty settings to switch things up further, OR on top of that you can tweak the settings to make a custom difficulty setting all your own. Again, there is practically limitless freedom with this one and it's worth every penny.
So, having just used Princess Luna from MLP through Metallica's cover of Stone Cold Crazy, I give this game the highest possible recommendation. Go buy it and make your own experiences.

Open ended sandbox, storyline exploration crafting game. Build a base, populate and grow it. Make weapons, vehicles etc. Explore the world and search for resources such as ores and plants that are found in certain terrains, then use them to craft everything you need based on schematics you earn or buy from npc's.
What it does right, it does very right. What it does wrong, is horrifically bad.
You can craft almost anything you can imagine. Guns, vehicles, buildings, etc. You make them. All of them. There are very few premades available in the game so you must make what you want or find the plans another player made. If you are creative, you can make almost anything. If you aren't and don't find other players plans, you shouldn't bother with this game. A year ago, there were numerous ISO's for everything you could imagine, but now there are very few since updates have broken previous ISO's and creators stopped making and updating them.
Vehicles include cars, bikes, planes, helicopters, boats, submarines, etc. They all share one thing in common. Movement with them sucks. Real bad. Helicopters can't seem to fly above the trees and that would be fine if they didn't get stuck on the trees if you hit one. The ground is so uneven that any ground transport bounces all over the place and hits everything in sight, or just flat out gets destroyed from bouncing and hitting the ground constantly. Turning vehicles is not as easy as you would think and often times hitting an object, backing up turning, then turning more going forward still results in you hitting the exact same object. Vehicles can get stuck on the ground, on the plants, on rocks, etc. Most areas of the map are actually faster to walk through than attempt to use a vehicle. Drive into anything and your vehicle gets damaged. Park near a predator and they will attack your vehicle until it is destroyed or they die. Fly a helicopter into a flying creature you didn't see because of lag and who knows, maybe it stalls and you drop to the ground and die while your helicopter blows up into pieces and leaves you stranded there.
The map is a limited use abstract with very little details but does allow fast movement between discovered points. The scanner map shows you more of the terrain, but is very difficult to decipher if you are looking for ore and quickly becomes useless if you are digging into a ore vein since it clutters up rapidly.
Lighting is almost useless since personal lights point directly forward with no means to use them to light up areas above, below or to the side of the character.
NPC ai is getting better but followers still get stuck on terrain sometimes and can easily be lost when you are crossing a long distance.
Combat is very basic with melee attack only or manually shooting a weapon.
Most quests are easily completed but some hunting quests give you only a name of a creature that is useless if you haven't been playing long enough to figure out what the different creatures are. Some creatures for hunting quests are also difficult to find since they can be very rare creatures or travel around a lot.
Updates are fairly slow in coming, but progress has been significant in the last year. Crashes still happen fairly often but autosave keeps you from losing more than a couple minutes of progress so they are a minor problem.
Overall, the potential for this game is great, but it does need more work to be really enjoyable. Mostly the vehicle controls and ground smoothing hamper the game at this point. When it takes forever to walk from known areas to new mission areas, it gets tedious fast when you know a vehicle would be faster, but are so not worth the trouble to use.
EDIT: I have played over 100 hours before I got this game on Steam.

I understand that SEGA did emulated games on Steam before, such as
, as well as other companies, such as SQUARE ENIX's
and
, but these games are excused.  Why?  Because they are nowhere near as video (or audio) intensive as the game in question, and therefore, there is no lag (and if there is, then why are you even using your horrible computer to play games?).  And I have no problem with framerate drops, usually, as long as it isn't drastic.  The thing about this game's low framerate is that it doesn't skip frames to make up for it; it slows the whole game down.  If you look at the timer in the top-left, you may notice that 1 second seems unusually long.  This is a problem, especially in a game that is all about speed; however, I do have to give credit on one thing: the music and sound effects don't slow down with the framerate, which is very nice.  It would be even nicer if the rest of the game didn't slow down!  All in all, I love this game, but seriously, get the Dreamcast version or Gamecube version, or if you have a PS3 or XBOX360 with internet, you can buy them off of their respective online shops, bringing up one more question: why do

Mount & Blade: Warband is a game that has such a wide variety of experiences among those that play it. I honestly can only speak for my experiences in the game and highly recomened you look at other reviews to see how they went about playing the game. The game drops you into the middle of a country torn by war among 6 factions. You create your character, their background and jump into the middle of a capital of one of the factions while being assaulted by bandits. The game can actually be played many ways with the overal goal being living your character's life the way you want to live it. At it's heart it is an RPG but it does have economy simulator, RTS, and even political simulator elements in the game. The goal of the game is...there isn't one. You can become the ruler of a trade empire, the ruler of a kingdom, the marshall of the armies of your liege, a ruthless bandit or anything you set your mind to. The game has a companion system with enough variety for any playstyle/morality to work. The companions even have dialogue with each other and develop friendships/rivalries depending on who else is in the party. The game has a wide variety of options and paths to pursue. Combat can be either as simple as charing your men at the enemy or forming up on the flanks with cavalry while infintry hold the line in sheild wall formation. The game actually centers itself around combat and even if you decide to be a trader you are going to need some bodyguards to defend yourself from bandits. The game promotes building your character to do whatever you feel like doing. Fighting off bandits, enemy nations, and trade caravans at your pleasure feels good with your troops. Your troops are recruited as the greenest of soldiers and have to work their way up through the trees to receive veteran unit status. Each unit receives xp individually so you know the soldiers that are getting stuck in are the ones leveling up. The game has a nice political and trade system as impoverished cities are the ones that are being constantly seiged/raided and are having their caravans and peasants slaughtered while the wealthy ones are receiving protection from enemy nations and bandits. Politically the game holds grudges and wars can be incited by the simplest bandit attacks on caravans, mistreatment of poor citizens, and trespassing. The fact that the kings are constantly declaring war, fighting, then taking their losses and leaving make for an always evolving map as towns and cities become destitute due to the heavy fighting. The system of marriage and lordship, including owning your own kingdom, is fun despite some issues and actually adds depth to simple things like feasts and tournaments as you fight for the love of lords and ladies, the wealth of the city, and a chance to place yourself higher in the realm. There are, sadly, plenty of issues in the game due to basically being abandoned by it's developer. There are a plethora of bugs that can ruin a game experience. For a game with a big focus on combat horse units are just some of the best in existence. The thing everyone knows is the heavily armored Swadian Knight which rides in on horseback slaughtering scores of men then if you manage to dismount the unit they are still a heavily armored infantry unit capable of fighting with sword and sheild and two handers. An army of all cavalry is quite honestly one of the best in the game as it is capable of outfighting a majority of units just due to the bonuses (Extra hp, damage etc) that riding a horse provides. The political system has it's flaws as you are not capable of directing the king to declare war, frame a nation for something without getting in trouble, and various other things. Following a marshall is fine until you realize the AI is derping around refusing to fight anything and you have to leave the Marshall's side to attack things or hope he likes you enough to trust you when you say that city over there only has 50 men in it.  Managing your towns basically  comes down to running fetch quests all over the region just to make your village/city wealthy enough to actually give you money. The game iteself does require the same thing over and over again due to the lack of a semi-competent AI. You have to fight many battles so you can win them as the auto-resolve will not actually work and will make you lose a good portion of your force. Even fighting your way though the entire enemy nation means nothing unless you leave 80+ men at each location you take due to the inability of your nation to capitalize on the death of the entire standing army of the enemy nation. It is also to be noted that the game will take forever to make meaningful progress as anytime your host nation gets any amount of pull in the world ALL other nations will declare war to curb it's power regardles of how much land they lose to their other enemies. The game itself has issues with even making your own kingdom. It trys to justify it by saying you need "Right to rule" but never really explains what that is or how to aquire it. It also doens't seem to matter as even with a large amount of it you will be beset by every neighboring faction as soon as you decide to make your own kingdom. The issues with owning your own kingdom are plenty with you being genreally unable to control your lords even in times of war. You basically have to pray that they are following the marshall/you around in times of war and are not just wasting their own time outside of the wars.  Fighting long wars doesn't seem to have  a lasting affect unless you take land as you can never truely get rid of a lord. Merely imprison him until the peace treaty. This means that although you can try as hard as you might the game is designed to drag itself out to absorb as much of your time as possible while still remaining just entertaining enough to keep you playing. Most mods for the game are complete overhauls turning the game into a Warhammer, Warcraft, LotR, or GoT version of itself all with their own problems and bugs. Although these mods typically vastly improve the gameplay of the vanilla version they are too varied to give a concrete rating. I rate Vanilla a 6.2/10

This is a fun, relatively short zombie platformer game. To me, it was very reminiscent of the original Prince of Persia game (going back to the '80s) and this was intentional on the developers part. Although only in "2,5D", meaning your character moves in the 2 dimensions, but you see the background move in 3 dimensions, the artwork is evocative and the settings are varied enough to maintain interest. I enjoyed the cutscenes, which used "graphic novel" style stills. The voice acting was adequate. The story was not the most original, though it did the job and even had a few affecting moments at the end.
I used an Xbox 360 as recommended, and didn't experience any issues in regards to responsiveness of the controls.
I flew through the game for the most part, though there were a few moments towards the end that were a little difficult where I even had to put the game down for a bit to think about how to complete the section. I respect this at a time when a lot of games don't challenge their players to think about puzzles and instead reward endless slot-machine-like drudgery. I recommend this to anyone who wants a short, light, zombie game that doesn't overstay its welcome!

Really recommend for those who like beautiful side-scrolling adventure/puzzle games.

This is the first game I've ever felt inclined to write a review for... I hope that says something. It's simple, polished, beautiful, and correctly priced; its become my preferred game whenever I want to relax or just kill some time.
It's surprisingly difficult at first, until your brain masters the translation from color/symbol to button press. After that point. however, the game is pure bliss. It produces flow very easily, and my mind often wanders as I'm playing... only snapping back to attention when I miss one. It's incredibly cathartic.
I will say that enjoyment of the game depends a lot on what kind of music you like listening to. When the game parses a song, it'll tell you how well it was able to track the music, either giving you the tempo (along with the game's confidence in that tempo) or simply reporting "energy peaks". I've found this rating to be fairly accurate in predicting the song's playability, and songs with high irregularity or "noise" (lots of background instruments, lots of different harmonies at once, etc) don't tend to be well suited for the game's algorithm (in my opinion).
Examples of music that works very well:
the entire Shatter OST
Pendulum - The Island Pt. 1
Pet Shop Boys - Axis
The Glitch Mob - Head Full of Shadows
I can't recommend this game enough!

Far Cry 3 is an action packed adventure. You have multiple objectives you can do and they don’t have to be done in order or you can simply never do them! You can find relics, raid outposts, explore, find treasure chests, and many more endeavors within Far Cry 3. The campaign reminds me of college students on vacation and things go south and rather rapidly. I don’t want to spoil anything, but the story itself contains mysteries, mystical happenings, and a crazy adventure that won’t leave a bad taste behind like other action adventure titles.
The game itself is open world and both islands are living, breathing entities. Whether its people driving around, guards patrolling, or a lion prowling in the tall grasses of the jungle, there is always some form of activity going on in the background or around you. To explore this vast world, one can obtain ATVs, vehicles, boats or air gliders and enjoy the beautiful scenery of the Rook Islands. The scenery has lush jungles, waterfalls, white sandy beaches, clear blue waters, swamps, and green grasslands. The developers put a lot of thought in this game and it seems they added a bit of every biome in this title.
You’ll notice outposts and telecommunication towers – the outposts provide you with a means of fast travel, a place to sell/buy items, and local militia to fight near your proximity. The telecommunication towers help you reveal large portions of the map so you can prioritize your next adventure or continue your way on the campaign. There are a few factions on the islands, but I won’t go into them since they may or may not be a spoiler (I’d rather be safe than sorry).
With any open world game there is customization or crafting (most of the time) and this game delivers, even though it is on a smaller scale than other titles. Your crafting consists of killing wildlife and using their hides to make a bigger holster, a bigger ammo bag, etc. in order to obtain more items (ammo, syringes, etc.). You can customize guns (paint, scope, magazine, etc.), but don’t assume the customization is big compared to Battlefield titles or other shooting games. They do bare bones on customization with guns, but they do improve a big portion of the stats relating to the gun (aim, ammo capacity, range, etc.). They could have added more customization/crafting options in the game, but I did like the quests that one must obtain to maximize their crafting potential.
The UI was clunky at times; I’d have to press multiple times of ESC to get back to the game as one example. The game was well enough to ignore the clunkiness of the UI and the game has a few years on it, so it isn’t ‘modernized’. I didn’t have any FPS drops or bottlenecking when playing this title. I never experienced any crashes or delays or audible problems that sounded off or distant. The voices were done in a way to have an emotional experience and trying to connect with the player when going through the campaign and experiencing the hardships from protagonist, his friends, and his enemies.
A title like Far Cry 3 needs no spoilers and I truly think most people who like action adventure games will enjoy this title. I might not have done everything (finding relics, treasure, etc.), but I did finish the campaign and I would recommend this title to anyone. There are still a lot of content for me to finish, so this game is worth its price.

I want to like this game, but it's getting more frustrating with each match. Now I'm not really experienced in the game and I won't touch on things that I have no clue about.
First of all, is it pay 2 win? When I hear that, I always think of being able to buy objects with real money that will give you a huge advantage over others, without the possibility to buy them with in-game currency. This is not the case in Heroes and Generals as far as I've seen, you can acquire almost everything with in-game money. You just gotta work real hard for it, but it isn't nearly as bad as it used to be.
So what is it exactly that I dislike about the game?
One is the fact that you don't get any of the most basic tools from the beginning. There's vehicles, but you gotta buy them first and they do cost a little. There's tanks but in the beginning there's nothing you can do about them. Even if you buy one later on, there's still matches where no one in your team seems to have anti tank utilities. So what's the issue? Vehicles are spread in the maps and there's rocket launchers lying around all over the place. That is right, still doesn't help me if there's a tank on top of the hill and no one's doing anything about them. And rarely there's vehicles nearby when you truly need them, when you spawn for example and there's recons hiding on top of two hills left and right, making it impossible to traverse an open field without getting shot.
Speaking of spawns, they are horrible at times. I can imagine that they've deliberately made it so that you sometimes have to walk/drive that long so you're more cautious and think in a more tactical manner. Thing is though, that it just raises the chance of your team losing quicker because often, you're the only one who pushes and your team is drinking coffee while one of the few remaining points are being taken. I always try to communicate in a civilized manner and when I tell my team to push forward because we're the attackers, I'm still left as the only one doing it.
Squads are a nice idea, but that doesn't work if your people don't follow the orders or spend the entire match whining about your orders and going to a different lane. Another new addition are the medipacks, the small one is completely useless. With one of the mouse buttons you can either heal yourself or allies when you stand in front of them, which makes a fancy little animation for a few seconds until you're done. Problem is, no one stands still if you want to heal, and when you're under fire, using it is bound to be suicide. And you can only carry one. Maybe I'm blind but I didn't have the option to carry more, which makes no sense at all as you can carry tons of grenades.
With a WW shooter that isn't so known and a little clunky you'd expect decent people to play it, but in reality, a good amount of them that I've met lacked common sense. Here am I in a house chasing an enemy near our objective. I and a team mate "cornered" him, and I threw a grenade into that room. My team mate, who was behind me and should've seen me, runs into that room and gets team killed. I got a warning immediately. Another time I was on the roof of a building, enemy jeep coming towards us. I throw a grenade at it to eliminate the threat, and there was this guy that I didn't notice before that ran right into our enemies with a G43 as if it was a weapon for such short distances. Immediately got a warning and flamed to hell. A game can't change the people that play it, but it can protect people with common sense from those that don't have it, and ruin it for everyone else.
Unless you're stoned, a masochist, in for some free and casual shooting or want to play it with friends, you've not missed anything if you haven't played this game. I'm pretty sure it won't replace any of the shooters you already own. I hope the devs address these issues one day but I kinda doubt it, as some of them were present months ago.

There’s always a dangerous line to travel when a sequel is made, especially when the previous installments are successful or have a healthy modicum of acceptance from consumers. Straying too far from the original formula can make the sequel feel removed and disjointed from what made the previous game good, and sticking too close to the original can come off as lazy or apathetic. Dennaton certainly did not have an easy job on their hands making a sequel to Hotline Miami, and while the gameplay from the previous game is as strong and snappy as ever, what additions were made end up bloating the new installment while punishing the player for playing wildly.
Oddly the biggest disappointment I have right out of the gate is the story-telling. The first game was quite memorable due to the story, which kind of didn’t really care if you were following along clearly or not. Sure, with enough observation and putting puzzle pieces together you could get some idea, but it never really stopped to explain things, just chugging along to the next scene to give you more violence and combos to build in order to get that high score. In Hotline Miami 2, I can’t help but feel like there was damage control because of that, and now there’s too much story being fed to the player. Many characters are brought in to flesh out the narrative, like the Fans who are following in Jacket’s footsteps, or Evan, the journalist writing about all the mayhem and getting involved in ways he wasn’t hoping for. Yes, this does mean you get a nice break between segments to be in someone else’s shoes and potentially have different playstyles (Evan’s lack of killing, the Fans acting as Jackets’ different masks from the first game), but I can’t shake the weird feeling that between Hotline Miami 1 and 2, it felt like there was an obligation to play catch up and bog down the game with narrative just for the sake of putting some clarity to the mayhem.
The second major disappointment comes from the larger, more densely populated maps the game throws you in. While bigger maps should mean more attack strategies, higher scores and longer combos to chain, we mustn't forget that a single, errant mistake means death and restarting the screen. In the first game, playing like a madman often had the end result of clearing screens by the skin of your teeth, adapting in the middle of a skirmish and having very hectic, though incredibly satisfying victories. A death would cost you very little, and only during the later acts when the maps got larger, and more risky did you have to slow down and plan a bit more thoroughly. The player was nearing the end of the game, so the increase in difficulty was to be expected. In Hotline Miami 2, the difficulty of larger, more involved maps starts far sooner than in the original, and is expected, reckless, wild rampages will be shot down far more swiftly and feel much more painful in the process. It’s not the difficulty of the game or the easy death of your character that’s the issue, it’s that the bigger maps that almost seem to demand that you lure waves of enemies into a bottleneck before you horribly end their lives time and time again, and any improvisation during a frantic deviation from this strategy has a high cost regarding your time and patience. Having to clear a level using turtle tactics and purposeful pacing rather than going bonkers through the place and getting a poor score/rating at the end of it all was a frequent reminder of why the first game was far easier to digest and have bloodier enjoyment of. And doors somehow have gotten worse. WORSE.
The soundtrack for me is the biggest shining point of this sequel, as while the first game had a far more memorable OST that stuck with me afterwards, Hotline Miami 2′s music feels much more solid across the board in out of game listening, but it lacks that memorable punch that the first soundtrack had. To say that the music is the most noteworthy part of the game doesn’t entirely speak poorly of Hotline Miami 2′s gameplay which, excluding the need to take encounters on a lot more slowly than intended, it remains as it was in the first game.
Even if we exclude the reported problems that rose during the Steam launch of Hotline Miami 2 of controller play not functioning, Windows XP support being sketchy and the fact that the godforsaken executable did not work on day one for many consumers, I walk away from the game feeling incredibly disappointed on a personal level, while feeling frustrated on the technical side of things. Yes, it is more Hotline, but the attempts of sticking to the original formula while shoving borderline fanfiction-esque narrative upon me made things more and more difficult to swallow, and the ending itself feels like a gigantic middle finger to the player for going through everything they had to see things through to the end. I can only recommend Hotline Miami 2 to those who greatly enjoyed the first game or those who found the first game much too easy. Too much disappointment has remained on a personal and technical level, and it’s because of this that I must unfortunately say that for anyone else curious about Hotline Miami 2, it’s a pass - The first game is your much better bet.

There are a lot of things that I like about this game, and I really, really wanted to recommend it - but I just can't.
The bottom line is this: the audio detection (the core game mechanic) is BAD, BAD, BAD. If it were merely average, or even just mediocre, my overall opinion would likely be different - but it really is that bad.
It does a fine job of tracking the basic background rhythm of a song, but fails horribly when pitted against even the simplest of melodies. Even when testing with the most mundane 5-chord pop-radio double-digit tempo BS (barf) I could dig up, all non-rhythm segments of the gameplay quickly become totally out of sync with the audio; I'm talking about constant audio/visual offsets in the triple digit milliseconds when any amount of polyphony was present, not just audiophile nitpicks. In contrast with the 0-latency, spot-on simple beat tracking, this made the gameplay awkward and clumsy at best - but mostly just outright discordant.
To clarify, this is not an issue of latency; the game interacts with (my) system audio output flawlessly - it just does a terrible job of translating the audio into visually-synchronous gameplay (orbs/obstacles). I found that the more attention I paid to the music, the worse I played - which is exactly the *opposite* of what I expect from a game of this sort. Calibration, while an awesome feature to have in this sort of game, is unfortunately useless if the audio algorithm cannot even track and synchronize significant components of an audio track individually... which it clearly cannot.
As it currently stands, the game is a linear, strictly visually-cued sidescrolling twitch-platformer that very loosely incorporates the *most basic* rhythm of the user's soundtrack. If you were to take away the audio library option, this would simply be a better-looking clone of thousands of similar, free, flash games out there - plenty of which execute their intended gameplay better.
With so many other excellent games in this genre out there, I can't get behind one that only works if you ignore the audio. Here's hoping this will be addressed by the development team in the future, in which case I'll happily revisit the game.

In my years of gaming, I have seen many great products come and go. Great products like Rainbow Six and SWAT as they made their mark in the gaming world. You tend to look back on those games and ask yourself this question. Does anyone still remember those days? How they helped pave the way for tactical strategy in games?
When Door Kickers came along, the answer couldn't have been more clear. "♥♥♥♥ yeah we remember!"
What's good about the game:
-The deep tactical planning, choose from a wide variety of weapons and equipment to plan your approach. (You can even change their names if you're into that sort of thing.) Use your troopers to their maxium potiental to get the job done and bring everyone home safe. Espically in Iron Man mode you will have to take your planning very seriously as every  trooper death only makes your job harder.
-Open-ended planning, missions can be completed in several different ways. It will be up to you to determine what is the best course of action.
-Random enemy placement. In most if not all cases, the odds will be stacked against you. You will face off against several tangos (bad guys) armed to the teeth and not knowing for sure of how many  are there or their location adds tenson to the action. Just because you have a plan figured out, doesn't mean things can't go wrong.
-The ability to do two different playstyles. The first being a pause, plan, action playstyle. Before your troopers get into the thick of it, you can pause the game and develop a course of action for them. Tell who to go where, where to look, where to strafe, etc. Then watch it unfold when you switch it to real time. The second being what I call wing-it mode. You can play the entire mission in real time and make things up as you go. So players that aren't into the whole stop and think style aren't forced to play that way.
-Numerous amount of missions and counting. There are several missions to be completed in this game, all of which have a lot of replayablity to them. Single missions, campagns, custom player-made missions, randomly generated missions. It feels practically endless to what can be done to have missions.  Furthermore, as of the time of this review, the developers are still adding missions, content, and improvements to the game.
-Mod support. Something about the game you want to change up? Things like new weapons,
Odds are there is a mod that fits the bill and there are quite a few to choose from.
-The bits of comedic relief. Though this game has an overall serious tone, there are bits of humor thrown in that is quite amusing to lighten the mood a little when needed. It's not obnoxious or intrusive ethier, it's well timed and unexpected.  I'm not to going to spoil them as I'll leave them to be discovered yourself. ;)
I honestly can't think of anything serious to complain about with Door Kickers. It's an overall well made and addicting tactical strategy game that is worthy of your money and time.  Even at full price, you get a lot for twenty dollars.

PROS:
- Great variety in mobs/animals and plants.
- A building system which allows you to place down whole walls at once, and allows you to save a building and then build it somewhere else if you have the resources.
- You can build your own guns, swords, shields, vehicles, and turrets.
- You can turn this into a Tower Defense game if you want.
- Pretty good crafting system.
- Excellent hand-held scanner which allows you to search for high-mineral deposits and underground caves.
- You have pretty much an in-game workshop in multiplayer, where you can download different things people have built and then use those blueprints (ISOs) in any game mode. Great for those less-creative/new users.
- The save system is pretty great, it generates 3 auto-saves over time, and you can also manually save at multiple points. This is useful if you accidently take on the hardest enemy base and then very quickly get killed when you respawn. (Like I did)
- Great customer support. I've asked them questions multiple times, and they have always responded within 24 hours, even when I've done so on a weekend. They will tell you what is wrong or will ask for more information if needed, and are very polite in doing so.
CONS:
- Lots of crashes, though really if you won't play this game because of it, why are you even looking at a game still in development?
- Developer Reliability:
(EDIT: They seem to be getting more and more consistant with updates, releasing at least one monthly. If they keep this up, then my review will continue to be positive.)
- Not a whole lot of variety in quests; most are just, "fight these things," or, "bring me this." This is fine, seeing as story mode is yet to be completed, but I'd like to eventually see more variety.
OVERALL/TL, DR:
-
This is an excellent game, and the developers seem to have learned from their mistakes. They've noticed the dwindling player base and have acknowledged that it is due to their previous infrequent update history. They're improving upon that and have begun monthly updates. They are also very responsive to suggestions and have a great customer support system, should it be needed. I'm looking forward to the future of this game.
Still TL, DR: Put it on your wishlist and get it on sale.

The game initially feels kind of like a cheap chinese knockoff, but as you play you'll be quickly disuaded from that idea (at least the cheap and knockoff parts; the dialogue still makes me think non-native speaker). While you need to mine for resources and are capable of building a variety of structures, terraforming the world is NOT the main focus of this game. Instead you primarily spend your resources building equipment, weaponry, and vehicles. These allow you to fight the hostile forces that reside in the sprawling world as you explore. Both the combat and exploration are really well polished, and those aspects alone are worth the fairly low price. The story has been added to throughout early access, and does a good job of providing distant destinations for you to travel to so that you can lose yourself along the way (not literally; you have a map).

The graphics are slightly outdated, but the game is still playable. This isn't even an issue, as I think they might've done it on purpose to increase the amount of people who can play it. Whatever the case may be, the graphics really don't matter enough here for people to turn away from the game.
Reliability loses a point because multiple people have reported crashing when you alt-tab. Switching out of the game and back in safely is important to quite a few people, so I think this is something that should be addressed by the developers. Besides that, I haven't actually crashed or encountered any bugs at all yet, so again, I didn't factor this one in either.
The game has an excellent replay value. There is about a million different ways to play the game. I'm not kidding, either. It would be too much for me to explain here. See for yourself! There are also, as mentioned above, many mods to pick and choose from, increasing this value even more.
Multiplayer. I haven't actually played it yet, but I have quite a few friends who play this that have reported that it is amazing. I can only assume it receives a 10 as well.
For the length of the game, it can really go for as short as you'd like, to as long as you want. Start out a serf, fight a couple battles, then retire? Go ahead. Want to play a 1,000 hour marathon of the game where you slowly conquer the entire land? Probably possible, maybe with the help of mods. I don't know if the game would even still be stable beyond that point, or perhaps there would be nothing left to conquer, but really I shouldn't be expecting more than this.
But yeah, if you fancy an actual medieval simulator, or perhaps a really fun game, get this one. It is worth it.

This is one of my favorite games of alltime. There are millions of other reviews, so I'll skip the gameplay mechanics and just stick to what makes the game worthwhile:
This game nails "sandbox" better than any other game I've played. The perfect mix between non-linear, open world aimlessness and just enough mini-questing to make the world feel alive. Essentially, the world exists just fine WITHOUT you, and you can go in and be whichever part of it you like. It is incredibly immersive precisely because you feel so small at first -- you are not a hero of destiny with any special abilities, but just another human that is just as fragile as the NPCs. In order to become more powerful, you actually have to GET BETTER at fighting. It comes with practice, and the learning curve is balanced perfectly. Failure is an essential component of this game, but unlike games like Dark Souls that are "artificially" difficult, it simply feels like it's a harsh world out there. It isn't always fair, but it's equally unfair for all the other inhabitants.
There are some noticeable flaws, but none of them are dealbreakers. Firstly, it looks about five years older than it is, graphically. Secondly, the dialogue is extremely limited and repetitive. Thirdly, it's definitely a little buggy.
But despite those three flaws, I've never played something that felt so immersive -- and that's really strange because all of those flaws SHOULD be immersion breakers. Yet this is the only game I've played where I subconsciously began to imagine lore for my own character, which is not something that comes naturally or easily for me like it would for, say, someone who does a lot of D&D. I'm not even sure why it has this magic to it. For example, I remember badly wanting a castle fief when I first become a vassal of a faction, but I knew that, as the new guy, it would be a long time before a property like that trickled down the totem pole. I grew impatient and led a ballsy, expensive siege on my own time and coin that resulted in the capture of a weak enemy castle. I requested ownership of the fief that I had conquered at great expense, but the king awarded it to some other guy.
I was actually OFFENDED. This character has maybe 15 pre-programmed lines, no voice acting at all, and a face that doesn't even move, and somehow I felt the deep, personal vendetta that I would feel for a real person that disrespected me. I literally went to bed ANGRY, thinking about how I would respond when I played the next day. It's unbelieveable how something so simple has gotten its hooks into my imagination.
Anyway, if you have any interest in this genre at all, this game is a must-buy. It's one of those rare gems that is clearly a bit flawed, but might actually be less desireable if it was more polished. It's the girl next door with the annoying laugh and weird birthmark that is somehow more beautiful than an airbrushed supermodel. It's got "charm" or "character" or something.
I don't know what it is, but it's an absolute classic. Try it out.

It's a Ubisoft sandbox game.
If you've ever played a Ubisoft sandbox game before, then this is all you really need to know. You start in an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-infested area with a big villain ruling over it, you gradually liberate said area by overtaking strongholds and you reveal the map by climbing tower and making the camera pan around it.
In this case, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-infested area in question is a tropical island with all kinds of wildlife and plants on it for you to hack to bits. Animal skins can be used to craft equipment like weapon holsters and wallets and plants can be used to craft drugs. There is only one plant needed for a health syringe though, and those were the only drugs I ever made in the game.
An advantage that Far Cry has over, say, Assassin's Creed 2 is that they didn't have machineguns, cars and tigers in 15th century Italy. This makes overtaking strongholds (and combat in general) way more fun. In Assassin's Creed you only had the choice of either stealthily stabbing people in the neck or not-so-stealthily stabbing people in the neck. In Far Cry 3 there's an infinite amount of possibilities. You can take people out from a distance with a sniper rifle, you can set them on fire, you can run them over with a jeep or you can shoot the lock of a cage in a stronghold and watch as a komodo dragon mauls them to death. Missions are challenging and varied, so they never become boring.
Besides the variety in gameplay, the story is also one of the games strengths. Especially Jason's character arch is really good. He starts out as a standard millenial tourist, and by the end of the game he's basically John Rambo with enough drugs in his body to floor a sumo wrestler. The rest of the characters are pretty hit-and-miss. On the one side, there are Vaas and Buck, two extremely colorful, charismatic villains, but on the other side there's the extremely generic tribe that helps you become a warrior. Luckily you spent a lot more time with the more interesting characters.
The variety in combat doesn't rub off on the sidequests. True to the Ubisoft formula the sidequests consist entirely of assassinations and navigating Tomb Raider levels in order to find a magic MacGuffin at the end. There are also a ridiculous amount of MacGuffins scattered around the map for you to collect if you really have nothing better to do. The map isn't all that amazing either. It feels like they made an area containing some hills, small villages and ruins and just copied and pasted it 20 times.
But in the end, the relatively samey map and bland sidequests do not change the fact that the main game is fun and the story is good.
