TL;DR:  It's a bit rough around the edges, but Sonic Adventure 2's a pretty fun 3D action platformer and solid entry in the Sonic series.
I'll start this by saying I bought as a part of the Sonic Everywhere bundle on Amazon a while back for $15 on sale.
Sonic Adventure 2: Battle.  Oh man, I remember this from the Gamecube.  It was my first actual 3D Sonic, since I entirely skipped the Saturn and Dreamcast.  I never thought I'd see it on PC, honestly.  This is a port of a port, but that's not all that bad.  I'll try not to mention anything related to the 2P mode or the Battle DLC additions.
The game is split into three sections told by two separate stories between Hero and Dark.  Sonic and Shadow are the typical high-speed platforming/rail-grinding/Homing Attacking gameplay where you get to the goal ring.  Tails and Dr. Eggman travel through levels in bipedal mechs and blow things up with some platforming elements.  Knuckles and Rouge climb, glide, and dig through large levels to find three Master Emerald shards or keys or so on.  The stories happen at the same time but are told by different sides, and by beating both Hero and Dark stories, Last Story is unlocked and through that the true ending to the game is revealed.
Gameplay is different from Sonic Adventure in that instead of merely choosing one character and using only that character until their respective ending, you pick between good and evil and you go through that side's stages alternating between Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles for Hero and Shadow, Eggman, and Rouge for Dark.  There are no Adventure Fields to traverse between levels, so the flow goes between Action Stages and story events with some boss battles sprinkled in.  Every character fights his or her opposing-side match one or more times in a boss fight, though there are some third-party battles too.
There is a good bit of content though you don't need to see it all to beat the game.  Every stage has five missions, though you only beat the first mission as you go through the story mode.  The other four missions are optional challenges, and every mission gives you a rank based on score.  Emblems are also awarded for clearing missions and other tasks, and getting all of them is a pretty big undertaking since there are 180 of them.  Getting all A-ranks in every mission is something a challenge-seeker would enjoy.  There is a leaderboard feature so you can compare scores between everyone or just friends.
The music is catchy.  Some of the songs during the stages have lyrics which doesn't really detract from the experience.  I hope you like rock and some hip-hop, though.  All of Knuckles' stages have lyrics present, a couple of the Sonic and Shadow stages have them, all of Rogue's stages have female singers present.  All six characters have theme songs too which pop up during the story, and if you want to listen to those or any other song in full, there's a sound test in the options, so that's nice.
Chao Garden.  Chao are cute little creatures found in Chao World separate to the story that you are tasked with hatching and raising, albeit optionally unless you want to get all of the game's emblems.  While only able to crawl around like an infant at first, by feeding them Chaos Drives and small animals found in the stages, they will grow and take on features of the animals.  Raised Chao can be entered in races, though you have no direct control over their performance outside of a little boost to speed.  There is some incentive to keep going back to the stages to get items to raise the little creatures and it is kinda nice to take care of them and watch them grow and change...and stop drowning in the little pond.
There is a lack of polish with this port, and at times they seemed to fix a couple of things but leave some others strangely untouched.  For example, the "wow, he's fast hey it's not his speed he's using the Chaos Emerald to warp" line during the story bit when Sonic first meets Shadow IS given a gap, but the "you're not even good enough--"  "I'll make you eat those words!" before Sonic and Shadow's first fight is not.  The mouths move with the Japanese audio and not with the English which results in some cutting off at times, or people talking after their mouths stopped moving.  Rouge's eyes actually went through her eyelids a few times, and the perspective of one scene put both of Amy's eyes on the same side of her face.  I didn't really have much problem during the gameplay, barring a couple of instances where hitting a boost pad the wrong way resulted in an unavoidable death.
I did not like the treasure hunting stages.  Even Tails and Eggman's sections I enjoyed even if they're not very Sonicy.  I dunno, I guess a big problem I have is that the radar only tracks the first item in a list.  You can be standing right next to a shard or something and the radar won't tell you unless it's the first in a line.  I understand why it's set up that way, but that's a problem I have with the core game as opposed to this port.  The stages are wide open and there are hint monitors, but they boil down to just hide-and-seek at best and pixel hunting at worst.  There are some interesting features like dodging the invincible enemy in Egg Quarters or adjusting the water level in Aquatic Mine, but at this point I'm just ranting.
Just pretend I said "treasure hunting but worse" here.
So in closing...it's an old game.  The graphics are visibly dated, the camera is a bit of a chore to fight against, and the story can be kinda hit-or-miss.  But I had fun with it, even for it not being new to me anymore.  I put in just 15 hours to clear the game this time around, and that was with giving plenty of time to Chao Garden.  Besides, this is the best game if you're prone to rolling around at the speed of sound, or if you feel apprehensive at the thought of somebody wanting to play with your emarools.  $10 ain't bad, and it's been cheaper before to boot.
Well, since Steam won't let me review a DLC that integrates into the main game, lemme go ahead and paste what I was going to say there.
The Battle DLC is, as you could guess from the name, related to the 2P versus mode found in the original Sonic Adventure 2.  It does alter a few things in the single-player version of the game, though I don't know if those changes carry over to the version of the game without this DLC.  It's a little hard for me to tell since I got them both at the same time.

I've been playing Vermintide since it officially launched, and I have to say that I am thoroughly in love. This game has all of the finer elements from the Left 4 Dead franchise that made it so replayable, and it puts them through the filter of the gritty Warhammer Fantasy universe. As a long time fan of Warhammer and Warhammer 40k, I am always watching for titles with the franchise name and giving them a thorough investigation before I would ever deem something that fell within my all time favorite fantasy universe great simply for having the name attached. Vermintide for sure delivers. You truly are pitted against the hordes of Skaven set during the End Times and it feels like a constant struggle to mix quick movement with thoughtful decision making. Sometimes you see a patrol that can easily be avoided or fought in a fierce melee, while other times you are moving safely through back alleys and suddenly a Gutter Runner has one of your party on the ground and a Packmaster is dragging another away and your group now dances on the knife edge of a full on wipe. These moments come all too often and really bring a good life to the game.
The loot system is another thing I found pretty interesting and acceptable. Loot is only earned on a successful mission completion, so it truly does force one to not rush forward hastily, however taking more time seems to draw in more ambushes and waves which can easily grow overwhelming.
Positioning is an important aspect of the game and is to be used at all times.
I really REALLY hope they make some Chaos force maps or other evil force DLC's, because thats what I think we'd all love to see.
Cons: The cons I do have are mostly with the servers and hosting. There is NO dedicated hosting, so hosts are on a player by player basis, which means that if your host decides to up and leave 3/4 through the mission, you are restarted back at the beginning of the mission with another player as the new host.

Do you really like tactical games? This is the game for you. Take control of a SWAT team and take them through various police scenarios such as hostage rescues, imminent hostage executions, drug raids, arrest warrants, and VIP escorts. There are many weapons that have their own individual stats as well as a variety of different equipment from different types of kevlar vests that protect more or less from different angles (front, rear, and sides), to different types of grenades (flashbangs, stun grenades). There's other ways of breaching such as using breaching charges, shotguns, bolt cutters, and much more. This game reminds me of the old Rainbow Six games and the SWAT games as well.

Team Alpha, go! Bravo, engage!
Pros:
- Doorkickers has a very great tactical element to it, allowing you to utilize unit sight lines to spy corners before entering and taking out the baddies before shots are fired. Using multiple units for cover and movement through doorways, flashing, flanking is very fun and very satisfying when it all goes according to the plan in your mind.
- The different classes to combine on missions is very interesting and with mobility meters could spell the difference between a good outcome on a mission or a very fatal end.
- Utilization of "Go-Codes" is always exciting when you are able to time your plan sequences in a smooth, fluid execution.
- There is a SKILL tree and Doctrine points to purchase weapons and gear (only once) for all of your units to use
- Lots of maps and creatable content to share with Steam friends and community.
Cons:
- I have to admit, sometimes the units can be a bit finnicky, and it gets a bit frustrating; there are two tangos in a large room on the other side of a locked door you cannot flashbang through - breaching with a hammer, lockpick, or breaching charge takes too much time to set up, you send a man through and direct his sight line to sweep, but instead of firing on the first guy he sees on side A, sweeps and shoots man in corner B instead and leaves the first man he sees in the shadows. Alongside the factor of friendly fire sight lines, its frustrating when you have 2 of your own units stacked on top of each other, but one will not fire in his designated direction due to a teammate being directly on top of him.
- I've found that enemy units are able to fire simultaneously and hit my units while they are in a line, while my units cannot fire through each other. Something I think will be patched in the future.
- Another issue I'm having is pathing selections: there are times where lines will overlap in a hallway and you wnat to change the sight line of ONE of your units, but you can't select his pathing line because the OTHER guys' line is on top of his. I tried to lock one unit's path with SHIFT, but doesn't seem to work. Something that can be fixed.
Conclusion:
All in all, I REALLY do enjoy the game. For $20? Sure. I honestly feel the game's INCLUDED content could have been more, the campaigns are a bit short, but the replayability with different tactics is refreshing. The focus on community map content is a bit harrowing, as I'm not one to really have time to download and configure all of it to work. I also feel that each class should have their own type of special ability in relation with the skill trees, instead of just access to a certain type of primary weapon. Different stat fluctuations, maybe? I don't know. It's still a great game to kill time and terrorists with.

The original was so impressive, it would seem that the successor had no hope of ever pulling off originality again. I don't think that's the case here. HM2:WN is, quite frankly, masterful story telling of Hollywood calibre via a gaming medium. Sure, the gameplay is mostly tweaked borrowings from the original, but there's absolutely nothing wrong with that. Dennaton Games really focused on the story telling this time around, introducing a boatload of new characters - some old characters revisted as well. From one act to the next, you are jumping into a new character's point of view with his/her own story to tell. Amazing stuff here. What we end up with is one hell of a roller coaster ride from beginning to end. Upon its completion, it was clear to me that I had just experienced something that could only be described as a 6-8 hour long acid trip. There's nothing subtle in Dennaton's whacked out artistic style. They really want you to believe you're tripping out - pretty much why the Hotline Miami games stand out.
All in all, I can attest HM2:WN lived up to the hype.
Also worth noting is the utterly brilliant soundtrack. Quite possibly one of the best, if not THE best, soundtracks ever for a video game.

Hotline Miami 2 is neither a step forward or a step back when compared to its legendary original. It is in some ways better than the first and in some ways worse. It is really up to the player to determine if it is as up to par or even better than the first. I'll sum it up quickly in a PROS and CONS list.
PROS
- Amazing soundtrack as usual. Not as iconic as the first but definitely more versatile.
- Slick retro graphics that are slightly improved and more vivid than the first. Soldier's missions also throw in a more hazy variety. And the last level...prepare yourself.
- Cleverly written and delivered story that isn't shoved down your throat. In some ways it is open to interpretation, but it is more focused and clear than the original's narrative.
- Interesting and engaging characters...whether you hate them or not (screw Manny Pardo though. You'll know why once you play the game).
- Core gameplay itself is as slick as ever. Nothing new as the system was good to begin with.
- Upcoming level editor for near endless replayability and experimentation.
- GOTTA GET A GRIP!
CONS
- Some levels have very annoying level design with an abundance of windows. Level design is NOT the same as Hotline Miami. It is one of the key break-offs and differences actually. Maps are significantly bigger and that is bittersweet. You will die a lot more times by a goon with a gun off-screen that you couldn't see. This may also be because of slightly smarter AI and I believe field of vision.
- Lackluster hard mode. The hard mode is filled with artificial difficulty to the point where it could be viewed as unfair. With the already larger maps, adding in even more windows is frustrating.
- Smooth gameplay experienced from the first can be notably delayed and interrupted because of the level design/hard mode (or both) in some levels.
NEUTRAL
- No more iconic mask catalog like you oh so loved in the first game. Instead, you have different characters with different abilities and playstyles depending on the chapter you are playing. The Fans are a group that have masks that each have their own unique ability, such as dual submachine guns, combat roll, or Tony's lethal punches. There's also the budget Batman known as The Writer, and The Soldier, who permanently wields a gun that can have refillable ammo on drops and a combat knife. These characters change how you play the game completely, instead of just perks like the masks in the first game. However, it really depends on what you like. The game is different because of this.
Overall, I personally loved this game. It is one of my favorites, period. I can't decide if I like it more than the first, but I'm definitely pouring more hours into it. I don't believe it SHOULD be compared to the first, but obviously that's inevitable seeing how legendary the first installment is. If you are a fan of the series, I definitely recommend this game. If you liked the first purely for the gameplay, you may be disappointed here as it is different in many ways.

I played this game for more than 36 hours in the first three days that I'd bought it. I believe this alone speaks to its quality. I have no doubt whenever my friends and I have the itch to play zombie shooters, it *will* be Contagion we return to. Three things about it to note; you should play with other people at least once, even if you don't know them, because it's a different game, although there is charm in playing alone; the sound system is amazing, and it will immerse you really well, plus it's incredible in Hunted; and they capture the feeling of the zombie apocalypse rather well.
Most of the charm in it for me is playing with other people, who can be scarce. Many of my experiences were better because a friend of mine rented a server so we essentially played whatever we wanted, but if you don't do that and already have three or four friends to play with, it can get a little difficult to find enough players to do what you want to do. Especially in Hunted, if you're stomping a round for a good 20 minutes, people tend to leave.
Other than that, the sound *is* fantastic, except for one regard - it doesn't handle vertical distances very well. Playing Hunted was amazing on Aurora Estates, but not so much on Biotech; in Aurora, you pinged, you knew someone was at least in your house, but in Biotech, you already knew they were nearby as it's a smaller map, but with there being three floors and four rough sections, you can't ever tell what section they're in, only that they're near you on the XY axis. That said, there's nothing like sitting in Ventrilo, in kind of silence, making vague jokes about what everyone else is doing but trying very hard to listen for quiet footsteps... and then someone shoots the shotgun *once,* and the whole game is galvanized.
Finally, the zombies. The goddamned zombies. You wonder in games like Left 4 Dead how the zombies actually killed anything, ever, if there were such violently competent survivors running about. I understand that there was a small percentage of the population which was immune, but that wasn't explained until a game later, as subtext for the end of a campaign; the thought remained long enough to disenchant me. Contagion, however, makes every zombie a threat, even without the possibility of you being infected. When they didn't infect you, a single one could take up too many bullets if they caught you by surprise, or you'd miss a lot, or you'd go for the sledgehammer kill to save ammo or be quiet and it would be this huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and now you're missing half of your health feeling like a moron. At the same time, I never felt cheated when a zombie got the better of me, because you don't die in Contagion due to the game screwing with you, it's because you ♥♥♥♥ed up. What's more, aside from the zombies' competence at genocide as a whole, once a single player went down, they became an infected player, and the hypercompetent player zombie always brought the game to a swift end soon after, in both Hunted and Escape. There were very few games that ended in a player victory in Escape with player zombies present, and in Hunted, many an infected survivor won by the skin of his teeth because the zombie players found the other final survivor, or both of them were infected and it was a time game, or one of them ran out of ammo but the other was infected - all kinds of stuff.
tl;dr it's outrageous fun, grab a friend, hell grab a four pack, get a server, play Escape and be the hero your friends deserve, play Hunted and be the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you were meant to be

Let me just state one thing clearly first, Deadlight is a very polarizing game when I played it so this recommendation is more towards neutral. With that said Deadlight is a zombie apocalypse 2D action platformer video game. The game has player character traversing a 2D plane with 3D environment with you assuming the role of Randall Wayne on a quest to find his wifey and daughter in this zombie hellhole with Randall narrating the his thoughts on the state of the dying world as you play along.
Notice the lack of survival in the genre list and that is because its not survival at all but rather a a linear experience with PC simply going from point A to point B jumping from platform to platform before triggering yet another cutscene. Not that Deadlight platforming section is terrible, it's good but I'll touch on that later. For now, the review.
Excellent, truly marvelous, and atmospheric. If I don't count some of the voice acting that is within Deadlight overall I can say that the sound design is spot on, there are moments where I actually got spooked due to the sudden change in music, audio cue and etc etc.
Meanwhile the voice acting especially for the PC is incredibly gravelly, like very much so. It's like he is incapable of speaking without a slight growl all the time. But if we ignore that [and a few other missed issues] it's actually pretty solid!
Cutscenes are rendered in still comic book art style and well to give a short opinion, it looks good but nothing to shout about. You have to get used to it seeing as it pops up quite often.
As for the actual graphic itself, I don't have much to say about it other than the fact at the time I'm reviewing this game it already looks kind of dated with a seemingly muddy filter covering the whole screen. The texture also looks muddy as well. I'm just gonna go ahead and say it looks ok for the atmosphere they were aiming for but not for the gameplay itself since zombies can sometimes blend in with the environment and effect glitches are plenty for the zombies as well.
Option Menu is disappointing. You have resolution controls, gamma, vsync but no individual graphical option settings. Instead they give you a slider with options from low to high and that's it. You can rebind control keys for keyboard but not for controller  and it plays better with a controller anyways except when it comes to aiming,
Now as for Performance, my computer isn't actually that powerful but I still find it baffling that I cannot run this on low at 60 fps. There are also random lag spike whenever the game loads new assets.
And bugs oh boy, Zombies can apparently grab you from behind doors at times, I even got stuck on a moving platform with my Character unable to respond to my controls. Certain sections also contains a lot of bugs that will be fixed upon reloading a checkpoint.
The character also sometimes does things that you didn't tell him to do and when it's located at the beginning of an area forcing you to redo it all over again it gets aggravating fast.
Simple stuff, you have walljump, ledge grab, and all those fancy smanky parkour moves so you can move around the environment nimbly. For dispatching zombies for those occasional moment you have several weapons and some can be aimed. The basic axe won't kill the zombies no matter how many times you hit them unless you use the finishing move on them while the gun will kill them in 1 shot provided you aim for the head because otherwise they can still chug along just fine.
While in the game you can collect collectible secrets, ID cards, and diary pages but these are just fluff. They don't serve a purpose.
Pretty much that's it, gameplay has you going from point A to point B while parkouring along solving easy puzzles and not end up as zombie bait.
Story - Too short, the plot twist is hideous and the ending itself is a terrible way to end a game. The whole big exposition they hyped to you about throughout the game turns out to be something that if you're genry savvy you can see from a mile away.
Inconsistent Tone - At first the story is about zombies wait sorry no, shadows. I hate it when zombie game pretend to not know the word zombie anyways, at first it was a story about shadow, then they shoehorn in an organization that we never even need to interact with, somehow everybody you interact with don't really move the story in any meaningful way, and then it very laughably tries to switch the main theme of the story halfway through before hurrying up trying to get back on course but by then it's too late, the train has already derailed.
The Ending - I will not spoil it for you but the ending of the game goes contrary to what you have been allowed to do i-game. Cutscene Dissonance Disorder. Thank goodness the whole thing was short because it felt like a slight waste of time.
Padding - There is so much samey environment that you will have to go through but at the end of the day the whole game is still short and it feels so unfulfilled and this combined with the myriad of issues almost tipped me to give it a solid no.
But the platforming section is unfortunately [or fortunately?] quite good so if you already have this game you might as well give it a try and rage at the story like I did. Plenty of issues, plenty of bugs, but a few saving grace kept this from being a bargain bin deal... actually scratch that, get it on sale or from somewhere as long as it is not full price. It's not that good to warrant the full asking price.
Scoring Methology:
-	S-Rank: excellent
-	A-Rank: very good
-	B-Rank: solid
-	C-Rank: satisfactory
-	D-Rank: inferior
Verdict: C- Passable. But just that.

A short but fun jump and run game in a zombie apocalypse setting. It's a 2D side scroller embedded in a 3D world that looks great, with lots of stuff going on in the 3D background and enemies coming towards the character and camera from there.
You are some rather faceless guy called Randall who searches for his family and tries to reach a 'safepoint' during another zombie apocalypse. You can collect notes and diary pages which explain a bit about the past and how it all began, but don't expect too much of the story. ;)
The jumping mechanics are great, and Randall can do many different moves (including a wall dash) to climb and jump over the  various obstacles in the partly destroyed city, while avoiding traps and the zombies which walk on the floor. You have some weapons like a pistol and an axe, but they are mostly tools to break into doors or shoot buttons. You can kill some zombies with them, and you have to do that in a few scenes, but you will have to avoid larger groups (and the majority of them throughout the game) by jumping, climbing and running.
I've finished the game in less than 5h, but I had a blast. During this time, it didn't matter much to me that the story is mediocre and that the characters are not that interesting. If you like 2D side scrollers, get this game for a few bucks, it's worth it.

You nail it and jump up onto the ledge and hammer jump furiously while Randall finishes his diary entry? Oh well. Randall develops fear of heights and won't jump to safety? The background sounds give it a nice ambience and coupled with the Shadows you'll have a few heart pounding escapes. Again, it looks fantastic. Enjoy the scenery.

Hotline Miami 2 is neither a step forward or a step back when compared to its legendary original. It is in some ways better than the first and in some ways worse. It is really up to the player to determine if it is as up to par or even better than the first. I'll sum it up quickly in a PROS and CONS list.
PROS
- Amazing soundtrack as usual. Not as iconic as the first but definitely more versatile.
- Slick retro graphics that are slightly improved and more vivid than the first. Soldier's missions also throw in a more hazy variety. And the last level...prepare yourself.
- Cleverly written and delivered story that isn't shoved down your throat. In some ways it is open to interpretation, but it is more focused and clear than the original's narrative.
- Interesting and engaging characters...whether you hate them or not (screw Manny Pardo though. You'll know why once you play the game).
- Core gameplay itself is as slick as ever. Nothing new as the system was good to begin with.
- Upcoming level editor for near endless replayability and experimentation.
- GOTTA GET A GRIP!
CONS
- Some levels have very annoying level design with an abundance of windows. Level design is NOT the same as Hotline Miami. It is one of the key break-offs and differences actually. Maps are significantly bigger and that is bittersweet. You will die a lot more times by a goon with a gun off-screen that you couldn't see. This may also be because of slightly smarter AI and I believe field of vision.
- Lackluster hard mode. The hard mode is filled with artificial difficulty to the point where it could be viewed as unfair. With the already larger maps, adding in even more windows is frustrating.
- Smooth gameplay experienced from the first can be notably delayed and interrupted because of the level design/hard mode (or both) in some levels.
NEUTRAL
- No more iconic mask catalog like you oh so loved in the first game. Instead, you have different characters with different abilities and playstyles depending on the chapter you are playing. The Fans are a group that have masks that each have their own unique ability, such as dual submachine guns, combat roll, or Tony's lethal punches. There's also the budget Batman known as The Writer, and The Soldier, who permanently wields a gun that can have refillable ammo on drops and a combat knife. These characters change how you play the game completely, instead of just perks like the masks in the first game. However, it really depends on what you like. The game is different because of this.
Overall, I personally loved this game. It is one of my favorites, period. I can't decide if I like it more than the first, but I'm definitely pouring more hours into it. I don't believe it SHOULD be compared to the first, but obviously that's inevitable seeing how legendary the first installment is. If you are a fan of the series, I definitely recommend this game. If you liked the first purely for the gameplay, you may be disappointed here as it is different in many ways.
9/10

For starters, if you haven't played the first Hotline: Miami, do so now.  Not because it's necessary to understand or appreciate the second, but because it's a great game in its own right.  Now, onto this sequel.
Wrong Number is a great follow-up to the first.  The gameplay is essentially the same.  You work your way through levels, each with an often-amazing music track accompanying the gory action.  There are some changes this time around, mostly in the level design.  The first thing you'll notice is that maps are a lot larger than they were in the first.  This is both good and bad.  While levels tend to be more diverse and interesting, it's very, very easy to get killed by off-screen enemies and this encourages you to play much more cautiously.  There's a "look ahead" feature as well as a lock on mechanic, but I can't help but feel that it alters the game play in a detrimental way at times by making the pace of action feel a little choppy.  Fortunately, the controls are still very tight and responsive and enable you to react quickly to the even-quicker reaction times of your enemies.
The visual design is, like the first, very unique and has an almost hypnotic quality to it.  You can run this game on any PC, by the way.  The only thing I can say hardware-wise is that if you have a good sound card it will only enhance the music which is...........
AMAZING!  The soundtrack is somehow better than the first.  Play this game with a good set of headphones.  The tracks are more diverse than the first game's and some of them are just monstrous.  I ended up buying the soundtrack after owning the game a few days, it's that good.
Story-wise, this game doesn't deviate from the first's vague method of plot exposition.  It jumps back and forth in time, with very little explanation as to what exactly is happening.  You'll probably be looking up plot summaries online afterwards, but it still has interesting enough characters that will make you care enough to do so.
In conclusion, Wrong Number is a great sequel.  As mentioned, it plays differently than the first due to the larger levels, but it's still the same great action and (I can't say this enough) the soundtrack is absolutely incredible.  It's well worth the price and you'll get around 12-15 hours out of it.

I have a long history with the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise. While this may make me slightly biased, I still feel that this game is an excellent platformer with elements of high-speed action, treasure hunting, and third person shooting. This 2001 entry into the Sonic catalogue was originally released on the Sega Dreamcast as a follow-up to 1998's Sonic Adventure. Both of these titles brought the blue hero into the world of 3-D on a level to match Super Mario 64 with more intricate and darker storylines and hard rock music to give them attitude. The game has obvious issues with the voice acting and the levels could have a better design to them, but the characters themselves and classic Sonic elements more than make up for it if you're willing to look at it for what it is. Whether you don't know about the games or didn't like past iterations, you should still give this a try. The story isn't fantastic and has some slight plot holes, but the graphics aren't terrible, the music is fantastic, and the sense of speed is pretty good for 2001. In case anyone wonders, the title track "Live and Learn" is done by the band Crush 40, featuring the renowned musicians Jun Senoue and Johnny Gioeli. I more than recommend this game, having picked it back up recently and still enjoying it a great deal despite whatever small problems the game might have.

My history with the Sonic series goes back over a decade. I've stuck with it and tried to keep an open mind through each of the games released from the mid-2000s to mid-2010s whose reception has, for the most part, been unspectacular. Even if Sega's ideas for the colorful creatures haven't always worked - and I will still contend that many games released during this time have - I very much respect them for branching out and flicking an angular, latex-gloved bird at the industry trend of using statistics to decide what kinds of games to create. So it's really a formality, after all, for me to review possibly the last Sonic game that's consistently respected. And boy, have I ever had a lot of fun with the game, so here it goes:
Sonic Adventure 2 has some serious problems.
The game's sunny, San Francisco-esque first level, City Escape, is unique but completely fitting. I've played through it dozens of times trying for the elusive A-rank and completing subsequent missions, and dozens more just for the sheer fun of it. The majority of later levels, though, are much less impressive.
Tails' and Eggman's offerings - the style is identical - are intelligence-insulting, slow, repetitive shoot-'em-up excursions that encourage the player to tap the shoot button for several minutes on end as fast as possible while executing platforming stunts with oddly realistic physics amidst, more often than not, vast expanses of abyss. To be fair, later levels do contact the player's brain for directions once in a while, as shooting certain hatches or covers can expose the level to the universe outside and thus suck the player in. I'm pretty sure that's not how gravity works, but forgivable. What's less forgivable is just how annoying this mechanic is; after being trained to shoot until I can physically shoot no more, I don't much appreciate being slapped in the face by a quick death.
Knuckles' and Rouge's levels I rather enjoy - the ones on Earth, anyway. Those feature much more interesting and varied scenery and more concise, inspired level design. No, it's not speedy, but I don't really miss that. Aside from some abysmal physics in parts of the level Mad Space, Emerald-hunting levels generally play very fluidly and without issue. They're also quite relaxing and force the player to get more intimate with Sonic levels than they may be used to.
Sonic's and Shadow's will likely feel the most familiar to players of not only the Genesis Sonics, but of other 3D titles as well; Sega decided this was the formula that worked the best. For the most part, they're right; the levels are exhilarating, expecting speed and precision as only levels in the Sonic series do. My enthusiasm, unlike Omochao's to help the player, however, is finite: the hedgehog levels occasionally display awkward physics and glitches, and the precision necessary to avoid cheap deaths can get ridiculous. Play or watch a Let's Play of one of the rail levels (particularly Sky Rail) or get acquainted with the homing attack - there's a narrow window of time and distance from a target when you have to press the jump button to neither plummet to your death nor get hit and fall backwards to your death - and you'll see what I mean. Hedgehog gameplay is fun overall, but it's imperfect.
It's high time now for me to talk about what I find by far the worst aspect of the game: the cutscnes. Sweet mother of Wisps, are they ever bad. I get that Sonic Adventure 2 is a Japanese game, but there's "non-native but kawaii and starting every other sentence with 'But,'" and then there's "voice actors literally interrupting each other and tire-hopping through their already stilted dialogue as they pitifully try to map it to the natural rhythm of the English language." In one scene, I kid you not, Knuckles interrupts himself. More mildly, but still effecting of distraction, Eggman's voice is way too quiet, and Tails sounds like an actual, gross, human 8-year-old boy instead of the parallel-universe fox we've grown to love.
It's a shame that the cutscenes of later games (e.g. Shadow's existential mopings, Charmy's inexplicable top-secret discs, Sonic's gooey romance that I'm pretty sure is illegal in 15 zones and Westopolis, with further legislation being drafted in Station Square) are the infamous ones, when they actually represented serious and respectable efforts to advance their games' stories. The FMV sequences in Sonic Adventure 2 don't only flop on a technical level; they don't even seem to take themselves seriously. As a result, I can't take the plot of the game seriously - well, any more than I otherwise would considering it's about talking animals, gigantic emeralds, and a truck the width of a street and both sidewalks. Honestly, it's completely fitting that the captions are all in Comic Sans. How would I summarize SA2's cutscenes? They stink, like echidnas do!
Like Sonic jumping from some height and being blasted far higher than before by a spring, however, I do have to give one aspect of the game the extreme, saccharine praise it deserves: the music. Each of the six characters has their own style, and every single time it fits both their personality and their gameplay style. Sonic corresponds to pop-punk, Tails jangly alt-rock, Knuckles rap, Shadow industrial rock, Eggman vaguely funky alt-metal, and Rouge smooth jazz. With a minor exception of Knuckles, I never get bored of it within each level, and even with him only because they can take so long. (Not a bad thing! Not a bad thing!) Even the game's intro theme changes time signatures a few times to ring in the characters, as if a conceptual overture to the radically divergent styles. I'm not sure much of anything could have been done to improve the game's tunes, and you know what, I don't even care that they almost drown out the voices during certain cutscenes.
It does sadden me to say that I can't recommend the game, despite all the fun times I've had with it. (Stop staring forlornly at me, you blasted thumbs-up! It's not your fault, but Sonic Adventure 2's had its chance!) It just doesn't claim the accessibility or polish that I would need to, in reasonable intellectual honesty, suggest to a friend who isn't experienced with the Sonic series' odd physics and gameplay style. Even I don't enjoy the Tails/Eggman levels much. So, while there is a lot I appreciate and would entreat the adventurous (no pun intended) consumer to try, I have to give it a "no" for the general public.

I recommend this game if you get it during a sale, because I don't think there is enough to make it worth 20 dollars.
BUT it does several things right for a zombie/survival/multiplayer/horror game.
It is SUPER IMMERSIVE. They went with a minimalist heads up display letting you focus more on the environment. The detail to sound is amazing. There will be footsteps, zombie growls, and eerie music that plays ever so quietly.
Next, this game is really fun with friends, mostly Hunted mode, but also maybe extracted. The rest of the gamemodes are not really worth bothering with. Hunted mode definately makes this game. The maps are big and detailed creating enough space for 12 people to scavenge for a bit of time without encountering each other, and for people to hide from everything deadly. The games are always intense, but can sometimes be frustrating when you are the first picked off.
Now finally, the horror aspect is done really well, though I'm not sure it was intentionally done this way. While zombies are theoretically scary, and the environment and setting are unsettling, the game actually poses a real threat for you to fear. In hunted mode, when you die you don't respawn, so its horrifying everytime you encounter another human (or a zombie, because you never know if they are a real player with an intelligence level high enough to kill you) So an unsettling environment and a real threat combine to create an effect that can actually scare you. It's best when played at night while your senses are dull and you can poop your pants in an instant.
Overall fun game, my piece of toast.

I got Melody's Escape around 3 months after it went into early access, and I ended up writing a rather haphazard and not very serious review. So, now that it's out of early access, how does the complete product fare, and is it worth $10?
The answer: Yes!
This is probably one of the most addictive music games I've played, helped by its simple gameplay, charming graphical style, and high quality music detection. I have no idea how the devs did it, but this accuracy is really damn good. There are hiccups on a few songs, but it was never the entire song in my experience.
The control accuracy is really good too, something vital to a game that requires precision. It felt like my fault when I missed an orb or an obstacle, as opposed to bad control accuracy.
There are also a lot of cool skins and visual mods on the workshop, and the game even gives you the template to make your own skins. Lots of fun ones to add to your list, lots of RWBY and MLP:EqG.
However, the game does have its flaws. The orbs can be a bit blurry depending on how fast they go by, though the devs have taken steps to fix that since well before the full release by redoing the orbs a bit so they're easier to see. You also need to have a large music library to get full enjoyment out of this game, though that's a given for a game like this.
My personal main problem with this game is that there are no leaderboards for individual songs. Hopefully this will be rectified in a later patch, because I really want to see how others fare on the songs that I play.
So, if you have ten bucks lying around, a lot of music on your computer, and like simple, easy to grasp gameplay, then this game is for you. I highly recommend it to any rhythm game fan.

I've been with ME since it came into early access around two years ago. There's been ups and theres been downs and this game has changed a lot during this time. But there is one thing that hasn't. This has been one of my favorite games to relax into since it first appeared.
To be honest I didn't think I was going to fall for melody's escape half as hard as I did. I saw it on steam and thought it would be worth a few hours of fun. As you can see by my hours a few turned into a lot.
ME has basic minimalistic visuals meant to stimulate you with popping colors and shifting moods with the music, don't be fooled though in the background it visualizes your music in the sky as an aurora and that can take quite a bit out of the average potato computer. Due to the fast movements and vibrant colors its also prone to screen tearing if your moniter is more than three years old, it refreshes too fast. It may look simple to run but be sure you really are up to specs to play it or you'll kend up with a giant headache!
ME's beat system is one of the best. Almost as good as audiosurf, but in a different genre. It was primarily made for 4/4 beats since thats what the average joe would normally try to play music wise. If you try to confuse it you will just like you can confuse audiosurfs beat detection. For the most part any song that has a strong beat and steady tempo works great, its amazing fun to jump and punch and kick your way through on the beat.
The difficulty is below that of audiosurfs for the most part. This is a game made to relax and enjoy your songs to, not make you rage and scream. The game is fun but most of it is just visualizing your music to pull you into your songs deeper. It's good for a chill out day or just trying to unwind after a hard day, but if you're a hardcore OSU player of audiosurf top ranker you may find this game lacking after a few hours play for challenges. If you go into this game trying to pump yourself up and tensing all your muscles for a keyboard smash fest you will be dissapointed, because thats not what ME is about, and it never was.
I love using this game to listen to new music, it really lets me focus in on things I may never have noticed in the songs before, and it really helps me get into a good mood for whatever I need to do next. Definitely recommend it for anyone who enjoys the little moments to just take a breather.

you do NOT get to choose your room. you do NOT get to choose your map. you do NOT get to choose your side.

all in all the game is NOT worth paying $60 for, but I got my copy for 1/3 of that. it's worth $20, but I wouldn't pay anything more for it.

This is definitely one of my favourite games of 2014. It may confuse people looking at the 2D grafics when I say this game is amazing in every aspect of it. But everything fits nicely: The grafics don't hide information and for me they manage to be detailed enough convey the narrative while giving my enough space for using my own imagination. The UI is simple and easy to use. The sound effects are subtle (which is important, as you are going to hear them way too often when trying to get a perfect rating on a map). And the equipment is surprisingly well balanced, and personally I prefer balance to realism (it is really hard to explain why two .223 rem rifles with 10" barrels, even if one is a long-stroke piston system and one short-stroke, would have so different power levels, but in the game, this makes both interesting). All leads to a very good immersion.
The difficulty level is somewhat self-adjusting, as most maps are easy to finish. But getting 3 stars, using only one plan, no interaction afterwards? That takes more than a lunch break.
It is not perfect yet, there could be some interface improvements when it comes to several troopers breaching the same door (whose tools are used) and a bit more synchronizing for cooperative action. And minor flaws like having female troopers but only a male voice set. And the three campaigns could do with some story texts. But these are trivial things that one will find in AAA productions, too.
From a software developer's perspective: Recently, I backed three games (on Kickstarter and elsewhere).  Two (Wasteland, Jagged Alliance: Flashback) were a huge disappointment. Doorkickers was the only game that managed to continuously improve, seemed to have tight feedback cycles and was thought through from the beginning, so huge features did not come in late and were error-prone. And they polished their product before release. This speaks of a great development process and makes "In the killhouse" a company I would love to work with (if I were a game dev).

The gameplay is pretty solid as far as the combat itself goes. There is a large variety of guns and you can choose to play sneakily or go all guns blazing. Gun and takedown animations are good. The story missions are mostly quite intersting and although the majority of them involve the same thing (that being "kill a bunch of bad guys to get to the end of the level, and get some story progression), they all take place in differing environments, which gives them a little more flavor to distingush themselves. The same cannot be said about the side quests, which are INCREDIBLY repetitive. There are three types of side quests. The "hunt X amount of animal with a given weapon" quest, the "Go stab an enemy with a knife" quest, and the "fetch X amount of these objects for me" quest. These three have been copy pasted around the map. Same goes for the enemy bases, you end up taking them out in basically the same way every time. Luckily though, they're completely optional and are fine to do while you're listening to a podcast or something. Radio towers are boring, frustrating little climbey things that are spread around the map and add no depth whatsoever to the gameplay.
Your "friends" however and most allies with the excpetion maybe being the german guy feel really awkward however and you don't really end up caring about them. The villains are a different story. Both have solid voicework and make for interesting characters, particalrily Vaas. Although, i would have hoped for more backstory being given, but even despite the lack thereof they're still cool and memorable characters. Also really didn't like the main charater's VO. The storyline itself starts off as kind of generic but gets better as you get to know your villains more it becomes more interesting. Any emotional impact is unfortunately taken away thanks to the characters being so boring that you don't care about them or their fate.
Overall though, i would recommend it.

Want to build a small band of bandits and raid caravans for quick cash? Want to build asmall army to kill bandits? Want to become a kind? Mount & Blade throws a shovel at you and shouts "Get to work."
Basically what you put into this game is what you get out of it.  All your hard labors at piecing together a 200+ man army could be completely destroyed at the hand of an enemy, which means you need to play SMART.  Very little can happen at points where you're just travelling to a quest, but the world seems much more alive once you get involved in the rigorous politics and government of the game.  Becoming the vassal of a king's kingdom takes quite a while, but the mods tend to make this approach a little more user friendly than the Native module.
My favorite mods are Gekokujo, Naruto, and the Blood in the West (Lord of the Rings) which I downloaded from
.  For some reason, the subscribed mods in the workshop aren't working for me despite my efforts to locate a solution.  But no matter, it's only slightly less convenient to download my mods from another website, and it's totally worth the wait.
This whole game is worth the wait. It takes days to load the menu, days to travel, days to get anywhere of importance before the rug just gets pulled out from under you.  It's all worth it though, because this game is literally as good as you play it.  Like I said, take the shovel, get to work, and maybe after five hours into developing a character you'll have made something of yourself in a world that feels like a real, complicated, competitive, and interactive experience.

is an uncomplicated, stylish side-scroller that plays as an action-platformer.  Simple to learn, fun to play, aweing to look at: all of the makings of a good game are present.  Beyond that solid foundation,
also boasts its own unique charm that ushers it into an elite echelon within its genre.  It can be quite difficult, though, and may be best enjoyed on a low difficulty just relishing the aesthetics and savoring the experience.

The gorgeous backgrounds and graphic-noir character models combine to create a very atmospheric experience— which is often difficult to achieve in a 2D game.  I personally feel that the aesthetic appeal alone merits a playthrough.  This immersive atmosphere of the game is coupled with a decent - yet minimal - storyline to create a sense of purpose as you progress through the campaign.  Perhaps not the most enthralling fable, but the narrative serves its purpose.
The actual gameplay is pretty simplistic in nature, yet the game itself can be quite challenging in certain parts, especially on the high difficulty.  The controls are not quite as fluid as one may hope, and unfortunately you may die a few times as a direct result.  This isn’t that bad for the average gamer as the checkpoints are frequent; but if you want to go for the “no-deaths” achievement (win in
), you may find this significantly more troublesome.  I found the “normal” difficulty to be perfect and extremely enjoyable; but I admittedly found the
to be not worth enduring for the final achievement.
If you are OK with just enjoying a game for the experience, and don’t need to 100% every game— it’s probably safe for you to assume
isn’t as overwhelmingly and generally difficult as some other people may lead you to believe.  However, if you are someone who wants every last achievement, you may need to be prepared for some frustration.
You should also be aware that
is not very long.  It only lasts about 4-5 hours on the “normal” difficulty.  I found it to be a pleasing length as I felt the game had served its purpose by the end; I enjoyed the experience and was ready to move on.  You will have to decide for yourself if it sounds too short or just right.

Torture by gaming and if you install this then you deserve to be punished for it, just like the developers meant you to be.
It looks great and to begin with you won't have any idea what the criticism is all about.
But then it just goes to pot and what could have been a good zombie scenario platformer turns into a lesson in why you are stupid enough to persist.
The controls are generally unresponsive, there are too many key combinations to remember and use to get past set pieces and while you know what you are supposed to do you will be punished time after time for not getting the key presses done in the correct order and speed.
And that is what you will get - repeating the same sections time after time until you grind your way past them to the next.
After each set piece grind it gets better, lulling you into thinking it is over with some reasonable sections until going back to punishing you again.
You know a game is bad and unfair when your response to being killed is swearing simply because you never stood a chance or that you have had to give up to have a break to see if you can get past that grind set piece the next time you load it up.
Overall, it is something you want to beat to prove it isn't you but actually getting to the end is a punishing chore.
How on Earth it is rated very positive is beyond me and I would suggest reading the other not recommended reviews before purchasing outside of a bundle.
Play it, beat it if you can then put it in the 'never to be played ever again' pile.

Deadlight is a very middle of the road title. I just finished it after playing it on and off for a year (Steam Shame Pile is real life), and I got around 8.5 hours of gameplay out of it. I unlocked Nightmare Mode after I finished, but the truth is, I don't even think I'll bother to play it again.
While the graphics are slick and I appreciate the side-scrolling style, the controls get in the way of your fun on numerous occasions. I lost count of how many times I died because of sticky controls or unclear instructions.
Another annoyance was the game crashing repeatedly on Windows 10. This might be fixed in the future, as it worked fine before I upgraded, but it's something to be aware of. I was sometimes in the middle of trying to shoot a zombie and everything would just crash to the desktop. WTF?
The story is pretty stupid, as well. Trying to follow it is a giant waste of your time. Just skip all the cut scenes (they are crap anyway) and shoot stuff. That's way more fun.
Lastly, the checkpoint system stinks. If you stop playing and come back, you'll get booted back 3-4 checkpoints. It's really frustrating.
If you can get past those cons, the game can be pretty enjoyable. I wouldn't buy it unless it was on a Steam sale, though. $14.99 is too much for this considering the much better games available here with more substance and replayablity.

The comparisons to Left 4 Dead are apt from a basic gameplay perspective.   This game, however, has a lot more depth to it.  The loot system is the most obvious addition and it is done quite well.  The rarity of the weapon doesn't have a major impact on the statistics of the weapon but instead adds 1 to 3 modifiers to the weapon.  You can salvage and fuse items together to try and get higher quality items as well if your luck with the loot rolls doesn't go your way.  The other major difference is the emphasis on melee combat.  Imagine fighting a Tank in L4D with melee weapons.  That's what it's like fighting a Rat Ogre.  The melee system is visceral and quite responsive.  Vemintide also has 5 difficulty settings with the two hardest settings adding friendly fire to your ranged weapons in addition to the hordes of rats being more difficult to kill.  Then on top of that you can make each map a bit harder for better chances at high quality loot by picking up grimoires in the maps that will lower your groups max HP.
Overall a very well made game with a lot of depth and a basic gameplay loop that L4D fans will love.  One of the few Warhammer Fantasy games that is worth your time.

I love this game!
In the 80s, there was a game called Roadwar 2000 for Commodore 64.  You start alone, find some weak and lonely people to join your gang, you train them up, and eventually, you lead a gang across America looking for the cure for the plague that has wiped out mankind, while engaging in strategic combat with armed rabble or militant groups.  Little by little, you make a name for yourself, and take control of towns, and explore.
This is the medieval equivalant for the 21st century!  I love games that don't dictate how you must play, but offer a sandbox.
If you want to play Trogdor and loot and burninate all the villages, you can do that!  You can be a villian!  If you want to play Conan the Conqueror, and fight with a giant axe, and build an army, you can do that!  If you want to play Merida, the horse archer, you can do that!  If you want to play the knight Lancelot, who lances (alot), you can do that!   If you don't want to fight, but want to trade between the warring nations, you can do that!  If you want to set up different enterprises within the cities, you can do that!  If you want to siege castles, you can do that!  If you want to participate in castle tournaments, you can do that!
Are you a first person gamer?  You'll love it!  You can do everything in first person, including walking around the towns, visiting merchants, visiting the locals in the villages, visiting the lords and ladies in the castles, and of course, fighting.
Do you prefer strategy?  You'll love it!  You can sit on your horse on the top of a hill and direct your archers to retreat while ordering your infantry to advance.  You can have allies spread out and hold a position while your cavalry follows you to wipe out their archers.
Do you prefer more RPG interaction?  You can find quests from most NPCs.  Do you prefer less RPG interaction?  You can bypass all of it.
Do you like to mod your games?  There's a large modding community!

If I should describe Deadlight, it might be a "side-scrolling platformer survival shooter game". It could've been a good platformer, could've been a good side-scroller, could've been a good shooter, it could also have been a good survival game. But which one it really is?
Pros:
+ The graphic art is gorgeous, it certainly aged well despite being 3 years old game. I don't think it's gonna feel dated anytime soon.
+ It has some nice soundtracks.
+ The atmosphere feels kinda creepy and gloomy, which really adds up to the whole experience.
+ Very enjoyable gameplay during the first half of the game. A fun platformer with simple puzzles and good amount of survival feel to it.
In-between:
o B-class voice acting, corny dialogue at times.
o The story is not bad, but nothing really distinguish itself from another zombie themed games / movies. There's a little twist at the end of the story, but some of you might find it predictable.
o This game has a lot of "instant death" (e.g. falling platform, spikes, drowning, etc.) which is quite common in platformer games. This could mean "annoying" to some or "challenging" to others.
o Shooting mechanism is nothing special, but does the job well on a controller. (haven't tried using m/k though)
o Platforming is actually kinda fun, but I died many times because of the main character's slow and clunky movement.
o You can't change jump direction in mid-air. I know it's not realistic, but I think it's quite essential for platformers.
Cons:
- The characters are not interesting enough to make you care for them.
- Pacings might feel odd sometimes. There are times where you have to sprint through an area, then do a puzzle in the next area, and sprint again.
- Rat Man's series of boobie-trapped puzzles are unnecessary, annoying and quickly become tedious. Even after you passed the "test" you'll still need to do another series of similar puzzles to get out of the place.
- There are some areas / set pieces where you need to perform series of action EXACTLY how it's meant to, and there are no other way (at all) to progress which added unnecessary difficulities. Miss a split second and you're dead. Probably the easiest way to explain is: "quick-time events" with no prompt.
- After the second half of the game, the "survival feel" is less present and feels more like the enemies has become a part of the puzzle. Sometimes there is no chance of killing / outrunning them all, and like what I've stated in the previous point, you can only do it the way it's meant to.
- Melee combat is awful. You have to perform "execution" in order to kill a zombie, and to do that you need to knock them off their feet first. However, there is no certain amount of how many hit you need to knock them off. Sometimes it took one hit, sometimes it took five.
- Sometimes you have a gun, sometimes you don't. The game decides whether or not you should have a gun for the sake of the game progression.
- Very Short. It says I have 4.6 hours on record, but that .6 hour was spent trying to get the game working (apparently stuck in "preparing to launch Deadlight" loop counted as game time).
The Verdict:
This game has so much wasted potential. IMO, it would be better if this game actually put more focus on one aspect instead of trying to cover everything on it's sight. This game might feel unfair for some people, and those who are not really familiar with side-scrolling platformers will find this game to be extremely frustrating. It's very short, I finished it in 4 hours. If you don't die at all (which is highly unlikely), you could probably beat it in 3 hours. The story ends with unsatisfying conclusion. No rewards for finishing the game and collecting "secrets", except for Nightmare Mode which is basically replaying the same game with the save feature disabled (No, thank you). Having said that, I got this game when it's on sale for $2 and at that price point I think this game is definitely worth it, but probably not more than $5.
I'm kinda torn whether or not to recommend this game. The first half of the game captivated me so much I find it hard to hate this game. In fact, if not for the second half of the game, I would proudly say "I love it". But for the whole experience, I feel like I have a guilty feeling for liking it. Would I recommend it to every gamer I know? Certainly not. However, I would recommend this game to anyone who's really into side-scrollers / platformers, or anyone who haven't played those genre for a while to simply quench their thirst.

2. AI is bad. Really bad. We had virtually no chance of completing the first level on hard due to us being swarmed by the enemies and our two bots couldn't handle for example hiding from the minigun rat and were decimated by him.

Has some degree of potential, but it really just isn't a very good game.  The combat system is pretty poor, and the music is nauseatingly bad.  Resource gathering relies too much on making the resources tedious to gather rather than dangerous or rare.  However, these flaws are not fatal flaws and easy enough to overlook.
Story mode has a very nice map, but limits equipment progression based on missions.  This wouldn't be too bad, but the missions are incredibly boring (think MMO style missions). The world has nice design sensibilities and exploration is a strength, but exploration also is locked behind progression.  Enemy "difficulty" scales very quickly, so if you go off the rails then you can expect to spend way too much time cheesing enemies that can take insane amounts of damage, or getting one-shotted by unavoidable attacks.  If you actually want to explore, you have to complete the tedious missions that will get you the requisite equiptment to survive the new area.
Adventure mode would curcumvent these flaws, if it didn't have its own issues. The terrain generator is lackluster.  The mode is very buggy and occasionally crashes. Performace is even worse than Story mode, which is saying a lot. The ludicrous "difficulty" scaling of enemies combined with the element of randomness in their distribution means that you are unlikely to encounter enemies that match your power level.  It seems that animal spawns were dramatically decreased to mitigate this problem, but that just results in an empty world. Even though you can explore and advance at your own pace, adventure mode is somehow even worse than story mode.
The game does have many good points.  Building is well implemented and the ability to create custom objects borders on revolutionary.  If you could play adventure mode on the story mode map then it might be worth the asking price to some people, but as it stands it really isn't worthwhile at any price.

Door Kickers is a pause and plan RTS with a focus on high energy, high impact tactical gunfights.  You normally control a team of 2-8 SWAT personnel and are charged with eliminating tangoes, defusing bombs, rescuing hostages and all sorts of other goodness.  The planning is intuitive & easy to implement.  It can be done entirely through mouse commands or by using the keyboard to trigger go codes.  Gameplay is fast and lethal - your SWAT wear body armor, but that doesn't mean they won't go down if someone empties a MAC-10 at them or if they step out in front of a shotgun.  As a result, you're constantly planning how best to win the fight before your man is ever in view - distracting the enemies by popping a trooper into view and then flanking them, stunning them with flashbang grenades or whatever other fiendish tricks you manage to pull off.
Enemy A.I. varies from cautious (hunker down and wait) to aggressive (investigate gunfire/other loud sounds) and changes between playings.  Most of the more complex scenarios offer several possible enemy set ups, deemphasizing puzzle-based planning and providing a more organic experience (is that room to the left clear or can it be safely ignored?).  The enemies carry a full range of weapons and can even load up on heavy body armor - there are an unrealistically large number of tangos, but this yields a more satisfying experience and you'll find yourself going along with it.
Moreover, I have been playing Door Kickers since the alpha and, with each new iteration, the game has continued to grow and evole.  The dedication of Killhouse Games to delivering the best product possible has been something to behold and I can say that from personal experience they are very receptive to feedback from the community.   They have worked hard to pack a lot of value into the package - at present there are over seventy single player maps, plus three campaigns, a random scenario generator and an editor to enable users to design their own maps.
The game itself offers a wide variety of experiences, from simple missions that can be knocked out in a few minutes (when you're just looking for a quick release during downtime) to large, complex hostage rescues which require both planning and precision to pull off.
In short, this is one of the best computer game purchases I have made over the last couple years - if any of the above sounds appealing then I highly recommend picking the game up.

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #43 - Deadlight
I'll start by saying I love the art style in Deadlight.  This is definitely the strong point of the game.  The entire game is a 2D side scroller, but the attention to detail is really well done.
Unlike other zombie games I've played, there isn't as much of an emphasis on combat in this game.  It's really more about using your parkour skills to keep finding a way forward.  More often than not I was running from zombies because it's easier to run than to fight.  This changes somewhat when you eventually get a gun, but even then your bullets are limited.
The game plays like an adventure game, where the main character Randall serving as narrator.  You progress through levels, and in between you'll get a little animated comic book sequence that tells more of the overall story.  You can also find pieces of Randall's diary along the way which also fill in gaps in the story.
Don't expect any kind of an open world here.  The gameplay is completely linear.  If you die you'll go back to your last checkpoint.  There's no visual cue as to where the checkpoints are, but there seem to be a lot of them.  I never had to repeat more than a minute or two of gameplay in any of the deaths I had.
In some ways this is a strange game because as a zombie game I wasn't that impressed with it.  As an adventure game the story is okay, but not what I would consider the strong point of the game.  It's the platforming elements where the game stood out for me, which I was not expecting going in to this.
I'm a little lukewarm about paying the full $15 for it, so I'd recommend maybe waiting for this to go on sale.  As it happens right now it's 75% off, so for just under $4 it's definitely worth picking up.  Regardless of the price, I had fun with the game and really enjoyed the art, so I can recommend it based on these strengths.

Edited Review:  The game will seem fun the first 10 hours when everyone is on an equal playing field...so any review pre 10 hours of play or pre level 3 reached is a review to be taken very lightly.
After 54 hours of play you will see that you have made some progress but not much...and with that progress you will unlock new items...however those items will be too expensive to use as the cost to upkeep them will outweigh the amount of credits you make.  Right there is a deal breaker for me and the grind just wasn't enjoyable.
Now lets say those issues didn't exist...what is the game like.  It is an average fps at best.  I like the WWII genre but when damage types don't reflect historical accuracy it kind of kills the WWII vibe.  I'm not gonna go into detail here becaues I don't really care enough. The game is free so try it if you want...you certainly will only lose time.
It is very buggy which is expected from a beta.  Their changelogs never show what they changed and there is lots of secret nerfing going on.  One day your weapon may do a certain dmg and the next day it doesn't.  The community is very divided over the above issue...there is a handful of players who really beleive all is well...perhaps that ones who invested in it.
When I brought up the issues mentioned above I was told "what gamer doesn't like grinding"...this comes from the fanboy side of the community.  The playerbase is low...id often see the same players in the same games over and over...most of the games you join you will join mid match in games that are already won or lost.  Rarely do you join a match from the beginning.
It has a similar system of World of Tanks but there aren't tiers...everyone is lumped together...so imagine for a moment...if you have played this game...tier 1 tanks playing with tier 9 tanks.  That is Heroes and Generals but with tanks, infantry, and airplanes.
Some nice ideas but it is just awful.  Maybe in a year or two they have things figured out but don't waste your time.  It's free if you want to try it but as a gamer with much experience...this is not a good game.

Minecraft and Alpha Centauri bumped into Skyrim and Spore leaving the over-budget rejects club. They all hooked up and had a weird four-parent-baby and named it Planet Explorers.
But enough about the game, lets talk about me. I have learned SO MUCH from playing Planet Explorers! I thought I needed friends and family and a life and a job and a future, but now I see those are all optional. All I really need is to mine more copper, find all the survivors, investigate the interference, learn more about the natives, help the earthlings and Martians get along peacefully, and always eat before I get a stomach ache because the ingredients for stomach medicine are so rare.
Planet Explorers gameplay is way too fun. I hate to admit it, but they may have finaly made a game that is better than real life. Some of the controls are quirky, and I'm sure that will bother a few at first. For example, RMB is for both moving the camera and stoweing your weapon/tool. So any time you are using your equipment, it gets put away the next time you move the camera. It is most annoying in combat but once you get used to it, it's fine.
The graphics in the game are way over-the-top. I have to run it on 'simple' just to get >10fps. I have an old computer though, so I doubt many people will share that experience. But, even on low graphics, the artwork is quite charming. It doesn't look -bad- until you get to the minimum setting.
The new content creation features are very well thought and add tremendous depth of freedom to the game. You can design almost anything- armors, weapons, tools, vehichles, buildings, etc. Getting your new designs into the game however is another story, as I have not yet been able to figure out how.
Problems- Combat gets interrupted frequently by poorly designed pathfinding and physics interractions. I've watched an animal run circles around a tree trying to get me while I stood still maybe ten paces away. It doesn't happen often, but it is annoying when it does. NPCs will run at trees. They seem to want to get someplace beyond the tree but they can't seem to see it, so they just stick to it and run in place until you chop the tree down. That happens a lot. While fighting, your body will sometimes get tangled up with and enemy's body and you can't do anything until they sepparate. So, you may die a couple times because one monster decided to get freaky with you while the other uses you as a punching bag. That happens way more than it should. In story-mode, you will sometimes encounter invincible enemies. They are invincible because they are part of an event or scene and not supposed to die, but you can't know they are invincible until you try to kill them, at which point they start chasing after you and there is nothing you can do about it, because they are invincible. That is a real pain. The build features (for placing blocks/dirt/etc) has no proper in-game introduction, and unfortunately isn't idiot-proofed. There is a sort of mini-tutorial, but after reviewing it I still had no idea how to use it. I think I am finally figuring most of it out, and now it's fun to use, but it is not intuitively designed. At one point (while trying to build something, though I don't know that is necessarily the cause) the game gave me a 'critical error' and my save-file stopped working, so I had to start the game over.
-YOU MUST SAVE REGULARLY AND USE MULTIPLE SAVE FILES-
Because you may play for two or three days (seriously, not a game for addicts) and then -CRITICAL ERROR- and all your progres is lost.
In conclusion, I happily accept the game's few, though dire flaws, and I'm sure you will as well! =D
And I feel bad about it really, because I bought maybe a dozen games in the steam winter sale and now the rest may never get touched.
