I waited and waited to review this game cause I had really high hopes for it. But after the long awaited 0.9 update I can't help but write this review, so that maybe I can save others from the useless expense that this game is.
It's new year's day and I'm still on a little hangover so i'll just list what i hate as things come to my mind. Forgive possible mistakes :)
- This game is overpriced. Highly overpriced.
- Optimization: this game will fry your GPU even at lowest settings. I don't have a monster GPU (Radeon Dual-x R9 380) but I can run almost every game at high settings without problems. Here, at fastest settings my gpu still works 100% at 78° with fan speed over 50%.
- Fastest settings will make game unplayable since fonts will become unreadable (really?!?)
- Even at fastest settings I'm having random fps drops and stutters.
- Character creator is always the same obvious placeholder, which was there 1 year ago or so.
- Controls are clunky, would best fit for an mmo in my opinion. By the way combat and object interaction are so bad... to gather materials from plants you have to target the ground under the plant, not the plant itself... really?!?
- Bindings are the most unintuitive I've ever seen. Alt+Y to open replicator menu? Really?!? Yes, you can rebind, but seriously?!?
- Updates come at a slow pace and seem to just introduce more bugs. They've changed the UI several times, onlyu to deliver another clunky and unintuitive UI.
- Music. It's nice for the first 5 minutes, After that you'll want to turn it off, since it's the same super-short song playing over and over again.
- A LOT of backtracking, in story mode. At the beginning you won't have a vehicle to ride, but still the first quests need you to go back and forth between points that are miles away from each other. That's boring as hell.
- The game, at least in story mode, never seems to demand that you build anything. What's the point of giving us the possibility of creatingour own guns and armor etc. pixel by pixel if I can just use the blueprints I find? Plus, creating object, as fun as it may seem at the beginning, it's super time coinsuming and I really cannot see myself craft more than a couple objects in an entire playthrough.
- About creating weapons and such: why should dps of a weapon be based on how much material you use to create it? I mean, why should a gun that uses the same barrel (and so the same bullets, I guess) as another one do more damage just because you've put a lot more wood or anything around the barrel?!?
- Monsters: You'll encounter thousands of identical monsters in each area, which makes the world boring and exploration super repetitive. Now I read they've randomized monster size, so you should have a little more diversity but it's just not enough.
Is it enough?
I really can't see this game getting any better, even in a year or so, plus there are a lot of better exploration and survival games that play, look and feel better than this that I really can't see the point of buying it, so beware...
oh and Happy new year to everyone! =) cheers

Doorkickers is a fun, challenging shooting puzzle game with a tactical paintjob and some forgetable RPG elements.
Let me start by saying that Door Kickers is not what I really hoped it to be: a spiritual successor to the Swat line of games. Remember those? They were the counter to most shooting games because you could get the best victory with the fewest shots fired. A careful and well-planned approach was more useful than  running and gunning. Being cautious was almost always better than being fast.
Door kickers has none of that. The goal is generally to kill everyone besides your team that has a gun on the map.
DK isn't a police simulator or even that much of a tactical simulator (for reasons I'll go into below)- it's a puzzle game. But it's fun and I found it delivered plenty. In general DK wants you to complete the mission without losing any of your guys and in the shortest time possible. This usually means killing all suspects but you're also tasked with preventing the execution of hostages and demolition of bombs. Keep in mind not only are the suspects absurdly numerous but they throw grenades at your guys. Yeah.
There are also some extra goals for each mission, like using a single trooper, not pausing, or using only one plan. These are sometimes neat little challenges but other times are frustrating or, sometimes, impossible due to the design of the mission (some impossible challenges have been removed in patches, I suspect more will be later). As I said there's not much cautiousness allowed if you want the full score for a mission. Instead you go in fast and if it doesn't work, just restart and try again. Repeat until you succeed below the time limit. It seems the newly added campaign missions are a little less strict for time.
You can build your squad but there's not much individualism there. You can put backer's names and faces in to personalize a trooper but that's it: no backstories, special skilles, interactions, etc. Fans of Jagged Allience (or to some degree Swat 2) shouldn't expect much here. Troopers advance in 3 skills as they go along but I honestly can't tell much of a difference between an expert and novice trooper.
You can gain your whole squad certain skills\upgrades which are sometimes useful but many are bizarre in that they replicate what should be normal behavior. For example: being able to hold fire when not under threat. Given the micromanagement elsewhere I don't see why it's even an upgrade instead of an inate ability. It's really tiring to be trying to do a stealthy approach and the guy you've armed with a carbine decides to blow away an enemy across the map who has no idea what's going on, thereby alerting everyone. The "skill" in question would also be much more useful if it were a toggle rather than the way it is implemented as a button that must be pressed every time one wants to fire. I'm also not sure how a squad needs to "learn" how to open doors instead of noisily kicking them. I've tried both, and opening a door is easier and more tactically sound!
There are lots of guns and devices. Most are redundent and add little but it's nice to have some variety. Some of the weapon stats are very unrealistic. It seems that a .45 caliber pistol is easily more powerful ('stopping power') than a UMP45, which is basically the very same cartridge in a longer barrel and therefore more velocity. Looking at the stats it might even be more powerful than a assault rifle! It doesn't make any sense and I'm not sure if it's as a 'balance' issue or rule of cool.
There really is no arresting necessary, except for those missions that present unarmed subjects specifically targeted for arrest. Nor is it easy to arrest suspects, as they never voluntarily drop their weapons and the troopers don't give them a chance to do so anyway. The only real way I've found to arrest armed suspects is to tase them and then cuff them while they are disabled. This is a tricky and very risky move when there's more than one suspect around and there's really no reason to do it since putting a bullet through someone leads to the same result.
The enemy AI is pretty dumb. There's a mod to leave dead bodies on the ground instead of having them vanish and I think I know why it is not the default... it looks absurd how many bodies will be lying in the same spot. You'd think once you kill the first 3 guys who walk out a door there would be a change in tactics. That would be a mistake. By all means, keep shooting them as they march out as if they're cattle. The only thing stopping you is the need to occasionally change magazines (from your unlimited supply) and the time ticking away. But on later missions the poor AI is hidden with absolutely STUPID levels of armor for the enemies who, while still dumb, will manage to murder your troopers immediately upon seeing them from 150 yards away.♥♥♥♥♥♥ why don't we hire these criminals? They're vastly better than anything the good guys can do. Plus they never have to reload (had a guy firing a shotgun at me for 2 minutes without pause).
Friendly AI is also robotic (the only thing giving the bad guys a fighting chance in addition to their absurd numbers and lots of access points). You need to micromanage everything if you want to get a good result, to the extent where you need to manually direct the troopers in a 'slicing pie' movement to clear a doorway (otherwise they'll tend to sorta just charge in and promptly get shot). Troopers will respond to being shot... eventually... but that seems to be the only stimulus that will get their attention. They seem to be of two minds as to whether they'll address a threat in an area not specifically designated as 'their' cover zone. Usually this means they'll ignore it if it's important and engage it like flies on♥♥♥♥♥♥if it's NOT important. So if there's two bad guys and one is disco dancing while the other is moving to shoot the hostage, it seems like the troopers go for the dancer. Well, okay, can't blame them for that, but I wish there was a way to designate a target out of several visible.
So if it sounds like I'm negative about this game, it's just because I wanted something a little more like Swat 2. But the game is addictive and if you buy it knowing you're getting a tacticalish puzzle shooter you can have a lot of fun. It's nice to play things out in slow motion and the RT\Pause action works quite well (on single story buildings). Watching the replay afterwards can be fun as it brings everything together. The dev-team seems responsive to the community and there is modding (as well as a mission editor). It strikes me as one of those games that just demands 'one more try' even when you should probably be out mowing the lawn. I believe I paid $15 for the early access and that seems to me to be a good price-point for the game.

An absolutely outstanding experience, I've really never played a game like it before.
Door Kickers is a top down, Real time strategy game unlike any other i have played before. you control a swat team of various size depending on the mission you pick, you can either chose single missions or play a campaign mode which is a set of specific missions with varying objectives that span all game types. Drug Busts, Hostage Rescue, Elimination, arrest warrant. and so on.
You have two ways you can do this, create a plan in the planning phase or just go all out and control the team members in real time (I do not recomend this) The planning is the star of this game, set each individual team members path of movement and direction they are facing, set certain way points such as getting them to hold a certain position until all hostiles in his field of view are dead or getting them to hold a certain position until you give them the go ahead to continue n their pre-planned path.
How well this plan is executed however is dependant on the equipment and upgrades you have unlocked. After each mission you are awarded EXP, how much EXP you are awarded is dependant on how many stars you were rated and how many challenges you completed within the mission.
EXP goes toward levels which span your entire team, each time you level up you ear stars and points, the stars can be spent on new and better gear where as the points are spent in the skill tree to improve your team members proficiency with certain weapons.
the game has classes, at first you just have the "point Man" class but you soon start to unlock the others. Assaulter, Shield, Breacher and Stealth. each one unlocking at a specific milestone. when you first start out you'll most likely spend a lot of time replaying old missions to get used to the mechanics but it's when you've unlocked every class that the game really picks up.
Customizing your team per mission with the classes certain missions may need.
The game comes with a mission creator though the UI in that map creator isn't very helpful, in fact it feels like more of a hinderence, text of items over lap each other to the point where you can't read them and the creator also offers you no help, no explanation on how to use the funtion.
it is a very in depth mission creator when you look at everything you are able to place and control but as i said, it offers you no explanation on how to use these things.
For example i clicked on the "Walls" tool, expecting myself to be able to place walls only for the walls not showing up at all in the test run of the map and since the creator offers you no help, i had no idea why this wasn't happening.
All in all i'd give this ame a 7/10 and that 7 comes from the main game alone, the map creator gets a 0 from me purely because it offers you no help what so ever, like it expects you to know how to use everything without ever having used it before.

Melody's Escape is a musically generated endless runner/platformer/rhythm game with a very simple setup and premise and features a sleek looking little visual package. Completing the package, you plug in your music and the game builds stages around each song's rhythm, and then you play a fairly simple game of DDR/Stepmania/name your music game to make Melody do all sorts of cool things in time with the music.  Ideally...
This is sort of the deal breaker, and where the game may fall apart depending on your taste in music.  The game's rhythm detection algorithm can really only detect very simple and pronounced 4/4 beats. Try throwing anything else at it, and you end up with a spastic spam of icons that are in no way in sync with the music or fun to play whatsoever.  Even detecting 4/4 beats, the generation still seems to vary in how each individual "note" may be off-rhythm.  For being the very core part of the game, this detection and level generation needed to be tighter.
It's a game that can wow you with some fun visuals when everything comes together and matches up to a song, but again, unless you're a fan of very specific types of music, it's probably best to pass this up.

This is my most favorite game of all time.
There aren’t enough tags to describe what this game has to offer. 1st person-3rd person-open world-sandbox-tower defense-base building-crafting-exploration-random gen-massively multiplayer-sci fi-RPG-survival-CO-OP, and much, much more.
But that being said… it needs so much work, and yes, I know it is still in alpha.
The ambition behind this game is incredible. The delivery is amazing. The overall quality… Not so much. Not yet anyhow.
Gathering resources is frustrating and time consuming. It’s almost impossible to dig a hole without having it be massive because where you aim and where you dig is different every hit. The animations make me angry. From swinging a pick to having to stop and kneel to pick up plants and flowers, most take too long and there’s no weight behind them. This makes playing survival or adventure mode very, very time consuming and almost always frustrating.
The game lacks any sort of explanation on how things work and you’ll find yourself either giving up in frustration or scouring the wiki and discussions for answers.
But underneath the very rough exterior is the most amazing and beautiful game I have ever played. The worlds are huge and richly populated with alien animals, monsters, lakes, rivers, oceans, mountains, and caves. Each player in a world gets their own settlement where they spawn, which could be anywhere (even in the middle of the ocean) due to the games randomly generated worlds. You can farm, mine, hunt, build, explore, swim, and battle massive enemies, robots, mutants and monsters. You can build a mansion on a mountain, or a bunker under one. You can fit your base or settlement with turrets and shield generators to help fend off would be attackers.
Seriously, check out some of the all-time popular screenshots in the community hub.
But none of that is where the game shines the brightest.
Everything from buildings, swords, shields, guns, boats, helicopters, jets, and anything with wheels can be built in a voxel editor. Anything that flies, floats, drives, shoots, blocks or swings. If you can think it, you can build it, and use it in the game. What you can create is almost limitless. This is the ultimate sandbox creative game. It just needs A LOT of polish and some time.
I would recommend this game in a second.
If anything you just read peaks your interest. If the video on the store page made your eyebrow raise.
Buy it.
But maybe hold off sinking your teeth in and getting a big bite… Just a little while longer.

Where to start? SA2 is one of my favorite 3D platformers to date. It's not just the nostolgia goggles either, I find myself replaying SA2 all the time because of it's fun gameplay.  A lot of people complain about how this was the downfall of the Sonic franchice, but I disagree. You're able to play as the hero and dark stories,  and both of them are more or less the same concepts with different characters and levels. Sonic and shadow are traditional "gotta go fast" levels, get from point A to point B, avoiding enemies and other hostile objects. Most of the stages are well thought out and genuinely fun to play through.
People seem to hate on Knuckles and Rouge's levels. But I enjoy them. It's basically a hunt for 3 chaos emeralds or keys. You're given an open level to explore and find them. Level design saves this otherwise tedious sounding task. Every level is different and utilizes new physics and actions as you progress.
My least favorite type is the Tails / Eggman levels. You're basically going from point A to B in a big robot walker that can shoot lasers. It's not really that bad, and these are more puzzle solving levels, but sometimes these levels drag on for a little too long.
Raising Chao are fun, but it's not nessisarry unless you want to 100% the game or get achivements.
The presentation is all awesome, the soundtrack is absolutely wonderful. Especially the Knuckles stage rap music. The lyrics are a bit silly, but the beats are downright fresh to death. The visuals are colorful and attractive, and the art design fits well (besides the humans in the game, they just seem out of place.)
SA2 is a much more polished version of SA1. They are both fun games, but I prefer to play SA2. This game is also in HD, which is rad.
Now for a little critisim:
1. The story is kinda lame. Go figure, it's about a blue hedgehog.
2. The voice acting is cheeeeeesey. It's not game ruining, it's actually quite funny and you'll get more than a few laughs.
3. Like SA1, this game has it's share of glitches, some more frustrating than others, but not as many as SA1.
4. Beating the game itself isn't that difficult, but getting all the emblems is almost torture.

One of my favourite games ever. The story is cheesy, with terrble but lovable voice acting and a somehow heartwarming final chapter. Essentially, Dr Eggman releases a super powerful weapon that his grandfather built years before, known as the ultimate life form - Shadow the hedgehog. Shadow tells eggman that as a reward for rescuing him, he will tell him of a way to achieve world domination. Shadow shows eggman to ARK - A space Colony that was abandoned when Eggmans Grandfather was arrested, and the place where shadow was made. On the ark is a weapon of mass destruction, the eclipse canon, which can blow up pretty much any planet when it has all 7 chaos emeralds. Rouge The Bat, a thief appears and agrees to help them find the emeralds. Sonic on the other hand is getting chased by the police, who somehow think the famous blue hedgehog hero guy is suddenly black.
Enough about the story, the main gameplay has 3 varietys, Sonic and Shadow have the speedy platforming levels. you have a spindash, you grind rails, get some great powerups, these are by far the best and momst interesting levels in the game. Next are the Treasure hunt levels, featuring knuckles and rouge. I personally enjoy these, the characters are fast, have good attacks, the levels are designed creatively, and knuckles music is usually pretty great, if incredibly cheesy. Finally, there are the worst levels in the game - Mech levels, in which you are Eggman or Tails, piloting a mech and shooting things. these levels aren't terrible, however until you get the jet booster (It lets you hover after a jump, to make platforming more accurate) they can be disgusting and offputting.
My least favourite level in the game is the 3rd level on the dark side, Sand Ocean. You're eggman, doing tricky platforming with moving platforms and stuff, it's very dark, the music sucks and you don't have the booster, making platforming horrendously tedius. To make matters worse, you're surrounded by quick sand, so missing a jump will result in death.
The game has quite a few bosses, some better than others. The standard GUN robots are easy and I wouldn't call them good bossfights. The last eggman/tails bossfight is challenging, the last 2 bosses of the game are pretty great, the second last being really difficult, the Last sonic v shadow fight is alright, it doesn't make it explicitly clear what you have to do though, so get creative. The game does have a bossrush mode, so Bosses are readily replayable. I wouldn't call this game hard, it's pretty easy to pick up and play, though it does have  maybe 2 partially difficult levels and a difficult bossfight, nothing you can't overcome
After the main gameplay is the Chao garden, you raise a chao as a pet. Take it from me, I've owned this game on 4 other systems, the Chao garden is just the best thing ever. So much charm, so much fun, so much personilisation. For those who wonder what I mean, try giving nothing but birds to a chao, and make sonic give it them. Within a few hours, it'll turn pink and grow jesters like a NiGHT character, Give it just tigers and It'll turn green and eventually blue, and grow sonic spines (Do it with shadow and it'll be black with red) This is just a few of the things you can make.
The music is just fantastic, Jun Senoue is back with more great music, alongside many other artists. The games main theme is 'Live and Learn' A great hard rock ballad, The pop rock 'Escape from the city' By Ted Poley accompanies Sonics first level, with a fantastic bassline. All of knuckles levels feature cheesy raps, but they aren't as bad as everyone says (A ghost tried to approach me and got married) Shadow has as Techno theme in his levels, Even if you aren't buying this game you should definately look up the soundtrack, in true SEGA/Sonic Team fashion the music is truely brilliant. Buy ths game.

This game is the textbook definition of "mixed" feelings (IN MY OPINION). Plot: its okay for the most part but there are a couple of things that, while not TOO important, could have gave depth to some characters but weren't fleshed out enough. Sonic/Shadow Gameplay: REALLY FUN! The only levels that i liked the least was Final Rush & Final Chase, if only because of the over abundance of rail grinding. Overall though, i had a lot of fun with these stages. Control was fluid & the level design was great. Tails/Dr Eggman Gameplay: Meh. Not a huge fun but Dr Eggmans stages, especially Cosmic Wall, were a lot of fun. Tails though has poor level design and was not fun to play as. Control was pretty stiff too. Knuckles/Rouge Gameplay: I dont know what to say, to have a good time with these levels you have to be patient alot of times. Although the control is great, you might have to be patient to get full enjoyment from these levels. I didn't mind them. Boss fights: Pretty easy in my opinion. Even the Biolizard and the Finalhazard were easy despite what people have said. Music: Great, but Adventure has a better soundtrack though (IN MY OPINION). The only music that i found REALLY memorable were, Live & Learn (DUH!), City Escape And Pumpkin Hill. I have a guilty pleasure for Pumpkin Hill and City Escape and Live & Learn are iconic. Voice acting:Okay, the voice acting in this game can mostly be good although there are moments where you will laugh at the delivery of some lines, Eggman "LET'S GET TO WOOOORKK!!!!" Overall: Sonic Adventure 2 has not aged as well as Sonic Adventure (which baffles me!) but for £5.99 (99p including the Battle dlc), it is recommended even if some of the mech stages (especially Tails's stages) can be poor in design and Knuckles and Rouges stages can require you to be very patient at times. Despite some of the negative things about this game, you should give it a go and hey, you may even like it! Score: I don't do scores as it makes the reader actually READ the stupid REVIEW!

For a game that has been in Beta for 2 years, its a bit awkward to play sometimes, but I can honestly say that this game has some promises in a RTS-style gameplay. This game just needs to properly update the bullets and fair gameplay in some ways. For example, the tanks are like mobile explosive sniper rifles in terms of accuracy as the bullet is unaffected by gravity or accuracy in any way. This makes them unusally unrealistic and sometimes incapable of properly hiding behind walls of a building with plenty of holes to kill an entire infantry by hitting the right place with an explosive shot on the cieling. In other ways, the community can sometimes be good, or they can be outright jerks. They can also use the friendly fire feature to kill the right amount of allies without having punishment while also insulting other players in a rude manner for no reason. As realistic as this can be for certain Germans in WWII, this can also be annoyingly handicapped in multiple ways since the reporting feature only happens with friendly fire. Some players won't bother to hit the report button, so you might as well hope that they are not in your next game.
As for the good sides, I can openly say that I am looking forward to future updates. There is only Russian, German, and US. The Russians are given an armor-piercing sniper rifle for their lack of a vehicle weaponry. The Germans are given superior vehicle fire power in exchange for their lack of... popularity? The US are given pretty much the standard gear with a Stuart being the superior armor in a tank fight for some reason and a Thompson that can pretty much be called the standard room cleaning gun with spray and fair RPM to assist the lack of aiming speed. In other words, I have had a fair time with some interesting experiences, and you will always encounter players who have no plan in desperate techniques. If you truly want to win a game, the best bet is having a plan and play it like a real RTS as a team. You are more capable than any individual NPC in a normal RTS, which means you have the advantage to be the hero. You must use your wits, help and follow your teamates, and work together to solve the hunt of the most dangerous game of all... a sentient human soldier aiming their sights at you. Failure to work together will result in your downfall. Failure to have a contingency plan will result in your downfall. Failure to outsmart the enemy will result in your downfall. How will you play? Will you die a hero? Or lead a team together as the General? It is up to you comrades.

Door Kickers: 6/10
Door Kickers is an interesting concept -- one that's been done before, but not as often as people hope. The cult classic Rainbow Six 3: Raven Shield being the quintessential example of this type of game, Door Kickers takes a similar approach in trying to create an atmosphere of tactical tension, albeit with a bit of levity involved in the presentation. In recent years, we've also seen the well-made Breach & Clear released, which was an underappreciated game that took the Rainbow Six formula, made it purely top-down, and focused the action in on three-second pseudo-realtime moments.
So, there is quite an audience for this type of game built in already -- many people love this type of tactical action for two reasons; as games, they provide a thrill unlike any other. This isn't Call of Duty, where rasberry jam will be smeared all over your character's face if you improperly clear a room: if you fail to properly check your corners, your character will die, and this creates a sheer tension towards entering and moving through buildings in any properly executed Tactical game. A second reason is more of a gritty tactical feel -- it's not really the thrill of playing a game, but the thrill of using real tactics, real equipment, and truly mastering these raids until you can defeat most levels on the first try. Rainbow Six leaned towards the latter. Breach & Clear aimed towards the former. Door Kickers gets stuck somewhere in the middle.
As a game, Door Kickers has a very 'hotshot' atmosphere. The achievements, menu tips, and even the interface all make it out as a Call of Duty-esque experience that challenges you to play. The gameplay can either be taken very tactically and slowly,  or in a more brash realtime mode where squaddies will just follow your mouse as long as you hold and drag them around. Neither of these modes works perfectly. For example; as a game, the gameplay quickly falls apart when you realize just how rote and routine winning each level becomes. Going back to Breach & Clear, each level was interesting enough, but sweeping rooms was really only half the battle. Using your items and abilities intelligently was really what carried you forwards. In Door Kickers, using items effectively is useful, but nonessential. Setting up intelligent fire zones and sweeping a room carefully will let you beat every single level in the game with the basic Assault class.
And speaking more towards classes, the RPG elements of Door Kickers are not as deep as those presented in other games. If you're going to put a character progression system into a game, it has to feel like your characters are progressing. Let me explain: XCom: Enemy Unknown is a perfect example. In the earliest parts of the game, your recruits are pathetic. They can't shoot, they can't hit anything, and they have no useful abilities. They'll get slaughtered. However, as you play more and more, you really begin to bond with them; you create little vignettes in your head of everything they've done as soldiers, and you see them come to life with powerful abilities and interesting weapons. You thrill at their victories, and gasp at their failures. In Breach & Clear, this also happens; you create a squad of soldiers and deploy them for the entire game, slowly levelling them to the point of creating a cohesive crack team of unique and varied soldiers. Door Kickers really just expediates this process to the point where it's completely pointless. I had a maximum-level squad within the first five hours of gameplay, and none of my squad members really stood out. The small stat increases they receive are fairly pointless, and it's really their loadout that affects things more than their actual skill. Furthermore, you can just swap all of them between classes at will, so there's no real reason to specialize anyone. You gain a lot of tactical freedom, but lose all of the characters and personality that could've been developed here.
So, Door Kickers isn't really a perfect game -- it's not too challenging, nor is it really relatable. So, is it, at least, tactical? To a degree, I would say it is, but in a very frustrating way. As aforementioned, it works as a room clearing simulator. Entering a room is interesting and fun, and you begin to pick up some actual tactical acumen as you play through the game. But then, you begin to suddenly realize what a dearth of options there really are in the game. You, of course, have five classes.
Pointman - which becomes entirely useless about twenty minutes into the game,
Assault - Which is the only class you really need to win every map,
Breacher - Which is a nice class to have, but becomes a short-ranged assault about three hours into the game,
Shield - Which is slow moving, doesn't do much damage, and is incredibly situational, and finally
Stealth - Which is very similar to Assault, but completely superfluous and is preferable in only a few tiny instances.
Now, the thing you may have noticed is that all of these classes seem to just bleed into the Assault class towards the end; the shield is, perhaps, the only one that remains entirely unique, and it's so rarely useable that it becomes like a health potion in a roleplaying game. You look at it, sigh, and say to yourself, "Maybe next time. I should save it." Furthermore, the inventories on all of the classes are almost entirely identical. Taking a game like Rainbow Six into account, you could arm any individual soldier with eight categories of weapons, each of which had twenty weapons, and several ammunition subtypes -- and that's not even getting into the modification system. In this game, each class has about 16 weapons available, and no modification system to speak of. As far as items go, the game is at a loss as well; this is a game about breaching and clearing rooms, so where the hell are the doorjams? Where are the fragmentation grenades? Where are the smoke grenades? Heartbeat sensors? Instead, you have some very basic options in the form of:
Flashbangs - The most useful item in the game.
Stingers - Very situational, not recommended.
Breaching Charges - Situational, but you need something to pad your inventory.
Lockpicks - Situational.
Hammer - Situational
Snakecam - Mandatory.
And a few others. Out of all of these, the three most useful ones are automatically equipped on the characters at the start of the game, making it pretty basic to load your troops out.
So, then you get into the tactical meat of the game, and you become inundanted in a complete nightmare of artificial stupidity. The game makes a point to challenge you to use one plan to clear the entire building from the start of the match -- this is standard. Rainbow Six 1-3 were based on this concept of planning, and the planning room in this game is a pretty close recreation of what those games had. The only issue comes with the AI; both friendly and hostile. Your own troops are, for the most part, somewhat intelligent, but have moments of immense stupidity that make you want to throw your keyboard across the room. Your men start approaching a door, 2x2 cover formation. The door opens -- they quickly blow away the mook with an AK on the other side, and..
They completely freeze in place. Why? Because I had them set to lockpick that door that he just blew open. The soldiers can't understand that the door isn't there, so they just stand and patiently wait. This is all well and fine when you have four guys stacked up, but when one soldier tries to pick the lock and a guy with a pistol opens the door, that soldier will just freeze, completely nonresponsive for minutes on end as the enemy tries to blow through his heavy body armor with the equivalent of an airsoft gun.
I'd type more, but I have to cut this short; the game is buggy, unfair, and pretty shallow, but it's the closest a game has gotten to the old Rainbow Six feel. If you like those games, get it. You won't regret it.

Melody's Escape is a side scrolling rhythm game. Melody herself will continuously run to the right as orbs and obstacles come towards her which requires corresponding buttons to be pressed in order to pass them.
The game itself comes with a handful of tracks itself, but the main feature of the game is that it can create levels based on your own music, which can be accessed by directly finding the files via the in-game file explorer, or alternatively you can drag files onto the game window itself to play them.
As the game relies on the algorithms to create levels, your experience with the game will be based on the genres of music you listen to, where clearer melodies will create much smoother levels. However, the algorithms are quite good, I've been able to play a variety of genres without much issues, such as Pop, EDM, Power Metal, Stoner Metal and Rock. The game will also often tell you how confident it is in the level creation.
The difficulty of the game, is very dependent on the setting you choose. There are 4 premade difficulty settings available, "Relaxing" is the easiest and it only uses one button at a time, Medium is the standard 4 button control scheme (W, A, S, D on a keyboard or Y, X, B, A / Triangle, Square, Circle, X for controller), "Intense" is mentioned as the full experience where you use the standard buttons for orbs but directional buttons for obstacles and finally there is "Overload" which is the standard buttons for orbs but requires both directional and standard buttons for obstacles in the same direction.
As you increase the difficulty, the tempo of the levels increase as does the variety in buttons required among other things. Luckily, there's a custom difficulty option that allows you to tailor your experience with options such as tempo, control schemes (Including a more difficult option where obstacles require differing directions for the obstacles and more varied buttons for orbs are used), grace periods and error margins. This both allows you to play a harder game if you desire but also lets you learn the more challenging controls at an easier tempo (I used it to progress from Intense difficulty up to Overload difficulty by using the Overload control scheme but at Intense tempo. I will also likely use it to progress into the most challenging control scheme once I'm confident enough)
All in all, the game is quite fun, it has a lot of customisation over difficulty to make a good place to learn rhythm games (Though, it doesn't appear to get to the mashy levels that many other rhythm games such as Guitar Hero or Project Diva get to) and due to it using your own music files, gaining new content is a simple as downloading (Or importing from a CD if you're old fashioned like me) new songs to play.
My only nit picks with the game are that the in-game file explorer can be a bit clunky at times (It also doesn't detect everything. I have some albums that it doesn't seem to find at all, but at least there's the option to drag them into the game manually) and that the favourite list doesn't seem to have a "Shuffle" function when using the "Play All" option, meaning that playing songs in a different order would require refavouriting everything each time.
Its a fun game, Looks nice and character customability which is a bonus

Competent, if ultimately dull Left 4 Dead clone. Might be a thing with a few months longer in the oven, but in it's current form, is largely unremarkable.
+ Makes great use of the Games Workshop source material.
+ Engine is pretty, and runs well enough maxed.
+ Tonnes of graphical settings to tweak.
+ Superwide screen support.
+ Framerate limiter in engine, without needing to use vsync.
+ Excels as a co-op game on harder difficulties, (if you don't mind extremely simplistic combat.)
- Is mind numbingly dull on difficulties appropriate to solo play.
- AI companions regularly freeze when faced with various mobs, will stand next to you when you need saving and let you die.
- Little to no over-arching story in the early stages.
- Level design is uninspired, often tedious to traverse.
- Horrid, horrid headbob that is motion sickness inducing for even the most seasoned of FPS players.
- FOV scaling produces insane fisheye unless you play in 21:9 resolutions.
Nice effort, but even at the lower asking price, offers little bang for buck.
Left 4 Rats

Pros-
-Levels feel like actual locations instead of linear paths.
-Cheesy yet appropriate voice acting complete with silly fake racism.
-Every weapon (so far) feels different and handles differently.  This gives loot a feeling of variety instead of just straight stat increases.
-Hacking into Skaven feels satisfying.
-It's challanging enough to ensure you'll lose but never really feels unfair.
-Proves that video games are the only media that you can straight up rip off what you took all your ideas from (L4D) yet still produce a really good game worthy of praise.
-Like weapons, characters feel unique and fill out their roles in different ways.  Even two builds of the same character can play out differently.  An elf with poison arrows might excell at clearing clusters of skaven while one with a long bow will more easily pick off specialist/armored rats.
Cons-
-The loot system itself is more punishing then rewarding.  Chances are you'll be getting the same white items over and over.
-Inconsistant framerates.  No this isn't my PC. Will be running perfectly fine then drop to 20 FPS, then 10 then shoot up to above 60 to "compensate" I suppose then go back to normal.
-Ranged weapons like pistols don't have the same feeling of impact as melee and other ranged weaponry.   Leaves them feeling that they lack feedback.
-Playing without a full team of players isn't viable. The AI is literally the most useless thing I've seen in a modern game.
-Sometimes waiting for a full team to assemble in the tavern can take awhile.  Expect to spend a lot more time then you'd want to shooting random crap inside the tavern.
-Buggy.  When I first wrote this I had not personally encountered any bugs but have since had my entire system crashed by the game.  Not just the game crash but my entire computer.  Very disappointing.

This is a pretty good game.  It's a bit on the repetitive side, but the overall concept is pretty awesome.
I'll go so far as to say that this is almost exactly what I've been looking for in a game for a long time.  I get the opportunity to level up my character, I can recruit an army, and I can level up each individual member of my army as well.  I can conquor towns and villiages, and I can upgrade them, too.  The problem is, it does all of these awesome things, but it doesn't do any of them particulary well.
The levelling is pretty lackluster.  At the beginning, it is made up for considerably because I get to level up so many people.  However, after a few levels, the realization begins to set in that there is nothing new to see here.
Even so, this game would probably have kept me entertained for much longer hours if the questing system wasn't so bland.  The problem is, it can be sometimes difficult to find a quest.  Then, even once a quest is found, there are only about a dozen or so different types of quests in the game.  Doing the same quests over and over again gets tedious.  Fighting the same battles over and over again is tiresome.
Overall, this game feels like a "Total War" franchise meets the Elder Scrolls franchise.  You just have to strip out about 90% of the stuff that makes each of those franchises feel cool to get to the final product.
After all of this negative talk, I am still recommending the game.  Why?  Because I feel it is one of the freshest ideas to hit the gaming market in quite some time.  The play controls are actually very polished.  It does have a moderate learning curve, and some of the play, inclusing some of the quests, are not very intuitive.  I logged over 30 hours before the monotony of the questing system started to drag me down.  The way I look at it, if I can get over 30 hours of game play for less than $20, that's a pretty good deal.  I must emphasize that the game did start out pretty awesome.  All it would have really taken to get me to have logged a good 30 more hours is a better levelling system.  Overall, I give it about a 6.5 out of 10.

I have a few hours in this game now, enough to say that I can write a review.
Firstly if you are into visceral melee combat in a game, this is your game. There are points where you are swamped by so many Skaven (Rat men to the non initiated) that swiping your attack through the heads of many is as enjoyable combat can get in any game.
While many play this sort of genre because they like zombies, and I forsee some not liking it because they are rats (My fiancé is a LFD2 fan 1500+ hours) but for anyone who just loves the play style then you will love this game.
Graphics: The graphics are modern, dark, dirty, medievalesque with a high attention to detail. The immersion brought on by the graphics is superb. Walking around a corner and seeing a Skaven shadow cast on the floor as it's creeping over the roof above you, to only be skewed by a teammates arrow as his head appears over the ridge, I have an asus gaming laptop and this game runs exceptionally smoothly at 1080 ultra wide with everything up to high, no slow down at all.
Sound: The voice acting is the most shining star in this the audiophiles torrent of sound. Each character, each script is perfectly chosen. The skaven themselves taunt you, talk amongst themselves when they think they are alone, and the ominous tone of the Skaven attack bell is enough to send a weight into the pit of your stomach.
Gameplay: Apart from the obvious afore mentioned viscaral combat, and what seems to be exceptionally balanced items. The gameplay is a good mix of horde/tank/scavenger gameplay with some interesting things into the mix. One of these things are that there are multiple paths and plenty of hidden areas to explore as you race through the map. Stay in place too long however unique rats, assasins, ratling gun skaven, packmasters, globe throwers are there to attack you at random. But these special rats are NOTHING when compared to the Rat Ogre. This brute can be agroed with ranged weapons with ease, however his blows are nothing short of untankable almost all the time. In harder difficulties these special Skaven can wipe your team in second. However for me, the sound I dread is the marching, clanking formation of the elite Skaven pack rats. Their high HP, high damage if allowed to surround your team will annhilate you faster than you can regroup.
One last thing. Expect to fail if you go alone with bots they can't cut it with only one real person in the team. Also expect to fail in your first couple of runs unless you are carried by your team. This game is over 10 years old. It's hard to believe it. This was a favorite from back during the dreamcast era.
So this game is a PC port of the re-released HD version for Xbox 360 and PS3. The port isn't really an HD remake. The textures are the same and cannot be upscaled. Anisotropic filtering? Nah. Higher resolution textures? Forget about it. Increase draw distance to remove annoying pop in? Nope. On release this game also had an issue with running the game in hyperspeed but has since been fixed thankfully.
Ignore the story, it's pretty dumb. 14 year old me loved it but I'm 26 now and yeah. XD
This game plays in three distinct modes, so I guess you can call it something like a 3 in one platformer or something.
Sonic/Shadow is sort of like a racing game with platforming. The physics feel very floaty, like somewhere between moon gravity and earth gravity when on the ground. This lends itself to some fun chaining with homing attacks and some rather impressive tricks for hitting perfectly timed shortcuts. The camera is sometimes your enemy as it swings wildly from side to side. This is easily the best part of the game.
Tails/Dr. Robotnik gameplay is a battle mech robot with lock on targeting for firing missles. The gravity in this game mode is very heavy, as if you were a planet twice as big as earth. There are some very boring slow platforming sections. The high weight and gravity on your character can become frustrating when you're rushing to platform but the robot can only jump 2 inches off the ground. You get points based on chaining your missle lock on. Again the camera is not your friend. This feels like filler.
Knuckles/Rouge gameplay is a treasure hunt style where you have to collect three of an object hidden in the stage. It uses the same physics from the Sonic/Shadow stages and is based on exploration. The aim is to find the items in the fastest way possible without any hints. The last two big zones are the best. Some of these stages can become tiresom when you just can't figure out where the last item is. It's alright but it's not for everyone.
So yeah this game plays like an old game. It released in 2001. It's now 2014. Hard to believe so much time has gone by. For sonic fans, def pick it up. For everyone else, pick it up on a sale and try it out. It's not bad and you'll get to laugh at the dumbest plots only an old video game can give you.
Oh. And I love the soundtrack of this game. I enjoy all the vocal tracks including the cheesy rap songs for Knuckles' stages.

Door Kickers is a top down tactical, turn based SWAT-style game.  The game also
allows for mods, and they provide the tools for player to generate new levels,
adding to the already large amount of content the game contains and encouraging
replay-ability.  Each level includes stars to encourage proficient play, as well
as challenges for the missions, which also encourages players to replay levels
to try for better scores.
The UI is basic click and drag, as you position your SWAT team members in each
mission to try to immobilize the enemy.  You cannot plan too far ahead, however,
as the enemies randomize their patrol routes and pathing.  The game
also utilizes
the restart function well, so that you can learn from mistakes and correct them.
Weapons have a skill set, and individual players have skill sets as well, which
gives the players a chance to customize the game to their preference.  The
different player abilities as well as the variety of weapons and their customi-
zation are very well balanced.
The abundance of variety in this game take away from any linear feel, as well as
the randomization of the enemies.  The game is very just, and at no time did I
feel like my time was wasted.  This game does everything that it set out to very
well.  I enjoyed my time playing this game, and can easily recommend it.

This is a great example of a game that was imperfect but had promise, and the developers have slowly began to deliver on that promise. It's a great game to try for those who enjoyed games like L4D or Payday but are looking for something new or different. While the game plays a lot more like L4D it's got a loot system comparable to Payday 2.
The problem to begin with was that the loot system was horribly punishing, where basically if you didn't play at the highest difficulties the loot you were likely to get was garbage. On top of that you were more likely to win the lottery than get a weapon you wanted or that was even viable. That however is mostly in the past, and while the game can still be rather punishing they have added a lot more conrols you can use to fine tune or upgrade loot as well as quests and contracts that reward more varied play so the game doesn't get so repetitive and feel so pointless even at the lowish levels.
The game and it's gameplay have also greatly improved, it runs a lot smoother than at launch and with a few fewer bugs. It's not perfect, and since last update I've noticed a dip in performance (had to bring my settings down to high). It definitely requires at least a upper midrange computer to play. The traits and trinkets can be incredibly confusing and might require some research. Even still, the developers have left some mechanics frustratingly mysterious which can be pretty bad in a game that punishes minor mistakes and details.
Personally after playing for a while and getting a good kit I'd say the game is most enjoyable at the hard difficulty, mainly because you don't have to worry about friendly fire which can make the game a lot more fun especially as the Bright Wizard. You also don't get quite all the frustrating try hards as much since most people grind for gear on the nightmare difficulty.
As for the DLC I'd say after you've played the game a bit and are certain it's your kind of game I'd grab the dwarf and vampire stuff. The levels are pretty good, and you can even try them if you find someone to invite you to a game who owns the pack. The new weapons are also pretty fun to play around with. The last stand game mode though isn't really necessary and kind of should have been in the base game. I'd skip it unless that really appeals to you.

The price point is too high, but this game does a great job of recreating the tense, twitchy situations of Zombie Panic. The atmosphere and sound is good at setting the dark tone, and the combat takes a more realistic approach, requiring precise aim and manual reloading. Playing a survivor is fun: scavenging for weapons, barricading a house, avoiding the undead and taking a few of them out silently, then sneaking up on a fellow survivor and executing them for their sniper rifle and vantage point is satisfying. Playing as a zombie is frustrating, but it is about as good as it can be. Player zombies have slightly better manueverability and the ability control the horde.
There are three main modes: extraction, escape, and hunted. Hunted is the true gem. It is a PvP game mode where everyone starts off in a random spot with a few supplies, and the only rule is to be the last one left alive. I always try to forge an uneasy alliance with whoever is around me early on, each of us knowing that if things go our way then eventually one of us has to die. Large gunfights attract zombies, and any players who die become a fresh walker ready to head straight back for the camping point they just died at. It can get very tense, especially while hiding in a closet with a revolver pointed at the door while gunshots, broken windows and screams echo around you.
Extraction is a co-op mode has you going from house to house and searching for survivors, then fending off waves of zombies as you lead them to safety. It's fun and challenging because each person is limited in what they can carry and do. If a person is barricading they cannot shoot, and it is useless to have a sniper and shotgun at the same time. The AI survivors however, are useless and will die without protection, even with a gun. The maps also last way too long, and most people will not make it to the end.
Escape is an objective based co-op mode that isn't really all that enjoyable. As you work your way through various obstacles and puzzles, anyone who dies becomes a zombie. In the beginning it is too easy as there are only a few zombies to deal with. The difficulty either stays that way because everyone works together, or it falls apart because too many people die and overwhelm the survivors. The puzzles are okay but using a smart phone to check objectives and locations of keys isn't really that fun.

At face value, this game had potential despite the mediocre writing and voice acting. But it's the controls that ruin it completely. Every action you take is delayed - from running and jumping to swinging a weapon and shooting. When it comes to action sequences/events that have to be timed correctly, it's a nightmare. An exercise is dying over and over because the controls won't respond. Jumping is so poorly designed. You can jump straight up like a middle aged man wearing ankle weights, or you can leap like a cheetah diagonally. Nothing inbetween. Oh are you 6 inches away from being squarely underneath a ladder? Nope, you can't grab onto it yet. You need to walk, stop, then jump straight up again. Otherwise you'll jump 15 feet away from the damn thing if you happen to press a direction while jumping. Sound was also missing from all cutscenes, and random textures fail to load throughout the levels.

But when we started MEDIUM difficulty, EVERYTHING changed. The seemingly limited moves helped fuel the struggle to complete the variety of commands being thrown at you. Make sure to check SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS and some reviews. The game requires a solid 60FPS for best synchronization. I had no issues running it with v-sync, but some may need to turn on some sort of Adaptive V-sync if frames drop below 60.

Developed by the Belgium devs from Icetesy, "Melody's Escape" comes with a premise to offer a fun game that generates platformer levels using any music (or audio file) you have on your PC. Supporting formats like MP3, OGG, WMA, FLAC, iTunes®, and even some video files, this game can read almost any track.
But where "Melody's Escape" stands above other procedural rhythm games like Audiosurf, Riff Racer or even Crypt of the NecroDancer? The audio detection algorithms of this game are based on notes/vocals detection, instead of beat detection, like the other games previously mentioned. Music compass plays a big role here too. While the levels synchronize perfectly with a tempo of 4/4, it goes great too with tunes far from the traditional, like Dream Theater and Soundgarden.
Above all things mentioned, “Melody’s Escape” is a joy to play. Yes, the gameplay it’s pretty simple: just run to the music track and try to beat your own score (no leaderboards included), but it’s also fun as hell. You can easily lose track of time playing this game, and there’s always a new song to try and some neat surprises I won’t spoil to you.
For a better experience and to avoid eye strain and headaches that some people experience, remember to turn off the blur and zoom out the playfield (75% instead of 100% is perfect), on the options menu. Have fun!

A truly great game.
This game is great because :
- It is free-roaming. You can explore to the edge of the world from the start of the game.
- It is hack and slash game. The combat is typical, but great enough. There are a lot of weapons, such as swords, shields, bows, crossbows, throwing axes, throwing knives, etc.
- It has a great modding communities. You could play using a Medieval Europe mod, or some AGOT Mod, or some fantasy-setting with elves mods. Some less-intrusive mods such as better troop system is also available.
- The graphics are acceptable, and no lags in major battles.
- Your character, while in individual basis is superior due to your skill, will require your troops support to win the battle, so it won't be like you could kill 1,000+ of troops in one sitting without getting a scratch.
- A limited economic simulator in the campaign map, where cities/villages/forts could change their wealth based on the actions of players and NPC.
- The NPC characters do something (though sometimes it is not very smart). All NPC will gather troops, patrol their own fiefs, conduct diplomacy, join tournaments, getting married, etc. In war enemies NPC will besiege your towns, loot your villages, etc. The NPC is more livable than most games.
- A lot of side activities : tournaments, feasting, marriage.
- Lots of skills to be trained on : tracking, path-finding, foraging, etc.
Downside :
- Lack of story. But you don't need story.
- Lack of mission variety. Most mission only encompass of kill X or escort Y. Some are do interesting, but not very much variety.
A great game that should be bought.

Your experience with Far Cry 3 will depend on whether you're a completionist or not. If you're not, Far Cry 3 is an awesome game. The story and the characters (especially the villains) are among the best i've seen. The gameplay is nothing that you haven't seen, but it gets the job more than done. There's upgrades via skill trees, crafting to get more space for items, and a real sense of progression. You'll explore 2 islands, the first being mostly jungle with mountains and the second being mostly plains and classic forest. The combat works, but 1 or 2 more enemy types would be welcome. Driving is also okay. There's a few minigames, and poker is very well animated. You'll feel that you're really playing in a real table. The soundtrack is decent, and the graphics good on PC. The optimization is decent. So, if you play the story and don't focus on many extra activities, the game is a great experience. However, completing this game to 100% is a chore unfortunately. Developed by the Belgium devs from Icetesy, "Melody's Escape" comes with a premise to offer a fun game that generates platformer levels using any music (or audio file) you have on your PC. Supporting formats like MP3, OGG, WMA, FLAC, iTunes®, and even some video files, this game can read almost any track.
But where "Melody's Escape" stands above other procedural rhythm games like Audiosurf, Riff Racer or even Crypt of the NecroDancer? The audio detection algorithms of this game are based on notes/vocals detection, instead of beat detection, like the other games previously mentioned. Music compass plays a big role here too. While the levels synchronize perfectly with a tempo of 4/4, it goes great too with tunes far from the traditional, like Dream Theater and Soundgarden.
Above all things mentioned, “Melody’s Escape” is a joy to play. Yes, the gameplay it’s pretty simple: just run to the music track and try to beat your own score (no leaderboards included), but it’s also fun as hell. You can easily lose track of time playing this game, and there’s always a new song to try and some neat surprises I won’t spoil to you.
For a better experience and to avoid eye strain and headaches that some people experience, remember to turn off the blur and zoom out the playfield (75% instead of 100% is perfect), on the options menu. Have fun!
:
*Plays well with keyboard and controller
*Can read almost any audio and video track
*Satisfying gameplay
*Steam Workshop support for skins and color schemes
*You can make it relaxed or tense as you want - 4 difficulty levels
:
*No leaderboards
*No multiplayer (would be a blast if this had co-op)

I have played Melody's Escape for a few hours now, and feel it is a fine rhythm game. It took some getting used to as the controls feel a little counter intuitive (the icon having me press right to vault over a wall, then changing to a different direction for the same obstacle), you learn to focus on the icons themselves for direction. This is disappointing, really, since it takes attention from the visuals, which are the selling point of the game for me. This game does a fine job melding visualization and game play, but since you are so focused on the button mashing, you don't appreciate the view. The casual setting is too easy, however, and leaves me wanting balance.
If it were possible, I would like to see leaderboards. I would like to know if I am the master of a particular song, a feature in Audiosurf that extends its play value.
I think, overall, I received value for my money, and will continue to play it again when I have a few minutes to kill.

So . . . this is a tough one for me. I'm NOT a twitch gamer. I thought the idea of being able to mash buttons in time to my own music was a cool idea and the graphics and art style of Melody's Escape speak to me. That said, I enjoy . . . harder music. Not death or speed metal (or really metal at all), but more of the post-hardcore, Vans Warped Tour band list variety. And herein lies my dilemna.
The game itself is fun and pretty to look at, in it's minimalistic way. But, with my own music imported, something feels . . . off.  I don't understand the reasoning (or even the rhythm) behind when I am to hit, tap, hold, etc the buttons for my songs.  It feels random, and worse so: off-beat.  Now, I understand that this is likely largely in part due to my music selections. But, that's what I want to play.
When I tap on beat to the song and I get offsync somehow with "error" or "too late" messages, I get a little frustrated. (BTW, I've been a drummer for over 25 years so I'm perfectly capable of keeping time). I know it's a game, and ultimately the score doesn't really matter, but to me - this does.
So, in conclusion, I enjoy the game in small doses, but until I get the feeling of actually playing my music (instead of a random level kinda-sorta timed to my music in parts, possibly . . . maybe . . .) I cannot recommend it.  At least not at full price.

Open ended sandbox, storyline exploration crafting game. Build a base, populate and grow it.  Make weapons, vehicles etc.  Explore the world and search for resources such as ores and plants that are found in certain terrains, then use them to craft everything you need based on schematics you earn or buy from npc's.
What it does right, it does very right.  What it does wrong, is horrifically bad.
You can craft almost anything you can imagine.  Guns, vehicles, buildings, etc.  You make them.  All of them.  There are very few premades available in the game so you must make what you want or find the plans another player made.  If you are creative, you can make almost anything.  If you aren't and don't find other players plans, you shouldn't bother with this game.  A year ago, there were numerous ISO's for everything you could imagine, but now there are very few since updates have broken previous ISO's and creators stopped making and updating them.
Vehicles include cars, bikes, planes, helicopters, boats, submarines, etc.  They all share one thing in common.  Movement with them sucks.  Real bad.  Helicopters can't seem to fly above the trees and that would be fine if they didn't get stuck on the trees if you hit one.  The ground is so uneven that any ground transport bounces all over the place and hits everything in sight, or just flat out gets destroyed from bouncing and hitting the ground constantly.  Turning vehicles is not as easy as you would think and often times hitting an object, backing up turning, then turning more going forward still results in you hitting the exact same object.  Vehicles can get stuck on the ground, on the plants, on rocks, etc.  Most areas of the map are actually faster to walk through than attempt to use a vehicle.  Drive into anything and your vehicle gets damaged.  Park near a predator and they will attack your vehicle until it is destroyed or they die.  Fly a helicopter into a flying creature you didn't see because of lag and who knows, maybe it stalls and you drop to the ground and die while your helicopter blows up into pieces and leaves you stranded there.
The map is a limited use abstract with very little details but does allow fast movement between discovered points.  The scanner map shows you more of the terrain, but is very difficult to decipher if you are looking for ore and quickly becomes useless if you are digging into a ore vein since it clutters up rapidly.
Lighting is almost useless since personal lights point directly forward with no means to use them to light up areas above, below or to the side of the character.
NPC ai is getting better but followers still get stuck on terrain sometimes and can easily be lost when you are crossing a long distance.
Combat is very basic with melee attack only or manually shooting a weapon.
Most quests are easily completed but some hunting quests give you only a name of a creature that is useless if you haven't been playing long enough to figure out what the different creatures are.  Some creatures for hunting quests are also difficult to find since they can be very rare creatures or travel around a lot.
Updates are fairly slow in coming, but progress has been significant in the last year.   Crashes still happen fairly often but autosave keeps you from losing more than a couple minutes of progress so they are a minor problem.
Overall, the potential for this game is great, but it does need more work to be really enjoyable.  Mostly the vehicle controls and ground smoothing hamper the game at this point.  When it takes forever to walk from known areas to new mission areas, it gets tedious fast when you know a vehicle would be faster, but are so not worth the trouble to use.

UPDATE:  Well after 1 year, I am eagerly awaiting full release of PE, and Grav, well, I stopped playing that last year.  Toxic community and not much depth.  PE is still amazing and even better now.
I don't know about the other reviews, the game is being very actively developed, just check the log.  There is a new beta release about monthly.   It's also Early access, bugs are to be expected and then you give feedback.  I see so many early access reviews complaining about bugs.
Pretty awesome game and it's still in early access.  I also got Grav around the same time and both games are fun but each is different in big ways.  I had debated on which one to get for a while but in the end I got both thanks to my brother and his generosity.
Both game are beautiful with  bright and varied environments.  This will not be a review of Grav, I'll just briefly touch on some of the main differences.
Planet Explorers Story mode is the single player mode.  It has NPCs, missions and a story line.  I've only been playing Grav solo because the free weekend seems to have brought some griefers into the multiplayer servers and I wasn't about to deal with that, so I can't speak too much to the public multiplay, though I did set up a server for a friend and me to play.  Grav's single player is more just about exploration, but there are some tasks that you get some rewards for.
The story in Planet Explorers is pretty in depth so far.  You'll meet a lot of NPCs, with a lot of missions and rewards.  The biggest difference is with the crafting systems.  Planet Explorers is insanely cool when it comes to this.  In Grav you're working with about 10 resources that you'll need to craft pre-designed items, such as a jetpack or monocycle.  You'll have different workbenches for creating different items.  Planet Explorers has a lot more resources for creating things.  And then you'll create a few things to create bigger things, and then there is a custom editor built into the game for designing weapons, cars, planes, etc...There is no pre-made car, you have to build the wheels, cockpit, engine, fuel cell and then build it and export it into your world.  For example when I had to build a car for a mission, I needed wood and rubber for the wheels, steel, iron and motherboard for the enginer, and to make that motherboard I needed plastic and copper wiring.  This may sound tedious, but it isn't because you can click on a component in the crafting window and it will then open that component so you can click on the ingredients and make them and traverse the heirarchy that way.  It's VERY easy to quickly make components and see which components will create which parts.  You then go into the ISO editor (the name for a custom creation is ISO), which is like a modeler if you're familiar with 3D Modeling.  You'll place the 4 wheels, cockpit, engine, fuelcell and then build your car however you want.  If you google Planet Explorer ISOs you'll find websites devoted to models that you can download and play with.  There are turrets and lots of guns, it's amazing what people have done with this.
Grav has been fun so far, it's a different game.. and Planet Explorers is amazing and fun too.
TL;DR: Planet Explorers is amazing because you can create a lot of custom content very easily using many parts and resources.  The story mode is very indepth.

I can sum this up real quick for you as Zombie Prince of Persia. Prince of Zombies? Zombies of Seattle? Also, I mean the old Apple II one.
Deadlight is a 3D side-scrolling platformer with the same precise yet tanky controls from two decades ago. There's running and jumping and turning in place and stopping on a dime, and God help you if you flub a jump. You play Randall, a gravelly survivor of the zombie apocalypse who wishes he had half the gravitas as Bill. You must guide him as he mantles up and over the thousand fences, crates, and fire escapes of Seattle in search of his three survivor buddies and maybe his family? I dunno, I was too busy wrestling the terrible combat controls.
Melee in this game is awful, as it only functions a certain distance from your character. Any closer and you harmlessly shove enemies away instead of whacking them. It makes mobs of zombies a proper death sentence, but in a game like this where it's easy to miss one running jump and land in a pit of undead, it can get frustrating fast. The gun is more effective but your ammo is rather limited and headshots are a must. I tended to do a lot more running from fights, which the game seems to support and often expects anyway.
Do not buy into this one for the story, for it is terrible. The characters are incredibly one-dimensional and the writing is bad to the point of nonsense in some places. It is a pretty game however, in that lovingly-rendered hellscape sort of way. There's a lot of detail in the environments (so much so that it can obscure your path at times), and plenty of little collectibles hidden in out-of-the-way spots or obvious deathtraps. Looks to be about a 5-6 hour game, quicker if you don't bother looking for goodies. Decent playtime for the price, but the rough edges lead me to suggest a sale purchase if at all.
If you thought Prince of Persia needed a modern reboot with zombies and bad combat, by all means give it a try.

Deadlight is an interesting little 2D Side scrolling, Zombie Survival game, where you solve puzzles, overcome obstacles, and try not to get overwhelmed by zombies. You can pick up melee weapons as well as ranged for protection, but avoiding a fight is preferrable if you want to survive. You have to manage not only health, but stamina as well, and can find power-ups along the way to help you out. There are also hidden items on the different levels you can collect. By doing this you unlock players diary entries, as well as other goodies and easter eggs.
I've played a lot of different 2D side scrollers over the years and this one visually looks nice, but the puzzles are overly simple and could have been more complex. It is still fun to play regardless, and should be given a try if it's on sale or part of a bundle.

-the zombies are actually menacing and very dangerous (in part, sadly, due to the awkward controls)
-decent plot with a good ending section: there's also an alternative ending- unlocked by beating the atrocious Nightmare mode- that gives you a different take on the events of the game, I recommend you look it up on Youtube once you've finished the game
-controls are sometimes unresponsive or extremely finicky, grappling a ledge or a ladder won't work properly unless you're positioned exactly right next to it, sometimes it'll take a split second too long to actually start jumping or running- due to delay in controls- and this'd easily spell your doom
-combat is so-so as firearms work well enough but melee combat is overly random: sometimes you'll decapitate or trip a zombie with a single hit while other fights see you bashing their heads repeatedly with little to no effect before getting overwhelmed and eaten
-some levels delve into trial and error affairs requiring you to memorize the whole sequence while also hoping the controls won't let you down: this isn't fun and can get frustrating
-Nightmare mode, where the game saves only at the beginning of each Act, is an asinine proposition considering you can often die due to unresponsive controls
-some assorted bugs due to it being a lazy port such as framerate drops, the game hanging and sometimes crashing while trying to access the start menu etc...some of those can be solved through workarounds posted on the forums but it's unacceptable nonetheless
-pretty short and linear, no real replay value
Deadlight does as many things right as it does wrong...the unresponsive and sometimes buggy controls, paired with some overly difficult sections, can really get in the way of your fun: this gets very clear during the second half of the game, with a few acts sporting truly annoying scenes where a single mistake or bug in the controls will see you die. Thankfully there's always a checkpoint near so you won't be losing much progress and it's not as bad as some reviews make it out to be, even though I'm not really into the genre I managed to get through said sections in a few tries.
While dodgy controls in a platformer are an unforgivable sin the game does manage to pull itself through thanks to a story that, while surely full of survival/ zombie cliches, is quite engaging and features a few twists to keep you interested. There's also a great atmosphere to be found in the game's bleak graphics, Seattle is truly a zombie infested ruin with abandoned vehicles, crumbling walls and corpses everywhere. Last but not least Randall was an enjoyable character to control with a strong voice acting and an interesting take on things through both its thoughts and diary pages.
Deadlight is a decent game overall if you can be patient with its obvious shortcomings and I feel it's worth a playthrough for any zombie fan: do not buy at full price though since it's simply not worth that much, wait for the big sales where it's under the 2$ mark.
