Once in a while the task of putting together a video review for a title is such a pain… mostly because you have to stop playing the game you’re really enjoying. I love Vermintide. This game came out of nowhere and has just truly impressed me.
Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide was developed by Fatshark, best known for Lead and Gold, War of the Roses, and Krater. Without a doubt, this is their finest product yet and one of my favorite games this year.
Vermintide shares a ton of similarities to Left 4 Dead (a formula I’m a little surprised hasn’t been emulated much). It’s a four player cooperative experience where you and a your team need to get from point A to B while fending off hordes of monsters. This time (thankfully), it’s not roaming herds of zombies. It’s giant rat men.
There are a total of five characters to choose from, each representing their own distinct class. The Dwarf Ranger and the Empire Soldier are primarily built as tank classes. The Elven Waywatcher and the Bright Wizard deal out heavy damage from from away. And the Witch Hunter falls somewhere in the middle, he can play as a ranged class or as a primarily melee class. But since it’s Warhammer, everyone carries ranged weapons to compliment their melee weapons. The game finds a great balance between the two styles of fighting for every character and the best players will know and when is ideal to quickly switch between the two
As you finish maps, you roll the dice to get new gear, and every piece of gear can drastically change how each character plays. There are opportunities to obtain more dice in each map to increase your chances of getting better loot. A sword and shield will play much differently than a two handed hammer or a one handed mace. There are a variety of bows with a range of special effects. The Bright Wizard can go from crowd control to dealing pure pain. And special weapons have traits that can be unlocked through the games simple crafting system. Increased range, reduced stamina cost, health vamping, and more. The higher level you are, you are likely to come across and develop more and more complex loot that will help in the brutally tough levels of the game. The loot in this game is what will keep players coming back for more.
But the loot isn’t the only draw. The world and map design is stunning. It’s just beautiful. The game doesn’t hold your hand either (thankfully). Finding your way to the end of a new map is a big part of the fun. The maps are all unique to one another, ranging from creepy graveyard ruins, to the outdoors, to vacated city streets, to a twisted MC Escher-esque wizard tower. The world feels like it was once lived in, but abandoned because of the catastrophe.
There’s a good number of maps, but also a great challenge to go along with them. Each map can be set either as easy, normal, hard, nightmare and cataclysm.
Most importantly, it’s fun. The realm of video games is in staggeringly short supply of enjoyable and challenging cooperative experiences. And though this is is heavily inspired by Left 4 Dead, in many ways it exceeds it.
There are a few elements that irk me a little. A couple maps, particularly the ones where you have to gather scattered supplies and bring them back to a central location, feel imbalanced to me. Even set on normal difficulty, these maps can quickly wipe a moderately experienced team.
Twice in my twenty hours of playing the game, I’ve had servers reset… or something. All of the players will stay in the game, but the map would restart and we’d all be playing as a different character than the one we selected. Really weird.
When playing with 2 people or more, the NPC bots do a great job of holding their own. Unfortunately, I found when playing solo, they tend to do some really stupid things, like getting stuck in the environment… or jumping off of buildings… and then the rest will jump off of buildings to save their buddies. I hope they get a little patch.
And finally, the game does NOT feature any competitive multiplayer like Left 4 Dead. I personally never enjoyed the competitive play in Left 4 Dead, but I know that might be a dealbreaker for some.
I’ve had a few different friends ask me about the game, if you only fight against rodents of unusual size. Yes, giant rats of various shapes and classes are the only enemy. If that sours the experience for some, I have to say the action and excitement far outweigh any minor issues I had with the game’s choice of enemies.
The developers have made promises for some DLC for the game and NO microtransactions. With a universe as rich as the Warhammer series, I’m hoping to see some greenskins, or maybe even some space marines action.
If you’re a PC owner, Vermintide is a must-own, especially at its budget price of $30. It’s just pure fun, cooperative arcade action set in a wonderful world.

Hotline Miami 2 picks up right after Hotline Miami 1 with difficulty, Hotline Miami 1 ended with the grade at 11, this game ends it at 27. If you got enough out of killing people you should move on, but if your bloodlust is still rising, this game will please you. There's more blood coming out of the enemies, there's more windows, more large black men to rush you, but fewer "masks". In this game, you don't use masks, you have different characters. There are The Fans, who are all different (Corey can dodge-roll, Tony has killing fists but can't pick up weapons, Alex & Ash are chainsaw and gun using sister & brother, Mark has two sub-machine-guns), there's Ethan who is completely non-lethal and unloads guns when he picks them up, and refuses to carry sharp weapons. There is The Son who is just like The Fans but without Alex & Ash. There's a Russian Hitman who you play as for 1 mission who doesn't do anything other than start with a silenced pistol. You also play as Richter, the rat in the first game who
.
The level design is a bit weird, for some reason they decided that putting windows ON EVERY ♥♥♥♥ING WALL was a good idea, once you see a dude through a window you have a split-second to shoot first, before he shoots you or rushes to your position. Also, in this game the dogs are EVIL.
The story... Oh boy the story. It continues on from HM1 a bit, but some actually take place before HM1,

Great "simple" tacticool title, albeit with some minor scuffs.
The game mechanics are VERY easy to learn, yet surprisingly complex, so you can easily get into the game quickly, but will be working for a LONG time to master the game. And yes, this is one of those games where you will WANT to 3 star a level. So, while the levels themselves aren't super diverse(some are, but most aren't), you will want to keep re-attempting them for that perfect run(ala R6).
The game definitely has some small issues still though, but ALL of these could be patched easily:
* still hard to properly orient your guys throughout the process. Yes, there are "two" modes of look direction(strafe + body facing), but the game doesn't seem to always follow what you have selected(sometimes you'll find your guys walking backwards into a room...)
* still issues with "overlapping" unit movement and proper selection. ie: if unit A and unit B are traveling close together...it's VERY hard to select A and orient him; oftentimes the game will make it hard to select A or B, so I would recommend a way to "dim" or outright remove other unit pathing temporarily during the setup process to avoid this
* randomness(a good thing and a bad thing): there are times when you'll just do the SIMPLEST layout(with no facing setup) and it will be flawless...other times you'll put lots of effort into a perfect run...only to see your "elite" soldier stand in a doorway and eat a magazine dump...
* some of the weapon options/classes are kind of pointless. Outside of a maybe 1-2 missions...there just isn't any use for the shield class. Same thing for weapons: there are a couple that are CLEAR standouts in their grouping...and you'll be using them 99% of the time...so yea...sucks for the rest of them
* "silent" mode is still buggy. Too many times you'll have your guys barge into a room and not fire, even when hostages/team members are in immediate danger, all the while...you have to press the "fire" button to give them permission(or at least override their behavior). Sometimes they work right, sometimes they don't. Kinda weird. Some kind of ROE options would be nice here or another planning option to let them override silent mode for a specific walk
* $20 price point is IMO a little steep for what it offers. The devs are awesome and they have been consistent with updates so far, so it's worth rewarding them for the time I've put into it. For a new player, I'd think $15 would be more the sweetspot(check out Steam sales later in the year).
tl;dr: The game boils down to attempting to perfect missions, ala R6. The base mechanics are easy enough to learn, but you will spend a fair amount of time retrying missions until things click together.

(Updated March 2016) No, Planet Explorers is NOT dead. It is still being updated with large substancial patches and currently aims to be released in 2016.
Yes, it took a long time since PE reached Greenlight in 2013, but game development simply does take a lot of work and time, especially when we're talking about such a large and refined (optionally) quest-driven sandbox-game with so many - nearly endless - possibilities (change the beautiful world with it's different biomes to your liking, craft all kinds of stuff from tiny decorations over equipment and vehicles to large buildings with the creation-system, keep up your comfort-level to stay healthy, hunt the naturally behaving awesome-looking animals, defeat giant boss-mobs for quests, defend NPCs and your own fully powered-up SF-colony with turrets, discover weird alien structures, scan and dig for ore, play the mainquest or try free survival on procedurally generated worlds...
Too many players being impatient and completely ignorant of all warnings about what Early Access means have created a bad reputation for the whole Early Access system. Sadly Planet Explorers is one of these games that have been slandered because of EA and some players even said that Panthea had "abandoned" this game, while in reality they have regularly kept on updating it.
In my personal opinion, Planet Explorers - even in its current state - is already the best of all games I've ever played.
* it features large, beautiful, variated and imaginative non-blocky 3D-game-worlds with different biomes and interesting flora. There's one predefined gameworld for the "campaign"-mode, plus procedurally generated worlds that players can create with different settings to choose from
* even better - these worlds are populated by fantastic creatures (six-leggers like in Martian Dreams!) endemic to each biome, behaving "naturally" - meaning herds sticking together while roaming the regions, carnivores hunting herbivores in packs, animals sleeping at night, flocks of birds flying off when getting close, etc. - plus giant boss-mobs too (you juast have to love the whale-like Ostrov Sharks)
* on the "campaign"-world you can discover awesomely weird looking alien ruins, dams, highways, great walls and camps with hand-made alien buildings
* in the campaign you can interact with a decent number of unique NPCs, each with their own personality and background-story - and of course quests, ranging from subquests (fetch me x herbs) to really large main quests (defend a camp with turrets, defeat giant robots/mobs, learn to grow plants, establish a whole colony with different powered structures)
* by now you can play PE both (or alternating) in first person and third person mode btw.
* you can build extremely large structures like bridges, walls and buildings etremely quickly directly into the game-world with the smootest gameplay mechanics ever. You can save your structures and then copy more of them into the world too - however logically you will need to collect all the necessary materials beforehand
* additional to that PE features an awesome creation-system that allows you to create, save, copy and share tons of stuff - all of the equipmant and vehicles you can build will even have certain stats and such will have a gameplay-impact within the game, depending on the materials it's been made of and it's shape. You can design every kind of object from tiny to large, from simple tableware and decoration items to furniture and streetlamps to large buildings.
* with the usual ingame-crafting-menu (replicator) you can craft a wide range of pre-set equipment and other stuff too without having to design it specifically. Most of these have a really nice and unique SF-look
* after prospecting/scanning for ores you can dig an infinite number of mineshafts and tunnels into the world. Well, you can even shovel away whole mountains if you're in the mood to do so
* building defensive walls and different turrets will help you with battling larger enemies, and you will need this after setting up a colony, because there will be irregular invasions, during which native creatures will try to get to the power core of the colony to shut it down
* you cannot only craft many different vehicles (also flying ones) in the creator-menu, but you can even build a refined monorail-system across your gameworld. You can dive into deep underwater caves with or without a wetsuit and you can fly by using a wingsuit or later on also jetpacks
* the campaign-mode features an RPG-like story with quests and a down-to-earth background-story that is unveiled bit by bit. While it might not be to everyone's taste, I personally like it
* there's a minecraft-like free creative/builder-mode with an infinite amount of all materials to freely build and craft with
* the third game-mode is a survival-mode for adventurers, featuring an optional skill-unlock-system on randomly generated game-worlds sprinkled with NPC- and alien-settlements and optional small quests - set your own goals there without the RPG-story taking you by the hand
* you can ask NPCs to live in your colony and defend the colony (together with your turrets) both in campaign-mode and also in adventure-mode
* lately a comfort-level and illnesses have been added to the game, together with medicine to cure your character that you can brew or buy from NPCs. So now it is advised to sleep regularly and not to get soaked in the rain for too long. And digging for seeds (that you can plant) in animal dung might have an affect on your character's health as well...
* there are multiplayer-options too now, so you can invite other players to your server or join them on theirs
* the performance on my 64bit Windows 7 prof. is totally alright, no problems with the FPS here. I very, very rarely experienced freezes or quest-bugs. No problems with the sound and also nearly none with the graphics. However the game might not run as smoothly on every existing system, and I still experienced frequent crashes after playing for a longer while in early 2016.

+ Solid mechanics. Simple and intuitive. Deadlight reminds me of classic platformers like Prince of Persia and Flashback. I do not understand reviewer complaints about control responsiveness.
+ Beautiful art direction. The game looks appropriately dank and gritty. The cutscenes are done in a limited animation graphic novel style which looks gorgeous and fits the world perfectly. Hugely amospheric.
+ An appropriately understated, mostly ambient soundtrack. Occasionally rises to greatness.
= Voice acting that ranges from acceptable to cheesy. (The bad dialogue doesn't help.)
= Very short.
- Truly terrible writing. Within the game itself, it's bearable. The unlockable diary entries are jaw-droppingly amateurish for such a high-quality game, including the occasional grammatical mistake. I was not surprised to learn Tequila Works is not a natively English-speaking developer. A weak translation might be to blame for some but not all of the issues. The plot itself is derivative in the extreme, though it does contain a few high points.
- Somewhat buggy. Some minor bugs, like specific death sounds playing after reloads instead of when you die, dialogue not playing after pausing and unpausing, and sound not playing during specific cutscenes. Some more serious ones, like puzzles not properly resetting after death. (Thankfully, being able to restart sections stops this from being game-breaking.)
TD;DR: It's short, but you'll probably enjoy it while it lasts. Recommended if it's on sale, you like zombie games with great visuals, and you enjoyed classic platformers like Prince of Persia or its gameplay clones. You'll have to overlook the poor writing and the flat characters.

First off, the story is a mixed bag of feelings. But it did leave me wanting more at the end. Oh, and if you're not going to be completing most of the side-quests, this game is extremely short. I finished virtually everything in the game (other than gathering some useless loot) in under 20 hours, and that's with a decent amount of dying involved.
However, the gameplay is fantastic and holds up easily in this day and age. Play as a sniper or a gung-ho machine gun toting maniac, it gives you the freedom to decide how you want to fight. THAT BEING SAID, it is rather unbalanced when it comes to completing certain sections of the game. For instance, stealth takedowns of outposts give ridiculously more XP to level up with than a standard, shoot-everyone takeover. It's like the game is forcing you to choose stealth over a more manly approach. At other times, being a stealth-based character can get you screwed as your abilities and weapons will be borderline useless. Try using that Sniper rifle and Bow in close-quarters combat, or when the whole island and their moms know where you are and are coming to kill you. Also, you can learn literally every skill in the game. What's the point in making choices, then?
It is still a ridiculously enjoyable shooter that you can burn through pretty quickly, before moving on. Definitely play this.

Rating - 76/100
Recommendation - Campaign makes Michael Bay look like Woody Allen
Disclaimer: I have zero interest in the multiplayer campaign. This review specifically covers the single player campaign, and is specifically FOR people who only want the single player campaign. There's co-op horde mode too, apparently, but I haven't gotten to try it yet. Oh, also, fair warning: Default FoV is VERY narrow, and is only changeable in multiplayer (which doesn't carry over).
Call of Duty is often at the center of video game controversy, and you would be hard-pressed to find any other series that can elicit such strong reactions from people. Reviews are usually either 10/10 or 0/10, and you will likely have friends groan at you if you claim to be a fan. There are no series other than sports that get pumped out with such regularity, and with so few innovations from game to game. It seems like sales of one game haven't even gotten a chance to cool off yet before another new one is announced. By all outward appearances, this is a terrible terrible series.
You know what, though? I have a soft spot in my heart for Call of Duty. It's a big dumb oaf of a series that you just can't help but smile at. It's very much a Hollywood Summer blockbuster movie, with non-stop action and explosions from the outset, getting your blood pumping while you're in the moment, and then making you go "...what was that?" when you're done.
Case in point, Ghosts. I played through the entire campaign in 5 hours (with very minimal repeating of sections), and was in a town that was getting bombed, then in space, then back in the bombed town, then on a military base, then scuba diving, then on a ship, then driving a tank, then doing bombing runs in an airship, then in space again, then fighting on an inverted high-speed train. While all that is going on, I was switching back and forth between past and present, and controlling probably 5 different characters (or at least it felt like it). The plot and action literally do not stop to even take a breath. How can you not love that!??
You should know what to expect when you're looking at a CoD game, and this one delivers.
I'm not fully up to speed on all the Call of Duty games' campaigns, but I have played a decent number of them, and this is one of the best if you're looking for a shallow, explosion-fueled adrenaline rush. If you want to feel like John Rambo, John McClane, and John Woo somehow had a baby whose life is being directed by Michael Bay, then look no further.
The graphics won't win any awards, but they're good and well-optimized (60fps at 4k maxed with a 980), sound design is solid, the gunplay is as good as ever, and there are tons of little one-and-done gadgets you get to play with throughout. If you're just here to hate all over Call of Duty, then downvote and move on, but if you're looking for some mindless action, I highly recommend this one.

UPDATE TO THE UPDATE: I've just passed 100 hours in the game. Still pretty much a lot of fun. The developers have announced they are working on new updates expected before the end of the year to include an enhanced editor and more gameplay modes. So even if you aren't interested right now, put it on your wishlist and it might be on an upcoming Steam Sale.
UPDATE: I'm posting a short update to this review. I've just passed eighty(80) hours in the game. The developers have released two updates, adding some new features and fixing some small bugs. The Steam Workshop community is very actively supporting the game (I have several mods there myself). Still highly recommended.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
If you are at all interested in the subject you should definitely give it a look. The game is already well supported by the community and the Steam Workshop has some excellent mods, weapons and levels already. It's the old SWAT or Rainbow Six from a top down, 2D perspective that puts more emphasis on planning than quick reactions. Check out some of the Let's Play videos out there, or some mission video captures posted on my YouTube channel for more information.
Now that it is in release, there are even more interesting features, the major ones being multistory buildings and drug busts where you have to race to seize the evidence before the bad guys dispose of it. Three campaigns have been added, which are a series of linked missions (also with some branched, optional missions) where you are limited to your existing roster. Without giving away any spoilers, there are a couple of really large maps set on a waterfront and a train station that combine long sight distances, dangerous approaches and unusual rooms and buildings.
The game is pretty much bug free due to the long alpha period, with only a couple of minor items that have to be addressed. There is an excellent level editor that works pretty well, the only really awkward part being the current need to edit the background image (which is the floor or ground of the map) outside of the editor, should you want one that isn't the default grey warehouse floor. The developers have stated that they intend to add that background editing ability into the in-game editor.
Also of note is the excellent Mission Generator. You select the size of the level and the amount of opposition and the game generates a random seed. Then you select either "KillHouse" (for a training map) or "House" (for a real world map) and the game generates a mission using one of the maps in the game. The mission could be just to eliminate hostiles, or escort a VIP, or run a drug bust, or rescue hostages. It's a real challenge because it's newly generated.
Overall this is an excellent value for the price; three campaigns, 80 official missions (once you enable the two new missions via the Mods interface), a Mission Generator and tons of mods already in the Workshop. Highly Recommended.

If you loved Left 4 Dead 1 & 2 but are too tired of those games to really go back, then this game might be for you. Fun, solid gameplay with level, loot, and difficulty progression are all good mechanics to keep you coming back.
*First, some positives:
-The game looks nice. Even on the lowest settings, it looks almost as good as Skyrim on High settings.
-The sound design is solid.
-Each of the 5 unique characters are fully voiced, and interact with eachother similarly to how the characters of L4D interacted. (With a more fantasy twist of course) They even say helpful things that let you know when you've gone into a dead end, or when a certain enemy is nearby.
-The gameplay is very good. It has "borrowed" most of L4D's mechanics, but that's not a bad thing. It does them well. The melee, and ranged play both have uniqe feels to them, and that is nice.
-The leveling, loot, and overall upgrade and progression system is fun, and keeps you wanting to play even when you've completed each mission a bunch of times.
*Now for some of the problems I've experienced:
-It's very resource intensive. Could most likely be optomized further. It seems to be somewhat random in whether or not your rig will handle it smoothly or not.
-The random loot drop system and loot rolling system is annoying in many ways, but does keep you wanting to play. You only get an item if you level up, or win a mission. There seems to be a higher chance for getting loot that is for your current character, but it is completely random. You will get items for characters you are not interested in instead of ones you want. The only thing you get for failing is a small amount of XP.
-If the host quits anywhere in a mission, it restarts the entire mission too.
Overall it is a very good game. It has lots of replayability, with optional extra challenge for each mission. The characters don't usually get on your nerves, and are fun to play as. Hopefully it will be improved over time, though what it is now is very fun. $30 is a pretty fair price for what it is. It has its bugs and issues, but under all of those it is a great, fun game.

I'm not really a fan of zombies or zombie games. They've never really scared me and they're a dime a dozen these days. So when I picked this up during a Humble Bundle sale for really cheap, I wasn't expecting much. However, this game surpassed my expectations and turned out to be one of the best indie games included in the bundle.
The game takes place in Seattle in 1986 after the outbreak of a virus that has resurrected the dead and turned them into zombies. You assume the role of Randall Wayne, a park ranger and survivor of the virus who is on his way to the last remaining safe point in hopes of finding his wife and daughter.
Deadlight combines elements of a platforming, puzzle solving and horror. You're always encouraged to run away from the zombies you encounter unless you have no other option. You're only armed with an axe, but as you progress through the game you'll come across a handgun and a shotgun. Ammunition is limited though, so you should only use when it's necessary. The meat of this game is the platforming. It makes good use of parkour, which is the best part about this game in my opinion. The game is very linear, but very fun to play. Included are several things to collect, which makes the experience more fulfilling as it offers something in addition to just playing through each level and progressing through the story. There's also an additional mode called "Nightmare Mode", which is basically the same as the main story except you're not allowed to die. If you die in Nightmare Mode, then you must restart from the very beginning.
The only negative for this game is it's length. It took me less than 7 hours to complete 100%. That's not always a bad thing. Not every game has to be 20 hours or 40 hours long. I just think $15 is a bit much to ask for a game that's so short. Sure, you could play Nightmare Mode. I'm sure that would add lots of time, but it's just more of the same on a much harder difficulty and doesn't really add anything new.
Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of platformers or zombie games. I'm not even a fan of zombies, but I still really enjoyed this game. The story is good and the gameplay is great. It's well worth buying, but because of it's short length, I'd suggest waiting for it to go on sale.

If there was ever a Sonic game that has been praised and hated the most at the same time, it is this game. Don't let that be a factor that makes you change your choice of buying this, though.
Sonic Adventure 2 managed to successfully continue the formula of Sonic Adventure in a slightly altered way. The game is split into three styles, the speed levels (Sonic/Shadow), the mech shooting stages (Tails/Eggman) and the very, VERY bad treasure hunting stages (Knuckles/Rouge).
The speed levels are the best part of the game. No doubt. But, they are slightly more linear than SA1's Sonic stages, which is a disappointment. Luckily, they are still awesome.
The mech stages are clunky but bearable. Just be ready for some annoyances.
The treasure hunting is despicable. Luckily the stages are usually rather small and are not as common as the other stages.
While SA2 is flawed in some major aspects, the game is pretty darn replayable. The game has an improved Chao Garden from SA1, which is very addictive. Plus, every level has 5 missions, and if you want to 100% the game, you will need to A Rank every stage and fully complete the Chao missions.
Also, SA2 has probably the best multiplayer in any main-title Sonic game. So that's a plus.
Ultimately, I do recommend SA2HD, and it is pretty cheap online. If you want to experience a bit of a 3D Sonic classic, then pick this up.

I’ve spent many, many hours playing Sid Meier’s Pirates!, and there’s the same addictive quality about Mount & Blade: Warband. There’s always just one more thing you have to do, just turn in this quest, oh, but you ran into some bandits on the way, oh, and now your fiefdom is being raided, so you have to go defend it, but you need to recruit more troops, and sell off the loot you got from the bandits too. This constant flow of tasks has no easily-identifiable break points, so you never feel like you can leave it alone, even though the reality is you can save and exit at any time, and pick up exactly where you left off.
I think what really keeps you playing a game like this is that you might not remember what you were doing when you return to it later. Because almost all of what you do, and the order in which you do it, is entirely up to the player, you have to take on the whole cognitive load of planning and scheduling tasks. This is what takes up the bulk of the player’s attention while playing Mount & Blade: Warband, and once they’re in that state, there’s a certain inertia to it.
So it’s actually fortunate that you can’t play Mount & Blade: Warband for too long without running into one of the seemingly endless array of bugs, that snaps you out of that cognitive state, often by making one of your tasks impossible to complete. Those bugs are why I eventually had to just give up on the game altogether, because any given thing you’re doing might turn out to be utterly futile.

This is a fun survivial based coperative game similar to ZPS/L4D with lots of potential and some great and not so great game modes.
"Escape" is a objective based game mode and the closest to L4D you will find, this is good but could do with letting the player know what they are expected more, as you will spend a lot of time running around empty hallways not sure how to continue when you first play the game.
"Hunted" was a PVP survivor vs survior game type that really did not fit the theme of the game at all as it is basically a FFA.
The game modes that really shined for me though was "Panic (objective)" and  "Panic (classic)" these are team based PVP (zombies vs players) and this is where I have had the most fun, in this you need to
barricade up rooms and hold out against player zombies as they pick off players turning them into zombies themselves. However with limited maps for this game type, the fun wore off quickly and has caused the game type to unfortunately died out online.
"Extraction" also felt very similar to "Panic" but with AI and a wait time to holdout, and left me wondering why this is not just merged with "Panic" game modes by giving server admins the option to enable/disable zombie AI.
I would love to see the developers focus more on this game type adding more maps that focus on defense and barricading as this seems to be the games best part.
Overall this game has a great foundation with good game mechanics in place and working, it just needs a little more polish and PLENTY more maps (especially for "Panic") to keep me coming back for more.

I tried with videogames BGM, Vocaloid, and Japanese/Korean vocal music (Anime OST as well).
The only minor lackluster part for me is the stock music selection. There are a couple of tracks finely mapped to be the best gameplay experience, but they are... not enough. The main idea of the game is using your own music, but some more manually mapped tracks are kinda necessary.
Even if you are not a huge fan of the rhythm game genre it's worth a shot, it's a promising game that I'm sure it will get even better with time and good feedback.

I got ghosts for 7$ and, for the price, it was a very cinematic and somewhat fun, if forgettable, romp: but I'd never shake the feeling that the game goes through the motions covering all the things a modern shooter is expected to have without any true effort. You'll be facing the same set pieces, dialogues and plot twists you've seen in many games and movies before, heck some of them come straight from previous CoD games: the few innovative levels (in space and underwater) still sport the same tired run/shoot gameplay and ultimately add very little.
The gameplay is basic and isn't very different from a shooting gallery with little between each enemy encounter: said enemies have a very simple AI and are dangerous just due to their numbers, grenade spam and accurate aim. Your teammates do little to help you, even getting in the way a few times, and Riley the dog is more of a novelty piece than anything else since you'll be using him just a couple times to explore enemy positions.
The story is likewise simple and so generic that you'll have a constant sense of deja-vu as events unfold, what's worse is that the characters are as generic as the plot and I never managed to care about them or their fate.
In the end playing Call of Duty: Ghosts was a decent way to pass a few hours but one can't shake the "been there, done that" feeling due to how generic and derivative everything is: it's simply one of the weakest entries of the franchise and thus I can't really recommend it.

Following up such a breakout hit as Hotline Miami, a game which blew away expectations and single handedly pioneered a new subgenre of frenetic twin-stick shooters, was never going to be easy. Part of the mixed responses to the sequel stem from expecting more of the same and being disappointed by change. Confusing, to say the least, especially when considering that Hotline Miami 2 is by far one of the greatest video game sequels in recent memory - one that improves upon and supercedes the original in almost every regard.
The enthralling, nerve-wracking and deeply satisfying gameplay is still here, made more complex by a larger array of characters with unique traits that the game challenges you to adapt to, accompanied by a pulsing soundtrack that against all odds manages to be even better than the first. The level design is more detailed and rich in variety, some being short and some being exhaustingly long. They're extremely difficult but rely on learning from experience and overcoming adversity through perseverence. ALL of the 25 levels are vital and they are all incredibly rewarding. All these positives are to be expected from a Hotline Miami game, surely. What I didn't expect, however, was the richness and intrigue of its story. It's a much more dense and narrative-driven game than the first, often erratically jumping between time periods, character viewpoints and locations. Convoluted? Naturally. Hard to understand? Sure. It's a Gravity's Rainbow, Hunter S. Thompson-ish kaleidoscopic tearing into postmodern American culture, as well as a scathing critique on the addictive nature of mindlessly violent video games. It's absolutely intoxicating.
Hotline Miami 2 is a perfect game. It never overstays its welcome, and offers a consistently entertaining and endlessly complex experience. There's still nothing else like it. If you haven't played it already, you gotta get a grip!

Deadlight has a good (if unoriginal) premise and a great visual style. Where it falls down is in the gameplay, which is trial and error guesswork platforming, but without the quick reset that makes games like Super Meat Boy tolerable.
The story can be dismissed out of hand as it doesn't do anything original or put any kind of twist on your standard "human drama in the apocalypse" zombie stuff. It's not badly done, but it doesn't stand out.
It can be difficult to tell what the game considers background art and what it considers mountable platforms. Many "chase sequences" are prevented from being as effective as they could be, because you have to be a mind-reader to guess what is going to happen next. It's respectable that the game has so many unique moments, but from a gameplay perspective this means you have no real idea of what you're in for. What this means is you end up repeating sections until you have died in all the traps and hazards, and can then memorise the run to execute it properly. In other words, by the time you complete the section you'll have seen it so many times that even if it was initially cool, you're soured on it in the end.
I had more frustration than fun in my playthrough, so sadly I can't honestly recommend it. It's so close to being a great entry in this genre, but it *just* misses the mark. I give it a tentative recommendation for the zombie obsessed, and the very patient.

Barely recommended (on sale for $10 or less!) for Vaas only! Vaas is one of, if not the best, lunatic boss character ever and probably the sole reason I am recommending this game. The voice acting and character modeling/rigging are superb.
However, the open world components are very repetitive and formulaic, with poor, if any, level design in most components (aside from the outposts) and there is ***FAR*** too much pointless running back and forth.
I usually play games like this to 100% completion, but once I finished the main campaign and the fun missions (outposts/wanted), the remaining items were too grindy and generic to warrant wasting time on.
PROS:
-Gorgeous environment
-Great voice acting (esp Vaas)
-Great modeling/rigging (the plot itself isn't great, but the scenes convey it incredibly well)
-"Wanted Dead" and "Outpost" objectives were both genuinely fun: both of these mission types basically ask the player to kill all enemies in a certain location. This lead to a variety of base types, enemy setups, and approaches, especially when combined with the alarm (and whether or not to disable it).
NEUTRALS:
-Loot system served no real purpose (it is basically all cash). You will quickly realize looting dead bodies is a complete waste of time as nothing can ever be found.
-Crafting system is similarly confused and borderline pointless, especially considering how easy the game is. The only crafting component that made some sense was using the various plants for syringes.
-Shopping system serves as a cash-unlock mechanic which is generic and alright, but once you have unlocked the gear you like, there is no reason to loot anything anymore.....and since missions give you the guns in shops for free, technically there is no reason to loot things ever.... (You can buy maps that show you collectible locations though I had an extreme overabundance of money throughout the game)
-Huge island, but its extremely generic with no reason to really explore
-No real reason to do any of the activities on the island, esp since they are mostly repetitive, grindy, and generic.
-There seem to be local leaderboards for the activities, but they don't link up through uPlay....even though uPlay connection is active while playing....
CONS:
-Some of the main characters actions make NO sense. He jumps through ridiculous hoops for side characters for no reason while freely killing hundreds of others without hesitation.
-The plot in general is silly and doesn't make sense, but the characters are very well portrayed.
-REALLY Easy. I played on the very hardest difficulty right from the start and found the game to be incredibly easy.
-uPlay.   Modernly it "links" to your steam account which sounds like a good idea, but mine didn't when I first loaded the game (and it DID the second time I loaded the game). Naturally, this resulted in a lovely bug and now I have 2 uPlay accounts with mismatched information that I have to waste time trying to sort with ubisoft. Not fun.
-LOTS of walking around. In the second half of the game you get the wingsuit, which helps (but doesn't fix) the problem. Unlike other games (like GTA) where vehicles are prevalent, in FarCry you can and will go long distances on foot. Combined with the generic island and nothing to find, this is the games #1 problem.
---The running problem is made worse by the fact that there are very few vehicles on the island and the island is so rocky most vehicles need to take crazy alternate roads to get anywhere, so you end up just ditching the car and going by foot.
-The excessive walking problem is made worse by the fact that most vehicles in the game drive like crap and can not get up even the smallest hills without a huge running start (no exaggeration). This means you will often have to ditch your vehicle and go on foot because it can't make it over the 3 foot hill in front of you.
-Collectibles are pointless and identical. Although 3 different collectible types exist, there is nothing that distinguishes them (other than their name). Collecting enough of them rewards you with a weapon/recipe...basically the same rewards.
-"Hunting" missions were pointless, repetitive, and boring. (Go to X place and kill 12 deer with a bow. Wow.)

Melody's Escape is a rhythm game with the skin of a platformer stretched over it. Like many other games in the genre (With maybe the expection of oddities like Crypt Of The NecroDancer or Gitaroo Man.), it doesn't matter who you are, or what is going on, your new goal in life is to tap those damn buttons to the icons on screen and either love it or feel like a ponce for being rhythmically challenged (Which, I'll admit, I am these days.). Thankfully, the developers realize this and included Steam Workshop support and wide library support (which is a godsend) so you can see a minimalist Madoka (or some various anime character of your choosing) do a face-plant while The Knife shriek about nerve itches in the background.
It's been years since I last touched anything remotely related to the genre, but Melody's Escape difficulties are descriptive but very far apart, with relaxing acting as a test to see if you're still breathing on one end and Overload reminding me of fitter, happier, Pump It Up days trying out nightmare. The two inbetween difficulties are probably going to be what most people settle on since they provide a healhier challenge.  If that doesn't satisfy you, you can craft a difficulty based of those presets into something where you're manically smashing one button for a minute on end or doing singular complex inputs every few seconds.
Since the main draw of the game come from the massive library and format support, it's only fair to mention that while the synch program is often great and hits the notes of the song, it's often a question exactly which ones that can mess you up. Some songs that I tried out like King Kunta (Kendrick Lamar), Burn the Witch (Radiohead) and various electronic/Hip-Hop/things with a pronounced beat things, were relatively flawless and easy to decipher, something more nuanced or jittery, like Ice Cream (Battles), or Sleep (Godspeed You! Black Emperor, which I really don't recommend trying out unless it's for some crazy marathon.) often had beats placed on different elements, where I'm doing more button presses during the calm intro than at the typical post-rock cresendo. To the game's credit, it tells you how well it thinks it gets the gist of the song, but I kinda wished that it did a little more.
While it seems like I've been ripping this game a new one out of some jealous jilted bitterness of days gone by, it's actually kinda fun to play once you understand the nuances of the game's algorithms and got your groove down, at least in short segments. While I personally think that some leaderboard support would be sweet, I'm content with what it has now and will enjoy future sessions of watching Kurisu Makise plummet to her temporary doom while Burzum is playing in the background.
Worth a full-price purchase if you're a fan of the genre, possibly worth it on sale if on the fence.

Okay, I'm preparing my self for this being a very unpopular review; but here goes.  Please also bare in mind that this review is purely and solely based on the single player side of the game - I will touch on the multiplayer side but only briefly.
Call of Duty: Ghost is the tenth game in the COD series, and was released in 2013 on PC, PS3, Xbox 360 and Wii U, and then re-released on launch of PS4 and Xbox One.
This was my first COD game that I had played in a while, so the problems people have had with the gameplay becoming stale and lack of innovation didn't effect me so much. Yes the gameplay is very much the same as all of the other Call of Duty games, however I still had fun whilst playing it. I have yet to play the multiplayer, and to be honest, I probably won't. The single player campaign follows the character of Logan Walker. You also play as Baker, Elias Walker (your father) and a new addition of playing as a combat dog, Riley.  There are no new elements to be seen in the gameplay, its very "Call of Duty", aim and shoot is pretty much the whole game with the odd quick time event thrown in. There are some really interesting levels when you are in space and underwater, however my favorite levels were the vehicle based ones; where you take control over tanks and helicopters - they add a little something extra to the game in my opinion, breaking up the monotony of the classic ground troop fights.
Graphically, Ghosts is very dated; I was playing on 4K resolution, and it still looked very poor. Textures when close up are so low res it's hard to imagine this is a game which was released in 2013. The game uses an engine which was used in previous COD releases, but with apparent "significant upgrades", however I don't really see a difference in graphic fidelity in Ghosts and any of the other "recent" COD games.
Ghost had a story which kept me interested right until the end, however I felt that the game's ending really did not do the game any justice. I really felt like I was getting a big two fingers up to me when it happened. Not sure whether people will class it as a spoiler, but the cliffhanger at the end really relies on there being a sequel in the Ghost franchise, however unlikely that will be. Up until the end though, it is a compelling story - maybe if you quit just before the end credits you'll enjoy it more!
This is another game where you will not die or fail on the single player mode; you are with a squad of other characters for the majority of the game; and you could very easily just sit back and watch the fire fights if you were so inclined and you would still not fail. Even when playing on higher difficulties, there is no real ramp in the challenges on show.
With the games extremely linear level design, it leaves you very little time to explore the world in front of you, that being said, there is no reason to want to either though. There are one set of "collectibles" to be on the look out for, and that's it - I guess it is to be expected from a COD game though. It would of been nice to maybe find little bits of extra plot and story through hacking computers, finding files etc.
The single player mode took me just about seven hours to finish - I thought that was an OK length for the game;  I wasn't growing tired of the gameplay by the end of the game but there is no reason at all to play it through for a second time - expect of course if you want to play on a higher difficulty; but even then, I wouldn't say it's worth it.  Where you are going to get your mileage out of any COD game is the multiplayer - however I still don't plan on playing it simply because I am not interested in the multiplayer side of many games.
Technically I didn't have any bugs or issues whilst playing. I was able to play on a steady 60 fps on 4k resolution the whole play through. At times the frame rate was even in the 100s. It certainly looks like the PC version of the game came out on top of the consoles on the technical side of things, since the consoles could barely even achieve 60 fps on lower resolutions, Xbox could only handle 720p. This game is better off being played with a keyboard and mouse, however the lack of FOV sliders did make me feel a little bit nauseous with the camera swaying around all of the time when moving. You can change this in .ini settings but in this day in age, PC games need a FOV slider as compulsory in my opinion.
In conclusion, whilst there may seem to be more negatives than positives in my review for Ghosts, I did have a lot of fun whilst playing it, however the price of £39,99 is absolutely ridiculously especially for a game which has been out almost two years now.  If like me you are just going to play the single player mode, wait for the game to be around £10, but if you are going to be jumping into the multiplayer side of things (there is still a very active community out there too!) I would happily say you can pick this up for anything below £15 - since you will get the seven hour single player as well as many many hours of CODs core element, multiplayer.

This review focuses primarily on the singleplayer aspects of Ghosts; I realize many enjoy the multiplayer aspect, and it is indeed good but I'm much too old to be berated by 12 year olds so I tend to avoid the multiplayer, likewise it's something that seems to get largely overlooked in the reviews. ;-D
The campaign is the usual CoD fodder: a Michael Bay movie with more explosions but dialogue that usually doesn't make you cringe. Essentially it follows the tried and true angry arch nemesis from the past route that every CoD game since Modern Warfare has done. While it certainly isn't horrible, it isn't spectacular either; unfortunately the first mission fills you with hope that everything is going to be a bit different from previous campaigns, perhaps you will be fighting predominantly locally as a guerilla fighter and being challenged with weaponry that doesn't completely trump your opposition, particularly since they portray a fascinating scenario in which the front lines have stagnated much like world war 1 with a no-mans land between the sides... no such luck. You go from guarding the wall with your awesome dog and Superman (your brother) to becoming a scuba diving, globe trotting, ninja in the blink of an eye with a bunch of indistinguishable and forgettable spec ops.
Overall, every level is decent in and of itself and the setpieces are spectacular, albeit sometimes the plans are more absurd than an A-Team episode (i.e. instead of destroying the pylons of an oil rig while you are already scuba diving below it, sabotaging said oil rig to explode while you're on it). Unfortunately just as soon as you begin to understand a mechanic it's gone forever. Riley your lovable and homicidal dog is only in the first few missions so just as soon as you get the gist of using him to attack he's no longer available. Similarly gadgets like thermal vision, tear gas, or strobe lights that blind and disorient the enemy are only utilized for a minute at most in the campaign leaving you thinking "that was fun, can't wait to try that again" only to eventually realize you won't ever get to try that mechanic again unless you reload that level.
In summary, the single player of Ghosts is overall enjoyable but it would have been a considerably stronger gameplay experience if they had focused more on a few mechanics such as fighting alongside Riley and done less globe trotting, basing the majority of the story in Southern California instead. Buy it on sale when it's about the price of going to a movie and you'll likely enjoy the singleplayer. Of course after the campaign you can always jump into the multiplayer and be berated by 12 year olds extending the value of the title considerably if that's your thing.

I played through the first game and loved it, with my only complaint being that the game was too short and the last few levels were effortless.
Hotline Miami 2 brings some interesting new things into the mix, but unfortunately the overall experience falls short. Compared to the first game, the level design is horrendous. You seem to have very few options a lot of times, and playing the whole game melee-only doesn't seem possible. Running into an area, guns-blazing, isn't a good way to beat the levels.
Many of the rooms are huge, and you can't even see from one side to the other with aiming. This is a real problem since it really hurts your ability to track enemies in the area. Ontop of this, many levels seem to just have an absurd number of interior windows... so if you walk into an open area, you are within line-of-sight of multiple different areas, all filled with rifle-toting enemies. You're going to get shot and have to restart a LOT. Because of this, the best way to clear levels is to play them out very slowly, not wasting a shot. This is the complete opposite of the first game.
The game is fairly buggy at times as well, compared to the first. Doors in particular are damn near broken. Enemies get stuck in doors frequently, seem to stop in doorways, lose sight of you in door ways, etc. In some of the more ridiculous levels I pretty much just abused doorways and made the enemies funnel into them just to thin them out to make the levels actually enjoyable. The AI is insanely bad as well, perhaps it's just a line-of-sight issue, I'm not sure. You can often kill a guy next to a stationary enemy, and that enemy won't even react. AI just seem to patrol paths more than anything, but on some levels killing a guy with melee causes enemies from all the adjacent rooms to swarm you. Pretty inconsistent behavior.
The game still does a lot well... The music is still great, the graphics are unique and interesting, there's some interesting design behind the pause menu, things like that. The story seems less interesting, but probably ends up about the same.
The game itself just seems much harder in general, and a lot of your deaths feel like it's due to a lack of information / clarity for you to react to, instead of you just screwing up.  An example being a black dog patroling across a black floor. You will pretty much never notice him until he kills you the first time. Also, there are a ton of random objects on the ground that prevent you from going around. I found myself getting snagged on them often while trying to dodge and run around. Some of them seem like there would be enough room to walk by them, but there's not. More frustrations.
I can't really recommend this sequel unless you're a huge fan of the first game, have played it multiple times, love to memorize levels or enjoy relying on your reflexes to carry you through levels.

This was a pretty solid platformer for the most part.  I enjoyed the story, graphics, gameplay and atmosphere.   It's a cool mix of survival horror flavor with old fashioned run, gun and jump antics. Nightmare mode was an absolute dog that took me 21 hours in and of itself to complete, doing it the old school way; no cheats, no walkthrough, no trainers and no memorizing.  If I could go back and do it all again...I wouldn't!  Ha ha ha, but I enjoyed the game enough to try to complete all of the modes available even if my own suffering was eventually nearly too much to bear.  As I don't use a controller for PC games, I have to say that there was just enough wonkiness to call the controls a decently royal pain in the butt.  I would hit the buttons to do the requisite actions when I had pretty much every segment of the game memorized but sometimes Randall wouldn't respond at all, do a completely different action than required or be a stubborn mule and do nothing at all, curiously making me inquire to the obstinate Mr. Wayne, "Please tell me what you're doing and why you did that.
Here's some traditional pros and cons for this mostly enjoyable s.o.b. of a game:
Pros
-Cool settings, graphics and sound
-When the platforming works it's alot of fun
-Plenty of challenge on Nightmare mode
-Good mix of situations and gameplay ideas
-Satisfying shooting
-Fun environmental puzzles (just challenging enough lending a little Prince of Persia/Castlevania fun)
Cons
-Way too easy on normal mode.
-When the platforming doesn't work, expect frequent calls to the suicide hotline
-Nightmare mode almost too difficult (even 2 lives would have been nice)
-Certain dialogue scenes not skippable (a real aggravator during Nightmare mode)
-More time in the overworld would be nice (the Rat's lair is kind of a stinker)
Though I missed a collectable or two and a few other achievements (I ended with 74%), I can honestly say I won't be going back to find them!  The 21 hours spent on Nightmare were more than enough for me.  Glad I have insomnia and stay up late even when I have to work or I would have never finished it.  Though Deadlight is far from perfect, there is something about it that keeps you coming back for that next exhilarting moment of dodging a zombie horde, nailing an impossible series of jumps/rolls and giving the undead both barrells of your shotgun.  It kept me going for about 5 days.  Nightmare Mode though...phew...good luck with that.
Overall rating:  7.5/10

Aaaah...Far Cry 3, where can I begin with you?? Far Cry 3 is an open world action-adventure first-person shooter video game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft on November 29, 2012. Far Cry 3 is set on a tropical island between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. After a vacation goes wrong, protagonist Jason Brody must save his friends, who have been kidnapped by pirates and escape from the island and its unhinged inhabitants. This game gave me so many emotions because of the well written story, missions, cut scenes and music! I literally cried at one moment. The gameplay is absolutly fantastic! You can do so many things in this game. Driving, flying, hunting, killing pirates with a large variation of takedowns and a very big gallery of weapons. Far Cry 3 gives a RPG feel to it by crafting skins, medicine and other stuff to help you during the game. The graphics and the open world are gorgeous! Every corner of the Rook Island is beautiful and pleasant to the eye. The A.I. is one of the most advanced I've seen in recent years, animals from the island not only attack you if they feel threatened, but they also attack the pirates or your allies. Far Cry 3 has one of the most memorable and iconic video game characters, Vaas Montenegro. You'll love every scene and every moment when he's present and you will want more from him. This game gives a good moral: How far will you go to save your familly and friends? Yes, the game's protagonist, Jason Brody is like Walter White aka Heisenberg. He will start beeing imature and party-dude kind of person and during the game until the end, he will be a different person. Far Cry 3 will give you the feel of a hunter, at first killing will feel wrong, but in the end, it feels like victory. During or after you complete the story, you have many things to do. Hunting and side missions are not making any exception. Overall, Ubisoft gave all they had to make this, in my opinion, masterpiece. It's one of the last good games that Ubisoft really gave interest. I highly recommend this game to anyone. You won't regret it!

Unfortunately, I can't endorse this game in any way.
While from a technological side, the game is reasonably impressive for an unknown team, the game falls very short in the field of gameplay. Now, I was just bored so I decided to kick the game up and play singleplayer.
First off, the game seems to be going for a much darker and edgier theme on zombies. So far, that's OK. The problem is that the game pretty much just drops you in, and sorta hopes you know what to do. The problem is, "what to do" is far from obvious. The game really is supposed to be a more suspenseful game than the L4D series, so wasting bullets isn't what you're supposed to be doing, but...when you're first let into the world, you just are...there? I mean, the first reaction of most players nowadays when presented with no objective is to find the nearest zombie and pump it full of lead. To top off this tedium is hilariously over the top creepy music while I'm pretty much just chilling in a garage, and nothing is really bothering me.
I mean, is this my life? Just sitting around, murdering zombies that go near me? Eventually the game takes pity on me or something and tells me that I should be barricading an activated house. That's...great. There are dozens of houses in this map. Is this a joke? Somehow, through no action of my own, the game then tells me to go to an extraction point after a few minutes. Again, this is far from clear. There's no objective marker, hardly a description of what I'm looking for, and the map is quite large. The end result was that I spent about 15 minutes ambling around, occasionally taking potshots at a zombie, and then quitting the game. I didn't even find any loot, the traditional reward for players who look around in a map in order to keep them at least *slightly* engaged.
And the combat isn't terribly fun either, the zombies are...kind of hard to kill, and killing them feels incredibly unrewarding. Overall, this game feels, and plays like a vastly inferior Left 4 Dead without anything resembling a UI, and is more expensive to boot. Even if you got this game already as part of the last Humble Bundle, like I did, I wouldn't bother playing this. I'm sure someone can tell me what the objectives *were*, but it hardly seems worth the effort to play a game with so little consideration for the user experience.
The dev team clearly has no small amount of technical skill, so I'm looking forward to seeing if they can produce another effort, with better done game design and user experience planning in their next game.

Voxel based creation/survival game just like Minecraft, Rust, Space Engineers and all the others in the same genre but with a few things thrown into the mixer! It feels more like an MMO RPG or 3rd person shooter when you play and move around the game world, this goes for the control system as well it's not like a first person sandbox most are used too.
The art style of this game is a sort of futuristic fantasy setting a bit like Phantasy Star.
Like all survival/creation games you start up, resource gather, build things and create stuff but Planet Explorers does try and do things that others don't which is why I'm giving it a good review.  It should be applauded for not being a total clone and has great potential the alpha is a solid 7 out of 10 bar a few bugs and missing content is very very playable for 20-30 hours.
Anyway... there's classes and a blue print designer which actually lets you design your own blocks, objects and textures in game to create buildings, transport and weapons. This is something other games like Minecraft don't have.  The game has sandbox mode which has no enemies it's just pure build mode with infinite tools and objects, adventure mode and normal survival mode are included too and that's why I like it and what makes it different. Adventure mode is the most fun and where I see this game doing well and succeeding, It still features building and crafting but there's NPC's that give quests, have shops you can visit and many types of mobs and enemies with decent enough AI.
Apparently tower defence and wave surivival might be added too at some point which could be fun with a sandbox element.
It may not be a complete game yet but a good attempt and for an alpha/beta is solid. It's a bit different from the other games we're all used to so when it's on sale go ahead and pick up a copy! I hope they continue to be a little different.

This is one of those games that reaches for the stars, but hasn't gotten there quite yet.  It has a creation system that has only been dreamed of by any other game that I've found and it falls short in mission interest because they tend to get boring after a while.  The creation system alone is worth playing this amazing game: it is challenging and logic driven, while also being so freeform as to allow you to create almost anything of almost any size.  You want a helicopter, just build it; you want a ship destroyer, just build it; you want a castle that reaches into the sky, just build it.  There is a survival mode, a story/survival mode, and a free build mode.  Multiplayer co-op or vs and single player.  The possibilities are endless and the developers should be commended for trying to create a game of such colossal scale.  It's obviously not done yet and still rough around the edges because it just entered beta, but when it does become finished it will be a one-of-a-kind experience.

Do you remember Rainbow Six's famous planning phase? Did you enjoy that part of the game more than the actual mission? If you answered yes to these questions, Door Kickers is a worthwhile investment.
The game's core features right now are quite good. There is a slight learning curve to get your guys moving the way you want. Sometimes you will feel like you are micromangaging movements especially if you want to execute proper room clearing techniques. And occasionally you get angry at the pathing system since there are numerous house plants and chairs which create impassable barriers. But it is still fun.
There are definitely a good number of missions available of varying difficulty. Some you will breeze right through, others will be the bain of your existence until you get that perfect plan with 0 casualties working just right. Also the random mission generator is always good if you are looking for a quick challenge. As well as replaying missions trying to achieve the single-plan and hands-off achievements.
The loadouts are varied and offer a decent sized arsenal. It is mostly reflective of what a police SWAT team would have available. One gameplay feature I like is how your team really practices good trigger discipline (single shots if possible). While the bad guys will often go full auto at the slightest of targets. One thing that is not completely apparent in the loadout section of the game is what effects do the equipment have on your team. You'll notice in cramped interiors, it takes the man with the M4 longer to train his rifle than the man weilding his pistol. But for those long corridor or outdoor shots, your Assaulter with his rifle is far more efficient than your rear guard weiding his shotgun. Sadly none of this is explicitly described in the loadout menu and will take some experimentation to figure out what the ideal loadout is based on your style of play and the mission.
The graphics and sound are good for a game. It is definitely not a high fidelity sound and graphics visual masterpiece, but that really is not necessary. It is the gameplay which makes this game shine. There are various mods which revamp the sound experience if you are unhappy with the tone of the firearms.
Overall, really fun game!

I played through the first game and loved it, with my only complaint being that the game was too short and the last few levels were effortless.
Hotline Miami 2 brings some interesting new things into the mix, but unfortunately the overall experience falls short. Compared to the first game, the level design is horrendous. You seem to have very few options a lot of times, and playing the whole game melee-only doesn't seem possible. Running into an area, guns-blazing, isn't a good way to beat the levels.
Many of the rooms are huge, and you can't even see from one side to the other with aiming. This is a real problem since it really hurts your ability to track enemies in the area. Ontop of this, many levels seem to just have an absurd number of interior windows... so if you walk into an open area, you are within line-of-sight of multiple different areas, all filled with rifle-toting enemies. You're going to get shot and have to restart a LOT. Because of this, the best way to clear levels is to play them out very slowly, not wasting a shot. This is the complete opposite of the first game.
The game is fairly buggy at times as well, compared to the first. Doors in particular are damn near broken. Enemies get stuck in doors frequently, seem to stop in doorways, lose sight of you in door ways, etc. In some of the more ridiculous levels I pretty much just abused doorways and made the enemies funnel into them just to thin them out to make the levels actually enjoyable. The AI is insanely bad as well, perhaps it's just a line-of-sight issue, I'm not sure. You can often kill a guy next to a stationary enemy, and that enemy won't even react. AI just seem to patrol paths more than anything, but on some levels killing a guy with melee causes enemies from all the adjacent rooms to swarm you. Pretty inconsistent behavior.
The game still does a lot well... The music is still great, the graphics are unique and interesting, there's some interesting design behind the pause menu, things like that. The story seems less interesting, but probably ends up about the same.
The game itself just seems much harder in general, and a lot of your deaths feel like it's due to a lack of information / clarity for you to react to, instead of you just screwing up.  An example being a black dog patroling across a black floor. You will pretty much never notice him until he kills you the first time. Also, there are a ton of random objects on the ground that prevent you from going around. I found myself getting snagged on them often while trying to dodge and run around. Some of them seem like there would be enough room to walk by them, but there's not. More frustrations.
I can't really recommend this sequel unless you're a huge fan of the first game, have played it multiple times, love to memorize levels or enjoy relying on your reflexes to carry you through levels.

Definitely not worth the $15. Maybe $10 at the most.

If your looking for a really unique action-adventure game with a blending of different types of gameplay styles well look no further. Sonic Adventure 2 expands upon the original Sonic Adventure, adding bigger levels (although sadly no more open world), more upgrades to find, more characters to play with, a tamogachi inspired Chao raising garden, Kart races, and even a 2 player racing and battle mode if your inclined to take part in.
If all of this sounds too good to be true, well you should be happy to know that won't be disappointed as long as your expecting a game that by all accounts isn't perfect, but its just so unique and has that Sega Dreamcast era charm and personality that it might as well be and you definitely be hard pressed to find similar games to it even to this day.
Now lets get down to all this varied gameplay I was talking about earlier, in this game there are specifically 3 different types of gameplay styles which include Sonic/Shadow which their levels are all about going fast, bouncing on enemies, and is generally the type of gameplay you would expect from a Sonic game. You then have Knuckles/Rogue levels where they have to have find Chaos Emeralds shards or keys in a level by listening to a radar to see if they are close and then either straight out picking it up or digging in the ground for it or even just killing an enemy. Last, but not least is the Tails/Robotnik levels which are essentially updated Gamma levels from Sonic Adventure 1 where you will go through a level locking on and shooting lots of enemies while trying to get to the end. It's also worth mentioning that going through story mode you will also sometimes come across the usual boss fights and even the occassional racing mini-game to add even more to the mix.
Now to the part where about half of you will love and the other will hate and thats the Chao Garden. You see, throughout each level in the game, you pick up these colored objects and even small animals that you can take back to the garden and feed to your chao to make it level up in a certain attribute which you can take to compete in races or even battle it out karate style! They also evolve and change depending on how you grow them and there are some secrets even to be had with them. The part however that some people do not like with this big part of the game is that it is essential to raise a chao to have high stats and do all the races/battles so that you can get 100% completion which unlocks a special level and raising chao is not a fast endeavor.
All in all, the game itself is great. The port however...has a few kinks to work out with getting it to work with Fullscreen mode now with a new patch, but is semi-easily fixed, so if you can get it working then you should have a great time with the game and this game will take you quite a while as well if you try to get all the Emblems and A-Ranks as well, so there's that, but if you just try and finish the story mode by itself with some or little chao raising then your looking at a solid 10 hour game.

I just finished Sonic Adventure 2, and I gotta say; Very few games are incredible. And this is one of those few. The plot is exceptional with a couple show-stopping plot twists at the end (I won't spoil them, you'll have to play it for yourself :)), the controls are great, and the level design is AMAZING. The bosses are amazing (some can be annoying, though), and it has plenty of replay value with the Chao Garden, and you should try to A-rank every stage (which of course I can't do XD) My only problem with this game might be with the grind rails in the final rush stage. But aside from that, this game should NOT be missed. It beats out the first game in the series by far.
Overall, I give this game a 10/10.

Aaaah...Far Cry 3, where can I begin with you?? Far Cry 3 is an open world action-adventure first-person shooter video game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft on November 29, 2012. Far Cry 3 is set on a tropical island between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. After a vacation goes wrong, protagonist Jason Brody must save his friends, who have been kidnapped by pirates and escape from the island and its unhinged inhabitants. This game gave me so many emotions because of the well written story, missions, cut scenes and music! I literally cried at one moment. The gameplay is absolutly fantastic! You can do so many things in this game. Driving, flying, hunting, killing pirates with a large variation of takedowns and a very big gallery of weapons. Far Cry 3 gives a RPG feel to it by crafting skins, medicine and other stuff to help you during the game. The graphics and the open world are gorgeous! Every corner of the Rook Island is beautiful and pleasant to the eye. The A.I. is one of the most advanced I've seen in recent years, animals from the island not only attack you if they feel threatened, but they also attack the pirates or your allies. Far Cry 3 has one of the most memorable and iconic video game characters, Vaas Montenegro. You'll love every scene and every moment when he's present and you will want more from him. This game gives a good moral: How far will you go to save your familly and friends? Yes, the game's protagonist, Jason Brody is like Walter White aka Heisenberg. He will start beeing imature and party-dude kind of person and during the game until the end, he will be a different person. Far Cry 3 will give you the feel of a hunter, at first killing will feel wrong, but in the end, it feels like victory. During or after you complete the story, you have many things to do. Hunting and side missions are not making any exception. Overall, Ubisoft gave all they had to make this, in my opinion, masterpiece. It's one of the last good games that Ubisoft really gave interest. I highly recommend this game to anyone. You won't regret it!
PERSONAL RATE: 10/10

Door Kickers is an Action/Strategy game which puts you in command of a S.W.A.T. team. you must use planning and tactics to complete the objective (such as rescuing hostages or defusing a bomb) and keep your squad alive.
The game is played from a top-down perspective and nearly all of the missions revolve around storming a building. there is a variety of weapons and gadgets to aid you in completing the objective. ( such as spy camera's to look under doors, or flashbangs to temporarily blind enemies) With the introduction of BETA. you can now customise the appearance of the member of your squad. as well as change their names and callsigns.
The game also includes a sort of skill tree which allows you to grant extra skills to your squad using points earned by completing levels. there is a variety of skills and more will be implemented as the game develops. (My favourite skill is the one that allows stealth members to hold fire until ordered to shoot)
The game also includes different types of S.W.A.T. members. like shotgunners. assualters. stealth ETC. each mission is different and requires careful planning and certain classes will be more efffective than others.
finally the game features steam workshop integration. making it possible to create and download user created maps, weapons, gadgets and more!
In conclusion. this is a game that is definately worth buying. if you like strategy games. You will like this. The game is currently in BETA and will be updated to include more gear and a campaign mode. i definately recommend it.

REVERSE WARNING: This is actually the only Early Access game that I bought without regretting it later.
Door Kickers is a solid top-down 2D tactical SWAT strategy / tactical / shooter title. You draw your troopers' paths with your mouse, place waypoints and commands and then watch the action unfold according to your plan. There is also the option to pause the action in real-time and switch orders on the fly. The game went through many iterations and improvements during early access, both frequent and meaningful in content and changes / fixes.
The biggest draws of the game (apart from the obvious - existing in a great genre that is virtually abandoned) is the fact that it has Steam Workshop support and an integrated level editor allowing for infinite content. When the core gameplay mechanics are as polished and as fun, even simple user-made maps can add tons of replayability to a game that is already quite large in beta form.
I bought this game in December 2013 and watched it blossom into the beautiful thing it is today, a couple of months before its final release. I recommend this wholeheartedly to anyone who is interested in the genre.
