I played through the first game and loved it, with my only complaint being that the game was too short and the last few levels were effortless.
Hotline Miami 2 brings some interesting new things into the mix, but unfortunately the overall experience falls short. Compared to the first game, the level design is horrendous. You seem to have very few options a lot of times, and playing the whole game melee-only doesn't seem possible. Running into an area, guns-blazing, isn't a good way to beat the levels.
Many of the rooms are huge, and you can't even see from one side to the other with aiming. This is a real problem since it really hurts your ability to track enemies in the area. Ontop of this, many levels seem to just have an absurd number of interior windows... so if you walk into an open area, you are within line-of-sight of multiple different areas, all filled with rifle-toting enemies. You're going to get shot and have to restart a LOT. Because of this, the best way to clear levels is to play them out very slowly, not wasting a shot. This is the complete opposite of the first game.
The game is fairly buggy at times as well, compared to the first. Doors in particular are damn near broken. Enemies get stuck in doors frequently, seem to stop in doorways, lose sight of you in door ways, etc. In some of the more ridiculous levels I pretty much just abused doorways and made the enemies funnel into them just to thin them out to make the levels actually enjoyable. The AI is insanely bad as well, perhaps it's just a line-of-sight issue, I'm not sure. You can often kill a guy next to a stationary enemy, and that enemy won't even react. AI just seem to patrol paths more than anything, but on some levels killing a guy with melee causes enemies from all the adjacent rooms to swarm you. Pretty inconsistent behavior.
The game still does a lot well... The music is still great, the graphics are unique and interesting, there's some interesting design behind the pause menu, things like that. The story seems less interesting, but probably ends up about the same.
The game itself just seems much harder in general, and a lot of your deaths feel like it's due to a lack of information / clarity for you to react to, instead of you just screwing up.  An example being a black dog patroling across a black floor. You will pretty much never notice him until he kills you the first time. Also, there are a ton of random objects on the ground that prevent you from going around. I found myself getting snagged on them often while trying to dodge and run around. Some of them seem like there would be enough room to walk by them, but there's not. More frustrations.
I can't really recommend this sequel unless you're a huge fan of the first game, have played it multiple times, love to memorize levels or enjoy relying on your reflexes to carry you through levels.

Perhaps in 5 years time, the game will be closer to what the developer envisioned. As for now, however, it will sit in my game library until it gets beyond a POC.

Door Kickers is an amazing example of tactical strategy done right.  It allows you to plan meticulously as you coordinate the actions of your team to deal with a multitude of law enforcement mission scenarios.  Once your plan is drafted execute and witness your officers engage; top down action rarely seems so tense.

Kicking down doors has never been so much fun. In fact, I don't remember the last time I had this much fun kicking down a door with my mighty boot of door bashiness.
I have been longing to play a tactical game of this sort. I was dissapointed by the previous Jagged Alliance (the kickstarter one looks nice, but time will tell), slightly bored like Frozen Synapse (which I might add, is a pretty damn good game, but the presentation didn't work out for me).  Door Kickers made the cut for me. Of course, we had the amazing X-Com. But there's something about Door Kickers. Is it the speed at which your plan is executed? The thrill of raiding a villa full of bad guys and unlucky hostages and making it out without a single casualty on the good guy side? Door Kicker is simply amazing.
Great presentation, sound and above all, gameplay. Amazing detailed top down views from your average training killhouse to villas and apartments. Great system for planning out your moves, and your swat guy armaments and tool are great, from trusty crowbar to m4s and boots of door bashing+1. Be it in real time or pausy-planning-unpausy-time, the gameplay feels rewarding. And it's always a pleasure taking down those horde of baddies :)
Door Kicker win the cake for me, as a rewarding, well thought out, tactical game.

Door Kickers. What can I say?
Door Kickers to me is a superb, real time, action-filled, strategic and sometimes infuriating Police game. Fancy taking charge of your own SWAT team that can kick down (almost any) door or blow it up? Want to shoot people and be overly happy when you complete a mission that took AGES but you finally mastered it? Of course you do and Door Kickers is it.
To be serious though the interface is very intuitive if sometimes a bit fiddly  and the stop-time FTL style mechanic means you can keep on top of everything even in the middle of a firefight. The only major thing wrong with Door Kickers is that you MUST be prepared to be patient and repeat missions: on more than one occasion I have yelled and got generally angry with both myself and the enemies, so yeah, be patient, it is worth it in the end. Few other minor things but excusable for a Beta!

Vermintide is a fantastic first person slasher/shooter game set in the Warhammer Endtimes universe.  It is very similar to Left4Dead: a team of 4 players tries to get from one point to another in each mission while completing objectives along the way. PROS:
*Each class has unique skills and further each weapon greatly changes how a class plays

CONS:
*If someone drops or you start a game with less than 4 players the computer AI companions are DUMB.  They split up, they don't get you up if you are down waiting for a revive... I've died while 3 computer AI players stood there fighting one ratling instead of getting me up (shouting at my screen the entire time, of course!)

Campaign review:
Mostly by-the-numbers Call of Duty campaign where you're taken on a linear, "roller coaster" and shown lots of whizz and bang without much interaction.
Some of the levels showed promise by allowing you to flank enemies and walk in more than one direction, but these innovative mechanics are short lived as you're taken back to the fun of pressing F to watch a bomb being planted, pressing F to watch an enemy being stabbed or pressing F to watch a door being opened.
Promise is shown further still as a lot of the levels revolve around the idea of stealthy infiltration, but again you're shackled by the game and end up watching most of what's happening which is a huge shame as some of the areas and scenarios could have been really fun.
The plot isn't actually bad, and the loading screen animations are quite nice to watch so following the story is easy. Unfortunately, they make you watch this fairly lengthy loading screen every time you change something in the graphics settings (They may have changed this in the latest patch).
Infamously poor optimisation, 'though not as bad as it was around release period. I also came across lots of odd behaviour from characters such as enemy deep sea divers doing the backwards swim animation but coming towards me extremely fast while shooting (Hilarious but also terrifying). Really, really poor texture work in places too.
I'd pick it up in the winter sale if it falls below the £5 mark but ultimately can't recommend it as it never allows you to have the fun it dangles in front of you.

Deadlight is a perfectly thrilling platformer for fans of Z-games and a catching one for the not-infected as well. Because I've already got fed up with the mindless beasts before they truly became popular in gaming culture, I cannot say that I'm flattered by their presence in the game. Yet, the athmosphere and the wonderfully crafted levels make it extremely fun - oh and by the way, not as easy as it first seems - to play.   The adventure doesn't take long really, it took me about 8 hours to finish it, passing the controller - with which the game operates smoothly! - to friends visiting at a party, fooling around to reach secrets, etc, so just taking my time.
It's another example where it clearly shows how much effort the dev-team has put into crafting and adjusting the environment untill they get the impression they have just dreamed of. If you have read any of my other reviews, you know just how much I appreciate that effort. Art to be more precise. You will actually be able to have a glance at the brainstorming that took place, as the team will grant you with additional artwork from the dev-phase. The best thing for me were the cut-scenes. Splendid 2D art smartly animated. Neat.
All in all you get your hands on a platformer that will stick you down to your seat, the action pushing you ever forward, while the astonishing athmosphere will surely blow your mind. Contagion is a zombie survival game with a number of game mode focused on online play. In the game you can either play as a zombie or as a person when playing pvp which is fun to play both sides. As the person you can do your basic FPS mechanics and as a zombie you are the normal zombie exept you have a small speed boost and you can call a horde to your side from any zombies near to you. Theres also an extraction game mode where you have to try to save civilians without letting anyone die. There are more game modes to suchas one that can act like a story guiding you through a map. I personally found myself playing a pvp all alone just for the fun of blasting zombies away without worry of someone else trying to kill me.
When it comes to inventory, you have 4 weapon slots and you can carry so much ammo it's not a worry, but that leads me into the next thing, getting ammo and supplies.
You start off every match witha random melee wapon and a pistol of some sort. From there, you must scavenge. You must break into peoples houses, movie theaters, malls, really anywhere and search high and low for things (don't worry about how the locals feel about this, they've already been infected). You can find anything from med kits to nail guns to wooden planks to assault rifles to varrying types of ammo to an occasional greanade (just try not to blow yourself up). This is a game where your shots count though and you shouldn't fire until you know it's going to be a head shot. A zombie can take a very large sum of bullets to the body or a single shot to the head.
Contagion did do a nive job with the models and what they look like when they take damage for the bodies. When you put a round in an undead's head, you can see a large exit would on the other side. If you blast their leg with a shot gun, it may come right off. If you hammer away at their chest, you may leave a nice cavity there. The point is, you can blast an enemy to smitherines and you'll be able to tell.
In the game you can also make a 'home base' type area such as when you're in the suburban map. The game provides nail guns and planks of wood if you look around to help secure an area. You can make this place a stock pile, a temporary place to just sit for a minute, or simply slow the zombies down for a few seconds while you run for your life out the back door.
Contagion also has large maps, especially the city one which I think is something like 9 full sized blocks (also if you look enough, this is the one game to put a gun store in it if you need a couple extra rounds. *wink wink, nudge nudge*) This is great when needing to run from another player or when you just feel like exploring.
The graphics in the game are good... but only at night. I've noticed that durring the daytime nothing looks as good as it could be, and though that may just be a time/budget thing to make it look good, just try not to look too closely at textures in the sunlight. When it comes to night time it does look very pleasing to the eye with their lighting engine and the reflections in everything. You can see this which helps to show off what it can do and with the lack of sunlight makes it so you don't focus on any below-par textures.
Lastly for what I have to say about the looks of the enviroment is rain. Just rain. It looks very nice compared to many other games I have played especially with the lighting engine to help show it off. You can see small ripples if you look close enough to where a rain drop has landed and little things like that.
Finally, I would just like to point out the sound. They did a great job with the sound like when you step on a piece of fallen fence you can hear it shake, of when you step on broken glass and hear it crack. My point is, it sounds nice.
The good-
-Great lighting engine (if anything it's a tad too bright with the flashlight, but that's fairly small depending on where you are
-Zombies look great when heavily damaged
-Nice sound
-big maps
-good, serious atmosphere
-if you look close enough, most of the little extra stuff like books do actually have titles and such.
The bad-
-player zombies feel a bit underpowered (but thats probably to help balence)
-map size can make multiplayer difficult
-revolves anound the same mechanics most of the time, it's more just who you're shooting at.
The ugly-
-It may just be me but I've noticed a case of "fuzzy screen" when playing this that usually doesn't happen with other games
-don't look at textures to close in the day time
Rating: 7.5-8/10

A very melancholy and nihilistic game focused on gruesome violence and horrible things happening to horrible people and somehow you still feel some pity… sometimes.  This game is more fractured than the original, frequently jumping between different times, characters, and locations.  The story takes a while to get into, and you need to play the first game to get the full emotional impact, but it is surprisingly good, thought provoking even.  If not very depressing.  Mechanically the game feels smoother for the most part, however I found myself frequently frustrated by enemies miles away killing me, getting stuck on furniture, and dying due to the crosshair jumping around after I killed an enemy it was locked onto.  Some new characters are fun, like the murder swans, but most play like Jacket… however dodge roll is kind of useless, it gets me killed more times than it saved me.  There are some odd level designs, and some levels overstay their welcome (like the boat level), but those minor issues aside, the game is pretty solid and a lot of fun, though it does make you feel a bit bad.  Beat it in 10 hours.

I thought about my review for a long time and came to the conclusion that several issues render me unable to recommend this game. Here's why:
The story of the game might be good, as well as the way it's being told - yet there are a lot of goofs I don't want to spoil right now.
Also, the port was done very poorly. It often crashes, especially after using ALT+TAB. I also often spawned only to find me falling through the map a few seconds afterwards, which required a complete restart of the game to fix that.
Controller controls are not very optimized. You will often jump into the wrong direction or fall even though you are sure you pressed the jump button at the correct time.
The way the character moves and behaves feels extremely bulky, which is very unfortunate for a survival game in which you need to avoid enemies most of the time.
Also, the level design is pretty boring. Every map feels like the previous one and so forth. But that might be an issue of 2.5D-games in general.

It's more of an action adventure game than ARK and more of a survival game than GRAV. It does both very well. The game world is interesting, the story is enjoyable, and the building/creation system is impressive (but mostly optional if you prefer to stick to adventure gaming). As you get farther into the game, throw in some colony management that reminds me a bit of Kenshi.
Although the game has been out for awhile it does still have some serious bugs (semi-frequent game crashes). The dev team is still active and the game recently went through an engine upgrade, so there is hope these will be worked out in the next few months.
Overall it's just a lot of fun, if you like survival adventure/creation in a sci fi setting.

I'll happily admit I'm not very good at rythmn games but I tend to enjoy them regardless. However this game had some issues which rendered it nearly unplayable, despite my greatest efforts to fix them.
Firstly, there's the incoming symbols and obstacles. They were nearly a blur and neigh impossible to focus on until I found out that you could zoom out the camera. That helped, but it wasn't quite enough. I also had to turn off the moving background to focus better.
Next there was the lag. I'm not entirely sure the reason for this but there was massive lag at the beginning of a song, and usually at the end as well. This may simply be the song sync and saving of my results, but it was a near-standstill until I returned to the menu.
I'm not sure if its just me, but I also found the symbols a bit confusing at times. I don't feel that there was enough indication to which direction to press, but as I said, that may just be me.
The good thing about this game is the fact that you can put any song or even video audio in and it'll auto generate a level and button prompts. This was something I would've loved in Kickbeat and it was done very well here.
I suppose that in summary, if you are a hardcore rythmn game player or just looking to drop £4 on a sale item, grab this. Otherwise, if you're more of a casual player of these games like me, or  sometimes struggle to focus on a screen when there's too much going on, go get something else.

If you see the screenshots, that's literally all the game is.  The menu is barebones, the options are nearly non-existant, and the running never changes.
That would all be fine, except for one MAJOR problem -- there is no way to create your own custom map, and the music autodetection is imperfect.  It's not *terrible* by any means, but with every song I tested (Mostly Vocaloid -- heck, it's Miku running there!), there were distinct times where the map I was playing did not match with the beat at all.  Most of the time, it feels like it *almost* matches what's going on with the song, but it never feels like a cohesive experience.
If this were a free game, I would recommend it.  It's flawed and feels incomplete, but there's some fun to be had when it works.  There are several games online, for free, with already created custom maps for most songs out there.  The bad autogenerated tracks coupled with the inability to customize your own really kills the experience.

Sonic Adventure 2 has finally made its way to PC here on STEAM.
If you've played Sonic Adventure you might want to know that in terms on in between levels, this game is vastly different as this time around you choose between two sides of the main story instead of 6 characters with each of their own story (all of them still being connected though). In this game however, the two sides follow one main story, just from different perspectives. There is the Hero side and the Dark side, each side has 3 playable characters with different game types of their own. The game types are Adventure Stages (Sonic/Shadow), Action Shooter stages (Tails/Eggman) and Treasure Hunting stages (Knuckles/Rouge). Though this game is, in my personal opinion, a very enjoyable game, it shows some aging with minor bugs/glitches throwing you through platforms and between the tiniest gaps, but that happens rarely. If you haven't got any ver. of this game yet (Dreamcast or Gamecube), I would highly recommend getting this as it is available here on Steam at a verry reasonable price. If you purchase the SA2 Battle DLC you will get additional game modes for the Multi Player section AND a new mini game in Chao Garden.

Love Sonic Adventure 2? This port is very faithful. You need a good cpu to run it, and if you don't, you're better off emulating it.
If you don't have a sense of nostalgia for this game, the controls take getting used to, and doing the ring dash is off at times. Worse case, when you have to do a ring dash in the air as Sonic after getting the Bounce Bracelet.
You have 3 main character types. Speed (Sonic and Shadow), Shooting (Tails and Eggman), and Treasure Hunting (Knuckles and Rouge). Speed is what you expect and works just fine for the most part except what I explained a bit ago. Shooting is much slower, but pretty fun to shoot things and gain huge combos. Treasure Hunting can either go in your favor, or frustrate you, depending on your luck. All 3 have really tight control, so you can stop on a dime.
With linking to a portable device gone, the Chao system is more limited now. You can't interact with Chao from other files, Special Chao and even Maria's theme are impossible. However, with the trainer linked at the bottom, it becomes possible. It'll depend on how you feel about using something like a trainer. The rest remains the same.
I very highly recommend a controller for this. It's much more difficult to control with the keyboard. With a keyboard, you can only run, never walk since a keyboard is digital and not analog. And you can never be precise with your movement. Even when I first tried a keyboard, I instantly got thrown off. Bottom line, use a 360 controller, or be like me and use a PS3 controller using the "Better DS3" tool.
What's really cool about this PC version is the amount of mods made by fans. So anyone who misses the cheats from the previous versions, can use them here. Most of the mods are for looks, but there's Character Selection, Spin Dash for the alternate speed characters (Amy and Metal Sonic), and even a Super Sonic mod.
Another mod that is note worthy is the Chao Stat Multiplier. This increases any stat increases a Chao gets by 5 times. So for example, instead of +2, you get +10. If you ever felt getting stats up took forever, this cuts down the fat. This is also good if you don't wish to use a trainer outside of getting the Maria theme.
Despite the downsides from this version and the initial game, if you can look past them, I highly recommend this game.

A zombie platformer which offers an interesting premise that falls short in writing, mechanics and game production. The games writing is often bland, or uses language that no one uses today, i.e. using sayings such as comrades instead of friends, or yelling towards a specific friend saying friend instead of their name. This is jarring and immersion breaking. Mechanics such as controls are ill tempered, and often fight with what the game wants you to do. Jumping is a pain, yet it places you through speed trials with unrefined controls. Finally the game is filled with bug such as audio not playing properly during cut scenes or rendering issues such as rooms missing objects, or completely going black.
A positive to take away from this game is that the premise is very interesting for a zombie game. It mixes a bit of survival, with platforming and puzzle elements. It was a fun experience if not short, but worth the 15 dollars. If you can get past the glaring issues this game has the potential to be a fun game.

I adored the first Hotline Miami. It was a masterpiece of insanely entertaining and rewarding action wrapped in an extremely visceral aesthetic and just a little hint of creepy weirdness.
This is just crap. The larger levels are probably the main reason everything breaks. Larger levels means more backtracking when you die (so you want to play safer), more deaths from off-screen (which is just brutally unfair), more reliance on guns (which aren't as cool as melee) and more use of that awful panning camera control. It all just boils down to standing behind a door and waiting for the idiotic AI to run through so you can kill with impunity.
Add to that the change to the mask system that mainly just limits playstyles without that many fun additions (The Duck siblings are cool, when the shooter duck doesn't get stuck in a doorway... which he does, all the time).
The core gameplay is great. Kicking in a door and killing 3 dudes with 2 melee weapons and a curb stomp in 5 seconds is exhilarating... but the first game did that. And it did it better.

Sonic Adventure 2 finally gets its deserved port to the PC platform. It's a fast-paced action platformer that expands on the gameplay of it's prequel. It isn't the most polished game out there and it is definitely showing its age, as it was an early 2000's title. If you like timed challenges, love racing the clock and enjoy spatial dynamics in a game then Sonic Adventure 2 is great for you. Players who prefer more abstract gameplay, dislike challenges involving physics and moving objects, or otherwise have a low affinity for platform games will not enjoy this title as much.
The port itself is a mixed bag. It supports high resolutions and the 360 controller, both of which make playing on PC a better experience. On the other hand, there are issues involving loading as the game will sometimes refuse to load if certain programs are running like flux and rainlendar (anything that uses rendered overlays). The launcher is also poorly designed.

Sonic Adventure 2 has an incredible reputation behind it, with many deeming it the best Sonic game ever created. While perhaps the most stylish, it is also poorly dubbed (with characters frequently interrupting and cutting each other off), requires you to complete the infuriatingly frustrating Knuckles, Rouge, Eggman and Tails levels to get to this game's little bit of meat, suffers from the Sonic series' infamous slew of bugs, and seems to constantly attempt to top itself in chauvinism. Even if you can look beyond the flaws of the game itself (as many have), or beat the game enough that you can just do the Sonic and Shadow stages, you have to be ready for this interpretation of the game to frequently disconnect due to its requirement of always on DRM that frequently malfunctioned on my machine (ironically making it easier to play a pirated copy of this game than a legitimate one).
This is a very disappointing sequel to the fantastic Sonic Adventure, which unless you're the most die-hard of Sonic fans, I suggest you avoid at all costs (especially the PC version).

I decided to play this game after beating DX on the GameCube only because it came in a Sonic Bundle that saved me $5 dollars on the racing games that were the only ones I cared about and included every other Sonic game on Steam as a bonus to me. The boss fights were fun, the stages were fun, the story was pretty good for revolving around a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ blue hedgehog. It really feels like a lot more work and thought went into this. The characters are annoying, yet I was entertained throughout. Sonic is an♥♥♥♥♥in this game. Anyhow there are still flaws in the fact that the treasure hunting sequences are broken more than they were in the last game and when you go to space as Rouge the bat you will want to break something. I stood up and went to grab a drink after another intense round of Vermintide.  I had some punishing rounds where the tide turned in favor of the Skaven in the blink of an eye.  And on the other hand I found a group that didn't seem to mind carrying me while I try to gain some levels and get some better gear.  After all this, the thought ocurred to me: Vermintide is repetitive.  I immediately had a flash of disappointment.
My initial impression was probably the chemical aftermath in my brain.  My first few rounds I was frantically scanning rooftops or looking over my shoulder worrying another rat was crawling out of a crack in the walls.  It didn't take long before I was ready to start charging up a power attack when I felt like a rat was behind me.  My eyes were darting across the screen, I was constantly worrying about keeping up with my teammates, or rushing to someone who had fallen.  After my first experience playing, I was probably recovering from the intensity of NORMAL.  I should have started on easy, but I'm glad I didn't.  I got to see how difficult and chaotic things can be from a random group.  I also got to feel that surge of excitement from a well organized vicory after a crushing defeat.
When I was cramming in a round before work the following moring, I thought: being repeatedly amazing is just what I want from a new release.  The satisfying *splak* of my axe swinging into a rat man's neck, picking off a Packmaster before he pulls one my teammates down an alley, and attempting to stand my ground to a rat ogre are just a few things that I could do all day.
The sound in Vermintide is very well done.  The voice acting from the character is entertaining and helpful.  The ominous sounds that surround you are enough to increase your heart rate.  You can hear the sinister voices of Gutter Runners while they wait in the shadows ready to pounce on an unsuspecting noob like myself.  When you hear the horn in the distance you might immediately realize you need to close the gap between you and your teammates.
Pair the sound with the dark and gritty feel visuals and you've got a fantastic immerision into the Warhammer universe.  The cities are on fire and abandoned, aside from a rat in every corner.You really do feel like one of the last remaining shreds of hope to expel the Skaven menace.

I adored the first Hotline Miami. It was a masterpiece of insanely entertaining and rewarding action wrapped in an extremely visceral aesthetic and just a little hint of creepy weirdness.
This is just crap. The larger levels are probably the main reason everything breaks. Larger levels means more backtracking when you die (so you want to play safer), more deaths from off-screen (which is just brutally unfair), more reliance on guns (which aren't as cool as melee) and more use of that awful panning camera control. It all just boils down to standing behind a door and waiting for the idiotic AI to run through so you can kill with impunity.

This game presents itself as "decent" and in many ways the game is good. However I feel this game isn't worth the money (Even if its cheap) for what seems to me a pretty terrible system of playing "To the beat" of your songs.
I already want to start with a simple fact. You are buying a game that generates the levels for you. Thats all the work that they need to put into making this. The rest is you using songs other people have made and being pleased with the outcome that in my opinion masks how terrible this generator can be.
The songs I used ranged a lot in quality and I played on all the difficulties to test whether or not the reason I felt the songs I was playing felt horrible was not based on how many notes they shoved in. I played Kanye, The 1975, Deadmau5 and countless others I can't be bothered to name. I feel like this game appeals to and pleases the people who mindlessly play in full belief that they are playing "To the beat" The truth is you are not most of the time. Sure if you want to just click away pretending you are playing "To the beat" because every so often you hear a beat as you click a note then be my guest. Many of the reviews are positive saying "Feels good" or the reviews are the usual joke reviews that actually offer no real information... I don't understand these people. All you have to do is actually pay attention to the song and you will notice that half the notes are just shoved in as filler and when the song has a part with a decent beat for some reason the generator ignores this and sends the character into a long note instead of several small ones "To the beat" This sytem of the level changing as the pace gets faster (or slower) is also pretty terrible. Several songs will go into full swing and the generator keeps my character in the same speed (yellow) The yellow speed is basically Melody (The character) at full running speed. This is a decent speed however when the song is at full swing with so much going on your adrenaline should be pumping for some reason the generator doesn't boost you into the pink speed in which Melody is flying at the fastest speed she can go. Every time this happened I would actually get angry because it feels so out of place and when I get angry at the game I start to loose focus and miss notes. Something to add is several times while at full speed the song might quickly drop to a slow speed for no more than 1-2 seconds I mean this in the sense that the creator of the song may have a quick drop in speed as part of the song or in something like Kanye when he takes a breath mid way through a verse. The generator sadly ruins the whole pace and suddenely my character is walking along at the slowest speed for literally 2 seconds then boosts to full again. It feels so horrible and looks terrible.
The difficulties are another issue. I don't think they are "Hard" instead the harder you go on the list the more notes they shove in your face. Not to mention when I played the highest difficulty the notes where still out of place. They placed more notes but most of them were still not "To the beat" You might think me quoting "To the beat" is getting repetative? Well that's because this game strives of it being a rythm game. If your main selling point is playing "To the beat" then I'd hope that I didn't sit there getting mad everytime the song just does not work. Some songs work well, the best song I played so far was "Endless fantasy" by Anamanaguchi. The song picked up in the right areas and I noticed a lot of notes hitting in time. However when I put this song into the highest difficulty it was terrible again. Parts of the song where one single note was in the song the game decides because this is the highest difficulty it will shove several notes one after another at different colours etc etc. That isn't good or even decent in my eyes. It's pointless.......
Basically buy this game in a sale and you can play it if have nothing else to play or maybe your internet is down and you are unable to log into Counter strike or some other game that needs internet. This game is good if you are happy with feeling like you are playing "To the beat" until you really take notice. Maybe I am just too picky but if a game is going to make me pay to use songs others made with the promise it will feel fluent and good then I am going to be very picky about this. I paid £3.99 for this and at the moment I have played less then 2 hours and don't intend to play much more unless I really am scraping the bottom of the barrel for something to do.

I like its aspects of realism and teamwork.
I don't like its lack of hitscan and animation sync. If you're close to a zombie, it literally hits you two seconds before it actually swings its arm, even with a low latency. Ironsights aim tends to be off with some weapons, and since a core 'feature' of the game is a need to conserve ammo, most of its bugs tend to be very counterproductive and make the game nearly impossible in some situations.
I also REALLY don't like the lack of configurable options. No option to turn off friendly fire even in strictly cooperative mode, no flexible dedicated servers, nothing. There are four difficulties, and they all affect the same thing without any variance: Damage taken & dealt, amount of ammo to be found, etc.
I'm not getting my hopes up with this game, yet. It seems to be one of those types of games fitting under a 'great idea, poor execution' category, but the game itself is still far from being 'complete' and is being worked on at a gradual pace, so maybe after several more patches and a few more updates, I'll be able to recommend this, but for now, I'd recommend staying away.

Pros
- Pretty good character animation.
- The guns (though used sparingly) feel nice and are satisfying.
- Environments looked pretty nice, y'know, as far the whole post-apocalypse thing goes.
- Puzzle sections aren't too bad, provided you aren't getting pressured by something. (See Con #4)
Cons
- Clunky movement in tight spaces and in combat
- Mostly poor voice acting
- A pretty short and fairly anti-climactic final level with a really dull twist ending with a side of annoying supporting character whining at you. Her actions in the last cutscene actually infuriated me, tbh.
- Any tense set piece (especially toward the end) can easily loose its grip when you die from missing a small environment clue or Randall not drawing his gun fast enough.
- Can't kill zombies approaching you from the background until they're right on top of you, even though you have a gun.
- Wanna jump or swing your axe in a certain direction? Just point one way and press the button you want and Randall will just do it in the opposite direction you wanted him to.
- The last half of the game in general was chalk full of frustrating little things overall (and that's pretty much everything I mentioned above).
That about sums it up. This is the first game I actually felt strongly enough to write a negative review about for the game itself, and not a botched port job.

I recommend this game because its fun to run around, dig, build, create.  One can experiment with architectural design.  That's enough for me to be satisfied but the game as a story has major problems:
Be prepared to be frustrated with bugs in the story line.  I've played this game on and off for a while, seen it go through quite a few versions.  On an earlier version I was able to play through story mode pretty far, as far as the developers had written.  My saves were erased with an upgrade and given the amount of time I had spent crafting a delightful and luxurious base, I became discouraged.  I tried to restart, to plod through the storyline with its many fetch-type quests but with another upgrade those saves got erased too.  Recently I came back to the game and have been having fun with it again.  Strangely, though, I cannot get very far in the story quests.  They are extremely buggy.  The story quests appear to have actually become quite a bit MORE buggy since the last time I'd played it.  I can't get past the first quest (a critical character has irretrievably disappeared, and was just reading about the second quest having a high likelihood of a massive game ending type bug also.
It is difficult to program games and I respect the hard work.  That being said, I recommend the developers focus on making the core gameplay stable instead of pursuing shiny, new, additional features with each update. I fear/suspect the game has been dropped as a serious development project and that core bugs will not be fixed.  It appears to be used as a template for experimentation instead.  That's cool but It would be nice to be able to actually play it.

Let me preface this brief review by saying: I am bad a rhythm games and have honestly never played one before, and will need significant practice to really get the fullest out of this game. Since this is my first rhythm game, I can't say what, if any, features come standard in games of its kind or what's unique about it. That said, let's take a look pro/con-wise.
TL;DR VERSION: fun, simple game, rather addictive once you get the hang of it; made for a pretty good intro to rhythm games imo; using my own music is great but not all music translates well (acoustic songs or "fuzzy" mastering rate poorly on compatibility); possibly better played with a keyboard rather than controller.
LONG VERSION:
PROS
-use your own library OR in-game tracks
-audio/visual latency calibration (can't vouch for how well it works though, didn't seem to change much tbh)
-slick visual design with a bit of avatar customization
-game will rate how well it can create levels out of songs (no tempo, poor, acceptable, good, excellent)
-customizable difficulty (allows you to use existing difficulty settings as a template, then change things like respawn time and sensitivity)
-flexible control scheme on controller (buttons and directions can be interchangeable on some difficulties)
-it's FUN, which is really important!
CONS
-works best with only certain kinds of music (This is most things with a strong, heavy beat. Songs with "fuzzy" sounding keyboards/snares will confuse the game even if there is a good beat. Songs with predominantly acoustic instruments also do not rate well. Sorry, jazz and swing fans.)
-probably best played with a keyboard (or my xbox controller is lame, but moving my thumb over the directional buttons caused a lot of mistakes while playing)
-slightly confusing menu when navgating your own libraries for music (uses only directional keys, a designated "back" button might be nice for going up folder levels)
-minor gripe: the "B" button/right direction icons are pink, and that's kind of confusing (I get it fits with the aesthetic, this isn't even really a complaint it's just me being petty)

Actually works pretty well - I find myself doing much better on levels generated from songs I know well.  Nice that it has many different difficulty settings (as well as a customizable one or a "the game plays itself" visualization mode).  Lots of visual mods for it as well as being easy to mod, itself (includes a mod tool to make it very easy to make your own characters and color themes).  Very full-featured, slick and relaxing.  And the game has as many levels as you have music in your library!  Definitely recommended!

This is quite possible the most frustrating game I have ever played in my entire life. And I have been playing video games since the original Nintendo. The gameplay design is absolutely atrocious.
In any modern game, when there is only a single important object that can be activated by the player, it is usually either highlighted with a bright outline or a button prompt appears for the button that should be used. Deadlight does this... But only when it feels like it. It is very inconsistent as there are many, MANY times where I VERY clearly noticed that this was not the case. There is often zero clue on what needs to be done and I guarantee many people will get stuck. Because I have been playing video games for decades, I could often figure it out. But I admit that there were a few times where the solution was so completely non-obvious that I had to look it up. And when I found out the solution, I cursed out loud at how idiotic of a game design decision that was.
The unfortunate thing about this is that it leads to you dying over and over and over and over again. If you enjoy dying repeatedly and re-doing sections of levels ad nauseam, then this is the game for you! If not, you will find this game incredibly frustrating like I did.
The problem is that often deaths are NOT your fault. It's not like Dark Souls where you die because of lack of skill or mastery. In this game you die because the designers simply want you to die and re-do the level.
- For example, there is one level where you are being chased by a helicopter and you are running away. All of a sudden, you trip over some boxes, fall to the ground and get shot by the helicopter. Those boxes weren't highlighted, and they look EXACTLY like any other stack of boxes in the entire game. The NINETY-NINE other times in the game the stack of boxes was in the background and you ran right past them, but only THIS time the designers decided that you would indeed trip and die. Since they're not highlighted, you would have no idea whatsoever to jump over them the first time you play this level. So you die and have to replay the past 5 minutes since the last checkpoint.
- Another example is when you are following a certain character and being chased. They crawl through a hole in a fence and keep going. So you crouch, but you can't go through the hole in the fence. You die and have no idea why. So you re-play from the checkpoint and die again. This time you notice that you were shot. But from where?? You re-play from the checkpoint and notice that you were indeed shot from NOWHERE. There is no enemy. You literally get shot and the bullet appeared out of thin air. WHAT THE F??? After looking it up, you realize that you have to climb OVER the fence. Why can the other character crawl through the hole in the fence, but you cannot? WHAT THE F??? Why???
These are just two examples. Multiply this DOZENS of times and you start to see why this game is incredibly frustrating.
Not only that, but the controls are sluggish and horribly tuned:
- Very often you need to climb a fence and then swap to the other side. Pressing right to swap to the other side for some unknown reason sometimes swaps you to the right side and BACK to the left side. What??? And then you die of course because you're being chased by something.
- Or sometimes you need to climb over a fence and drop off of it. But there is some sort of delay that you cannot simply climb over and drop off. The game makes you wait a second or two while you mash the drop button, but it's too late. So of course, you die once again and have to replay the past 5 minutes.
- Or the game makes it so you have to time your jump PERFECTLY at the last centimeter before the end of a platform. Otherwise you die and have to replay the section again.
- Or you run, jump, double-jump, wall hang, etc all perfectly and are proud of your having gotten through it. But the building is crumbling so even though you think you're safe, you get crushed by concrete, die, and have to repeat it all.
- Or sometimes you run and jump past zombies on the screen. Sometimes you do the exact same thing and the zombies are like an impenetrable wall. Of course you die.
- Or you're running to the right (hold Shift and D) and have to jump and climb often (W and Space). Put your fingers on these buttons. Or imagine doing so on a keyboard. Now, you also have to crouch quickly to roll through a fence hole (press Ctrl). Try pressing Ctrl while also pressing all the other buttons on one hand. It's very awkward, and almost impossible to get perfectly in the heat of battle like the game expects you to. I had to move my right hand under my left hand to reach Ctrl. And of course, needless to say, getting it right meant a lot of deaths.
The story itself is too sparse to be worthwhile. The story is basically just to find your family, but the story sequences are about 1% of the game with the other 99% of it being frustrating gameplay as described above. When I got to the end all I thought was, "That's it???" Moronic beyond belief. The only reason I finished the game was so I could delete it without having the game staring at me in my Steam backlog. Now I can get rid of it forever and never have to see it again.
If you dislike frustrating gameplay, I GUARANTEE you will be better off having skipped this game.

Deadlight is, to be sure, an interesting game. It has a decent enough storyline, and has gorgeous art. But these positive traits can't save it, first and foremost from its clunky and often frustrating controls. A platform, especially one with a number of timed and scripted sequences, needs to have crisp controls. Not only are the controls often disagreeable, performing actions you never intended, but there are a decent number of sequences where the 'correct' path isn't obvious - a man will appear at the end of a long hallway you're running down to avoid being shot and will shoot you. That isn't intuitive level design, but instead a necessity that the player repeat, and fail due in no part to their abilities, a sequence in order to finish it. Finally, the voice acting is below average, removing any real semblance of immersion I felt.

Great use-your-own-song game with a fantastic song analysis algorithm. Recommended.
First generation technology of this sort of thing was pretty bad. Vib Ribbon for the PS1 is the first game I know of that tried, but Audiosurf and Beat Hazard made it very popular in the early 2010's. While they improved the formula significantly, it still mostly seemed to just detect the BPM and 'pulse' the levels to the rhythm, changing gameplay elements as the song's speed or volume changed. These games required a pretty good deal of your imagination filling in the blanks to really feel like you were playing the song, not just playing a game with background music.
Not so with Melody's Escape, which feels very, very 'right'. I played through an album's worth of music with varied tempos, musical styles, and instrumentation and I would say that it felt like I was playing a hand-crafted track about 85% of the time. This absolutely blows previous games of the genre out of the water.
As for the gameplay, if you ever played Vib Ribbon, this is pretty much exactly that. It's very solid and time-tested rhythm gaming. Hit the button when you see the symbol.
This is a good way to chill out and experience an album in as relaxed or intense of an environment as you like. The difficulty options in this game are very varied.
If you like rhythm games or just listening to music, Melody's Escape is your go-to game. Once you try it, you won't be able to go back to Audiosurf.

Sonic Adventure 2 is, in my opinion, one of the best Sonic games of all time. Hell, it's my personal favorite. It has two story modes, the Good side and the Dark side. The good side features the characters Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles. The Dark side features Doctor Ivo "Eggman" Robotnik, and two new characters that made their debut in this game, Shadow the Hedgehog and Rouge the Bat. Both sides offer speed stages, which feature the two hedgehogs, treasure hunting stages, featuring Knuckles and Rouge, and mech suit shoot-em-up stages, featuring Tails and Dr. Eggman. This game did so many things right, I can hardly point out any flaws. Some of the gameplay mechanics get repetitive, the power-ups can seem like too much of a hassle, and getting the highest rank on every mission requires weeks, if not months of dedication. All in all, I definitely reccommend this game to any fan of Sonic the Hedgehog, or just SEGA in general.

Super little game. Fun enough at the moment that even if development stopped for some reason I'd not feel I'd wasted any money and they're adding plenty of other features/content as development goes on anyway.
If you played the old Rainbow 6 then it has similarities to the planning phase of that but can play/pause as you go (and control the officers while they're running your plan for desperate tweaks etc); I'd be tempted to compare the positioning etc to Frozen Synapse too.
The idea is to achieve the goal of the level; at the moment one of, kill everyone, rescue the hostage/s, make the arrest or disarm the bomb.  There are other goals to get better ratings on each level which are to beat a certain time and to keep as many of your chaps up as possible.
Advancement is both by individual cops gaining in ability and rank, and "Squad Doctrine" group training options.
Gear is selectable both by a class (which can be changed per mission) and choices within that class- which specific guns, armour and gadgets your chap will carry into the mission.  Some of the choices at the moment are fairly irrelevant and down to small preferences, others will have a big effect on how you go through the mission.
POST RELEASE additional comments:
There are a selection of single missions; randomly generated single missions; mods from the workshop and campaigns.  The single missions are sort of training for the campaigns really, both yourself, and leveling your troops/unlocking gear.  The campaigns themselves are perma-death but with restarts though there is iron-man mode which doesn't allow restarting. All in all a pretty vast amount of prepared content and then there are all the mods and randomly generated content making for a pretty near infinite game...and you'll almost certainly want to do individual bits multiple times too.
I've gone through the single missions multiple times now and there's still tactical improvements, nuances etc to learn.  They've updated adding more content and more is still to come.
If you like tactical stuff just do yourself a favour and buy this game.

Doorkickers is an indie RTS/Puzzle game which involves you leading a SWAT team through missions. I've been following this game since late Alpha and have enjoyed it since it's early form. The gameplay is quite simple, but is hard to master.
Basically you give your team check points to go to through the mission area. You tell them where to go, where to face, what to use and so on. It's somewhat similar to the mission planning of the old Rainbow Six games but now in live action, with a live pause available.
The game features five classes that your officers can pick from. Pointman, Assaulter, Breacher, Stealth and Shield. The Pointman is the fastest through the door, but only wields a handgun. The Assaulter packs either an SMG or an assault rifle and is best at ranged gun fights. Breachers wield shotguns and can blow doorlocks off. Stealth wield silenced weapons and move quieter. Shield men wield large shields that stop bullets. In my opinion, most of the classes are useful, but I don't really use the shields as they are slow, and are doomed if they are flanked.
There is about 80 single missions, 3 campaigns, a random mission generator and an simple editor so there is a lot of content on offer. The campaigns aren't very story driven, at all. There isn't a paragraph describing any story. I'm not saying it ruins the experience but it would have been nice to have that. Officers do take injuries during missions and can die, but this only really affects the campaign. The campaigns are quite short, but entertaining, and are worth replaying for experience points and stars (explained later).
Although this game is mainly about planning, there is a bit of luck involved. I'd say it's 9/10 planning and 1/10 luck. Just know that♥♥♥♥♥♥poor planning leads to♥♥♥♥♥♥poor performance. One great thing about this game, is you can wing it, or plan the whole mission out (which gives a bonus in EXP).
You unfortunately do have to unlock equipment during the game. Troopers level up during missions, and your entire squad levels up as well. Leveling troopers grants them better speed with shooting and using tools and accuracy. Leveling the squad grants doctrine points which grant all members improved abilities such as accuracy boosts, and one shot door breaching. It also gives access to more classes, as you only start with pointmen.
Another thing worth noting is that you have to unlock weapons, by acquiring stars during missions. You get one for completing, one for having all troopers alive and one for beating it under time. It can be challenging getting all 3 stars on some missions but the rewards are worth it.
One complaint I will make is that you have to erase all of your checkpoints ahead of a checkpoint if you want to make changes. This can make it more time consuming to change plans. I also find that sometimes I accidentally erase points which can be very frustrating.
Another issue is the new story mechanic. Some missions have multiple levels but to be honest changing between them is quite awkward in my opinion and I feel the game would be better without them.
My other complaint is that this game doesn't have a solid tutorial. Fortunately you can practice all you like on the single missions without an issue.
The graphics of this game are quite simple, but I honestly think it's unfair to expect better from a 3 man indie team considering the scale of this game, and it's certainly better looking than a Unity engine game and to be honest the menu background looks great.
Doorkickers has been my first adventure into PC indie gaming, and easily the best. A small, and passionate team who actually listen to the players, and use the advice to develop a competent and entertaining game that was realistically achievable. I'd give Doorkickers a 9/10.

This is for the MP aspect / I'm not a hater of C.O.D and I haven't played Advanced warfare or BO2 enough to compare but in my opinion this game is by far the worst Call of Duty I have played.
-Reason one - Optimization! -
This game runs like sh!t, I can run BF4 60fps but this game dips below 30 more than it should and stuttering and slowdown in critical moments make this the main reason this game sucks, but not the main reason the game is the worst in the series.
-Reason two - Netcode and general gunplay -
Call of Duty in my experience over the years when it comes to netcode has always been "OK", nothing special but i've never encountered it as a problem until now. The death's around corners and the constant non registering of hits are what bring this game down.
The gunplay suffers hugely to the netcode, my reason for thinking this is that ive noticed the "Time to death" which is the amount of time on average it takes to kill or be killed during encounter is around half a second'ish lower than the other games. You're probaly thinking by that "what differance does it make?" well the other C.O.D's gave you chance to react to being attacked in the other games (to a degree, insta kills still happened) and this gives the impression of one sided encounters more than there should be.
-Reason three - Unlocks and Progression -
This is less of a technical critique but more of a personal taste issue so you can discard this one if you so choose.
I have zero problems with using currency for unlocks but I feel this game has abandoned the Joy that was felt by players who used to love "Ranking up", there was a certain lust for the powerful weapons and equipment in the past games. A player would spent tonnes of time playing to earn the weapons and feel a sense of achievement, thats now been scrapped and replaced with a half baked "Earn points = get anything" when  it comes to the weapons and that for me ruins one of the things the C.O.D series always did right and thats progression. (This doesn't apply to Perks)
Side note: Killstreaks are really, really sh!t.

Overall I don't recommend this game, but it's not completely without merit.
I enjoyed the atmosphere--I'm impressed that a side scroller was able to create the atmosphere that this game creates. The tight graphics (especially the backgrounds) and sound (music, background noises, and voice acting) contribute immensely to the atmosphere, as do the zombies popping up and surprising you just enough to keep you on your toes but not enough to feel obnoxious. The classic limited resources also help provide an air of desperation.
Many other reviewers report a buggy experience, which I have to say I did not have at all. The game ran flawlessly for me from start to finish.
The story works, but I didn't find it incredible. Many people praise the ending, while many others seem to despise it. I found it unexciting and overall derivitive, but I was buying a zombie game so I guess I wasn't expecting James Joyce.
What I disliked, and the reason I can't recommend the game was the gameplay itself. The controls are what I would call... loose. Sometimes I would try to climb a fence and simply push against it ineffectually. Sometimes a wall jump wouldn't work. Swinging your axe takes a while to complete its arc. At the beginning of the game, all of these things were fine, because I mostly had time to think out my next move. In fact it could add to the sense of desperation and realism because there would be a zombie right behind me, and I wouldn't be able to jump the fence in one go so I'd get eaten, or just barely escape. In the first third of the game I definitely died many times, but each time I died I learned how to progress, until the light came on and I figured out the optimal sequence of moves to beat that section.
However, towards the middle of the game several sections have a chase/time limit mechanic that absolutely killed the gameplay for me. Suddenly all the little things that didn't bother me much in the beginning were what was holding me back from progressing--and I didn't feel like I was learning anything to try differently and achieve success. When I would finally beat those sections, I didn't feel good because I don't think that my skills factored into my success--I got a lucky run where every fence I saw I jumped on the first try.
If I could choose a "Meh" recommendation I would, but honestly my ambivalence would probably lead me to review every game that way. I got the game for pretty cheap on sale, so I'm not mad about it. First two hours were great, and it slid downhill from there to kind of end leaving a bad taste in my mouth. I think that people more into zombie stories than me will probably really enjoy it.
Summary:
Atmosphere, Graphics, and Sound: Good to great
Gameplay Mechanics: Start out good but a slippery slope into downright frustrating territory

+ The game looks terrific - graphics are stunning in the foreground and the background - movements look lovely and realistic.
+ Wonderful atmosphere all the way throughout. Very post-apocalyptic and somewhat unsettling.
+ Generally fun gameplay with puzzles and platforming. Game is not centered around combat - but survival. Conserving ammo is crucial.
+ Main character is not a superhero, rather an older looking man weary of life. He' s not an Olympian, so he can't continue swinging axes, and holding on to edges ad infinutum.
- The games lovely movements sacrifice precision for aesthetic. This can make the platforming very frustrating.
- 2.5D graphics make it difficult to differentiate background from foreground, and the graphics are dark enough to not be able to find things like crawl-spaces easily. (The latter, I should note, is not much of a con to me.)
- The PC port is not amazing. My game glitched on about half of the cutscenes, muting the audio. At least there were subtitles, however it was somewhat detrimental to immersion - something crucial with an atmospheric game such as this one. Graphics are stuck at 30 FPS.
- Very short, probably frustratingly short for anyone who didn't nab this out of a bundle - story mode can be completed in 3-4 hours, and these are NOT speed runs.
- Another detractor from the immersion is the tendency to include split-second reactions that pretty much force you to die, a lot. Dying is fine, but the frequency of it makes it hard to stay in Randall's shoes, it's too often reminding you that it's a game. Personally, I enjoyed the puzzles and the fast paced reactions, although it was at the cost of some of the atmosphere of the game.
Story was so-so, and acting was also so-so. There were times where the main character was just Captain Obvious, and his voice was pretty emotionless through the entirety of the game. I loved the Rat's dialogue, however. It was funny, creepy, well-written and well-acted.
Soft 7/10 - not a bad buy in a sale.

Let me start off by saying, this game is extremely unkind to newcomers. Now that that has been said, I do deem this game as good, or at least in my own opinion. Now to describe the game itself, first off, there is no set story, only what is played in multiplayer. There are five modes to play: Escape, Hunted, Extraction, Panic, and Panic Objective.
Escape:
Escape is the basic objective driven game mode, you use your phone to follow written objectives like "Go to Chuck's Gunstore, and stock up." The maps are fairly open, however, it is linear, people who haven't played it before will find it difficult to find their way, even with smaller maps; the best thing to do, is to follow someone who knows what they are doing, and try to remember what they did.
Hunted:
Hunted is your basic pvp arena type situation, boring and uneventful with people constantly trying to get the upper hand.
Extraction:
Extraction is another objective game mode where you have to follow objectives on your phone, however, you are following a map this time, and your goal is to extract the Computer Survivors. In most games, it ends up in a holdout type of situation, boarding up the house and trying to survive the horde. (Never try to holdout in a house).
Panic:
Panic is my personal favorite game mode. In the begining, one person starts out infected, after they turn into a zombie, it is their job to kill the rest of the survivors, with the added perk of respawning each time as a SWAT zombie. The survivors either try to survive for 20 minutes, or kill all of the lives of the zombies, working together can achieve this goal, but can also get boring quickly.
Panic Objective:
Panic objective is a mix of panic and escape. The game mode is an objective driven quest to escape the map, however there is a twist; there are no longer any Computer Zombies, instead someone will start off infected like in Panic and they will try to kill the group before they can escape.
All in all, I think that Contagion is a decent game, it is entertaining and can get quite lively!
P.S. If you see that I am a zombie, you had better run like the wind.
Edit* There are very few people who play this game anymore, and there are no plans to further the game, I wouldn't recomend buying it anymore.

Okay, so it's time to write a review for this game since I finished it a week ago and would like to bestow my opinion on those who are on the fence about picking up this game. Lemme start this off right away by saying that
I loved playing this game and
I would recommend it for those looking for a fast-paced-top-down-arcadey-twitchy-shooter with some kickass heartpounding music.
One aspect of Hotline 2 that I actually really appreciated was the way that each individual character was handled. In Hotline 1, you played as the same character and had an arsenal of masks at your disposal. A mask was chosen at the start of the level and the mask you chose would essentially determine your playstyle for the level. In Hotline 2, you play as a cast of multiple people who each have their own small set of selectable playstyle-providing attire. While some might disagree, I enjoyed being forced out of my comfort zone in HM2. I often found myself choosing the same mask over and over in the first game and as the game progressed I became accustomed to using the same mask. Hotline 2 forced me out of that zone and it was refreshing to mix up the playstyle every so often!
Another thing I adored was the music. Both of the games had great music in my opinion and it would be hard for me to compare the two. There is one specific track in the game that is perfect for the fast-paced and intense level it is featured in and I LOVE IT. The music is very atmospheric; eerie and spooky n' stuff when some zany♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down and insane fast-paced techno for when you are running from room to room causing chaos.
I also loved the story. Without spoiling too much, the story is told out of order and as a player it is appealing to rearrange each event in order in attempt to figure out what is really going on. Some levels make an effort to be truely unique and throw a curveball at you and when the game does this it is fantastic. There is much more I could say but I don't want to spoil anything.
Some of the level design is just... ugh. Not to say it isn't bad. This is the major issue that some people have with the game. The problem is that some stages are very large and it is not common to get shot from somewhere offscreen. That plus the insane amount of windows littered around these places makes the game frustrating rather than challenging sometimes. On one specific occasion I had just cleared a large stage only to discover that there was one more enemy awaiting me. Lo and behold, before I can react my character is knocked on to his♥♥♥♥♥♥by some offscreen shooter. Dead. Press R to Restart. In a game designed to chain together combos, it is a little counter-intuitive to hide around a corner waiting for an unsuspecting enemy.
If you like dthe first Hotline Miami, I would say that you should pick this game up. You may not like it as much as it's older borther but it does a great job improving (for the most part) on what made the first game great. If you have never played Hotline Miami, this game may be a little bit difficult to you. It is almost as if the difficulty curve was designed with veteran players in mind. If you aren't afraid of a challenge, I would give Hotline Miami 2 a shot.
All-in-all, I found Hotline Miami 2 to be a great experience that I would recommend to those looking for a challenging top-down shooter.

Original Review:
After playing for an hour, I can say this: it's incredibly simple, painfully difficult, and addictively fun.  Think of this game as a cross between DDR/Guitar Hero and any Runner game.  The levels are generated based on music from your PC, which is really cool, but it does work better with some songs than others.  Be warned: there is a massive spike in difficulty between the Relaxed and Medium settings, and some songs will be easier than others.  The level-generating algorithm is nothing too revolutionary, but it gets the job done, and on higher difficulties you'll be too preoccupied to care.  All-in-all, this is a lovely little game and a thoroughly enjoyable time-killer.

The game was amazing. I played it for 2 hours without end and it felt great to play.
I'll start with cons, since there are some that I want to mention.
- No "early press" allowed. Some dodges I prefer to start slightly early, but this counts as a miss and disables the dodge and causes you to lose a lot of possible points.
- Rhythm detection only follows 4/4. This means that 3/4 songs don't detect nearly as well.
- Camera motion sometimes hides suprises like two consecutive presses/moves and won't give you nearly enough time to see it.
Pros!
- Really lets you play any song you want, even full instrumentals, and detects them well.
- Gameplay is consistent, without any song being too difficult or any being too easy.
- Awesome graphics. I was super suprised at some of the 'extra' animations that occur at various points.
- The middle mode (between Relaxed and Intense) is perfect for playing casually, allowing you to mash buttons rather than directions when you start panicking.
This is an amazing idea, and if developed further, could easily overrun other custom-written rhythm games like osu!. The fact that I can play any song whether or not someone else has written the beat for it is awesome, and something I've been searching for for a while.
8.5/10 would recommend.
1.5 -> would ask developers to improve timing sensitivity (or at least give an option to whether accuracy is between so-and-so milliseconds, etc)

Constructing anything seems needlessly complex, which makes producing anything not so much a challenge but a grinding task. Some may enjoy this but I find the cost/reward to be very imbalanced.

The vehicle construction is fun and I like the option to design your own weapons, too. I also enjoyed the variety of transport methods like jetpacks, helicopters and motorbikes.
Planet Explorers is mediocre and there are many games that do each element better, but perhaps few that combine them into a singular game.
This game has taught me a valuable lesson. Never buy an early access game!

Old Rainbow Six/SWAT, with a bit of Hotline Miami goes FTL.
Well, that's a rather weird explanation of the game. In sense, it is a top-down fast paced tactical shooter. You don't really "play" a person, but rather manage the operation as a overseer. You control an (I assume), SWAT team and plan their movement through various buildings. It shares the pausing of time to plan your move much like FTL does. The way you ravage your team through the environment has quite a lot of similarity with Hotline Miami.
The game is really enjoyable and rather fast paced, with short levels(think 30 second operations). Getting it right at first requires a bit of effort and can be challenging, but once you get the hang of it it becomes very enjoyable and pleasing to see your planned route work.
The game is in Beta, but for it's state it is very, very featured. Everything regarding planning and working out your entry seems to be there, including loadouts. Outside of that, there still seems to be still a bit less game but I am sure that will change in the future.
Reaction to sound seems a bit lacking, and your team seems to lack own thought. They will happely ignore a gunshot next to their head when they haven't spotted the hostile or if the hostile isn't on your path. This is in contrast with the hostiles, which seem to be having much better ears.
It's a really fun game and already feels to be worth the price.
Maybe be in alpha, but this game is already compelling, fun, and challenging. A winner in the making.

I've enjoyed Rhythm Games on the go, and this is fun to play with if you got time to kill. I certainly did. Though I will say it does have some shortcomings.
Visuals look clean for what it is. Minimalistic and with vibrant colors. Melody's design certainly has that anime aesthetic which clearly isn't much of a problem for me. An added plus is the fact that you could mod Melody's appearance, and I plan to mess with that later on. While I do like the visuals, some representations of some hold arrow notes took me a while to figure out how long they should be held. While some are clearly distinguishable, others (slightly impressed grounds) aren't so clearly visible. I think a white motion path (or white outline along the slightly impressed ground) that changes color as you go along with it would help first time players.
As far as gameplay goes, I really liked how it played. Easier difficulties from Relaxing to Medium is easy understand. It's when you start having to use Both WASD and the Arrow Keys where things start to get confusing and difficult. And I think that's fine, since all I say to that is practice! Now one of the main draws to this game is the ability to use your own music. And does it work...? Well, I think it's hit or miss. The game tries to detect a 4/4 measure. And if it doesn't, it relies on the waveforms audio peaks. While the few songs I had worked for the former, it went well, but with the later, that's where we start hitting the miss territory. Granted it still works for what it is, but sometimes I wish it did detect notes I would expect it to detect. I feel like this game would benefit from a map editor because generated maps aren't perfect, and I'd personally like to go into it and improve what the game generated for me. That personally would have sold it for me.
Overall, I like this game. Definitely would recommend for Casuals, but Hardcores might wanna wait till this game is discounted (which was the case for me) before one considers this game. And if the game is still worked on for improvements, even better! I honestly do hope that's the case because I wanna see more coming from this.

Though the elephant in the room is whether the game can properly translate your music into gameplay. To that I say... yes and no. What I mean by that is that I found the game to be exactly what I expected it to be using various songs, which is either a mess that you need a lot of practise at higher difficulties to conquer, or a beat-by-beat stroll through colours that you get to enjoy for a bit and move on.
However, I didn't think that was the game's fault. Even in games that try to be as accurate as possible like Guitar Hero, you need a lot of practise to truly appreciate it. You need to learn the exact timing that each button has to be pressed and need to play a track over and over again to memorise and master it. I am talking hours upon hours, not just a few songs and call it a day. Or just play at a lower difficulty that gets boring after a while.
So yeah, it's a fun game overall, just don't expect to go in it and be able to master it in minutes.

Somewhat generous checkpoint system, it's nice they give you a checkpoint after one or two rooms so you don't constantly have to repeat the majority of the map, but as I mention below the game is largely trial and error in some spots and whichever sadist of a dev decided to put so many dialogs right after savepoints is truely cruel, in parts you're stuck on you can hear the same piece of dialog upwards of 10 times and it makes you want to break your controller in half.

Has some bugs, I swung my axe accidently while I was interacting with something and started walking into the background where you're not allowed to go. I shot a zombie with my shotgun blowing off her top half only to have her legs get up and bite me in a one hit kill.
The controls have some iffy spots, when jumping on a ledge that's not against a wall it's sometimes hard to line up right, holding a direction at all will cause you to leap in that direction instead of jumping directly upwards like you'd want.

Deadlight is a great, fairly short 2.5D zombie platform/puzzle game.
This is an Xbox360 arcade port. I’d recommend a controller, although I didn’t even try the keyboard/mouse controls.
The 2.5D is wonderfully done with smooth transitions between screens. It also has a really nice graphical style. A lot of elements are very shadowy and dark. In fact, your character is basically a silhouette. There is also a blurring or out of focus effect on the edges of the screen. You may not even notice it unless you’re looking for it. It’s subtle but adds to the whole environment feel.
At its core, Deadlight is a puzzle platformer with zombies (called shadows in the game). You get very basic weapons. Pistol, shotgun, axe and slingshot. The ammo for these is somewhat sparingly put around the game. You certainly cannot go blasting away, you’ll run out of ammo very quickly. The puzzles scattered throughout the game are not very hard and you won’t be stuck on any for long.
Speaking of combat. The zombies are very lethal in this game and any more than 2 will quickly overwhelm you. I like this approach as it makes you think about certain situations more to avoid them. One gripe with attacking the zombies…If I sprint at a zombie and tackle it, I should not have to fight it off of me. It should’ve been a quick way to get a zombie on the floor and then use your axe to kill it.
The story moves along nicely with good cut scenes done in a series of images with narration. The voice acting varied to me. Sometimes it was great, other times it felt a little forced. But that’s a minor gripe.
A few issues I came across. The controls. They need some tuning as it feels very floaty and sometimes when trying to reach a ledge you will unexpectedly leap forward instead of jumping straight up. You need to be completely stopped before trying a vertical jump. I had several deaths that I felt were directly related to the iffy controls.
I also ran into more than one cut scene having no sound.
The game was very stable, never crashed and ran at 60fps. There were a few stutters possibly when loading a new area but it didn’t take away from the game.
+Great graphics style and environments
+Sounds effects and music are good
+Puzzles are not too hard and fun to complete. Wish there were more.
+Good collectables that are not too hard to find
+Story is decent and fleshed out through his diary
+Floaty and imprecise controls
Deadlight really is a nice game and I’d recommend it to anyone into zombie or apocalyptic settings. It’s hurt slightly with floaty controls but fantastic visuals and light hearted puzzles made me want to keep playing until the end. Get this on a sale, as $15 is a little steep for ~6 hours of gameplay with little to no replay value.
