Door Kickers is a great game and has the makings of a great CQB training aid.  The survival of your officers is heavily based on your ability to control your tactical angles.  Real tactics, techniques, and procedures work (for the most part).  As an added bonus, you can create videos of your playthroughs, which you can then edit and use it to help train your team, whether it be a video game clan, paintball, airsoft, or even actual military and law enforcement.  By having a clear display of each officer's field of view, you can accurately portray sectors of fire and emphasize an understanding of the importance of angles.  Add to this that you can create your own levels with nothing more than some photo editing software, and you have the ability to create any training aid or game level you wish, complex or simple.
Currently, this game is in Alpha.   Right now, the game has a feel of many Android or Apple games, with a bunch of sequentially harder scenarios that you attempt to earn three stars on.  Time is the primary factor for achieving the three stars, which is somewhat counter to how a SWAT team actually acts.  Slow and safe is often preferred to fast and loose.  Things have gotten a bit deeper as the game has progressed through its Alpha stage, with the addition of different classes, levels of armor, rank progression of your officers, and training unlocks.  Updates have come at a very steady pace, and have consistantly added new great features that make me happy I bought the game.
This game can be as simple or as complex as you want to make it.  Do you want to intricately plan out your entire team's movement with go codes and then press play and see what happens?  Or do you want to work through the scenario as it plays out, pausing and unpausing to make changes on the fly or control an officer's field of fire directly?  Either way works, and it's up to you.
This game is so much fun.  You can run through a quick scenario to get your fix, or you can try for the best score on a hard level for hours.  With new scenarios being added constantly by the community, and the ability to create random missions from any map, you have an endless amount of replay value.

I've just recently started a single player storyline version of this game. Overall I have to say I am enjoying it. There is not much to not like. Sure, there is a slight grind collecting materials (if you've played MMO's like WoW, I don't think it's as painful as their grinds!!). While collecting materials however you're immersed in a vibrant world with creatures fighting between themselves for survival.
The UI is straight forward but I haven't started base building or item creation yet. The basic replicator usage to create 'recipe' items is very easy, and I like how you can click up and down through the layers of items you need to build up towards a more complex item - for example, you need gunpowder and copper to make bullets. But you have no gundpowder, simply click on the gunpowder Icon and suddenly you're looking at the gunpowder creation screen... how intuitive! There are a few tricks with the UI that had me briefly confused, such as 'do not have the inventory box open while trying to loot animal corpses or interact'.
The story line is easy enough to follow, and the quests are interesting enough. The side quests are optional but you can get a lot of handy stuff like the recipes you use in the replicator section. Buy the recipes in shops from NPC's, don't waste your meat (meat is money) on the actual item. Meat also can be converted to fat... fat plus charcoal equals gunpowder... you get the picture... A few tools like made of copper or iron, and suddenly you're collecting resources like a boss!
This game has some slight challenges, a sizeable world to explore, but most importantly it is thoroughly relaxing to play with it's intuitive gameplay and music...ok, so I have my music turned down but I haven't turned it off completely like I do in most games!

Before I get into my full review, I'd recommend anyone and everyone playing this game to turn VSYNC off. Leaving it on will leave you with choppy gameplay, and for a game that needs you to be on point at all times, a choppy gameplay will be absolutely frustrating.
As many can tell, this game isn't very demanding on your PC system, so you shouldn't need anything special to make it work. I would recommend a comfortable keyboard, or at least a place to rest your hand while playing, since it's very dependent on the arrow keys (or WASD keys, if you prefer that).
Now, with the playing aspect of the review.
Yes, I do recommend this game for those who are looking for a new rhythm game to play.
However, I've noticed when playing songs that I have in my library, the synchronization software isn't really accurate. I know, of course, that nothing can be perfect, especially with things like these. However, I was expecting at least a more accurate depiction of my songs, not just random obstacles and things that I need to press. There are some songs that work perfectly well that accurately depict what this game is meant to be like, but half the time it's just nonsense.
However, you can't blame the developers for not integrating a better software for this game. Before each level, it analyzes your song and displays how confident it is in its analysis of the song's beats. It's more of a Play-At-Your-Own-Risk type of thing, as you can decide if you want to play to a song that won't be accurately represented.
Aesthetically, this game is minimalistic and I love it. Instead of overloading your eyes with lots of flashy details, everything is kept simple so you can focus on the task at hand.
Overall--
PROS:
- aesthetically pleasing
- great algorithm for detecting frequencies and tempos, even if it isn't competely accurate
- cute concept
- i'm loving the personal library integration
- community mods for customization
CONS:
- song synchronization software isn't as good as you would expect it to be
- gets extremely repetitive really fast
I highly recommend this game.

I've had an awesome time with this game. I have an extremely extensive music library of electronic music and it's been really fun trying out different genres and styles with this game. The BPM detection system is surprisingly quite accurate. Even when it can't detect the BPM it reads the audio peaks and places the notes accordingly, which is often times still very effective. The customization options are limited, but it's not a big deal at all.
It's only fair I list a few complaints to balance out the review, so I'll say that if you don't know anything about BPM and various genres' BPM standards, then your play experience isn't going to be as enjoyable. A song's difficulty is more often than not linked directly to the BPM of the song you're playing, so it's no fun imputting random songs without knowing that all your nightcore music is going to be very difficult. This also means that if the game incorrectly reads the BPM in thirds, which it sometimes does, then the track is basically unplayable. I've also had an unusual glitch with the game stuttering every once in a while, disorienting me and causing me to miss a few notes, but this happens pretty rarely.
The game also determines difficulty based on "overall intensity," meaning that genres like trap music tend to have rather lack-luster levels designed for them as the game doesn't read the drops as anything important. If your song has vocals then the game prioritizes the vocals assuming they're the most intense part of the song and focuses on building the pattern around the singer rather than the song, which isn't necessarily a bad thing depending on the kind of music you listen to. It helps to have a lot of music to experiment with, otherwise you might find yourself disappointed with how the game reads the few songs you have.
I wish I'd found out about this game sooner, as the beta's been playable for over 2 years. It's lightweight so it shouldn't strain anyone's PC too bad, but even if you can't run it in 60 frames there are graphical adjustments in the menus. It's got great controller support so I've been straining my thumb mashing buttons to all my drum & bass music.
10 dollars can seem a little pricey to anyone who might only enjoy the game for a few days before the novelty wears off, but if this looks like something you'll frequently come back to then I would definitely recommend it. This is honestly the best rhythm game I've found on steam, as far as audio detection and overall involvement goes. If you're still unsure about the purchase, then look up some gameplay on youtube. There's a ton of different songs that people have recorded themselves playing so you can get a feel for how the game's audio detection works.

Please note that playing COD Ghost in good conditions requires a rather powerful PC with a recent GPU and a least 8 Go of Ram. In addition, the PC version was ridden with technical problems which is totally unacceptable in general and even more so when it affects one of the most respected and lucrative franchise in the industry.
So why do I recommend this game?
Simply because when you put technical issues aside, COD Ghost is amazing.
-a very interesting setting : the game universe is a post-apocalyptic America  at war with a powerful south american federation. the game environments are rendered in great details and have a desolate beauty to them that I find almost poetic
-a great diversity of design (SP) : all missions include a nice twist on the design formula.
You infiltrate a compound, you navigate underwater, you take part in a full scale tank assault.
It's still COD but it shows that the designers went to great lenghts to keep the game exciting
-a good story (SP) : the game focuses on a small group of elite units.
It is a more personal theme and although there are plenty of action, it drops the bombastic tone of former entries for something more subtle and grounded. You feel part of a unit playing a small yet vital part on a bigger war front.
-Great multiplayer (MP): the conventional MP is great and packed with amazing maps which are a blast to play and still convey that post apo vibe. In addition, there is an extinction mode which is more or less COD meets Left4Dead.
You are a team of soldiers fighting  beast-like aliens and you have to use special abilities to stand a chance.
All of this makes Ghost my favorite entry in the COD franchise.
It's just a pity that so many people seem to dislike the game.
It makes me wonder if they even gave it a chance...

Easy difficulty is not at all easy.  It feels like the director is tuned for only one setting and difficulty level only effects health pools.

Poorly planned out classes.  The ranged classes have prohibitively small ammo pools and ammo pick ups are RNG spawned so you can pick a ranged class and end up playing melee.  Except for the bright wizard, who gets unlimited "ammo" but can literally burn herself to death while dealing with one of the director's psychotic events.
RNG loot.  It uses the worst possible RNG loot system from hyper monetized F2P games.  I have no idea why.  There is no option to buy loot boxes or a subscription time.  On top of that you only get to roll for loot at the end of a win, you only get one roll, and it's not specific to the class you played.
Oh and if you have significant latency to your host, dodging and specials are near impossible to accomplish.
The game has its plus sides.  If you really want a melee focused Left 4 Dead this game offers it well.  If the Warhammer fantasy setting gets you off this is a must have.  The game is fairly well polished and bug free.

>>> An incredible blend of Left4dead and the Warhammer franchise<<<
Gameplay:
Very SOLID gameplay with classic features like healing items/bombs/potions
Very SOLID and SATISFYING melee system; all weapons FEEL real. Axes chop, hammers bash, swords slash.
It is such a pleasure to brawl through hordes of rats!
Each character really plays differently than the others and it's really cool to find out which one(s) suit your style best (even better considering each of them can also be customised to play differently). So many team variations!
The special rat enemies are well though, they both respect the lore AND play great for the gameplay. We've got the classics like the "posion rat" the "catcher" the "tank" the "assassin" but also original stuff like a "gunner" rat or some "armored ones" you're actually better of avoiding in most cases when you hear them (the audio for each of them is amazing)
At the end of each mission you roll to get a chance at dropping loot that can be better than your regular gear (but not too much so it works as an incentive but not a gamebreaker if you just want to play the game casualy).
Plus how can you make a fantasy game without loot?!
Lore:
Set during the Endtimes of Warhammer (an apocalyptic period where every army throws everything they have at each other in one climactic final campaign. To give you any idea of the clusterfrak, the world explodes after it!); the game really respects the setting with a really grimdark atmosphere.
The ambiant/flavor audio between characters is spot-on
In conclusion:
A great revamp of a classic gameplay with the addition of an innovative melee system
A very good use of the Warhammer Ip (and boy was it mistreated recently)
An enjoyable audio experience with spot-on music and audio queues
A GREAT coop game
Some room for "expansion" (if at a later date they wanna add more heroes, maps, etc)
Congratulations to Fatshark, they put a lot of work and love into it and we can clearly see that in the final product

I’ve played most of the zombie games recently available. Contagion is easily my favorite. The only other game that comes close is the Nazi Zombies series.
As an adult gamer, I don’t have much time. I play at least once a week with my friends online. We use a mumble server. Voice chat is absolutely necessary as teamwork is insanely important in this game. You will not be able to run off by yourself and survive. I have a dedicated private server. Which is easy to set up and lets us play without trolls or kids. We prefer the coop “escape” mode.
The best thing about this game is how brutally hard it can be. Head shots are the only practical way to kill zombies. Ammo is so scarce every single shot counts. It is common to be down to your last two or three shots with zombies on your tail. You can run away, but eventually you will have to stand and fight. Finishing a level is very satisfying and a real accomplishment.
The levels are enormous, but well laid out. Some game modes do not have a map, so getting lost is possible.  Once you learn them you will not get lost, as most are fairly linear.
The downside is that there are not many maps. The game needs about twice as many maps as it has now. A few people have released maps via the workshop. While most of these are very good, there are not many and few people play them.

Contagion is a very good game, and I tend to find that i can come back day after day and still have fun. That said, I dont usually spend more then an hour or two a day playing this game because of the hand full of faults that cause some problems with gameplay.
pors:
+very fun to play after you get the hang of the game
+the fact that zombies can be killed similar to most other zombie games results in a shallow initial learning curve
+the zombies pose a real threat. player zombies even more so (yes, you can be a zombie)
+different weapons need different types of ammo, forcing players to share supplys
+loot is generated randomly unless it is preset to spawn at a specific area
+most situations can be solved through a bit of good teamwork
+the game is affective at creating a scary atmosphere
+controls are very effective and responsive
+graphics are very good
cons:
-zombies are subject to a handful of bugs that ruin immersion
-good teams are rarer then winning the jackpot at the lottery
-escape and extraction can a bit repetive
-hunted is really just a contest to see who plays the most call of duty
-lack of weapon variety (total of 3 pistols, 2 smg's, 2 shotguns, etc...)
-all to often, people fail to realize that not all ammo works in the guns that there carrying
points of interest:
-feels like a more polished version of no more room in hell, although that game is free
-a free dlc pack is supposed to be realesed that will include new weapons
Overall the game is very good. The games flaws do cause some problems but not enough to ruin the game. Most of my problems with the game are centered on the lack of attention and teamwork among a good chunk of the player
community. Focusing on the game and the quality of the game on its own, contagion deserves a solid 9/10.

What a game! Like Audiosurf but on a more platformer level. The arrows on the level indicate which directional arrow you hit on your keyboard which will give you points based on your reaction time and accuracy. Choose from bundled tracks or from your own library, it supports many - if not all - audio formats: MP3, OGG, AAC, FLAC, WMA and I think there is more!
- Simple, intuitive and hella' simple. It's hard to keep up based on the tempo of the song, but that's just the added challenge! Hit the key at the right time, and hold it if necessary, that's all it is!
- Choose from bundled sets (from one of my favourite artists, Shirobon!) or from your own library. SFX are straight forward and a very nice touch.
- Not revolutionary, but not garbage either. Really awesome effects and looks like any platformer would. Backgrounds are cool to look at!
- Easy to navigate, follows the "three-click" rule and doesn't overcomplicate things; a monkey could do it.
- Download off the Steam workshop no sweat and load it into the game, choose customization and select how you want to appear in-game i.e. I use an Asuna skin and theme: it looks awesome! Colours are nice and vibrant, plus you can change your theme at any point!
Level Design: 8/10
Audio: N/A
Graphics/Art: 7/10
GUI: 9/10
SW: 10/10
+ Great Fun
+ Various types of customization available
+ Easy GUI Navigation
+ Looks Great
+ SW Support
- Sometimes the tempo gets the better of you and it's hard to recover from (hardly the game's fault)
- It's not something that's revolutionary, but it's still a fantastic game
Definitely recommend to anyone of any age and any gender!

First, this game has a lot of potential.  However, none of the potential is being reached;  there are so many problems with the game that it seems like an early Alpha, not a Beta.  To begin, several of the maps are unbalanced as anything I've ever seen.  On top of the unbalanced maps, it would seem as if the Americans get an early game advantage as it is incredibly easy to get the Stuart once going down the tank line, while tanks of other nations and equal in rank cannot reliably penetrate it from the front.  They also seem that it is fair to throw new players into the game with no real tutorial and into games with veteran players with advanced weapons such as their scoped rifles.
Besides the ridiculously unbalanced gameplay, I have two more serious problems with the game.  One is that the audio is ridiculous; the guns sound like staplers and you hardly notice when you're being shot in a tank.
The second is the more major of the two; this game is a massive money grab.  While I can see a slightly higher price for newly unlocked tanks, I don't think 130,000 in game credits of around $15 in actual currency is an allowable price for a gun that is unlocked at rank 5.  One could throw a hundred bucks at the game and ignore the massive grind most people have to experience, and can get the best equipment in the game.
There's a lot of potential here, but none of it is being reached and it seems like the devs couldn't care less.

I'm a massive fan of the original Hotline Miami, both are definitely great games and a lot of things about them are amazing. As far as Wrong Number goes, it still has a lot of the same things, which is -good-, a great soundtrack, storytelling, and most of all, fun gameplay.
However, as great as it is, there are a few things I dislike about it, along with a decent amount of others who have played the original. First of all, the maps are far larger than the first game. This wouldn't be -that- bad if there were more rooms, but I came to find some very open, large areas that were very difficult to progress through due to the fact enemies just shoot you almost outside your view.
I'm not gonna ruin the ending but it was great. I heard some people disliking it but that's likely over how they didn't understand it, there's a lot of cool twists inside of the game and people are too busy killing to care. One other issue I had with the game is that enemies seem to oftenly get stuck in corners, particularly against doors, and dogs seem to go around in circles at random points.
Maps and minor things aside, the game is really fun, certainly one of my favourites, and a worthy sequel.

Prince of Persia meets Zombieland. The game is easy to pick up and fun to play, at least initially. Whilst the animations and gameplay are fluid, the story that holds it together leaves a little to be desired. It tries a little too hard to be gritty, but ultimately is clumsy and shallow.
Often you can move through the game and just react to situations on the fly, and this is where the game excels. Quickly doing some swift parkour moves to escape in the nick of time feels great. There are however some very annoying sequences that require you do very specific moves at specific times or you instantly die. This isn't a huge problem, because you just start again from your previous checkpoint, and they are never far behind. However, it can really slow down the excellent momentum the game has up until those points.
The whole game will take around 5 hours to complete, and was definitely worth it (especially if you get it on sale).
The weak story is a bit of let down, but all in all, a great little experience.
There is some replay value, in that there are secret collectables and a "nightmare" mode when you finish the game, however, I personally will not be going through that again!

Alright, so, I like a lot about this game. building is fun, the world is decently interesting, I had few bugs, and only one of them prevented me from ever completing the main story. (npcs I need to complete one quest involving a certain queen of certain crab monsters won't spawn, even after starting an all new game and playing through a second time)
But here lie the problems:
-that's the only place TO have fun. either you play an easily bugged, massive open world adventure mode where you get to experience everything or you play the survival mode.
-survival mode spawns you in a rather small piece of land with only one biome. In the center of the map is a town, revealing that you are a SECOND generation colonist, taking away all sense of "roughing it." All you can do is walk out into the wasteland and get a little iron or copper, but never enough to really build anything good or give a sense of progression. You'll probably end up making a stone hut 10 meters from the town, cowering from enemies you lack the resources to face. this is especially disheartening because it shows that the only way to get to the fun colonies and giant robots part of the game is to play the hours-long adventure mode.
-there's a creative mode, but you get the same little patch of land with nothing to do but build with no challenge. pretty standard.
-although building is cool, creatures can just knock it down, which means building a home is pretty pointless, because it won't protect you from anything anyway. (unless you want to build a mess of turrets that run out of bullets)
-a large portion of the main quest involves walking in straight lines for miles at a time, sometimes just to look at something, then fast travel back. (which costs money)
-followers constantly get stuck.
-the game has little cutscenes where the camera will pan in to show you something of interest, but these scenes are unnecessarily long.
a few days of my life I'll never get back... out of ten.

Where do I start?  Sonic Adventure 2 is one of those games that you'd call a masterpiece.  Put together much more tightly than the original Sonic Adventure, Sonic Adventure 2 has three types of gameplay - fast-paced high-speed stages featuring the Blue Blur himself and his dark counterpart, Shadow the Hedgehog, shoot-out style stages with Miles "Tails" Prower and Dr. Ivo "Eggman" Robotnik, and treasure hunting stages played by Knuckles the Echidna and Rouge the Bat.  With 155 missions spread across 31 levels, a multiplayer mode, and the Chao Raising system, there's quite a bit to do in this game.  I'll rate the following:
Gameplay:  Top notch, for the most part.  With four different styles, it doesn't get boring.  Players will dash through Sonic and Shadow's levels, shoot out robots in Tails and Eggman's levels, and hunt for treasure in Knuckles and Rouge's levels.  The kart racing levels can be a tad hard until you have the controls down though.  Thankfully there aren't too many stages with that style of play.  The Chao Raising system is relaxing - you get virtual pets to take care of at your own pace.  Chao Racing and Karate, however, require a bit more involvement - you'll be playing plenty of the main game to raise your Chao for 9 of the 180 Emblems for 100% completion.  So, overall, I give gameplay 4.5/5.
Controls:  The game controls quite well on a keyboard, especially due to the fact that you can map the keys as you see fit.  The slight snag I see is you have a tad less accuracy when aiming in shooting stages.  And when I mean "slight", I mean very slight; it's barely noticable.  The game does support controllers - an Xbox 360 controller works very well with this game.  Overall, I give controls a 5/5.
Level Design:  Superb.  While the stages do start out easy, they get deviously more difficult as you progress - you'll have a fairly easy time in the city-themed stages, it starts getting difficult at the desert-themed stages, and the ARK-themed stages get to be about as difficult as other end-of-game stages from other Sonic games (like Scrap Brain Zone from Sonic 1 or Metropolis Zone from Sonic 2, for example).  While there is a somewhat steep curve, the challenge keeps things interesting - you ask yourself questions like, "Where can I cut a corner to save a few seconds?", or "Is there another way to reach that platform"?  The design of the levels just rocks, period.  I give it a 5/5.
Graphics:  After more than 10 years, this game still looks pretty dang good.  The HD is just icing on the cake here.  5/5.
Music:  One of the best soundtracks for any Sonic game.  It's pretty easy to get the case of the Ear Worm with several tracks - music from City Escape, Pumpkin Hill, Radical Highway, Metal Harbor, Green Forest, White Jungle, Security Hall, Pyramid Cave, and all the ARK stages have awesome music.  The main theme, Live & Learn, is also quite nice.  5/5.
DLC:  The DLC contains all the multiplayer characters and levels from Sonic Adventure 2 Battle, as well as additional themes and Chao Karate from said version of the game.  To put it plainly, one may ask, "Is this worth the three extra bucks?"  I say yes.  Even if you don't play multiplayer that often, it's still worth the Chao Karate mode for its antics and additional challenge - especially if you had Sonic Adventure 2 Battle for GameCube instead of Sonic Adventure 2 for Dreamcast.  And 20-some additional levels for multiplayer is definitely not a bad option for $3.  Overall, I give the DLC a 5/5.
Replayability:  If you're going for 100% completion, it's going to take at least 50 hours on average (on average being the key words here), especially if you're raising your Chao the honest way.  With 31 levels and five missions per level, there's plenty to do.  Records are also saved for each mission - your best time, the highest amount of Rings you finished with, your best score, and how many times you played a mission.  I would say that Leaderboard support would also add replayability, but sadly, that's nerfed to a degree.  Plenty of dishonest people on those Leaderboards, but if you have friends who own the game, you can compare and compete.  Leaderboards aside, I give this a 5/5.
Other Notes:
- Many complain about the camera system, especially if they're new to this game.  But they also need to remember that this is a port of the game; not a remake.  That, and several 3D platformers lack a "perfect camera", especially ones made back in the early 2000s.  So I can forgive the camera - the rest of the game is just too dang good.
- As stated, keyboard controls work great - they just might not work for everyone.  Luckily, the game supports USB controllers, so there's essentially an option for everyone.
So, there you have it.  Sonic Adventure 2 is a great game, hands down.  One of the best released on Steam.  With great gameplay, great level design, awesome music, a rock-solid framerate (provided you meet the requirements), and responsive controls, it's just as good now than it was 12 years ago.  This masterpiece is not to be missed.
Overall rating, 5/5.

Vermintide is a game that doesn't do anything particularly new, but what it does do; it does it very, very well.
It is a multiplayer, 4-player coop game where you battle off swarms of heretical rodent furries hence the name Vermintide.
It borrows much of it's gameplay from similar titles such as the L4D series, healing items work in much the same way, reviving a player works much in the same way, if they die they will reapear in an area to await rescue just like L4D.
At this moment graphics aren't the best optimized, but on a decent rig it will run smoothly though the developers are still currently ironing out bugs.
I've run across minor connectivty issues, and there are a few things I do have with the game that irk me.
- There's positively no way to play this game without an internet connection as of this moment, though there is bot AI for your companions.
- Aforementioned optimization issues that I'm fairly sure will all be fixed
- Sometimes it feels like there's little variation between the characters, the only one feeling like it has a particularly unique ability being the Fire Wizard
- Often it's hard to get in at the beginning of a mission, there's no option to search for open lobbies/inns at the moment to join a party BEFORE it begins. It would be nice to see some more matchmaking filter options.
I'm tired of coming into a new mission during the final battle because I don't want to host and wait for players to join myself.
Besides these small things I can think of off the top of my head, overall the gameplay is great, melee combat feels very solid and you really feel your hits "connect" unlike some other games.
The director AI (another thing borrowed from L4D) is pretty damn solid and will definitely figure out how to throw you a curve ball at the worst of times.
Getting loot, and the loot system in general is fun; you'll get an item when you level up, and after every mission you roll some dice to find out what you get, and how high you roll will factor into the rarity of your item; though no items I've come across have felt particularly unbalanced.
Visually (optimization besides) it's very impressive, the art direction is fantastic and the maps are lavishly detailed, there's even a nice amount of variety in the Skaven hordes, and as of the moment there's definitely a good amount of levels to tide you over until more pop out with further development.
The chit-chat between the characters is quite good, and sometimes funny enough to elicit a mild chuckle; I had heard some people complaining about the content of some of the Witch Hunter's dialogue, and while I haven't heard everything he's said there's nothing particularly stunning or outworldly or horrendously sexist outside the realm of what we're used to when it comes to video games, I mean I'm sure he says something off-kilter but, again, there's a certain level to be expected with the current state and maturity of the media mentioned; and considering the fact that I heard people complaining, I've really not found anything that offended my own sensibilities yet.
To make things short, Vermintide does nothing new, but what it does do, it does fantastically. It's absolutely great fun and I definitely recommend it in it's current state.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number, seems like the perfect way a sequel should be executed. In theory. The game features significantly MORE of everything, there's larger maps, a considerably longer campaign, more playable characters, more missions, overall going with the assumption that Bigger=Better. This is generally true, as it is not a sequels job to evolve gameplay in significant ways, thats the job of new IP's. What a sequel is generally supposed to do, is take an already stellar concept, and add on to it, refine it, fine tune every small detail until it reaches the potential it always had. Wrong number does this in many ways, and for the most part does it beautifully. However, as I was about 2 hours in to wrong number, I noticed something that greatly concerned me. I had stopped playing it. The original Hotline is in my opinion perfect. Every single aspect of the game was executed flawlessly, the tone, the atmosphere, the soundtrack, the vague and ambiguous story, the incredible adrenaline rush as you murdered dozens of faceless mobsters for the thousandth time that level, and how you snap back into reality when the music stops, and you realize the horrific atrocities you've just committed. And then you do it again. Anyway, there was not a single time for my entire first playthrough of the original Hotline Miami where I stopped playing. Even though the game was, when you think about it, very repetitive, I was never bored. It concerned me when the sequel didn't have the same effect. Granted, it's considerably longer, but I don't think that's the only reason. I decided to delve deeper and try to find out what exactly went wrong in Hotline Miami 2. Let's start with the pros.
The story in Wrong Number was absolutely fantastic. It opted to drop the Vagueness of it's predecessor, to  great effect. Wrong Number tackles significantly bigger topics then HL before it, and ends up succeeding with flying colors. For the first few scenes, I was somewhat concerned that the story would be more convoluted than Season 6 of Lost, but as it progressed, I understood the tale the writers had in mind, and really enjoyed it. You play as a multitude of "Protagonists" this time around, all of which have unique personalities and motives for their actions. There's a film star, a Corrupt Cop (Clear inspiration from Showtime's "Dexter") An actual serial killer, A soldier in Vietnam, a drug Kingpin, a Failed writer, a group of Vigilantes hoping to recreate Jackets rampages throughout the first game, and numerous others. Each story was well written, intricate, and differed greatly from the others. Without venturing into spoiler territory, You're in for a treat. Another positive note, is that the fast, fluid, adrenaline fueled gameplay returns in full force. There aren't any significant chances to the formula, besides a few new enemy types, however I'm pleased that they kept the flawless gameplay virtually untouched. Obviously the soundtrack is phenomenal. Like, its freaking awesome. The game is also SIGNIFICANTLY more difficult than the original, including an unlockable hard mode, for those who require practice in punching computer screens. The difficulty change is both a blessing and a curse, which I'll get to in a minute. Now for the negatives.
Wrong number is a hard game. If you haven't played the original, PLAY IT FIRST OR ELSE YOURE BONED. I was still able to eventually beat it, but some of the levels  I was forced to exploit AI problems to win. However, Wrong Number, unlike it's predecessor, often feels unfair. Anytime I died in HL1, it was due to my own poor timing or slow trigger finger. with enough patience and skill, you could tackle any situation the game threw at you, everytime. Less so with it's sequel. As I mentioned earlier, the levels are much larger. And considerably denser. And whoever designed these apartments, clubs, and military bases has a very strange obsession with windows. THEY. ARE. EVERYWHERE. I can not even count the number of times I cleared a massive area, which often took minutes (Which because of the multitude of restarts, minutes+Wrong Number=Hours) and as I rounded the corner, some unbelievable accurate enemy spotted me from across the dimension, shot at me with pinpoint accuracy FROM OFFSCREEN, and I was forced to play this one FREAKING area again for the billionth time! THIS GAME MIGHT BREAK YOU! So yeah, unfair difficulty. Next point. Something I always loved about the original Hotline, was the freedom given to you at each level. There was a massive selection of masks, each giving significant buffs to Jacket, which helped you find a playstyle that worked for you. There were also a multitude of paths that can be taken through the level, based of your both your play style and preference. This is reduced heavily in the sequel, and I think I found out why. Its essentially because in HL1, gameplay drives story. You do whatever you want in a level, and the game doesn't care. It gives you a number of options, you pick one, and you go on a majestically brutal murderous rampage. you're given a blank canvas to draw a picture of some drug lord choking on his own large intestine. However in HL2, story drives gameplay. You play almost every level exactly as the developer intended, with only a few levels straying from the beaten path, and even then only slightly. Because there are specific characters for specific levels, you dont get to choose a mask at the beginning of each level. The only times you get to choose a mask (I believe)  Are for the fans/kingpin, where you get either a BARREL ROLL, killing blows (But unarmed), dual characters armed with a chainsaw and an interchangable firearm (this one was pretty amazing) or dualweilding machine guns. And then theres the one snake guy who either get's a nailgun, killing throws, or I think (I dont remeber this one) like some martial arts thing. Even though the mask system is present, its also considerably more limited, and often times restrictive. Why can't tony carry weapons? Why cant the bear drop his weapons at will, or at least reload when he wants to? These questionable game design choices are pointless and frusturating, and very dissapointing. In addition, the different ways each character plays, and the lack of choice makes for a more linear and, in my opinion, watered down experience.
I've said a lot in this review, but I haven't answered the one, simple question. Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. I said many negative things about this game, and I stand by those. This game is a mixed bag. Full of good and bad, overall it is an enjoyable game, but I wouldn't recommend it unless you have already played and enjoyed Hotline Miami. Hotline Miami 2 has a load of small problems that add up over time, but the large problems are really frustrating almost from the start.
Among the small problems are things like pathfinding glitches. Enemies occasionally get stuck on doors and become invincible or lose their vision of you when going through a door and just kinda sit there. Dogs are extremely guilty of this. There are also some hitbox problems, it might look like you punch someone yet they still kill you. Some pieces of terrain have hitboxes that are way larger than it looks like they should be. As for major problems, I'd say the most irritating one for me is the level design. It's nowhere near as good as the original and can be extremely frustrating at times. Levels in Hotline Miami could be beaten with several different routes, using any weapon, and on your first try if you were careful and quick. Levels in Hotline Miami 2 are more linear, and although you can beat them taking multiple different routes, there is usally one single route that is the easiest. A huge complaint of mine on many levels is that you are often shot and killed by enemies that you couldn't actually see. A couple levels in Hotline Miami had things like that but they were very rare, and typically you were just supposed to avoid the area entirely. Last complaint of mine about the levels is that it's often hard to tell whether or not something counts as full LoS blocking cover, or it it's only movement blocking. The levels do look nicer with the extra details, but not knowing whether something will keep you alive or not gets very frustrating.
The music, much like Hotline Miami, is great. However, it is much louder and completely overpowers many other sound effects. It also has a very different feel to the original's music, in neither a good way or bad way, just... different.
Finally, the masks. Hotline Miami had a massive variety of masks, many of which you would never use. Hotline Miami 2 has changed that by having each chapter use different characters, each of whom only has a 3-4  very different and specialized masks to choose from. For instance, if you've ever played Hotline Miami you'd be familiar with the Tony mask, which makes your punches kill instantly. That mask still exists in HM2, but now you cannot pick up any weapons. The variety is nice, but I would've liked if after you've completed the game that you could go back over any level and use any character/mask.
In the end Hotline Miami 2 is still an enjoyable game, but I cannot recommend it unless you have already tried, enjoyed, and wanted more of Hotline Miami. I went back to get the secret ending, every weapon, and an A on every level on Hotline Miami, but I have no desire to go back and do the same for Hotline Miami 2.
Note about play time, I beat the game while offline.

Soemtimes it will feel like the story gets in the way of the gameplay. I found myself annoyed when I had to sit through lengthy (Although meaningful) dialogues. This may sound petty, but when a game tunes you for second-to-second action sequences and fast restarts the long dialogue may throw you off from the fast paced gameplay.
Sometimes you will be killed by out of sight enemies, and in the end level knowledge will be you best friend. Knowing where to be when is esential in this installment. Sadly you will find yourself less empowered in this game, there are far less times when you actually roll through the level. But this can also be seen to add to the challenge, so take the news as you wish.
Overall I enjoyed this game very much, and would highly reccommend it even with some minor faults.

TL;DR The game is fun, but pay attention when it says it found/couldn't find a beat when you know it shouldn't/should. As compared to other user-supplied music games, this one is the most like DDR/Guitar Hero, so proper beat location is important.
Music test so far:
Monster Killer - TheEnigmaTNG. I picked a recent addition to my library with a solid, obvious beat. Game performs as intended.
Honor Thy Father - Dream Theater. Dream Theater is my "how good is the algorithm" go-to. The game helpfully told me that it could not find a 4/4 beat, which is accurate. The fallback algorithm performed well.
Panic Attack - Dream Theater. I like this song, so I gave it a go, even after I did the stress test. Oddly enough, it said that it found an acceptable beat, which Panic Attack definitely doesn't have, and the gameplay showed it. I'm a little disappointed.
Feathers (Original Mix) - Archie. In Audiosurf, this is my favorite go-fast song. Reds practically all the way. Here, it was not fast all the way. Accurate beats, and it was still fun.
Sound of Silence - Disturbed. I had to run a slow song test, and I recently discovered this excellent cover. Seriously, go listen to it. When the song was really going, the algorithm's adherance to the vocals was great, but in the slow parts, it was a bit patchy. The revelation that "slow songs are a bit boring" is not really news to fans of other music games.
Overall, I'm glad that there is a rhythm game that is really trying to hit the beat accurately. Even Audiosurf is a bit loose with the beat. It's not perfect, but it is very fun.
Still holding out for iTunes playlist integration. Then again, I'm holding out for that in Audiosurf 1/2, Symphony and Beat Hazard, so there's that.

In this post-modernistic masterpiece, we follow the turbulent inner struggle of Sonic T. Hedgehog as he grapples with issues of identity, a fitting follow-up for the first game's exploration of his sexuality and search for belonging in a world he does not feel like he fits into. He is constantly besieged by a mysterious apparition known only as "The Shadow" - which, to educated players, should be immediately apparent as an overt application of Jungian psychology, as The Shadow represents the parts of Sonic that he desperately tries to not aknowledge, as well as manifesting his insecurities: where Sonic attempts to be heroic, noble, and fast, The Shadow is a cruel, villainous sort, heralding Sonic's constant inner battle against his latent nihilism and pro-capitalistic attitude, an aspect of his character that is also explored in his obsession with "Rings", the main currency of Hedgehog Earth. Worth noting is that The Shadow does not have Sonic's speed - instead opting to have his racing prowess augmented  by a pair of rocket-enhanced shoes, symbolizing Sonic's constant insecurity and fear - running is all he is good at, what if he one day could not run as quickly without aid? What use would there then be for him? He literally can not see himself as anything else than someone who runs fast, and his self-esteem suffers for it. There are some Kafka-esque overtones to this subplot, punctuated by Lynchian dream sequences in which Sonic takes on the appearance of Doctor Eggman, his therapist, as he rampages through a derelict shipyard in a large robot, freeing animals from the cold clutches of other, slightly smaller robots. These scenes are often contrasted by the non-chronological vignettes wherein we play as Tail The Hedgehog; these ultimately only exist to expand upon the backstory of Sonic's relationship with Jamie Hedgehog, however, while the Doctor Eggman scenes tend to revolve around Sonic's trust issues. There is also a minor subplot concerning Knuckles The Hedgefund, and his supposedly controversial inter-racial relationship with Rogue The Boat, but this is ultimately only inserted to make the game an appropriate length (five and a half hours) and these stages were all removed in the Director's Cut.
All in all, this is a classic that you owe it to yourself to experience. I have faith that if this game had been released before Johnny "Jaws" Ebert died, he would have realized that sometimes, video games CAN be art - SEGA's creative mastermind, director Shigeru Miyamoto, has certainly proved that much with this interesting (though thematically dense) narrative.

Personally I can't endorse this game.
Hotline Miami 2 picks up where hotline miami 1 left off in difficulty and gets harder. So far so good right? Well no, the game goes from encouraging an open play style to locking down the player into very specific playstyles if he wants to succeed. NPCs have gone from being fairly lax with their gun use to being crack shots, secondly the look function has been nerfed, you can only look half as far as you did in the first game but levels are often twice, or four times the size leading to more than a few surprises. This is bad because you will often get killed by enemies wielding guns from outside your range of sight, add into this that tony is no longer capable of picking up weapons and throwing them or using guns AND he's forced into an RNG execution animation when it comes to killing dogs and he's made into a widgety character who will get killed by RNG. Corey's dodgeroll takes a lot of experience to use but it's just not useful enough to be seen as anything as a gimick mark's SMGs are undroppable making him vulnerable to certain enemy types if you try to play the game on hardmode and alex and ash's pathfinding are awful. This isn't even covering the over use of guns, glass, and special enemy types, the use of RNG to make a level sometimes unbeatable without restarting and the fact that the story is disappointing and winds up feeling short due to how the narrative bounces around between something like 4 or 5 different viewpoints.
as a whole the game feels less like a sequel capping off a series and more like a calculated insult to the person who bought the game.
my advice would be to pirate it, if you enjoy it, if you feel the devs deserve your money. Then by all means purchase your edition of choice.
if not, well you didn't lose any money.

This is absurdly fun, extremely addictive, and absolutely fantastic in everything it does. Hard mode gives it a good amount of replay value too, for a relatively short game - I squeezed 24 hours out playing through on Normal and Hard. You can really tell the difference and it kicks up the (already considerable) challenge a lot.
The music is utterly gorgeous, with over 3 hours of absolutely killer songs (look out for the song that plays on Scene 12, Death Wish - that's my favourite) from a bunch of very talented artists. As a sequel, Hotline Miami 2 makes itself unique in the range of characters, each with varying playstyles, and you really do play very differently with each one. I miss the masks, definitely, but having all these characters to get into is worth the loss.
It's a shame Hotline Miami ends here, because with this upward trajectory the next game would have been phenomenal, but on the same note this is a fantastic game to end on. An absolute must-buy for fans of the first, no questions asked.

Instead of taking the easy route for the sequel, Dennaton Games decided to advance Hotline Miami's gameplay and story. Less forgiving than the first you'll find yourself much more weary of windows and gunman. In return you’ll find guns to be much more favorable throughout all levels. Arguably the game suffers from “Artificial Difficulty” in the sense that you’ll get shot off screen on every level. While it may be frustrating, especially on hard mode, it makes completing a level all the more satisfying. You learn from every death, slowly crawling your way to the end on a first playthrough. In a weird sort of way it trains you for a “speedrun” if you plan on replaying a level. Hotline Miami 1 felt free flowing for almost the entire game while its sequel takes awkward stops and skips for playstyle/story. This really gives Hotline Miami 2 its own very very very unique feel. I highly recommend this game. Also the soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥ing great.

Intial Review: This game is very fun to play with 4 people. I have been able to get alot of the people who use to be big on l4d1 and l4d2 into a game which has good replay value and the same underlying concept of utilizing team work to get a know acomplishment. I would give this an 8 out of 10. Due to a few things needing to be polished, or lack what I would consider a great game.
Positive: There are many maps around (15 I think) which you can play, which is a lot more than the orginal 5 maps l4d orginally offered. There is a wide variaty of styles and combat choices that each individual player can play. There are 5 various levels of game play averaging from easy to nightmare mode. There is an upgrade system for weapons. There is a good variaty of enemys to play against espically against you storm vermin....... It also offers another higher risk vs reward where you can collect tombs (which take hp spots) to grimoires which lowers your overall teams hp to get better dice rolls for weapons and other trinkets. This game constantly keeps the player on the move, unlike in l4d where there were slow parts with no zombies or very little.
Negatives: There are still many bugs and glitchs espcially for special vermin. The pack master and vermin runner (hunter) are by far the most glitchy. From teleporting across openings, to having bad hit boxes, to not having shoving not affect them or your fellow ally. There is a drop system and basically to get good drops you as a player will have to grind on specific levels getting grimoires and tombs for the ones that do have them. This will also encourge people to utilitze glitches to get past harder parts of those levels which offer grimoires in the game. The levels that dont offer this, well there is not much reward in itself other than beating a level to get the final experience and open more levels (you can still get a chance of getting a drop, its just must lower without tombs and grimoires). The drop system is also very noticable in weapon damage, for example one of the characters I like to play I only have grey items (lowest level) it takes about 2-3 hits to kill (not a headshot) 1 average rat. Yet when I play with others who have golden level items they will kill the same enemy in 1 hit (not including head shots). Enemys seem to spawn ontop of players more than one occasion and sadly that can be a pack of storm vermin which insta kill you or even a rat ogre.... yes I have had both spawn ontop of me.....it ended badly.
Final: Overall this game is very fun despite the very apparent glitches and screwed up special vermin. If some of the items listed in the negatives area be improved I think the game will do very well. Espeically not having tombs, or grimoires on all levels. As long as FatSHark provides good support and timely fixes i think this game will be high up on those who enjoyed l4d's list (I just hope Fatshark doesnt make the same mistake that TRS did with evolve). This game provides alot of potentinal just as evolve did on intial release, but because of the lack of support of inherent glitches, and imbalances in the game is one of the main reasons why most later on gamers who stuck to higher levels of playing shyed away from  the game.

This game is something new and great. The way this game works is that you download a music file and the game picks it and analysis it to pick out the beats. It then adds obstacles to the beats and depending on how long or short the beat is depends on the length of the obstacle. One it maps out the level it then adds orbs that go to the beats. All of the orbs and obstacles are activated by a key press on the keyboard(W, A, S or D). Each orb and obstacle need to be pressed with a different directional key. When there is a high BPM (Beats per Minute) there a more obstacles with less time in between them so a higher BPM it is a lot harder. Also do not forget to calibrate the game before you play to make everything sync up.
Overall this game is very good but some work could still be done analyzing the music to create more accurate obstacles.

Definitely recommend this for fans of rhythm games.
Bear in mind, the engine makes far better levels for beat-heavy games. If you go from something with a strong bass line or regular drums/cymbals to something else, the results can be pretty jarring.

We've really only played the Escape game mode, which for just the two of us is great.  And it seems a lot of the maps have randomly generated objectives when you play them.  Like some times a door may be blocked, but the next play through you can go through it and explore a different path to escape the map.  It makes replaying maps more enjoyable.
When you die, you become a zombie.  It'd say it's more fun on a public server with multiple players, but in a 2-player co-op setting, it's not that fun.  But I can see the effects it would have on a 6+ player server.
All in all, it's a pretty decent game.

If Left 4 Dead and Killing Floor are one side of the Zombie shooter coin, which primarly focuses on fast-paced shooting action, then Contagion is the other side, focusing on scavenging, survival and a more realistic approach.
This is the closest I've got a to a Walking Dead experience.
The escape mode is pretty good, Barlow Square is great albiet the routes can be too hidden and difficult for newer players. Although this would be a blast playing it with known friends, I've got mostly a good play experience from the community of strangers, where we would actually work together. But once in a while you get players who will sprint away so they can scavenge everything. When your character dies, you play as a Zombie, constantly trying to overwhelm until no survivor is left. It's actually really fun, again, mainly because of the pacing. You'd spend a good 4-5 mins scouting and stalking the survivor before even trying an attack.
The gameplay sure as hell needs polish. Another drawback is the voice acting. Jessica's sprinting sound could have someone in your house mistake you for watching porn.
On a high note, the Graphics are as good as it gets and the ambience and soundtrack is impressive!
It's clearly not worth $19.99, but decent at 5$

I wanted to like the game, but it fell short in many regards. In the end I was just frustrated and unsatisfied.
-
(I cannot argue with that fact that this game looks great. The rain, the sewer water, the decrepit buildings of a ruined Seattle. It all came together to paint a nice picture.)
-
-
(Any tiny bump, any attempt to 180, ANYTHING made you pretty much lose all momentum. This is particularly annoying when you're running from a certain death situation and you bump into a tiny cardboard box and go tumbling to the ground. On top of that he is just unresponsive. I jump, he waits a couple seconds; I spam to climb away from the zombies, he bashes his face into the wall before eventually deciding "oh hey, I should get away from these zombies". Some people might say "It's a more realistic movement system. If you bump into something you'd trip". To that I'd say "Well that's fine and dandy but it has to be fun. This is a game, all of the mechanics in the game should help the game overall be more fun. This system only frustrates the players.")
-
(What I mean by Rinse-and-repeat is that sometimes it just comes down to memorization. Jump here? Dodge that? Shoot that? Miss one of those steps and you die, then get sent back to the start of the puzzle and have to do it all over. Other than going back and collecting the rest of the stuff you missed and playing the Nightmare Mode, there isn't really a point in playing through the game a second time. PROS:
-Nice Aesthetic
-Platform style is executed well
CONS:
-Audio issues (cut scenes lose audio)
- Lagging when accessing the start menu
- Voice acting and scripts are bad
- Puzzles could be more challenging
- Ranged Weapons are almost pointless to include

The Good:
- This game is incredibly atmospheric. The art design and in-game cut scenes are extremely well done, and definitely adds to the allure of Deadlight.
- While brief, I found the story to be engaging, and I was satisfied by the ending. The voice acting was good too, and helped carry the story along.
- Deadlight ran without any problems; I didn’t experience any issues with crashing or sudden drops in the frame rate.
The Bad:
- While I found the story engaging, there could have been a little more substantive content to prolong the story until its conclusion.
- After completing the game there is very little reason to go back unless you’re trying to unlock all the achievements.
-Nightmare mode is ridiculous (check points only at the start of each chapter, and reset after the game is exited). The game’s chapters/acts are spaced unevenly, and so chapter/act 2 destroys any fun you might have trying to unlock this achievement. Additionally, the controls can be unresponsive at times. The normal mode provides numerous check points, and so this issue is minimized. However, in Nightmare mode where there are only two checkpoints, dying due to unresponsive controls is absolutely rage inducing.
Final Verdict:
Overall, this game excels in its atmosphere; however, due to its short length and limited replay value, I recommend buying this game on sale.

Deadlight for me is one of the best indie titles i have played. The story and the pace of this post apocalyptic zombie title are one of the best out there. There arent many zombie games that will make you understand and feel what its like to live and survive in a post apocalyptic world, where every ounce of humanity people have, has been discarded for the sole purpose of survival. Its a game that builds on those emotions, especially during the cutscenes were we can witness first hand what it means to be both a hero and a villain.
The game contains stunning  visuals as well that combined with an awesome soundtrack provide an even more immersive experience to the world and daily life of the main char. A main char whose story begins with the usual cliche of finding his family but as the game progresses it becomes so much more than that. Every arc is building up for the ultimate conclusion, which trust me is one i enjoyed to the fullest.
The gameplay for the most part plays smoothly and without many shortcomings. You must for the better part use your brain rather than your muscles. Its easier to avoid the zombies rather than to fight them, but when you have to fight the combat itself is not so difficult. There are some bugs concerning the way you move and how you face the zombies themselves but that wont be an issue after a while. The puzzles themselves arent that hard, but they have their moments especially during the end, where you have to show that you mastered everything the game has taught you in order to survive.
To sum up this was a game that i loved from the beginning to end. I recommend it to all zombie fans and indie lovers.

A strong, though flawed, follow up to the ultra-violent Hotline Miami. Wrong Number manages to deliver both more of the same thrilling action and new ideas, but it’s not perfect.
8-10 hours (Main game)
8/10
The first Hotline Miami was an extremely fun, hyper-violent, top down action game. Needless to say, I loved the game and was eagerly anticipating it’s follow up. The core mechanics of the sequel remain much the same as the first, and as such, I won’t spend too much time talking about them, and instead recommend you read my review for that game. The basics of it are that it’s a top down action game where you must kill all the enemies in the area, through a combination of firearms and melee weapons.
Now, let’s talk about what’s different. One notable change is how the gameplay has a much heavier emphasis on gun based combat compared to the first, and melee combat gets a much smaller spotlight this time around. Whether this is a good or bad thing depends on personal preference, personally I’d have liked a slight bit more melee combat in this game, but in the first game I wanted a bit more gun combat in the first, so on the whole it balances out for me and I regard it as a neutral.
In the first game you played as a single character and equipped different masks that slightly altered your abilities (excluding of course the trio of post-game bonus levels that let you play as the biker). This time around, you’re given a few different characters that you get to play as. You don’t get to choose your character for each level, but each one does come with their own set of “masks” that you can choose from. (I put masks in quotes because sometimes it’s choosing your weapon, or even the one where choosing a different masks gives you what is essentially different character).
The variety added to the game by these different characters and playstyle is one of the strongest points in the game’s favour. It’s something the game does very well as a sequel, as even with the new additions and changes, the core gameplay mechanics remain intact: frenetic, high speed, blood drenched murder.
So let’s talk about these different characters. Now of course, some of the characters play very much like the first game, where you commit your atrocities as straightforward slaughter. On the other end of the spectrum, one of the characters does not kill his targets, and won’t use lethal weapons. Another takes place in flashbacks to a war, where you are given one gun and a knife and must fight your way through enemy territory. When you run out of bullets you must find more ammo to pick up, as with this army character you cannot pick up weapons dropped by the enemy.
My favourite character to play as though is the one I made mention of earlier, where the different masks give you a different character to play as, specifically you can choose from 4 different masks with this character. One is able to dodge roll, even under enemy fire. Another has fatal unarmed melee attacks, but cannot use weapons. The final two are the ones I’m particularly fond of though. One dual wields machine guns, even being able to point them in opposite directions. The other (and my personal favourite in the game) allows you to control two characters at once; one wields a chainsaw, and the other a firearm. It’s absurdly fun to enact a chainsaw massacre while carrying out a mass shooting at the same time.
The first game received a lot of praise for its soundtrack, and I’m in the minority in that I was mostly lukewarm on it, though I did some of its tunes. Wrong Number’s soundtrack however caught my ear much more than the first, and the soundtrack is pretty strong throughout the game, and fans of the first game’s music will likely feel the same.
The game also makes some small improvements compared to the first game in the form of its options. You can now pick your resolution from inside the game, instead of before loading it up, as well as supporting higher resolutions than the first. It’s now possible to remap the controls, which is something every game should let you do (though I find the default work just fine for this series).
A review wouldn’t be complete without criticisms, and while Hotline 2 does a lot right, it does bungle a few things. For one, while there’s better variety in the game, the level design is weaker than the first. This stems from two main problems with the game’s level design:
1). There are a lot of times that there are enemies that are off screen and will kill you before you can even see them (even if you’re using the shift key to look further ahead of you, they’re still off screen). This is frustrating and adds nothing to the game but artificial difficulty, and it will lead to many unfair deaths.
2). There are a lot more windows in this game, which enemies will shoot through to kill you. This forces you to be much more careful in proceeding through levels and sometimes interrupts the pace of the game. This is compounded by my first point about the off screen enemies being able to kill you before it’s possible for you to even spot them, as the two issues are not mutually exclusive.
While the faults in the level design are the biggest issue with the game, they are sadly not the only ones. When using the shift key to look further ahead in a level, the mouse seems to be much more sensitive than it is when playing normally. This isn’t a problem I recall experiencing in the first game, and while I did adjust to it, it’s still an annoyance, especially given how much more you need to use that feature in this game.
Aside from that, the game has some odd glitches that pop up now and then. Enemies (mostly dogs) will sometimes get stuck and spin in circles as if you’ve already lobotomized them with your pistol. When you play as the two characters, sometimes one of them will bugger out and not move with the other character as it should. There are other occasional glitches that sometimes occur during gameplay, but these are the ones I noticed repeatedly.
The game was supposed to have a level editor, but as of yet this feature is unreleased. Hopefully it’ll be released soon, as I’m quite interested in trying that (hopefully we can download user made levels online as well).
All in all, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number gets a few things wrong, but it also gets a lot right. It’s a strong follow up to the first game, and while there are some things about it that are much better than the first game (the character variety in particular), on the whole I think it’s slightly inferior. That said, it’s still a lot of fun, and fans of the first would do well to pick this up. If you haven’t played the first game, then you should absolutely do that, and do so before playing the second.  In the end Wrong Number manages to build upon the first game and keep the essentials intact, and it’s certainly worth your time and money.

Would I recommend Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number? Yes...for the most part, and No.
Story
-----
The story takes place right after HM1, and then it doesn't.  You jump from present day 1991 and back into the past constantly in nonlinear fashion constantly.  It's easy to get lost or confused at what's going on.  The story is interesting, but not as compelling as the first game. The game is less subtle about its story and has a lot more dialogue than the first game, and this works against the game. The beauty of HM1's story was how players interpretted the actions of the main character. Here, you know your character's objectives from the get-go and it takes the mystery out of it.  Another issue is the addition of multiple characters. With so many characters, they all don't get the characterization they need despite HM2's focus on telling its story. Not only that, with what little they're given, they're not particularly likeable either. Top that with questioning what's really happening and what's not and you got a crazy plot with a somewhat disappointing ending.
Design
-----
HM2 remains similar to HM1 in structure: you pick a "Scene", sometimes pick your character, and you proceed to kill everything in the level. This base structure is what HM sets out to achieve, and it does it well. Here's something odd: "sometimes pick your character". At certain points of the game, you either get to don a couple of masks (And by a couple, I mean at the most 4) or you're given control of a specific character. The former is like HM1 in that regard; it's the latter that's quite different. These characters either have a unique trait not found with the masked characters (I.E. a soldier wielding a knife and gun at the start but unable to use other weapons; journalist that ejects the magazine clips from guns, promoting non-lethal kills) or they don't have any special ability at all.  This injects variety into the game for those who play HM with, say, one mask, but it feels forced and goes against what a lot of people liked about the first game. In addition, levels are huge in comparison the the first HM, with tons of glass windows. These levels result in many cheap deaths where you get shot by an off-screen enemy or someone hiding behind the glass windows. Not only that, a lot of levels are designed to be played in one way, meaning going off to find a different way to tackle the mission usually results in death. For those who played HM1 one way, this isn't an issue, but I can see this being one for those who want to get creative.
Gameplay
-----
"Smooth" is the word I'd describe playing HM2. The controls are nearly perfect; my only gripe would be that I'd wish the camera would zoom out more to compensate for the huge levels. When you die in a close fight, you only have yourself to blame. There's not much to say about how it runs; when you play it, it feels right.
Presentation
-----
Is there anything else I can say about HM2's presentation that hasn't been said; it's candy for your senses.  HM has always been known for its style and it delivers; the wide color palatte brings the world to life. The clash of colors is appealing and at times, it's overwhelming. The soundtrack, like the first game, is perfection. Compiling the best artists for the game that HM2 is, it's a natural fit and the soundtrack alone warrants a listen to anyone who fancied the first game's soundtrack. Sound effects are all there and feel as powerful as they should.
Conclusion
-----
The big question is, is Hotline Miami 2 a game for you? If any of the issues I described above is something of concern, then I would say it's safe to skip this game and let the original game stand on its own. Door Kickers is a Indie, Simulation, and Strategy game developed by the folks over at Killhouse Games. It was added to steam on September 3rd, 2013. The game features a mix of real time strategy with a tactical stop and go pause mode that allows you to analyze situations, and make your plans for each map. There is a small amount of customization in the current build of the game but that is simply due to the early access nature of the game.
The gameplay is pretty great, however it can be rage inducing at times. The main idea is to kill the bad guys and have at least one of your own team mates left standing at the end. In some cases there are hostages to rescue which can put a timer on the level. All the levels can be completed in a small time window . Ultimately you want to play a level as fast as possible with little to no casualties.
The game is a early access game and thus has many features missing. With that said the game is great as it is right now. Of course a few flaws that I’m not sure are bugs or overlooked design. For example there are times when I open a door and my character is looking directly at a person and will mow them and 3 other people down without being shot. Then there are times where the same guy will open the door and sing love songs to the enemies and thus getting domed (shot in the mother♥♥♥♥ing skull). It feels like r.n.g and less bug but who am I to say. This was the only real issue I had with the game. Especialy on the one level at the beach where I had one guy left, and there was one enemy left. My guy opens the door to the bathroom and both the ai and my character stand their in a stand off for about fifteen seconds before the ai shoots my guy in the face…..
The levels can be played in many ways, the best is just to find a style that suits you. For most of my levels I set a path for my guys to run and it worked. I very rarely had to pause the game after my initial plan. However if you want you can breach doors. After breaching a room, you can pause the room to setup what to do next. The breaching, and or DOOR KICKING is the core of the game. You have several ways to breach. You can just kick a door in and hope your guys don’t get blasted before they can see through the door. You can also breach with a flashbang where they open a door and throw a flashbang in. Again however if your guy is standing directly infront of the door you risk getting shot and killed so it is best to do it from the side. Then there is the breaching charge where you setup a charge on the door and can detonate it. This stuns most of the people in the room giving you an advantage. You can also use a snake cam to see under the doors.
The game has no multiplayer but the developers say it MIGHT come later. The game also has a mission editor , however I did not play around with that yet. It does mean the game will have many mods and games with mods are always better because of it! The game as single player is a lot of fun and I definitely suggest anyone who likes tactical strategy games to make this purchase. The game is worth every god damn dime. As far as early access games go this is one of the better ones on steam. I will of course do a re-review of the game upon full release of the game.

I'll get straight to it: Vermintide is fantastic.
Play with three other teammates and fight off the Skaven hordes in a class based, Left 4 Dead style melee centric FPS. If you're familiar with L4D then it is much like that, and although it loses the versus game mode, it gains a great deal from an elegant melee combat system and varied character classes.

"Melee-focused Warhammer L4D" is the short description of this game, but it doesn't quite do it justice.
The addition of loot (with special properties as you get to higher grades), loadout customisation, etc, adds a lot of variation to the formula. The five classes (besides the bright wizard) start out feeling very similar, but as you collect more weapon choices for each they start feeling much more distinct. And weapons can completely change how a class plays and how you deal with specific threats. I'm pretty impressed with how different they all feel.
The maps are very well designed - my absolute favourite is "Wizard's Tower". It's a delight of level design, you can really tell they pulled out all the stops for it. I wouldn't want to spoil it, but I'll mention that it is a bit different depending on which class you enter as.
At the time of this review, it's a bit buggy (not to a terrible degree, mind you, and they've been fixing it up very well). They've made some mentions about future content that if they hold true will give this game some great longevity. I for one hope for a Warrior-Priest character.
Also, the netcode is pretty good. As an Australian, I'm able to play with my American friends (ping to the US tends to be about 200-240ms) without too much visible lag - sure my hits take a little time to register, but it's playable. Higher difficulties where every bit of damage you take counts for a lot more may be much more difficult, but for now it works well.
