I started out liking this game, theres a lot of potential in a Warhammer-IP clone of Left 4 Dead, but its got a few issues that start to take the shine off the game after further playing:
The game has a general feeling that you're the puppet of the RNG god. This can actually be fun when theres some setup to allow you to at least tailor the results later. In this case, theres nothing of the sort. Loot dice, tomes and grimoires may increase the chance of getting a better ranked item, but have no effect on whom that item is going to be for. Even fusing items has the exact same result, an item you have no control over the results of. This can easily lead to you getting tons of gear for a class you may not use/have access to (Maybe your regular co-op team mates already use that character.) This taints what would normally be really cathartic gameplay by making it feel like a grindfest for no guaranteed rewards.
The issue that has most put me off, however, is the feeling of ranged weapons in the game. The focus is more on melee than in L4D, as it should be, but ranged weapons are still an essential tool, whether it be a scatter gun for clearing packs, or a sniping weapon to pick off specials before they grab someone. The former works fine, a good blunderbuss will take out a horde of skaven and really take the pressure off swarms, but the latter has some serious hitbox issues. Regardless of playing as a client on a multiplayer game, or soloing with no lag factor at all, it seems that the head hitboxes are very poorly done. Arrows will sail through a skaven's head and do no damage, unless you hit whats a very narrow centerline of the face, so narrow that you can literally shoot a gas rat in the eye and it doesnt register as a hit.
An overhaul of the Skaven's hitboxes, and maybe some way of tailoring crafting more to one's specific needs would really help to tighten up the rest of the game, which is still an overall quality product, and one of the best Games Workshop IP games to come out other than Blood Bowl and Dawn of War.
In the end, I had to think hard over recommending or not, and I think for now its a tentative no. It hasnt quite got the same polish as the L4D series, which although they dont have the RPG elements, are more spot on with the gameplay. Hopefully with a tweak or two, the game can become the addictive, cathartic rat-smashing-fest it deserves to be.

Would I recommend Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number? Yes...for the most part, and No.
Story
-----
The story takes place right after HM1, and then it doesn't.  You jump from present day 1991 and back into the past constantly in nonlinear fashion constantly.  It's easy to get lost or confused at what's going on.  The story is interesting, but not as compelling as the first game. The game is less subtle about its story and has a lot more dialogue than the first game, and this works against the game. The beauty of HM1's story was how players interpretted the actions of the main character. Here, you know your character's objectives from the get-go and it takes the mystery out of it.  Another issue is the addition of multiple characters. With so many characters, they all don't get the characterization they need despite HM2's focus on telling its story. Not only that, with what little they're given, they're not particularly likeable either. Top that with questioning what's really happening and what's not and you got a crazy plot with a somewhat disappointing ending.
Design
-----
HM2 remains similar to HM1 in structure: you pick a "Scene", sometimes pick your character, and you proceed to kill everything in the level. This base structure is what HM sets out to achieve, and it does it well. Here's something odd: "sometimes pick your character". At certain points of the game, you either get to don a couple of masks (And by a couple, I mean at the most 4) or you're given control of a specific character. The former is like HM1 in that regard; it's the latter that's quite different. These characters either have a unique trait not found with the masked characters (I.E. a soldier wielding a knife and gun at the start but unable to use other weapons; journalist that ejects the magazine clips from guns, promoting non-lethal kills) or they don't have any special ability at all.  This injects variety into the game for those who play HM with, say, one mask, but it feels forced and goes against what a lot of people liked about the first game. In addition, levels are huge in comparison the the first HM, with tons of glass windows. These levels result in many cheap deaths where you get shot by an off-screen enemy or someone hiding behind the glass windows. Not only that, a lot of levels are designed to be played in one way, meaning going off to find a different way to tackle the mission usually results in death. For those who played HM1 one way, this isn't an issue, but I can see this being one for those who want to get creative.
Gameplay
-----
"Smooth" is the word I'd describe playing HM2. The controls are nearly perfect; my only gripe would be that I'd wish the camera would zoom out more to compensate for the huge levels. When you die in a close fight, you only have yourself to blame. There's not much to say about how it runs; when you play it, it feels right.
Presentation
-----
Is there anything else I can say about HM2's presentation that hasn't been said; it's candy for your senses.  HM has always been known for its style and it delivers; the wide color palatte brings the world to life. The clash of colors is appealing and at times, it's overwhelming. The soundtrack, like the first game, is perfection. Compiling the best artists for the game that HM2 is, it's a natural fit and the soundtrack alone warrants a listen to anyone who fancied the first game's soundtrack. Sound effects are all there and feel as powerful as they should.
Conclusion
-----
The big question is, is Hotline Miami 2 a game for you? If any of the issues I described above is something of concern, then I would say it's safe to skip this game and let the original game stand on its own. If not, it's well worth looking into at some point. As for me, I liked it, but if there was another HM made like this, I'd skip it. Dennaton Games set out to make its last Hotline Miami game different from its predecessor, but what we get is something that will divide the fans on what Hotline Miami truly is: a game we play for its story, or a game we can replay differently each time.

Okay, so. Here's the thing. Pretty sure I said this on my HLM1 review, but it bears repeating. This is not a comfortable game to play. At every turn, at every second, with every gunshot or blood splatter or death you suffer, every achievement you unlock, every stage you playthrough, every cutscene you watch and every choice you make, you are constantly aware of how WRONG everything is. How brutally uncompromising the violence is. The previous game always kept making you go back through the level without the pulse pounding music and adrenaline to keep you going, with just an unnerving, slow drone to sober you up after your bloodthirsty rampage, to SHOW you the destruction you left in your wake, to remind you what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are for enjoying such awfulness.
This game does that and way more. This game makes you question your motives as a gamer. Is it truly right to enjoy an excuse plot, to enjoy a game that both rewards AND punishes you for butchering people left right and centre with little to no explaination or reason as to why, AND to have finished that game, and DEMAND a sequel? You want MORE of that? ... Well okay then. But you'd best work for it, you sick ♥♥♥♥.
So that basically sets the stage. This game departs a little from the first's formula. You aren't Jacket any more. Instead you are SEVERAL characters. You play one of a cast of surprisingly interesting and intriguing characters, from an aspiring, down on his luck writer with apparent anger issues, a maverick cop who has a very well kept secret, an ultranationalist murderous idiot who worships the people who send him the phonecalls, a group of kids who are emulating Jacket simply because they're BORED and want to hurt people, Richter, Beard, the son of the Russian Mafia boss (who looks like Tommy Wiseau) and the new boss's right hand man. All of them have their stories, their backgrounds and their particular gameplay mechanics. It'll take some getting used to all of them, but you'll pick it up I'm sure. It's all very nicely done, and if anything the game is greatly improved by the changes in characters, keeping the action fresh, interesting and the difficulty JUST HIGH enough to not be overly frustrating. Think tactically, think quickly, react even quicker, and you'll make it through...
This game likes to hide things, just like the first did. Be sure to check out newspapers, answering machines, desks you might be sat at for example... Pay attention to the actions of all characters, minor or major. This game has many, MANY little details that are easy to miss but are wonderfully executed... pun definately not intended. Yikes.
but... really... You KNOW how this story ends, don't you?
Ah well...
Leaving this world isn't as scary as it seems...

I really love the idea behind Melody's Escape.  I can tell there was a lot of work into trying to get a working level generator like audio surf, but in a more interactive and vibrant way.  The game is a step in the right direction, but it really just doesn't work yet.
Before I go on I'd like to mention that, yes, I had VSYNC disabled and I'd recommend anyone else playing the game to disable it, as VSYNC will butcher any chances of proper on-beat gameplay.
Unfortunately, most of the songs that I personally tried to play just didn't sync up in an enjoyable way.  A few of the songs I tried were:
Shirobon - Regain Control (this song actually worked exactly how I thought the game should function, but was the only song to really do so, for me anyway)
Mystery Skulls - Magic Animatic
Rage Awakened - Kingdom Hearts 2.5 OST
Hataraku Maou-sama! - The Devil is a Part Timer OST
Dog of Wisdom Remix (Blue Version) - The Living Tombstone
The main issue with the songs is that half the time, there was on-beat gameplay and it felt great, and the other half I couldn't tell what the program was trying to get me to tap to.  The synchronization software seems to work better with songs that have slower, defined beats.  That way, the game can recognize shifts in the song and adjust the visuals accordingly.  However, even in those slow songs, sometimes I couldn't discern if the beats for me to tap were going along with the song's actual beat, or the vocals.  So, in my experience, slower songs sort of work, and fast songs just don't work.
The level builder in Melody's Escape does very good at attempting this synchronization, however, and is probably the best I've seen so far, so I have to give it that.  But, the reason I just can't recommend it is because it just doesn't work as well as one would expect it to.
The gameplay itself is entertaining at first but quickly becomes more tedious than relaxing, primarily due to the fact that, as I said, most songs aren't actually properly to the beat.  I understand that the gameplay is more of an aid for a visual experience than an actual fleshed out game itself, but in that respect I still can't say it's very good feeling to me.  If the goal is for visuals to shift in tune with the music, then I don't believe that's been achieved.  This is very, very close, but it's not there yet.
Overall, I don't hate Melody's Escape.  In fact, I really like it a lot.  But, it just doesn't play the way that I'd hoped.  Maybe in the future the game will perform better with personal music, but until then I'd wait on purchasing it.

Door Kickers is a Fantastic Game!! -- One of the best I've ever played, and there's still lots more to come! Door Kickers offers an enjoyable, realistic and informative peek into the world of tactical response police and special forces that is very secretive and usually hard to find (portrayed even semi-accurately at least) in the entertainment world. In a simple, fun, and effective way it showcases realistic tactics, weaponry, gadgets, radio chatter and movements in a variety of hostage, bomb defusal, room clearing and even tubular assault scenarios.
Door Kickers is particularly enjoyable if you're into Police or Military Tactical Response/SWAT or Special Forces, but even if you're not, it's still an amazing and rewarding tactical game that enables you to think, plan and execute different strategies in a variety of different scenarios. It's NOT an exceedingly difficult game by any means, but there is plenty of room for perfectionist work if you so desire. Although the trailers play at full speed, there is a tactical pause feature that lets you think, plan and execute your strategies as fast or slow as you want.
Would recommend Door Kickers to everyone! Lots of very cool new stuff is promised in the near future, such as Snipers, Ballistic Shields, Tazers, and a Campaign (in addition to the dozens of single missions currently available). The updates have been released very regularly so far - the devs obviously care about the game and have already implemented alot of suggestions from the community!   In short, you should get it!  You won't regret buying this game!    11/10!

Overall, I wouldn't recommend it. Unless it's on sale and you have a couple hours to spare to look at the pretty pictures.

This game is good at times and frustrating other times.

It had potential to be great, if not such a linear one-way to do everything (unsure how to do that with this style of 2-D game, unless if more stealth or paths) and a bit more content, but it was short (5 hours) and sweet.
Verdict 7/10 pick up on a sale for under $10 and its worthy.

As a zombie fan I had to try this Deadlight since the moment I saw the first trailer for this game. I've waited and waited and finally decided to give it a try thanks to the price drop in this 2015 Summer Sale (for about €2.39). At first I liked what I saw: the graphics were nice, not great but functional and detailed, the atmosphere was spot on but then there's the gameplay, the very foundation of every single game on this planet. Well, even tho it is simple and rather easy to get in, it suffers from small problems like it has a mind of its own, especially during those moments where quick reflexes are needed and the controls must be close to perfection. In Deadlight that's not the case and it can lead to some frustration, more so if played in Nightmare Mode, where there are no checkpoints (only between chapters). Also, the game seems only to work with Xbox360 controller, I've tried a PS2 controller with USB adapter and nothing happened (literally)! The sound is a mixed bag in my opinion. The ambient sound and sound effects are ok but the voice acting lacks something and sounds bland and dull for most part. Also, the sound seems to mute during some of the cutscenes for some reason I don't know (some other players complain about this issue as well). And don't expect a long game, it will be over in no time, lasting about 5 hours tops.
My verdict? Buy it for cheap, it's not bad but not great either.

Everything I wanted from Left 4 Dead can be found in Contagion.
I have primarily played the Escape mode (start at point A, make your way to point B), with some time spent in the Extraction mode (go from place to place rescuing other survivors), both of which are coop modes so this review is purely based on the coop and solo experience but the game does have versus multiplayer.
Where other games have focused on special infected units, this game has only two: zombies and riot zombies (the latter in riot gear making them harder to take down).
Every playthrough of a level is different; there's different loot in different places, different pathways blocked, and even different endings. With that said, once you play the game a bit you'll get the hang of things. It seems each map has two different ending points and various paths throughout that are either blocked or open. Bullets, medpacks, and weapons are sparse, leading to a much more cautious playstyle that I quite enjoy. Not only do you not want to get hit by a zombie because medkits are in short supply, but you can also become infected yourself. It will not immediately become apparent but as you continue you'll...well...start to become a zombie.

it lacks what triple A games have but still a very worthy game that deserves support and possibly a sequel.

Ah Contagion.....Do I love you? Or do I find you utterly redundant? Maybe a little bit of both. You see, this is a game that provides some innovative mechanics into a familiar video game theme. I have had this game since it's early days, so I have had the chance to watch it grow, and grow it has. I personally find the art style nice, and the graphics quite good, so I have no complaints in those departments. The physics are fine, and I absolutely love how the zombies can only die with a proper shot to the brain. I feel like this game has really improved my overall skill and precision using a mouse for aiming. The game consists of a couple modes, only two of which I personally find interesting. There is mainly just co op modes, but there is one mode that shines, and it's called "Hunted". In Hunted, it's every man/woman for his/herself with weapons and pathways randomly generated, but there are of course, zombies everywhere. Now the thing that makes this game different, is that when you die, you actually BECOME one of the zombies, and have multiple abilities, including the power to call a horde of up to 15 zombies to follow you, zombie sight (Basically night vision for the deceased), and the ability to blend in with the NPC zombies. Sounds cool right? It's not. I'll be honest, it gets very tedious running around as a zombie, as people RARELY work together and use strategy to take down the remaining survivors, and it's simply not as fun as being human. The factor of fear completely disapears and I think that's actually the issue with this game. It's very shallow and one of the only things that makes it interesting would be the fear factor. Hiding in a house, then you hear a player walking in, for example. The maps are very well created, and I give props to the designers responsible, but it still doesn't save this game from being mediocre at this current time. One thing that's cool, is that the devs have stated that all the upcoming DLC will be free, and they apparently plan on implementing more features, but I have no idea if any of that is actually true in the long run.
Okay, so the game is original, and has style, but what does it lack? I shall start with the fact that there is absolutely nothing to unlock, or achieve, other than steam achievements. It does not matter how many matches you win, all you will ever recieve is a little message, and "awards" like "Hunter" that actually hold no weight whatsoever to your profile or game at all. I know some people prefer this style of online game, but I find it totally destroys replayability and makes the game feel pointless. I think this is a great game to play in SHORT bursts but only with close friends on a mic. I find going online solo, only lasts me about 25 minutes before I have to turn it off due to how repetitive and redudant it had become.
To sum things up....
The game is well made, and bursts with creativity, considering the genre. Although it's creative, looks good, and the bugs are extremely rare, the game lacks content and feels very shallow in comparison to other modern, multiplayer online games.
PRO:
-Creative take on the zombie game genre
-Very nice visuals and not too hard on your PC.
- Interesting weapon selection/Small selection of maps, but they are well done.
- Virutally no bugs (100 hours of playing and I have yet to encounter many past full release.)
- All upcoming DLC are going to be given to us free (They say they plan on POSSIBLY adding a ranking system of some sort, but only want to add it to "Escape" mode which absolutely baffles my mind.
CON
- No Ranking/No unlockables whatsoever. Nothing to achieve.
- Small map selection
- Only ONE proper pvp mode (It's good though)
- The other modes are boring (Escape isn't terrible but as I explained, there is no reward for completing it other than a steam achievement)
- Lack of replay unless you have close friends to play with using mics. I have friends that play but even then I find it redundant, so it's truly hard to say.
- NO CHARACTER CREATION/NO CHARACTER PROFILE FOR ONLINE
- The head developer of this game will reply in anger to criticism on the forums, defending his game to the very last breath, even if it means he is so completely incorrect about the subject at hand. -Warning-
If you enjoy FPS games with a zombie theme, and enjoy a minor horror touch, then go ahead and buy this...If it is ON SALE. I would never pay more than $10 for this game in it's current, shallow state.

Mount & Blade: Warband Wall-O-Text Edition
I often get asked, "What is it about Mount and Blade? Why do you keep playing this game?"
If you've never played Mount and Blade or M&B: Warband, that's an understandable question. If you've only scratched the surface of it (turned it on, tried the tutorial or a quest or two) you probably really wonder "What is it about Mount and Blade?"
It's not a cheap "Oblivion" knock off. It's not like "Gothic" or "Total War." It's not "like" anything, really. It's a very unique creature - a true-blooded, genuine, bona fide, Indie-made, diamond-in-the-rough PC game!
It's a strange home-brew of strategy, diplomacy, resource management, role-playing, and, most of all, first or third person melee (and ranged) combat!
Perhaps the greatest thing about Mount and Blade - and Warband - is that it allows you, the player, to make of it what you will!
Of course, that kind of freedom comes with a greater responsibility. The game gives you all the tools to have as much fun as you desire... The question is, how will you use them?
Mount and Blade and Mount and Blade: Warband will not hold your hand. They'll teach you a bit about how to fight and pretty much kick you to the curb. The game world is open for you after that, to do with exactly as you please.
Players who are accustomed to a more thorough tutorial may feel a bit jilted. I, myself, believe in thorough tutorials, but somehow, for me, Mount and Blade/Warband works!
I felt as if I were part of that world; I had only basic skills and I was set loose to find my own destiny...
There were no restraints on what I could do! I could join up with a faction, I could wander aimlessly. I could turn bandit, or merchant, or earn my keep traveling from tournament to tournament!
When I first started the first Mount and Blade, it took me a while to figure out that, while I could travel entirely alone, I could gather companions to my side - and even hire recruits to form a raiding party or the start of an army!
I found out quickly that I, myself, could level... It took me a bit more time to find out that my companions could level, as well! Not only that, my army could level!
My army could literally change from a bunch of ragged peasants to elite warriors by gaining experience through training and combat!
Now, rather than drifting through the world alone and in peril, I was a force to be reckoned with!
In time, kings and sultans, lords and khans sent me offers of vassalage, hoping to lure my ever-growing band to their cause...
In my first games, I took their offers. I fought small skirmishes and great battles! It was not uncommon to find myself in the midst of 200+ warriors, mounted and afoot, thundering across the battlefield seeking each others' lives!
It. Was. Glorious!
And then, it wasn't enough...
I'd captured castles and cities, destroyed armies 4, 5, even 6 times my own size! (And, yes, it's extremely difficult.)
However, I'd done it all for the king. While he sat on his bum in his keep, feasting and passing out what I'd captured to other lords, I was out killing and bleeding for him - for someone else...
That had to stop.
It did. I rebelled against my "rightful lord" and made him pay a higher price than all his foes... I even started my own Empire, capturing town after town, castle after castle and bringing them under my banner!
I promoted my faithful companions to lords - vassals now serving under me! By my right of rule do they gather armies and chastise my foes! By my right of rule are they awarded fiefs of towns, villages, and castles.
That, my friends, that is Glorious!
If you've never played Mount and Blade/Warband, but you've played, say, a Real-Time Strategy game like Warcraft 3, or, perhaps better, something from the Total War series, you've captured or razed villages, destroyed armies, perhaps even engaged in diplomacy...
In Mount and Blade/Warband, you're not leading your army from some celestial cloud with a drag-selection box and right-click. You're on your horse with mace and bow! You're literally standing on the field with sword and shield and you can alter the course of battle!
You can walk through the cities and castles! You can assault the walls in siege towers or on ladders! You can defend your holdings, firing bolts from the parapets or standing shoulder to shoulder against the foe!
This isn't some detached strategic simulation... I've made more difficult decisions in M&B/Warband than any other "strategy" game.
Last night, I was besieging a castle. Defenders outnumbered my forces 3+ to 1. While I was preparing a siege tower, the defenders sent a force of 145 to try to destroy my army of roughly 100.
I shattered them.
However, my forces were wounded, but I had time to heal as I continued work on the siege tower. That was when a group of about 400 rode in over the horizon.
I could break the siege and run. That would be easy. It certainly wouldn't be bold.
I decided, instead, to rest my troops while I could, get them healed as much as possible.
Within a few hours (mere moments in game-time), the group of roughly 400 was upon me.
I'd been fighting this faction, the Sarranids, for a very long time. I now controlled most of their territory - all but a small handful of castles and one city.
My troops were battle hardened.
Their troops were green.
My decision to heal got me back to almost full strength. The 400 attacked me in open plains. In 4 successive battles, we destroyed all but 13 of them!
Those cowards ran away...
After that battle, I still had enough time left on tower construction for my now slightly diminished army to heal. I was also able to hire on captives that the broken opposing army had held!
A day later, the castle was mine!
These are the experiences that no other game - that I know of - can give you! And this is just the tip of the iceberg!
You can play the righteous vigilante and right wrongs, slaughtering bandits and saving the innocent! You can woo and marry nobles! All of this is in the "vanilla" game!
The mod community, however, is astonishingly rich and vibrant!
Mount and Blade and Warband are the treasures you always hope you'll find in gaming... They're the unsung joys that keep on delivering fun and depth long past more polished triple-A products. They're roughly half the price of those triple-A products even when they're not on sale, to boot!
If you're the kind of player who enjoys depth and is willing to forgive a few blemishes to explore and experience, Mount and Blade/Warband may just be for you...
If you're the kind of person who really needs to have their polish and linear story, you should probably look elsewhere, or perhaps, to a mod.
All that being said, if you have ever wondered what it would be like to have hundreds of cavalry riding alongside you, swords clashing, tack ringing, screams and cries echoing all around... If you've ever wanted to feel your hair stand on end as you ride down a hated foe... If you've ever wanted to see your kingdom spread across the land...
Mount and Blade/Warband might just be for you.

Melody's Escape is great, but it has two enormous problems.
The only things really hindering it are that there is no reason the controls should be split between being displayed in the air and being displayed on the ground. It violates every instinct to be required to press up even though the icon telling you to press up is BELOW the last one you had to press. Similarly, when the icon is to the left of the slide indicator, every instinct in the body screams "Anything but right," but the placing of the arrow on the slide has absolutely no relation to what button is actually required. It's really hard to describe how jarring that is. But these two problems MUST be fixed. A streamlined approach is needed--such as having all the button inputs being in the air or on the ground, and having the "Hold Right" indicator being redesigned so that the right arrow is actually on the right side... How these flaws made it through testing, I don't know. The game is great, but these two things are huge hindrances and will be responsible for 80% of the missed notes.
A smaller problem (which may be mentioned somewhere on the store page, I don't know) is that playing any song that isn't 4/4 is really hit-and-miss. It handled Tool's "Right in Two" (11/8 timing) very well, but practically fell apart under A Perfect Circle's "Judith" (6/8 timing). It also had issues with some 4/4, like with Korn's "No Way," but handled Pink Floyd's "Have a Cigar" beautifully.
The main problem is with the interface, though... Every human instinct is to press down when the next button is actually positioned lower horizontally than the last button you pressed, and every human instinct is to press left when the indicator is on the left side of the bar that indicates the button needs to be held.

I really don't know what to make of the CoD franchise.While playing Ghosts, I constantly feel like I'm watching hundreds of thousands of dollars burn away in front of me. Each scene is so grand, so flashy and fantastical that I can't say I've seen much like it in any other series.
And yet, I'm walking down the same corridor shooting the same "bad guys" with a machine-gun I can't remember the name of. It's abysmally mindless, and I'm left wondering how this could possibly be the most popular, best selling bunch of videogames on the market. What if something intelligent had this sort of budget? What if Vampire Bloodlines, Armored Core, Deus Ex or S.T.A.L.K.E.R (to name a few more interesting games from the top of my head) had this sort of money to blow on grandiose environments and production? Sure, it's in the name of accessibility, but I feel like I'm being treated like an idiot by the game.
It's the equivalent of a Michael Bay film -- fool the audience with flashy explosions so they don't question the content behind them. It's dull, repetitive, and I have to say I'm a little disappointed that this is the new norm.

The pricetag may seem a little steep but don't be surprised if you find yourself putting 100 hours into this.
It feels a lot like Minecraft but it improves in a lot of areas where Minecraft falls short.
Similarities:
-Voxel based building
-Crafting
-Pre-generated monsters (not randomly generated)
-Swords/Axes/Pickaxes on your 1-2-3~9 slots, like you'd expect
-Healing items/food/drink
Differences:
-World is not randomly generated (I've only played Story so far)
-Build a community and bring all of the humans together to help your cause (even in multiplayer)
-Non-Voxel based digging
-MEAT IS MONEY (for a good while anyways)
-Aggressive NPC villages
-VOXEL BASED ITEM/OBJECT BUILDING: Make your weapon look like whatever you build it to look like.
-VOXEL BASED VEHICLE BUILDING: Build a Car/Helicopter/Submarine/Weird Jumping spinning orb thing/ chair on a propeller/ rocket seat/ anything you can make move
Problems:
-Light does not get stopped by the dirt you dig, making it bright in the day, and dark in the night, underground, regardless of how far you go. Underground bases are very easy to make though.
-Combat is really clunky, and shooting is not very user friendly. [TAP left click to enter aiming mode, then left click to fire, tap right click to put your gun down.] {Suggestion to change it to HOLD right click to aim please!}
-Weapons have really deliberate animations that move your character in an unusual manner and the slash isn't quite the spot you'd expect it to go. But there are Daggers/2H/ and 1H/Shield styles now, so that fixes it a bit.
-NPC pathing is non-existant and functions on a teleportation system
-That damn poo quest lol
MULTIPLAYER SPECIFIC:
-Randomly generated
-Contains randomly generated dungeons that are pretty fun
Cons: You can delete voxels that other people placed, even within their own colony. You can also steal their Sentries and prefabs. It even gives you the materials. This is a Pro if you're a troll. :P
Steam has a REFUND SYSTEM! Give this game an hour's worth of your time and if you don't like it, simply refund it. I encourage anybody who loves Minecraft (especially if you modded it a lot) to try this game.

Epic game, lots of fun if you like building games. For $24.95, even at full price this game is well worth the value. The developers have made good on many of their promises, though they may have set their own bar too high. As it stands, if this game never got another update I feel like a certainly got my moneys worth - much better than many AAA games that costs $49 or $59 on Steam. No Man's Sky will have a lot more stuff to do (a similar game on the horizon), but it will also be a $60 game. ;)
So a couple points about Planet Explorers:
Build Tools ROCK! Love how easy it is to just pull and drag out whole walls, columns, floors you name it. What might take a few days in a game like Minecraft to build you can get done in 1 day since the tools make building both faster and more fun. The barrier to entry in regards to building your first castle right from the start is almost none.
Exploration is pretty cool. You can walk around for hours discovering new stuff, new mobs, locating hard to find resources. If you like to just explore and see what the world has to offer, this is a good game to do it in.
Smooth Voxel epicness! No more Minecraft cube clone with this game.
Combat is OK. It could use a little more fine tuning obviously, but it is there, it works and plenty of weapons to craft to take down both standard enemies and bosses. Yep, it has bosses and they are HUGE and dangerous. ;)
Colonies and multiplayer. Multiplayer just makes it great - team with friends, load up a previously worked on world and work on building your empire together. I currently play this with two other friends and we always have fun.
Active developers. It is a small team so what you can expect for a game of this complexity? As I stated before, in it's current state, $24.95 is a steal for how many features are in this game. If it never got another update I would be fine. That being said, the developers, while sometimes a little slow, stay on top of the project and continue to work on stuff and make it better and bigger.
In conclusion, with the transition to Unity 5 an already great looking game just got even better looking. Don't expect lightening quick updates and constant patches every couple weeks or month - and honestly, this game doesn't need it. It is stable, it is fun and offers something differnt from all the cube based Minecraft clones out there.

Door Kickers is one of the most extreme tactical SWAT games I have ever played. It offers hugely evolving gameplay and a load of weapon combinations to suit your playstyle. You will be able to use armories from multiple countries (Germany, France, UK, US, etc.) and also have different forms of each weapon (Silences, or non-silenced) for you to be able to in stealthily or blow your way into the enemy lines. You will also have the option of creativity as each time you do a mission you will want a new strategy, and it allows you to have multiple ways of getting into a room, from pick-locking a door to blowing it down with C4 or shottgunning the lock. You will also enjoy the challenging gameplay of only having a limited amount of men and will likely be outnumbered, forcing you to strategize and plan instead of rushing them like it's a Third-person shooter.
Also note this game is being created by a small, indie team. So you will not get updates every other day, but it seems so far they have been having extremely large updates every two weeks, which likely means they love there buyers so much they are over working themselves.
If you have the money, and enjoy planning and then watching your men burst in and dominate the enemy or have one thing go wrong and watch your team get slaughtered, then buy the game. It's fairly cheap and really innovative to the market, it's also in early access so there is so much more to come and it's completely playable and almost bug free in its current state.

The first half of this review contains no spoilers the second will, I will warn you when the spoiler part starts.
So firstly my thoughts: I first bought and played Hotline Miami a couple months ago and completely fell in love with it, the graphics were perfect, the music a big bonus, the controls were simple for anyone to learn it and the difficulty hard like it should be and with Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number they get all this right again and improved on the story aspect making it 10 times as good as the first in my mind, the new weapons blend in nicely, but I normally used the original shotgun when I could. This game reminded me of the biker missions in the way that every character is different in some way, e.g. the cop seemed more like Jacket, but his friend who I nicked name the pacifist only used blunt weapons to knock out opponents which made fighting anyone with a gun a problem (My least favourite moments). The difficulty has increased for sure in this game, in the first game I made it through levels dying once or twice and in the first level I died over and over reminding me of playing some of the last levels in the Jacket missions for the first time. I loved all the missions with Tony and the mask gang they were very fun with all the different masks, my favourite being the twins.
Now spoilers ahead since this is the part where I review the story.
On a story stand point this game is great, it tells a detailed story from many characters, but sometimes I wanted to learn more about certain characters like what happened to Jacket, I understand he went to jail and all but maybe a bit more information would have been nice. Other than that I quite liked it, the writer was found out more about the guy you kill as Jacket in the mission assault and I like that we see the stories of the different people from the original game, like the guy who you see in a couple of places in the Jacket story and how he was in Afghanistan, or that one fat guy you see shaving his head in the bathroom in one of the times you go into the bar in the first game. The amount of unexpected things in this game were crazy, one of my favourite missions has to be the final one Apocalypse was very fun and showed the head of the Russian mod killing all of the mask gang, I did like how they showed the different abilities they had, like with the twins, one head moved towards you attacking you with the chainsaw but looking like a head, the other trying to stay away shooting at you. The ending was perfect for this game, with the nukes going off and everyone dying, or did they because the final thing that happens which sort of annoyed me was the sneaky little thing they did hinting at a third game by putting you in the title screen of Hotline Miami 3 and then a couple seconds later rewinding and going back to Hotline Miami 2 title screen which I also found entertaining.
So what I thought, with everything said above I will give this game a 9/10 this game did very well to show what it wanted to show, but I just wanted more story about Jacket, other than that the story had some faults killing off a lot of characters before we learnt more about why they do what they did and I found that a bit sad.

Everyone loved Hotline Miami, your grandma loved Hotline Miami and was probably humming the soundtrack while she cooked Sunday Dinner. Not everyone loves Hotline Miami two, still you should give it a go just for the experience, you won't find a game more offensively difficult, fascinatingly broken and contemptuous of any standards of decency not only in it's bloody cartoon violence but also in it's story's giant screw you to narrative logic.
When it all goes right and you're in the zone you become Chow Yun Fat, Tony Jaa and Jason Vorhees rolled up in one, gunning your way through a room full of gangsters is a lot of dangerous fun, I like it even more because you being so fragile makes every second like dancing on a knife edge. Although if you actually want to succeed then you might want to be quieter than I was.
It's gameplay breaks one of the cardinal rules of game design, if you're going to demand precision and pixel perfect judgement from the player, you shouldn't expect them to be lucky also. As always, if you make one mistake it's over, but if some fat guy falls in the wrong direction, someone on the other side of the map turns around at the wrong time or a bug temporarily renders a mobster invincible, then it's over as well. Failure isn't always your fault.
It takes the diffficulty of the first game and ratchets it up to levels you might call unfair. It's less tolerant of improvisation and recklessness even when the soundrack practically screams at you to go totally blooddrunk. But most of these flaws are rendered harmless by the R key. Because restarting is painless and quick, and most of the levels don't require you to revisit massive chunks of a map because you didn't see someone hiding in a bush, then it's less of a problem to have to go through it a million times. Later on you do get levels that are big and complex enough to make you wince at the thought of doing all that work again, but still Press R To Restart is the best thing about this game.
The best way for me to describe the story is thus: Hotline Miami took a sledgehammer to a previously cosy world, smashing it into a hundred pieces and sending irregular bits everywhere. Hotline Miami 2 takes each of these fragments and examines them, before jumbling them up in no particular order. Both a sequel and a prequel, it focuses on a number of different characters who's lives were effected in some way by the 50 Blessings conspiracy, as well as revealing the organisation's horrifying ultimate objective. Jaket is on trial, the Russian President is planning a visit, a group of bored vigilantes are waging war against crime with their own collection of animal masks, the son of a dead boss from the first game is trying to rebuild his father's criminal empire, we flash back to a US-Soviet war in Hawaii (presumably standing in for Vietnam), Richter and Jake have cameo roles, a formerly respectable actor is shooting a violent slasher flick seemingly inspired by the wave of violence and a writer and detective are both busy trying to make sense of it all. They do not succeed.
As a medium games are very good at telling "fuzzy" stories, that is a story that leaves as much out as it can get away with and relies on the player to fill in the gaps with their own sick imaginations. Almost every plot point in Hotline Miami 2 is suggested to us, rather than told, and several of those suggestions are hidden away somewhere and deliberately obscured. The downside to this kind of thing is the risk of the whole narrative being constructed of red herrings, that nothing actually goes anywhere and it all starts to fall apart if you look closely at it (remember how impressed you were with the moivie Memento when you first saw it? Remember how dissapointed you were when you actually tried to make sense of the plot?). The upside is that you sometimes get a story that really is better than the sum of it's parts (Silent Hill 2 for instance). Hotline Miami 2 lands somewhere between those two, not all of the numerous new characters really 'need' to be there and I can't help thinking that it could have used a tighter narrative with fewer perspectives and more oddness (The Vigilantes versus The Son and his Russian mob or something). But taken on their own each of the plot threads make sense as a private descent into hell, with series mascot Richard the Rooster appearing here and there as a kind of "Ghost of Christmas Future" laying down warnings of a disaster to come if they dont change their ways.
I like the little touches you find sometimes, how Pig Butcher's story mirrors the "rescue the princess" nonsense you used to see a lot of, how The Writer is trying hard not to go as crazy as the other characters, how the game pulls a Ruggero Deodato on us right in the tutorial section and how the trick is reversed at the end, The Detective's Cynicism coming back to bite him and Richter's concern for his mother preventing him from becoming a total monster. If you play through it all at once it can be frustrating but once you unlock all the chapters and can pick and mix the parts you want it becomes much easier to digest, but taken as a whole it becomes the kind of story that treats it's most important plot point as a throwaway reference at the start of one of The Soldier's levels and has a big twist that has so little foreshadowing it seems at first like a joke, but you can tell they had no other way to end it.

Mount & Blade: Warband Wall-O-Text Edition
I often get asked, "What is it about Mount and Blade? Why do you keep playing this game?"
If you've never played Mount and Blade or M&B: Warband, that's an understandable question. If you've only scratched the surface of it (turned it on, tried the tutorial or a quest or two) you probably really wonder "What is it about Mount and Blade?"
It's not a cheap "Oblivion" knock off. It's not like "Gothic" or "Total War." It's not "like" anything, really. It's a very unique creature - a true-blooded, genuine, bona fide, Indie-made, diamond-in-the-rough PC game!
It's a strange home-brew of strategy, diplomacy, resource management, role-playing, and, most of all, first or third person melee (and ranged) combat!
Perhaps the greatest thing about Mount and Blade - and Warband - is that it allows you, the player, to make of it what you will!
Of course, that kind of freedom comes with a greater responsibility. The game gives you all the tools to have as much fun as you desire... The question is, how will you use them?
Mount and Blade and Mount and Blade: Warband will not hold your hand. They'll teach you a bit about how to fight and pretty much kick you to the curb. The game world is open for you after that, to do with exactly as you please.
Players who are accustomed to a more thorough tutorial may feel a bit jilted. I, myself, believe in thorough tutorials, but somehow, for me, Mount and Blade/Warband works!
I felt as if I were part of that world; I had only basic skills and I was set loose to find my own destiny...
There were no restraints on what I could do! I could join up with a faction, I could wander aimlessly. I could turn bandit, or merchant, or earn my keep traveling from tournament to tournament!
When I first started the first Mount and Blade, it took me a while to figure out that, while I could travel entirely alone, I could gather companions to my side - and even hire recruits to form a raiding party or the start of an army!
I found out quickly that I, myself, could level... It took me a bit more time to find out that my companions could level, as well! Not only that, my army could level!
My army could literally change from a bunch of ragged peasants to elite warriors by gaining experience through training and combat!
Now, rather than drifting through the world alone and in peril, I was a force to be reckoned with!
In time, kings and sultans, lords and khans sent me offers of vassalage, hoping to lure my ever-growing band to their cause...
In my first games, I took their offers. I fought small skirmishes and great battles! It was not uncommon to find myself in the midst of 200+ warriors, mounted and afoot, thundering across the battlefield seeking each others' lives!
It. Was. Glorious!
And then, it wasn't enough...
I'd captured castles and cities, destroyed armies 4, 5, even 6 times my own size! (And, yes, it's extremely difficult.)
However, I'd done it all for the king. While he sat on his bum in his keep, feasting and passing out what I'd captured to other lords, I was out killing and bleeding for him - for someone else...
That had to stop.
It did. I rebelled against my "rightful lord" and made him pay a higher price than all his foes... I even started my own Empire, capturing town after town, castle after castle and bringing them under my banner!
I promoted my faithful companions to lords - vassals now serving under me! By my right of rule do they gather armies and chastise my foes! By my right of rule are they awarded fiefs of towns, villages, and castles.
That, my friends, that is Glorious!
If you've never played Mount and Blade/Warband, but you've played, say, a Real-Time Strategy game like Warcraft 3, or, perhaps better, something from the Total War series, you've captured or razed villages, destroyed armies, perhaps even engaged in diplomacy...
In Mount and Blade/Warband, you're not leading your army from some celestial cloud with a drag-selection box and right-click. You're on your horse with mace and bow! You're literally standing on the field with sword and shield and you can alter the course of battle!
You can walk through the cities and castles! You can assault the walls in siege towers or on ladders! You can defend your holdings, firing bolts from the parapets or standing shoulder to shoulder against the foe!
This isn't some detached strategic simulation... I've made more difficult decisions in M&B/Warband than any other "strategy" game.
Last night, I was besieging a castle. Defenders outnumbered my forces 3+ to 1. While I was preparing a siege tower, the defenders sent a force of 145 to try to destroy my army of roughly 100.
I shattered them.
However, my forces were wounded, but I had time to heal as I continued work on the siege tower. That was when a group of about 400 rode in over the horizon.
I could break the siege and run. That would be easy. It certainly wouldn't be bold.
I decided, instead, to rest my troops while I could, get them healed as much as possible.
Within a few hours (mere moments in game-time), the group of roughly 400 was upon me.
I'd been fighting this faction, the Sarranids, for a very long time. I now controlled most of their territory - all but a small handful of castles and one city.
My troops were battle hardened.
Their troops were green.
My decision to heal got me back to almost full strength. The 400 attacked me in open plains. In 4 successive battles, we destroyed all but 13 of them!
Those cowards ran away...
After that battle, I still had enough time left on tower construction for my now slightly diminished army to heal. I was also able to hire on captives that the broken opposing army had held!
A day later, the castle was mine!
These are the experiences that no other game - that I know of - can give you! And this is just the tip of the iceberg!
You can play the righteous vigilante and right wrongs, slaughtering bandits and saving the innocent! You can woo and marry nobles! All of this is in the "vanilla" game!
The mod community, however, is astonishingly rich and vibrant!
Mount and Blade and Warband are the treasures you always hope you'll find in gaming... They're the unsung joys that keep on delivering fun and depth long past more polished triple-A products. They're roughly half the price of those triple-A products even when they're not on sale, to boot!
If you're the kind of player who enjoys depth and is willing to forgive a few blemishes to explore and experience, Mount and Blade/Warband may just be for you...
If you're the kind of person who really needs to have their polish and linear story, you should probably look elsewhere, or perhaps, to a mod.
All that being said, if you have ever wondered what it would be like to have hundreds of cavalry riding alongside you, swords clashing, tack ringing, screams and cries echoing all around... If you've ever wanted to feel your hair stand on end as you ride down a hated foe... If you've ever wanted to see your kingdom spread across the land...
Mount and Blade/Warband might just be for you.

Do you remember when you were playing Medieval: Total War and thought "Oh man, I wish I could be down there bashing skulls by myself", or when you were playing Chivalry: Medieval warfare and thought "I wish this was an RPG and I would get fame and fortune from quicking all this people's♥♥♥♥♥quot;? It's both a strategical and political (albeit not extremely deep) simulation, and a real time large scale battle in first/third person, with all the classical elements of RPGs: A party, levels, skills, equipped items, loot and money.
You can work as a commoners man, protecting the peasants from bandits and doing quests, work as a mercenary for the big lords, swear fealty to one of them and keep loyal so that the king grants you towns, castles and cities (which you can assault and conquer), support a pretender, or declare yourself a king and form your own faction. Extremely frustrating. The first half of the game (around 2 hours) isn't too bad, the protagonist Randall is introduced along with the basic mechanics. As the game spills over into it's second half however, it decides to just throw scenarios at you where you literally can't guess what's going to happen, unless you're the MacGyver of gaming. So you end up in a vicous cycle of dying constantly and getting slightly further each time. Ultimately, it can end up taking around 5 minutes on one small puzzle section, and these sections get more persistent towards the end.
On top of that, the only thing strong about this game is its visual presence and how it incorporates set pieces. However, even the really cool moments where it actually feels like you're playing a decent game are soiled by constant deaths, the ending sequence with Stellar was particularly bad.
I can understand making a platformer 'challenging' but throwing death obstacles in the final leg of the game and ultimately negating the impact of the cool part is a sure-fire way to sour the experience. In the last quarter of the game you're just wishing it would be over, and it's only four hours long...dear oh dear.

I don't recommmend buying this game unless you've beaten the first one; this game is longer and harder to beat than the first, so you may get frustrated if you're not already familiar with the tactics necessary to progress. For example, I was surprised at the difficulty of the first non-tutorial level.
This game is not perfect; a lot of the criticisms people point out in these reviews are things that I agree with. I just still think this is one of the most-fun games I've played in years.
I was worried the music would be considerably worse than that found in the first, but I was pleasantly surprised: while it isn't quite as good, it's close, and still great. The first one probably had the best music I'd ever heard in a game, so I can't hold it against them for having trouble getting music to quite the same level.
The missions in this game have a TON of enemies, way more than in the first game. This means you may frequently need to lure people one-at-a-time around corners to narrow down the numbers before you can get more aggressive. Other people have been pointing this out as a criticism, but I just think it's a way to increase difficulty for people who've already mastered the first game. I've seen videos of people who are still able to rush through the game once they memorize where the different enemies are.

I loved the first Hotline Miami and very much enjoyed the first few acts of this game.  The second half of the game, has been a totally different story.  Your focus will switch from doing levels more effieciently (higher combo and less time) to being desperate to finish them.  Why is this you ask? Well the later levels are specifically designed to be very cheap. Enemies are placed strategically to off screen snipe you. The game turns into a memorization and luck game.  Here are some examples of what you will find:
Lighting will be changed on one level to make it very hard to see.
You will shoot blindly down halways hoping to kill the offscreen sniper that killed you last time that you cannot use the camera movement to find.
You will constantly find yourself asking, "who shot me?" or "how did i die?"
While windows are obvious, several other graphics are not obvious whether not you can shoot through them or not.  You will learn on that level which ones are once you get shot through it several times.
The game will ask of you extreme accuracty and response of an aiming system that makes it very difficult.
Do not get me wrong, this is not a bad game. It has been well made with a few bugs (AI getting stuck on doors).  However, it is not my type of game.  It initially has the spirit of Hotline Miami, which is lost as the game progresses.  I find myself pleading for it to end.

Do you like this game ?

Extraction: A mode that i found to be the most boring. you  go around rescuing NPCs, holding out for a while, sending them off, rince, repeat. Boring, repetitive.
Escape: When i saw the map "biotech" i was psyched since it was my favorite ZPO map in ZPS, but i couldnt play though it because when 1 person died they absolutely crushed everyone else as a zombie, but more on that later. Despite my attempts i found the maps much larger than they had any business being, spawns for zombies were either too close or too far from the survivors from what i played, and running around doing objectives felt a lot more like a chore than anything else.
Hunt: The only mode i found fun for a while until i realized that it's just a rush for the power weapons and that's it. Go for a machine gun and burst someone down when they can't see you and you've just about won it. What's more is that it basically comes down to who sees who gets the jump on who. You become a zombie when you die, but that's got its own issues.
Survivor play: It felt like i was playing a clunky version of No More Room in Hell. You have some zombies that are fast, some that are slow, but the problem is that some of them are players.
Zombie play: Dart around and either eat up or dodge their shots, when they reload go in for an easy kill. not to mention there is a grapple mechanic so go behind them and bite someone to infect them and you've basically got an easy kill or more than just 1 easy kill.
I wouldn't recommend this game at all. If you want PVP go on ZPS if you want PVE go on NMRIH. They should have just focused on making Hunt mode its most attractive feature, but in its current state i get the feeling that 2 of the modes are useless and one is just potential that i highly doubt can be realized because of the mechanics and overall feel of the game.

Hello gamers!  Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number was recently released to the masses, and I have taken a break from popping heads and making meth in Payday 2 to bring you a quick review of this game.  Full disclosure: I never played the first game but I am familiar with it, and I only purchased Hotline Miami 2 to get the bonuses that were being offered within Payday 2.  That being said, I am glad that I did pick it up.  Let’s get down to it!
Developed by Dennation Games and published by Devolver Digital, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the sequel to the very successful Hotline Miami.  The game’s story is a little confusing, and I’ll be honest I had to look it up online to understand it better.  You play as a whole slew of characters in Hotline Miami 2.  Like the first game, each character or mask has different abilities that make them handle just a little bit differently than others.  At the end of Hotline Miami, the character Jacket was captured and is seen on trial in Hotline Miami 2.  This plays a small part in Hotline Miami 2, but the constant shift between different characters, time periods ultimately forms the story in this game.  You play as characters such as The Pig Butcher, Martin, starting out filming a violent snuff film, going onto TV and giving an interview so bizarre that suddenly Tom Cruses couch jumping antics seem totally normal.  Following the arrest of The Pig Butcher, you end up in a police station and then fight and kill your way through until you ultimately find out that it is all part of the film.
The gameplay is absolutely awesome.  Some characters start out a stage with a weapon, while others may simply use their fists to get the job done.  You will punch, beat, strangle, chop and shoot your way through floors of enemies and paint the walls and floors with their blood.  Hotline Miami 2 is a wonderfully explosion of blood and pixels and sometimes it is your blood.  Yes, you will probably die several times throughout the levels.  Like this.  Or this.  Or like that.  Despite the near assurance of several untimely endings, it isn’t really all that bad and the levels go quickly enough that it never gets too frustrating.  There really is no set way to finish each floor, allowing the player to dream up their own way to slaughter everyone in their path.  The AI is at times kind of stupid and pretty easy to dupe, making some areas way easier than what they should probably be.
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number has a great soundtrack that keeps you engrossed that keeps up with your movements.  This isn’t your mama’s slow dance, the fast paced electronic beats will never lag behind your merciless run through each stage.  Crank that♥♥♥♥♥♥up and get ready to experience a true killer’s soundtrack.
Overall the game is really entertaining but a little short.  Dennation Games has said that a map editor is going to be released.  I couldn’t find any information from Dennation Games that specifically said that there would be Steam workshop support, but I would guess that a map editor released along with Steam Workshop integration would make a lot of sense.  At any rate, a map editor is coming which should inject a healthy amount of life into this game and allow you to create levels for the gamer masses to play and enjoy.

As a huge fan of the first game, I simply cannot recommend this one.
The music style, plot style, and visual style are all the same (as to be expected) and still fit really well into the whole neon theme they got going on. Depending on your personal tastes they might have even improved on these aspects.
They completely dropped the ball on gameplay though. The first Hotline Miami was fast, action-packed, and rewarded risky gameplay thanks to the tight and short level design.
This sequel however has large sprawling levels with huge corridors and windows, forcing you to take a slow and calculated approach or risk being spotted and overwhelmed. Certain bulky enemies cannot even be killed in close quarters, but have to be shot. This puts a greater emphasis on hiding behind corners and constantly popping out to shoot. The situation where you desperately need a firearm but don't have one or any ammo for it will pop up frequently, which was never the case in the first Hotline Miami.
All in all, you might like this game. It's just that the gameplay took such a drastic turn for the worse that it's left a bad taste in my mouth. I could not bring myself to finish it.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.
Hotline Miami 2 takes place during the aftermath of the first game along with going back in time to fill in the story line that was in the first game. The features are the same but with a few added ablities and characters to play as from the store clerk in his army days. To the fanatics that attempt to follow in the foot steps from the lead character in the first game. While charging through dark hallways to even subway tunnels to even hawaii where a fictional war takes place. Hotline Miami 2 delievers the same memorable game play with some new weapons and enemies to be thrown at you.
Gameplay:
If you're familiar or have played through the first game the same is to be mostly expected in HM2. Using doors to knock enemies over and using mask to give you different abilities to help you throug the level. The level design us much larger this time around and you'll find yourself dealing with enemies that are far out of sight. So you'll be relying on moving from cover to cover and tricking enemies to chase after you when peaking around corners. This whoever can be extremely frustrating as you will find yourself time and time again picked off from a lone enemy just out of sight. Whoever with there being no serious penalty for being killed you'll spawn in again, and again, and maybe you'll make it this time. But that's what makes Hotline Miami so challenging is figuring out what you're next move should be when going from room to room as you dispatch one heavily armed bad guy after the next. As the story moves forward you'll have to rely on using tactics and a fast reaction to push through large groups of enemies out for your head. This is what makes this game such a rush to play through over and over again. Though with there being some uses with the controls or enviroment getting in the way when it really shouldn't it's a minor set back to the rest of how the game plays. Which is fast and vicious.
Graphics:
The game looks and feels like an old school top down shooter. With flashy 80's colors and set pieces in the game to really set the game in the mood. You can tell there was some great deal of work that was done up when this game was put together. In all it's 16-bit glory this game may not be in super HD 3D graphics but the art style and choice of art direction makes this game stand out from the rest of the games that are out. Bright and vibrant colors on the chapter and loading screens are just an awesome thing and really just add to the world that Hotline Miami conveys. And with each new place you venture through is a different look and feel with the color pallets that are used.
Story:
Hotline Miami is a mixed bag of wild, confusing, and very interesting story. I won't try to delve to much on it's as to not ruin it for anyone who hasn't played the first or the second game. Wrong Number fills in some answers that left players asking questions while still leaving things up to the players to figure out for themselves. While showing some back story to some well known characters and introducing new ones and some characters that leave you unsure as what they contribute into the story itself. The story being hard to explain I'll will just say it leaves you wanting to see what happens next and where it will twist and pile on more of the plot.
Music and Audio:
With a crazy amount of violence and intense situations the soundtrack is the literal cherry on top when it has come to the Hotline Miami games. Heavy techno blars as you run in guns blazing as a duel sub machine gun bear mask wearing fanatic. To slicing up people in a strip club with a sword it all just fits so perfectly and the developers chose their soundtrack perfectly to help tell the story and push the action. Though sound effects are a bit on the mild side with guns sounding a little quiet and most weapons making the same sound when you hit an enemy its really a minor detail that I didn't see as a big of a problem. Since Hotline Miami is a game well known for the soundtrack this game brings it back in spades and you'll find yourself jumping back into levels just to hear the songs over and over again. Now if only I could get my hands on the full soundtrack I think my life would be complete.
Replayablity:
Hotline Miami has another feature that is great for anyone trying to beat their own highscore or just trying to see how fast they can get through a level in the game. Hotline Miami is awesome when it comes to being able to replay levels that you've already beaten. And for the perfectionists you can't go wrong with being able to easily replay old chapters to see if you can do better than the first time around.
Final Thoughts:
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number delievered very well with being a sequel and they did it right with enough added features and a larger story from the first game. The music and visuals are stunning and it really breaths in an amazing world and story that leaves you wanting more and seconding guessing yourself and you go from room to room bashing heads in. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is all and all a great game and something different from the typical norm that is released almost yearly.
I strongly recommend picking up Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number and give it a play through you won't regret it.

Hotline Miami 2 is a hot mess compared to its predecessor, but a great game nonetheless.
For those who have played HM1:
HM2 is a great game overall, but falls short of the first one.
-Too many guns, makes the action less intense when it's a lot of spray-and-pray in the overly large rooms.
-On the levels, some are just WAY too big leaving the player wide open for one random bullet to put an end to all their hard work.
-Lack of masks was dissapointing (to me anyway); I anticipated having a more refined/polished mask system, which was present, but on a much smaller scale than the previous game.
-Forced characters puts too much emphasis on narrative and restrictive gameplay, something that was not present in HM1.
-Along with the narrative, it's convoluted to say the least, and supplementary information shouldn't be required to understand it.
-Addition of roll-dodge is neat, but is EXTEMELY annoying when trying to perfom an execution.
-Personally, the game is missing some of the close-quarters, high-intensity gameplay from HM1 (which is not necessarily a negative thing).
-Four main additions to this game: Guns, Glass, Thugs and Dogs
Annnnd on a lighter note...
-The music is stellar on most levels, though some levels have forgetful songs.
-Alex and Ash is a badass mask (in my opinion of course).
-The game as a whole is still Hotline Miami and is still worth a playthrough by fans of the series.
-The addition of hard mode (as if this one wasn't hard enough) offers more replayabilty.
Overall, fans of the series will enjoy this, however, expect more frustration than the first HM, and don't expect it to trump the first HM. It's strangely hard to recommend this, but it's still the same♥♥♥♥♥kicking fun that was to be had in the first game.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a game that shares many similarities with the Left4Dead series, with the main difference being the removal of PvP modes and a heavy focus on aquiring better equipment for your character(s), of which there are 5. Each Character feels very unique from the others, and has an impressive array of primary and secondary weapon varients to unlock. (Gear is unlocked by a single drop at the end of each mission, regardless of length.)
Unfortunately, the same loot system that offers such a wide variety of playstyles and customization also drags the game down into what is essentially a grind for the best gear. Bonus objectives (tomes and grimoires) can be picked up throughout the level, and improve your chance at better rewards if carried to the end of the level, while the difficulty chosen decides what loot can be dropped at the end of the mission.
Because of this design, players often run short, high difficulty missions repeatedly with the same bonus objectives each time. Adding to the monotony is the lack of randomization in each level that Left4Dead showed with it's Director system. It often feels that player skill and game knowlage takes a backseat to your equipment and knowlage of cheese strategies for the level, which feels even worse without PvP.
TL:DR It's a co-op survival with well made combat and classes but suffers from grindy progression and over-reliance on equipment rather than player skill. Reccomended for Warhammer fans or fans of Borderlands, Warframe, etc.

At the time of writing this review, I had about 1.4 hours invested in the game.
Melody's Escape is a fun game for what you pay. If you typically enjoy rhythm games, then this game will be perfect for you. This game is still in early access however, so I advise that you spend some time considering everything before buying it. Melody's Escape uses your own musical library to then generate a track for you to traverse. Tempo of the song is analyzed and the track is created based on that.
PROS:
+Nearly any PC can run it.
+Theoretically unlimited gameplay.
+Difficulty ranging from incredibly easy to brutally punishing.
+Has a sort of Sandbox mode where you can just chill.
+Simple backgrounds that don't distract from gameplay.
+Options for different characters, including ways to input a custom character.
CONS:
-The game is in development, and hasn't had an update for several months.
-Any graphical slow down could cause you to mess up a song.
-Frequently unstable framerate (see above)
-Animations are stiff and at times don't feel natural. While this doesn't exactly detract from the value of the game, in my opinion a finished game should have fluid animation that makes sense.
TL;DR
Melody's Escape is a charming game that is worth playing, however it doesn't look like the game will be "finished" and there is one problem that has a negative impact on gameplay.

Sonic Adventure 2 is one of the better 3D Sonic Games. Is it the best? No. Is it still really fun? About half of it is. There are six different characters in Sonic Adventure 2 and only three playstyles. Each very different from eachother.
The First playstyle is Sonic and Shadow's. Their playstyle is full of fast paced platforming, great level design, fantastic controls, and amazing music. They are the best characters to play in the game. But out of the 30 levels in the game, they only get 10.
The Second playstyle is Tails and Dr.Eggman's. Their playstyle is quite different from Sonic and Shadows. Both Tails and Dr. Eggman control a Mech. They go around shooting enemies, moving at a moderate pace, and dealing with Castlevania type knockback. The sad thing is about Tails and Eggman is, only Eggman is fun to play as. Tails on his mech feels like it was just thrown in there and his levels are horribly designed. Eggman on the other hand has levels that work perfectly with his playstyle.  Atleast both Tails and Eggman get good music in their  levels.
The Third playstyle is Knuckles and Rouge the Bat's. Their playstyle is all about treasure hunting. Now with these two, nothing is wrong with how they control. They are fast, they can glide through the air, and they are able to climb walls. They go around in non-linear levels and search for three objects. Once all objects are found, the level is over. At first I enjoyed this. I found it fun... until I got to the later levels. As you prgress through the game the levels become more open and the three objects you're searching for become harder to find. The harder they are to find, the longer you spend in the level. The longer you spend in the level, the more annoyed you become. The more annoyed you become, the more you hate their playstyle. Rouge has some really nice music in her levels while Knuckles is plagued by really bad Rap.
Overall, I only like half of the game. Sonic, Shadow, and Eggman. The characters I could not care for. As for the story, I have to say that the story in this game was actually decent. Sonic Adventure 2 is a good game, but I found it impossible to enjoy all of it.

A dark, paranoid parkour trip through the gritty 1980s streets of Seattle during a zombie outbreak as the middle-aged Randall makes for a fantastic 2D platformer through ravaged streets and tunnels in a world dripping with atmosphere. Deadlight never got the attention it deserved, and as one of the few indie game on the platform at that time, it launched on X-Box and flew under the radar, and was then quietly added to Steam later, which is a shame because it's surprisingly well made 2.5D platformer, and has plenty of character and a strong atmosphere and art design, offering a bit more than you'd expect.
What could've been a flat 2D platforming experience has become an interesting world with history and characters worth paying attention to. The detail and the art style make this a fun experience rather than just another game.
* Great art and level design, there are a few times when you'll get frustrated at repeating a section or two, but they're few and far between
* Fun, albeit simple mechanics (like the Yo-yo) keep it form being boring
* Rich, interesting variety of collectibles and easter-eggs
* The PC Port was frankly very lazy and poorly done. At least one section of gameplay seems to have been time limited based on frames rather than microseconds, meaning problems occur when changing FPS, which is presumably why they've locked it to a mere 30 FPS. Check Recommendations below for a guide on changing FPS, and enabling SLI. Poor controls, poor graphics and optimization options and more add to the problems of the port.
* A few small design mistakes make some moments feel cheap and annoying
Deadlight is fairly short, and comes in at around 5 hours playtime, which will feel too short for some, but it fits well for the world and underlying story, and Deadlight doesn't overstay its welcome. The addition of good collectibles and achievements also add something for completionists.
Available for £9.99/11.99€/$14.99 on Steam, the soundtrack is fairly nice, but not worth paying for. Deadlight is also available on X-box, and does come up in indie bundles from time to time.
* You can remove the 30 FPS lock by editing the config files, there is no in-game option to do so. Note that there may be problems at certain stages of the game as a result due to the poor reliance on frames for timing.
.
* Interestingly, Deadlight supports multiple GPUs, but has SLI disabled by default. You can enable it
.
* There are some interesting easter eggs including shoutouts to games like Portal and Cthulu, collectible hand-held game consoles, and references to real world serial killers.
* It's playable on a keyboard, but much smoother on a controller.
