A good sequel uses the original game as a springboard, taking the concepts and ideas and evolving them naturally, taking the good parts and improving on them, and trimming the misused or outright bad aspects down to manageable levels, or removing them entirely if possible. Hotline Miami 2 is not a good sequel.  The core gameplay, that of chaotic violence to the tune of a fantastic soundtrack, is relatively intact. Everything else, however, has changed, in my opinoin, for the worse.
Hotline Miami was not an easy game by any means, but the gameplay revolved around that. It accounted for that. Death was cheap, and respawning was instant, your player character going from a bloody stain on the floor right back to the front door in a second flat, ready to try murdering an entire building one more time. The levels were mostly compact and there were plenty of separated rooms for you to take advantage of, the formula changing slightly as the game went on to add organic challenge and force you to adapt to situations you can't prevent. Due to the game's top down nature, the entire level was not always in frame, especially as the game went on, but you didn't typically have to worry about someone off screen killing you from across the stage because there were rooms between you and them, not one long hallway that you can't see down.
Hotline Miami 2, on the other hand, makes death feel absolutely annoying. Levels are significantly larger, the enemy population growing accordingly. And there's a lot of empty space to traverse. Ordinarily, this wouldn't be too much of a problem, were it not for the greatly emphasized focus on guns. Half of your deaths will absolutely come from off screen because a goon saw you and blasted you from an angle you couldn't account for. You respawn just as fast, of course, but instead of getting right back into the flow without a care, you feel the loss of progress. There's a lot of guys to kill, and if the last ones get the better of you, you are going to feel the pain. The gameplay itself becomes a chore, and the most successful way to get through stages goes against the entire point of the game: taking it slow and steady, holding down the shift key the entire time to make sure the big area you're traversing doesn't have a guy with a gun who'll pop you the second you enter his line of sight. The basic game design has remained the same, while the scale of the actual game has outgrown it and taken things in a different direction that the design wasn't built to handle.
Another factor that Hotline Miami 2 boasts is several different characters. There's actually a ton. And in my opinion, that makes things less compelling. Especially because at least half of them don't even wear masks, and as an effect, don't have special abilities beyond two that specifically come to mind, both with glaring downsides and with no sizeable buff to compensate. One of them is "nonlethal", the air quotes being present because you can be lethal, but only with downed enemies. He refuses to use bladed weapons or guns, choosing to unload picked up firearms and make it so enemies can't use them instead of using them himself. It makes sense in character, of course, but adjusting to his gameplay takes time, especially because, again, a lot of enemies use guns. The other character starts with a gun you choose at the beginning of his segments. That gun sticks with you. You can never drop it, only switch to your knife. You can reload it at ammo boxes, but confusingly, he doesn't fully restock, even though the ammo boxes can be used forever. Dropped enemy guns taunt you, because as that character, you cannot pick up any weapons.
The story has expanded accordingly, aiming to expand on how the events of Hotline Miami started, and conclude them. Taking the Pulp Fiction approach of presenting events in anachronic order, the story jumps from character to character at various points in time, not too much of a far cry from how the first game was handled. However, because there is now an overarching story that isn't laid out piece by piece for you to put together, and is instead thrown directly at you, there is dialogue everywhere. Characters talk, and talk, and for some reason, that doesn't feel too "in the spirt" of Hotline Miami, the expanded roster making the experience less of an utter mind screw and more of a crime thriller with the chapters all mixed up. Not a bad thing ordinarily, but because it is a direct sequel, it does need to be compared to the original.
Thankfully, the soundtrack remains one of the defining aspects of the game. It was always good in Hotline Miami, and it's thankfully unchanged here. It's one of the unquestionably best parts of the game, and I recommend getting the soundtrack and looking into the various artists that contributed, Perturbator being my personal favorite.
Occasionally there's a level where you get into the groove. You tune out everything but the music, and just jump right in, going right in and playing the game the way it was meant to be played, never stopping, every second punctuated by the death of a pastel suited goon, grabbing his weapon and using it on his buddy in the next instant, the way the game wants you to play it. Unfortunately, those levels seem to be few and far between, most of them throwing guns at you and expecting you to wade in amidst a wall of instant death. Curiously, every character seems to have a degree of resistance to bullets, able to take maybe one or two before dying. However, you won't notice that unless you're lucky. Shotguns kill you instantly, and the ability to take one hit doesn't matter when a thug with an automatic rifle sends several rounds your way. And amidst my major issues, there's a bevy of errors and glitches, the masked twins act as one character, yet the partner AI gets frequently stuck on walls and often fails to give you back up when you storm a room. Some levels have a strangely bright filter thrown over them, which makes your cursor hard to see. On the upside, I haven't seen a single boss encounter or stealth section. That's...about it.
It's strange to see a game functionally unchanged, but feel wholly different. It's a sequel that aims to expand, but does so ungracefully and with surprisingly short sight. At the time of writing (March 21st, 2015), I cannot recommend it at full price. If you must play another Hotline Miami, wait til it's on sale. One of the few redeeming aspects of the game is its cross promotional deal with Payday 2, making Jacket a playable character in that game if you buy the special edition of Hotline Miami 2.
All in all, 5/10. The end result has changed while keeping the basic formula intact, but the game expects you to play it like the first one when doing it in such a way will get you killed more often than not and just lead to frustration. It's a sequel that aims high, but performs worse than its predecessor and falls short of the mark.

Hotline Miami 2, from what I have been told, was a much anticipated sequel to a game I never played. I like Payday 2, so I bought this as a DLC for Payday, and I thought I might as well play it.
And To be honest, I quickly fell in love with this game, I enjoyed the fast paced game play, planning a route, and I wasn't even made when I died.
For the first few levels at least.
Quickly I became frustrated, even angry with the way levels would spin out of control the second I walked out a door, after being shot by an enemy that I couldn’t see, even when zooming off-screen as far as I could go, I still got blindsided by a bullet that when thru 3 windows and a half open door. I ended up using Trial and Error to figure out which hallways to spray down when, and hoped I would hit the one enemy that keeps killing me, only to die to a new enemy that Just now decided I existed. I had assumed this was the Hotline experience, that is until I bought the first game.
Now, after having completed both games, with secrets unlocked, I can compile a review for this one.
+Better AI (Kind of)
+More Variety
+More Game play
=Equally Frustrating AI
=Equally Confusing Story (Maybe a bit more, but at least it cleared a few things up)
=Equally Charming Music and Atmosphere
=Higher Difficulty
-Much Worse Level Design
-Less Flexibility
Hotline Miami falls into the common pitfall of Horrible AI with superhuman Powers, they won’t see you blast the guy they’re staring at in the back of the head, but if you take a step 50 feet behind them, they whip around and shoot you before you can pan your screen to see them. It was hard to believe at first, but the AI is actually better in Hotline 2, for the pure reason its more streamlines, and the enemies actually react to you walking into a room.
In My opinion, this game has Hotline 1 Beat over Variety. In Hotline 1 you could choose 1 ability that was based on your mask, every level or so, you got a new mask. In Hotline 2, you occasionally get a choice between Characters or masks, depending on the level. The most Variety are the 'Fan' Levels in which you can choose 1 of 4 characters (Technically 5, but one is a Duo) or being able to choose which gun you use for an entire level. The Least Variety being no choice at all. In the middle of the game I found myself saying 'I wish I could play as the guy from the last level'. While restricting the player, this is almost a smart design choice, as it encourages the player to flexibility; I learned how to use all of characters, instead of 1 (For the level I had to use them for, at least). This prevented a Trend I noticed myself doing in Hotline 1, which was choosing a favorite mask, and only using that. While I think this was smart, it also feels restricting, as the player is forced to step out of their comfort zone.
When it comes to game play, this game just took me more time; I don't know if its difficulty, or more levels, but I beat Hotline 1 in like, 1 sitting, Hotline 2 took me a few days at the least.
The AI is just as frustrating, still feels brain-dead, a bit smarter, but none of them think to stop running around the corner hugging the wall, even though there’s at least 7 dead people on the ground next to said corner. Same thing with rooms. They just keep running in.
This game cleared up a lot about the story, mainly the back-story of the main character of Hotline 1, but it still makes no sense.
The Music and atmosphere are amazing, in both games, this is strictly a plus.
What I didn't know, is this game is MUCH harder than Hotline 1, to the point where, having played Hotline 2 first, I breezed thru the First game, in like 2 hours, granted I didn't go for 100% or anything like that, but it was still a walk in the park.
As you may have noticed from many reviews, the level design is horrid as the game goes on, open areas are not fun to be in a game like this, and it comes to a point where levels are strictly larger than you can see, and you get blindsided more than anything, It was the biggest downfall of what could have been the perfect sequel, in my opinion.
As stated before, The game has less flexibility, while it stops me from using the one mask I like, it does so by force, many would feel if they want to use the same ability they should, and while I loved a lot of the game play elements brought to the table, I still developed favorites, that I would use whenever presented with a choice, and late level design makes half of the abilities seem almost useless.
Deadly Fists (But No Guns) Was a common ability that I hated, I felt like the open areas punished me for choosing my fists, and when I can get a Chainsaw-SMG tag team, that does the same thing, but better, I didn't feel compelled to do so. I also didn't feel the score bonus I would offset said challenge of picking my fists, but others might disagree.
Starting Weapon (With Limited Ammo (With Exception)) Felt useless when the length of levels were taken into account, even if I got a kill with every bullet, I would have to drop the weapon, and use something else, normally worse. Because of this I much preferred other abilities.
Also this game has less abilities overall, making it seem like they skimped out on the personal flair you could add to a strategy, that only worked using your favorite mask.
*Enemies getting stuck in Doors
*Enemies becoming Immortal in Doors
*Not being able to throw Thru an Open Door
*Executions taking longer while holding (About half of the) weapons VS your bare hands
*Not being able to restart after receiving your grade, and having to sit thru a cut scene you don't want to see
*Confusing scoring system (In my opinion) that gives me an unclear target goal, and sometimes gives me an A+ for...   reasons?
*Enemies wandering away from their spawn point, seemingly at random
*Bonus points awarded at random, in which enemies will be downed instead of killed, awarding kill points, and bonus execute points
While still being a fun game, that I think is worth about 10 bucks, it doesn't hold up as a sequel to the original, so don't buy it as that.

This game's okay.
Yes, you can sense one certain faction being noticeably superior to the rest. Don't expect to win as Germany a lot, and even less as the US.
Yes, they pressure you to spend real money in order to advance. For example, I play as US infantry and wanted the Thompson. However, you have to purchase the grease gun, another American SMG, and actually using it is necessary in order to unlock the Thompson. The grind to unlock the Thompson itself isn't bad, however you're met with an insanely high cost of 126k standard in-game currency, and it takes quite a while to rack up just a few thousand if you're a player of average skill level.
No, I wouldn't say it's a pay to win. You're still perfectly capable with what you already have in the game. Other players can shortcut the entire game and get some pretty good gear, but it goes both ways.
Yes, it's historically inaccurate for the most part. The Russians and US shouldn't be at war with each other. But there isn't any kind of ally system in the game, presumably for the game's sake. You can figure that out for yourself with the game's "War" mode. Each faction battles for parts of the map, taking place all over Europe. Eventually, the US and Russians collide for territory, and I'm pretty sure that they're enemies to each other in this game in order to keep the game rolling and balanced (as far as balanced goes in this game).
No, this game doesn't have the best gameplay mechanics or graphics. It can be pretty rage-inducing from time to time. It can be really fun some of the time. Overall it feels somewhat empty and just not there. There are tons of maps (in War mode at least), but after some time everything from the scenery to the firefights start to feel repetitive. Textures are pretty basic, which doesn't help the repetitive factor much.
Yes, teamwork, coordination, and tactics are key to succeeding in this game. However, don't look for that here - you'd be lucky to find anyone communicative on your team other than around 3 or 4 people at a time at most. In other words, you're likely to be stuck with people that have no clue what they're doing or are playing as an individual.
Yes, this game is F2P. Not only that, it's in Beta. I don't have high expectations for this at all, but when it's no longer Beta and the full version is out, I would hope that the developers listen to the community to make it a better game for all.
No, I would not recommend this game. It's definitely a love-hate relationship, and definitely has some potential behind it. However, in its current state, it's worth a check-out at the most, but don't expect to be wanting to stick around for long.

Whatever you do, do NOT purchase this because the atmosphere looks cool.  Yes, it does look cool.  You know what's not cool?  Literally everything else about the game.  The overall mechanics, controls, story, voice acting...all atrocious.
What's worse than the worst controls you've ever experienced in a game?  How about attaching those controls to a character who can't swim and can barely swing an ax (slowly, I might add) more than a few times before needing a nap?  Sounds like a perfect candidate for zombie apocalypse survival, right?
Have fun watching yourself die over and over again, but not JUST because of the controls.  Oh, no.  The infuriatingly unintuitive trial-and-error design will make sure you die repeatedly, as well.  But don't despair!  The game ALWAYS makes sure you figure out what to do.  Shortly after you die.  And after you die, you can enjoy largely terrible checkpointing, often complete with painfully narrated cut-scene garbage, adding to your ever-blossoming rage.
The positives, aside from atmosphere?  It's only a few hours long.  And some of it is bad enough to cause the sensation of near laughter, but that laughter will sadly be stifled by your seething hatred for this atrocity of a gameplay experience.

This game has managed to age well and may very well be even better than it originally released (especially if compared to sonics that follow it) It feels as though sega did some soft tweaks to the engine for this port and as such some of the bugginess of the original and gamecube versions, such as sudden slides or homing attack flipping out, are far less common though the flame ring priority over light dashing problem is still as strong as ever. The game still has some bugs however and should be handled with care, many of which will show their head in final chase/rush.
The game play of the "adventure" series has always been varied, sonic being speed, knuckles being
treasure hunting etc. This one is no different but with the twist that you can play as both the heroes and villians of the story who all play as mirrors of each other. These end up mirrors in gameplay to each other. sonic = shadow, tails = eggman, knuckles = rouge. while this isn't absolutely horrible, the sameness may leave you desiring more and since story is always been kinda a laugh in Sonic games, the story wont really be a huge motivator to push through the sameness. Another problem with this game it was part of the era where sega thought super should remain exclusive to sonic and it be cinematic only. You cannot go super in any of the ordinary stages which is a serious no fun allowed feeling.
This game was also the last of the games to have one of the greatest addictions of that era: chao. Chaos were an addicting tamogachi like pet system that one could lose hours of their life playing around with, Adventure 2 had the most expanded upon chao garden and thus the most features.
For replayablilty there is alot to do: chaos, finding hidden powerups, going for all A ranks and emblems. There's plenty one can do to keep entertained. In all I highly recommend this game because it was one of the last good main series sonic games until Sonic Generations.

Contagion is a great game, it doesn't meet all of its potential, but a great game none-the-less.
The premise is a slow paced survival horror game in a zombie infested area. Any and all game modes start you with minimal equipment and a general idea of what to do. Now you must search for equipment and start your objectives.
There are a small variety of game modes and maps, but they all feel drastically different, so the repetition is not as noticeable until you've logged a few hours.
Escape - In this game mode you are working together with your party to find your way out of a bad situation and get to an extraction point. You'll need to unlock doors, remove hazards, and find alternate paths. Somewhat similar to Left 4 Dead but with the slow pace and true zombie threat more similar to 7 days to die or DayZ. This mode can be fun and is generally very entertaining, though it can be somewhat overly challenging when playing alone. It can also get very repetitive though the game does try to address this. The developers have made some maps shift slightly between games so that certain routes or actions aren't available and you have to take alternate courses to finish the game. That said, it's still the same location and the same extraction point, so after a few games you might have gotten all you'll get from a certain map.
Extraction - Here you are wondering through the areas gathering weapons and avoiding zombies until you lock onto a house that has stranded survivors. You follow your GPS to the house, grab the survivors, and hunker down until extraction is ready. This mode can be fun but it lacks much variety and really requires a group, but a small one at that. If you have no group you can get easily overwhelmed while a large group can take out all tension or difficulty.
Hunted - My personal favorite. This is classic PVP infection in a map littered with the undead. Here you start out spread across a map with a melee weapon and basic pistol. You must scour the land for equipment and refuge against the zombies and other players. You can might alliances, but entirely based on yourself, no game mechanics involved, so people can turn on you at any moment. Once you die, or last long enough after infection, you become a zombie and must now hunt down the survivors until only one remains who is deemed the winner. As a zombie you can control up to 15 npc zombies as a sort of leader, though their A.I. isn't the best and can be difficult to get them to do what you want.
General - The game does have some decent graphics with some nice effects such as water and lens flare. The sound design is really nice with great. powerful, and recognizable sounds. Mixing on the other hand can be off at times. I've heard gunshots that sound as if they are right next to me as they are fired from across the street in the opposite direction. The community is a mixed bag featuring your silent players, your talkative friendly people, your power players, and the classic trolls.
missed potential - While the game does have its moments and is generally fun, the idea of a fully over run zombie world with fragile alliances and conflicting goals is far greater than what this game actually is in practice. Perhaps in time with updates more game modes or tweaks to the existing modes will help the game reach its real promise. Maybe a hunted mode with side objectives, changing maps not just in escape, or maybe the ability to actively change the layout (besides just boarding up doors and windows). Maybe the source engine just isn't diverse enough to realize this or maybe the independent team isn't large enough or doesn't have enough money, but currently the game is a collection of zombie modes that can be found in other games. I think completely original game modes that can't be found anywhere else is where the greatness of this game may lie.
Verdict - If you like the zombie modes in games like infection from Halo or the COD zombies mode you'll likely enjoy this. It has some interesting ideas and can definitely be fun, but it's much better with friends and it currently doesn't step too far away from the common practice zombie modes.

This looks like a great idea for a game, but I couldn't get the controls. So, if you don't have awesome reflexes, this game might not be for you.
The game appears to be very solidly made, but be careful which songs you play, because it can make a huge difference in how difficult the gameplay is.
Not that there is no penalty for missing the orbs, unlike, for example, DDR, where missing too many notes will stop the song. Only the obstacles cause you to lose the ability to keep going seamlessly, and those only drop you out for a second or two.
In the end, I didn't enjoy this game, because my reflexes weren't up to the challenge, but I'd still recommend it to people who like rhythm games and have better skill than mine.

I don't normally indulge in rhythm games. The only one I would say I frequently play and have somewhat become adept in is Cytus on my tablet. I stumbled upon this game while browsing early access titles on sale, and what intrigued me the most was A) the art style, and B) the fact that you play with songs from your own library. Mainly the latter. So I was pretty excited to pick it up.
At first I was a little wonky, as per usual whenever I delve into a rhythm game for the first time. I was a bit disappointed that there was no real tutorial in the game, however. There is a "how to play" guideline that somewhat helps you get started, but I feel like a tutorial would have been a more hands-on experience. I certainly hope they'll add one in the future.
But with that aside, once I got used to the controls, I had a lot of fun. A controller and keyboard are both viable methods of playing. It all comes down to your preferred play style and which would suit you the most. Personally I found both to be quite fun. You can also customize the difficulty, which I thought was handy. So if you ever think that the set difficulties are too easy or too hard, you can create one that's just right for you. It's quite impressive that the levels tailor themselves to whatever song you pick. One small detail that I really appreciated was, one of the songs I picked had a drop in it, and right before the drop there's this dramatic slow-motion sequence that I thought was really, really cool.
If you're a rhythm game connoiseur, then you will DEFINITELY enjoy this game. Heck, even if you're not, like me, chances are you'll probably enjoy it too.

When writing this review, i had a really tough time thinking of any possible cons for Melody's Escape. In all honesty, Melody's Escape is as smooth as its simple art style, which i personally think is very reminiscent of an advertisement for ipods.
The concept itself is also very simple, you control Melody as she runs through the chosen track, hitting buttons to the corresponding beats. Similar to Audiosurf; Melody's Escape allows the player to use their own music, and given how easy it is to obtain
music from the internet (or whatever shady site you download from), the sky's the limit! The game's simplicity is complimented by its high level of customization that the player is given. You get to decide Melody's hairstyle, clothing (or skin, some options from the workshop are more like reskins than clothing options) and the colour scheme for the game itself. If you feel limited by the default selections you can turn to the Community Workshop for even more options to pick and choose from. And if that’s still not enough customization for you, then there’s a “ModStudio” tucked in the steam program files that allows you to start from scratch and make/edit  your own unique hairstyle etc. (Might take some figuring out but there are a few guides that go over the process). There’s also an option to make your own custom difficulty to play with; which is a nice touch.
However, at the core of any game is its gameplay and its controls. So how does Melody’s escape score in these areas? Wonderfully well. the controls are nice and tight (although personally i would recommend using a controller over a keyboard). The gameplay of Melody’s Escape can be pretty difficult at times but the game’s learning curve is never unfairly difficult (unless you’re using an insanely high tempo song then well, you’ve only yourself to blame). Each is level is generated by some technical algorithm that analyses each song, but i’m no expert on the details. Despite the minimalistic amount of content you’re given in the actual game not counting your music, i seem to always come back to it. When buying Melody’s Escape, bear in mind that this is a game that’s best played in short bursts, not just because you’ll get bored after about one to two hours of back to back playing, but also because your eyes will get sore. Very, very sore.
The first issue with this game stems from the visuals. Don’t get me wrong, i love the art style and bright colours, but i’d be lying if i said that my eyes didn’t get strained after about a half hour of playing. Though the issue can easily be remedied with a couple tweaks to the settings as well as following general health and safety tips.
In summary, Melody’s Escape is a perfect game to just pick up and play casually whenever you’re bored, waiting or need to relax etc. It has a great visual style and it’s customization is boundless. The difficulty only enhances the feeling when you beat your high score; and as long as you don’t play for too long in one go than you’ll have a blast! It's also a great entry point into the rhythm genre.
Definitely a good game to have in any steam library.

I wish I could give this game a 2.5/5 because it isn't bad, it's just not good for me. I have played games like DDR, Stepmania, Beatmania, and the like for over a decade. All that those games have ingrained in me have made it very hard to adjust to how this game is set up.
Anyways, I'll try to keep this list short-ish
-There is no indicator to where the game thinks the beat of the song is... and the game will occasionally put commands off the beat to match a specific sounds.
-The game is framy at higher FPS... I don't know how this is possible, but I can see bad stutter unless the game is locked to 60FPS... and even when trying to lock it to 60FPS I will get higher and still stutter on occasionally.
-When you miss some commands you dissapear, and often reappear directly infront of another obsticle, causing chain-failures... This can be slightly alieveated with the custom mode, but when the game doesn't quite have the beat of the song right, can chian for quite a while.
-Some of the obsticles have unintuitive directions. such as hitting left (backwards) to fly upwards sometimes, or up to dive downwards sometimes? Not that you actually know if your airborn path is going up or down, as you can never see your landing point.
-The shapes for the circle type commands are too uniform, thus you kindof have to play by color.
If you're looking for a casual rythem game, I would recomend this over audio surf... but for a skill rythem game, I'll stick to my Dance Dance Revolution.
But if you're looking for a well tuned rythem game, be prepared to grit your teeth.

This is an enjoyable game. It is hard to find a lot wrong with it besides the fact that it is a dated game. So graphics, AI, and so on are not at the best. What the game does make up for, is how it handles itself. The game follows some simple tactics, get money, build up an army, then you either join a nation, or one of its uprisers, or go into being a king/queen yourself. What I personally love about the game, is the combat. It still has a hack and slash feel sometimes, but when your horse has been knocked underneath you and you have a dozen guys bearing down on you, it does show just how well you can handle it. Thrusts, slashes, chops, it's like Medieval Chiveraly, but earlier. The battle mechanics work on the same concept, but now you have horses, bigger maps, and different terrain. Being an old game the ap variety can be a little lacking, and spawning on the side of a mountain is never fun, but it does add a little bit of randomness to your battles. Since half of the game is on a 'running' around screen, it doesn't take much to play this, so even some low level computers might be able to handle it. Again, after playing over 20 hours you can get a little bored, but I enjoyed it, and still enjoy it as I am determined to beat it one day.

Until level three, this game plays very much like you're playing Day of Defeat but with more open maps and some working light vehicles, like bikes, jeeps, trucks, halftracks.  The infantry combat is quite solid.
Then you hit level three.  Now there are bigger maps.  They feel a bit like a slog, but it's nice to mix it up and maybe it'll be cool to see the vehicles in play.  Then you hit the tanks, and make a bunch of really unpleasant realizations.
First, if you've been using your grenades, you probably have the RPG.  Great- it'll be nice to be able to defend yourself against any tanks that you can get close enough to, right?
So, you try to equip it and realize that the equipment carrying limit is so low that you can carry exactly your rifle and the RPG, and nothing else- no grenades, no SMG, etc.
That's fine... except you also can't swap loadouts mid-battle.  So, you either need to commit to a loadout that'll leave you at a disadvantage over much of the now rather long battles.  More problematically, if your team collectively doesn't have enough anti-tank firepower to deal with the enemy you can't do anything about it without leaving the battle.
One thing you personally can do is buy multiple characters, and then- here's the real problem- level up and equip each of them.
I'd happily pay $5/loadout to unlock some more loadouts.  F2P developers need to get paid somehow, after all.  However, I'm not going to commit to going through the entire F2P grind and economy for each loadout I want to be able to field in a battle.
Also, that RPG you unlocked?  Each shell costs 710 credits.  At level 3, you're making something like 1500 credits per battle.  On the first battle where I managed to get into RPG-ish range with tanks I racked up over 5000 credits worth of ammunition costs getting one tank kill and some damage.  Bit of a price tag, that.
This, incidentally, also only got me about 1/50 of the way towards unlocking the first of the AT grenade/mine line, which are weapons I could carry in my inventory and still have room to swap out my rifle for an SMG or carry some grenades or do something else.  So much for that plan.  I'm neither willing to grind nor pay for that.
So, maybe you try being a tank crew instead- you can convert your infantryman into a tanker at this point.  Alternately, you could pay to buy a second pre-trained tanker.
Your first tank?  It's got a machine gun as its weapon.  You can kill other people in their first tank, but you're mostly just fodder for people who have ground or paid their way up to higher tier tanks.  Definitely rubs the progression in your face in a bad way.
Unsurprisingly, with all of these factors combining, it's not that hard to find yourself fighting a better-armored enemy and not being able to do anything about it.
The larger maps are also something of a tedious slog to play and should be revisited, and the prevalence of huge open fields and- especially- narrow bridge chokepoints also accentuates the badness of the tank system heavily.
It's also worth noting you're paying credits for both ammunition and repairs on all your gear each match.  For those first couple of levels, this doesn't seem like a big deal, but I assume it'll scale up ala other F2P games so that at higher levels you need to choose between using lower level gear or paying real money to be able to afford ammo and repairs.  Not necessarily the end of the world- I'm a big fan of World of Tanks which uses the same system- but what I've seen of the game so far leaves me no trust or interest in getting further and discovering what else H&G has to offer.
There's the core of a really good game here.  The infantry combat is good fun, and some of the Battlefield-esque chaos the infantry, gear, and vehicles can produce can shine through.  However, the bigger maps/missions need work and everything related to armored combat is an unenjoyable mess that rubs the need to invest more time and money into the game in your face.

The gameplay consists of directional button presses according to the rhythm akin to the old DDR tradition, which is deepened by the variables the game offers, such as the difficulty level's adjustment of the frequency of obstacles, as well as the ability to use one or two sets of directional keys for the two present obstacle types. Overall, it's quite a pleasing and addictive atmosphere and experience.

only 6.5 hours of gameplay yes, but Ive gotten a feel for the game. I love it so far. Combat feels satisfying. Every class has their own playstyle. A lot of people have been comparing this to L4D. And at first I didn't see that. It's a game set in medieval times where you fight against mutated rats with swords, magic, old flintlock guns, and archery.
Then I saw the giant brute rat. Much like the giant hulking zombie in L4D.
Or the packmaster that picks you up, and drags you away from your party. Much like the smoker in L4D.
You also can only carry one healing supplies at a time.
But then the combat and atmosphere make it feel much different. Theres also a variety of weapons to choose from. At the end of every mission, you get a random weapon. But these aren't randomized loot. If you get enough junk items you dont want, you can go to the forge and trade 5 weapons you dont want for a new one.
You can go back and replay levels, change the difficulty, etc.
Grinding the same levels over and over again will actually make your quality of weapons you get worse, from what Ive heard. I like this so you dont join rooms that want to do the same level over and over and over again.
There seems to a bit of optimization issues, but overall it feels like a really solid game.
EDIT: I just looked at recommended GPU, and its a GTX 780. I have a 770. It actually runs quite well then since Ive been running it at high this whole time.

So I have put quite a few hours into this now, which gives me enough of an impression to actually write this. That is not to say that time played by default makes my opinions correct, or at all helpful, but I will try.
So I have been keeping an eye on this game since pretty much the start, maybe 2 years, not sure. But so far I have noted these key points.
The Developers:
#The developers seem quite dedicated.
#They seem ambitious, almost to a fault but not quite.
#They are a recent announcement to upgrade to unity 5 shows they wish to improve even what seems to be set in stone.
#They are slow, but they are also detailed, few game crushing bugs have ever popped up.
#They are a small team, and not as vocal with their community as I would like.
(keep this last one in mind when I describe the game, as it means alot when it comes to visual assets.)
The Game:
#Graphics are pretty good in some ways, but a letdown in other.
#The art style for humans leaves them feeling a little less real, and can be seen as a little cartoonish
#Character customization leaves a lot to be desired but has come a long way since earlier versions.
#Animation leaves a lot to be desired but it has been already announced they are going over the animations from scratch and making very impressive leaps, set to be released in 0.90 along with Unity 5 engine.
#Combat is currently clunky, ranged weapons are your only real weapon, use a bow at first but aim for a laser weapon ASAP and a large supply of batteries. Combat in melee is not an option at the moment but in a recent video they have shown great progress in the combat system coming in 0.90 Unity 5 update.
#AI is parted into what seem to be factions, often you will see animals fighting in clear and defined rolls of hunter and prey, truly one of the fantastic parts of this game.
As for my impression of the game as a whole?
I like it, I played through all the story that is currently there, and when I hit that first message saying I could not take this mission because it was not currently complete, I was left begging for more.
However I do worry the 0.90 update will require a total restart of my play through, but with all I have learned, and baring major changes, I will be able to do everything even better and even faster next time round, I know where you hid my aluminum you sly dogs!
I would buy this game again, but there is one fact I must stress to all consumers. So please read this and take it to heart.
This is an early access game, you may end up with something you did not expect, it may be bad, it may be good, it may be total trash, but you knew this going in, you paid for an unfinished untested product and it is your risk alone to take!

Planet Explorers - If you build it you can play with it.
I love this game, with over 150 hours in it and so much to do.  I will say Planet Explorers is a missleading name.  At a glance it would seem you just hop from planet to planet and explore them, but there is only one planet.  Of course you can have a different planet each play through but you can't jump from one planet to the next.  What I mean by this is in adventure mode you can generate the type of planet you will explore, A mix of desert, trees, water, grassland etc...
You can make your own weapons - riffles, pistols (lasser or bullets).  When I say make you can use a preset weapon to craft, or you can build your own and play with it in the game. Deadlight is a 2.5D parkour action, but almost puzzle platformer in a post apocalyptic zombie infested Seattle set in 1986. If it sounds an awful lot like that other first person parkour action platformer in a post apocalyptic zombie infested game named Dying Light, you'd be wrong. Dead wrong. No, this is a game more about traversal than fighting waves of the undead that are named shadows. Everything in the foreground is black and shadowy including the zombies, yourself, the terrain, ladders and so on. The backgrounds are beautiful, diverse environments that you won't get to explore so much as gaze in awe of throughout the game. This makes the game feel a kin to Limbo, but in color without the painful and vague puzzles.
Its really a five hour journey that takes you through the city. From your safe house, through the city, up buildings, underground in a trap laden labyrinth made by a madman, to trailer homes of suburbia, a stadium, a hospital and even a militia camp. That's what I took away from this game were the beautiful vistas that looked like a team must have spent a lot of time on for what is essentially a budget title.
But how will you get there? You've got a lot of land to cover, piece by piece. Climbing ladders, hanging from ledges, sliding down rooftops, jumping over gaps, running from helicopters, wall jumping, crouching under doors, rolling from high leaps, crawling through air ducts, pulling boxes, pushing over things to barricade doors from zombies. You can even yell, call and taunt zombies to your location. Its all simple and easy. You'll even get a fire axe that can smash open doorways and boarded up windows. It can also smash through zombie heads! Its not a gory game though. You won't see blood in the game, but you will see art blood in the cut scenes.
You've got stamina so every time you swing the axe, that stamina goes down. You'll get slower with your swings, everything will become slightly blurry until you rest. This makes you vulnerable to zombies. Normally you can button mash to shake them off you, but when you're groggy, you're susceptible. Even with one block of health left, you can still do a good job of shaking them from  you, unless a zombie sneaks up behind. Fighting zombies is a rare part of the game, most of the time you just avoid the ones in the foreground and the ones in the background shuffle to the foreground. When you kill a zombie, they disappear into smoke after a some time goes by and they'll appear in the background to do it all over again.
The stamina drains as you hang from ledges or wires. Once your stamina is gone, you fall most likely to your death. Speaking of death, there are electrified pools of water that you'll need to turn off the power to get across.
I can't call the game a survival horror, even though there's zombies and limited ammunition. You'll get a revolver that you need to load each bullet and its quick enough. Shooting involves using the right thumbstick to aim a full 360 degrees and pulling the right trigger to fire. There are of course keyboard controls, but its a game from Microsoft, I'd recommend using the 360 controller in this case. You can find more ammunition on bodies strewn about the game. I never felt like ammo conservation was an issue. The same body will always have more ammunition. There's also a shotgun, which ammo is very limited and a slingshot that you'll get for one part of the game. This slingshot has unlimited ammo and you can always bounce your rocks off walls to hit triggers. Other than that, you'll need guns to shoot out windows, locks and other things. The game always makes sure there's an ammo corpse somewhere.
Everything you'll need is highlighted with a slight glowing tint. You can turn this off, but it really helps and at some point, I think the game realizes that you know what you're doing, so the tint becomes less present. There are twinkling sparkles on ledges. There's a big emphasis on ledges and climbing, you can even hang from a ledge and drop down. Otherwise, falling great distances hurts if not kills you. Oh it also kills the zombies too.
Since you're so burdened with stuff, you can't swim, which makes for some brief water puzzles where you'll raise and lower the water. With all of the light puzzles in the game, I never felt like anything was too difficult or vague. Its an easy and enjoyable journey through Deadlight, but there are moments you'll need to run and get things correct. The last moments of the game it seems like a puzzle against soldiers in order to do the right thing at the right moment. If you jump off a fence, you'll get gunned down, but if you drop off the fence, then you can shoot the soldiers. Stuff like that. Other times, you'll need to run to avoid zombies chasing you or a helicopter's gunfire.
For the most part, zombies are a big part of the game, but other times its about a para military group chasing you. Its really just a helicopter. There aren't any soldiers outside of the final moments of the game. Your biggest foes are still the zombies.There's a sense of dread as they come closer or overwhelm you, but for the most part, they're easy to avoid either by taunting to lure them in and jumping over their head to knocking them down and running past.
At some point, the danger becomes traps as an old man forces you to run through his rat maze to the end. You'll need to be quick to avoid falling spike traps, crumbling platforms and its all interesting stuff and the traps look believable within this art style and setting. I just know some people that play zombie games only do it for the zombies, but this is a game about traversal and staying alive, the zombies are just in it.
If you die, you'll merely restart from the last checkpoint. I can't say that the game is too death heavy outside of a few rare points. There are health packs here and there, but every death refills your health, so they almost feel pointless. There are a lot of other collectables and secrets. I can't say there's too much exploring or secret areas, it feels like a very linear experience, but still a fun, enjoyable one. For those that find the game too easy, once you complete the game, there's a nightmare mode with no save and only one life. Its possible I'm sure.
Throughout the game, you'll hear your character Randall Wayne talking with his smoky gravely voice, explaining things. So you'll always have a hint at what to do or how to do it. He's a good character, but his voice seems out of place from everyone else in the game. Its only noticeable in cut scenes. To flesh out who Randall was, there are a few flashbacks that hint at things as well as explain how he learned to fire a weapon. There are a few nightmarish hallucinations where the skies turn red and zombies in the background are giant.
Between the actual game, there's beautiful yet grim artwork during cut scenes. I'd much rather have these sort of still frame art style than something in the game's engine. There are a few things done in the game where you lose control, but they're brief and rare.
I did manage to find a few bugs here and there. Pausing coming out of a save seemed to freeze the game. There was a cut scene where the audio just ended and didn't resume until after the scene. Its nothing that ruined the experience.
With all of that said, it was a fun five hours. Easy enough to be relaxing and let me use my brain. I think the beautiful vistas really helped my enjoyment. I found myself looking at things and taking screen shots.

Deadlight shows a lot of potential, especially early on. It's a tense, dark side scrolling platform with a great art style and wonderful attention to detail.
Sadly this only lasts for the first Act. Eventually the ideas ran out and the cohesive world building and fourth wall are broken for no apparent reason. Instant kill traps for no good reason, forced combat situations, cliche story, and trial and error fill up the rest of the remaining two acts.
I'll explain a bit more about the trial and error as that is what truly causes this game to deserve a thumbs down. This is a game that will make you want to throw a controller/smash a keyboard. I'm fine with tough platformers, but not if the problem is the controls. The tight controls from the begining of the game do not hold up to the advanced "we put this death trap ridden jungle gym of a house falling apart just becuase" sections throughout the game.
An example: in one level you are tasked with sprint running through a door, making a jump over water, running fast through a corridor, wall jumping to grab a ledge, vaulting over and then rolling through the escape. Any slip makes you restart. The kicker? This is literally impossible if you long jump (sprint + jump) on the first jump. But you are already sprinting through the door so you have to stop sprinting, jump, then sprint. This is the only puzzle that requires this and there is no hint as to why you die in the corridor because you long jumped. After restarting 20ish times you either look up the trick online, or figure it out by mistake/trial and error. By all means google a few youtube videos of it, the level is called Fallen.
Bad game design and a lack of polish ruined a game that showed great potential, and really, that's too bad.

Let me first say that my playthrough of this game was, on the whole, a positive experience. Why do I not recommend this game, then? Because everything that it does has been done much better in other franchises.
The "New Flu" came to our world and began to kill large swathes of people. Unfortunately for the rest of us, the sickness was not over when its victims died. Instead, the dead bodies would lift up, a shadow of their former selves. These shadows only cared about one thing: eating those that were not yet one of them.
Randall has fallen in with a small group of survivors after being separated from his family, but there's quite a bit of tension when he's forced to kill another survivor's infected sister. The noise from the argument draws too many shadows, and Randall is forced to flee using a different route. Now, he must track down the group of survivors to which he's become attached while still looking for signs of his wife and daughter.
In other words, a standard zombie apocalypse opening. That's fine, as there are only so many ways to launch a zombie apocalypse. Very early on, though, it becomes very obvious what direction the story is heading and, as much as I don't like twists for twists' sake, it was quite disappointing to get to the end of be utterly unsurprised by the conclusion.
Still, excellent execution can make up for a cliche' plot. I realized that I wouldn't be able to give them credit for that when a sewer stalker was revealed to have been watching Randall the entire time he was in Seattle. "The Rat" tells him that he must complete his obstacle course to earn his trust then rescue the Rat's son from a militaristic group of survivors before he'll tell him where his companions are. Randall agrees, even acknowledging the insanity of this clearly crazy man. That's when I stopped caring about the story.

Collect sacks of grain or gunpowder, defend something, destroy pillars with hacking them or destroy pillars with explosives ballers. All the while slaying a horde of rats.
The enemies are as follows: Naked Rats, Rats, Rats that steal you and take you to their dungeon to do unspeakable things to you, Assassin Rats, Rats in Shining Armor, Rat Oger, Gas Rats, Loot Rats and Gatling Gun Rats. The game play is solid L4D action. There is a loot system, XP system, blood, gore, hilarious dialogue and a good setting. There are no complex menus and everything seems really simple. I just hope that this was like Ground Zeroes and the best is yet to come.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide
Besides being a mouthful of a title, Vermintide is a 4-player co-op survival game set to the theme of the Warhammer fantasy universe. This game takes many elements from the Left 4 Dead series, so I can't really review this game without making the comparison.
Visuals: The game is beautiful, without question. It sets the mood well, and though it is filled with drab greys and browns, this is quite intentional to invoke the atmosphere the game is aiming for, and it does manage to break that up from time to time with a bit of different scenery to admire as you hack your way through the skaven horde.
Sound: The banter between the characters adds a lot to this game and can be pretty entertaining. One of the weakest parts of the game however is it's music, which at times is lacking entirely, and at other times is repetitive.
Gameplay: To those familiar with the Left 4 Dead franchise; This took the formula you have grown used to and improved upon it, while sharing many of the core aspects that made it work in the first place. Hordes are more threatening, and ranged options, while varied, are limited, making ammo conservation important as well as not always being the best tool. Skaven that share similarities to L4D's special infected are present and in some ways, greatly improve on the design, one of the most obvious being the Packleader, a reimagining of the L4D Smoker. The different heroes add depth and customizability to the game, but with a limited roster to choose from and the inability to run duplicates, this may mean playing a few games as someone you would rather not. To those that haven't played Left 4 Dead, it will be a tense but enjoyable adventure to play with friends - and you will need friends, which brings us to the weakest part of Vermintide.
AI: The AI for your companions if you are lacking a player to fill that spot, is abysmal, and will be an even greater enemy to you than the skaven themselves. If you are not looking for something to play with friends or at the very least, something you can tolerate playing online with strangers, this will not be the game for you, as the AI will do more to hamper your experience than improve it, and it is very clear this was only done as a band-aid while you wait for real players.
Overall, as the Left 4 Dead series has nothing new on the horizon as of this writing, this fills the void nicely and even does it better, with more unique qualities. If you have 1-3 friends that are willing to suit up for pest control, this will prove to be a very fun experience and worth the price.

Concidering the game takes a bit to learn, you'll be replaying the same level from the beginning over and over....and over, never feeling like you have accomplisherd anything.  Frankly, this game would be 'must have' if each map was broken into multible stages which you unlocked as you moved forward.  Dying after 2 hours of gameplay and returning to the beginning is never fun.  Graphically it's not bad, and the presentation is far more professional than most other zombie games on Steam.  It really comes down to your tolerance level.
At first Contagion would appear as a Left 4 Dead clone, however it quickly sets a dramatically different pace more in line with a survival horror rather than L4D's run and gun frenzy.  You explore area's and clear out the zombies, while figuring out how to move forward.  Which brings us to problem #2.  Many times you find yourself lost wandering hallways with no clear idea of what to do next.  This is par for the course for survival horror games where you can save, go eat a sandwich, and than get back to it later.  Contagion however has the save system of an areana shooter, and the gameplay of a FPS horror game.  I gaurantee if you play for a few minutes you will fall in love with Contagion.....until you die and revert all the way back to the beginning....than you will hate it.
In the end it's a fun game with a cool concept, and your enjoyment depends on your tolerance for horrid save systems.  Oh, and there are these armored zombie that take a million bullets to kill.  They suck like crazy.  Contagion is fun enough, but has so much potential it will drive you insane.  With a better progress system, and fleshed out abilities (cover system, hiding, dodging) this game could become legendary.

I'm writing this review fresh after finishing Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number, and I have to say, I fairly enjoyed this game. Instead of writing down a massive wall of text for what I did and didn't like I'll just sum it up in bullet points ranging from good, meh, and bad.
The Good
+ More levels.
+ More Characters.
+ More awesome music.
+ Much harder than the first game.
+ Basically just more Hotline Miami.
+ None of the new characters feel "Gimmicky" for lack of a better word.
+ More backstory for old characters.
+ The ending.
+ Additional Hard mode.
+ No awful stealth chapter.
+ Constant fast pace.
+ More gore.
+ The Alex and Ash combo is absolutely kick♥♥♥♥♥
The Meh
+/- Can't pick up knocked out enemies and use them as shields anymore.
+/- No stealth executions.
+/- More Story.
+/- Much longer than the first game. (10 hours as opposed to the 3-5 of the first game.)
+/- Ending is a bit confusing.
+/- Many executions are automated.
+/- Bigger emphasis on gunplay.
+/- Game expects that you played the previous one first. (Only a "meh" for new players.)
The Bad
- The Beard levels are awful. (The combination of the color changing and the music gave me headache on one level.)
- Way too many windows.
-  Levels can feel too big at times.
- Some levels are the length of several levels from the first game.
- Many story arcs go nowhere and end abruptly.
- The ending just happens. There no real build up that the end is coming and it just hits you like a brick wall.
- All of The Son's abilities are just taken from The Fans minus the really cool chainsaw/pistol combo.
- The AI is REALLY bad at times, like borderline "special" kid bad. (May be patched out by the time you're reading this.)
- Less masks than the first game.
- Story can be a bit disruptive.
Overall I really enjoyed Hotline Miami 2 and if you need a numerical grade I would give it a solid 8.5/10. It is a really great game and a good sequel but it has a few issues that hold it back from being better than the original. There is apparently an upcoming level editor so that should add more content to the game and more reasons to obliterate our "r" key.

Gameplaywise exactly like the first game, just a little bit harder(especially hard mode :o).
The story is even more fragmented than in the first one since there are multiple storylines, so it may be a little hard to follow the first time around, but even the story gives a huge amount of replay value since there is always some minor detail you missed in the last playthrough.
Puzzleing out the motives, backgrounds and relations of the characters you play makes the story itself more interesting than Jacket's story in Hotline Miami 1, I must admit.
The best thing about the game however is the way it mashes story and gameplay together. It just works so perfectly that the story doesn't hold back the gameplay and vice versa.  "You really seem to like hurting other people..."
Another thing worth mentioning is the soundtrack, which is absolutly phenomenal, since it features many of the artists from HM1. Everything from the calm theme on the main menu to the adrenaline pushing "Roller Mobster" while you are basically killing and dying every second fits so perfectly that I could listen to it all day and not getting tired.
There are however some things that are bothering me, namely general A.I. problems and occasional flaws in level design (random enemy shooting through window across the hallwall without even seeing you, wtf xDD).
It's nothing brand new compared to the predecessor, but it is superior to it in almost every regard.

I can honestly say I really like playing this game, it's a fun way to listen to your music and kill some time by playing this rhythm platformer.
Since it's in early acress, I can easily spot some things that need fixing/improving, but overall it's a pretty solid game, especially since it has been getting updates here and there such as visual improvements, new difficulty, mod support, etc.
When playing this game, I'd recommend anyone starting off at medium difficulty right away, then when getting used to getting 4/5 stars on your songs, jump to insane difficult. Reason for this is because it makes the game a lot more fun. It's challenging while you get to do even more than before + the rhythm detection gets a little better for every + difficulty.
Most songs do play fine. The detection is decent and very pleasuring once you play the right song such as Stitches" and "Uptown funk" since the game seems to be able to detect the rhythm to these songs very well... however on most songs the detection function seems to be lacking 20/50% of the song since it can't find the peaks of certain songs or is just plain boring and it makes no sense when unsyncronized orbs and arrows come at you.
This definitely need some more work.
Another thing I have to adress is how the game runs. Most of the time I'm able to hit all the arrows and orbs at any speed... however I am sometimes having latency problems when it comes to the slow pasing orbs. Rest are usually fine.
Another thing is the screen resolution. I can't for the life of me ever try to play this game in fullscreen mode. The eyestrain is real where it seems like the whole screen is in motion blur constantly and my eyes can't focus on the character and the upcoming orbs/arrows. So currently I'm stuck playing in 600x800 resolution, which is small, but it's the one I'm most comfortable with for my eyes... even though it still gives me eye strain after 3 or 4 songs.
All in all though, I definitely recommend this game and I can't wait to see how this will improve over time!

Have you ever wanted to play a serious hardcore survival horror game online with your friends? Well, you've found Contagion.
Contagion is a survival horror game with zombie virus as theme, and has online multiplayer support, both co-op against the AI and playing against human zombies. Different modes for different gameplays. You can escape a building full of infected zombies and scarce resource, cross a city looking for a safe place, escort civilians out of a small town or even go crazy and play with your friends as humans and zombies. If you are looking for multiple gameplays, I'm happy to tell you the items and the scenario changes, forcing you to handle different threats and unexpected situations. The game really has this aura that brings you into the survival mood. It makes you want to save ammo, to stick together with your friends, to work as a team.
I recommend Contagion. It has a lot the features and the atmosphere of a survival horror, and brings the best of your solo or co-op play. Its only downside is the need of more maps. Most particularly for the "Escape" game mode.

Admittedly it's certainly a niche market and obviously not for everyone if they just want to shoot some zombies, but get some like-minded friends in on the action with a private server and you'd be surprised at just how enormously replayable the (currently) small roster of Escape maps can be, especially on Extreme difficulty. Hell, even joining public servers full of randoms manages to go against the usual online experience and can often wind up being remarkably fun. A game that will sometimes feel a little rough around the edges the more you play and experiment with things, but certainly not enough in any way to ruin the experience.

I'm writing this review fresh after finishing Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number, and I have to say, I fairly enjoyed this game. Instead of writing down a massive wall of text for what I did and didn't like I'll just sum it up in bullet points ranging from good, meh, and bad.
The Good
+ More levels.
+ More Characters.
+ More awesome music.
+ Much harder than the first game.
+ Basically just more Hotline Miami.
+ None of the new characters feel "Gimmicky" for lack of a better word.
+ More backstory for old characters.
+ The ending.
+ Additional Hard mode.
+ No awful stealth chapter.
+ Constant fast pace.
+ More gore.
+ The Alex and Ash combo is absolutely kick♥♥♥♥♥
The Meh
+/- Can't pick up knocked out enemies and use them as shields anymore.
+/- No stealth executions.
+/- More Story.
+/- Much longer than the first game. (10 hours as opposed to the 3-5 of the first game.)
+/- Ending is a bit confusing.
+/- Many executions are automated.
+/- Bigger emphasis on gunplay.
+/- Game expects that you played the previous one first. (Only a "meh" for new players.)
The Bad
- The Beard levels are awful. (The combination of the color changing and the music gave me headache on one level.)
- Way too many windows.
-  Levels can feel too big at times.
- Some levels are the length of several levels from the first game.
- Many story arcs go nowhere and end abruptly.
- The ending just happens. There no real build up that the end is coming and it just hits you like a brick wall.
- All of The Son's abilities are just taken from The Fans minus the really cool chainsaw/pistol combo.
- The AI is REALLY bad at times, like borderline "special" kid bad. (May be patched out by the time you're reading this.)
- Less masks than the first game.
- Story can be a bit disruptive.
Overall I really enjoyed Hotline Miami 2 and if you need a numerical grade I would give it a solid 8.5/10. It is a really great game and a good sequel but it has a few issues that hold it back from being better than the original. There is apparently an upcoming level editor so that should add more content to the game and more reasons to obliterate our "r" key.

This game is hands down one of the best conclussions to a series I've seen so far in all of my gaming careers.
Mainly because unlike most games I've played, this one doesn't produce 2 or more sequels. Just the one sequel/prequel/alternate perspective story. It puts into perspective all these metaphors, and motives, while also making you think the creators are just intentionally screwing with you. Do you even care? No. Because, you're more focused on killing about 15 men in 45 seconds.
And if I get anything from this series, it's that not every ending is predicted. It's that karma can be achieved in 2 hours if you're that insane. And I've learned a lot about myself and the style of story I like from a game. Is it important? No, you can just play the game for senseless violence, like the first one. But, unlike the first, they've taken time to actually make a visible and interlocking storyline between very unlikely people.
The first game was good. Hard? Yes.
The second game was better. Harder? Yes.
The level editor is going to open up so many possibilities as well, effectively bringing the community together for the sheer challenge of who can make an amazing story, and levels harder than Tony's fists.

There really needs to be more games like Contagion. Think Left 4 Dead, but a less theatrical, and more realistic rendition of Z-Day that doesn't involve mutant monster zombies that throw rocks and spit acid. Also refreshing, is how Contagion has more of an emphasis on ammo conservation than most shooters in general, making for another layer of conflict when encountering hordes of undead. Really makes you think twice before deciding: "Shotgun, or sledgehammer?"
Zombies are not nearly as squishy as most of us would like to think, with our prior video game knowledge. While headshots are always the goal, they are pratically paramount in Contagion.
Refreshingly enough, there is split screen co-op if you have a buddy and another controller. If you're playing online, that's cool too. You can have way more than 3 other buddies playing along - so there's yet another leg up on the L4D series, in my opinion. The only critique I can possibly offer for Contagion is: the lack of content. My friends and I don't really do PvP - we're more about the coop stuff. Unfortunately, there are only a handful of coop missions, and though they are rather lengthy, and they all tend to play a little differently every time, there is still something lacking with the progression. At it's core, it really just just a load of blasting, slashing, running and gunning, but there's so much potential here for something more that just isn't quite there yet. I've really been pulling through for Contagion to introduce more content, and I'm still hopeful that there's more to come, but I can't be too sure.
Regardless, as is, it's still a superb game with some really tight controls and shooting mechanics. Bullet physics are wonderful, and each and every headshot you get is so satisfying that you likely won't notice until after getting a few hours in that you've been doing the same thing over and over again. One of my favorite coop games in existence. If you're looking to blast through some zombies with some friends, this is it. It's also quite pretty, to boot.

I have thoroughly enjoyed this game so much that I wanted to write a review. The game modes are some of the best, you can play escape mode which is more objective and obviously you do the objectives to get to the end to escape. There is Hunted mode which is PvP based and is so much fun, there aren't any Panic servers I don't know why but I haven't gotten to play that game mode. Extraction is very challenging, especially if anyone died and becomes a zombie, you really have a tough time and adds to the suspense.

If you die too many times as a zombie though you will stop respawning and you become a spectator which can really bum you out, Only negative thing about the game is that. I love playing all the game modes however, and there are plenty of people to play with. They really emphasize the headshots in this game, and if you dont you will run out of ammo SO fast and you will die.
I have nothing bad to say about this game, and the developers are still working on this amazing game and are about to release a free DLC to us buyers with 2 new maps 4 new guns and more.

Remember the two bonus levels ("Highball" and "Exposed") from the end of Hotline Miami? The poorly-designed, wide-open levels that nobody particularly liked but played anyway? That is basically every level in Hotline Miami 2.
After you finish the introductory mission designed to help familiarize you with the controls again, the missions are very hard. Not challenging, just hard. With enough repetition, you will memorize where the enemies hide off-screen and the best corners to hide in, but it doesn't feel like the same controlled chaos of the first game. Hotline Miami rewarded you for the creativity, variety and speed with which you dispatched enemies, but HL2 never quite gives you the same autonomy; you basically have to stick to one particular path in order to complete a mission and stay alive.
The new character abilities feel more like gimmicks than helpful tools. I never found a practical use for shooting two guns in two directions. The combat roll is bound to the same key you use to execute downed enemies; it got me killed more than it saved me. The twins (which you control at the same time, similiar to the Ice Climbers) don't work well together, either. The secondary character follows you around and can use a gun, but it's not possible to peek corners with her or effectively mow people down. I used her as an attention-getter for luring people into the primary character's melee weapon around the corner more than anything else.
I have high-hopes for the user-created content, but between the poor level design and half-baked masks and weapons, the campaign felt very forced compared to the first game. All that said, it's hard to say this is a "bad" game. It just doesn't seem like it builds on what Hotline Miami created; it's just more of the same but with longer, more frustrating missions.
If you enjoyed the first one, it's worth playing. Just don't expect much.

A fantastic game which, despite one or two flaws, does justice to its famous predecessor and delivers an improved and more enjoyable game experience.
Characters
------------
There are significantly more characters this time than in the first one, which only let you play as 2 different ones. In this installment, there are 12 characters with various skills and abilities which change the way you approach levels. Examples include a maniac in a Zebra mask who can roll and dodge bullets, and a grizzled detective who can wield his shotgun one-handed. They also possess a voice and personality, unlike Jacket in HM1, leading you to have a better understanding of the characters and their differing motivations.
There is also a larger variety of enemies and NPCs, leading to a more immersive experience as you constantly encounter new and interesting people throughout the game. The number of boss battles has also increased, and there's nothing more satisfying than taking down one of these unique enemies in a violent way.
Levels
--------
The levels are far larger to an almost overwhelming scale sometimes, which can ramp up the difficulty because of the increased enemy count. Maps still possess the same features, such as doors and windows, but there is not really any need for anything new anyway as it would just feel 'gimmicky'.
Weapons
-------------
There is an increased number of weapons- all of the old ones make a magnificent comeback, but there are also exciting new kill machines such as a flamethrower and a sniper rifle.
Story
--------
The story, although confusing at first, ends up being a fascinating novel full of plot twists and developments. Although the ending feels slightly adrupt and out of place, you are left with a feeling of satisfaction and conclusion after you fully grasp the meaning of it.
Negatives
------------
The game possesses a few irritating bugs, such as enemies sometimes sticking in doorways and abnormal movement patterns. However, on the whole it is a smooth experience and I did not experience a single game-breaking bug or crash in my gameplay.

Ive done my waiting! 4 Years! And still we dont get a decent successor of minecraft!
Planet Explorers has the first engine which look decent. Other than other Unity voxel games it goes a new way, away from the block shaped minecraft clone worlds.
What is the engine capable of?
- generating a very nice looking 3D environment, with rivers, lakes, hills, mountains and endless oceans. A whole map can be 40x40km, thats not even close to be as big as a minecraft world, but still big enough to satisfy a great number of players.
- having a lot of free roaming animals, that even work in groups, defend each other or fight other species.
- having building sized boss enemis, with a great amount of different attacks (I mean seriously building sized, they are ♥♥♥♥ing huge).
- complete voxel based 3D mapping. You can dig through every mountain for ressources, still the areas arent made of simple cubes, also you dont have a restriction of placing objects in a square system. And sometimes you can find gigantic caves, that even have lakes and rivers inside of them, big enough to fly through them with helicopters.
- oh yeah, the game also has vehicles and guns. And the best part is: You can build them all by yourself (this would be maybe the current core element of the game)
- A colony system with real working NPCs like a Real Time Strategy Game
What are the cons?
- lack of actual exploring stuff
- lack of balance (if you start on a gold and iron / aluminium spot, you can make your end equip in 30 minutes, or you die over and over again, because there is an enemy alien camp right ahead and constantly raiding you)
- from patch to patch fluctuating between super stable and crashing every 15 minutes
- you need a high end PC
- you need to be very creative in crafting, or you are bound to other players workshop stuff
- overpowering open world bosses are way to easy
- sometimes annoying gamebreaking bugs like selfkill with a melee weapon
- lack of content to do
The main course:
Crafting:
The game comes with a complex editor, that allows the player to design his own guns, swords, shields, vehicles, boats and helicopters. It also allowes to craft free style objects without deeper purpose, that can be used as furniture, from a simple chair to a laptop with detailed screen.
Being awesome as it is, the editor doesnt glance with user friendlyness. Even making a corner or edge or diagonal structures can be a pain, creating round, sharp, beautiful looking or complex filigrane objects are only possible by...I dont know...havent figured it out jet. And the other players arent really helpful in answering this question.
Also using material for your objects changes its abilitys. Every ressource has stability and weight, with aluminium being the most useful ressource, due to its strength and low weight. Creating a good looking weapon and also giving it good stats can be a painful balance act. For example I figured out, that a strong gun should have 40 aluminium as building costs. That way it would have 170 damage and exactly 100% accuracy. Every try of building it bigger would decrease the accuracy under 100% so that the gun wont shoot a straight line anymore.
Swords are even worse because I still havent figured out, how to craft sharp blade structures with the editor. But the damage of the blade is calculated from the size of the weapon and how sharp the front is. I have found a workaround, but I dont think this is the way the game should be used.
Building vehicles is awesome, but currently the game restricts you, wherever it can. You are not allowed to use every vehicle part for every type of vehicle. You have restrictions of maximal parts of one type. I dont know if that is supposed to be some sort of balancing...
For example you can use big thrusters instead of rotors for your helicopters, but you cant use those thrusters in other vehicle types. Yeah, maybe it doesnt work this way, but...why do I also cant use the helicopter energy cells on ground vehicles? I can use them on boats, why not in a car? That way, a tank rapitly runs out of fuel and ammo and isnt capable of doing long range scouting + fighting great amounts of enemys.
All in all you still can do a lot with the editor. More options are already announced (armor crafting).
Colony:
While in minecraft you only build houses to feel happy (and be save at night), here you can build up a functional colony, with defence systems, factorys and farming. Also you are able to recruit NPCs to work for you. This currently only works in Singleplayer.
All in all Planet Explorers is a decent try of a open world sandbox, where you finally literally can do, what you want. I hope they wont let us down.

-Combat:
Combat doesn't have a sense of connection to the attacks and reactions of things being hit. There is no real reason to go melee over ranged unless you want to spend more repairing all your armor.
Despite these things I mentioned, the rest of the system is so fun they didn't really matter to me.
